artigo.texto: Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners announces EUR 270 million investment in new Scottish battery storage project Kilmarnock South is a 350MW four-hour duration BESS project located in southern Scotland. Now under construction, the project is expected to commission in early 2028. The project represents an investment commitment of over EUR 270 million, further strengthening Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ (CIP) contribution to UK energy security. KILMARNOCK, Scotland, Oct. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), through its fourth flagship fund, Copenhagen Infrastructure IV (CI IV), has taken Financial Investment Decision (FID) for Kilmarnock South, a 350 MW / 1,400 MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) located in south Ayrshire, southern Scotland. Construction is now underway with commercial operations expected in the first quarter of 2028. At four hours of duration, once operational, Kilmarnock South will be the longest-duration asset in CIP’s growing UK storage portfolio. The battery will store surplus Scottish wind power that would otherwise go unused and release it to the grid when the network has capacity. Kilmarnock South is CIP’s fourth investment in transmission-connected BESS projects in Scotland, joining Coalburn 1, which reached commercial operations in August 2026, Coalburn 2, and Devilla. Upon full commissioning, CIP’s four Scottish BESS projects will collectively offer a total energy storage capacity of 4.4GWh, the equivalent of almost a third of Great Britain’s operational battery energy storage today. CIP’s Scottish BESS portfolio (Coalburn 1, Coalburn 2, Devilla and Kilmarnock South) will have total power capacity of 1.85 GW and 4.4 GWh of energy storage, equivalent to the electricity demand of over 5.5 million households, across a two-hour period. Nischal Agarwal, Partner at CIP, said: CIP is pleased to add Kilmarnock South to our growing portfolio of UK battery projects, which, once commissioned, will be the longest-duration BESS asset in our UK fleet. ”Well-sited battery energy storage projects provide valuable power system flexibility which enables the full benefits of low-cost renewables to be captured, strengthening security of supply and helping to both cut and stabilise energy bills for consumers.” Michael Shanks, UK Energy Minister, said: A former coal mine at Coalburn is now home to one of Europe’s largest batteries storing clean power, while at Kilmarnock South, a new GBP 232 million battery will store even more Scottish wind power for when it’s needed most. ”Together, these projects mean less homegrown power going to waste, greater energy security, and lower bills over the long term.” READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners announces EUR 270 million investment in new Scottish battery storage project, source

artigo.texto: Nvidia e Broadcom estão relativamente protegidas contra o agravamento da crise de energia nas centrais de processamento de dados dos Estados Unidos, afirmou o Morgan Stanley em relatório nesta segunda-feira (5). Porém, qualquer atraso resultante nas implantações de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial pode afetar os fabricantes de chips de memória, componentes ópticos e outros processadores secundários. O banco estimou no mês passado que os desenvolvedores de data centers nos EUA enfrentarão um déficit líquido de energia de 34% até 2028, equivalente a 32 GW. O boom da IA gerou bilhões de dólares em investimentos em data centers, mas as enormes necessidades de computação e eletricidade da IA generativa estão cada vez mais esbarrando nos problemas de fornecimento de eletricidade nos EUA. Tanto Morgan Stanley quanto Goldman Sachs sinalizaram restrições crescentes à expansão dos data centers nos EUA; o GS espera um impacto limitado no curto prazo devido à resistência política, enquanto o MS vê desafios relacionados à mão de obra, energia e política. O Morgan Stanley afirmou que não vê os gargalos colocando em risco as previsões da Nvidia ou da Broadcom para 2027, citando a visibilidade dessas empresas quanto à alocação de chips, à expansão geográfica e à coordenação entre centros de dados, fornecedores de chips e a cadeia de abastecimento de energia. Se a capacidade de produção de chips não puder ser implantada, os clientes poderão adiar entregas ou cancelar pedidos, sendo que componentes de memória, óptica, gerenciamento de energia e analógicos são os mais expostos a problemas de fornecimento, afirmou o Morgan Stanley.

artigo.texto: Posted on October 5, 2026 Technology group Wärtsilä has today closed the transaction of the joint venture for its Energy Storage business, following the agreement with German engineering company RCT Solutions GmbH announced on 15 June 2026. Under the arrangement, Wärtsilä and RCT Solutions each hold a 50% ownership stake in the joint venture, called Valo. The joint venture combines Wärtsilä’s global energy storage capabilities with RCT Solutions’ engineering expertise and is designed to provide a strong platform for long-term growth in the rapidly evolving energy storage market. Wärtsilä’s Energy Storage business employs approximately 450 people globally, and in 2025, it generated net sales of EUR 694 million. The transaction represents less than 5% of Wärtsilä’s total net assets. Energy Storage ceased to be a separate reporting segment in Wärtsilä in the second quarter of 2026. Up to the completion of the transaction, the Energy Storage business is reported in discontinued operations. During the third quarter of 2026, Wärtsilä recognised a write-down of capitalised R&D related to the Energy Storage business before the establishment of the joint venture, rather than within the joint venture as previously expected. It is expected that the new joint venture will generate operating loss in 2026 and positive results towards the end of 2027. With the transaction now completed, the joint venture will focus on executing its growth strategy and serving customers globally as an independent company jointly owned by Wärtsilä and RCT Solutions GmbH. The joint venture transaction can be discussed in more details on Wärtsilä’s pre-silent call today at 15:00 EEST; please register for the call here. artigo.texto: Residents filled the seats and hallways of the town hall’s rotunda for a nearly four-hour Bethlehem City Council meeting on Tuesday to participate in a public hearing on data centers and proposed amendments to the city’s zoning ordinance. The council passed the zoning ordinance amendments in a 7-0 vote. Rachel Leon, the council’s president, said this attendance was “anomalous” for the council. Most of the residents came for the public hearing or to comment and left when it concluded, nearly three hours into the meeting. City’s zoning ordinance amendments proposed Cathy Fletcher, director of planning and zoning for Bethlehem, presented the zoning ordinance text amendments to council at the public hearing. Fletcher defined data centers as facilities that house physical hardware to support digital systems and said the demand for data centers has grown rapidly. She said municipalities must allow for all land uses, so data centers can’t be banned. Fletcher also said local governments can determine how land is used and the specific development requirements to account for a municipality’s characteristics. Specifically, she said the city can regulate height, scale, setbacks, noise, light, access and safety standards. According to Fletcher, data centers fall under the industrial land use category and are permitted as a special exception in the industrial district that requires any proposal to go to the zoning hearing board. She said data center impacts aren’t always predictable. The zoning ordinance amendments will require all plans, studies, evaluations, assessments and strategies to send these documents at the time of application: - Environmental impact assessment and proposed mitigation strategies - Water utilization report and wastewater disposal documentation - Energy management plan and a power usage effectiveness analysis - Electronic waste and decommissioning plan - Emergency response plan and documentation regarding hazardous materials - Thermal impact mitigation plan - Photometric study that shows compliance with Article 1318.25, the lighting control section of the zoning ordinance - Full spectrum pre and post-construction sound study measured at the lot line The amendments also alter design standards, including increasing yard setbacks from a minimum of 20 feet to 80 feet and buffer yards from a minimum of 15 feet to 40 feet. The amendments also make a setback for residential districts at 1,000 feet and change building height limits to include rooftop structures within an 80 foot limit. Residents raise concerns about data centers Laurel Chuss, a Bethlehem resident, lives 200 feet from a proposed data center. She shared her concerns about the center being so close to her house in the public comment section of the meeting. “I’m heartbroken that regulation comes too late to protect my home,” she said. “No family should have to choose between unexpectedly moving or experiencing the negative lifelong impacts of living too close to a data center. I ask you to please protect other families in Bethlehem from my family’s current reality.” Shelby Carr, also a Bethlehem resident, said she believes the city should enforce a ban on non-disclosure agreements for data centers. She also expressed the importance of community meetings. “I hope it’s not lost on you how desperately people don’t want a data center in our community and while we can’t outright ban them, we should be doing as much as we can to safeguard our community and its resources by crafting tough ordinances,” Carr said. Mike Pipestone, Bethlehem resident, said he would like to see more post-construction reporting done. He said if the city gives away all the water and power it generates, all that’s left is a “smoking, intemperate mess,” and that’s not doing right by the community. “In this room today, I’ve heard all of our councilwomen show us the way forward with both courage and wisdom,” Pipestone said. He said voting for this amendment is a starting point and emphasized the importance of participating in midterm elections. Bethlehem resident Bret Becker also voiced his concerns about the water usage of data centers. He said he’s worried about his property value decreasing because of data centers being built in the area. “Bethlehem is preparing to allow one data center with no substantive guardrails,” Chuss said. “More will follow. Three data centers using three million gallons of water and now you’ve exceeded the water of Bethlehem Steel with 300 jobs to show for it.” According to Company Histories, Bethlehem Steel employed about 300,000 people at its peak production. Michael Bianco, Bethlehem resident, recommended the council to experience a data center visit. He said to stop data centers, development and fees can be made more expensive so it’s not as attractive. “The first thing I would say is to increase the fine because the purpose of a fine is to hit these people where it hurts for abusing our water, for abusing our land, for abusing our airspace and for abusing our communities,” Christian Maldonado, Bethlehem resident, said. Council’s response to the amendments Leon said there are currently no regulations on data centers in the city of Bethlehem. “I’m very much in support of (the amendments) for the main reason that it’s currently, in our zoning ordinance, a wild west,” Leon said. artigo.texto: HAILEY, Idaho — Blaine County commissioners passed an emergency moratorium pausing data center permitting, giving the county 182 days to draft new rules as artificial intelligence drives growing demand for the facilities. County Commissioner Lindsay Mollineaux said no influx of data center permit applications has hit Blaine County yet, but she is not going to wait around for it to happen. "I remember reading about things growing up and thinking, oh, that's never going to happen in Idaho. That's not the world anymore," Mollineaux said. Bannock and Kootenai counties already have moratoriums in place on data centers, and Mollineaux said she expects more counties to follow suit soon. She pointed to what other states have already experienced as a signal for what could be ahead. "Just like other states have seen potentially a big wave, we might be next, and so again, you want some time to get everything in order," Mollineaux said. The commissioners agreed, adopting the emergency moratorium to pause permitting until the Planning and Zoning Department can draft an ordinance to address data centers. Outside the courthouse, resident Alexis Limburg told me laws governing data centers should be in place before they are needed. "Before anything can come in without people really agreeing to it, you know, they should have a chance today to put those laws in place," Limburg said. Resident Heidi Bynum gave her public comment during the meeting. "Just say nix, I just wish you could just say nix," Bynum said. Mollineaux said other states have taken the lead in setting rules and guidelines for data centers, but in Idaho, it is up to each county — or even each municipality — to figure it out. "And so it's put, I think, a huge burden on our counties and cities to really think about things. We never thought we would have to think about," Mollineaux said. Mollineaux said the moratorium gives the county time to update its code and hold public conversations before anyone moves forward under old rules. "While we have time to sort to get everything together and update the code and have those public conversations, there's not the opportunity for someone's going to come in under the old rules, which we've already decided you don't need to be tightened up," Mollineaux said. She said the county's work on data center regulations is only just beginning. "And so my anticipation is, this will be the start of the conversation, but not the end of it," Mollineaux said. artigo.texto: Cooling battery cells directly in liquid creates an engineering challenge: keeping that liquid away from electrical equipment. BYD has filed a patent application for a two-chamber cabinet that separates submerged battery modules from electronics and routes their connections through the upper part of the liquid-filled compartment. The China National Intellectual Property Administration published the application, numbered CN 122868832 A, on October 5, 2026. Filed in March 2025, it describes battery cabinets and energy storage equipment that use dielectric fluid to absorb heat directly from the modules. The design places electrical equipment in a dry upper chamber and battery modules in a wet lower chamber. Its focus is the boundary between those spaces, where connections must pass through without allowing cooling liquid to reach components intended to remain dry. Bringing cooling liquid directly to the cells Many battery systems remove heat through an indirect cooling arrangement. Liquid circulates inside aluminum cold plates positioned against battery modules, drawing heat through the cell casing and materials between the cells and plates. Immersion cooling changes that heat-transfer route. Battery modules sit directly in a non-conductive fluid, allowing heat to pass from their wetted surfaces into the surrounding liquid. This shortens the thermal path, but containing the fluid becomes part of the cabinet’s design. Electrical equipment and connection points that are not intended for immersion still require protection from the liquid. More from Transportation See All BYD’s application specifies dielectric cooling fluids, including hydrocarbon- or ester-based formulations. These fluids provide electrical insulation while cooling the submerged modules. Moving connections higher to reduce pressure The proposed cabinet divides the battery and its electrical equipment into two isolated compartments. The lower chamber holds the immersed modules, while the upper chamber houses electrical components outside the liquid volume. Electrical and signal connections pass through the upper portion of the wet chamber before entering the dry compartment. The arrangement avoids routing those connections through the floor or deeper sections of the liquid-filled chamber. That positioning matters because hydrostatic pressure increases with depth. A sealing interface near the top experiences less liquid pressure than one farther down, reducing the pressure acting on the boundary between compartments. The design therefore combines an insulating fluid with a physical separation between cooling and electrical equipment. The cabinet’s layout addresses how connections cross that separation while keeping sensitive components outside the main liquid volume. A storage cabinet awaiting commercial plans The application covers battery cabinets and energy storage equipment. It does not identify a passenger-vehicle application, so the filing does not establish that BYD intends to use this arrangement in an electric car. Existing systems use different cooling layouts. BYD’s MC Cube-T specifies liquid cooling, while CATL’s EnerOne and EnerC storage systems use cooling plates outside their battery modules. CATL’s Qilin vehicle battery places a liquid-cooling plate between adjacent cells. BYD’s filing instead places the modules inside the cooling fluid itself. The application remains under substantive examination, and the company has not announced commercial production plans for the proposed cabinet.

artigo.texto: Blaine County leaders on Tuesday are scheduled to consider approving an ordinance to establish a temporary emergency moratorium on the issuance of development permits for data centers. The proposed ordinance—put forth by Commissioner Lindsay Mollineaux—would disallow county officials from the “receipt, processing and approval of applications” of permits for the construction of data centers in Blaine County for 182 days. The emergency moratorium also mandates that county officials in that six-month period develop a plan for a “permanent solution” to a list of “problems” associated with data centers, including the developments’ typically industrial-scale consumption of water and energy. The proposed moratorium was placed on the Tuesday agenda of the Board of County Commissioners just two days after the commissioners asked the county’s land use director, Rachel Martin, to initiate the process of drafting amendments to the zoning code to define any allowances for data centers on industrial-zoned lands. “Internally, we have been discussing for quite a while data centers and their effects on neighboring properties and the community as a whole,” Martin said to the board. “Many local jurisdictions in Idaho have started adopting codes to regulate data centers and their use.” Martin said the Land Use and Building Services Department has determined that the often-controversial developments could potentially be allowed in the county’s light-industrial zones, but only with “carefully considered” regulations and “specific parameters.” In an interview Monday, Mollineaux said she determined that the county needs to implement the emergency moratorium to allow time to analyze the complicated issue and implement appropriate regulations before any applications are made. No applications for data centers have yet been submitted to the county, Martin said last week. However, Mollineaux said, in the absence of a moratorium, any incoming applications would have to be processed under the existing zoning regulations, which don’t adequately address data centers. Data centers are buildings—sometimes extremely large—that store, process and distribute digital data and information through a vast network of electronic equipment. The rapid growth of the use of artificial intelligence—which relies heavily on data centers—in different applications has fueled a high demand for the developments and a subsequent boom in their construction. However, as more data centers are constructed, evidence of some significant negative impacts has surfaced. Detractors of AI data centers across the nation have cited water usage, energy requirements, environmental pollution and provision of a relative lack of long-term jobs as significant negative factors. Meanwhile, promoters say the developments provide thousands of well-paying jobs, fuel economic expansion, boost communities’ tax bases and help meet the needs of modern technology. The three-page proposed Blaine County moratorium cites an array of potential negative impacts, especially massive water consumption in a region stricken by drought and under strict state management of existing water resources. It states that: - “A medium-sized data center can consume up to 300,000 gallons of water per day for cooling, roughly the daily use of 1,000 households,” and that large centers can consume up to 5 million gallons per day. - “Most large data centers use evaporative cooling, which consumes water and removes it from the local watershed rather than returning it.” - Major water draws for data centers “can reduce streamflow during drought, harm aquatic habitat, and increase competition with agricultural and municipal water users.” The proposed ordinance also states that data centers: - Use a variety of dangerous chemicals and consume up to 100 megawatts of electricity, enough to power tens of thousands of homes. - “Are often at least 1,000,000 square feet in size, or approximately the size of 17 football fields,” and newer proposals are calling for even bigger facilities. The proposed moratorium concludes that the impacts of an improperly regulated data center “constitute an imminent peril to the public health, safety, and welfare of the citizens of Blaine County.” Blaine County currently has only three areas zoned for light-industrial uses, Martin said. They include: a small area south of Ketchum along state Highway 75, around Clear Creek Drive just north of The Meadows; a small area just north of Hailey along Highway 75, around Bartholomew Road; and a larger area around Glendale Road southwest of Bellevue. In crafting regulations for data centers to be added to the zoning code, the county will have to consider matters such as establishing a clear definition of data centers, what size might be permitted and what limitations might be placed on water and energy consumption, Martin told commissioners last week. The process—which will require extensive research by staff, reviews by the county’s Planning and Zoning Commission and final approval of the Board of Commissioners—should include “quite a bit of public input,” Martin said. Mollineaux said Monday that data centers have “been on everyone’s mind for a while” but she learned of the “imminent” nature of the issue at a recent Idaho Association of Counties meeting. Other counties have already taken action to regulate data centers, she said, and details of other developments in Idaho that are moving forward have come forth. Idaho is now in the “bullseye” for data centers, she said, and Blaine County needs to establish proper control. Even though industrial-zoned land in Blaine County is limited, land can be rezoned and developers can seek loopholes in existing regulations, she said. As for whether developers might propose to build a data center in one of the cities in the county, Hailey City Administrator Lisa Horowitz said she and Hailey leaders are not planning for that scenario. artigo.texto: The Maryland Public Service Commission has conditionally selected two transmission-connected energy storage projects totaling 440 MW for Energy Storage Capacity Credit awards under the first round of the state’s Next Generation Energy Act procurement. The Commission regulates public utilities in Maryland, and the storage procurement is designed to support financing by providing a more stable revenue stream against uncertainty in future PJM Interconnection capacity market prices. The Chalk Point Storage Project would provide 400 MW at the existing Chalk Point power plant site in Aquasco, Prince George’s County, while the 40 MW Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project would be a combined solar-and-storage facility on a reclaimed coal mine in Barton, Garrett County. Together, the projects would provide 440 MW with four-hour durations under flat, 15-year award terms, with an estimated combined cost of 6.98 cents per month for a typical Maryland residential customer. Round 1 targeted 800 MW, while the Next Generation Energy Act requires at least two solicitations for a cumulative 1,600 MW of front-of-the-meter, transmission-connected energy storage with a minimum four-hour duration. The Commission selected Chalk Point and Jade Meadow III as the most cost-effective and highest-ranked remaining proposals after public and evidentiary hearings, while the 500 MW Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project was not selected. Both selected projects must still apply for Commission construction approval, and the Round 2 Request for Applications will be issued by January 1, 2027. Maryland selects 440 MW of energy storage in first round Two four-hour storage projects totaling 440 MW secured conditional 15-year awards in the first round of Maryland’s energy storage procurement. artigo.texto: Canadian Solar Inc. has announced that its energy storage solutions business, e-STORAGE, has signed an agreement to supply and commission a 100 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) for OX2’s Muswellbrook Solar Farm and Battery project in New South Wales, Australia. Shipments for the project are scheduled to begin in the third quarter of 2027, while commercial operations are targeted for the third quarter of 2028. The battery cells and SolBank systems will be manufactured at Canadian Solar’s own facilities, providing greater supply-chain visibility and quality control. Under the agreement, e-STORAGE will deliver an integrated energy storage solution based on its SolBank 3.0 battery containers, along with power conversion systems, plant controls and its proprietary EQ-S Energy Management System (EMS). The EMS has been developed in-house by e-STORAGE’s North American software team. The company will also undertake R1 grid connection studies, provide a hybrid power plant controller to coordinate the battery system with the co-located solar farm, and lead the overall integration and commissioning of the hybrid facility. The project is backed by a 20-year long-term service agreement (LTSA), covering hardware, proprietary software and long-term system performance under a single service arrangement. Located approximately 2.5 kilometres east of Muswellbrook, the solar-plus-storage facility will be developed on land at a former coal mine within the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. The project comes as the Hunter region prepares for the retirement of aging coal-fired generation capacity in the early 2030s. The two-hour battery system is expected to store surplus solar generation during periods of high daytime output and dispatch electricity during evening peak-demand periods, supporting grid reliability as conventional thermal generation declines. Once operational, the BESS will support OX2’s long-term hybrid power purchase agreement for the project. By combining solar generation with dispatchable battery storage, the facility is designed to provide firmer renewable electricity while supporting the Hunter region’s transition away from coal-fired power. Steve Symons, Vice President of OX2 Australia, said the storage system would transform Muswellbrook into a hybrid facility capable of capturing solar power when available and supplying it when required by the grid. Jeff Roy, President of e-STORAGE, highlighted the growing role of battery storage in regions transitioning away from coal generation, adding that e-STORAGE’s integrated approach covers battery cells, energy management software and long-term servicing. artigo.texto: A revisão técnica do padrão corporativo Corporate Net-Zero Standard, conduzida pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), estabelece novos critérios de integridade para corporações que buscam neutralizar impactos climáticos. Sob as novas diretrizes regulatórias globais, mecanismos genéricos de compensação perdem prioridade em favor de intervenções diretas nas cadeias de suprimentos das próprias empresas. De acordo com análise apresentada por Rodrigo Oliveira, diretor-presidente da Green Mining e vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Empresas de Logística Reversa (ABELORE), essa orientação reposiciona o crédito de carbono gerado pela reciclagem como um instrumento central para neutralizar emissões residuais de embalagens nos setores de bens de consumo, varejo, cosméticos, higiene, e-commerce e alimentos. Segundo o executivo da entidade, a reformulação normativa atinge diretamente a governança ambiental de conglomerados que operam sob alta intensidade de empacotamento. Em pronunciamento institucional, a empresa de rastreabilidade logística sustenta que a compra de créditos climáticos tradicionais, desvinculada do ciclo produtivo dos resíduos descartados no pós-consumo, torna-se insuficiente para atender a investidores institucionais e reguladores internacionais. Para a organização, a redução de pegada ecológica nesses segmentos exige vinculação direta com a logística reversa e a substituição efetiva de matéria-prima virgem por materiais reaproveitados. Pressão do Escopo 3 na indústria de consumo Nos cálculos de inventários de gases de efeito estufa (GEE), a gestão de resíduos sólidos e materiais embalados concentra a maior parte do impacto ambiental fora dos limites fabris imediatos. Conforme expõe a Green Mining, os setores de comércio varejista e bens não duráveis registram o grosso de seu passivo ecológico no chamado Escopo 3. Esse parâmetro técnico abrange as fases de extração de insumos, frete logístico terceirizado, manuseio no ponto de venda e, de forma crítica, a destinação final dada pelo consumidor aos frascos, caixas e recipientes plásticos, metálicos, celulósicos ou de vidro. Na avaliação da entidade setorial, estratégias como redesign estrutural de recipientes, diminuição da espessura de invólucros plásticos, ampliação de modelos de refil e troca de insumos fósseis por componentes biodegradáveis diminuem expressivamente os inventários absolutos. Contudo, a Green Mining argumenta que essas medidas não eliminam a integralidade das emissões associadas à produção primária e ao frete de retorno. Mesmo diante de saltos de ecoeficiência industrial, persiste um volume residual contínuo de resíduos que demanda soluções de compensação aderentes à matriz de materiais de cada organização. Mecânica operacional do crédito lastreado em resíduos A tese defendida pela companhia estabelece que a integridade climática requer paridade entre o vetor de poluição e a ferramenta escolhida para mitigação. No entendimento manifestado pela diretoria da Green Mining, companhias que comercializam recipientes em larga escala cometem inconsistência metodológica quando tentam saldar passivos materiais exclusivamente via projetos florestais distantes ou iniciativas energéticas desconectadas do ecossistema de manufatura. - A coleta é auditada em pontos georreferenciados para garantir a adicionalidade do volume recuperado. - Pesagem e triagem são registradas eletronicamente para impedir duplicidade de notas ou contagem fictícia. - A homologação de transformadores industriais atesta o reprocessamento de insumos secundários. - O cálculo de carbono abatido compara o gasto energético da reciclagem contra a produção virgem primária. A alegação técnica da Green Mining pontua que o benefício mensurável desse modelo deriva da substituição da matéria-prima virgem — como bauxita no alumínio, areia e barrilha no vidro ou derivados de petróleo no polietileno — por insumos secundários que demandam fração sensivelmente menor de energia calorífica e elétrica durante o refundimento industrial. Ao documentar e auditar esse percurso de ponta a ponta, a companhia sustenta que a operação gera lastro técnico verificável para emissão de ativos ambientais. Gargalos estruturais da cadeia reversa brasileira O mercado brasileiro apresenta uma disparidade estrutural entre o volume de materiais descartados diariamente e a capacidade de reprocessamento das usinas nacionais. Dados setoriais defendidos pela assessoria da Green Mining ressaltam que o país detém uma das mais expressivas redes de reciclagem social do planeta, ancorada no trabalho de cooperativas e operadores autônomos. Apesar dessa capilaridade de campo, os índices gerais de retorno pós-consumo permanecem muito aquém do potencial de mitigação das cidades. Sob a ótica detalhada pela entidade, o valor de venda de materiais como vidro ou plásticos flexíveis não remunera adequadamente os custos agregados de frete, triagem mecanizada, formalização trabalhista e armazenamento intermediário. A Green Mining argumenta que o crédito de carbono gerado pela atividade opera como uma alavanca de capitalização privada capaz de cobrir o déficit financeiro de coleta nas municipalidades, viabilizando a inclusão socioprodutiva de catadores e a expansão de tecnologias de leitura óptica e rastreamento serial. Critérios de integridade e auditoria corporativa À medida que diretrizes internacionais como a SBTi intensificam as exigências de comprovação contra o greenwashing, fundos de investimento e comitês de auditoria passam a exigir comprovação de adicionalidade nos investimentos ambientais. Conforme postulado pelo relatório corporativo da Green Mining, compradores institucionais de crédito não se contentam mais com atestados estáticos de equivalência métrica; o foco migrou para a auditoria de processos que gerem benefícios econômicos e sociais comprováveis nas regiões impactadas. - Comprovação documental de que o material recolhido não seria absorvido sem o incentivo financeiro adicional.

artigo.texto: OS DATA CENTERS CRESCEM DE IMPORTÂNCIA E JÁ SERÃO TEMA DE UM DEBATE INTERNACIONAL QUE COMEÇA AMANHÃ EM SÃO PAULO A primeira edição do Data Center World Brasil começa amanhã (6), no São Paulo Expo, em um momento em que decisões sobre energia, tributação, conectividade e capacidade computacional ganham peso na definição de onde e como serão instalados os próximos grandes projetos de data centers no país. A programação reúne debates sobre condições regulatórias, investimentos, disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, refrigeração, operação e capacidade computacional, diante de uma nova geração de aplicações de inteligência artificial que exige infraestruturas mais robustas e eficientes. Um dos temas que chegam ao congresso é o Redata, novo regime especial de tributação para serviços de data center, criado para estimular investimentos no setor. A medida será discutida às 10h30, na Opening Arena, durante o painel “Infraestrutura digital como ativo geopolítico: competitividade, investimentos, regulação e o que precisa mudar”. A conversa aborda os efeitos do programa sobre a atração de investimentos, a competitividade do país e as decisões que podem influenciar a infraestrutura digital nos próximos cinco a dez anos. O debate passa ainda pelo impacto do Confaz e do ICMS sobre a competitividade do setor. A energia é outro fator decisivo nessa equação. O avanço da inteligência artificial elevou a demanda por capacidade computacional e trouxe novos desafios para a implantação e a operação dos data centers. Localização, disponibilidade energética, eficiência e continuidade operacional estão entre os temas que atravessam a programação do congresso Na sequência, às 11h30, a roundtable “Energia como gargalo estrutural: disponibilidade, intermitência e viabilidade real” discute a oferta efetiva de energia, modelos de geração, armazenamento e alternativas para garantir estabilidade às operações. Às 14h, o painel “Como grandes empresas escolhem data centers na prática: decisões reais de custo, risco e performance” traz a perspectiva de quem utiliza essa infraestrutura e precisa equilibrar localização, latência, custo, segurança e continuidade dos serviços. A discussão sobre investimentos volta às 16h, com a roundtable “Financiamento, viabilidade e expansão: por que projetos travam — e como viabilizar na prática”, que reúne representantes do Ministério das Comunicações, BNDES, Brasscom e Patria Investments. O debate aborda capital, crédito e as condições necessárias para tirar grandes projetos do papel. A conectividade também ganha espaço entre os assuntos que ajudam a explicar a expansão do setor. O avanço das redes de alta capacidade reforça a importância de conexões estratégicas para sustentar data centers, serviços de cloud e aplicações digitais cada vez mais intensivas em processamento. No dia 7, quarta-feira, o painel “Latência, rotas globais e edge: onde a infraestrutura decide o jogo”, às 10h30, aborda a relação entre localização, conectividade e desempenho. Às 15h15, o painel “Desafios dos Hyperscalers: como planejar capacidade em um mercado imprevisível” coloca no centro da conversa o desafio de ampliar a capacidade diante do crescimento da demanda impulsionada pela IA. Logo depois, às 16h, o estudo de caso “Continuidade operacional em data centers: como se preparar para falhas, crises e eventos extremos” contempla estratégias de preparação para situações capazes de afetar as operações. Para fechar o segundo dia, às 16h30, o LATAM Leaders Panel “Data centers na América Latina: investimento, expansão e decisões de arquitetura” amplia a discussão para os movimentos de investimento e crescimento do mercado regional. A inteligência artificial ganha ainda mais espaço no último dia do congresso. Na quinta-feira, 8 de outubro, às 10h30, o C-Level Panel “Expansão na era da IA: decisões que definem bilhões em investimento” discute escolhas de infraestrutura, energia e capacidade diante da nova escala de demanda. Às 14h, o painel “Data centers AI-ready: densidade, energia e novos requisitos de infraestrutura” mostra como cargas computacionais mais intensivas estão mudando a arquitetura dos empreendimentos. O aumento da densidade dos racks pressiona sistemas elétricos e térmicos e acelera a adoção de tecnologias de refrigeração mais eficientes, como o liquid cooling. Para Leonardo Benedicto, diretor do Data Center World Brasil, a transformação provocada pela IA exige que o setor olhe para os data centers de forma mais ampla. “A inteligência artificial está mudando rapidamente a forma como pensamos os data centers. Não é apenas uma questão de aumentar capacidade. É preciso considerar energia, refrigeração, espaço e a possibilidade de ampliar as instalações ao longo do tempo. O desafio é construir uma infraestrutura que acompanhe a velocidade dessa transformação e esteja preparada para as demandas que ainda estão por vir.” A expansão do setor também tem reflexos sobre a economia. Estudo da FGV aponta que 100 MW de capacidade instalada em data centers podem representar cerca de 12,5 mil empregos, evidenciando o alcance dos investimentos em infraestrutura digital para além do mercado de tecnologia.

artigo.texto: Verlume conclui testes hiperbáricos de sistema de bateria submarina de 500 kWh antes de implantação no Mar do Norte holandês A Verlume, especialista em baterias submarinas e sistemas de gerenciamento de energia com sede no Reino Unido, testou seu sistema modular de armazenamento de energia submarino de 500 kWh em Aberdeen antes de uma implantação planejada no Mar do Norte holandês, de acordo com a Offshore Energy. O sistema está previsto para se tornar a primeira bateria submarina formadora de rede co-localizada com energia eólica offshore após a instalação. A Verlume informou em 1º de outubro que havia concluído os testes hiperbáricos de seu invólucro submarino Orah na instalação de testes hiperbáricos da JFD em Aberdeen, um passo que a empresa descreveu como um importante marco de qualificação antes da implantação planejada do sistema no parque eólico offshore OranjeWind. Esse projeto está sendo desenvolvido pela RWE e pela TotalEnergies na costa holandesa. O sistema modular de armazenamento de energia submarino de 500 kWh foi projetado para fornecer suporte autônomo de rede para parques eólicos offshore. O Orah utiliza química de bateria atual e é gerenciado pela plataforma de gerenciamento de energia Axonn da Verlume. Segundo a empresa, essas tecnologias se combinam para formar uma solução modular de armazenamento de energia e suporte autônomo de rede destinada a ajudar a viabilizar sistemas de energia offshore mais flexíveis e resilientes. Com peso de 10 toneladas e dimensões de 7,2 metros de comprimento, 2,4 metros de largura e 2,4 metros de altura, o sistema é descrito como o maior vaso já testado no centro hiperbárico da JFD até o momento. O programa de testes submeteu o invólucro a um perfil de pressão controlado que representa seu ambiente operacional submarino pretendido. Ele se concentrou em três áreas críticas: qualificação de pressão e profundidade, integridade do invólucro e desempenho funcional sob pressão. Depois que o sistema completo de 85 toneladas for implantado no parque eólico offshore OranjeWind, ele representará a primeira bateria submarina formadora de rede co-localizada com energia eólica offshore. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado de acumuladores elétricos de íons de lítio (exceto usados) nos Países Baixos, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. Cobertura do Produto Acumuladores Elétricos de Íons de Lítio (Exceto Usados) abrange células e baterias secundárias de íons de lítio novas e não utilizadas, projetadas para armazenamento e fornecimento de energia elétrica, incluindo separadores, em formatos retangulares, quadrados, cilíndricos, prismáticos ou tipo bolsa. O escopo abrange acumuladores completos prontos para integração em equipamentos, bem como células individuais e módulos que fazem parte de um sistema de bateria maior. Acumuladores usados, gastos ou resíduos destinados à reciclagem ou descarte são excluídos. Incluídos - Acumuladores de íons de lítio com formato retangular ou quadrado - Acumuladores de íons de lítio com formato cilíndrico - Células e baterias prismáticas de íons de lítio - Células e baterias tipo bolsa de íons de lítio - Módulos e pacotes de baterias de íons de lítio - Acumuladores de íons de lítio com sistemas integrados de gerenciamento de bateria - Acumuladores de íons de lítio de alta densidade de energia para veículos elétricos - artigo.texto: The Alabama Public Service Commission voted on Tuesday to keep a ‘deemed approved’ process that lets Alabama Power’s electricity contracts with the largest data centers take effect without a vote of the commission. The new rule extends the review period from 10 days to 90 days, but retains the previous rule of automatic approval for Alabama Power data center contracts if the commission fails to make a decision within 90 days. Energy Alabama advocated for a public vote on all applicable data center contracts in written comments this summer. “For three decades, rules built for manufacturers let contracts take effect without a vote of the Commission. Data centers on this scale are a different animal,” Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, said. “Ninety days is better than ten, but silence still counts as yes. A contract this big should never take effect because nobody voted. Alabamians deserve to see their regulators decide, in public.” The Alabama Attorney General's Office also submitted comments on August 6, calling for a vote by commission members on contracts between Alabama Power and data centers. “The elected and appointed members of the Alabama Public Service Commission must actively participate in the decisions of the commission by voting on large load contracts, especially when the matter involves an assessment of public benefits or a determination of the public interest,” Olivia Martin, division chief of consumer interest with the AG’s Office, said in August. The new rule requires Alabama Power to file a public petition naming the data center customer and its parent companies, the city or county where the facility will be built, and the maximum amount of power it has contracted for. Other aspects of the contract would be confidential. All three members of the commission said they wanted future commissioners to vote on the contracts, but still approved a “deemed approved” process where contracts could be approved if the commission doesn’t vote within 90 days of the petition being submitted. According to the rule approved at Tuesday’s meeting, “Contracts submitted under this process shall be approved or disapproved through a commission vote within 90 days of the submission of the filing of the petition. If the commission fails to vote within 90 days, the petition is deemed approved.” “I feel strongly that we should take a public vote as a commission on data centers. We should not follow the deemed approved process that we’ve been following for a number of years,” Cynthia Almond, Public Service Commission President, said. “It should be a very public process we go through, I believe, because the public is very interested in this, very concerned about it. If we don’t take a public vote, that to me is not doing our job.” Almond and other commission members, Jeremy Oden and Chip Beeker, also voted for the new rule. Oden and Beeker both lost their Republican primary races in May. The commission is set to expand to seven seats in January 2027 under a new law passed in the 2026 session. artigo.texto: CATL, Sungrow, Tesla and BYD are leading the global battery energy storage system market in 2026, but their leadership differs significantly across battery shipments, system integration, software, regional market share and mega-project execution. Battery storage has become one of the fastest-growing parts of global power infrastructure as utilities add batteries to integrate solar and wind, manage peak demand, provide grid flexibility and improve energy security. Global battery storage additions reached 108 GW in 2025, up 40 percent, according to the International Energy Agency. Installed capacity is now 11 times higher than in 2021. Around 80 percent of new capacity was utility-scale, while lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, accounted for approximately 90 percent of deployments. China represented around 60 percent of global additions, followed by the United States and Europe. Growth accelerated further in 2026. SNE Research reported global lithium-ion ESS battery shipments of 461.3 GWh in H1 2026, up 71 percent from 269.7 GWh a year earlier. Markets outside China accounted for 258.7 GWh, or 56 percent, exceeding half of global shipments for the first time. The global battery storage market is therefore moving rapidly beyond China, even though Chinese manufacturers continue to dominate battery-cell production and system integration. Which Company Is the World’s Largest Battery Storage Supplier? There is no single answer because the industry uses different measurements. CATL is the world’s largest ESS battery-cell supplier by H1 2026 shipments, delivering 125 GWh and capturing 27.1 percent of the global market. Sungrow ranks first in Wood Mackenzie’s 2026 Global BESS Integrator Comprehensive Ranking, which evaluates companies across technology, safety, R&D, supply chains, vertical integration, financial strength and other criteria. Tesla remains particularly strong in North America, while BYD combines cell manufacturing, system integration and large-scale project execution. The distinction matters because battery-cell manufacturing and BESS integration are different businesses. Global Top 10 Battery Storage Companies in 2026 Wood Mackenzie’s comprehensive 2026 BESS integrator ranking places the companies in the following order: The ranking demonstrates why BESS procurement is moving beyond battery price toward efficiency, safety, financial strength and lifetime performance. 1. Sungrow: World’s Top BESS Integrator Sungrow ranks first in Wood Mackenzie’s 2026 comprehensive assessment. Its advantage comes from combining battery systems with power conversion systems, controls and global project-integration capabilities. That is important because PCS efficiency, thermal management, grid-forming capability and system controls directly affect lifetime project economics. Sungrow also leads Europe’s BESS integrator market and has established a particularly strong position in the Middle East. 2. Tesla: Megapack and Software Create a Different Model Tesla ranks second globally in the comprehensive assessment and remains the leading BESS integrator in North America. Its Megapack strategy combines utility-scale battery hardware with Autobidder software, which can optimize battery participation in electricity markets. Tesla’s strength demonstrates why the storage battle extends beyond battery chemistry. Software capable of determining when to charge, discharge and participate in energy or ancillary-services markets can directly influence project revenue. 3. CATL: 125 GWh Makes It the ESS Battery-Cell Leader CATL dominates when measured by battery-cell shipments. The company shipped 125 GWh of ESS batteries during H1 2026, up 81 percent year over year, increasing its market share from 25.6 percent to 27.1 percent. For comparison, second-ranked EVE Energy shipped 48 GWh, while Hithium delivered 46.2 GWh. CATL therefore shipped more ESS batteries than the next two suppliers individually by a very wide margin. Its huge LFP manufacturing scale provides significant cost advantages, while continued investment in alternative technologies including sodium-ion could broaden its future storage portfolio. 4. BYD: Vertical Integration Meets Mega-Scale Storage BYD combines battery-cell manufacturing, electronics and complete storage-system integration. Its H1 2026 ESS cell shipments reached 35.7 GWh, giving it 7.7 percent global share. Its project footprint is equally important. BYD’s total contracted battery volume with Grenergy for Chile’s Oasis de Atacama project has reached 6.5 GWh across project phases. BYD is also gaining ground in Europe, where it moved from fifth to second among integrators. In the Middle East, BYD and Sungrow together captured 87 percent of the BESS market in 2025, demonstrating the scale of Chinese supplier expansion. 5. Envision Energy: Combining Renewables, Storage and Digital Control Envision and Trina Storage share fifth position in Wood Mackenzie’s comprehensive global ranking. Envision’s strategy extends beyond batteries because the company participates across renewable generation, storage and digital energy management. It ranked third in Asia-Pacific behind CRRC and HyperStrong. Combining wind, solar, storage and digital optimization could become valuable as utilities move toward integrated renewable-energy projects rather than procuring individual technologies separately. 6. Trina Storage: Utility-Scale Integration Trina Storage has developed its BESS position around the Elementa platform and utility-scale LFP projects. The company’s integration with the broader Trina Solar ecosystem also creates opportunities in solar-plus-storage. For developers, greater system density can reduce land requirements and some balance-of-system costs, while integrated battery and power-electronics design can improve project efficiency. 7. artigo.texto: Judge dismisses DC Blox lawsuit challenging Metro Nashville’s actions surrounding proposed data center near zoo The judge said some of the claims were too unclear about what rights DC Blox said Metro took away. What This Story Is About - The DC Blox lawsuit that challenged Metro Nashville’s actions surrounding a proposed data center has been dismissed and its subsequent request for a preliminary injunction has also been denied. Why It Matters - DC Blox was vying for a property next to the Nashville Zoo for a data center that sparked a petition with more than 600,000 signatures as well as responses from local celebrities. What Happens Next - The judge said DC Blox can try again with a clearer explanation, within 21 days by filing either “an answer or a motion to dismiss” the amended complaint. For Context Catch Up NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - The DC Blox lawsuit that challenged Metro Nashville’s actions surrounding a proposed data center has been dismissed and its subsequent request for a preliminary injunction has also been denied. In August, DC Blox sued Metro Nashville in federal court and challenged the city’s data-center moratorium and its decision to halt permit processing for the company’s project that was proposed next to the Nashville Zoo. DC Blox alleged that the site had operated as a data center under a previous tenant, Asurion, and claimed Metro’s actions violated due process, equal protection and constitutional protections against taking property without just compensation. Overall, DC Blox brought nine claims to the judge. Four federal constitutional claims and five claims seeking declaratory relief which include the following: - Substantive due process: The Moratorium reportedly interfered irrationally with DC Blox’s protected property, use, pre-existing-use or vested permit rights - Equal protection: Metro allegedly treated DC Blox differently from similar developers, including RadiusDC, without a rational basis. - Procedural due process: DC Blox claims metro place their applications on hold despite asserted protected rights without adequate process - Takings: The moratorium allegedly took DC Blox’s property rights without just compensation - Pre-existing use: a declaration that DC Blox asserted protected data-center use under Tennessee law had not been terminated - Vested permits: A declaration that DC Blox’s July 17 application vested rights and should be judge under the law in effect when filed - BZA Authority: A declaration that the amended moratorium was invalid because it was not referred back to the planning commission for review - Validity of the moratorium: A declaration that the amended moratorium was invalid because it was not referred back to the Planning Commission for review - State-law preemption: A declaration that the moratorium was preempted by Tennessee’s vested-property-rights statute. Of the nine claims, the judge dismissed three. The judge said some of the claims were too unclear about what rights DC Blox said Metro took away. The judge said DC Blox can try again with a clearer explanation, within 21 days by filing either “an answer or a motion to dismiss” the amended complaint. Councilmember Courtney Johnston said that Metro has both the right and the responsibility to determine appropriate land uses through its legislative and zoning processes. “DC BLOX had every right to challenge those decisions in court. They did. This was the result,” Johnston said in a Facebook post. Read the full lawsuits and claims below. Copyright 2026 WSMV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Atmos Renewables, an Australian renewableenergy firm, has reached financial close on two Capacity Investment Scheme-backed projects in Australia: the 400 MW/1,600 MWh Teebar BESS and 470 MW Parron Maam Marang Wind Farm. Atmos Renewables is the Australian renewable energy business of Igneo Infrastructure Partners, developing, owning and operating utility-scale wind, solar and battery storage assets. The four-hour Teebar BESS will be built beside Powerlink’s Teebar Creek substation in Queensland’s Fraser Coast region. Parron Maam Marang will be developed in Western Australia’s Wheatbelt and supply electricity to Synergy under a long-term PPA. Together with the 100 MW/400 MWh Merredin BESS, Atmos has taken 970 MW of CIS-backed capacity through financial close over 16 months. Atmos will retain ownership of both projects during construction and operate them after completion. Its national portfolio now exceeds 1.5 GW of operating and under-construction wind, solar and storage capacity. Atmos closes financing for 400 MW Teebar BESS, wind farm Atmos Renewables reached financial close on 870 MW of CIS-backed battery and wind projects in Queensland and Western Australia, expanding its portfolio. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no EXCLUSIVO CNBC: Marvell projeta mais de US$ 30 bilhões em receita de data centers em 2028, diz CEO Publicado 07/10/2026 • 16:53 | Atualizado há 14 horas KEY POINTS A Marvell projeta uma forte expansão de seus negócios ligados à infraestrutura de inteligência artificial e data centers, com receita implícita superior a US$ 30 bilhões em 2028. Em entrevista exclusiva à CNBC, Matt Murphy, CEO da Marvell, afirmou que a estimativa representa uma forte revisão em relação à projeção de US$ 15 bilhões apresentada pela companhia dois anos atrás. “Dois anos atrás, estávamos em Nova York, no mesmo hotel, no mesmo local, falando sobre nosso crescimento em IA e data centers. E estávamos falando, naquela época, sobre US$ 15 bilhões de receita da Marvell para 2028”. Segundo Murphy, o consenso atual dos analistas já aponta para uma receita de data centers superior a US$ 30 bilhões em 2028. “Ela basicamente dobrou nesse período”, disse. O executivo afirmou que a companhia vem atualizando os investidores conforme o mercado de inteligência artificial evolui e que os resultados alcançados ao longo do caminho reforçaram a confiança nas projeções. A expansão também ocorre em um momento de aumento das expectativas para empresas de semicondutores ligadas à inteligência artificial. Murphy comentou a declaração feita por Jensen Huang, CEO da Nvidia, que afirmou em junho que a Marvell poderia se tornar a próxima empresa de US$ 1 trilhão em valor de mercado. “Não foi ensaiado e foi chocante quando Jensen disse aquilo”, afirmou Murphy. Segundo ele, porém, uma avaliação desse tamanho não seria necessariamente incompatível com as perspectivas de receita da companhia nos próximos anos. Para o CEO da Marvell, uma das principais oportunidades está menos na capacidade de processamento individual dos chips e mais na infraestrutura necessária para conectar diferentes componentes dos sistemas de IA. Murphy explicou que o avanço da inteligência artificial inicialmente foi acompanhado por uma forte expansão da capacidade computacional, seguida por uma grande demanda por memória. O próximo gargalo, segundo ele, está na conectividade entre esses componentes. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC “Não há o suficiente na camada de conectividade para conectar todas essas coisas. Você tem muita computação instalada, muita memória instalada. Mas adivinha? Elas todas precisam conversar entre si através de interconexões ópticas de alta velocidade, redes de comutação”. O objetivo, segundo Murphy, é evitar que unidades de processamento ou memória permaneçam ociosas por falta de comunicação eficiente entre os componentes. A necessidade de conectividade também aumenta com a diversificação dos sistemas de IA. O executivo afirmou que aplicações de IA generativa, agentes e modelos de raciocínio estão ampliando a variedade de tipos de computação utilizados nos sistemas. “Quando você começa a falar sobre IA, agêntica e modelos de raciocínio, há cada vez mais tipos diversos de computação. Então, a camada de conectividade fica ainda mais complexa”. Murphy considera essa expansão o próximo grande desbloqueio do mercado de semicondutores. Segundo ele, o negócio da Marvell relacionado à conectividade acelerou desde que essa tese passou a ser apresentada aos investidores. O executivo também comentou a expansão do mercado de silício personalizado. Em abril de 2024, a companhia estimava um mercado total endereçável de US$ 40 bilhões para esse segmento. Agora, a projeção apresentada por Murphy é de US$ 235 bilhões até 2030. Segundo o CEO, a discussão sobre a viabilidade do mercado mudou significativamente nos últimos dois anos. “O debate era, na verdade, se o personalizado poderia sequer se materializar como uma fatia do mercado. Agora, você avança no tempo e não somos apenas nós. Todo esse segmento foi claramente consolidado como algo real”. A Marvell atua nesse mercado em diferentes áreas e estabeleceu uma meta de US$ 30 bilhões em receita com silício personalizado até 2030. A companhia espera alcançar mais de US$ 12 bilhões nesse negócio em 2028. Considerando a projeção de US$ 235 bilhões para o mercado até 2030, Murphy afirmou que a meta da Marvell representaria cerca de 13% de participação. “Nosso negócio em 2028 será de US$ 12 bilhões ou mais em personalizado. artigo.texto: A Plattsburgh man planned a data center in Chateaugay. Locals are pushing back The rumors started swirling a few months ago. Chateaugay, a small farming town in northern Franklin County, may soon get a data center. But little was known about the project, including who was behind it and what stage of development the data center was in. Chateaugay joins a growing list of towns across the country that developers are eyeing as demand for data processing sites grows amid the artificial intelligence boom. Last Monday evening, dozens of people showed up at the Chateaugay town board meeting looking for answers about the potential project. Turnout was so much higher than normal that the meeting was moved to a larger room. Paula King, who lives in Chateaugay, was among those who expressed some skepticism about the project. "I am all for local development, but I like to be sure that we’re mitigating any harm to the environment, to the people that live within the communities and that we maximize benefits from this," said King. Details of the proposed project The property where the potential data center would be built is a few miles south of downtown Chateaugay. The 19-acre property is the site of a former wood chip factory. In 2022, Joseph Church from Plattsburgh purchased the property for $500,000. Church is a veterinarian and a former partner at the Plattsburgh Animal Hospital, where he worked for more than two decades. According to his LinkedIn, Church is also the founder and CEO of New York GreenCloud, a company focused on "developing data center infrastructure powered by renewable energy.” A year after he bought the property, Church presented his data center proposal to the Chateaugay town board. According to his company's website, the data center could consume up to 15 megawatts of power, which is much smaller than the project currently under review in nearby Massena, which would be designed for 635 megawatts. Developer of the site in Chateaugay faces problems When it was first proposed, Chateaugay Town Supervisor Don Bilow said he was open to it. "When they presented the project, it looked like a nice project, but now we’re starting to get doubts about it," said Bilow after last week's meeting. Bilow said he hasn’t heard anything from Church in three years. Church also did not respond to multiple requests for comment for this article. Along with the site in Chateaugay, Church is also planning to build a data center at the Buena Vista biomass plant in Amador County, California. A local newspaper reporter from the Ledger Dispatch in northern California interviewed Church earlier this spring and asked about the project in Chateaugay. Despite it being listed as "in construction" on his company's website, Church admitted that the project has been stalled. "The problem with Chateaugay- it’s not abandoned due to any issues; it's that the site is not in the condition that Buena Vista was in," said Church. There was some work done on the site in Chateaugay a few years ago. Church hired an electrical company from Clinton County, but according to public court records, he never paid the company, so they sued. A judge ordered Church to pay back more than $38,000. In recent years, he has also been sued by two credit card companies over unpaid debt. In those two cases, Church was ordered to pay back a combined $54,000. Skepticism and fears arise over the proposed data center When he was interviewed earlier this spring, Church said he was still hopeful his business will take off, and he claimed that the community in Chateaugay was supportive of his project. "Chateaugay welcomes the restart of that place," said Church, later adding that "they would love to see it come back." But that’s not an accurate reflection of the local sentiment now that more people are aware of the project. According to some who were at Chateaugay’s town board meeting last week, most commenters were either skeptical of the data center or against it. "I fear that there’s too much unknown with what a data center is actually capable of," said Cecilia Merrill. Her top concern is about the environmental impact of a data center. Along with requiring a lot of power, data centers also need a lot of cooling capacity. The property Church owns is about 1,000 ft. from the Chateaugay River, where Merrill goes fishing about five times a week. "The brook trout in it are still thriving; they’re beautiful," said Merrill. "There’s wild fish in there, and there’s a color pink on some of them that I’ve never seen on any other spectrum of light.” She’s worried all that would be at risk if a data center was built near the river. Meanwhile, some others at the meeting said the area needs more industry. Griffon Wilde, who owns property in Ellenburg Center, said she is skeptical of the project, but she’s also sympathetic to the local economy. "There needs to be new industry coming here. There needs to be more opportunities for people to be something other than prison guards," said Wilde. "There’s got to be more coming in for this place to survive.” "It sounds like there's still time for Chateaugay to potentially stop something like this," added Wilde, "or at least make sure that it will be a positive and bring enough jobs to make it worth it." Drafting up a moratorium At its meeting last week, the Chateaugay town board heard about 30 minutes of public comment on the potential data center. In the end, the board agreed to work on a one-year moratorium that would ban any data centers from coming to town. There is currently a statewide moratorium in effect, but it only applies to projects larger than 50 megawatts, so it would not apply to the proposed project in Chateaugay. After a local moratorium expires, town supervisor Don Bilow said if a data center is officially proposed in the future, he’d treat it like any other development. "Any project, we always look at it and go from there. If it looks like it’s going to benefit the community, we definitely move forward

artigo.texto: NY hit pause on large data centers. A massive project in Massena may be exempt Over the past year, a proposed data center project has been the center of a tense community debate in Massena. New York Digital Investment Group (NYDIG) and its affiliate cryptocurrency operators, North Country Collocation Services (NCCS), want to build a 1.5 million-square-foot, 635-megawatt data center near the St. Lawrence River. That equals around 70% of the power produced at the huge Moses Saunders hydroelectric dam nearby. If approved, it would be one of the largest data centers in New York State. Close access to this hydropower has made Massena an ideal location for data center developers. This project is planned for the shuttered Alcoa East/Reynolds industrial site. The company's website says initial construction is slated for later this year. Earlier this year, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order temporarily restricting development of new hyperscale data centers exceeding 50 megawatts. These facilities used to power A.I. are controversial across the country. The moratorium gives state agencies more time to assess their impact. But the Massena project could be exempt from this statewide restriction. That’s because the moratorium isn’t a blanket ban on new data centers. It orders the DEC not to issue any new discretionary permits. But Massena officials say NCCS doesn’t require additional permits because it already applied for them back in 2020. Jason Pfotenhauer, director of St. Lawrence County's Planning Office, said that NCCS's exemption could be legitimate. "If they don’t need a state permit, then the moratorium wouldn’t be applicable," he said. "The applicant is saying, 'We don't need any official approval from the state because we're not going to meet any thresholds that would require us to get a state permit. So because of that, the moratorium doesn't apply to us.'" State officials haven't confirmed if NCCS is still subject to this moratorium. Massena opens the door Massena’s Town Board recently cleared a path for the data center by voting 3-2 against a local moratorium. Deputy supervisor Samuel Carbone and board members Adrian Taraska and Jared Hollander voted no. Hollander said the project is worth exploring. "Data centers, they are being built whether we have a say in it or not, not across the country alone but across the whole globe. So the opportunity that we have in front of us is control," he said. Supervisor Raymond Lancto and board member Kristy Baker voted in support of the data center restriction. Even if this project is exempt from the state moratorium, that does not mean it’s good to go. Hurdles remain, including those from the local government and the state. Massena’s Town Supervisor, Ray Lancto, said developers are just in the beginning phases. “There’s a review process," Lancto said. "It will have to go through the SEQRA process through the state and through DEC, and then it’ll have to gain all those approvals.” The DEC would evaluate the environmental, social, and economic impacts that data center construction and operation could have on the area. Data center controversy This data center has been controversial. Residents across the North Country are concerned it will drive up electricity bills, consume massive amounts of water, and cause noise and air pollution. NCCS says no local water will be used for cooling the data center because they're designing a fully sealed loop system. The St. Regis Mohawk Tribe issued a statement opposing all hyperscale data centers, saying they “pose known and unknown risks that could impact the health and well-being of our community.” "We met with Town of Massena representatives and sincerely hoped that the Town would not issue authorization for the continued growth of data centers in our area,” the Tribal Council said in a statement. Akwesasne has a long history of industry giants like Alcoa, General Motors, and Reynolds polluting the land and water around this data center site. Neddie Thompson has lived in Akwesasne her whole life. At a recent anti-data center protest in Massena, she said the town needs to take its time to learn more about this project so history isn’t repeated. "I grew up right on that river right next to that GM plant. We didn’t know nothing about what’s going on. We were little. And thyroids started first, then heart trouble, then our organs and our kidneys. We’ve got to get the facts on what this data center is, the noise pollution, the contamination of our water." Some people in Massena are supporting this data center because they hope it’ll provide jobs and boost an economy that’s struggled for decades. Mark Ryan was born and raised in Massena and was at a recent town board meeting. "When you look at this piece of paper and this information [on the developer's website], it talks about all the money they’re going to commit to invest in our community. If this is going to be good for our community. How could we turn it down? The community needs a lift," Ryan said. The company says the data center will provide 200 full-time jobs and an estimated 2,000 construction jobs. It's also pledging millions to support local schools, emergency services, roads, and other public services. Even if this data center project is exempt from a moratorium, Pfotenhauer from the county Planning Office said he doesn’t expect it to start anytime soon. "Projects don't happen overnight, right? Even if there were some requirements for the moratorium at the state level — this is not going to happen within a year. This project is not going to be built and developed in a year," Pfotenhauer said. During that time, he said there could be more regulation that comes out of the state moratorium. Massena's next town board meeting is Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, at 4:30 pm. It's not clear yet if the data center will be included in the day's discussions.

artigo.texto: FLORIDA – The race for Florida governor is drawing sharp contrasts on some of the state’s most pressing issues. Democratic candidate David Jolly and Republican Rep. Byron Donalds sat down separately this week to answer questions on artificial intelligence, hyperscale data centers and Amendment 3, a property tax relief measure heading to voters next month. Here is where each candidate stands: Recommended Videos AI Data Centers Jolly said he would issue a moratorium on hyperscale data centers on his first day in office, arguing the industry is rushing into a state with a favorable regulatory and campaign finance environment before the public health and environmental questions have been answered. “This is moving too quickly,” Jolly said. “Big tech and big data are rushing into a relatively unregulated or favorably regulated environment.” Jolly pointed to a data center community in Northern Virginia where, he said, four children had been treated for respiratory conditions, one had been hospitalized, and several had been treated for hearing conditions. He said nearly 75% of Florida voters oppose the facilities. “Florida’s voters are saying, don’t do this. And I’ve said, I’ll issue a moratorium on my very first day in office,” Jolly said. Donalds took a different approach, saying the decision belongs to local governments — not the state. “County commissioners issue building permits, not governors,” Donalds said. “Local communities do.” Donalds said state law, signed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, already puts siting decisions in the hands of local communities. At the state level, he said his administration would focus on two guarantees: utility bills would not increase because of data centers, and fresh water would be protected through existing water use permit requirements administered by water management districts. Donalds also noted a study commissioned by the state is due back June 1, 2027, and said he would release it publicly. “We are going to maintain that,” Donalds said of the existing permitting framework. “This is not a new phenomenon.” Artificial Intelligence Jolly called himself an AI optimist but said the technology’s integration — not its promise — is the critical issue. He cited concerns about job displacement, children’s privacy and the role of AI in classrooms, arguing teachers should use AI as a tool, not be replaced by it. “AI should not replace a teacher,” Jolly said. “But I think teachers could benefit from AI.” He also cited what he described as a corrupt campaign finance system quieting public concerns. “The public is saying, hey, pump the brakes, slow down. Even the inventors of AI at times are saying, slow it down,” Jolly said. On job displacement, Jolly drew a comparison to trade adjustment assistance programs created during NAFTA and CAFTA, saying Florida may need a similar retraining and assistance framework if the federal government fails to act. Donalds said AI is already embedded in everyday life and cannot be put back in a box. “If you got rid of the models at the top four or five companies, there’s probably 500 young computer scientists and engineers who are already making up their own model,” Donalds said. He said Florida should focus on protecting children, safeguarding name, image and likeness rights, and empowering parents. He also pointed to commercial space development on the Space Coast as an example of AI-powered economic opportunity, calling it a potential $1 trillion industry generating high-paying jobs across multiple fields. “The question is, how do we protect families? How do we protect communities and how do we protect children?” Donalds said. Amendment 3 Both candidates acknowledged the property tax burden on Florida residents, but they land on opposite sides of the measure. Jolly said he anticipates voting no on Amendment 3, aligning with sheriffs and law enforcement groups who have warned the measure would cut funding for public safety services. “That’s essentially what Amendment 3 is gonna do. It’s gonna defund law enforcement along with critical services that communities need,” Jolly said. He said the measure was rushed through without a sufficient funding backstop and noted that Gov. DeSantis, who initially proposed a version of the idea, is not actively campaigning for it. Jolly said he would instead pursue targeted relief — a homestead exemption of up to $250,000 for first-time homebuyers, income-based relief for seniors, and returning expanded exemption authority to local governments. “Let’s target first-time homebuying tax relief,” Jolly said, noting the average age of a first-time homebuyer in Florida has risen from 28 to roughly 40 or 41 years old. Donalds said he supports Amendment 3, arguing property taxes on Florida residents have effectively doubled over the past seven years. “It’s not our money. It belongs to the citizen. It belongs to the taxpayer,” Donalds said. He said the amendment’s language requires public safety to be funded first before any cuts take effect. For fiscally constrained counties, he proposed a dedicated funding formula so those governments would not need to lobby Tallahassee for help. He also argued larger counties had the option to roll back tax rates as property values rose over the past six years and chose not to. “Local governments have to live within their means, the same way the state government has to live within our means,” Donalds said.
