artigo.texto: SMM, October 7: Key points: During the National Day holiday, the solid-state battery sector showed a pattern of “hot policy, slow industry.” Seven ministries’ 15th Five-Year Plan set 2030 as the target for large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries; Sinocera’s sulphide production line was completed, Chuneng’s polymer GWh-level line went into operation, and a 100 GWh project was signed. Overseas, Samsung SDI/EcoPro cooperation and BMW real-vehicle validation moved forward. However, materials are seeing “rising volumes and falling prices,” and the transition from pilot production to mass production still requires 2–3 years, with cost reduction, yield, and client validation remaining the three major hurdles. Around the National Day holiday, the solid-state battery industry received a dual boost from “policy direction” and “industrial implementation.” Many enterprises arranged early holiday breaks, and actual industrial implementation remained slow. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other departments jointly issued the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New-Type Battery Industry, setting a 2030 timetable for the large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries for the first time in a national-level special plan. At the same time, China’s first polymer GWh-level production line went into operation, Sinocera Materials’ sulphide electrolyte production line was completed, and a project with over 100 GWh of capacity was signed. The industry is accelerating its transition from an “intensive pilot phase” to a “mass-production validation phase.” However, SMM believes there remains a clear gap between policy enthusiasm and industrial reality—the trend of “rising volumes and falling prices” on the materials side has not yet reversed, and the window from pilot production to mass production still requires 2–3 years of validation. I. Policy side: First national-level special plan released, 2030 timetable officially set During this holiday, the biggest variable for the solid-state battery industry came from the policy side. On September 28, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other departments jointly issued the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New-Type Battery Industry. This is China’s first national-level special plan in the battery sector, explicitly proposing that by 2030 all-solid-state batteries will achieve initial large-scale application, and top-tier players’ product defect rates will reach the PPB (1 part per billion) level. Notably, the plan places special emphasis on key technology directions such as interface contact, high ionic conductivity, long cycle life, and engineered pressure system design, while also proposing to promote the integrated application of high-voltage cathode materials and new-type lithium metal-based anode materials. This indicates that policy orientation has shifted from “encouraging R&D” to “engineering implementation,” targeting the core bottlenecks in the industrialisation of all-solid-state batteries. II. Materials side: Sulphide electrolytes see “rising volumes and falling prices,” capacity construction enters the “mt era” The core highlight on the materials side during this holiday was the acceleration of capacity construction and the continued downward shift of the price center. Sinocera Materials’ sulphide electrolyte production line completed. On October 5, Sinocera Materials disclosed that its automated sulphide solid-state electrolyte production line had been successfully completed, with initial mass-production capability established. The first line is planned to have an annual capacity of 30 mt and is expected to be completed and put into operation within 2026; the second line is planned to have an annual capacity of 100 mt and will be advanced in an orderly manner based on the industrialisation pace of downstream battery enterprises. It is worth noting that Sinocera Materials is simultaneously laying out both oxide and sulphide technology routes, but its current strategic center is focused on the sulphide route, and its product performance has been highly recognised by downstream battery enterprises. SMM believes that sulphide electrolytes are in the typical early-industry stage of "rising volume and falling prices"—production is increasing, but capacity utilization rates remain low, and price pressure has been the dominant theme since Q3. The commissioning of 100 mt-class production lines means the industry is crossing from the "kg-class" to the "mt-class" threshold, but there is still some distance from truly meaningful large-scale supply. Battery cell side: Polymer route achieves GWh-class breakthrough, "three dominant players" landscape begins to emerge In battery cell manufacturing, the most noteworthy event this holiday is the GWh-class mass production breakthrough on the polymer route. China's first polymer solid-state battery GWh-class production line has been commissioned. On 29 September, Chunlv New Energy's Hukou 1 GWh solid-state battery intelligent manufacturing base officially entered production, marking China's first solid-state battery mass production line using the polymer process route. The project is planned to be built in two phases, with total capacity reaching 5 GWh once fully ramped up, covering diverse scenarios including grid-side ESS, industrial and commercial ESS, passenger NEVs, drones, robots, and marine power. artigo.texto: Colleton County settles lawsuit, creating exclusion zone for data centers in ACE Basin WALTERBORO, SC (WCIV) — Colleton County has reached a settlement with the Southern Environmental Law Center that will prohibit data center development across much of the ACE Basin, ending a legal challenge over a county ordinance that opened rural areas to large-scale data center projects. The agreement resolves a lawsuit filed in January by Colleton County residents Miles Crosby and Jennifer Singleton, who challenged county zoning changes that allowed data centers in rural portions of the county through a special-exception process. Under the settlement, Colleton County will establish a "Data Center Exclusion Area" as part of its Comprehensive Plan, identifying areas deemed unsuitable for data center development. "This historic settlement agreement sets the framework for legislative action that will ensure responsible conservation of natural resources while securing the economic future for citizens of Colleton County," Colleton County Council Chairman Scott Biering said in a statement. The agreement follows months of intense public debate surrounding a proposed Eagle Rock Partners data center campus south of Walterboro. The project, first unveiled in late 2025, called for an approximately 859-acre, 1,000-megawatt development near the headwaters of the Ashepoo River in the ACE Basin, prompting strong opposition from residents concerned about impacts to the environment, water resources and the region's rural character. READ MORE | Colleton County residents raise concerns over proposed data center, power plant projects According to the Southern Environmental Law Center, the exclusion area will cover most of the ACE Basin within Colleton County, including ecologically sensitive lands along the Ashepoo, Combahee and Edisto rivers. The exclusion area also includes the roughly 850-acre tract where the original Eagle Rock proposal was planned. "The original data center complex that was proposed would have surrounded my property on three sides and completely changed the area," Miles Crosby said in a statement released by SELC. "I'm thankful we could reach an outcome that not only prevents data centers from surrounding my home but also protects the majority of the ACE Basin in Colleton County from data center development." Jennifer Singleton, another plaintiff in the case, called the settlement a compromise that protects one of South Carolina's most significant natural resources. "It's been a long and winding road to get here, but I'm thrilled we were able to reach a compromise that establishes a 'Data Center Exclusion Area' in Colleton County," Singleton said. "The ACE Basin is a treasure we must all work together to care for." County Administrator Thomas Higgs said the settlement demonstrates that economic development and environmental protection can coexist as South Carolina continues to attract new investment. "We understand South Carolina currently faces many economic development issues. Data centers are a current national security topic and developers have their eyes on South Carolina," Higgs said. "In every economic development scenario, the challenge is to protect South Carolina itself, and moreover, its natural resources." The ACE Basin encompasses roughly 1.6 million acres across the Ashepoo, Combahee and Edisto river systems and has long been recognized as one of the nation's most significant conservation landscapes. More than 300,000 acres have been permanently protected since the formation of the ACE Basin Task Force in 1989, according to SELC. SELC South Carolina Director Chris DeScherer called the settlement "a significant victory for the ACE Basin" and said the organization looks forward to working with county leaders to ensure future data center projects are developed responsibly. County officials said they hope the agreement can serve as a model for other South Carolina communities seeking to balance economic growth with conservation.

artigo.texto: A australiana AirTrunk pretende elevar para até US$ 30 bilhões seu investimento total em data centers no Japão durante os próximos cinco anos, segundo declaração de seu fundador e CEO, Robin Khuda, ao Nikkei Asia. O montante representa cerca de três vezes o investimento da operadora no país. Apoiada pela Blackstone, a empresa busca ampliar sua capacidade para atender ao aumento da demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial na Ásia. Khuda afirmou que os clientes aceitam pagar um valor adicional para instalar capacidade de processamento no mercado japonês. O executivo também avalia que a Ásia pode ser a principal beneficiária de uma eventual desaceleração dos Estados Unidos, embora os dados fornecidos não detalhem os projetos, o cronograma dos aportes nem as fontes de financiamento. Principais fatos e números - A AirTrunk planeja investir até US$ 30 bilhões no Japão em cinco anos. - O valor projetado triplicaria o investimento total da empresa no país. - A expansão busca atender à demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial na Ásia. - Robin Khuda disse que clientes aceitam pagar mais para instalar capacidade no Japão. - A operadora australiana de data centers é apoiada pela Blackstone. Por que isso importa para empresários e investidores O plano indica uma expansão relevante da infraestrutura digital japonesa e pode abrir oportunidades para fornecedores de energia, equipamentos, refrigeração, construção e serviços de conectividade. Para empresas que utilizam inteligência artificial, a oferta adicional de capacidade local pode ampliar alternativas de implantação no Japão, embora não haja informação sobre preços futuros ou datas de entrada em operação. Investidores devem considerar os riscos de execução de um programa de até US$ 30 bilhões, incluindo a disponibilidade de energia e a concretização da demanda. A fonte não informa localidades, projetos específicos, estrutura financeira ou compromissos já contratados.

artigo.texto: ATHENS — The town of Athens wants a little more time to think about the industries it wants to welcome within its borders. The town board moved Monday to allow Supervisor Michael Pirrone, if he deems necessary, to extend moratoriums on cannabis farming, data centers and battery-energy storage into next year. "It is always a proper approach to take things at the proper pace to evaluate all the current information, research available," Pirrone said Tuesday. "This way it will stimulate input from the people. That helps us make better decisions." He added the decision to review the bans together helps him keep a "handle" on their deadlines. The longest-standing moratorium, which covers the development of battery facilities, may extend into its third year as the town seeks to pass a local law regulating their development. Ahead of an approval vote, the town will hold a public hearing on the issue at the Rivertown Senior Center at 6 p.m. Oct. 19. Battery-energy storage facilities The soonest priority of the three industry for Athens is establishing guidelines for battery-energy storage facilities within the town. The current draft of local law No. 5 of 2026 seeks to "regulate the siting, design, installation, operation and decommissioning of battery energy storage systems." Athens is looking to hold facilities to storing a limit of 400 kilo-watt hours, to create a specific zoning district and to establish emergency response plans among other requirements. If Pirrone sees it valuable, the moratorium, set to expire Dec. 1, could be extended until June 1, 2027. "(The moratorium) was the result of people coming to us at meetings and telling us about the dangers and issues with battery storage facilities," he said, especially concerning potential fires. New York suffered from four battery-energy storage facility fires in 2023. The federal Environmental Protection Agency advises battery fires to be isolated and managed rather than put out. The EPA reports the rate of fires dropped 98% to 0.03 fires per installed gigawatt in 2024 from 1.5 fires per gigawatt in 2018, while gaining nearly 300 gigawatts of storage in the same timeframe. "These are all things the town has been concerned about," Pirrone said. The moratorium on such facilities was initially established March 4, 2024, amid public outcry that eventually halted the development of a storage facility in the town of Catskill. Eolian Energy withdrew its application for a battery-energy storage system Nov. 6, 2024, citing the negative reception from residents of Catskill. "Unfortunately, the actions taken by the planning board showed us that the community was not yet ready for this step into a cleaner and more secure energy future," according to the company's letter of withdrawal. Pirrone said Tuesday he doesn't want to see the same fiasco in Athens. He said the board has spent the last two-plus years gathering information to develop a law before potential applications are considered. "We feel that we have a more-than-adequate law that we hope will pass," he said. Cannabis farming The town's temporary ban on commercial cannabis cultivation is its newest. Pirrone, in June, described the moratorium as preemptive because of a lack of zoning regulations in the town. The municipality has received some inquiries from potential growers to create farms ahead of its decision to pause development June 15. "The town is a farming community and is seeing how cannabis farming fits under the general terms of farming in the town, and adopting the proper regulations for it," Pirrone said in June. On Tuesday, he said time is still needed to gather the facts around zoning regulations and other issues. The current moratorium, set to expire Dec. 15, could be extended by Pirrone to June 15, 2027. "We're looking to make sure we have the right information, and also the state has the right procedures for someone to operate," he said. Data centers There's not much need for the town to extend its moratorium on data centers, but Athens may do it anyway, Pirrone said. "We just want to make sure we keep it in front of our eyes," he said. Gov. Kathy Hochul established a one-year statewide moratorium on the development of new hyperscale data centers July 14. In the meantime, the state is working to make money available for communities and repeal sales-tax exemptions for data centers. Athens established its one-year moratorium Dec. 1, 2025, seven months before Hochul's moratorium. An extension by Pirrone would last until May 30, 2027. He said Tuesday a pause independent from the state's may continue to be necessary. "It's very important for me as the supervisor to do all I can to ensure the safety and the welfare of all residents within the town of Athens," Pirrone said.

artigo.texto: [ESPAÑOL ABAJO | PORTUGUÊS ABAIXO] Colombia’s new government will initiate proceedings to lift a 50% cap on carbon credit retirements against CO2 tax liabilities – handing a win to voluntary carbon market (VCM) sellers, and boosting the significance of compliance measures in response to trade pressures from the EU. Minister of Environment and Sustainable Development Fabio Arjona announced in Medellin that the new government of right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella would propose the change to Congress. Latin American and Caribbean countries enjoy relatively low trade exposure to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which prices in the embedded carbon of goods entering the bloc. Still, Colombia ranks just behind Brazil as the most EU CBAM-exposed Latin American or Caribbean countries. Colombia’s COP 29,070.49 ($8.76) per tonne CO2 tax rate may alleviate some of the border carbon burden by creating an EU-recognised domestic carbon price that’s deductible from CBAM fees. In its current form, the European Commission’s draft implementing act would make the price paid for carbon credits retired under the tax eligible for deductions, too – enhancing the role of the VCM to address both domestic and international carbon pricing compliance. Arjona simultaneously announced the revocation of Ministerial Decree 0973 on the VCM, which established restrictions in line with former President Gustavo Petro’s criticisms of the market and was published in early August. EMISSIONS TRADING SYSTEMS Both Colombia and Brazil are working to implement emissions trading systems – called the ‘PNCTE’ in Colombia, and the ‘SBCE’ in Brazil. These schemes could also create EU-recognised carbon prices. In Brazil, carbon project co-developer Earthshot Labs Brazil has seen some foreign investors take a cautious approach due to uncertainty in the SBCE’s final design, Carbon Pulse reported last week. That does not mean that investment in the Brazilian VCM has halted, according to the co-developer’s director Rita Croce – rather, some investors are holding out for projects that could potentially generate Article 6 Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) in the future. Brazil’s increasingly crowded carbon asset ecosystem would include SBCE allowances, called CBEs; SBCE-eligible voluntary carbon credits, called CRVEs; voluntary credits bearing a Letter of Authorisation; and regular voluntary units. Purchasing either CBEs or CRVEs for use in the SBCE could potentially fall under the European Commission’s draft vision for a ‘carbon price effectively paid’ in a third country, for CBAM purposes. Meanwhile, Colombia’s Ministerial Decree 0969 from the now-departed Petro administration stated that up to 3.3% of PNCTE compliance units could be sourced from the VCM – a far lower percentage than what was initially pitched in a Sep. 2024 consultation document. The fate of the PNCTE under De La Espriella is unclear. J-REDD+ QUESTIONS Meanwhile, a Brazilian state and Argentine province grappled with thorny implementation questions for jurisdictional REDD+ (J-REDD+). A proposed road in the Amazon could result in up to 133,800 hectares of additional deforestation over 20 years – putting Brazilian state Acre’s J-REDD+ goals at risk, according to a report published by NGOs Amazon Conservation and SOS Amazonia. Acre’s J-REDD+ programme is registered under the ART standard’s TREES protocol. Researchers noted that the modelling is not meant to predict actual future losses, but that plans for new road developments placed Acre at “a critical juncture”. In Argentina, senators for the province of Misiones – itself promoting a large-scale, Verra-registered J-REDD+ programme – are mounting partial opposition to a national bill they helped draft. Senator Sonia Rojas Decut has taken issue with the bill’s definition of ‘project owner’ (Spanish: titular del proyecto). The definition would effectively require written consent from thousands of native forest owners to implement programmes at the provincial level, she argued. The bill would therefore “make it impossible for Argentine provinces to implement jurisdictional programmes”, she wrote. Argentine media has reported that while the bill disappeared from the agenda for last week’s Senate session, members of ruling party La Libertad Avanza have indicated that they will participate in ongoing negotiations with Misiones in hopes of bringing the bill to a future session. artigo.texto: KALAMAZOO, MI (WKZO AM/FM) – It has been one of the least controversial issues the Kalamazoo city commission has had to deal with this year, but one of the most emotional. Opinions have been nearly unanimous that the city needs to brace itself, and thoroughly prepare for the day someone wants to build a data center, or any other potentially worrisome high-tech facility in town. They have scheduled a final public hearing and a vote this evening. Kalamazoo city commissioners are set to finalize a one year moratorium, to buy time to redraft zoning codes to make sure if a data center or large battery energy storage system is proposed, that it won’t become a problem for its neighbors or the community. Assistant City Planner Bobby Durkee says that one year clock begins with tonight’s approval. “The goal of the moratorium is to develop those zoning standards and appropriate land uses, and to study for a transparent public process. For staff in the community to research the topic, understand the topic and draft regulations because you cannot outright ban a use.” He says as recommended by the planning commission, staff will set up a working group to assist in the research. “You know I look at things like public utilities, private utilities, residents, neighborhoods, the industry itself.” Several commissioners implored him not to make it top-heavy with industry and utility experts and to make sure it represents community and environmental interests too. Commissioner Chris Praedel says it’s “so critically important that there are people sitting in those seats that are just everyday people, you know, that care a lot about this issue.” While communities have some flexibility in how it sets up its own zoning regulations, it’s still a process that is guided by state laws and technical requirements and must be detailed and specific if a community wants to avoid legal challenges, or leave gaps or loopholes. Data centers have become a major state and national issue this election year with national polls showing 65 to 70% of the public opposed to having a data center in their community and only 20% supporting. The numbers are even higher for Democratic and younger voters.

artigo.texto: COLDWATER, MI (WTVB) – Coldwater city officials are in the process of trying to make the community as unattractive as possible to potential developers of data centers. This comes after a joint session on August 19 involving Coldwater government boards. They heard a presentation that evening on data centers from Jean Hardy of Michigan State University whose research centers on the role of technology in rural economic and community development. City Planner Robert Hawley told the Coldwater Planning Commission on Monday night they and their consultants from McKenna and Associates are currently working on zoning ordinance amendments that would define data centers. Mayor Tom Kramer emphasized there was no desire among City Council members to bring a data center to Coldwater. But Kramer added that by law, they have to offer something to potential developers. A draft could be presented to the Planning Commission on November 16 with a public hearing possibly taking place in December. Hardy said in August that the backlash across the state from communities opposing data centers has now caused those companies to rethink the prospects of building new facilities in the state. In other business, the Planning Commission approved a new Master Plan and sent it on to the City Council for final approval. It was compiled after a year of community surveys, steering committee meetings, and focus groups. The Master Plan for Coldwater has not been updated since 2017. It outlines goals and infrastructure strategies to guide the future growth of Coldwater.

artigo.texto: KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): The deferment of the carbon tax implementation is aligned with the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry’s efforts to establish a complete regulatory and policy framework before enforcing emission caps. Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup said the government decided to delay the tax, originally planned for this year, following global geopolitical developments that led to volatile energy prices, providing affected industries with a necessary buffer. Speaking during a Concorde Club dialogue session at Wisma Bernama on Monday, he said the postponement is also timely as the ministry works towards solidifying the required legal structure, including the National Carbon Market Policy and the upcoming Climate Change Act. “[The postponement] is also right because we need to have the proper framework and all that in place first. That’s why we’ve been successful in launching the National Carbon Market Policy and I hope that we can table the Climate Change Act soon. “Once that is up, then we have the framework and the policies all clearly in place, including the regulation, enforcement, the regulatory powers to give us to set the emission ceiling, and then we can know anything above the ceiling, then the carbon tax will come into place as a penalty to the polluters. “So, we’re not looking at this year for the carbon tax,” he said. Meanwhile, on Clean Air Regulations exemption, Arthur said exemptions for industrial plants under the regulation would only be extended to factory operators who demonstrate proactive measures toward technology adoption. He said while no new blanket extensions are being issued, factory operators whose exemptions expire by January next year must show clear steps toward compliance, with 2030 set as the final deadline for total compliance across all industries. “We had the Clean Air Regulations, which came into force in 2014, where plants, factories are not allowed to pollute above the 600 milligram per cubic metre...that was the regulation set...however, they have been enjoying exemptions up to this year. “So when I came in as the minister, I decided that I will not be issuing any more exemptions because the technology is available, the technology is accessible and if we are to meet our target of net zero emissions by 2050, we need to have all this in place and we definitely need the cooperation from the industries as well,” he said. He added that while operators need adequate time for feasibility studies and modifications, strict progress is required to qualify for temporary extensions. The session, titled “Building A Resilient Malaysia: Environment, Climate And Our Future”, was moderated by Bernama chairman Datuk Seri Wong Chun Wai. Also present was Bernama chief executive officer Datin Paduka Nur-ul Afida Kamaludin, as well as members of the local and foreign media based in Malaysia. Uploaded by Tham Yek Lee

artigo.texto: UAE-based real assets investor and developer ROX Capital Group has launched the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform, targeting utility-scale and commercial energy storage projects in the UAE and Oman while exploring opportunities for regional assembly and manufacturing. The platform will evaluate a range of storage technologies, including vanadium redox flow, lithium iron phosphate and sodium-ion batteries, as well as long-duration solutions such as CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage. ROX plans to establish partnerships with selected technology providers based on their track record in deploying large-scale storage projects, long-duration storage expertise where applicable, financial and operational capacity, and ownership or control of core technology intellectual property. The company said it will prioritise providers with bankable systems, established manufacturing capabilities and the ability to offer long-term technical support, performance guarantees and warranties. The platform and its partners will pursue upcoming energy storage tenders and assess local assembly or manufacturing opportunities where commercially viable. “The Gulf is building some of the world’s largest solar projects. The next challenge is ensuring that clean power remains available after sunset and during periods of peak demand,” said Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group. “No single technology will meet every requirement. We are building a platform that matches the right technology to the needs of each project and, where viable, supports the development of local manufacturing capability.” “Lithium-ion batteries have transformed energy storage and will remain an important part of the solution,” Antony added. “However, the Gulf’s climate, load profile and energy-security priorities create a need for a broader portfolio of technologies. High summer temperatures can increase cooling requirements, while solar-heavy systems require storage over longer periods after dark. We see an important role for technologies including vanadium flow batteries, CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage and thermal storage alongside lithium-ion solutions.” -TradeArabia News Service

artigo.texto: Chinese New Energy Vehicle Startups Are Collectively Venturing Into the Deep Waters of the Battery Sector The crazy September saw a boom of automakers' in-house R&D on batteries. On September 4, Xiaomi released its Longjia Battery and announced partnerships with CALB and Sunwoda Power; on September 7, Li Auto announced that its in-house developed batteries will be gradually installed on all its vehicle models; on September 16, Leapmotor claimed that it has achieved 100% in-house R&D of battery cells; the next day, He Xiaopeng, Chairman of XPeng, stated at the G9L launch event: "Starting from this year, XPeng will develop all its batteries on its own." * Source: Xiaomi The motivation behind in-house R&D is that automakers no longer want to be mere battery buyers. Most of their previous battery budgets went to CATL, the king of batteries. Spending money is not the top concern — the fact that the right to define battery solutions and the initiative of the supply chain are in the hands of others keeps some automakers up at night. As a result, some call this a "de-CATL" trend, while others argue that "in-house R&D" is just a new guise. Judging from various incidents in the battery industry in the past, in-house R&D is far from being that simple. 01 "The auto industry camp stages a collective 'rebellion'" The direct reason for automakers to extend their reach to the battery industry chain is that they do not want to "pour too much money" into battery suppliers. In 2022, Zeng Qinghong, then Chairman of GAC Group, publicly stated that battery costs accounted for 40% to 60% of the total vehicle cost, and uttered the famous line: "Aren't we just working for CATL?" Objectively speaking, CATL's profit performance does make automakers extremely sensitive to the distribution of benefits across the industrial chain. Financial reports show that in the first half of this year, CATL's net profit reached 47.031 billion yuan, up 45.31% year on year, with a net profit margin of about 16%. In contrast, the total net profit of 15 mainstream automakers listed on the A-share and Hong Kong stock markets was only 21.048 billion yuan, and a large number of automakers have a net profit margin of less than 5%. * Source: Xueqiu Thus, conflicts emerge. Automakers have to bear the pressure of vehicle price competition and sales, while a large part of battery procurement costs is determined by the supply chain. Battery prices can rise along with upstream raw material costs, but automakers dare not raise vehicle prices arbitrarily, otherwise it will arouse consumers' resentment and do more harm than good. Tiny fluctuations in battery procurement prices can directly determine whether an automaker makes a profit or loss, which in the eyes of automakers is an unbearable inversion of power. Not only that, at this stage, if automakers want to truly develop their own differentiated products, they have to delve deep into battery development inevitably. In the past, battery procurement was largely similar to "off-the-shelf selection". Suppliers provided mature products, and automakers selected products according to requirements for cruising range, interior space and cost, then completed vehicle adaptation. Even if the two sides carried out joint development, the openness of material formulas, manufacturing parameters and production data still depended on the specific cooperative relationship. * Source: Internet However, with the development of 800V high-voltage platforms, ultra-fast charging and cell-to-chassis (CTC) integration technologies, such boundary is increasingly difficult to maintain. The "three core electric systems" today are equivalent to engines and gearboxes in the era of fuel vehicles, belonging to core technologies that directly affect the final user experience of vehicles: The structure of the battery pack affects cabin space, total vehicle weight and body rigidity; thermal management affects continuous fast charging capability; the battery management system affects cruising range estimation, power output and service life. Batteries are deeply coupled with the vehicle architecture. If automakers want to define products in depth, they have to rely on battery enterprises, which is unacceptable for them. Therefore, among the latest batch of in-house R&D cases, the change in the relationship between automakers and suppliers is the most obvious. The Longjia Battery released by Xiaomi on September 4 is led by Xiaomi in battery pack design and development, and Xiaomi participates in in-depth R&D of battery cells with its partners. CALB and Sunwoda Power provide battery cell R&D and manufacturing capabilities, while Xiaomi participates in product definition and vehicle adaptation. He Xiaopeng commented on in-house R&D like this: "It's not just about battery cells. Investing in battery cell companies still leaves the core technology in others' hands. We have also invested in three battery cell enterprises, but starting from this year, we will develop all batteries on our own." * Source: Internet According to public information, the three companies are most likely CALB, Sunwoda and SVOLT. XPeng mainly carries out in-house R&D and manufacturing of battery pack systems, while battery cells are led by its partners, whose purpose is to increase supply sources to grasp more initiative. It can be seen that this collective "rebellion" is essentially a move by vehicle enterprises to change their right to speak in the industrial chain. As for whether they can become real definers, it depends on how much capability they master, rather than how loud slogans they shout. 02 "After technology popularization, in-house R&D becomes a bargaining chip" The reason why automakers can enter the battery field today is related to the gradual maturity of mainstream technical routes and the increasing number of battery supplier options. At present, both lithium iron phosphate and ternary lithium batteries have formed mature industrialization route

artigo.texto: By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Oct. 5: Headway Earth and Rezonance, led by international carbon-market expert Dr. Divaldo Rezende, have launched the Carbon Market Development Mission Nepal to help develop the country’s emerging carbon-market and climate-finance ecosystem. The initiative aims to build Nepal’s capacity to develop climate projects, strengthen carbon-market infrastructure and connect Nepali projects with international climate finance, investors and carbon buyers. Nepal has significant potential in areas including forests, agriculture, renewable energy, waste management, biochar and other climate solutions. The mission seeks to turn this potential into bankable climate projects, investment, employment and sustainable development opportunities for Nepali communities and businesses, said Pratik Karki, Founder and Managing Director of Headway Earth. The mission will initially focus on three areas—capacity development, project development, and climate finance and market access. Under capacity development, the initiative will seek to strengthen knowledge, skills and institutional capacity among government agencies, financial institutions, businesses, communities and other stakeholders on carbon markets, climate finance and international climate policy, Karki added. Similarly, it will identify, design and develop high-quality climate and carbon projects across the country, with an emphasis on projects capable of attracting investment and delivering measurable environmental, social and economic benefits. The mission will also seek to connect Nepali projects with international investors, climate funds, financial institutions, development partners and carbon buyers, creating pathways for Nepali climate projects to access global markets. A key objective of the initiative is to help establish the institutional and financial infrastructure needed for a functioning national carbon ecosystem. Highlighting the opportunities in Nepal, Dr. Rezende said Nepal has an opportunity to strengthen international confidence and position itself as an attractive destination for climate investment. “The world wants to come to Nepal. Nepal is committing to zero corruption, and this can create a new level of confidence among international investors and climate partners,” he said. Dr. Rezende brings extensive international experience in carbon markets, climate finance and sustainable development. He will work alongside Headway Earth to support Nepal’s integration into global climate-finance and carbon-market opportunities. As part of its long-term vision, Headway Earth and Rezonance plan to work towards developing a Carbon Fund and Carbon Bank for Nepal to mobilise domestic and international capital for credible climate projects, said Prakash Gyawali, Chief Executive Officer of Headway Earth. The initiative also aims to support the development and integration of a national carbon registry and carbon marketplace to improve transparency, traceability and market access for Nepali carbon and climate assets. Technology and transparent measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) of climate impacts will form an important foundation of the proposed ecosystem. According to CEO Gyawali, the initiative is not limited to generating carbon credits but aims to establish the wider ecosystem required to support the carbon market, including projects, technology, finance, capacity, a registry, a marketplace and access to international markets.

artigo.texto: As if Emporia’s data center debate needed any more controversy. With the general election essentially a month away, Emporians for Progress spokesman Casey Woods says the ordinance language behind the petitions hoping to ban data centers and battery energy storage systems don’t reference city Planning and Zoning regulations currently on the books. The petitions reference Article 15, but Planning and Zoning code uses Sections instead of Articles and only goes up to Section 12. Emporia Neighbors United founder Jay Vehige sees things differently, although he admits there was a “drafting error” before the petition was turned in. The original petition and ordinance were submitted July 14, according to City Manager Trey Cocking. It was certified by the Lyon County Clerk’s Office on July 21 and was passed by the Emporia City Commission on August 5. Cocking says Vehige tried to submit revised petitions August 7, but he tells KVOE News cities have no ability to alter what was originally submitted — meaning residents have to vote on the original package due to KSA 12-3013. This is the second clerical or drafting error in this petition process for Emporia Neighbors United. The original petitions submitted were invalidated because petition circulators didn’t verify they witnessed petitions being signed. Vehige has told KVOE News that issue was due to a paperwork error in attaching circulator forms to signature petition forms. Woods says Emporians for Progress sees this as one reason to oppose the ballot questions. Vehige counters Woods’ assertions, saying his guidance indicates the Article 15 reference would not invalidate both petitions in their entirety. Vehige also says he has spoken with City Attorney Christina Montgomery, who was out of the office last week and is currently unavailable for an interview. Cocking sent a statement to KVOE News. saying the Article 15 reference will be one issue to be addressed by the court for effect and “enforceability.” He also says the city is not speculating how this will be addressed in court with that process a distinct possibility. Woods sees potential lawsuits throughout the 10-year halt if the questions are approved. The city has asked for rulings on whether the petitions are legislative or administrative in nature. Administrative rulings would likely invalidate the petitions — and, if the petitions are approved but Kansas Senior Judge Glenn Braun rules the petitions are administrative after the Nov. 3 general election, the vote results would be invalidated as well. Vehige believes Judge Braun will side with Emporia Neighbors United. There is no date for when Judge Braun will rule on the nature of the 2 ballot questions. This continues a busy time for news when it comes to data centers locally. A lawsuit filed by Emporia City Commissioner Erren Harter against Recall Committee members Haley Bradford, Kathleen Lamb and Vehige — also including Lyon County Legal Counsel Molly Priest and County Clerk Amie Jones as defendants — ended Thursday with an “agreed upon order” that essentially says this version of a recall petition cannot move forward under any circumstances. Priest and the case paperwork say this does not stop future petitions seeking Harter’s recall cannot move forward. A grand jury determining whether Harter conducted misconduct in office will be empaneled Monday. Meanwhile, Amanda Mendoza, Kenneth Bruner, Ann Bruner and the separate Bruner trusts have filed a lawsuit against the city of Emporia, alleging the zoning part of the Digital Infrastructure overlay was not properly handled. The lawsuit, LY-2026-CV-124, says the Emporia Planning Commission did not have either the jurisdiction or the authorization to review applications for zoning classifications that did not exist when applications were filed — meaning, according to the lawsuit, the city’s decision to approve the overlay was unlawful and the subsequent rezoning of 11 tracts of land was unauthorized and without proper jurisdiction. On top of that, Vehige says Emporia Neighbors United will push to bring 2 more petitions to the ballot by early next year. One would change the form of city government from its current at-large City Commission structure to a 4-ward City Council system with one at-large position. The other would change the method of filling unexpired City Commission or City Council positions from appointment to public vote. In separate news related to the Emporia data center project, the Flint Hills Digital Campus website is no longer public-facing. The website went public in early June as the data center project was announced. Project spokesman Garrett Nordstrom says flinthillsdigitalcampus.com was meant to be an informational site before rezoning and was meant to “dispel misconceptions.” Nordstrom says the website still exists but is internal now and is being shared with potential end users. Nordstrom says no end user has been selected for the proposed data center in west Emporia. He also says it would be unusual for a public website to document a private development project. The data center ballot questions will be part of KVOE’s political interviews later this month ahead of the general election Nov. 3. Appearing at 10:06 am Oct. 20 will be Vehige and Edgar Esparza from Emporia Neighbors United, as well as Woods representing Emporians for Progress. Our remaining interview slate is as follows: *Tuesday: Candidate Profile with Kansas House 13th District challenger Democrat Mark Remmert. Incumbent Republican Duane Droge did not confirm interest in a forum-style interview *Thursday: Candidate Forum with Kansas House 60th District challenger Democrat Maddison Glover and incumbent Republican Mark Schreiber *Oct 13: Candidate Forum with Kansas House 76th District nominees Democrat David Claridge and Republican Russel Stukey Click here for the KVOE Voter Information Guide courtesy Community National Bank & Trust.

artigo.texto: Strategic partnership targets commercialization of sulfide-based solid-state batteries Companies to jointly develop solid electrolytes and cathode materials for all-solid-state batteries Ecopro BM announced Tuesday that it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Samsung SDI to cooperate on developing materials for all-solid-state batteries, with the goal of commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries by 2027. The two companies plan to deepen cooperation across the entire development process — from early-stage research through quality evaluation and the establishment of mass production systems — to raise both technological maturity and business competitiveness. They also intend to expand the scope of collaboration to cover a broad range of key materials, including cathode materials for all-solid-state batteries, cathode electrolytes and separator electrolytes. Under the agreement, Samsung SDI will advance cell development and refine its mass production technology for all-solid-state batteries, while Ecopro BM will take charge of developing the key materials. All-solid-state batteries are widely regarded as a next-generation technology capable of improving safety and performance at the same time. Because they offer longer use per charge and reduce the risk of fire, they are considered a core technology for future industries such as electric vehicles and humanoid robots. Ecopro BM has developed proprietary process technology in sulfide-based solid electrolytes — a critical material for all-solid-state batteries — and operates a pilot plant with an annual production capacity of 40 tons. The company is strengthening its technological edge through powder-control and quality-management capabilities, which are central to solid electrolyte development. It is also developing cathode materials suited to solid electrolytes, drawing on its high-nickel cathode technology. In recognition of these research and development achievements, Ecopro BM was selected in August for the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's "Super-Eul Project." The program is a government-backed research and development support initiative aimed at nurturing key materials, parts and equipment companies capable of leading global supply chains by securing world-class, first-of-their-kind technologies. Companies selected for the program submit their own growth strategies and technology development plans to the government, which then evaluates them through a review of the proposal, technical verification and a comprehensive assessment. Ecopro BM passed the government's evaluation with its sulfide-based solid electrolyte project. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy plans to provide selected companies with large-scale research and development support of 20 billion won ($14.7 million) per project over seven or more years. The ministry released a "Battery Industry Technology Roadmap" last month, designating all-solid-state batteries as a core strategic technology for the future battery industry. The government said it plans to support the early commercialization of next-generation batteries by strengthening joint research and development between cell and materials companies and deepening supply chain cooperation. Ecopro BM had earlier outlined a full value-chain roadmap for all-solid-state batteries at an investor relations event for retail investors in July. Gong Bo-hyeon, executive vice president for research and development at Ecopro BM, said at the time regarding solid electrolyte development: "We are currently reviewing trial production with leading customers, and we expect the earliest mass production timeline to be 2027. We have completed the design of the mass production line and are preparing to break ground immediately in line with customer demand." Meanwhile, Song Ho-jun, chief executive of Ecopro, was named incoming chief executive of Ecopro BM in a reshuffle of Ecopro Group's presidential-level executives last Wednesday. Under Song's leadership, Ecopro BM plans to strengthen its role as an intermediate holding company overseeing secondary battery materials. The company also intends to complete management systems at its overseas subsidiaries in Hungary and Canada, and to focus on building future growth engines through investment in the BNSI smelter in Indonesia. likehyo85@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: We sat down with Norfolk-based artist Rhashida Bess to talk about jewelry making and upcoming programs. Who is Rhashida Bess? Rhashida is the owner and operator of Alodeuri (pronounced al – oh – durr – ee) Artisan Jewelry, an African-inspired, cold form metal smithing and jewelry-making business. A skill she first learned in high school and advanced through self-teaching, jewelry making launched Rhashida into the world of entrepreneurship when she was looking for a way to turn her hobby into a way to provide for her family. Rhashida’s adornments (the term she uses for her handmade, sustainable, intention-based jewelry pieces) incorporate materials such as copper, brass, cowrie shells, semi-precious stones and crystals. How did she get started with NPL? Rhashida started working with NPL after attending a program. While talking with another library patron about her personal business, she was approached by a staff member who asked if she, with her wealth of experience, might be interested in teaching a program at the branch. What does Rhashida love about working with NPL? Rhashida loves teaching library patrons about the history of traditional jewelry and supporting them on their jewelry-making journey. Rhashida believes in teaching people both new skills and how to use those skills to achieve future financial stability. While Rhashida’s true love is copper-based jewelry, particularly chains, she dabbles in a variety of types and techniques, including beading and paper rolling. Some of the many programs Rhashida has done with NPL include Weaved Words Bangles, Maasai-inspired earrings and Crystal Point Necklaces. Upcoming Programs This fall, Rhashida will be holding The ARTisan Academy at Jordan-Newby Anchor Branch. Join her select Thursdays from 5:30 – 7:30 p.m. to invest 24 hours in yourself to change the rest of your life! This vocational pathway to creative entrepreneurship will teach you how to create adorned jewelry and birth a microbusiness. Fun Fact: Alodeuri is a blend of her children’s names. Fun Fact 2: Her favorite material to work with is copper.

artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have recently been drawing growing attention in the battery industry. While solid-state batteries, noted as the ‘dream battery’ for their high energy density, have attracted interest for future industries such as robots and high-performance electric vehicles (EVs), ‘price competitiveness’ is becoming crucial for applications such as energy storage systems (ESS) and mass-market EVs. Sodium is the English name for natrium, and SIBs are also called ‘salt batteries’. They charge and discharge by sodium ions, rather than lithium ions, moving between the cathode and anode. Because sodium, the key raw material, is abundant and sourced from a relatively wide range of regions, it can reduce raw-material price volatility and supply-chain risk. They are safe and maintain performance at low temperatures, raising expectations for broad application from ESS and EVs to automotive auxiliary power and uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) for data centers. This is why SIBs do not hide their ambitions to be an ‘all-weather battery’. Batteries, is ‘performance above all’ not everything? Humanoid robots and the like are emerging as new future sources of battery demand, but the largest markets remain EVs and ESS. Market researcher TrendForce estimates annual demand for solid-state batteries for humanoids at 74 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2035. By contrast, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA) and BloombergNEF, EV battery demand in the same year is projected at 4,0005,000 GWh, with new ESS installations reaching 972 GWh. The issue is that the importance of the ‘price factor’ is growing in both markets. In EVs, high-energy-density batteries are drawing attention for large, long-range, high-performance vehicles, while cost-competitive batteries are in focus for compact, urban models. ESS, where weight and volume constraints are relatively modest, is no different in the importance of price. The overall leveling-up of batteries is also heightening the importance of price. According to the IEA, the latest SIBs reach up to 175 watt-hours (Wh) per ㎏, falling short of the latest lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries (205Wh/㎏), but they have risen to the range of typical LFP levels (150~200Wh/㎏). China is moving to preempt the SIB market. After unveiling its SIB brand ‘Naxtra’ last year, CATL this year revealed a passenger car equipped with SIBs together with Changan Automobile. For ESS-use SIBs, it is targeting cumulative shipments of 1 GWh by year-end. According to the IEA, more than 95% of SIB production capacity in 2030, combining existing and planned facilities, is expected to be concentrated in China. Three Korean battery makers say, “This time is different from LFP”…gearing up to target SIB Korean battery makers are also accelerating development of batteries such as SIBs. This is because global SIB production capacity is still just over 1% of that of lithium-ion batteries, making it an early-stage market. A battery-industry source said, “There was a case in which domestic response to LFP was delayed in the past, so there is a mood not to fall behind in the early leadership race for the SIB market.” According to an announcement by SNE Research on the 2nd, global EV battery usage reached 844.2 GWh in JanuaryAugust this year, up 19.7% from the same period last year, but the combined share of the three Korean firms fell from 16.6% to 12.7%, down 3.9 percentage points. Meanwhile, the share of LFP batteries, where Chinese companies are strong, rose from 52.2% to 57.3%. SIBs are therefore also a future strategy to gain a competitive edge in the mass-market battery segment centered on China. LG Energy Solution is testing 12V (volt) and 24V packs for automotive auxiliary power on customer vehicles. It has completed technology validation in the hundreds of ㎿h(megawatt-hours) range with long-cycle ESS customers, and from next year plans to ship trial volumes to global customers. SK On plans to develop an ESS-use SIB prototype next year and commercialize it in 2028, and is also reviewing SIBs for EVs. Samsung SDI is developing SIBs for UPS and power ESS. The Korean government has set a goal of securing an SIB energy density of 160Wh/㎏ by 2027 and raising it to 220Wh/㎏ by 2030 for commercialization. ‘Will it catch LFP, or remain a niche?’…diverging views However, opinions diverge on whether SIBs will grow enough to threaten the position of LFP. Those who view SIBs as a future growth engine are pinning hopes on price declines with future mass production. Because supplies are nt concentrated in specific countries as with lithium, raw-material supply instability is lower, and aluminum can replace copper for the anode current collector, reducing costs. If pack structures are simplified by leveraging SIB safety, system-level costs can also be reduced. Conversely, as LFP is also raising energy density and compensating for weaknesses through design improvements, there is analysis that it is uncertain whether SIBs will fully replace LFP. Because each battery type has different strengthssuch as low-temperature performance, energy density, output, and safetySIBs should be seen as just ‘one option’ to broaden the battery portfolio. Can Korea catch up with China, which is in the lead? For Korean companies, the key question is whether they can secure competitiveness that surpasses China. In particular, in the early SIB market, how quickly they can narrow the mass-production gap with China and, at the same time, secure non-China material supply chains and customers will likely determine future competitiveness. In this respect, the United States push to build a de-China battery ecosystem is a positive factor. However, it is a burden in practical terms that China is already ahead in industrialization. artigo.texto: A recent study in PRX Quantum from the University of Oulu identifies key limits on quantum battery reliability and shows how different charging protocols can balance high power output with steady, predictable energy and power delivery. The findings help clarify what “dependable” performance will require in practice, bringing usable quantum energy-storage systems a step closer. Quantum uncertainty imposes a fundamental trade-off in quantum batteries, limiting their ability to deliver steady power and reliable energy simultaneously. Quantum batteries are an emerging area of research, with progress coming from theoretical work and early proof-of-concept experiments in small quantum systems. Unlike the chemical batteries used in everyday devices, quantum batteries store and transfer energy using quantum states. Researchers are exploring them as potential power sources for quantum processors and other quantum technologies. Much of the early work has focused on how quickly and efficiently these batteries can be charged. In their recent study, the team identified fundamental limits on fluctuations in both the energy a quantum battery delivers and the rate at which it supplies that energy. A quantum battery ideally should not only be fast and powerful but also needs to charge or deliver energy in a reliable and stable manner at the same time. Our work shows that quantum mechanics places fundamental limits on the reliabilities of quantum batteries. Brij Mohan, Study First Author and Postdoctoral Researcher, University of Oulu The researchers show that a familiar cornerstone of quantum mechanics, the uncertainty relation, prevents energy fluctuations and power variations from being minimized at the same time. In other words, a quantum battery cannot be tuned to deliver both highly reliable energy transfer and perfectly steady power at the same time. Here, “stability” and “reliability” mean keeping fluctuations small relative to their average values. The trade-off arises because, in closed quantum batteries, work and power are represented by non-commuting operators, much like position and momentum in standard quantum mechanics. The team then examined how this trade-off relates to methods for charging multiple quantum battery cells. In parallel charging, the cells function autonomously. Collective charging involves all cells simultaneously. Hybrid charging represents a midpoint between these two approaches, in which groups of cells interact during the charging process. The findings indicate that more robust collective charging increases power but also amplifies power fluctuations, which reduces power reliability. This suggests that evaluating quantum-battery performance based solely on maximum power is inadequate. Our results show that there is a meaningful way to balance power enhancement and the reliability of work and power. Intermediate-range interactions based charging scheme can provide a useful compromise between high power and stable operation. Tanmoy Pandit, Research Scientist, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland The researchers further investigated quantum batteries with transverse Ising-type many-body interactions and found a similar qualitative trade-off between power and reliability. This finding suggests that the phenomenon is not limited to the most basic theoretical framework. The reliability limits connect quantum fluctuations with many-body quantum physics in a direct way. They provide useful charging strategies that are practically advantageous. Manabendra Nath Bera, IISER Mohali “Quantum batteries offer a fascinating link between quantum information, thermodynamics, and many-body physics. Understanding their fluctuations is essential if these systems are eventually to become useful technological resources,” added Maciej Lewenstein, ICFO, Spain. The researchers' next goal is to explore the limits of reliability in more practical environments, accounting for factors such as noise, energy loss, open-system behavior, and experimentally relevant quantum platforms. Quantum batteries represent an ongoing advancement stemming from the extensive research conducted by the Nano and Molecular Systems Research Unit at the University of Oulu. This research focuses on the theoretical and modeling aspects of quantum devices, including superconducting qubits and quantum processors. Journal Reference: Mohan, B., et al. (2026) Fundamental Limitations on the Reliabilities of Power and Work in Quantum Batteries. PRX Quantum. DOI:10.1103/fnv6-yqmk. https://journals.aps.org/prxquantum/abstract/10.1103/fnv6-yqmk.

artigo.texto: Can AI navigate qualms about data centers, long-term debt? Q. When we speak about data centers, what exactly are we talking about? A data center is basically an industrial-scale computer farm. It's a large facility with a whole bunch of servers, storage and networking gear. The concept really predates AI. If you're storing your data in the cloud, you're basically a data center consumer in some sense. You're consuming storage and data retrieval services from a data center. The difference with AI is that AI dramatically increases the amount and consumption of these services. It's no longer just storing your data in the cloud and retrieving it when you want, but it's also actually doing computational work. For that reason, the scale of the infrastructure needed is enormously larger. For AI in particular, it needs really high-tech chips made by Nvidia and others. Also with large-scale computing, you need large-scale power and cooling infrastructure. All of that comes together in these data center projects. None of that is new, but the scale of it is new because of how much AI increases consumption. Q. How do data centers make money? It’s useful to think of the data center operator as an entity that finances the construction of all of that infrastructure and then monetizes it by leasing that computing capacity to a consumer. The consumer might be a large tech firm. Sometimes these data center operators are affiliated with one of the large tech firms. From our perspective, it's just useful to think of the data center operator as the part of the enterprise that builds out these data centers and leases out computing capacity. Q. The scale of data center construction appears to be unprecedented. Exactly how big is it? This is where you sort of forget the billions and you move into the trillions. There are many estimates of the cumulative CapEx (capital expenditures). If you look at the cumulative amount of CapEx that these firms will end up making over the remainder of this decade [roughly five years], the numbers are of the order of magnitude of $5 trillion. If you look at the cost of a data center, it seems to be in the ballpark of $30 billion to $40 billion per gigawatt used. So, a good way to measure the scale of these data centers is by the amount of power they consume. A gigawatt, by the way, is the equivalent electricity consumption of about 800,000 average homes. It seems that about half of that cost, maybe 60 percent, is the actual servers, chips and so on. The remainder is physical infrastructure, [providing electrical] power and the physical buildings. It's good to think of it as a [cumulative] run rate of $1 trillion a year, certainly not insignificant in the context of the overall economy, certainly not insignificant in the context of the amount of financing that needs to be raised. Q. Who has been funding the data center build-out? In the early stages of the build-out, it was mostly self-financed from the operating cash flow [of such firms as Meta, Microsoft and Amazon]. The numbers are now so large that you really have to tap into every available source of financing and then some. Wall Street research analysts have estimated where this money might come from. It's a combination of sources—20 percent of the overall CapEx might be operating cash flow and/or some sort of equity, maybe 30 percent will be in the form of unsecured debt in the high-grade debt markets. There will be some fraction coming from private lenders—private debt, potentially foreign investors. Then there's sort of a TBD [to be determined] fraction of it. Some of this is getting figured out as the build-out happens because this is a rapidly evolving landscape. If you just look at projections of debt supply in November [2025] versus now [September 2026], you know it keeps going up. This year, for instance, there's been about $200 billion in high-grade bond issuance to finance this. And about 70 percent of that is actually in the U.S. These borrowers are also tapping non-dollar currencies, the European bond markets, [the] yen and Swiss franc markets. A main takeaway is probably that the scale of this financing is large and, therefore, every possible avenue can and will be tapped. The positive side of that story is that tech firms have historically been very light on their debt footprint. Even though it's growing rapidly, at least in the initial stages, our contacts tell us that there's a lot of demand for this debt because a typical corporate bond investor is rather light on tech names. They're actually quite happy to take that issuance because in a sense, they're diversifying by buying debt from tech firms. Of course, there's a limit to that, and at some point, we'll get through that and the dynamic might change. But certainly, we seem to be in the relatively early stages, and there’s a willingness on the part of investors to buy tech company AI-related debt. Q. With so much AI debt going to market, what’s that doing to bond rates? Perhaps the best way to answer that is to look at what's happening among longer-term maturities [largely 10-year maturities]. The question of whether other borrowers are getting crowded out is difficult to answer at this stage of the game, but the impacts on long maturity sectors are becoming somewhat clearer. In general, there are a lot fewer issuers in the long end of the [yield] curve. Predominantly, the supplier of that debt is the [Department of the] Treasury—sovereign debt. Most firms tend to borrow shorter than that. Data center operators seem to prefer longer-term debt financing right now. Part of the reason could be the long-lived nature of the infrastructure. It could be issuers’ willingness or desire to just lock in financials for a longer period of time. It's hard to tell precisely why, but that's the observed dynamic. artigo.texto: EcoPro BM is strengthening its cooperation with Samsung SDI on materials development aimed at commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries. EcoPro BM said Oct. 6 that signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Samsung SDI to develop materials for solid-state batteries. The two companies will jointly develop battery cells and key materials, targeting commercialization in 2027. Their cooperation will span from early-stage research and development through quality evaluation and the establishment of mass-production systems. Samsung SDI will advance solid-state battery cell development and mass-production technology. EcoPro BM will develop key materials, including cathode materials for solid-state batteries, electrolytes for cathodes and electrolytes for separators. EcoPro BM operates a pilot plant with an annual capacity of 40 metric tons for producing sulfide-based solid electrolytes. The company is also developing cathode materials suited to solid-state batteries using its high-nickel cathode technology. EcoPro BM was selected in August for the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's "Super Eul Project" for its sulfide-based solid-electrolyte technology. In July, the company identified 2027 as the earliest possible timing for mass production of solid-state battery materials.

artigo.texto: India is stepping up investment in battery energy storage systems (BESS) to stabilize its power grid. The government plans to invest 500 billion rupees to deploy 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of BESS by 2033. According to industry sources on Oct. 6, the Indian government approved the third phase of the Green Energy Corridor (GEC-III) on Sept. 30. The project will expand transmission networks and BESS in line with the country’s growing renewable energy capacity. India plans to build transmission infrastructure capable of accommodating up to 135 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy by 2033. It will also install 50 GWh of BESS. The total project cost is 1.864 trillion rupees. Of that amount, 500 billion rupees has been allocated for BESS deployment. The government has not disclosed detailed conditions for the batteries to be used in the project, including battery chemistry, storage duration and procurement methods. The actual amount spent on batteries and systems could vary depending on those conditions. On a simple calculation, India will need more than 7 GWh of batteries annually for grid-scale energy storage systems (ESS) alone. But local battery production capacity is only about 2 GWh a year, meaning the country will have to rely heavily on imports. India has largely met demand through imports as it was late to establish a lithium-ion battery manufacturing base. Chinese-made batteries accounted for 75.2% of India’s lithium-ion battery imports in fiscal 2024-25. According to the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA), India’s lithium-ion battery production capacity could reach 60 GWh to 70 GWh by 2030 if announced investment plans are implemented as scheduled. Over the same period, capacity for assembling battery packs and BESS using imported cells is expected to rise to 180 GWh to 220 GWh. Local cell production is therefore expected to lag well behind the expansion of BESS manufacturing capacity. Wood Mackenzie estimates that it will take India 10 to 15 years to build a self-sufficient battery industry with competitive pricing. It estimates that locally produced battery cells will cost 25% to 40% more than imported cells. High financing costs and an underdeveloped battery-materials supply chain are among the reasons. As India needs time to expand domestic battery production, it will have to rely on overseas technology and supply chains for the time being. That could create an opportunity for Korean companies to enter the market. Indian companies have traditionally worked mainly with Chinese battery makers because of their price competitiveness. But the business environment is changing as political tensions between India and China persist. Korean companies are also seeking opportunities to enter the Indian market. AI battery startup DeltaX signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Toptec in July to cooperate on targeting India’s ESS market. “India is expanding localization across its renewable energy industry, including requiring the use of domestically produced solar panels,” DeltaX Chief Executive Kim Soo-hoon said. “Local solar and renewable energy companies are also expanding into assembling and selling battery modules and packs for ESS, and are actively considering cooperation with companies outside China.” The growing adoption of Korean-made battery equipment in India is another positive factor. A key example is a battery plant with annual capacity of 40 GWh being built in India by Agratas, a Tata Group company. A number of Korean battery-equipment makers, including Yunsung F&C, PNT, Philenergy, Hana Technology, J's Robotics and Axvis, have been selected as suppliers for the project. Business by Korean battery manufacturers in India remains limited. LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI operate local sales subsidiaries, but their main business is supplying small batteries for smartphones and other information-technology devices. Their operations in India remain small in both scope and scale compared with major overseas markets such as North America and Europe. LG Energy Solution leads among companies in energy-related patents, having filed 2,225 patents in India. “Indian ESS companies have traditionally sourced battery cells mainly from Chinese companies,” an industry official said. “They also prefer lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, so opportunities for Korean battery companies to enter the Indian market could expand as they increase their LFP-related businesses.” India also built a large-scale power grid under previous phases of the Green Energy Corridor program. Phase I involved about 9,100 kilometers of transmission lines, while Phase II is adding about 7,900 kilometers across seven states. As transmission investment expands under Phase III, demand is also expected to rise for power equipment from HD Hyundai Electric, LS ELECTRIC and Hyosung Heavy Industries, alongside BESS.

artigo.texto: South Korea's power semiconductor industry has begun research aimed at improving the efficiency of power supply systems for data centers as electricity consumption from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers continues to rise. Park Sang-min, a Ph.D. researcher at the Korea Electronics Technology Institute (KETI), presented an overview of domestic power semiconductor research for AI data center power systems at the Power Semiconductor Industry-Academia-Research K-Forum, held at Hotel Nongshim in Dongnae, Busan, on Oct. 7. AI data centers require more power than conventional data centers because GPU performance requirements and the number of GPUs installed are increasing, driving up electricity consumption. While conventional data centers required about 10 to 20 megawatts (MW), data centers consuming more than 100MW have emerged. A 10MW load is roughly equivalent to the electricity used by 10,000 households at the same time, while 100MW corresponds to about 100,000 households. South Korean research institutions are focusing on improving server power-conversion efficiency. Electricity supplied from the external grid to a data center goes through six power-conversion stages before reaching the GPU. Power losses occur at each stage, reducing the amount of electricity ultimately available to the GPU. KETI is seeking to improve data center power efficiency with a focus on server power supply units (PSUs). A PSU converts electricity supplied to a data center into power that can be used by servers. KETI is also leading a government-funded project. The institute is demonstrating a 100MW-class data center power system compatible with the Open Compute Project's (OCP) Open Rack v3 (ORv3) specification. The project applies compound power semiconductors such as silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN), which offer faster switching speeds than silicon (Si). KETI is developing high-efficiency, high-power power supplies and building the system at the rack level. The resulting system will be validated by NAVER Cloud. KETI is also researching power supply architectures based on 800-volt direct current (DC). Racks currently use DC power at around 50 volts. As power consumption per rack increases, the existing distribution architecture is approaching its limits. The voltage supplied to racks can be increased to as much as 800V, reducing the current required to deliver the same amount of power. This can lower power losses during distribution. There are limitations to immediately applying 800V DC to data centers in South Korea. Converting existing power infrastructure to 800V DC would require changes to existing power equipment. One alternative is to generate 800V DC inside the data center while maintaining the existing external infrastructure. This approach would modify only part of the current architecture. In the longer term, the industry is considering the use of solid-state transformers (SSTs), which use power semiconductors to convert voltage. An 800V DC architecture distributes power inside a data center at 800V DC after converting the several-thousand- to tens-of-thousands-of-volt electricity entering from the external grid. Raising the voltage reduces the current required to deliver the same amount of power.
