Targeting Commercialization by 2027 Joint Development of Sulfide-Based Solid Electrolytes and All-Solid-State Cathode Materials Expanding Collaboration from Cell Development to Core Materials and Mass Production Systems Ecopro BM is joining forces with Samsung SDI in developing core materials and building a supply chain, aiming for the commercialization of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries next year. Ecopro BM announced on the 6th that it has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Samsung SDI for cooperation in developing materials for all-solid-state batteries. The two companies plan to strengthen collaboration from the early stages of development through quality assessment and mass production system establishment, with the goal of enhancing the technological completeness and business competitiveness of all-solid-state batteries. Image of all-solid-state battery materials unveiled by Ecopro BM at InterBattery in March. Ecopro BM View original image Under the agreement, Samsung SDI will be responsible for developing all-solid-state battery cells and advancing mass production technology. Ecopro BM will be in charge of developing core materials for all-solid-state batteries. The two companies will expand the scope of their cooperation to include not just cathode materials for all-solid-state batteries, but also electrolytes for cathodes and electrolytes for separators. All-solid-state batteries are next-generation batteries that use a solid electrolyte instead of the conventional liquid electrolyte. They are considered key technologies for future industries such as electric vehicles and humanoid robots, as they can improve energy density and safety. Ecopro BM has secured proprietary processing technology in the field of sulfide-based solid electrolytes, a core material for all-solid-state batteries, and operates a pilot plant with an annual capacity of 40 tons. Leveraging its powder control and quality management technologies, the company is enhancing its competitiveness in solid electrolytes while also developing cathode materials optimized for solid electrolytes using its high-nickel cathode technology. Based on its sulfide-based solid electrolyte technology, Ecopro BM was also selected in August for the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's "Super Eul Project." The Super Eul Project is an R&D support program designed to foster materials, parts, and equipment companies capable of leading global supply chains. The government plans to support each selected company with more than 20 billion won of long-term R&D funding per project over at least seven years. Last month, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy released the "Battery Industry Technology Roadmap," designating all-solid-state batteries as a key strategic technology for the future battery industry. The government plans to support the early commercialization of next-generation batteries by strengthening joint R&D and supply chain cooperation systems among cell and materials companies. artigo.texto: At the end of 2024, Texas’ grid operator had 63 GW of large new customers in its queue. By this June, that figure reached 474 GW, more than five times record peak demand, about 90% of it data centers. Then Texas hit pause. What began as directions for data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades has since escalated to a freeze on all new permits. If you care about AI and American reindustrialization, this is important to understand. Why did it do this? The upcoming election is part of it, but the underlying issues are worth digging into. The first is the interconnection queue. This pause is just as much about how projects apply for approval as it is about the projects themselves. Developers routinely spam projects across several sites, and many are speculative builds with no customer yet. Often these new developers have never even plugged in a GPU, let alone a power plant, so dealing with low-quality submissions puts ERCOT, which runs most of the state’s grid, in a tough spot. Planners can’t tell which are real, and they don’t want ratepayers paying for upgrades built for projects that never show up. The second issue is community alignment. Noise, water, emissions, and power bills are top of mind for anyone who lives nearby. And regardless of the reality of these issues, people deserve straight answers when a data center comes to town, and they haven’t always gotten them (as of June, only 28 of 377 companies had answered a state survey on their resource use). In Hood County, commissioners were asked to support a tax waiver for “Project Patriot” without knowing who it was. To be fair, code names are common while companies shop for sites since a famous buyer can drive up prices, but that logic becomes tougher to defend once officials vote on tax breaks. The broader political backdrop is important, but I’ll be focusing on the energy side: why it’s so hard to power a data center, all the ways developers are trying to do it anyway, and where things are likely headed. What connecting to the grid actually means How Amazon purchases power helps illustrate what’s changed. For the last decade, they’d find a utility with network capacity, sign up as a large load, then enter long-term contracts to match their use on paper. These were often purely financial, meaning you didn’t always have to prove the power could reach you, and the grid connection was easy because utilities had spare network capacity. That’s no longer true. The grid is stretched thin, and almost any new large load or generator now requires an upgrade. Power flows across every connected path, so buying from one plant doesn’t reserve a route to your building (there are even markets for transmission congestion rights). So buyers went after firm power (available around the clock) they could claim more directly, typically by restarting retired plants or by building next to existing ones. Neither was a true escape, and some of the loudest fights are over “colocation,” which ERCOT describes as drawing power from a neighboring plant before it reaches the grid: - Susquehanna: Amazon bought a campus next to Talen’s nuclear plant, but FERC, the federal grid regulator, rejected Talen’s bid to send it more power directly. Utilities had argued it would let the campus dodge grid fees and push fixed transmission costs onto everyone else. After they restructured the deal, Amazon pays for delivery like any other customer. - Freestone: CyrusOne’s 760 MW campus beside Constellation’s gas plant needed approval from the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT), since it effectively takes much of the plant’s output from everyone else. The PUCT said yes in May, as long as the campus can cut its use or switch to backup power within 30 minutes of an ERCOT call. - Armstrong County: Two Crusoe data centers beside a wind farm got the same rule, and the second, approved in July, must also shed its entire load, so together they’d cut nearly twice what the wind farm can produce. Interconnection studies are how grid planners identify the wires and substations that need upgrades for any addition to the network. ERCOT used to review studies individually under rules built for 40 to 50 large loads at a time, but 2025 brought 225 new requests by mid-November. So this June, the PUCT approved a new batch approach. Under “Batch Zero,” ERCOT studies large loads of 75 MW or more together and allocates grid capacity among them. Primarily, the studies ask what happens when something breaks. NERC’s standard, the baseline for reliability across North America, covers a broad set of outage scenarios, with ERCOT adding its own requirements. Planners might simulate a transformer outage, then knock out a line or generator on top of that. Maintaining that reliability standard without shedding more load often means building additional infrastructure. A newer risk is load dropping off the grid all at once. Many data centers switch to backup power at the first voltage dip to protect their hardware, so one bad fault can pull an enormous load off the grid in seconds. This happened earlier this year in Virginia, but was fortunately handled well. Texas has even less room for error since ERCOT’s grid is largely isolated. Under some conditions, ERCOT can lose only about 3.2 GW of load at once before causing issues. A new voltage ride-through rule now requires new data centers to stay connected through routine faults, and I’ve even heard of labs running dummy jobs after a training run fails just to keep load from dropping abruptly. All of this can sound overly conservative, but the system was designed to put reliability ahead of cost. Put simply, the grid is built for the hot summer days and frigid winters when failure can mean life or death. That duty is what makes sizing the grid so hard; you build for a few peak hours but pay for it all year. So who does pay for all this resilience? artigo.texto: Novo regime tributário reduz custos para o setor e pode acelerar investimentos em data centers, enquanto a HostDime prepara em João Pessoa uma estrutura de R$ 250 milhões voltada a aplicações de inteligência artificial avançada O novo Redata pode provocar uma arrancada dos data centers no Brasil nos próximos anos. A avaliação é do CEO da Positivo Tecnologia, enquanto João Pessoa já aparece nesse movimento com um projeto de R$ 250 milhões voltado à inteligência artificial. Redata pode destravar uma fila de projetos no país A capacidade instalada de centros de processamento de dados no Brasil pode dobrar ou até triplicar nos próximos dois ou três anos. A projeção foi feita por Hélio Bruck Rotenberg, CEO da Positivo Tecnologia. Segundo o executivo, havia projetos aguardando uma definição sobre os incentivos tributários antes de avançar. Com o novo regime aprovado, a expectativa dele é de uma corrida por servidores, componentes e outros equipamentos necessários para colocar esses empreendimentos de pé. - Nova ponte de R$ 6,2 milhões vai sair do papel em Erechim e licitação já tem data marcada para começar - Multinacional alemã prepara investimento de R$ 712 milhões em Santa Catarina com construção de nova fábrica e expansão capaz de elevar produção em 130% - 40 mil pessoas a pé no meio dos caminhões: Via Dutra fecha 45 km de faixa com cones e leva à ANTT plano de calçada até Aparecida - De olho na indústria de rochas do ES, grupo italiano investe R$ 60 milhões para ampliar fábrica e elevar produção de 18 mil para 30 mil toneladas ao ano O Paraíba Business destacou que esse cenário já alcança o Nordeste e colocou a Paraíba no mapa dos novos investimentos, especialmente por causa da expansão da HostDime em João Pessoa. Rotenberg resumiu sua expectativa sobre o tamanho desse salto: “Acredito que deva duplicar ou triplicar nos próximos dois ou três anos”. A previsão é do executivo e, portanto, não representa uma projeção oficial do governo. Lei do Redata corta tributos e cria contrapartidas O Redata virou lei em 15 de setembro de 2026. A Lei nº 15.504 criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter e entrou em vigor na data de sua publicação. O programa prevê benefícios tributários para equipamentos e componentes destinados aos centros habilitados. Entre os tributos abrangidos estão Imposto de Importação, IPI e PIS/Cofins, incluindo cobranças incidentes sobre importações. Não é simplesmente uma liberação de imposto. Quem entrar no regime precisa cumprir contrapartidas, incluindo investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação e regras relacionadas ao atendimento do mercado brasileiro. De acordo com o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, ao menos 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenagem e tratamento deverá ser disponibilizada ao mercado nacional ou destinada, nas condições previstas, a instituições científicas, tecnológicas ou ao poder público. Para projetos localizados no Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, a própria legislação prevê redução de 20% em determinadas contrapartidas. Esse ponto ajuda a colocar regiões fora do eixo tradicional do Sudeste na disputa pelos novos empreendimentos. Antes da aprovação, entidades empresariais apontavam uma diferença pesada no bolso. Segundo manifesto do setor produtivo, instalar um data center no Brasil custava 26% mais que nos Estados Unidos e 35% mais que no Chile. Data center de R$ 250 milhões coloca João Pessoa nessa corrida Na Paraíba, o projeto mais concreto é da HostDime Brasil. A empresa anunciou investimento de R$ 250 milhões para ampliar sua infraestrutura de data center em João Pessoa. A estrutura terá capacidade energética de até 15 megawatts e será preparada para cargas de inteligência artificial. A própria companhia também cita tecnologias de refrigeração líquida para lidar com servidores de alta densidade. A HostDime já mantém operação na capital paraibana. A nova estrutura representa uma expansão bem maior e mira aplicações que exigem muito poder computacional, justamente o tipo de demanda que cresceu com modelos de inteligência artificial. Há, porém, uma diferença importante nas datas divulgadas. A reportagem do Paraíba Business publicada em 5 de outubro informa que o novo centro deverá operar em 2027. Já comunicações da própria HostDime publicadas em setembro colocam o início da operação em 2028. Também há variação sobre o começo das obras: um conteúdo da companhia, de 8 de setembro, mencionava início ainda em 2026; outro, publicado em 16 de setembro, indicava construção a partir de 2027. O investimento de R$ 250 milhões e a capacidade projetada de 15 MW permanecem nos materiais da empresa. Expansão no Brasil também mexe com fabricantes O movimento não interessa apenas a quem constrói os galpões cheios de servidores. Para fabricantes de equipamentos, uma expansão rápida dos data centers pode abrir um mercado grande dentro do país. A Positivo Tecnologia já atua na fabricação de servidores e vê no Redata uma oportunidade de ampliar essa frente. Rotenberg também defendeu que a política permite trazer tecnologias ainda não produzidas localmente sem retirar espaço da indústria já instalada no Brasil. A lei diferencia ainda a tributação de bens importados. O regime suspende impostos dentro das condições previstas e estabelece regras específicas para estimular investimentos, ao mesmo tempo em que exige aportes em pesquisa e desenvolvimento. O tamanho real dessa expansão, no entanto, ainda será medido nos próximos anos. Dobrar ou triplicar a capacidade é uma projeção do CEO da Positivo, não uma meta legal do Redata. Por enquanto, o que já está definido é o novo regime tributário. E, na Paraíba, há um investimento anunciado de R$ 250 milhões que coloca João Pessoa entre as cidades que tentam ganhar espaço na nova infraestrutura digital brasileira. Fonte: Paraibabusiness.

artigo.texto: Novo projeto de infraestrutura em Dubai integra 2.000 MW de energia solar com um sistema BESS de 1.400 MW / 8.400 MWh para suprir a rede durante a noite. A transição energética no deserto de Seih Al-Dahal enfrenta o desafio de manter o suprimento elétrico estável quando o sol se põe. Para resolver essa intermitência em larga escala, a concessionária estipulou uma infraestrutura capaz de estocar gigawatts-hora diretamente na rede de transmissão. Por que um sistema gigante de baterias é necessário em um parque solar no deserto? Quando ligamos aparelhos elétricos à noite, a rede precisa entregar energia instantaneamente. O painel solar tradicional produz eletricidade apenas enquanto recebe radiação solar direta. Essa diferença entre o momento de geração e o pico de consumo é equacionada com sistemas BESS (Battery Energy Storage System). A nova etapa utiliza baterias com capacidade de injeção de 1.400 MW e armazenamento total de 8.400 MWh. Isso significa guardar seis horas seguidas de geração máxima em módulos estáticos. Assim, a energia captada sob o sol do deserto abastece as cidades durante o período noturno. Quais são os números e a capacidade técnica da 7ª fase do parque solar? A infraestrutura planejada pela Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) combina painéis fotovoltaicos com um dos maiores conjuntos de baterias estáticas do planeta. Os dados estruturais demonstram a escala desse projeto de engenharia elétrica: Geração fotovoltaica instalada: adiciona 2.000 MW de potência através de módulos de silício monocristalino bifaciais montados em seguidores solares de eixo único. - Capacidade de potência do BESS: sistema de baterias dimensionado para injetar até 1.400 MW continuamente na rede elétrica. - Volume total de armazenamento: capacidade de 8.400 MWh para sustentação do fluxo elétrico por seis horas consecutivas. - Interconexão em alta tensão: integração direta em subestações de 400 kV e 132 kV para minimizar perdas de transmissão. - Química das células de armazenamento: baterias de lítio-ferro-fosfato (LiFePO4) escolhidas pela alta estabilidade térmica e vida útil prolongada. Como funciona o armazenamento e a entrega de energia na prática? Durante o dia, os inversores bidirecionais convertem a corrente contínua dos módulos e enviam parte dos 2.000 MW para carregar os contêineres de baterias. O sistema de controle monitora a frequência da rede e ajusta a carga em milissegundos para evitar variações de voltagem. Ao entardecer, quando a demanda por ar-condicionado atinge o topo, o sistema inverte a operação e descarrega até 1.400 MW nas linhas de transmissão. Dessa forma, a usina atua como uma geradora de base contínua, mantendo o sistema elétrico equilibrado sem falhas. Onde ver a estrutura do Parque Solar Mohammed bin Rashid em operação? O parque solar em Dubai ocupa uma área contínua no deserto de Seih Al-Dahal. A visualização das fases operacionais e do Hub de Inovação demonstra a organização espacial dos arranjos fotovoltaicos e das usinas de armazenamento. Acompanhar esses registros técnicos auxilia no entendimento da escala física necessária para instalar milhões de módulos e contêineres energizados sob altas temperaturas ambientais. Abaixo, um vídeo do canal oficial da DEWA Official que aprofunda o tema: Quais normas técnicas de engenharia garantem a segurança de grandes baterias? Sistemas de armazenamento em escala de gigawatts exigem conformidade com normas rígidas, como a IEC 62933 para integração de BESS e a NFPA 855 para proteção contra incêndios elétricos. Para testar a resistência contra fuga térmica em células, aplica-se o padrão UL 9540A. Os projetos incorporam barramentos isolados, paredes de contenção corta-fogo e resfriamento líquido acoplado aos contêineres. Seguir esses parâmetros impede o superaquecimento em climas secos com temperaturas superiores a 45 °C, garantindo a integridade dos equipamentos. Quando é necessário contratar um engenheiro eletricista especializado em energia solar? Projetos fotovoltaicos comerciais e industriais que incorporam armazenamento exigem a atuação de um engenheiro eletricista. Somente esse profissional pode calcular a capacidade dos inversores, realizar o estudo de curto-circuito e projetar a proteção contra surtos de tensão. A instalação sem dimensionamento adequado pode causar derretimento de cabos, disjunção incorreta e danos permanentes à rede do imóvel. Não é um trabalho que você faz sozinho porque envolve lidar com altas correntes contínuas e normas rigorosas da concessionária. Contexto importante: Este artigo é informativo. Para projetos estruturais e elétricos locais similares, recomenda-se avaliação de engenheiro eletricista, especialmente em contextos de risco de comprometimento elétrico, surtos de tensão e superaquecimento de baterias.

artigo.texto: São Paulo recebe, desde esta terça-feira e até esta quinta um dos maiores eventos globais de tecnologia voltada ao setor empresarial. O Data Center World Brasil, realizado no São Paulo Expo, é focado em soluções para companhias em áreas estratégicas, algumas das quais o Rio Grande do Sul tem sido um player cada vez mais competitivo, como a instalação de data centers, com oportunidades em negócios nas áreas de hardware, equipamentos e investimentos em geral. Prestes a completar 30 anos no Brasil, a Kingston, mais conhecida no mercado consumidor tradicional como fabricante de memórias e pendrives domésticos, busca acelerar sua atuação na infraestrutura corporativa no mercado latino-americano com outros produtos complementares, inclusive voltadas a relacionamentos, como parcerias com marketplaces. O Brasil, atualmente, concentra 58% da fatia de mercado da Kingston na América Latina e somente as vendas da linha enterprise cresceram 42% no primeiro semestre deste ano. “O Brasil hoje é o principal polo de data center na América Latina. A gente tem muita energia limpa no país e já possuímos vários cabos submarinos. Hoje um dos principais gargalos de construir data center no mundo é a questão da energia, e isso o Brasil tem bastante”, destacou o country manager da Kingston no Brasil, Paulo Vizaco. Para ele, a inteligência artificial está indo “para todos os lados”, em meio a uma “uma corrida gigante de players investindo até trilhões de dólares na criação de infraestrutura”. E o Rio Grande do Sul, como região que está recebendo projetos bilionários na área de data centers, como o da Parks, em Cachoeirinha, e o Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul, é um local onde há uma atenção concentrada, por meio de oportunidades de parcerias. “Obviamente que vemos monitorando todos esses projetos. Estamos em contato com a maioria deles conversando, vendo o que que a gente pode agregar”, comentou Vizaco. Para ele, a Kingston também acompanha de perto as discussões e iniciativas regulatórias e tributárias no Brasil, a exemplo do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado a nível no mês passado. Data Center World Brasil 2026 e participação da Kingston no evento Corrida global pela IA acelera Conforme o executivo, a consolidação de incentivos como este é fundamental para reduzir o custo de infraestrutura no Brasil e tornará o ecossistema nacional de data centers ainda mais competitivo frente ao mercado mundial. “Como uma empresa de capital privado, temos a facilidade de se mover muito mais rápido do que qualquer outra. Então nos adaptamos bem a estas condições, principalmente tributárias. Temos uma flexibilidade muito grande neste sentido”, disse ele. O gerente de Tecnologia da Kingston, Iuri Santos, comentou que as empresas de maneira geral têm visto inclusive ideias de voltar a viabilizar grandes projetos de infraestrutura tecnológica, ao verem na Kingston economia, suporte local e qualidade que, eventualmente, seja um gargalo em outros fornecedores. Na visão de Santos, “nunca se produziu tanto semicondutor na história da humanidade”, porque a corrida global pela IA gerou uma demanda sem precedentes por componentes de altíssima velocidade e capacidade. Para ele, os preços destes atingiram um novo patamar global, e é irrealista buscar comparar os orçamentos atuais com os de anos anteriores. “Não devemos olhar para os preços que tínhamos antes, porque aquilo é um mundo sem a IA. A gente mudou, a tecnologia mudou. As empresas que estão ficando para trás são as que ainda estão olhando para o passado em vez de olhar para o presente imaginando se preparar para o futuro. Virou uma questão de sobrevivência: eu preciso me digitalizar”, apontou ele.

artigo.texto: A major improvement for Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE), Valeo’s aluminum heat exchanger delivers a 38% increase in cooling capacity, a 25% reduction in electrical consumption, and over a decade of proven corrosion resistance. October 7, 2026 – SAN JOSE, Calif. — At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit 2026 (October 12–15), Valeo will present, with OVH Cloud, the validation status of its breakthrough aluminum heat exchanger technology for data center thermal management. This technology is applicable for the rear door cooling modules of rack or fan wall in the core space of data centers (white space). It represents a paradigm shift in the industry. With over two years of dedicated development in the sector, Valeo is demonstrating its industrial capability and readiness to scale production. Leveraging decades of automotive thermal management, heat exchangers and corrosion know-how, Valeo develops solutions aimed at supporting the AI industry’s exponential scaling needs. Pascale Herman, Data center & BESS Vice President at Valeo, said: “Presenting our ongoing work at OCP 2026 represents an important step in our journey within the data center ecosystem. Over the past two years, we have made significant progress in evaluating how aluminum liquid cooling can meet the rigorous reliability and performance standards required by modern high-density facilities. By combining these early testing metrics with our decades of automotive thermal management expertise, we are working to develop scalable thermal solutions to support the industry’s evolving infrastructure needs responsibly and effectively.” A validated breakthrough for data centers cooling As artificial intelligence (AI) workloads push rack densities to new heights, aluminum heat exchangers are being evaluated to provide a powerful, lightweight, more efficient, and scalable alternative to traditional copper hardware. Valeo’s aluminum solutions deliver a 38% increase in cooling capacity and 65% in power density versus traditional copper solutions, while simultaneously reducing fan electrical consumption by 25%. These validation results establish a clear technological breakthrough, directly optimizing Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE) and Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), ideal for retrofitting existing or for new racks. Automotive-grade reliability: pushing the boundaries of endurance To evaluate long-term feasibility, and directly address industry concerns regarding aluminum corrosion, Valeo has implemented a comprehensive, accelerated long-run testing framework to simulate long-term reliability and OVH Cloud has been running real time and conditions tests for several months. Testing on Valeo’s specific coating has already successfully reached the equivalent of more than 10-years operating life, fully aligning with the standard infrastructure lifespan of the data center industry. Valeo is currently pushing tests up to 15 years ensuring the material unconditionally meets the stringent, long-term lifespan expectations of data center operators. This ongoing research aims to establish a clear pathway toward production-grade aluminum infrastructure for next-generation data centers. A comprehensive liquid cooling vision addressing the data center industry evolution While the aluminum exchanger takes center stage at OCP 2026, it is part of a broader liquid cooling ecosystem engineered to challenge traditional data center thermal limits and address the industry’s rapid evolution. Valeo’s technology portfolio also includes Direct-to-Chip (DLC) systems (both Single-Phase and Two-Phase) for high-density racks, as well as Zero-Water Immersion Units for Micro-Edge compute applications. By applying decades of automotive thermal expertise, stringent quality standards, and a vast global manufacturing footprint in all regions, Valeo brings a new industrial perspective to data center cooling. As accelerating AI demand reshapes digital infrastructure, Valeo combines high-volume production scale with cutting-edge innovation to power the digital transition. About Valeo Valeo is a leading global technology company creating innovative solutions and systems for automotive and technology partners worldwide. Valeo is structured around its POWER, BRAIN and LIGHT Divisions, and Valeo Service, the augmented service partner, for the aftermarket and new forms of mobility. Valeo is committed to making mobility safer, more sustainable and affordable to all. The Group is playing a vital role in shaping the Car of Tomorrow: which will be electrified, safer and software-defined. Valeo is leveraging its global industrial footprint and its technological leadership in electrification, advanced driver assistance systems, lighting and software to capture an increasing share of value per vehicle. Valeo is listed on the Paris Stock Exchange. artigo.texto: Growing up in Northern Virginia meant reaping the benefits of proximity to our nation’s capital. From field trips to the Smithsonian museums, walks across the National Mall and many hours spent on the Metro (objectively the best public transportation system on the East Coast), I was spoiled from an early age. People forget, however, that driving out of the city offers its own benefits. My favorite outside-of-DC stop was always Manassas, Virginia. Manassas is home to the historic Battle of Bull Run battlefields. My neighbor and I would drive through the battlefields on our way to summer camp at a farm in Manassas. I’d stare out the window at the cannons littered across open fields, the wooden fences leaning with time. Now? There’s a data center right next door. The farm my neighbor and I used to spend hot summer days at is being replaced by computer systems enclosed by sterile white buildings. Right next to where Robert E. Lee faced the Union Army. You can imagine my non-surprise when I found out about the proposed data center projects around South Bend. Because what goes better with tailgates and Touchdown Jesus than fiber-optic cables and AI systems? But on a serious note, the Northern Indiana data centers — and data centers in general — are more than just road trip eyesores. Sophomore Katherine Spiller spent her summer doing research and fieldwork in the St. Joseph County Kettle Lakes Corridor, just west of South Bend. The area is home to a sensitive sphagnum bog habitat, containing many endangered and rare species. A proposed data center project would pose huge environmental threats to such a rich habitat. Already, some of the lakes are drying up, and the massive amounts of water used to power data centers would cause even more drainage in the kettle lakes. Without water — or a home — the species that live in the lakes would cease to exist. “I believe hearing from those who see what the Corridor experiences ... is key to touching hearts and enacting positive change,” Spiller said. She asserted that over half of the people she interviewed brought up concerns about the effect of the data center on the local community, something that should compel tech companies and bystanders alike to step back and consider what they are supporting. We live in a next-step world where society is constantly coming up with ways to optimize and streamline our daily lives, and data centers fit into this future-focused mindset. But they’re almost counterproductive to the things that truly matter. In Virginia, a historical site backdropped by mass innovation provides a scary juxtaposition between past and future. In Indiana, a local ecosystem is slowly being sucked away by the hand of AI. Sure, ChatGPT is great and all, but is this really what we want? Is this really what it means to live in 2026?

artigo.texto: Zelestra and EDP strengthened their collaboration in Spain with two new hybrid PPAs that will incorporate 462 MWh of battery storage to 181 MWdc of solar capacity. The agreements pertain to the Pedroso project in Seville and the Valkyria project in Castilla-La Mancha. In both cases, additional measures will be added BESS systems to existing photovoltaic installations, which will allow part of the solar generation to be stored and its delivery shifted to other times of the day. Zelestra will own the projects while EDP will act as the energy buyer through new long-term power purchase agreements. The hybrid PPAs will incorporate four-hour batteries. In Pedroso, Zelestra will combine a 31 MWdc solar plant with a 25 MW BESS system and a 100 MWh battery storage capacity. Valkyria, meanwhile, will have 150 MWdc of photovoltaic generation and a 90.45 MW battery storage system with a 362 MWh capacity. The two systems will have approximately four hours of storage capacity. Together, they will provide the additional 462 MWh included in the new hybrid PPAs. This configuration allows the electricity produced during peak solar generation hours to be harnessed and stored for later use. In this way, batteries can increase the flexibility of power plants and reduce their reliance on production tied solely to hours of sunlight. Zelestra and EDP exceed 1 GWh of contracted storage The Pedroso and Valkyria agreements bring to four the number of solar energy and storage projects included in the collaboration between Zelestra and EDP in Spain. In 2025, the companies agreed a PPA for the Trujillo project in Extremadura, which combines 170 MWdc of solar capacity with 400 MWh of battery storage. Subsequently, in 2026, both companies expanded their collaboration through Pizarroso, a 50 MW solar plant in Cáceres where a 160 MWh BESS system will be incorporated. With Pedroso and Valkyria, the storage capacity linked to the four agreements reaches approximately 1,022 MWh. Unlike Trujillo, developed as a new solar project with storage, Pedroso, Valkyria and Pizarroso take advantage of photovoltaic plants existing ones to incorporate batteries. Batteries increase the flexibility of solar plants Hybridizing operational facilities allows for the addition of storage using existing infrastructure such as land, generation, and grid access. In addition, the model makes it easier for some of the renewable electricity produced during the day to be shifted to the late afternoon, evening, or other periods of higher demand. For independent power producers, this capacity opens up new commercial opportunities within PPAs. solar generation it is no longer strictly linked to the moment it occurs and can be better adapted to the buyer’s consumption profile. Zelestra has transferred to Europe some of the experience gained in markets such as Chile, where contracts combining renewable generation and storage have a longer track record. Likewise, the company is expanding this type of commercial structure in other European markets through hybrid PPAs and long-term storage contracts. Spain gains energy storage capacity The new operation also reinforces the role of BESS systems within Spanish renewable growth. Jaime Burguete, head of Zelestra in Spain, pointed out that the four joint projects demonstrate the viability of energy storage in the country and predicted that this segment will have a growing importance in the coming years. For its part, EDP seeks to use the combination of renewable generation and storage to provide a more flexible electricity supply and make better use of the energy produced by renewables solar installations. With the new agreements, Zelestra and EDP are expanding a strategy that links long-term supply contracts with large-scale batteries, a formula that can facilitate greater integration of solar energy within the Spanish electricity system. artigo.texto: A Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada, mais conhecida por MEX, pretende tirar partido das vantagens oferecidas por Macau para promover a negociação de activos ambientais – incluindo de créditos de carbono, certificados de energia verde e outros instrumentos similares – entre a China e os Países de Língua Portuguesa. Meng Meng, Directora-Geral da entidade, revela que a plataforma de negociação operada pela MEX já listou mais de 30 projectos ligados a países lusófonos e de língua espanhola, envolvendo uma redução total de emissões de carbono superior a 14,13 milhões de toneladas Como foi criada a Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada (MEX, na sigla inglesa)? Quais são os seus objectivos estratégicos? A MEX foi criada a 30 de Outubro de 2024. Recorrendo a tecnologias de informação avançadas e padrões de referência no sector, integra produtos e oportunidades relacionados com o clima a nível global, proporcionando à China uma solução específica com características de Macau para se conectar aos mercados internacionais de finanças verdes. A Região Administrativa Especial de Macau (RAEM) é um porto franco, com regras financeiras alinhadas com as normas internacionais. Além disso, a cidade situa-se na confluência de duas importantes estratégias nacionais – o projecto da Grande Baía Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau e a Zona de Cooperação Aprofundada entre Guangdong e Macau em Hengqin. Neste sentido, possui um conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas que lhe permite posicionar-se como um “superconector” no mercado internacional de carbono. A nossa tarefa é transformar gradualmente esse conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas numa realidade concreta. A nível nacional, trabalhamos no sentido de apoiar as metas de “duplo carbono” estabelecidas pelo país [atingir o pico das emissões de dióxido de carbono antes de 2030 e alcançar a neutralidade carbónica antes de 2060], proporcionando um canal mais aberto para que o mercado de carbono da China possa estabelecer ligações com capital, tecnologia e regulamentações internacionais. A nível global, estamos a construir uma plataforma de cooperação no campo da acção climática, ao mesmo tempo que promovemos o alinhamento de padrões com as normas internacionais e a sua implementação prática, divulgando o progresso alcançado pelo mercado de carbono da China. Em paralelo, a MEX encara o comércio de carbono como um motor para alcançar a neutralidade carbónica e desenvolver as finanças verdes. Oferecemos também a diversos sectores-chave em Macau soluções ligadas à neutralidade carbónica, ferramentas associadas a certificados verdes de absorção de carbono e instrumentos de financiamento verde, transformando a transição para a neutralidade carbónica numa vantagem competitiva para as indústrias da RAEM. Qual é o modelo operacional da MEX? A nossa plataforma pode ser entendida como um mercado digital de negociação de activos ambientais. Os produtos listados na MEX incluem créditos de carbono, certificados de energia renovável e outros itens similares. Apoiamos a negociação de certificados verdes internacionais e chineses e somos a única bolsa do género na China a disponibilizar contratos padronizados de créditos de carbono de elevada qualidade com cobertura global. Nas áreas não directamente relacionadas com a negociação de activos, prestamos serviços de dados e estudos, formação, consultoria e outras soluções. Publicamos regularmente relatórios sectoriais para ajudar os participantes no mercado a compreenderem melhor tendências, a identificarem oportunidades e a mitigarem riscos. Além disso, disponibilizamos programas de capacitação que ajudam as empresas a aprofundarem o seu conhecimento sobre os desafios associados à acção climática. Prestamos igualmente serviços personalizados ao longo de toda a cadeia, desde o inventário de emissões de carbono e o planeamento de trajectórias de redução de emissões até à definição de soluções de compensação. Através deste modelo integrado, que combina actividades de negociação e serviços não transaccionais, procuramos criar um ecossistema sustentável de activos ambientais e serviços verdes, permitindo que as empresas que necessitam de soluções nesta área as encontrem na MEX. Quais os principais marcos já alcançados pela MEX? Em primeiro lugar, concretizámos o nosso posicionamento estratégico de utilizar Macau como ponto de apoio para ligar a China ao mercado internacional de carbono. Macau tem vindo, gradualmente, a afirmar-se como um centro activo do mercado de carbono na Ásia. Até Agosto deste ano, o volume acumulado de créditos de carbono negociados através da MEX tinha ultrapassado 1,17 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO2-e). Já o volume de certificados de energia renovável negociados ascendia a 2,07 milhões de certificados. Contamos actualmente com 146 membros registados na nossa plataforma. Logo no dia da nossa inauguração, concluímos as primeiras negociações envolvendo cerca de 870 mil toneladas de créditos de carbono, abrangendo uma dezena de sectores em cinco países. Esperamos que, através da adopção de um conjunto de normas rigorosas e de uma governação sólida, os produtos disponibilizados através da MEX se tornem sinónimo de elevada qualidade. Somos a única instituição de Macau que é membro da Associação Internacional de Comércio de Emissões. Estabelecemos igualmente parcerias com outros membros e organizações internacionais e mantemos uma cooperação aprofundada com diversas instituições académicas e industriais de referência a nível mundial no sector. Estas colaborações, ao promoverem o reconhecimento mútuo de activos, a integração de sistemas e a harmonização de normas, posicionam Macau como um verdadeiro pólo de ligação entre os vários mercados de carbono da Ásia e do mundo. A nível nacional, a MEX formou alianças e assinou acordos de cooperação estratégica com várias instituições, com o objectivo de promover conjuntamente o desenvolvimento de um ecossistema de finanças verd

artigo.texto: Uma das maiores empresas de auditoria e consultoria do mundo, a PWC, projeta US$ 11,4 bilhões em investimentos em data centers no Brasil em 2026. O valor é 49,3% maior em relação a 2025, que foi de US$ 7,6 bilhões. A informação foi publicada no jornal ‘Folha de S. Paulo’. No entanto, o mercado ainda aguarda a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenters (Redata), sancionado pelo governo no dia 15 de setembro. Há indefinições com relação a impostos estaduais na implantação de projetos de centro de dados. O cálculo é que o Redata abra caminho inicialmente para planos de investimento de R$ 20 bilhões no Brasil. Entre as empresas que devem fazer esse aporte incluem as americanas Ascenty e Scala, a britânica Terranova e a brasileira Takota. O Brasil é o quinto maior destino de recursos em datacenters no mundo em 2026. Os investimentos são liderados pelos Estados Unidos (US$ 448,4 bi), seguidos da China (US$ 48,9 bi), Índia (US$ 28,2 bi) e Alemanha (US$ 16,7 bi). No mundo, os investimentos devem chegar a US$ 828,4 bilhões só este ano. Um estudo recém-divulgado da FGV Projetos estima que a implantação de um único datacenter, incluindo a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, mobiliza cerca de R$ 25 bilhões em investimentos totais. A instituição calcula que aproximadamente 12.560 empregos diretos e indiretos são gerados durante a fase de construção e implantação. Desse total, cerca de 1.860 postos são permanentes, incluindo equipes de operação, manutenção e serviços de apoio ao empreendimento. O setor calcula investimentos de R$ 500 bilhões até 2030 em centro de dados. A capacidade atual dos datacenters no Brasil gira em torno de 730 MW, mas a previsão é de saltar para 3,2 GW em quatro anos, com foco em atender o processamento de inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: 07/10/2026 - 13:34 Os FIIs de data centers abrem uma nova frente de financiamento para a infraestrutura digital no Brasil. A AZ Quest Panorama estruturou um fundo para adquirir ativos da Scala, enquanto a Alianza mantém em avaliação a criação de um veículo listado dedicado ao segmento. As estratégias buscam transformar imóveis e instalações de data centers em fontes de renda por meio de contratos de longo prazo. O avanço ocorre em paralelo ao Redata, regime tributário voltado à atração de investimentos para o setor. AZ Quest capta R$ 482 milhões para fundo de data centers O AZ Quest Panorama Data Centers (AZDC) captou R$ 482 milhões na primeira emissão e reuniu mais de 7 mil investidores, conforme as informações apresentadas pela gestora. O fundo adquire ativos da Scala e os aluga de volta à companhia. A estratégia inclui um data center em Fortaleza e três subestações, com contrato de dez anos e janelas específicas de recompra. Para Marcos Freitas, gestor de fundos imobiliários da AZ Quest Panorama, o modelo acrescenta uma alternativa às fontes de capital já utilizadas pelas empresas, como dívida corporativa e financiamento de projetos. “A gente traz uma nova fonte de capital, que é usar os ativos imobiliários que elas possuem como forma de financiamento do capital de giro e dos investimentos dessas companhias”, explicou ao InfoMoney. Remuneração depende do prazo e das condições de recompra O AZDC foi estruturado como fundo cetipado, com prazo determinado de dez anos. Segundo Freitas, a remuneração prevista parte de IPCA mais 9,5% ao ano, no cenário de permanência até o décimo ano. Em determinadas hipóteses de recompra antecipada, pode alcançar IPCA mais 10,5% ao ano. Os percentuais correspondem aos cenários descritos pela gestora e dependem do cumprimento das condições da operação. A proposta é oferecer exposição a ativos existentes, sem investir diretamente no desenvolvimento de um novo data center. “É um fundo que tem começo, meio e fim”, afirmou Freitas. A gestora informa que os rendimentos são isentos, enquanto ganhos de capital e amortizações têm tributação de 20%. A isenção dos rendimentos não se estende, portanto, a todos os valores recebidos pelo investidor. Alianza mantém plano de separar ativos do ALZR11 A Alianza considera transformar sua exposição a data centers em um fundo listado específico. O projeto de separação dos ativos, conhecido como spin-off, permanece condicionado à melhora das condições de mercado. Fabio Carvalho, sócio da gestora, aponta o nível dos juros e o tamanho crescente dos projetos como obstáculos. Segundo ele, empreendimentos que antes demandavam cerca de R$ 200 milhões passaram a alcançar R$ 700 milhões. Essa escala dificulta a compra integral por um único fundo. A Alianza avalia formas de participar de projetos maiores sem adquirir a totalidade dos ativos. O ALZR11, de estratégia multiestratégia, é citado pelo executivo como um veículo com flexibilidade para investir no segmento. Contratos longos sustentam a tese de renda Para Carvalho, a duração dos contratos é uma das características centrais dos data centers como ativos imobiliários. A carteira existente conta com contratos com mais de uma década restante. Novas operações poderiam ser estruturadas com prazos de 15 ou 20 anos, conforme o executivo. Essa duração favorece o planejamento das receitas, mas a criação de um fundo dedicado ainda depende da viabilidade das aquisições e das condições de financiamento. Redata amplia perspectiva de investimentos no Brasil O Redata foi sancionado em setembro de 2026 e prevê incentivos tributários para equipamentos utilizados em data centers. O acesso aos benefícios exige autorização do Ministério da Fazenda e contrapartidas das empresas. Freitas avalia que o regime, combinado às características energéticas e à posição geopolítica brasileira, pode favorecer projetos destinados ao mercado doméstico e a clientes de outros países. A Associação Brasileira de Data Centers estima R$ 500 bilhões em investimentos até 2030, com aumento da capacidade instalada de 730 MW para 3,2 GW. Para os FIIs, a expansão representa uma oportunidade de adquirir ativos com contratos longos. A concretização de novos veículos dependerá do custo de capital, da escala dos projetos e das condições negociadas com os operadores. artigo.texto: Nigeria is set to strengthen the integrity and credibility of its emerging carbon market through the deployment of robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) systems, as the Federal Government seeks to attract large-scale private investment into climate action. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs. Omotenioye Majekodunmi, disclosed this at a high-level roundtable on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) Protocols,” convened under the European Union Climate Dialogues programme in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. Represented by the Director, Energy, Transportation & Infrastructure of NCCC, Mr. Michael Ivenso, the Director-General said Nigeria was determined to ensure that carbon markets translate the country’s climate commitments into tangible economic opportunities while preventing greenwashing and protecting the interests of communities, investors and project developers. According to the Director-General, “carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits,” stressing that Nigeria would not accommodate a carbon market that lacked transparency, credibility and environmental integrity. Mrs. Majekodunmi said the country’s objective was to ensure that carbon projects delivered real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes, while contributing to community development, environmental protection and fair returns for project developers and investors. READ ALSO: Nigerian President Approves Carbon Market Framework The Director-General said carbon markets were not a panacea for Nigeria’s climate and development challenges, but argued that, when supported by transparency, credible MRV systems and effective stakeholder collaboration, they could become a major catalyst for sustainable development. The NCCC Boss, therefore, urged participants at the roundtable to move beyond discussion and develop an actionable and time-bound roadmap capable of positioning Nigeria as a leading destination for high-integrity carbon investment in Africa. “A major component of the new approach is the operationalisation of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry. “The registry is expected to provide a digital record of carbon credits generated, issued, transferred and retired in Nigeria, thereby helping to prevent double-counting and strengthening the integrity of carbon transactions.” She explained. The NCCC also plans to accelerate the adoption of digital Measurement, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) technologies, including remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies. The technologies are expected to reduce the cost and time required to verify carbon projects while improving the accuracy and reliability of emissions data. The Director-General explained that without effective MRV systems, buyers would be unable to determine whether claimed emissions reductions were genuine, regulators would face difficulties tracking emissions and safeguarding against double-counting, while communities could struggle to monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. The NCCC called for stronger collaboration among federal ministries, state governments, private-sector operators, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. Head of section, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms. Yolanda San Jose, said carbon markets are playing an increasingly important role in supporting emissions reductions, mobilising finance, and encouraging investment. According to her, this is why Nigeria took a very important step last year by adopting its National Carbon Markets Framework. It established a structured legal and institutional system for domestic and international carbon trading under the Climate Change Act (2021) and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The Framework is the foundation for confidence, trust, and effectiveness in Nigeria’s emerging carbon market system. Ms. Jose noted that, for Nigeria, the development of a strong national carbon market system is both imperative and a significant opportunity, and would help align climate targets with development priorities, support investment, and create an enabling environment for a low-carbon future. “Today’s event is intended to help shape that pathway. In particular, we aim to align stakeholder views around Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework and to discuss a preliminary roadmap for its operationalisation. We will do so by emphasising the robustness of so-called Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) practices, to ensure that this market mechanism delivers credible results for both the Nigerian people and the environment.” She added that the European Union is pleased to support this process in partnership with Nigeria. Representing the Ministry of Environment, Mrs Halima Bawa-Buhari said the ministry is working towards a partnership that will lead to a robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system and a high-integrity carbon market, contributing significantly to the Securing Nigeria’s Forest Future (SNFF) financing roadmap. One of the development partners, UKPACT Officer, Ms Folakemi Aletan, said a well-functioning carbon market in Nigeria represents more than a climate policy instrument. She said it provides an opportunity to mobilise investment, support sustainable development, strengthen competitiveness and ultimately mobilise climate finance. The representative of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), Mrs Nifesimi Ogunkua, said; “the organisation is supporting the National Council on Climate Change through a partnership agreement to strengthen the operationalisation of Nigeria’s carbon market framework.” She said the support includes the design and deployment of a digital portal for managing the lifecycle of carbon credit projects. Please enter the email address you use for your account so we can send you a link to reset your password: Local opposition has exacted a much higher cost for developers than has been previously understood, according to new Heatmap Pro survey of public records and financial information. The country’s largest technology companies are expected to spend more than $800 billion this year investing in data centers and artificial intelligence. But new data suggests the local backlash to data centers may be taking a meaningful bite out of that boom. At least $260 billion of data center investments were canceled this year after sustained local opposition, according to new Heatmap Pro data. The pace and size of those cancellations is picking up. About $130 billion in data center investment — or about half of the total — was canceled in the three months ending on September 30. And in dollar terms, the size of canceled projects in the third quarter of 2026 exceeded the size of all data center projects canceled last year. Roughly $1 trillion in data center investment now faces some kind of sustained or meaningful local opposition, according to Heatmap Pro data. About half of all projects that have met local backlash this year were ultimately canceled, our data suggests. Our market intelligence service Heatmap Pro tracks local projects and regulations affecting clean energy, batteries, and data centers. We run a continuous survey of public officials, regulatory filings, and local media to monitor energy and data center cancellations nationwide. Our investment figures, which have not been previously published and are larger than other estimates, are likely an undercount. Only about 60% of data center projects disclose the size of their planned investment, especially during a proposal’s early stage when it is most likely to run aground. These figures also do not include every project currently stalled because of state-level data center moratoriums in Texas and New York. But the totals show that the surging backlash to data centers is beginning to kill a sizable share of large computing projects. In August, a Heatmap Pro and Embold Research poll found that 75% of Americans would oppose a data center getting built near where they live — a striking change from a year earlier, when Americans were roughly split over the projects. “The number of canceled data centers speaks to the vast and growing grassroots opposition to these projects in communities across the country. The fact that many of these projects were defeated in just the past few months speaks to the upward trajectory of this opposition movement,” Mitch Jones, a policy director at Food and Water Watch, an environmental group that opposes AI data centers, said in a statement. A spokesperson for the Data Center Coalition, which advocates for the industry, did not respond before press time. Most canceled data center projects in our database are terminated because they fail to secure a local permit or face a hostile local government action. Hundreds of U.S. counties and towns now maintain a ban or moratorium on data center construction, our data shows. The Senate’s bipartisan permitting reform proposal would not affect towns or counties’ ability to prohibit data center development under their jurisdiction.

artigo.texto: Côte d’Ivoire has shortlisted developers for two 100MW solar photovoltaic plants, each paired with 33MWh of battery storage, as the country moves to close the gap between its 45% renewables target by 2030 and a grid that currently runs on thermal power for roughly two thirds of its installed capacity. The two sites — Dabakala in the north east and Niakaramandougou in the centre of the country — will each be awarded as 25-year independent power producer (IPP) concessions covering design, financing, construction, operation, and maintenance. The concessions run through Ci-Energies, the state electricity utility, and the procurement was launched last year before advancing to shortlist stage, according to Africa Energy. The scale of the ambition is thrown into relief by the starting point. The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) counted just 40MW of installed solar capacity in Côte d’Ivoire at the end of 2024. Thermal generation accounted for approximately 69% of the country’s 2,907MW of installed capacity as of 2023 — a grid profile that makes absorbing intermittent solar generation difficult without storage. The 33MWh of battery storage specified at each site addresses that integration problem directly. A predominantly thermal grid has limited tolerance for the midday surges that solar produces; battery systems capture that output and release it when demand rises after dark, smoothing the load curve and reducing curtailment risk that would otherwise undermine the economics of new solar investment. The procurement sits within the Pacte National Énergie, the government’s overarching framework for reaching 45% renewables — including hydropower — in the national electricity mix by 2030. The framework also encompasses Côte d’Ivoire’s ambition to position itself as a power exporter to neighbouring countries, giving the grid stability question a regional dimension: reliable, dispatchable renewable capacity is a prerequisite for cross-border supply agreements. West Africa’s power interconnection landscape makes that export ambition credible. Côte d’Ivoire already supplies electricity to several neighbours through the West African Power Pool (WAPP), the regional body coordinating grid integration across the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Adding dispatchable solar-plus-storage capacity strengthens the country’s ability to honour export commitments regardless of time of day or weather conditions. For developers shortlisted on the two concessions, the 25-year contract horizon and the involvement of Ci-Energies as the offtake counterparty provide the long-term revenue visibility that project finance for utility-scale renewables typically requires. The move to award stage will be closely watched as a signal of how quickly Côte d’Ivoire can translate procurement ambition into contracted capacity.

artigo.texto: Developer and creator Tom Shaw sat down with Meta’s Head of Infrastructure, Santosh Janardhan, to talk about Meta’s approach to building infrastructure to power the future of AI. Santosh explained why Meta is more than just a software company, how AI is different from any other technology, and why data centers are essential for building AI. artigo.texto: harhar38/Shutterstock Save for later Print Download Share LinkedIn Twitter The essential role that battery energy storage systems (Bess) will play in the energy transition is widely recognized, and investment continues to flood into battery assets. But to make the best use of these, it is essential that operators have a clear picture of all aspects of operations. And the only way to ensure that picture is complete is to collect, assess and analyze data in detail. Battery technology continues to advance across a broad front, with cell density and cycle performance achieving new limits alongside developments in battery chemistry and improvements to degradation curves. In this context, it is unsurprising that the International Energy Agency should have reported that global battery storage deployment expanded “strongly” last year, with total capacity additions reaching 108 gigawatts, up around 40% from 2024. Indeed, batteries are now big business, but hardware doesn’t hold the keys alone: It is harmony between strong software and strong hardware that generates the best results. In recent years, there have been no technological breakthroughs significant enough that an operator would consider wholly replacing a fleet of batteries years before the end of their operational life. It is therefore all the more important that asset managers maximize the potential of hardware that is already in place — and software is key to this. Shifting Mindsets: Viewing Energy Assets as Data Generators There is a constant trade-off in the energy industry between “revenue today” and “revenue tomorrow.” For batteries, this is especially important, as every decision influences the wear and tear on the system: Push them too hard during the early years and you shorten their useable lifetime, but hold out for future revenue and you risk this never actually materializing. To help asset managers strike the best balance, every choice — across both commercial and technical asset management — needs to be as robust as possible. And data is the golden thread running through these twin tracks of decision-making. Modern batteries continuously generate vast amounts of operational intelligence and data on a sub-second basis, from state of charge and thermal metrics to state of health and electrical values. Collecting all this information is a vital first step. Then this needs to be put to work to help site operators improve an asset’s performance and “lifetime value” — i.e. the total revenue across an asset’s lifespan. This metric is the ultimate north star for an asset manager in Bess. For example, a leading Bess owner saw a $110,000 uplift per annum from a single existing 75 megawatt, 1-hour system on Ercot, the Texas power grid system, by realizing the benefits of a more accurate “state of energy” reading and embedding this into their operations. Data as the Money Maker An essential part of commercial asset management is ensuring that the highest-performing technical asset is transacting in the most suitable market at the right time to make the most money. There are three main markets when it comes to Bess assets. Firstly, there are the core energy arbitrage possibilities — charging when the price of energy is low and discharging when it is high. Then there are also capacity/reserve markets (when the battery is paid to be available for a given period) and grid stability services whereby system operators, such as the National Energy System Operator in the UK, procure batteries to help maintain system stability by having them respond in milliseconds to fluctuations in the frequency of the grid. Decisions around which market to monetize a battery in typically fall with third-party optimizers, who are in turn reliant on technical asset managers maximizing the availability of the portfolio. Each party can utilize data to inform and elevate their judgements at different stages of the process. The more visibility into metrics around availability, reliability and underlying performance which stakeholders can exploit, for instance, the more they will be able to position their strategy for targeting the best market at the best time — to make the best returns. Minimizing Downtime Dig deeper into the technical management of a battery asset and it again becomes clear how crucial data is in achieving the perennial aim of having a battery system perform at as close to 100%, as much of the time as possible. With this in mind, leveraging insights can enable asset managers to streamline their approach to maintenance. There are several key performance indicators that asset managers need to track constantly. These include the headline concerns around availability and degradation, as well as round trip efficiency (how much energy is lost between a charge and discharge cycle), cycles per day (how much energy has flowed through the battery for a given time period), and warranty compliance (is the system operating within the bounds of the manufacturer’s warranty). The recent heatwaves have also thrown a spotlight on the issue of temperature performance and the need to adjust cycles/market choices when it is extremely hot. Granular data can help asset managers spot more quickly when a system is falling short against one — or more — of these metrics, and to see not just the symptoms of a problem but the root cause. Asset managers can then look to harness data to target the most efficient window to take assets off line for maintenance, whether it be opting to accelerate a maintenance intervention to make an asset ready for a predicted high revenue period or deciding that the cost of a higher tier of service level agreement from a maintenance contractor is worth it to bring a battery and its income-making potential back on line faster following an issue. The cumulative effect of each optimized technical decision quickly builds to a meaningful difference in results and competitive standing. artigo.texto: BETHLEHEM, Pa. — Bethlehem City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday to give initial approval to the city’s first zoning rules for data centers, which face a final vote Oct. 20. Bethlehem’s zoning code currently treats a data center like any other industrial use, with no added limits, Planning and Zoning Director Cathy Fletcher told council. The new rules would add a public hearing, require studies on water, power, noise and heat, and keep data centers at least 1,000 feet from homes and schools. The rules will not cover the one data center already proposed in the city, a project on Industrial Drive that could not be built under them. During the nearly three-hour hearing, Councilwoman Jo Daniels said the rules fall short in the areas that matter most to residents. Other council members argued that passing them now is better than leaving data centers unregulated. Get the latest laws & regulations news and updates from across the Valley. By subscribing, you agree to our Privacy Policy and consent to receive updates. Most of the 24 people who spoke during public comment urged council to pass the rules and strengthen them over time. Daniels and Councilman Bryan Callahan both said during the hearing that they did not expect to vote for the rules. Both voted yes. The Industrial Drive project The proposed data center is a two-story building with a 65,000-square-foot footprint at 2184 Industrial Drive, replacing the former Crowder Service Center building along Route 22. Boyle Construction and Paxos, both of the Lehigh Valley, and Tensor IQ of Newark, Del., proposed the project. The site is in the city’s Planned Industrial district, where the ordinance would not allow data centers. City zoning and parcel maps also show every part of the 6.75-acre lot is within 1,000 feet of residentially zoned property. Because its application was filed before the amendment, it will be reviewed under the current code, Fletcher said. The project goes before the city Planning Commission at 5 p.m. Nov. 12 in the Town Hall Rotunda, where the public can comment, Council President Rachel Leon said. Get the latest laws & regulations news and updates from across the Valley. By subscribing, you agree to our Privacy Policy and consent to receive updates. That local review carries added weight under a state order. Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order on data centers on Aug. 18. Under it, the state Department of Environmental Protection will not issue a permit unless the project “has received all required local approvals.” The order also bans nondisclosure agreements, which keep project details secret, on data center projects. What the rules do State law requires every municipality’s zoning to allow every legitimate land use. That means Bethlehem cannot ban data centers or write rules so strict that one could never be built. Under the amendment, data centers would be allowed only in the city’s Industrial district, not its Planned Industrial district, and only by special exception. That means an applicant would need approval from the Zoning Hearing Board at a public hearing, in addition to the usual Planning Commission review. The city Planning Commission voted 4-0 on Aug. 25 to recommend the rules. In a review letter, the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission called them “a thoughtful and intentional response to a complex land use.” Applicants would have to submit several studies and plans with their application, including an environmental study, water and sewer approvals, an energy plan, an emergency plan, a decommissioning plan, a heat plan, a lighting study, and noise studies before and after construction. Noise would be measured at the property line. The post-construction noise study would be due one to 12 months after the city clears the building for use. Buildings would have to sit at least 80 feet from property lines, up from 20 feet for other industrial uses. The setback grows to 200 feet next to any non-industrial lot. It grows to 1,000 feet from a residential district or an existing home, school, day care, park, hospital, or recreation center. That is 50 times the current 20-foot minimum. Larger buildings would also require larger lots. Fletcher said a data center under 50,000 square feet could cover no more than 50% of its lot, down from 65% for other industrial buildings. The limit tightens as buildings grow, she said. Councilwoman Hillary Kwiatek later returned to the rule to walk the audience through it. The rule means “the bigger the building gets, the even huger the lot size has to be,” Kwiatek said. Under the ordinance, each square foot of building between 50,000 and 250,000 square feet needs 3 more square feet of land. Above 250,000 square feet, each added square foot needs 5 more. By that math, a 250,000-square-foot data center would need a lot of about 16 acres, and a 500,000-square-foot one would need about 45 acres. Where the rules stop Fletcher said the city cannot require yearly reports once a data center opens. Zoning Officer David Taylor said post-approval inspections would largely be driven by complaints. Councilman Justin Amann said a zoning fine of $500 a day “is not going to be an issue” for a data center operator. City Solicitor Jack Spirk said the city could also seek a court injunction to stop a violation. Jill Seitz, chief community and regional planner for the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission, said state law limits what zoning can cover. The state Department of Environmental Protection oversees air quality, and the Public Utility Commission oversees electric service, she said. A regional planning commission guide on the meeting’s materials table, “5 Questions for Legally Defensible Data Center Regulations,” makes the same point. It says local rules hold up best when they address measurable effects, such as noise, lighting, building height, and setbacks. artigo.texto: DeepSeek is close to raising at least 80 billion yuan, or about $12bn, in a new funding round, Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday. Tencent and the battery maker CATL have committed some of the largest sums, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. The Chinese AI lab had first set out to raise about 50 billion yuan. Demand grew after the launch of its latest model, Bloomberg said, and the final total could approach 100 billion yuan. DeepSeek has not announced the round. At these levels, it would top the company’s first outside funding earlier this year. That round raised about 50 billion yuan at a valuation of $52bn to $59bn. Founder Liang Wenfeng was the largest investor in that first round, putting in about 20 billion yuan of his own money. Tencent added roughly 10 billion yuan and CATL about 5 billion yuan, alongside JD.com, NetEase and China’s national AI investment fund. Those same two backers now lead the new round. Tencent runs the WeChat messaging app and a large cloud business. CATL makes batteries for electric cars and is working on solid-state batteries. For Tencent, becoming more closely associated with DeepSeek could enable it to keep up with its domestic competitors. This was reported by Reuters in June when the first round of the comparison was being prepared. Last month, Reuters reported that DeepSeek had secured CITIC Securities to prepare for a possible initial public offering on Shanghai’s STAR Market, a market board for technology companies. However, they said that the timing, valuation and scale of the listing had not yet been determined. DeepSeek originated from High-Flyer, the quantitative hedge fund which Liang set up. The laboratory attracted widespread attention around the beginning of 2025 due to its R1 open-source model and launched its V4 models this year. artigo.texto: Google has been ordered to halt work on two data centers it's developing in Finland, a month after the tech giant committed to investing $15 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure in the country. Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency, or LVV, on Tuesday issued a notice to Google subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend building work for data center projects planned for Muhos and Kajaani until the environmental impact assessments have been completed. The suspension request applies, among other things, to the removal of trees, removal of topsoil, excavation, quarrying, crushing, transfer of soil masses, ditching, and the construction of roads and storage areas, according to a Google translation of an LVV press release. "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance," a Google spokesperson told CNBC, adding that it would follow the LVV's guidance. "We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas," the spokesperson said. "As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares [320 acres] at Muhos." The LVV ordered Google to halt work no later than Oct. 23. The request does not apply to planning, measurements, soil surveys, or other measures with minor impacts that can be easily restored. "In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure," Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at the Finnish licensing and supervision authority, said in the statement. 'Texas of Europe' Finland has emerged as a key location for data centers amid the AI boom, with hyperscalers and developers eyeing its available land and power, which is in short supply throughout most of Europe. Several data center projects with potential capacities of hundreds of megawatts have recently been announced in the country. The rise in demand has led to Finland being dubbed the "Texas of Europe." The U.S. state has become one of the leading locations for AI data centers globally, with a number of huge projects announced by hyperscalers and AI labs, including Google, Meta, Microsoft and Anthropic. Google's $15 billion plan for Finland will mark its largest investment in Europe. The capital will be deployed through 2028 into data centers and other supporting investments like energy projects, the company said in a statement at the time.

artigo.texto: The tech industry would build data centers twice as fast without the supply constraints they face, the CEO of Nokia told CNBC, underscoring continued demand for AI even as top executives debate slowing down the pace of development. "I don't think you can say in any manner we're overbuilding today because reality is that if we could build 2x faster, our customers could build 2x faster, they probably would," Justin Hotard told CNBC's "The Tech Download" podcast. "So that gives me confidence that we're still in the early days" of the AI buildout, Hotard added. Shortages of key memory chips and energy are among the supply constraints facing the sector. Nokia, one of the world's biggest telecommunications equipment makers, has pivoted to become a key player within the AI infrastructure space. It sells the technology required to connect racks of chips within data centers as well as technology that interconnects data centers across different locations. Nokia's growing role as a "picks and shovels" player in the AI boom appears to have won over investors, with the stock up around 130% over the past year. But there's been continued debate over whether the industry is building data centers too fast and whether demand will be there to sustain it. Investments in the AI buildout from data centers to chips and related infrastructure will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032 — an average of 3.63% of U.S. gross domestic product per year, according to research presented at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity. Companies are using debt, joint ventures and other complex financing mechanisms to raise investment for these projects, which depend on sustained demand for AI services over the long term. Concerns about the pace of the AI buildout were exacerbated by safety worries sparked by an Anthropic researcher's warnings on the existential threat of the technology, which prompted the company's CEO Dario Amodei to call for a slowdown in the development of the most advanced models. That sparked a knee-jerk sell off in AI-related stocks last month. Hotard said that demand for AI is not just predicated on frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI releasing new models. "I think the reality is that we're even where we are today is so early in the deployment, and the power of these models is so massive that there's a lot of there's a lot of demand to run in just deploying," Hotard said. "Even if we didn't have another frontier model released in the next three years, we could probably make tremendous progress just deploying the technology that's there today."
