artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution Targets EV Commercialization on 2029, Focusing on Cost and Application-Specific Designs While Samsung SDI Pushes Faster Mass Production With Supply Chain Deals and Sulfide-Based Technology As the commercialization of solid-state batteries comes into sight, technological competition within the domestic battery industry is also beginning in earnest. While Samsung SDI is accelerating efforts up to establishing a material supply chain with the goal of mass production next year, LG Energy Solution puts more weight on securing technological differentiation and cost competitiveness rather than the timing of commercialization. According to the industry on Oct. 7, LG Energy Solution is aiming for the commercialization of graphite-based solid-state batteries for electric vehicles (EV) in 2029, and the commercialization of anode-free solid-state batteries for next-generation applications such as humanoid robots in 2030. A solid-state battery is a battery that changes the electrolyte, the pathway through which lithium ions move, from the existing liquid to a solid. It is also called a ‘dream battery’ as it does not use a flammable liquid electrolyte, thereby lowering the risk of fire and increasing energy density. However, complex manufacturing processes and high production costs are considered challenges that need to be solved for mass production. Rather than rushing commercialization, LG Energy Solution has chosen a strategy of subdividing its technology to fit actual applications. The plan is to secure competitiveness by varying the battery structure according to the required performance, rather than targeting all markets with a single solid-state technology. The company is also developing dry electrode technology to lower high manufacturing costs. This is interpreted as a strategy to lower equipment and process costs as well as production time by reducing the organic solvents and drying processes required in the existing wet process. This comes from the judgment that securing both mass producibility and economic feasibility is important for solid-state batteries to compete in price with existing lithium-ion batteries. In comparison, Samsung SDI is stepping up to establish a supply chain with the goal of commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries faster around next year. It recently signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with EcoPro BM and agreed to cooperate from the development of core materials such as sulfide-based solid electrolytes and cathode materials for solid-state batteries, to quality evaluation and the establishment of a mass production system. EcoPro BM is operating a sulfide-based solid electrolyte pilot plant with an annual capacity of 40 tons. The two companies, which had previously been cautious about disclosing their specific cooperative relationship, have formalized their collaboration for the commercialization of solid-state batteries through this MOU. An industry official said, “The solid-state battery is a market where technological prowess determines competitiveness,” and added, “Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution will engage in a competition for dominance with differentiated strategies that utilize their respective strengths.”

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI See Combined Share Fall 11.1 Percentage Points Amid Weak North American Demand and LFP Shift South Korea’s three major battery makers are losing ground in the global electric vehicle battery market outside China. While the overall market grew by more than 20%, battery usage by Korean companies fell by double digits, sending their combined market share down more than 11 percentage points in a year. At the same time, Chinese battery makers continued to expand their presence, putting further pressure on Korean companies. SNE Research, an energy market research firm, said Oct. 7 that total EV battery usage in countries outside China reached 360.5 gigawatt-hours (GWh) from January through August this year. The figure was up 23.7% from the same period last year, exceeding the 19.7% growth of the global EV battery market as a whole. Despite the broader market expansion, combined battery usage by LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI totaled 96.5 GWh, down 12.8% from a year earlier. Their combined market share consequently fell sharply to 26.8% from 37.9%, a decline of 11.1 percentage points. The primary factor behind the deterioration was weakening demand in North America. The three Korean companies’ combined battery usage in the region fell to 25.3 GWh from 47.4 GWh a year earlier, a 46.5% decline. The demand gap that emerged following the expiration of the U.S. EV tax credit has dealt a direct blow to Korean battery makers. By company, LG Energy Solution retained second place in non-China markets with battery usage of 58.1 GWh, but its market share fell 5.1 percentage points to 16.1%. SK On dropped from fourth to fifth place after its usage declined 14.4%, while Samsung SDI fell to seventh after recording the steepest decline among the top 10 companies, with usage down 32.0%. As Korean companies saw their market shares shrink, Chinese battery makers continued to gain ground. CATL ranked first in non-China markets with 121.3 GWh, up 43.3% from a year earlier, giving it a 33.7% market share. BYD, which ranked third, also increased its usage by 66.5%, raising its market share to 11.0%. Several smaller Chinese battery makers also posted triple-digit growth, further increasing competitive pressure on Korean companies. Gotion, SVOLT and EVE Energy recorded growth of 147.2%, 105.2% and 185.6%, respectively. The combined market share of six Chinese battery makers reached 56.2%, surpassing half of the non-China market for the first time. The shift in market share coincides with the rapid expansion of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. LFP’s share of the non-China market rose 11.9 percentage points in a year, from 15.6% to 27.5%. The growing adoption of lower-cost LFP batteries in Europe and North America is creating a more favorable environment for Chinese battery makers, which have maintained a stronger position in the LFP segment. Korean battery makers are seeking to offset weaker utilization in North America by tapping demand for energy storage systems (ESS) and data centers. Battery usage in Europe increased 5.2%, maintaining modest growth, but the continued expansion of Chinese-branded EV sales in the region could make it more difficult for Korean companies to regain market share. An SNE Research official said local production capacity and price competitiveness, along with supply chain traceability capabilities needed to prepare for the battery passport taking effect next February, will determine companies’ market positions. The ability to respond to regional policy changes and diversify demand sources is expected to be critical to Korean battery makers’ efforts to recover market share.

artigo.texto: O Brasil se prepara para realizar, em dezembro de 2026, seus primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade destinados especificamente a sistemas de armazenamento em baterias. Mais do que introduzir uma nova tecnologia no sistema elétrico, os certames podem criar uma classe de ativos de infraestrutura, com contratos de longo prazo e potencial para movimentar uma ampla cadeia de equipamentos, engenharia, software e serviços. Para aprofundar as reflexões sobre o assunto, a KPMG produziu a publicação Armazenamento de Energia: a nova indústria que o Brasil pode construir. O interesse do mercado já é expressivo. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) recebeu 6.091 projetos, que somam 296.807 MW de potência. Trata-se do maior número de inscrições já registrado em certames do setor elétrico promovidos pelo governo federal. O volume cadastrado, entretanto, não corresponde à capacidade que será habilitada ou contratada. Os projetos ainda passarão por análise técnica, e o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) estima contratar entre 5 GW e 6 GW nas duas modalidades previstas. Por que o Brasil precisa de sistemas de armazenamento? A expansão das fontes solar e eólica aumentou a disponibilidade de energia renovável, mas também tornou mais complexa a coordenação entre geração, consumo, transmissão e segurança operacional. Durante o dia, a produção solar reduz a demanda atendida pelas fontes controladas pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). No fim da tarde, essa geração diminui rapidamente enquanto o consumo permanece elevado. O sistema precisa, então, disponibilizar um grande volume de potência em poucas horas. As baterias podem armazenar energia nos períodos de maior oferta e disponibilizá-la quando o sistema mais precisa. Sua resposta rápida também pode contribuir para a estabilidade da rede, reduzir parte do curtailment — o corte ou a limitação da geração disponível — e, em situações específicas, postergar investimentos em transmissão e distribuição. O armazenamento deve, portanto, ser entendido como uma infraestrutura que proporciona flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico. Seu valor não se limita à capacidade instalada, mas inclui a contribuição para a confiabilidade da rede, a integração das fontes renováveis e o melhor aproveitamento dos ativos existentes. Como funcionarão os primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia? Os certames estão previstos para dezembro de 2026. O primeiro deles será destinado a sistemas que comprovem o uso de baterias com fabricação nacional, de acordo com critérios cuja verificação caberá ao Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). Já o segundo será aberto aos demais projetos elegíveis, inclusive aqueles que utilizem equipamentos importados. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início do suprimento previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. Requisitos anunciados: - Potência mínima de 30 MW. - Capacidade de descarga durante quatro horas. - Eficiência mínima prevista de 85%. - Despacho centralizado pelo ONS. - Possibilidade de até dois acionamentos diários. - Prazo máximo de seis horas para recomposição da carga. A remuneração será realizada por meio de uma receita fixa mensal vinculada à disponibilidade do ativo. Quais fatores determinarão a viabilidade dos projetos? A previsibilidade da receita cria uma condição importante para o financiamento dos projetos, mas não elimina a complexidade dos empreendimentos. A localização será um dos fatores decisivos. Como a bateria funciona como carga durante a recarga e como fonte durante a descarga, o ponto de conexão precisa suportar os fluxos nos dois sentidos. A capacidade remanescente da rede e os eventuais custos de reforço também poderão influenciar a competitividade do projeto. Outro aspecto central é a degradação. As baterias perdem gradualmente parte de sua capacidade à medida que são utilizadas. O modelo econômico-financeiro deve prever como o sistema continuará atendendo às obrigações contratuais durante os 15 anos, considerando sobredimensionamento inicial, reposição de módulos, manutenção, eficiência e exposição cambial. A escolha dos fornecedores também não pode ser orientada apenas pelo menor preço. Histórico de desempenho, capacidade produtiva e financeira, garantias, segurança contra incêndio, cibersegurança, assistência técnica e disponibilidade de peças são elementos essenciais para a sustentabilidade do ativo. Qual é o potencial para a indústria brasileira? Um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (Battery Energy Storage System - BESS) envolve muito mais do que células e módulos. A cadeia inclui inversores, transformadores, sistemas de gerenciamento, proteção, climatização, combate a incêndio, automação, software, contêineres, obras civis, montagem, integração, operação e manutenção. O Brasil já possui competências em engenharia, equipamentos de potência, automação industrial, construção e montagem. Nos primeiros ciclos, o conteúdo nacional poderá se concentrar nessas atividades, enquanto a dependência externa tende a ser maior em células e determinados componentes eletrônicos. Para que os leilões gerem desenvolvimento industrial, será necessário combinar conteúdo local, competitividade, escala e previsibilidade. A continuidade das contratações poderá ser tão importante quanto o volume do primeiro certame para estimular investimentos produtivos e desenvolver conhecimento no País. Como transformar contratação em criação de valor? Os projetos mais sólidos não serão necessariamente aqueles que apresentarem apenas o menor custo dos equipamentos. A criação de valor dependerá da capacidade de integrar localização, conexão, tecnologia, financiamento, tributação, conteúdo nacional, contratos, execução e gestão do ciclo de vida. Os primeiros leilões podem representar uma nova etapa para a infraestrutura elétrica brasileira. O desafio será transformar o interesse do mercado em projetos seguros, financiáveis e capazes de gerar valor durante toda a vigência dos contratos.

artigo.texto: Créditos de carbono: Não olhe apenas para o preço. Os créditos de carbono não só abrem novas fontes de receita, como também ajudam as empresas a melhorar suas capacidades de gestão de emissões, atender às demandas do mercado e criar valor agregado à marca. O valor de um crédito corresponde a uma tonelada de carbono reduzida. O mercado de carbono vietnamita está entrando em uma fase operacional com muitas oportunidades, mas também com maiores exigências para as empresas. Investir em créditos de carbono requer custos com tecnologia, medição, inventário, verificação e gestão de dados, enquanto a receita da venda de créditos nos estágios iniciais pode não ser suficiente para fornecer incentivos financeiros diretos. No entanto, o valor dos créditos de carbono não reside apenas na receita das transações. O processo de criação de créditos também está ligado à melhoria da capacidade de gestão de emissões, ao atendimento aos padrões de mercado, à ampliação do acesso ao financiamento verde e ao fortalecimento da posição da empresa na cadeia de suprimentos. A história da Thanh Thanh Cong - Bien Hoa Joint Stock Company (AgriS) é um exemplo disso. A empresa registrou 4.375 créditos de carbono provenientes de seu projeto de fertilizante orgânico Verra (VCS), que segue padrões internacionais, e emitiu 25.000 certificados de energia renovável I-REC. A planta de Ba Tra, especializada no processamento de subprodutos agrícolas, deverá gerar aproximadamente 9.600 créditos de carbono anualmente. A AgriS também firmou um acordo bilateral de transferência de créditos de carbono com um parceiro de Singapura , nos termos do Artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris. Segundo a empresa, a receita direta proveniente da venda de créditos de carbono atualmente não contribui de forma significativa para sua estrutura financeira. O que motiva as empresas a continuarem investindo? Em sua apresentação no Fórum de Carbono do Vietnã 2026 “Da Política à Ação”, o Sr. Tran Tan Viet, membro do Conselho de Administração da AgriS, afirmou que a participação precoce no mercado de carbono contribui para fortalecer a reputação e o posicionamento das empresas no mercado internacional. Diversos fundos de investimento e instituições financeiras têm explorado essa possibilidade de forma proativa, abrindo assim mais oportunidades para que as empresas acessem fontes de crédito verde. O ponto crucial é que nem todas as atividades de redução de emissões geram automaticamente créditos de carbono. O Sr. Nguyen Tuan Quang, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente , afirmou que os projetos devem atender aos requisitos de complementaridade, integridade e sustentabilidade; a quantidade de redução de emissões deve ser mensurada, validada e comprovada por dados suficientemente confiáveis. Esse requisito estabelece a base para a qualidade do mercado de carbono. Quando os créditos são utilizados em transações domésticas ou em mecanismos de cooperação internacional, a capacidade de mensurar e verificar as reduções de emissões é um fator crucial para a aceitação no mercado. Quando a demanda do mercado impacta a produção Você também pode gostar A pressão para reduzir as emissões já não provém apenas das políticas ambientais. Os requisitos para o desenvolvimento sustentável, a responsabilidade ambiental nas cadeias de abastecimento e os novos mecanismos comerciais estão a impactar cada vez mais as atividades de produção e exportação. De acordo com o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, Chefe Adjunto do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono da Agência de Alterações Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e do Ambiente, os processos relacionados com os créditos de carbono precisam de garantir transparência, rigor e conformidade com as práticas internacionais. No que diz respeito à cooperação internacional ao abrigo do Artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris, a Agência de Alterações Climáticas está a coordenar com os parceiros o desenvolvimento de formulários, diretrizes e procedimentos detalhados. O Dr. Nguyen Hung Minh, Vice-Chefe do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono da Agência de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, afirmou que o Vietnã está aprimorando seu sistema de políticas e leis de resposta às mudanças climáticas. A Lei de Proteção Ambiental de 2020, cujo Artigo 139 estabelece a base legal para a organização e o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono, juntamente com as regulamentações subsequentes, concretizou gradualmente o inventário de gases de efeito estufa, a medição, a comunicação, a avaliação, a alocação de cotas de emissão e a operação do mercado de carbono. Entretanto, as exigências dos mercados internacionais estão se tornando cada vez mais claras. O Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) da União Europeia impacta diretamente diversos setores, como aço, cimento, alumínio, eletricidade e hidrogênio. No setor da aviação, o CORSIA também gera demanda adicional por créditos de carbono. Essas mudanças tornam a capacidade de gerenciar e fornecer dados de emissões cada vez mais parte integrante dos requisitos para atividades de produção, negócios e exportação. Para empresas que participam de cadeias de suprimentos internacionais, a capacidade de demonstrar desempenho ambiental pode afetar sua capacidade de atender aos requisitos de parceiros e expandir a cooperação. Segundo estimativas, o Vietnã poderá enfrentar um déficit de carbono de aproximadamente 2,3 milhões de créditos de carbono até 2028, o que equivale a uma necessidade de financiamento de cerca de US$ 92 milhões, caso o preço por crédito se mantenha em US$ 40 por tonelada. Esses números demonstram que o mercado de carbono está cada vez mais integrado a diversos setores da economia , da produção industrial e exportações à aviação e finanças. Em nível empresarial, o planejamento antecipado pode, portanto, oferecer certas vantagens. O Grupo TH é um exemplo disso, tendo começado a medir as emissões de carbono em toda a sua cadeia

artigo.texto: Chinese Battery Makers Grab 34% Share Outside China; South Korea's Big Three Slump to 27% Chinese battery manufacturers are rapidly expanding their market share in the global EV market outside China. From January through August this year, usage volumes for Chinese players including CATL and BYD surged sharply in non-China markets, while the combined share of South Korea's three major battery makers—heavily reliant on North America—fell below 30%. According to data released on October 7 by SNE Research, a specialized energy market research firm, total battery usage in battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) registered outside China from January through August reached approximately 360.5 GWh. That represents a 23.7% increase year over year, outpacing the global overall growth rate of 19.7% by 4.0 percentage points. However, the monthly growth rate for August alone slowed to 9%. SNE Research attributed this to the impact of the North American demand vacuum becoming more pronounced in monthly figures. Broad-Based Growth for Chinese Players CATL solidified its No. 1 position with 121.3 GWh of usage, up 43.3% year over year. Its market share climbed 4.7 percentage points from 29.0% to 33.7%. In Europe, usage rose 30.4% from 61.8 GWh to 80.6 GWh, while in Asia it more than doubled to 24.0 GWh. BYD maintained third place with 39.7 GWh, up 66.5%. Its share rose 2.8 percentage points from 8.2% to 11.0%. Usage grew broadly across Europe (14.5 GWh, +65.6%), Asia (13.2 GWh, +41.7%), and South America (6.2 GWh, +138.5%). Growth among later-entrant Chinese players was even steeper. Gotion High-tech surged 147.2% to 14.4 GWh, SVOLT jumped 105.2% to 11.4 GWh, and CALB rose 77.6% to 8.4 GWh. EVE posted the highest growth rate among the top 10 companies at 185.6%, reaching 7.5 GWh. South Korea's Big Three Fall Across the Board on North American Weakness The combined market share of South Korea's three major battery makers dropped 11.1 percentage points from 37.9% to 26.8%. The decline in usage was concentrated in North America. The trio's North American usage fell 46.5% from 47.4 GWh to 25.3 GWh, while Europe rose 5.2% from 49.9 GWh to 52.5 GWh and Asia increased 33.0% from 11.2 GWh to 14.8 GWh. LG Energy Solution posted 58.1 GWh, down 5.8% year over year, but held onto the No. 2 spot in non-China markets. European usage rose 9.8% to 31.3 GWh and Asia grew 44.4% to 9.2 GWh, but North American usage tumbled 42.3% from 25.2 GWh to 14.6 GWh, dragging down overall results. Its market share fell 5.1 percentage points from 21.2% to 16.1%. SK On remained in fifth place with 24.8 GWh, down 14.4%. Its share slipped 3.0 percentage points from 9.9% to 6.9%. North American usage fell 41.8%, and Europe also declined 1.5%. Samsung SDI posted the steepest decline among the top 10 companies, falling 32.0% to 13.6 GWh. Its share contracted 3.0 percentage points from 6.8% to 3.8%. European usage was roughly flat year over year at 8.3 GWh, but North American usage plummeted 62% from 10.4 GWh to 3.9 GWh. Japan's Panasonic ranked fourth with 29.7 GWh, up 1.8%. Tesla's North American volume underpinned its performance, but with growth well below the non-China market average, its share fell 1.7 percentage points from 10.0% to 8.3%. Non-China Market Usage and Share by Major Player Note: January–August 2026, excluding China market. Share change is versus the same period last year. Gotion High-tech's share was not disclosed. Policy and Supply Chain Capabilities Will Be Decisive SNE Research projected that regional policies and customer diversification will determine supplier competitiveness going forward. The research firm said, "Local production capacity, price competitiveness, and supply chain traceability capabilities in preparation for the battery passport regime taking effect next February will be the key variables determining market position." The rise of Chinese players reflects simultaneous penetration of the European market and expansion across Asia. South Korean manufacturers, by contrast, took a direct hit from slowing North American EV demand driven by policy shifts including the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Given their heavy North American exposure, the shock of market contraction was proportionally severe. Investors and industry observers see the key question for South Korean battery makers as how quickly they can capture the timing of a North American demand recovery while sustaining growth in Europe and Asia. Given the pace of Chinese players' price competitiveness and production capacity expansion, securing next-generation battery technology and supply chain transparency—beyond simply defending market share—is expected to be the crux of long-term competitiveness. artigo.texto: For nine months, the Rev. Edward Moultrie of St. Paul CME Church and his congregation filled county meetings, urging officials to reject a proposal for a massive data center near their church and homes. They warned that the project near Walterboro, South Carolina, would threaten the waterways they rely on and bring pollution to their doorstep. On Monday, they won. In January, two weeks after Capital B first wrote about the proposal, residents sued Colleton County over its effort to change the zoning code to allow data centers in rural areas. This week, the Southern Environmental Law Center reached an agreement with the county to resolve that lawsuit. The fight in Colleton County underscored a pattern in where these facilities are proposed. Last year, after a majority-white county in Georgia blocked a data center, the data center developer, Eagle Rock Partners, proposed a similar project in Colleton County, where the share of Black residents is nearly twice as high. Analyses have found that communities closest to U.S. data centers regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency are “overwhelmingly” nonwhite. Moultrie said the settlement “is a relief.” “I can’t preach to my people that God is making a way for them and offering them hope, and then have something like this come into the community to take people’s hope away,” he said. “Black people here have worked hard all their lives to survive and thrive and protect their land. It gives us some kind of sense of pride knowing that we’re not going to go by the wayside or be destroyed or taken for granted — for now.” With the settlement, the county has agreed to establish a “Data Center Exclusion Area” that prohibits data centers across the majority of the ACE Basin in Colleton County, which is a rural area home to ecologically sensitive animals and some of the most important waterways in South Carolina. The exclusion area includes the land where the data center was proposed in December 2025. The data center would have been over 800 acres, making it one of the largest in the South, which has become the epicenter of data center development. “I have lived in the ACE Basin my entire life, right here in Colleton County. My family has been here for generations. The original data center complex that was proposed would have surrounded my property on three sides and completely changed the area,” said Miles Crosby, one of the residents who brought the lawsuit. “I’m thankful we could reach an outcome that not only prevents data centers from surrounding my home but also protects the majority of the ACE Basin in Colleton County from data center development.” In the first half of 2026, at least 115 data centers nationwide were blocked by local residents. The blocked projects’ price tags totaled roughly $200 billion, according to Data Center Watch, a group tracking data center development. At the same time, data center development continues to climb. August saw the most money ever spent on data center construction in the U.S., up more than 73% over the past 12 months. The struggle for local Black communities is not over. A new fossil fuel plant, partially proposed to keep this and other data centers running, is moving forward in a majority-Black area located in Colleton County. The methane gas power plant would result in more than $30 million in local health care costs as residents begin to struggle through respiratory illnesses, according to a pollution analysis by the Southern Environmental Law Center. The pollution from gas power plants — fine particulate matter known as PM2.5 — can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer. Black Americans have the highest death rate from such pollution in the U.S. Chris DeScherer, the South Carolina office director for the Southern Environmental Law Center, said the group will continue to “help ensure that any data center projects in Colleton County and beyond are developed responsibly with respect to surrounding communities and natural resources.” Read More:

artigo.texto: BYD Sealion 6 Adds All-Wheel Drive in South Korea…Dual-Motor Setup Hits 100 km/h in 5 Seconds BYD Korea has added an all-wheel-drive (AWD) trim to its plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV, the Sealion 6 DM-i, and began taking pre-orders on the 6th. The strategy is to broaden choices beyond the existing front-wheel-drive (FWD) single configuration to respond to diverse driving environments and consumer preferences. The newly unveiled Sealion 6 DM-i AWD places electric motors with peak output of 150 kW (204 horsepower) on both the front and rear axles. The front motor produces 300 Nm of maximum torque, while the rear motor delivers 340 Nm, giving the rear axle greater rotational force. The vehicle accelerates from a standstill to 100 km/h in 5.0 seconds, a configuration that emphasizes the instant acceleration response characteristic of electric motors. Along with the AWD system, dedicated Mud and Sand terrain modes have been applied to ensure driving stability on rough surfaces such as unpaved roads. The goal is versatility that spans urban commuting as well as weekend leisure and outdoor activities. Battery and Charging Performance The vehicle is equipped with a 26.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery. It can travel 93 km in pure electric mode under South Korea's Ministry of Environment certification, allowing daily short-distance driving to be operated like a fully electric vehicle. On the charging front, it supports approximately 18 kW DC fast charging and features V2L (Vehicle-to-Load) capability with up to 3.3 kW of external power output. This allows the vehicle battery to power electronic devices during outdoor activities such as camping. Convenience features have also been upgraded compared to the existing trim. The audio system uses HARMAN's premium brand Infinity sound system, with a total of 10 speakers including a subwoofer. A head-up display (HUD), multi-color ambient lighting, metal door sill plates, and dynamic ceremony lighting have been applied to elevate the interior ambiance. The driver's seat supports 8-way power adjustment with memory function. Pricing and Market Strategy The Sealion 6 DM-i AWD starts at ₩41.9 million (approximately $31,000). BYD Korea stated, "By adding AWD, we have broadened the range of choices according to customers' driving environments and preferences," adding, "We plan to continue introducing products that consider the diverse lifestyles of South Korean consumers and to continuously strengthen product and service experiences." artigo.texto: Berlin-based ebike startup Lemmo has been shaking up the European market with a small selection of handsome mid-range models since 2022. It's now got something in the works for families and more adventurous riders with a versatile SUV ebike that promises to take you places while delivering an exceptionally comfortable ride. The Lemmo 3 is a long-tail ebike with room for cargo in the front and rear, plus pannier bags and up to two child seats. It sports a full suspension setup, a hydraulic seatpost, and all-terrain tires to soak up bumps and make it a breeze to cover all kinds of surfaces. The brand says this model is three years in the making, and includes plenty of tech for safety, performance, and convenience that you'd expect to see on the latest ebikes. It's also capable of covering longer distances than just your usual city commutes. Let's talk suspension first. A high-load spring for the rear suspension affords 80 mm of travel to ensure your little passenger is comfortable. Up front, you've got hydraulic forks that deliver 80 mm of travel too. Meanwhile, the seatpost offers 20 mm of travel as well. Closer to the asphalt, 65 mm wide all-terrain tires offer cushioning and stability while riding with heavier cargo. Lemmo's gone with a 960-Wh semi-solid state battery, which reportedly allows for up to 110 miles (180 km) of range and won't go up in flames from punctures or thermal runaway incidents. This pairs with a rear hub Bafang H720 motor that's rated for 750 W of continuous power in the US (500 W in Canada, and 250 W in Europe), and a three-speed automatic gearbox. This setup allows for a pedal assist up to 28 mph (45 km/h). With this kind of kit, the Lemmo 3 should be up to the task of tackling steep inclines and all manner of rough terrain. The brand says its direct steering makes it easier to maneuver than conventional cargo bikes, despite its long wheelbase. Riders ranging from 5ft1 (155 cm) to 6ft5 (195 cm) can enjoy a comfy upright riding position thanks to the adjustable stem and seat. If you plan to take this out on the trail on camping trips, it'll happily handle up to 176 lb (80 kg) of gear in the rear, and an additional 44 lb (20 kg) on the front rack. There's some neat tech on here too, including GPS tracking and a motion detection alarm for security, a 3.5-inch touchscreen displaying your riding metrics, a rear-approaching radar with automatic brake lights, and keyless start. That makes this a compelling option for people looking for a more versatile ebike than the vast range available for riding only around town. Lemmo is scheduled to crowdfund this model on Kickstarter later this month, during which the Essential model will be available at about US$2,155. That's discounted down from its expected MSRP of €3,390 ($3,890) – but it requires an early reservation on Lemmo's site with a refundable $45 deposit. You can add on a belt drive for an extra $193. There are also a couple of bike bundles which include accessories like a passenger guardrail, seat pads and foot boards, pannier bags, and a front rack. With that, Lemmo's set to go up against the Amflow TL Carbon we saw earlier this year. That's another capable SUV ebike, with a powerful motor and swappable add-on battery – at a slightly higher price above the $4,000 mark. Check out the Lemmo 3 on the company's site, and head here for the Kickstarter campaign that's yet to go live at the time of writing (you can sign up to be notified when it takes off). If all goes as expected, orders are estimated to begin shipping next April in the aforementioned regions. Source: Lemmo

artigo.texto: Elon Musk's data centers are pushing out a family that's owned land since "before people of color were allowed to" On a 2-acre property in Mississippi, 52-year-old Krystal Polk's family lived off the land for generations, raising chickens and pigs, growing onions and herbs and trading their peaches for pears. The land, on the border with Tennessee in the city of Southaven, was her family's survival, Polk said. "We lived a very simplistic life," she told CBS News. While life there may have been simple in Polk's view, the circumstances surrounding her home rarely ever were. Her family acquired the property "before people of color were allowed to have land," she said, and it's been passed down for four generations. When Polk's parents first moved in, they discovered "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill of their property, she said. Holding on to the land was made more difficult a year ago when a noisy neighbor appeared across the street — a power plant so loud, it drove the family away. Since then, the land has sat mostly empty, occupied only by an unrelenting hum. The plant, which is powering Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the Memphis area, has sparked backlash from Southaven residents concerned about noise and air pollution. A petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plant has over 1,400 signatures. Polk said she remembers when she could hear the birds chirping at her family home. Now, she said the plant's "constant roaring" lingers in her ears even after she leaves. "It's like you're in the middle of the airport where the planes are taking off, but they never take off," she said. SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, recently said in a July press release that it is investing millions of dollars in sound walls and silencers with "advanced quieting technologies" around the plant. Southaven residents have told CBS News that one sound wall installed so far has provided little reprieve from the noise. "We gathered there" Over the course of two years, Musk has expanded his footprint in the Memphis region starting with the construction of his Colossus 1 data center just north of Southaven in 2024. By January 2026, two more data centers were announced. This July, Musk quietly confirmed the construction of another local data center, "Minihard," in a reply to a post on his platform X. Musk's SpaceXAI projects will total more than $20 billion in investments to Southaven, which Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a press release will "bring amazing opportunities to its residents for generations." But for Polk, the development has meant a new kind of strain on her family. "We don't know the future," she said. "So we're not sure what to invest into it." Polk moved away from the family home after getting married, and for years, it bounced between relatives. It was where Polk churned her own ice cream as a child, held her rehearsal dinner when she got married and hosted the holidays each year. "We gathered there and we thanked God for what we had," she said. "It was always a celebration." She planned to return as a retiree and eventually pass the property down to her children. But now, those plans have been put on hold. Apart from the "24/7" noise, Polk said she and her family have asthma and are concerned about fumes from the gas turbines at the plant. "I'm afraid that we will be the ones that everyone looks back on and says, 'Hey, remember they tried to tell us that these things were hazardous to our health and causing harm,'" Polk said. "I'm afraid that we're going to be those casualties." The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and other groups sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in April, alleging that the plant "emits significant amounts of harmful pollutants." In June, SpaceXAI filed a motion to dismiss the case, and the Department of Justice also moved to intervene and dismiss the case. The Justice Department said in a statement that the matter "concerns national security and Mississippi's lawful action regarding permitting" and that the NAACP's lawsuit "could hinder the War Department's use of AI for national defense." CBS News reached out to SpaceXAI multiple times for comment and has not heard back. The company has entered into an agreement with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality that includes removing the 69 temporary turbines at the plant and replacing them with 41 permanent turbines over the course of a year. But a study conducted by EmPower Analytics Group found that the plan to install dozens of gas turbines would increase air pollution in the area and would be concentrated in communities that are disproportionately Black. The study was commissioned by the Southern Environmental Law Center, which is co-counsel for the plaintiffs in the NAACP's lawsuit against xAI and MZX Tech. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said in a statement that it doesn't comment on "third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation" and that it "remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations." MDEQ said that as part of the permitting process, MZX Tech was required to demonstrate that the proposed facility would not violate air quality standards. Still, residents are not convinced. Shannon Samsa, a 27-year-old physician assistant living in Southaven, is concerned about the plant's impact on her community's health. She's become an outspoken advocate against the plant, speaking up at city meetings and leading the Safe and Sound Coalition as its director. "It's not just my neighbors, it's not just my family and friends, it's my future patients," she said. "It's also a huge healthcare issue." artigo.texto: A moratorium on the facilities that enable artificial intelligence would last 45 days and could be extended to 22 months. The data centers powering artificial intelligence technology — and the accompanying public outcry — are officially something San Francisco city leaders can’t ignore. The San Francisco Board of Supervisors on Tuesday unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on data centers that would pause city approvals of the facilities and task the Planning Department with studying their impacts and developing long-term controls. The moratorium now awaits action from the mayor. “During this period, we are looking at issues including energy, water, air quality, land use, and community impacts, while working toward stronger protections and meaningful community input, as well as a data center definition that is clear to everyone,” said Supervisor Shamann Walton, who authored the moratorium. Tuesday’s vote is a significant step as city leaders grapple with the wider land use and infrastructure impacts of one of the city’s biggest exports. By November, city leaders will convene a hearing about progress by the Planning Department and its findings on data centers. The moratorium could be extended to 22 months, but it’s unclear whether city leaders would entertain the idea. Walton represents District 10, which stretches from Visitacion Valley and Bayview Hunters-Point to Potrero Hill and Dogpatch. His district has two of the six data center sites in San Francisco, according to market intelligence firm Data Center Map (opens in new tab). His district may have been eyed for a third one. In August, a lobbyist for a private equity firm advertising a 1.6-acre data center (opens in new tab) met with two of Mayor Daniel Lurie’s policy chiefs about planning and building permits for a waterfront plot of land in Dogpatch. The cities of Oakley, Richmond, and Gilroy already have moratoriums on data centers, while Oakland and Hayward are considering it. The Land Use and Transportation Committee advanced Walton’s proposal to the full board. At the committee’s Monday meeting, more than a dozen people showed up in support of the moratorium on new data centers. Among them was Arieann Harrison, a Bayview resident and executive director of the Marie Harrison Community Foundation (opens in new tab). She said her community already deals with worse health outcomes than other parts of the city, triggered by the industrial facilities located in District 10. “We need for this committee right here to stand on business when it comes to the health outcomes of our districts,” Harrison said at the Monday meeting. Walton’s proposal is among his final priorities in office. He was first elected in 2018 and will term out in January. All three of the frontrunners in the race to replace him on the Board of Supervisors are supportive of a data center moratorium. “Transparency about water and energy demands enforceable community benefits and a real opportunity for residents to weigh in before projects are approved, not after,” Walton said at the Monday committee meeting. Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the moratorium takes effect immediately. It awaits action from the mayor. More about the author Omar Rashad reports on San Francisco government and politics.

artigo.texto: First Look: West Feliciana’s data center Parish president says tax revenue and transparency were priorities in deal WEST FELICIANA PARISH, La. — A data center under construction in West Feliciana Parish will serve as a processing hub for Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence model when it opens in just over a year. Water usage and energy consumption are top concerns as Louisiana positions itself for a national A.I. build-out. Size and scope The data center will measure roughly 10 football fields long once completed. Projects of similar size elsewhere in the country have raised concerns over groundwater usage and rising electric bills for nearby residents. Parish President Kenny Havard said protecting the community against those issues was part of his goal. The developer Hut 8 is partnering with Entergy for a new substation on site that will power the project, fully funded by the company. On top of that, the data center will be using a closed-loop coolant system that replaces the need for tapping groundwater. “One was water and the other was taxes, we wanted to make sure everyone in West Feliciana Parish pays the same taxes whether you’re big industry or the local grocery store,” Havard said. Tax revenue and community funding Havard said the data center will bring in $90 million in tax revenue every year. That money will go back into the community through funding, infrastructure projects and rebates on property taxes. “We would have to build 6,000 houses to pay for one mile of road the way the taxes are distributed so this allows us to keep the quality of life that makes West Feliciana such a special place,” Havard said. Transparency in the deal process The agreement was made without non-disclosure agreements or private negotiations, according to Hut 8’s Hailey Miller. “Working with the parish president and parish council, a deal was done in public view, in open, transparent and for everyone to have input and consideration,” Miller said. State and political reaction Gov. Jeff Landry has pointed to more than $200 billion in industrial development during his time in office. Landry pushed back against critics of transparency in deals, who say secrecy is sometimes necessary to attract large projects. “Everything we’ve done to change policy in this state has been in the public so the public gets to grade us on that, this just says when these companies come in we don’t tell anybody they are coming in. Why? Because we want to keep them here!” Landry said. Many of Hut 8’s data centers across the country mine bitcoin rather than power artificial intelligence models like the one at River Bend. That connection brought bitcoin investor Donald Trump Jr. to the site. “People understand generally that you need AI, its the space race of 2026, its a really big deal there’s another reason why China is funding 200,000 bots on Twitter trying to vilify AI, its not because its bad for America, its because America leading is bad for China and we need to do that while still addressing the needs of the community,” Trump Jr. said. Construction timeline About 1,200 construction employees are working day and night to complete the project. The data center is expected to be operational by the end of 2027. artigo.texto: Em Brasília, a CNA recebeu na terça-feira (6) integrantes da Nuffield, rede global de produtores e especialistas do agro voltada à formação de lideranças e ao intercâmbio de conhecimento. O grupo reuniu representantes de Brasil, Holanda, Irlanda, Malaui, Zimbábue e Austrália. Elena Castellani, responsável pela área internacional da CNA, destacou o perfil produtivo brasileiro e explicou frentes da CNA, do Senar e do Instituto CNA, como inteligência técnica, capacitação, defesa de interesses, representação e apoio gerencial e técnico a produtores. A comitiva passou ainda pelo Instituto CNA, onde viu tecnologias voltadas ao setor agrícola. A ferramenta de dados da CNA despertou dúvidas sobre como as informações são coletadas, analisadas e implementadas. PSA, sigla de pagamento por serviços ambientais, e mercado de carbono regulado foram apontados como desafios comuns a vários países. Para Jackie Morrison, da Nuffield Austrália, o encontro ampliou a leitura que o grupo fez do Brasil. Segundo ela, os participantes entenderam que o país pode ser concorrente e parceiro de cooperação. Criadora de mel em parceria com o marido, ela investiga desde 2023 o Manejo Integrado de Pragas (MIP) para apoiar a apicultura australiana diante do ácaro Varroa destructor. Luciana Kliemann, que integra a Nuffield Brasil e cultiva grãos em Mato Grosso do Sul, considerou relevante apresentar a CNA ao grupo após uma programação internacional voltada a soluções, inovação e contato com produtores. Além do Brasil, o roteiro passou por Austrália, França, Romênia, China e Cingapura, com atividades em setembro e outubro de 2026. No período, os participantes analisaram modelos de produção, políticas, inovações e desafios ambientais e comerciais do campo.

artigo.texto: Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson’s recent defense of data centers presents a fundamentally flawed economic development narrative (“When judging data center incentives, don’t ignore the revenue,” Sept. 30). While he touts short-term revenue, his ledger ignores the long-term, structural costs these facilities impose on local communities. First, using job creation to justify data center subsidies is a sleight of hand. While $1.2 billion in construction permits is impressive, they’re short-term bumps in revenue. This masks the reality that data centers are essentially ghost towns once operational. They consume prime industrial real estate but employ only a small number of permanent staff members, meaning taxpayers are often subsidizing millions of dollars per permanent job. Furthermore, major tech companies rely on specialized, traveling construction crews. The economic multiplier effect largely leaves town when the concrete dries. Second, the mayor’s claim that Class 6B incentives don’t harm homeowners ignores the basic math of Illinois property taxes. When a data center’s assessed value is artificially slashed, the local tax levy doesn’t shrink. The burden simply shifts onto everyone else, driving up residential tax bills for 12 to 24 years. This is compounded when tax increment financing districts are used, such as the one Elk Grove Village created for the Vulcan Construction Materials site in 2022. While the mayor suggests schools stand to benefit, it should be noted TIFs divert new tax revenue to pay for project costs for up to 23 years, meaning schools and municipal services wait decades for the promised windfall. Worse, once operational, these operators frequently deploy aggressive legal teams to appeal their property assessments year after year, forcing municipalities to spend taxpayer dollars defending their own revenue. Finally, while data centers don’t add students to classrooms, they place enormous, invisible strains on our infrastructure. Their construction increases wear and tear on local roads from construction vehicles. Once completed, they are massive consumers of municipal water for cooling and place unprecedented demands on the electrical grid. These upgrades are eventually paid for by everyday ratepayers. Subsidizing heavily automated server farms that hollow out industrial parks, generate negligible employment and strain our grid is not the “pro-growth” policy our region needs. — Donald Guisinger, Strong Towns Oak Forest Will data centers pay fair share? Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson in his op-ed completely ignores the higher cost of water and electricity that his constituents will face subsidizing these monstrosities. Will he demand that data centers pay their fair share for the high volume of water and electricity they use? Or is it too late? — Ken Perez, Wood Dale Department of Justice’s credibility I am hopeful that with the recent focus on the “Broadway Six,” in particular due to the reporting of Tribune reporter Jason Meisner, the public will begin to understand that when prosecutors go unchecked, victims face extreme consequences for which they have very little redress. In recent years, the credibility of the U.S. Department of Justice has fallen to all-time depths as it has been weaponized against those with whom it disagrees, both political and nonpolitical, taking up positions not supported by the facts or even the law. This is on full display in Chicago. U.S. District Judge April Perry is being asked to consider disciplinary action against the U.S. attorney’s office for alleged misconduct in the grand jury investigation and prosecution of the “Broadview Six.” No justice system can function effectively if there are components within it that disregard the rules and mechanisms of checks and balance. The public relies upon this system to keep prosecutors in line, to punish misconduct and to send a message that misconduct cannot be tolerated. Misconduct is anathema to justice. — Michael Segal, U.S. National Title Services, Chicago Celebrate parking meter deal? No. Regarding Chicago’s parking meter deal, what a demonstration of ineptness and buffoonery — this is the 2026 edition of the 2008 disaster. As a Chicago resident and motorist, I have one simple question: Will it cost me less to park? Nothing I’ve read about this deal — a transfer fee, percentages of a future sale and net income, a “city wallet” program and 25- to 50-cent-per-hour surcharges for non-Chicagoans — suggests that it will benefit the great majority of drivers in Chicago. And as for the City Council’s self-congratulation over the deal: same-o, same-o. A final question: Where’s Mayor Brandon Johnson? — John Mjoseth, Chicago I support the arts in the city Thank you for the editorial regarding suburbanite parking in Chicago ( “Chicago may charge suburbanites more to park. How neighborly,” Oct. 1). I am a suburbanite who supports the Joffrey Ballet, the Chicago Architectural Center and the Art Institute with subscriptions to their events. I do attempt to take public transportation when I can, but that is not always feasible, since as the editorial mentions, timing for public transportation is sparse on the weekends. For example, a friend and I have Joffrey season tickets for its Sunday matinees, but trying to coordinate Metra and “L” train times with that is difficult. Although driving into town is stressful, we brave it by going down early to enjoy a great lunch at Italian Village before the show. And yes, we look for cheap parking because we’re already supporting businesses and cultural events. Also, because we are both in our 70s, we cannot park too far from the venue just to find an extremely cheap parking lot; we would then need a taxi to get to the Lyric Opera House. In short, considering our generous monetary contributions to the city of Chicago, asking us to pay more for parking really takes the cake! — Dianne Casuto, Lake Forest Naperville’s welcoming vibe Thank you for say

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) planeja avançar nas políticas para data centers, cabos submarinos, rodovias e inclusão digital ainda neste ano, afirmou nesta terça-feira, 6, o secretário de Telecomunicações, Hermano Tercius, durante o evento Futurecom, em São Paulo. Um passo importante nesse sentido deve ocorrer na quinta-feira, 8, quando o secretário vai apresentar a política nacional de data center e de cabos submarinos à Casa Civil. A expectativa é de que os planos saiam do papel ainda em 2026. Tercius deixou claro que "apenas o Redata não resolve" as demandas do setor de data center. O anseio do MCom é estimular a instalação de infraestruturas pelo território brasileiro, tanto data centers de borda como complexos para hyperscalers. No caso dos cabos submarinos, o secretário afirmou que a política setorial deve ampliar os pontos de ancoragem pela costa brasileira – atualmente, ainda estão bastante concentrados em Fortaleza, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador e litoral de São Paulo. Segundo exemplificou Tercius, a implantação do cabo Malbec em Porto Alegre já atraiu mais de R$ 4 bilhões em investimentos para a região Sul. Desse modo, a ideia é viabilizar pontos de ancoragem para cabos em outras localidades do País, como Belém e Recife. "Já mandamos para a Casa Civil a política pronta. Uma parte pode vir por portaria, outra tem que ser pelo Congresso", disse o secretário. "Com isso, a gente espera atrair para o Brasil mais data centers e fazer um cinturão digital nos próximos quatro anos", pontuou. Inclusão digital e rodovias O secretário ainda afirmou que a Política Nacional de Inclusão Digital (PNID) deve ser lançada em novembro – no mais tardar, no início de dezembro. A pasta ainda avalia se a política será implementada via portaria ou decreto. Em conversa com jornalistas, Tercius adiantou que o plano prevê um voucher para contratação de banda larga fixa ou móvel, de modo a subsidiar parte dos custos com o serviço, e medidas de letramento digital. Já a Política Nacional de Conectividade de Rodovias (PNCR) deve ser publicada ainda este mês, após alinhamento com o Ministério dos Transportes. Cada pasta deve publicar uma portaria, indicou o secretario. "A política vem sendo executada desde o início do ano. O que a gente vai fazer é uma portaria para dar um salto, levando em conta a questão do roaming, que queremos liberar e obrigar. [O ministério dos] Transportes vai pôr isso em concessões para ter cobertura nas rodovias federais", sinalizou.

artigo.texto: Silicon anodes can store around ten times more charge per gram than graphite and can support faster charging, but silicon swells by 300–400% as it charges, which has historically wrecked its cycle life. The silicon anodes now reaching EVs are silicon-graphite (or silicon-carbon) hybrids that deliver around 20% more range than graphite equivalents, with fewer charge cycles and a higher cost. Graphite remains the industry standard, but silicon is now in production cars. Lithium-ion batteries are the cornerstone of EV technology and most consumer electronics, and their basic architecture hasn't changed dramatically for decades. While cathode chemistries have evolved to give batteries different properties, the anode has almost always been graphite – sometimes with a few percent of silicon oxide blended in for a small capacity boost. Graphite became the staple anode material because it is stable and low cost, but there are other anode materials with a much higher specific capacity that could make EV batteries far more energy dense. The problem has been commercialising them. Related:Volkswagen and Gotion plan flexible LFP cell production across EV and energy storage applications Silicon is the best example of an anode material with huge potential that has been difficult to commercialise. It has around ten times the specific capacity of graphite and could enable faster-charging, more energy-dense EV batteries with a much longer driving range. However, silicon undergoes large volumetric expansion during charging that has historically degraded cells very quickly and made them unsuitable for commercial use. That is now changing. We're still not seeing pure silicon anodes in EVs, but hybrid anodes that combine silicon with graphite or other carbon materials have reached the market, and Mercedes-Benz has become the first carmaker to offer a high-silicon anode battery in a production vehicle. Silicon vs graphite anodes at a glance How do silicon and graphite anodes work? The silicon vs graphite anode debate has been running for a long time. The anode is a critical part of any battery: it stores lithium ions while the battery charges and releases them when it discharges, sending electrons through the external circuit that powers the EV. Silicon's theoretical specific capacity is roughly ten times that of graphite, which on paper makes it an ideal EV battery anode material. Depending on the material and form, silicon's theoretical specific capacity sits between 3,400 and 4,200 mAh/g, whereas the top end of battery-grade graphite is 372 mAh/g. In theory, a pure silicon anode could hold up to ten times more charge than a graphite anode of the same weight. That doesn't mean a battery with ten times the energy, though, because the cathode and the rest of the cell stay the same – and today's silicon hybrid anodes sit well below silicon's theoretical limit, somewhere between graphite and pure silicon. Related:Geely, NIO partner for Chinese battery swapping network However, specific capacity doesn't tell the whole story, and there's a reason graphite has been the industry standard since the 1990s. Graphite's inherent safety and stability have been key to its longevity, whereas silicon anodes have suffered from rapid degradation as they expand and contract during cycling. Battery safety is paramount to avoid EV fires. Graphite anodes also form a very stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, while silicon's is less stable – one of the reasons current silicon anodes also contain carbon as a stabilising material. Even so, graphite is nearing its practical capacity ceiling, and as demand for longer-range EVs grows, new chemistries are needed to push further. Enter silicon, which offers higher energy density – translating into longer driving range – and the potential for faster charging. Silicon itself is a relatively cheap and abundant material, and there is already a large global silicon supply chain serving the electronics and solar sectors, even if a dedicated silicon anode supply chain is still small. However, making silicon anodes is currently more complex and expensive than making battery-grade graphite, which benefits from decades of high-volume production that have driven costs down. Silicon is already used safely in many high-power electronics, so the main barrier to battery safety and lifespan is the anode's expansion. Related:UK to invest over US$9 billion into EV batteries, but must make up 55GWh supply gap Energy density: How much better is silicon than graphite? Because silicon's theoretical specific capacity is so much higher (3,400–4,200 mAh/g against graphite's 372 mAh/g), its potential energy density is much higher too. But today's cells use silicon-graphite hybrids rather than pure silicon, so they don't come close to silicon's theoretical limits. Most practical hybrid anodes have a specific capacity of 600–1,500 mAh/g – still well above graphite, but the real-world gains are smaller than the headline figures suggest. At cell level, that currently means around 20% more energy density, with up to 40% expected as the technology matures. The gain comes from making the anode smaller. In a lithium-ion cell, the cathode supplies the lithium, and the anode has to be large enough to store it. Graphite's relatively low capacity means the anode takes up a large share of the cell. Silicon offers about ten times graphite's capacity by weight and roughly three times by volume, so a much thinner anode can store the same amount of lithium – freeing space for more cathode material, and therefore more energy, in the same cell. At the upper end, silicon alloys with lithium so that several lithium ions can be stored per silicon atom. The highest theoretical capacity (4,200 mAh/g) comes from the Li22Si5 phase, but the more practical figure demonstrated in studies (3,579 mAh/g) comes from the Li15Si4 phase. artigo.texto: Nigeria will not allow carbon markets that lack integrity or amount to greenwashing, the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) has warned. The director-general of the NCCC, Omotenioye Majekodunmi, yesterday at the European Union Climate Dialogue programme organised by the NCCC in partnership with the EU Global Gateway and funded by the European Union. Majekodunmi, represented by the NCCC director of Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, Michael Ivenso, said the country was determined to ensure that carbon projects delivered measurable environmental and economic benefits. He said global carbon markets offered a major opportunity to mobilise private capital for climate action, but warned that the market would collapse without credible systems for verifying carbon credits. “Global carbon markets present one of the most promising avenues to mobilise this private capital. “However, as I have repeatedly stated, carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits. “A carbon market without rigour is merely an exercise in greenwashing—a scenario that Nigeria will not accommodate,” he said. Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon projects must deliver “real, additional, and permanent mitigation outcomes” while benefiting communities, protecting ecosystems and ensuring fair returns for investors and project developers. She said climate finance was critical to powering clean energy transitions, restoring degraded lands, modernising agriculture, improving waste management and expanding access to clean technologies across the country. The NCCC boss said the operationalisation of Measurement, Reporting and Verification systems was central to building confidence in Nigeria’s emerging carbon market. “Frameworks on paper do not trade carbon—transparent and verifiable data does. This brings us to the core theme of today’s roundtable: Operationalising Measurement, Reporting, and Verification,” he said. “MRV is the backbone of market credibility.” He explained that without credible MRV systems, buyers could not determine whether carbon reductions were genuine, regulators could not properly track emissions, and communities could not ensure fair benefit-sharing. Majekodunmi disclosed that the government was operationalising a unified national carbon registry to prevent double-counting and ensure the integrity of carbon credits generated in Nigeria. “Every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred, or retired in Nigeria will carry a digital footprint to prevent double-counting and guarantee baseline integrity,” he said. He added that Nigeria was moving towards digital MRV using remote sensing, Internet of Things sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to reduce verification costs and improve accuracy. The NCCC identified three immediate regulatory priorities, including finalising carbon market regulations, publishing sector-specific MRV guidelines and establishing local capacity-building hubs for Nigerian auditors and technical experts. Also speaking, the Director-General of the European Commission’s CLIMA Task Force on International Carbon Pricing and Markets, Jop Watering, said the European Union was prepared to deepen its engagement with Nigeria on high-integrity carbon markets. Watering said the EU had 20 years of experience with domestic carbon pricing and was now opening its climate strategy to high-quality international carbon credits. He warned that carbon markets would not succeed if issues surrounding integrity, transparency and accountability were not properly addressed. “If you don’t get the integrity right, the market will just not take off. It will just not be there,” he said. Watering said international carbon-crediting mechanisms had so far failed to fully realise their potential because of accounting loopholes and weak checks and balances. He said the EU wanted stringent methodologies, transparent registries, fair transactions and equitable benefit-sharing to underpin the international carbon market. The Head of Section, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms Yolanda Josaid, credible systems were necessary to ensure transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. She said Nigeria’s National Carbon Market Framework, adopted last year, provided the foundation for domestic and international carbon trading under the Climate Change Act and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The official said a credible carbon market could align Nigeria’s climate targets with development priorities, attract investment and support the country’s transition to a low-carbon economy. The Director of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa Buhari, said Nigeria’s forests remained central to the country’s climate response. She said forests served as carbon sinks, temperature buffers and sources of livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. Buhari warned that carbon market development must support forest conservation rather than create incentives for further exploitation. She called for stronger forest inventories, remote sensing, satellite monitoring and the use of appropriate artificial intelligence technologies to improve carbon measurement. “Forestry, I’d like to remind us all that the forest sector is central to Nigeria’s climate response because forests are both carbon sinks, temperature buffers, reducing natural disaster risk, livelihoods, humans’ primary food source, and famine, among several others,” she said. She also called for stronger coordination among institutions responsible for collecting, managing, validating and reporting forest carbon data. artigo.texto: Panelists debated issues surrounding data centers at a panel sponsored by the O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs on Tuesday. It was moderated by Ken Richards, an O’Neill professor of economics and sustainability. Nationally, just one in nine Americans support the construction of data centers in their communities. Opponents of data centers, which includes all four of the panelists, argue that downsides like noise and air pollution, strained infrastructure and higher utility bills outweigh the potential benefits, which the panelists described as unclear, for local communities. Panelist Justin Ross, a public finance, economics and policy analysis professor, noted the positive economic impacts of data centers. “If you take a look at, like, roads, they don’t directly employ anyone,” Ross said. “It is still crazy to think about their contribution to the economy.” Ross drew parallels between roads and data centers, which often employ few workers, but he argues they could still contribute to the local and national economy. Studies have found employment, wages and income all increase after the construction of a data center in a community. However, panelist Bryce Gustafson, an organizer for the Citizens Action Coalition, Indiana’s largest and oldest consumer and environmental advocacy organization, feels this is an oversimplification of the truth. “Not a lot of local jobs,” he said. “They are specialized jobs.” Gustafson explained that data center employees, who he said are often not local to the area, and the companies who own the centers benefit most from their construction. Gustafson also pointed to the 50-year tax breaks Indiana offers some data centers, which benefit the data center companies and deprive the local community of tax money. Panelist Saul Levin with the Global Center for Climate Justice criticized a frequent Meta talking point, which the company has often raised on what he described as a “press offensive around the country.” “Meta has been advertising all over the country that the Rayville, Louisiana, data centers are responsible for local teachers being granted $50,000 bonuses,” Levin said. “None of the marketing documents mentioned that this was already in local statute.” According to the New York Times, a local ordinance in Rayville mandates that 1% of local sales tax revenue goes to teachers; the huge bonuses for teachers in the town this year are partly due to sales taxes paid by construction workers working on the data center, who will leave after it is built. The panelists also discussed the power dynamics between local communities and data center companies. Levin explained this dynamic by asking guests a simple question. “Raise your hand if you’d be comfortable negotiating against a lawyer who makes $500,000 a year,” he said. No one raised a hand. Wu agreed, asking “(If this is a win-win,) how much win do they get and how much does the community?” The panel also discussed artificial Intelligence bubbles, which is the concern that more money is being poured into AI than the amount of revenue generated. Attendee Wade Catt raised concerns of noise pollution from data centers. He said the noise from data centers poses risks of cardiovascular disease and other negative health impacts. He pointed to Monrovia, a town in southwest Indiana where a data center was recently built. Catt said he knows people living by data centers in Monrovia and elsewhere who have struggled with noise pollution and said their homes have lost equity as a result. Catt also expressed his frustration with a lack of transparency in data center construction, noting that communities often aren’t adequately consulted before construction. “We don’t have the power to resist this,” Catt said to nods of agreement. “It is something that is happening to us.”

artigo.texto: U.S. District Court Judge Eli Richardson on Tuesday handed a significant win to Metro in the lawsuit filed by data center developer DC Blox in August. Richardson dismissed DC Blox’s claims. The company, which is seeking to build a data center at a site adjacent to the Nashville Zoo, had alleged that Metro’s “relentless efforts” to block the development illegally singled out the company. The lawsuit is focused on Metro’s implementation of new zoning regulations and a moratorium on new approvals of such projects, not on the city’s pending effort to seize the property using the condemnation process. “Plaintiff may believe, and is entitled to believe and contend, that it received a raw deal from (or was sandbagged by) the imposition of the Moratorium after it purchased the Property,” Richardson wrote in his opinion. “However, a raw deal or sandbagging — real or imagined, without more — does not a federal lawsuit make.” The legal battle is far from over, as Richardson gave DC Blox 21 days to amend some of the dismissed claims, and other avenues of relief remain outstanding. “I have said from the beginning that Metro has both the right and the responsibility to determine appropriate land uses through its legislative and zoning processes,” Metro Councilmember Courtney Johnston, who represents the zoo area, wrote on social media. “DC BLOX had every right to challenge those decisions in court. They did. This was the result.” A request for comment from the DC Blox legal team remains outstanding. “I am pleased with the ruling and remain confident that Metro has acted lawfully in its dealings with DC Blox and in the enactment of the moratorium on data center permitting,” Metro Legal Director Tyler Yarbro said.

artigo.texto: AI infrastructure is reshaping more than the servers inside data center racks. As GPU-intensive workloads push rack densities higher, Eaton, NVIDIA, Google, Microsoft and others are advancing direct-current power architectures designed to deliver more power with fewer conversion stages and less physical infrastructure. For solution providers, integrators and infrastructure partners, that shift could broaden the scope of AI infrastructure projects. Moving from traditional AC designs toward rack-level 48/50V DC and, eventually, 800 VDC affects not only power distribution but also backup systems, cooling, rack design and serviceability â forcing partners to think about those systems as an interconnected architecture rather than separate infrastructure purchases Why AI is pushing data centers toward DC power The broader demand curve explains why power architecture is receiving so much attention. The International Energy Agency projects global data center electricity consumption will roughly double from 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh in 2030, with consumption from AI-focused data centers growing even faster. Inside the facility, higher density creates another challenge: current. Delivering more power at lower voltages requires greater current, which can mean larger conductors, greater losses, and more heat. Higher-voltage DC distribution can reduce current while eliminating some power-conversion stages between the utility feed and IT equipment. 48V, 50V and 800 VDC architectures take shape The transition is already visible at the rack level. Open Compute Projectâs Open Rack V3 ecosystem uses 48V DC busbar architectures, while Eatonâs upcoming 50V DC system is designed for both conventional 19-inch racks and 21-inch ORV3 racks, with power ratings ranging from 33 kW to 132 kW per rack. Eaton specifically identifies system integrator builds, enterprise and colocation environments, AI/HPC deployments and OCP migration projects among its intended applications. The next step could be significantly larger. NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft are collaborating through OCP to establish 800 VDC as an open architecture for next-generation AI data centers. NVIDIA says moving from todayâs lower-voltage rack architectures toward 800 VDC reduces current, copper requirements and cable bulk while allowing fewer power-conversion stages. More than 80 equipment and infrastructure companies are participating in the ecosystem. Eaton is among them and is developing 800 VDC infrastructure alongside its current ORV3 and 50V DC offerings. DC power creates a broader infrastructure role for partners That does not mean every enterprise data center is about to switch to 800 VDC. In fact, the emerging market is better understood as a continuum. Existing facilities can continue operating AC infrastructure while introducing DC closer to high-density compute. Rack-level 48/50V systems offer another path, while 800 VDC is being positioned for future AI environments with substantially greater density. NVIDIAâs own roadmap explicitly includes hybrid architectures designed to introduce 800 VDC power racks into facilities with existing AC infrastructure. For the channel, architectural knowledge is increasingly important. Partners accustomed to selling servers, UPS systems, racks and power distribution as relatively discrete infrastructure categories may need to approach AI projects more holistically. Power density affects distribution, backup requirements, cooling, physical rack design and serviceability, meaning infrastructure decisions become interconnected earlier in the design process. Eaton similarly argues that power and cooling need to be planned together as AI densities rise. The opportunity, then, isnât simply selling a different power product. It is helping customers determine when existing AC infrastructure remains sufficient, when rack-level DC makes sense, how to design hybrid environments, and when future workloads justify a more fundamental architectural shift. Hyperscalers may be setting the direction today. Channel partners should be watching closely for when their customers begin following it.
