artigo.texto: Executivos da indústria de telecomunicações apontaram que o 5G RedCap, tecnologia que usa uma capacidade reduzida da quinta geração móvel para conectar dispositivos, ainda deve ser explorado no Brasil, especialmente em redes privativas e edge data centers. Em painel no Futurecom 2026, nesta quarta-feira, 7, em São Paulo, o diretor de Novos Negócios e B2B da TIM, Alexandre Dal Forno, afirmou que a operadora já tem condições de utilizar o RedCap em redes privativas, com base na tecnologia 5G standalone (SA). Contudo, disse que ainda não houve demanda e o custo dos dispositivos compatíveis ainda tem sido um impeditivo. "A grande dificuldade do RedCap é o custo dos dispositivos versus o 5G full", afirmou. "A tecnologia é bastante recente. Gosto de compará-la ao NB-IoT em 2017, quando ainda estava começando. Todo mundo ia para o 4G full", completou, em conversa com jornalistas. De todo modo, Dal Forno reforçou que vê espaço para adoção da tecnologia em redes privativas. Inclusive, apontou que, quando os módulos de RedCap forem incorporados a dispositivos, o custo da tecnologia deve cair. O executivo da TIM também indicou que a vertical deve ganhar tração com o desenvolvimento do parque de edge data centers pelo País. "O próximo passo da infraestrutura digital vai ser um aumento na quantidade de data centers distribuídos. Vejo o IoT e o RedCap ganhando uma oportunidade de fazer o upload para processamento no edge data center. Isso pode ser um motivo para investir na tecnologia", destacou. Massificação de dispositivos conectados Na avalição da Aisla Ezequiel, head de vendas da NLT Telecom, especializada em IoT e M2M, o RedCap vai encontrar mercado em operações com equipamentos que não precisam da velocidade oferecida pela rede 5G. Ela projeta que a tecnologia terá um custo menor e será menos complexa para operar. Já Sandro Tamman, diretor da Unidade de Negócios de IoT e Network Solutions da Allcom Telecom, vê o 5G RedCap avançando para conexão de dispositivos de gás, água, energia, iluminação pública e automóveis. No mesmo painel, Wilson Cardoso, assessor de Tecnologia do Senai-SP, indicou que o RedCap pode se tornar uma solução de redundância de conectividade. Como exemplo, ele citou maquininhas de cartão. Em determinados estabelecimentos, utilizam o Wi-Fi disponível no ambiente. No entanto, em caso de problema com a rede de fibra, os dispositivos poderiam continuar conectadas por meio da tecnologia baseada 5G de capacidade reduzida.

artigo.texto: Origin plans a 500 MW, 4,942 MWh battery at Eraring Origin proposes adding a 500 MW storage system at the Eraring power station site. The project, which still has to clear the approval stages, would target commercial operations between early and mid-2031. Origin is proposing Eraring BESS North, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with a discharge capacity of 500 megawatts (MW) and an accessible energy storage capacity of approximately 4,942 megawatt hours (MWh). The project would require up to 22 hectares on Origin-owned land at the Eraring power station site in New South Wales. It is located in the suburb of Eraring, within the Lake Macquarie local government area. A combined facility of about 1,200 MW The project would operate alongside the existing Eraring BESS, part of Origin's generation portfolio. The existing project received State Significant Development consent SSD-15950052 on 10 May 2022. According to the project document, the two facilities together would provide a combined maximum registered active power capacity of around 1,200 MW and an accessible storage capacity of approximately 8,600 MWh, subject to detailed design. The storage sector is drawing other projects from Europe to Asia. ML System secured two energy storage contracts in Poland worth â¬4.1 million, while Vena Energy won a 46.8 MW battery storage contract in Japan. In power transmission, Iberdrola expanded its alliance with GIC in Brazil. Company Origin Energy: company profile ORG A regulatory pathway ahead Origin expects the project to qualify as a State Significant Development (SSD) under Section 2.6(1) of the 2021 Planning Systems state environmental planning policy. It would be subject to Part 4, Division 4.7, Section 4.36 of the 1979 Environmental Planning and Assessment Act, as an electricity generating works development whose estimated cost exceeds the set thresholds. An environmental impact statement will have to be prepared in line with the Secretary's Environmental Assessment Requirements. The existing BESS received a "not controlled action if undertaken in a particular manner" decision on 19 July 2021 under the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 [2021/8956]. The new project includes approximately 11 hectares of vegetation clearance outside the previously assessed disturbance area. Origin says it reviewed alternative locations and consulted key stakeholders and the community to limit impacts. Components and timeline The project covers construction, operation, decommissioning and rehabilitation as far as reasonably practicable. It would include transmission works to connect the BESS to TransGrid's switching station, along with an extension of the existing substation. It also provides for extended water supply infrastructure, new electricity buildings, internal access roads and new operation and maintenance compounds. Construction is expected to start in 2028 and last about 2.5 years, with commercial operations anticipated in early to mid-2031, subject to approvals. Operations would run for up to 25 years, with a possible extension. Works would be staged, including site establishment, then earthworks for the battery compound and transformer yard, and finally civil and foundation works. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 % Origin presents the project as a response to the National Electricity Market's shift from coal toward variable renewables, supported by dispatchable storage capacity. The New South Wales roadmap targets at least 12 gigawatts of renewable generation and 2 gigawatts of long-duration storage by 2030. The Australian Energy Market Operator's 2024 Integrated System Plan forecasts that the market must triple grid-scale variable renewable capacity by 2030.

artigo.texto: Oakland has joined several other Bay Area cities in hitting pause on data centers. The City Council on Tuesday unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on approvals for new data centers. The moratorium can be extended by the council. Councilmember Carroll Fife, who authored the moratorium, has said the goal is to give Oakland time to study the impacts of data centers and make any needed changes to the city’s planning and building codes to protect residents’ health, safety and welfare. People across the country have become skeptical of data centers as tech companies, especially those developing artificial intelligence, have moved fast in recent years to build massive computing warehouses in cities and rural areas. Because data centers consume large amounts of water and electricity, generate noise and take up huge swaths of land, many communities have opposed their construction. Oakland hasn’t seen a boom in data center construction, likely because land and electricity prices are high here. However, a developer has proposed building a data center in a downtown building that used to house a supercomputer. Many of the people who showed up to Tuesday’s council meeting said they’re not just worried about the potential effects on their utility bills or the neighborhood’s quality of life, but they have broader concerns about the AI industry’s vision for the future. “The luddites were onto something,” a District 2 resident named Charlotte told the council. “They understood that what matters about a technology is not just what it does but who controls it and what kind of power it has to concentrate power. We do not control this technology. I think it is a big mistake for us to gamble with the future of our city and trust that the oligarchs have a place for us in their vision at all.” Dohee Kim, an organizer with the Local Clean Energy Alliance, said Oakland’s moratorium is part of a nationwide pushback. “Moratoriums are temporary solutions, but our communities deserve the right tools and the proper avenues to determine meaningful accountability and oversight when AI Data Centers directly impact our energy, water and land usage during a worsening climate crisis,” Kim said in a statement released after the council meeting. According to the Stop AI Data Centers in Alameda County coalition, at least 26 cities in California are considering or have passed similar moratoriums. San Francisco also approved a 45-day moratorium on data center approvals at the Board of Supervisors’ meeting yesterday. Richmond approved a moratorium in September. Some Oakland residents are opposed to the moratorium. Mindy Pechenuk, who is running for mayor, showed up to Tuesday’s council meeting to urge city leaders to reject any pause on data center development. Pechenuk, who uses AI to generate campaign ads, likened the AI boom to the American space program of the early 1960s, which she said united the nation and led to significant scientific advances. “I oppose wasting taxpayers’ money on a moratorium,” Pechenuk said. Sharon Taylor, who described herself as a lifelong Oakland resident, said her family was able to flourish in the city decades ago because there was ready work. “Data centers will bring jobs, they will not take jobs away,” she told the council. Andrea Ingram said Oakland needs tech industry investment. “Oakland is good at driving those things out of the city, and then we turn around and say, ‘Why don’t we have enough money to give city workers?’” Moratorium supporters see the economic implications of the AI boom very differently. Arbaz, a District 2 resident who spoke at the council meeting, said many Oaklanders are worried about rising rents, food prices and utility bills. “We shouldn’t be siphoning off our resources and mortgaging our people’s future on an AI bubble that will likely be leaving us holding the bag at the end.” Fears that the hundreds of billions of dollars major corporations have poured into AI might lead to an economic crash are shared by some high-profile investors and top economists. Rene Coe, another moratorium supporter, said Oaklanders should be wary of the promises of the AI industry and data center developers. “The best-case scenario: AI will replace people,” Coe said. “If it doesn’t, the bubble will burst and cause a recession worse than 2008. Oaklanders know what happens when billionaires make bets on our homes and jobs.”

artigo.texto: Após dobrar a área de manufatura em fevereiro, a Adata prepara nova operação industrial em Manaus para montar e testar servidores de alta potência, enquanto avalia projetos para automação e setor automotivo em 2027 também A fábrica da Adata em Manaus vai ganhar uma nova frente industrial em dezembro de 2026, quando a companhia pretende iniciar a montagem e os testes de servidores, incluindo equipamentos de alta potência destinados a data centers. Fábrica da Adata em Manaus dobrou área de produção em 2026 A expansão faz parte de uma estratégia que vem sendo colocada em prática desde 2021, quando a Adata iniciou sua operação industrial na capital amazonense. Desde então, a unidade recebeu investimentos para ampliar capacidade, automatizar processos e aumentar o portfólio produzido localmente. Um dos movimentos mais recentes ocorreu em fevereiro de 2026. A empresa dobrou sua área de manufatura ao incorporar um segundo galpão industrial à planta de Manaus. - Gigante americana Sukup coloca Mato Grosso no radar e avalia instalar fábrica em Lucas do Rio Verde para produzir sistemas de armazenagem de grãos em um dos maiores polos do agronegócio brasileiro - Duas gigantes chinesas negociam novas fábricas de geladeiras e lavadoras no Brasil enquanto setor supera R$ 7 bilhões em investimentos e amplia corrida pela produção local de eletrodomésticos - Grupo Michelin amplia presença industrial no Brasil com nova fábrica da Fenner em Guarulhos e projeto prevê aumento de 40% na capacidade para atender mineração, cimento, siderurgia e outros setores pesados - Indústria da soja acelera no Brasil, capacidade cresce 13% em um ano e setor prepara R$ 7,65 bilhões em novas fábricas e expansões para adicionar 7,4 milhões de toneladas ao processamento nacional Segundo Nivaldo Gagliardo, vice-presidente de Operações da Adata Technology Brasil, essa nova estrutura começará a contribuir com o crescimento das operações locais ainda no último trimestre de 2026. A companhia não informou, na entrevista, o valor aplicado na ampliação nem divulgou a capacidade de produção que será acrescentada pelo segundo galpão. Unidade já monta módulos DRAM e SSDs Hoje, a operação de Manaus realiza a montagem eletrônica completa de módulos de memória DRAM e SSDs utilizando tecnologia SMT, além dos testes desses produtos. Os principais componentes utilizados, como circuitos integrados de memória DRAM e Flash destinados aos SSDs, são fornecidos pela fábrica da própria Adata localizada em Santo Antônio de Posse, no interior de São Paulo. A produção ocorre em ambiente com controle de temperatura e umidade. A planta também utiliza equipamentos automatizados para manipulação e inspeção de produtos e ferramentais. Parte dessas soluções emprega inteligência artificial e foi desenvolvida no Brasil em parceria com institutos de Manaus, dentro de projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Servidores para data centers entram na linha em dezembro O próximo salto será a entrada no mercado de servidores. A partir de dezembro de 2026, a Adata pretende começar, em Manaus, uma operação destinada à montagem e aos testes desses equipamentos. A fabricação será realizada em regime de manufatura sob contrato. Entre os produtos previstos estão servidores de alta potência voltados à utilização em data centers. Com isso, a planta amplia suas competências para além de memórias e unidades de armazenamento, entrando em uma área ligada diretamente à infraestrutura de processamento de dados. A expansão ocorre após a empresa ter um projeto de diversificação aprovado pelo Conselho de Desenvolvimento do Estado do Amazonas, o Codam. Automação e setor automotivo estão no radar para 2027 A Adata também avalia novos caminhos para sua estrutura industrial em Manaus. artigo.texto: San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors today passed a temporary, 45-day moratorium on data centers citywide, halting the construction of new centers including one proposed in Dogpatch. The move follows increased fears surrounding the potential environmental impacts of data centers, many of which are planned or already exist in District 10, the city’s industrial southeast. The measure, first proposed by District 10 supervisor Shamann Walton and co-sponsored by supervisors Connie Chan, Jackie Fielder and Cheyenne Chen, will take effect immediately. Sources close to Walton’s office say the supervisor hopes the moratorium will result in a permanent ban. The San Francisco Planning Commission will assess during the ensuing 45 days whether the several data centers throughout San Francisco, including larger facilities in District 10 and smaller, regional ones downtown, pose an environmental threat to nearby residents. During the moratorium, the planning department will study the data centers’ impact on water, energy, air quality, land use, and the surrounding community. In the legislation, data centers are broadly defined as any “facility, or part of a facility, that houses computing infrastructure, including graphics and central processing units, servers, storage devices, networking equipment, and associated power and cooling systems, for the primary purpose of processing, storing, or distributing electronic data.” If the data centers are found to have a significant environmental impact, the moratorium could be extended up to 22 months — or alternatively, result in permanent controls or restrictions. At the conclusion of the 45-day period, the planning department will hold a hearing to present its findings. The moratorium will pause the expansion of NOVVA, a 7.6-acre data center at 400 Paul Ave. in Bayview, which was slated to increase output from nine to 36 megawatts by 2028. Though permits have been filed for an additional, 160,000 square foot datacenter in the Dogpatch at 1215 Michigan St., no construction has yet taken place — though an extended moratorium could put plans to expand data centers in San Francisco on hold for an undetermined period. Walton’s term will end in January 2027, potentially before the end of a moratorium if it is extended beyond four months. But strong regulations on data centers — and potentially an all-out ban — has gained increasing support among the candidates racing to replace Walton. Each of the front-running candidates, Theo Ellington, J.R. Eppler, and Dion-Jay Brookter, have expressed support for a moratorium. Brookter was, at first, the only candidate to propose a permanent ban, but during a recent candidate forum, all the others said they would support one, too. District 10’s Bayview-Hunters Point, which has two of the city’s largest data centers, has experienced a disproportionate level of air pollution for decades, including from increased truck traffic and a since-shuttered PG&E power plant. “We need to know what these impacts are,” said Walton, at the time he announced his plans to introduce the moratorium. “Until we know what that is, it needs to stop.”

artigo.texto: Maryland nets 440 MW/1,760 MWh in first bulk energy storage procurement This story was originally published on Utility Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Utility Dive newsletter. Dive Brief: - Two transmission-connected energy storage projects are slated to receive awards in the first round of the Maryland Next Generation Energy Act energy storage procurement, the state public service commission said on Thursday. - The finalists are Flatiron Energy's 400 MW/1,600 MWh Chalk Point Storage Project in south-central Maryland and REV Renewables's 40 MW/160 MWh Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in the far western part of the state. Both will receive flat pricing for 15-year terms at a combined cost of 6.98 cents/month for the average Maryland residential customer, the public service commission said. - The award will help address the PJM Interconnection's capacity woes, which Federal Energy Regulatory Commission chair Laura Swett last week called a "mess." The grid operator faces a capacity shortfall of 6.8 GW for the 2028-2029 delivery year, up 300 MW from the previous period, as capacity prices remain at the $325/MW-day cap. Dive Insight: Passed in 2025, the Next Generation Energy Act requires Maryland to conduct at least two solicitations for a combined 1.6 GW of energy storage capacity. Eligible projects must be designed to discharge at full power for at least four hours. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced the awards for the first solicitation round on Thursday, the statutory deadline. By law, it must open bidding for the second round by Jan. 1, 2027, and announce project awards by Oct. 1, 2027. Evan Vaughan, executive director of the regional clean energy group MAREC Action, said Thursday's selections will help mitigate the effects of PJM's high capacity prices. "These projects can help meet growing electricity demand while reducing exposure to volatile capacity prices that ultimately affect customers' bills," Vaughan said in a statement. Also known as the Mid-Atlantic Renewable Energy Coalition, MAREC Action consists of more than 50 developers and manufacturers serving the region's utility-scale solar, wind and battery storage industry. Flatiron Energy and REV Renewables are both members. Flatiron's project will be located at NRG's oil- and gas-fired Chalk Point power plant in the southeastern corner of Prince George's County, according to the Maryland Public Service Commission. REV will site its project on a portion of a reclaimed coal mine in mountainous Garrett County, near Maryland's border with West Virginia and Pennsylvania. The commission said it chose not to award the 500-MW/3,000-MWh Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project nor a 135-MW/540-MWh expansion Flatiron requested for the Chalk Point project in a revised filing after the first-round application window closed. The commission said Flatiron could reapply for the Chalk Point expansion and "invited [Oystercatcher] to consider participating" in round two, citing the "desirable electric grid location and characteristics" of the project's northeastern Maryland site while noting "the need for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County if the project is pursued further." In addition to near-term cost pressures due to PJM's capacity crunch, Maryland has ambitious clean energy goals, including a statutory 2045 target for statewide net-zero emissions and a 2035 goal for 100% carbon-free electricity set by gubernatorial order. In a statement, Maryland Public Service Commission Chair Kumar Barve called the first-round award a milestone in the state's effort to meet its energy policy goals, while acknowledging its relatively modest contribution. "While we are disappointed that these awards are below our 800-MW target for Round 1, our Round 2 solicitation is expected to attract many more offers due to a pool of over 40 additional energy storage projects from PJM's Cycle 1 interconnection process," Barve said.

artigo.texto: Sistemas de armazenamento de energia elétrica, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, estão vendendo como nunca no País. Enquanto o leilão do Governo para contratar grandes projetos de baterias continua agendado para dezembro mas enfrenta incertezas, o mercado encontrou seu caminho no varejo. Instalações menores em indústrias, comércios, condomínios e residências, muitas vezes associadas a sistemas solares em telhados, têm movimentado a indústria num ritmo recorde. Em 2025, o volume vendido e contratado atingiu 730 MWh, mais do que o acumulado dos cinco anos anteriores. E só no primeiro semestre deste ano foram mais 504 MWh, a caminho de uma nova marca histórica para o setor, segundo um levantamento da consultoria Greener. “O leilão é importante, claro, mas o BESS de uma forma distribuída, vamos chamar assim, vai ser em minha visão uma das grandes fontes de flexibilidade para o sistema elétrico no País,” Marcio Takata, o CEO da Greener, disse ao Brazil Journal. Ele fez uma comparação com a indústria de energia solar, que começou a se movimentar com leilões do Governo para grandes projetos e nos anos seguintes teve uma disparada puxada pelo mercado de pequenas instalações em telhados e miniusinas. A capacidade em geração solar distribuída hoje soma mais de 53 gigawatts, contra 23,6 gigawatts em usinas de geração centralizada, segundo dados da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). No momento, o acumulado em sistemas de baterias no País representa 1,9 GWh, com empresas incluindo WEG e Grupo Moura apostando no setor. O leilão programado para dezembro deve contratar pelo menos 2 gigawatts para operação durante 4 horas diárias, segundo sinalizações de Brasília, o equivalente a 8 GWh – embora parte do mercado já espere volumes maiores. O Ministério de Minas e Energia também programou leilões anuais, até 2029, para contratação de reserva de capacidade, nos quais haverá espaço para sistemas de baterias. Esses certames, porém, vão promover uma disputa da tecnologia com termelétricas e hidrelétricas, incluindo as chamadas hidrelétricas reversíveis – que na prática funcionam como uma bateria, ao guardar água para produzir mais nos momentos em que o sistema precisa. A contratação dessa reserva de capacidade é vista como importante para que a rede elétrica possa lidar com a variação da geração eólica e solar, que por vezes resulta num excesso de energia, obrigando usinas a paradas forçadas, conhecidas como curtailment. “Hoje o tema mais quente no setor são as baterias. E as hidrelétricas reversíveis. Até por essa necessidade do sistema,” disse o diretor da consultoria Thymos Capital, André Millions. Apesar do intenso interesse de investidores, o leilão de dezembro está sob risco devido a discussões sobre quem vai pagar o custo dos projetos de armazenamento, segundo diversas fontes do setor. A legislação atual define o rateio dos custos entre todas empresas de geração, uma regra que gera ameaças de judicialização. No momento, empresas do setor se movimentam para convencer o Governo a trabalhar pela aprovação de um projeto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim que alteraria a lei para repassar a conta aos consumidores, como ocorre nos demais leilões do mercado de energia.

artigo.texto: Denver’s mayor and city council Wednesday announced a “working group” of 26 citizens and experts on data center growth that will make policy recommendations amid a city building moratorium, putting developers on notice the ban could be extended past May. “It will be Denver, not corporations, that decide if and how data centers may operate in our city,” Mayor Mike Johnston said, in a statement accompanying the working group appointments. City officials said more than 250 people expressed interest in joining the panel. “This group brings together people with different perspectives to help us get this right: setting clear rules, protecting Denver’s resources, and putting the interests of Denverites first,” Johnston said. City Council approved a one-year moratorium in May, amid rising controversy from residents in the Elyria-Swansea neighborhood of north Denver for opposing a 600,000-square-foot data center under construction by CoreSite. Globeville and Elyria-Swansea residents and advocates point out they have long been the victim of excess pollution from interstate traffic, the Suncor refinery, past Superfund polluters, the Purina plant and other industries. Denver’s pause also comes as communities up and down the Front Range launch their own intensive debates about whether and how to site other massive data center proposals. Brighton’s City Council on Tuesday night approved a one-year ban on data centers, as neighborhood groups protest a 2.5 million square foot proposal in the northern part of the city that extends into Weld County. A city council member said that application had been withdrawn. Date Center opponents in Weld County are now circulating petitions for a public vote on a ban there, after commissioners rezoned for a large Global AI data center in an unincorporated part of the county near Windsor. Aurora, Colorado Springs and a handful of other cities are also debating data center rezonings and potential moratoriums. Denver data centers permitted before May were not impacted by the City Council moratorium. Denver officials who jointly announced the new working group emphasized it includes representation from the neighborhoods most impacted by potential data centers, as well as “union, utility, and industry representatives,” nonprofits, healthcare and air quality experts. The meetings will begin Oct. 9 and will be streamed. The group “will put community voices and community solutions at the center of Denver’s data center debate because the people who live closest to these projects should shape the rules that govern them,” said Council Member Darrell Watson, who represents many of the affected neighborhoods in District 9. Working group members listed as community representatives include Solicia E. Lope, Erin Overturf, Andrea Nemer, Precious Lawrence, V. Quintana, Dr. Brandon Scott, Alfonso Espino, Rebecca Trujillo, Jessica N., Gilbert Herrera, Rev. Terrance D. Carroll and Marcus Weaver. Union representatives include IBEW Local 68 representative Julian Aguilar and Cecil Courtney from Pipefitters Local Union 208. Appointed from utility interests are Melissa Almond, corporate economic development manager, Xcel Energy; and Andrew Hill, government affairs manager, Denver Water. From industries related to data centers, members include Steve Jackson, CEO, Empowercom; and Matt Gallagher, senior manaer of strategic partnerships, Satoshi Energy. Nonprofits in related fields will be represented by Courtney Fieldman, director of utility programs, Southwest Energy Efficiency Project; Ean Thomas Tafoya, vice president of State Programs, GreenLatinos; and Jim Garcia, CEO and founder of Tepeyac Community Health Center. Air quality and healthcare members include Priyanka deSouza, assistant professor, Department of Urban and Regional Planning, University of Colorado Denver; Dr. Kate Jennings; and Abi Balajee. voices from academia include Mark Orrs, teaching associate professor in the Department of Engineering, Design, and Society at Colorado School of Mines; and Benjamin Xie, assistant professor of computer science, University of Denver.

According to reports from Chinese media on the 6th (local time), this patent, filed in March 2025 (publication number CN 122868832 A), features an innovative two-chamber enclosure architecture designed to simultaneously maximize thermal management efficiency and electrical safety for high-performance batteries. According to the disclosed patent details, the battery cabinet system is physically divided into two independent compartments. The upper compartment consists of a dry chamber housing vehicle electronics, key electrical equipment, and connectors, while the lower compartment is designed as a liquid chamber where multiple battery cell modules are fully submerged in dielectric cooling fluid. The core engineering challenge of this structure—electrical connections at the liquid-sealed interface—was resolved by safely routing wiring and connection points outside the liquid volume through the upper dry chamber. The crux of the patent lies in a design that actively leverages the excellent insulating and cooling properties of the coolant while thoroughly separating and maintaining the insulation and operational stability of electrical components and contacts that must not come into direct contact with the coolant, through the physical layout of the cabinet. This patent should be viewed not merely as a method of using individual cooling fluids, but as an emphasis on enclosure cabinet structure design that physically isolates liquid cooling environments from electrical equipment. With this patent, BYD has gained a key to further refreshing its image as a technology company. The process of watching how this patent will be commercialized remains ahead. *This content was translated by AI.

artigo.texto: Volunteers Scott Foreman and Irene Purcell, right, encourage fellow Raton resident Betty Poe to sign a petition against a data center on June 20 in front of a grocery store. The Raton City Commission has voted down a proposed one-year moratorium on new data centers. Raton resident Pat Walsh, who has helped lead the charge against a data center in Raton, says she is disappointed by the City Commission's recent decision to vote down a proposed one-year moratorium on such projects. An attempt to pump the brakes on data center development in Raton went down in defeat last month after members of the City Commission voted 3-2 against a proposed ordinance that would have put a one-year moratorium against such projects. The Sept. 22 vote came after commissioners were presented with a petition signed by nearly 500 Raton residents expressing opposition to data centers in the Colfax County community of about 6,000 residents just south of the Colorado border. The City Commission’s decision stands in contrast to an August vote by the Colfax County Commission to adopt a one-year moratorium on data centers in unincorporated parts of the county. That made Colfax the fourth county in New Mexico to adopt such a restriction, joining Santa Fe, Sierra and Socorro counties. Raton Mayor Lori Chatterley and City Commissioners Daniel Campbell and Mark Honeyfield voted against the moratorium, while Commissioners Linde Schuster and Sally Hoger, who proposed the measure, voted for it. Campbell, who did not respond to a request for comment from The New Mexican, said at the meeting last month he saw no point in adopting the measure. “I can’t see that it gains us anything to be the first municipality in New Mexico that does this,” he said. Campbell noted Raton lacks the electrical power and water necessary to operate a data center, and the city’s ownership of the utilities that control those commodities serves as an adequate hedge against any potential development. “The data center issue was never going to happen to the degree that that’s been discussed because we don’t have the power to do that,” Campbell said. Hoger, however, described it as a commonsense measure and dismissed the idea the city already has adequate safeguards in place. “I don’t agree with that,” she reiterated in a recent interview. How it got started The issue arose in Raton earlier this year after leaders of Atterix LLC, a Denver-based company incorporated in late 2025, signed a memorandum of understanding with Raton officials to conduct a feasibility study for a data center project. That agreement, signed in February, gave the company six months to conduct the study; during that time, the city was prohibited from soliciting a similar project from another company. Atterix officials had floated the idea of creating a three-phase project in Raton that would have been constructed over several years, vastly increasing the city’s consumption of electricity. The company has not submitted the results of the feasibility study to the city, Hoger said. Chatterley said at the Sept. 22 commission meeting there was no project for the city to consider. She did not respond to The New Mexican‘s request for additional information. Kimberle Burke, owner and operator of a local ice cream shop, presented a petition to the commission Sept. 22 opposing a data center, warning against negative impacts a project might bring to the city when it comes to water, noise, the economy and “long-term repercussions that we may not know about right now.” Burke said people who signed the petition are anxious to understand what value a data center would provide to the community and who would benefit from it. “We want a moratorium so the community’s concerns can be addressed and we can all be aware of what’s going on, when and why,” she said. “Something of this magnitude should be decided by the community by the majority, not just a few.” Another resident who spoke in favor of the moratorium, Max Holland, reminded commissioners the adoption of a one-year moratorium would not permanently ban data centers from Raton. “A moratorium is not a no,” he said. “A moratorium is a timeout. Let’s utilize that time to inform ourselves and make sure we are doing the right thing.” Raton resident Pat Walsh, who co-founded Protect Our Resources, residents who oppose a data center in the city, said last week she was disappointed but not surprised by the commission’s action. She believes the issue is a long way from being dead in Raton. “We are going to keep an eye on various parts of city government to stay vigilant to see if any applications come through for power, utilities or water, or planning and zoning so we don’t get blindsided,” Walsh said. “I don’t want to take a chance on it being done,” Walsh said. “Nothing I can see would prevent someone else from coming in.” Hoping for a remedy Walsh and Hoger said they are more optimistic an ordinance regulating data center operators will get the commission’s approval, especially after the mayor has spoken in favor of such a measure. “I’m still very much in support of an ordinance of having strong guardrails,” Chatterley said Sept. 22. Hoger said she is part of a committee that has drafted an ordinance, which has been submitted to the city’s legal staff for review. She said it includes provisions that would require data center operators to work with local utilities to determine how much water and power they could use, establish minimum distances between such facilities and the nearest residence, and set limits on the amount of noise they could generate. She said the measure is based on similar ordinances adopted in other communities across the country. Hoger said she isn’t sure how to assess the data center battle in Raton with the defeat of the moratorium and the regulatory measure awaiting legal approval. artigo.texto: Azul Conecta fecha acordo com Auren para compensação de emissões de todos os voos de 2026 Parceria com a Auren Energia prevê compensar cerca de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente com créditos de carbono de projetos eólicos no Piauí e em Pernambuco A Azul Conecta anunciou uma parceria com a Auren Energia para compensar as emissões de carbono associadas ao consumo de combustível de todos os seus voos realizados ao longo de 2026. A iniciativa, batizada de Conecta NetZero, prevê a utilização de créditos de carbono certificados e não terá custo adicional para os passageiros. A Azul Conecta é a operação regional da Azul voltada à ligação de cidades de menor porte aos principais centros urbanos da companhia. Com aeronaves menores, principalmente do modelo Cessna Grand Caravan, a empresa atende mercados que não comportam os aviões utilizados nas rotas comerciais de maior demanda. O anúncio, portanto, vale apenas para os voos desta divisão regional da companhia e não para os voos feitos em outras linhas e aeronaves menores. A estimativa é que sejam compensadas cerca de 10 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e) ao longo do ano. Os créditos utilizados são provenientes dos complexos eólicos Ventos do Piauí I e Ventos do Araripe III, integrantes do portfólio de geração renovável da Auren. Segundo as empresas, os créditos seguem o Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), programa administrado pela organização Verra, e passaram por processos independentes de validação e verificação. Eles também tiveram sua elegibilidade reconhecida para a fase piloto do CORSIA, mecanismo criado pela Organização da Aviação Civil Internacional (ICAO) para lidar com as emissões da aviação internacional. Depois de utilizados na compensação, os créditos serão aposentados no registro da Verra em nome da Azul Conecta. A aposentadoria significa que as unidades deixam definitivamente de circular e não podem ser revendidas ou utilizadas novamente para compensar emissões. A medida busca dar rastreabilidade à compensação e evitar a dupla contagem dos créditos — uma das questões centrais nas discussões sobre a credibilidade do mercado voluntário de carbono. O programa, no entanto, é parte de uma estratégia mais ampla de redução de emissões da companhia aérea. A compensação não elimina as emissões produzidas pela queima de combustível das aeronaves, mas procura neutralizar, por meio de créditos certificados, uma quantidade equivalente de emissões contabilizadas pela companhia. A Azul afirma que sua estratégia de descarbonização também inclui renovação e modernização da frota e medidas de eficiência operacional. Entre 2019 e 2025, segundo a empresa, a intensidade de carbono de sua operação caiu cerca de 20%. Para César Grandolfo, diretor de Relações Institucionais, Tributárias e de Sustentabilidade da Azul, o programa representa mais uma etapa da estratégia climática da companhia. “Ao compensar integralmente as emissões associadas ao consumo de combustível dos voos da Azul Conecta por meio de créditos certificados, reforçamos nosso compromisso de combinar eficiência operacional, inovação e responsabilidade ambiental”, afirmou. A Auren afirma que já comercializou mais de 7 milhões de créditos de carbono para clientes em mais de 20 países. A empresa também informa possuir um portfólio de créditos associado a projetos de geração renovável e conservação de florestas nativas. “A parceria mostra como a geração de energia renovável pode contribuir também para a descarbonização de outros setores da economia”, disse João Guillaumon, vice-presidente de Clientes e Comercialização da Auren Energia. Compensação não substitui redução das emissões A iniciativa ocorre em um momento em que empresas aéreas enfrentam o desafio de reduzir sua pegada climática em um setor particularmente dependente de combustíveis fósseis. Mesmo com ganhos de eficiência, as emissões totais continuam crescendo à medida que aumenta a demanda por voos. Em 2024, as companhias aéreas emitiram globalmente cerca de 942 milhões de toneladas de CO₂, segundo a Associação Internacional de Transporte Aéreo (IATA), alta em relação aos 882 milhões de toneladas registrados em 2023. No mesmo período, porém, a intensidade de carbono da operação — medida pelas emissões por tonelada-quilômetro transportada — caiu 3,7%, sinal de que as aeronaves e operações estão ficando mais eficientes, mas que esses ganhos ainda não são suficientes para compensar o crescimento do tráfego. Embora avanços tecnológicos, eficiência operacional e renovação de frota possam reduzir o consumo de combustível por passageiro, a aviação ainda depende majoritariamente de combustíveis líquidos. Com isso, sozinha, a aviação responde por cerca de 2,5% das emissões globais de CO₂, de acordo com análise baseada em dados do Global Carbon Project. Contudo, seu impacto climático é maior quando considerados outros efeitos além do CO₂, como a formação de contrails ( aquelas linhas brancas que aparecem atrás dos aviões no céu) e alterações na química atmosférica. Para o setor aéreo, o desafio permanece maior do que compensar emissões: trata-se de reduzir, de forma estrutural, a quantidade de carbono emitida por cada voo. Nesse processo, tecnologias mais eficientes, combustíveis sustentáveis e mudanças operacionais deverão ter papel central — enquanto os créditos de carbono aparecem como uma ferramenta complementar na transição. A lógica é que uma tonelada de CO₂ equivalente emitida pela atividade seja compensada por uma unidade certificada correspondente a uma tonelada de emissões evitadas ou removidas em outro projeto. A efetividade climática desse mecanismo, porém, depende da qualidade, adicionalidade, rastreabilidade e integridade dos créditos utilizados. A certificação e a aposentadoria das unidades são, portanto, elementos importantes para demonstrar que os créditos empregados não serão utilizados por mais de uma empresa. artigo.texto: Renewable energy company Zelestra has entered into two new power purchase agreements (PPAs) with EDP to add four-hours of battery storage to existing solar plants in Spain. The deals will bring about 462MW-hours (MWh) of battery capacity to 181MW-direct current (MWdc) of solar power across two sites, Pedroso in Seville and Valkyria in Castilla-La Mancha. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. Under the new agreements, Zelestra will install a 25MW battery energy storage system (BESS) with around 100MWh of capacity at Pedroso, which already operates a 31MWdc solar plant. At Valkyria, a 90.45MW (approximately 362MWh) BESS will be added to the existing 150MWdc solar facility. EDP serves as the current offtaker for both sites. EDP global energy management CEO Pedro Neves Ferreira said: “At EDP, innovation goes beyond deploying renewable generation. We are continuously developing new solutions that combine technology, market expertise and flexibility assets to unlock greater value from clean energy. “By integrating storage with renewable generation, we can enhance system resilience, improve efficiency and accelerate the electrification and decarbonisation of the economy.” With these transactions, Zelestra and EDP’s joint portfolio in Spain now comprises four hybrid projects, with more than 1GW-hour of contracted storage capacity. The companies’ cooperation began in 2025 with the country’s first combined solar and BESS PPA, involving a 170MWdc solar installation and 400MWh of storage at Trujillo, Extremadura. Earlier, in 2024, the companies signed another agreement for a 160MWh BESS at the 50MW Pizarroso plant in Cáceres, reportedly the first PPA in Spain to hybridise an operational solar plant. Zelestra Spain CEO Jaime Burguete said: “Zelestra and EDP have built something together that is unique in the Spanish market: a commercial partnership that is unlocking large-scale storage capacity that will benefit the wider energy system. “These four hybrid projects show that energy storage is bankable in Spain, and we expect this segment of the market to be the main growth area in the years ahead. “It also means that every megawatt-hour moved into the evening or early morning is clean power the system would otherwise have had to find elsewhere.” In July 2026, Zelestra and EnBW signed a long-term tolling agreement for a 300MW share of a planned battery energy storage project in Emilia-Romagna, Italy.

artigo.texto: Just days after Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman declared that a gigantic proposed data center in the city “must be stopped,” a spokesman for the company behind the project said the 860,000-square-foot facility should be “evaluated based on verified facts.” Coffman posted his thoughts about Vantage Data Centers’ Trident project late last week on Facebook, saying the project “must not go forward.” His post followed a City Council meeting last week during which hundreds of people living in neighborhoods near the site came out to decry the data center, which would be among Colorado’s largest. Residents voiced concerns about the facilities’ large water use and electric consumption, along with worries about noise. Several cities in the state, including Denver, Thornton and Commerce City, have imposed temporary bans on new data centers as larger and larger — or hyperscale — facilities have sprouted. Hyperscale data centers are engineered for large-scale workloads and are at the heart of the burgeoning data-hungry artificial intelligence sector. The Aurora council narrowly rejected a moratorium on data centers in August, but the city is hammering out rules for the facilities, including a just-passed ban on the use of water-hungry evaporative cooling systems by any business across the city. Aurora, Coffman wrote, “must explore every available option, to include my calling the proposed Trident data center up for a public hearing and then asking the members of City Council for a ‘no’ vote to stop it from being built.” The mayor said he would do this regardless of any litigation Vantage might level against the city. Mark Freeman, vice president of global marketing for the Denver-based company, wouldn’t answer a question from The Denver Post about whether Vantage might take legal action against Aurora should the city kill its project. Freeman said the company’s proposed data center on a 108-acre site just inside the E-470 beltway at East 48th Avenue would use a closed-loop system that would require one initial 600,000-gallon injection of water and 2,200 gallons a day as part of ongoing operations — “about half the amount used by a similarly sized office building.” It would be designed to use 334 megawatts of electric power, he said, to run both “cloud and (artificial intelligence) workloads.” By comparison, nearby Denver International Airport uses 45 megawatts of electric power. Freeman also said the site plan will comply with all noise ordinance standards in the city, with sound levels from the facility expected to be “similar to a typical office building or a dishwasher running in the next room.” Aurora Councilwoman Amy Wiles, whose ward covers the proposed Trident site, recognizes the city is in a tricky position given that Vantage has been following the city’s approval process for more than a year and the site where it wants to build its center is zoned for that use. “I wish this had been done sooner — I brought it up months ago,” she said Monday. “Ideally, when (the area) was first re-zoned, I wish it had been looked at a bit more closely to balance the need for business while also prioritizing our residents.” Wiles said she still has questions about low-frequency noise and vibrations from data centers and how those might affect nearby neighbors. Coffman, in his Facebook post, said the project received preliminary administrative approval without a public hearing “because a data center is a permitted use under the current zoning.” The parcel Vantage wants to develop was zoned “airport district” by the city four years ago — a designation that permits businesses like data centers. The mayor is not against data centers per se, but he said more scrutiny needs to be applied in terms of where they are built. “We need to update our development code so that we have realistic distances between residential developments and data centers,” he told The Post in a text response to questions Monday. “The city of Aurora has a land mass a little larger than Denver and about a third of our city is undeveloped, so there definitely are suitable locations for data centers that are far enough away from homes.” Get more Colorado news by signing up for our daily Your Morning Dozen email newsletter.

artigo.texto: How AI is Reshaping Data Center Financing The race to build computing capacity for artificial intelligence is reshaping data center financing in the United States. As projects become larger, more capital-intensive and increasingly developed in phases, sponsors need financing that can adapt to changing capital requirements while still providing certainty of execution on increasingly compressed timelines. Some of the largest developments now represent multi-billion-dollar investment programs encompassing multiple buildings and years of construction. Rather than financing a single asset with a defined completion date, sponsors may be funding a campus that grows in stages as new capacity is added. The result is a financing model that increasingly needs to evolve alongside the project itself. Financing a project built in phases A large data center campus is rarely developed all at once. Sponsors may begin with land and site infrastructure before moving into the first buildings, then add capacity over time as customer demand develops. Each phase can bring different capital requirements, construction milestones and operating considerations. That makes flexibility increasingly important. “Five years ago, you were looking at a very different type of data center project,” says Michael Lardieri, Managing Director, Institutional Client & Financial Sponsors at BBVA USA. “Today we're talking about campuses that can require billions of dollars of investment and are being developed in multiple phases. That changes how sponsors think about capital and what they need from their banks.” Financing can therefore become part of a longer development strategy rather than a single transaction. Sponsors and lenders need to consider when capital will be required, how later phases relate to earlier ones and how the financing may need to evolve as a project moves from construction into operation. Speed is changing the equation At the same time, the expansion of AI infrastructure is putting greater pressure on development timelines. Suitable land, power capacity, equipment and construction resources are all in demand. Once those elements have been secured, delays elsewhere in the development process can become costly. Financing is no exception. For sponsors, having access to capital is essential, but so is knowing that financing can be executed within the project's timetable. Large transactions may require substantial underwriting commitments and coordination among multiple institutions, often while other parts of the development are moving simultaneously. “Clients don't only want to know whether the capital is available,” Lardieri says. “They want confidence that it can be delivered on the timeline the project requires. As the market has accelerated, that certainty has become increasingly important.” The asset cannot be viewed in isolation The infrastructure surrounding a data center is also becoming more relevant to financing decisions. Power is the most visible example. Large AI-oriented facilities require significant electricity capacity, and the timing of that capacity can influence when a project is built and when capital needs to be deployed. "The challenge is not simply the amount of capital required." But the same principle extends to other parts of a development, from connectivity and construction to customer commitments and the timing of future expansion. For lenders, that means understanding the financing increasingly requires understanding how the project itself will develop. Financing the next phase of growth AI is expected to continue driving significant investment in digital infrastructure. As it does, the financing supporting that expansion will have to keep pace with a sector that is changing quickly. The challenge is not simply the amount of capital required. It is matching that capital to projects that are being developed at greater scale, in multiple phases and under increasingly demanding timelines. For sponsors and financial institutions alike, that is making data center financing a more dynamic part of the infrastructure landscape.

artigo.texto: A agenda climática deixou de ser um capítulo isolado dos relatórios de sustentabilidade e passou a orientar decisões de investimento, contratos com fornecedores e a reputação de marcas inteiras. Nesse cenário, dois termos se tornaram onipresentes nos comunicados corporativos — Carbono Neutro e Net Zero. Embora sejam tratados como sinônimos, eles descrevem compromissos com profundidade, prazo e rigor bem diferentes. Segundo o Monitor do Mercado, entender essa distinção não é apenas uma questão semântica: é o que separa uma meta climática consistente de uma promessa sem lastro ou, em casos mais graves, de greenwashing. O que diferencia Carbono Neutro de Net Zero Ser Carbono Neutro significa que uma empresa equilibra a quantidade de dióxido de carbono que emite com uma quantidade equivalente removida ou evitada em outro lugar. Na prática, funciona como uma conta que precisa fechar em zero: de um lado ficam as emissões medidas; do outro, as compensações. Essas compensações costumam vir da compra de créditos de carbono ligados a projetos de preservação florestal, energia renovável ou captura de metano, de investimentos em reflorestamento — que aproveitam a capacidade das árvores de absorver CO₂ durante a fotossíntese — ou ainda de aportes em fontes de energia limpa. O ponto central é que a neutralidade de carbono não exige, necessariamente, que a empresa reduza suas próprias emissões antes de compensá-las. Ela pode manter o nível atual de emissão e simplesmente pagar pela compensação em outro ponto da cadeia. Trata-se de um modelo mais acessível e mais rápido de alcançar, o que o torna útil como primeiro passo, mas limitado quando tratado como meta final. Net Zero: escopo mais amplo e exigência de corte real O conceito de Net Zero representa uma evolução desse compromisso e parte de uma lógica bem mais exigente. Em vez de olhar apenas para o CO₂, a meta abrange todos os gases de efeito estufa, incluindo metano, óxido nitroso e hidrofluorcarbonetos. Além disso, a compensação só entra em cena depois que a empresa tiver cortado a maior parte possível de suas próprias emissões ao longo de toda a cadeia de valor. Isso envolve normalmente três frentes de emissão, conhecidas como escopos. O escopo 1 cobre as emissões diretas geradas por fontes controladas pela própria empresa, como frota própria, caldeiras e processos industriais. O escopo 2 está ligado à energia elétrica comprada. Já o escopo 3 abrange as emissões indiretas espalhadas por toda a cadeia de valor, da matéria-prima ao descarte do produto, e costuma ser a fatia mais difícil de endereçar. Só depois de reduzir drasticamente essas três frentes — e não apenas uma parte delas — é que se admite compensar a fração remanescente, considerada tecnicamente inevitável no estado atual da tecnologia. O que a SBTi considera uma meta Net Zero legítima A Science Based Targets initiative, conhecida como SBTi e principal referência internacional para validar metas corporativas de clima, reforça essa distinção. De acordo com a avaliação apresentada, uma meta Net Zero só é considerada legítima quando a empresa demonstra uma trajetória de corte real de emissões, geralmente entre 90% e 95% do total, antes de recorrer a qualquer compensação para o restante. O Carbono Neutro não segue esse mesmo nível de exigência. Esse padrão vem sendo continuamente aperfeiçoado. Em 2026, a SBTi atualizou seu padrão internacional de metas Net Zero corporativas, reforçando critérios sobre como as empresas devem comprovar, monitorar e reportar essa redução real ao longo do tempo — um sinal de que o mercado está fechando o cerco contra metas anunciadas sem lastro técnico. Hoje, milhares de empresas ao redor do mundo já têm metas climáticas validadas por esse tipo de padrão, número que cresce ano a ano à medida que reguladores, investidores e consumidores cobram mais transparência. Por que a diferença importa para quem investe É essa diferença de rigor, alcance e prazo que explica por que uma empresa pode se declarar carbono neutro já hoje, com relativa facilidade, comprando compensações suficientes para equilibrar suas emissões de CO₂ em um recorte específico da operação. Uma meta Net Zero, por outro lado, costuma levar décadas de reestruturação de processos, fornecedores e tecnologia para se tornar realidade. Justamente por essa diferença de complexidade e percepção pública, quanto mais a sustentabilidade influencia decisões de compra, contratação e investimentos, maior é a tentação de usar esses termos de forma solta. Uma empresa pode anunciar neutralidade de carbono comprando créditos de projetos de qualidade duvidosa, sem nunca reduzir de fato sua produção — o que, na prática, não resolve o problema climático, apenas o desloca no papel. O que observar além do rótulo Por isso, especialistas recomendam observar não o rótulo usado pela empresa, mas o plano por trás dele. Existe uma meta de redução real, com etapas intermediárias verificáveis? A compensação é usada como complemento ou como substituto da redução? Há transparência sobre os escopos 1, 2 e 3? Segundo a análise, essas perguntas dizem mais sobre o compromisso climático de uma empresa do que qualquer selo isolado. Na prática, os dois conceitos não são excludentes e costumam ser etapas de uma mesma jornada. Em um mercado onde compromissos ambientais se multiplicam, entender a diferença entre Carbono Neutro e Net Zero tornou-se essencial para interpretar o que as empresas realmente estão fazendo para enfrentar as mudanças climáticas. A neutralidade pode representar um ponto de partida relevante, mas o Net Zero é o que revela o grau de ambição e transformação envolvido. No fim, a pergunta mais importante não é qual termo aparece no relatório, mas quais ações concretas estão sendo implementadas para tornar essa promessa uma realidade. O texto é assinado por Renata G. artigo.texto: Stevens Point starts data center conversation STEVENS POINT, Wis. (WSAW)— The city of Stevens Point added an item to Monday’s planning commission meeting for a public discussion on data centers, with city leaders saying they want the community to drive how the city reacts if or when a data center looks to move in. Current zoning rules “At this point, if a data center wanted to build one of those massive things, what safeguards would there be for the community?” said Alder Mary Kneebone, Stevens Point Planning Commission. The planning commission says there isn’t much. As of now, data centers can’t be built in residential or commercial zoning districts. They would be allowed in the city’s industrial zoning districts. Developer interest While the city hasn’t had conversations about constructing a data center, data centers have reached out to the city about interest levels. “It was a conversation that, we didn’t talk about it,” said Jarod Kivela, director of community development, Stevens Point. “They have been, I guess not responded to until we have this conversation.” Public concerns During public comment, many expressed concerns over the environmental impacts in a city built on the outdoors. “If I saw that there was a data center being built in Stevens Point and I was a prospective college student...like, if I went back to when I was looking just out of high school...I would’ve said no. I wouldn’t have come here,” Reemus said, an environmental studies student. Other concerns were lack of economic impact after data centers are built, as well as want of transparency between the city and the people if a project were to start. Federal candidates weigh in The issue of data centers is more of a city and state-level policy, but it can be influenced at the federal level. Both candidates for the 7th Congressional District are hearing from voters about them. “We are way behind in regulating this entire sector,” said Fred Clark, (D) 7th Congressional District candidate. “We need to treat AI like we treated nuclear energy in the 1950s. And, and the federal government is the only game in town to make that happen.” “This is where I think it’s so important to have young faces involved in this rise of AI,” said Michael Alfonso, (R) 7th Congressional District candidate. “You know, AI has the ability to put out of work so many workers. But I actually think if done properly, it can actually empower workers.” Clark says the state needs to regulate how they’re built. Alfonso adds that should include supplying their own power, not use up waterways and let local leaders make the decision. artigo.texto: Northfield council moves away from data center ban, toward tiered regulation After more than two hours of public comment and council discussion, the Northfield City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday night to reduce the required setback between data-processing facilities and parks or trails from roughly three-quarters of a mile to 200 feet. But the setback change was only part of the story. In a separate motion, the council also directed staff to explore a tiered regulatory framework for data-processing facilities as part of the upcoming Land Development Code update, looking beyond just power consumption to include water use and other emerging concerns. The change to the setback had been in the works since 2024, when the city passed an ordinance regulating data-processing facilities. That ordinance required a 3,950-foot setback from any existing or planned park, trail, or recreational feature. It also required a 200-foot setback from residential structures. Community Development Director Scott Wopata acknowledged the moment was about more than one number. “This one's going to be hard,” he said. “In any example I look at around Minnesota or the Midwest or nationally, there aren't a lot of examples where communities have figured out a way to have this conversation and learn from each other and to empathetically see things from different perspectives. There's a lot of negative examples of how elected officials and staff members in different cities have signed NDAs, dismissed the public, not listened to public concerns.” Wopata framed the night as an effort to rebuild public trust after a year of conversations that started long before any application existed. "In 2024, we put a moratorium on all data-center development so that we could develop policies before we had a project application," Wopata said. "That is what we did. We have been following those best practices." The city's regulations include 17 performance standards covering noise, water use, glare, vibrations and more. They also require a conditional use permit triggered by any water use. “If we read anywhere anything about data centers, [there] is a very well documented track of negative externalities,” Wopata said. “There are water quality issues. There's water quantity issues. There are stories of communities losing water pressure. There's stories of communities where residents have seen significant spikes in their utility bills because the data centers moved in and this corporate development has happened.” But he also drew a distinction between prohibition and regulation. "Regulating is often a more strategic and sophisticated and just successful approach than prohibition," Wopata said, listing alcohol and cannabis prohibition as negative examples from history. "Bringing something into the light and regulating it can often help ameliorate some of the biggest harmful negative externalities." City Planner Mathias Hughey explained the rationale for the change. The 3,950-foot setback made every industrial parcel in the city undevelopable, and it was originally drafted without a clear rationale. "This is still much more restrictive than other industrial uses," Hughey said. Hughey said the planning commission had separately recommended that data-processing facilities be prohibited outright and that staff research a tiered regulatory framework. Because that recommendation was not part of the published public hearing notice, the council had to proceed with the setback item as written. Competing priorities More than a dozen residents spoke during public comment, most urging the council to keep the moratorium or reject the setback change. One Northfielder, Trisha Brunk, even led the room through a song. Councilor Kathleen Holmes acknowledged the volume of opposition in the room but said the council has to weigh competing priorities. “While there is a high number of people who have spoken out against data centers, we, those of us decision makers, policymakers up here, have to hold many priorities,” she said. “And while we have heard the thoughts, the feedback, the opinions on data centers, I would say probably all of us here more often and more frequently hear 'Lower our taxes.’ … I take this as the belief that the path forward is through regulation and not prohibition.” Councilor Jessica Peterson White said she saw parallels to hog feedlot debates from the early 2000s. "But when we were talking about hog feedlots, the scale was a really important part of the conversation," she said. "I don't have a clear sense myself of what scale of data center or other types of development is where we should set a regulation, but I believe that the regulations that we have make it vanishingly unlikely that we will get a hyperscale data center, and that seems good." She also addressed the equity dimension. "There is a history in this country of affluent white communities sort of offshoring their industrial needs to communities that don't have the same resources, don't have the same organizing power, and those industrial uses are then underregulated and create issues for poorer and less white communities," she said. "And I hope we don't play a role in that." No one is saying ‘Let’s build a huge data center’ Councilor Davin Sokup said he was voting yes despite his own uncertainty. "But I just really want to highlight that what we're considering here tonight, I think, in my opinion, does show an openness to having a data center in Northfield," he said. "I'm not willing to say that it couldn't possibly be that in the future." Councilor Chad Beumer said he understood the distrust but believed the city's regulations were already strong. “I don't think there's a single person sitting up here that is saying, ‘Let's build a huge data center out there that's going to burn up all kinds of energy and waste a whole bunch of water,’” he said. “I think our ordinance 1098 clearly dictates that that's not going to happen.” Mayor Erica Zweifel closed the discussion by noting the s

artigo.texto: Climate experts and other stakeholders yesterday gathered in Abuja for the European Union Climate Dialogues programme ( EUCDs2) for Nigeria’s carbon market roadmap. The event, which focuses on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets Through Robust Monitoring, Reporting And Verification (MRV) Protocols,” brought together government officials, development partners, private-sector operators, investors, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon market must be built on integrity, transparency and credible data, warning that the country would not tolerate practices capable of undermining confidence in carbon credits generated in Nigeria. Represented by the Director, Energy , Transportation and Infrastructure, Mr Michael Ivenso, l she said that the council had issued about 26 million carbon credits so far from projects previously executed in Nigeria, describing the development as evidence of the country’s capacity to participate in international carbon markets. According to her, Nigeria’s objective is to ensure that carbon projects deliver “real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes” while protecting communities, ecosystems and the interests of investors and project developers. The Director-General said the operationalisation of the National Carbon Markets Framework would provide the institutional foundation for a credible carbon market capable of mobilising private capital for clean energy, agriculture, forestry, waste management and other climate interventions. The NCCC boss said a key component of the strategy was the establishment of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry through which every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred or retired in Nigeria would have a digital record. “This will help prevent double-counting and strengthen the integrity of carbon transactions,” she said. She added that Nigeria was also moving towards digital MRV, leveraging remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to improve the accuracy of carbon measurement while reducing the cost and time required for verification. Majekodunmi said effective MRV would also enable regulators to track emissions trajectories, assure buyers that claimed emission reductions were genuine and help communities monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. She called for stronger coordination among federal ministries, state governments, project developers, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. She said the Council was working with relevant stakeholders to ensure that future carbon credit transfers under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were supported by credible national systems. The Director, Federal Department of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, said the forestry sector remained central to Nigeria’s climate response and could become one of the country’s biggest opportunities in the carbon market. She said forests served as carbon sinks and temperature buffers while providing biodiversity, soil protection, water regulation and livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. “We must therefore ensure that carbon-market development supports forest conservation rather than creating pressure for further forest exploitation,” she said. Bawa-Bwari stressed that credible carbon markets could not be built without credible data, particularly in the forestry sector. She said Nigeria needed reliable information on forest cover, degradation, deforestation, biomass and carbon stocks to determine how much carbon was being stored or removed and how those changes occurred over time. She called for continued strengthening of the National Forest Inventory and forest monitoring systems, as well as increased use of satellite imagery, remote sensing and artificial intelligence. However, she cautioned that satellite information must be complemented with ground-based measurements and field verification. The director also called for increased capacity among federal and state forestry institutions to collect and manage forest data. “MRV should not be developed as a stand-alone carbon-market activity. It should build on existing national systems for forest monitoring, greenhouse-gas accounting, REDD+ data, land-use planning and climate reporting,” she said. Bawa-Bwari urged relevant agencies to avoid establishing parallel systems that collect similar information, calling instead for clear institutional responsibilities for the collection, management, validation and reporting of forest-carbon data. On it part, the European Union said Nigeria’s efforts to develop a credible carbon market could help attract much-needed finance for climate action while supporting sustainable economic growth. Mr Jop Weterings, a member of the Task Force on International Carbon Pricing And Marketing Diplomacy at the EU said the bloc had stepped up cooperation with Nigeria on carbon markets over the past year, describing the roundtable as an important milestone in the partnership. The EU said its shared interest with Nigeria was to scale up high-integrity carbon markets capable of strengthening global climate action, channeling resources into Nigerian initiatives and driving sustainable economic growth. It noted that Nigeria’s adoption of the National Carbon Markets Framework had provided an important foundation for building confidence and trust among investors, buyers and other market participants. The EU representative said the focus should now be on operationalising the framework, particularly through strong MRV systems that would ensure carbon credits generated in Nigeria represented credible climate outcomes. artigo.texto: The Public Utility Commission of Texas is asking a Travis County judge to block the release of information showing where data centers and virtual currency mines operate, saying those details could aid terrorists. The lawsuit filed Monday pits the state agency responsible for regulating utilities against Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office over the scope of Texas’ public-records law and the state’s protections for critical infrastructure. At the center of the dispute are two seemingly basic geographic details: the county where a facility is located and the regional water planning area in which it sits. The PUC argues that those details are “privileged information” and become sensitive when combined with other information collected through its survey of the industry, including electricity demand, actual electricity consumption, projected peak demand, water consumption, water sources, cooling technology and the utilities and infrastructure serving a facility. The commission is not asking the court to declare the entire survey confidential. Instead, it wants the court to rule that the two geographic fields are exempt from disclosure under the Texas Homeland Security Act, which is meant to “protect against homeland security threats and hazards . . . and prevent significant criminal and terrorist attacks.” The lawsuit does not represent a final ruling on whether the information ultimately must be released. But it does come as Texas officials are seeking more information about the state’s data center industry. Gov. Greg Abbott has ordered state agencies to conduct additional reviews of data centers seeking to connect to the state’s electric grid, including reviews of electricity and water use, cooling systems and other information. He has also directed the Texas Water Development Board to take enforcement action against data centers that fail to comply with required water use reporting. What’s in the PUC water and energy use survey? In 2025, Texas lawmakers directed the PUC to collect information about water and energy consumption at data centers and virtual-currency-mining facilities to better understand the growth of the industry. The effort reflects a growing concern among state officials and Texans about the resources required by large computing facilities. Data centers can consume enormous amounts of electricity because of the thousands of servers operating inside them. Depending on their cooling systems, they can also require substantial quantities of water to help keep their servers cool during operation. The PUC developed its survey in cooperation with the Texas Water Development Board, the state agency tasked with overseeing the state’s water planning process. The information was intended to help state officials better understand the relationship between electricity demand and water consumption and to inform future planning. The Legislature also directed the PUC to share information with other state agencies and produce a report on its findings. The survey was sent to 377 facilities and sought information including a facility’s location, county and regional water-planning area, electricity load and consumption, projected future peak demand, cooling technology, water consumption and sources and information about the facility’s connection to the electric grid. The response was limited and called “pathetic” by one state representative during a June legislative hearing where PUC officials said 28 companies representing 92 facilities had responded to the survey. Lawmakers questioned whether the resulting data would be sufficient to support long-term policy decisions. The PUC later reopened the voluntary survey for an additional 10 days in July. As of August, 13 virtual currency mining and 77 data center facilities had filled out the survey, according to an email from a PUC spokesperson. The PUC lawsuit The PUC dispute with the attorney general’s office began after a resident from McLennan County and four journalists, including a reporter at The Texas Tribune, sought the survey responses through open records requests. The PUC denied those requests, saying that the information should be protected from disclosure in its entirety. Those requestors have an opportunity to participate in the open records dispute if they choose. Under Texas law, when a governmental agency believes requested records aren’t open to the public, it can ask the Attorney General’s Open Records Division for a ruling. That is what the PUC did. The commission argued that at least some of the survey information was protected under the Texas Homeland Security Act, which makes certain information concerning vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure confidential. But the PUC, the government entity seeking to withhold records, must establish that the statutory exception applies. That distinction is at the heart of the dispute. The Attorney General’s office issued two rulings concluding that the PUC had not sufficiently established that the disputed information identified the kind of technical vulnerabilities covered by the Homeland Security Act. The PUC is now challenging those rulings by asking a court to reach a different conclusion.
