artigo.texto: Tech giants are trying to win over communities that oppose data centers as they pour billions into the infrastructure powering their AI ambitions. Amazon’s latest approach is to invest more than $1 billion over five years in job training, free community college, and energy efficiency upgrades. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman announced the Built Together program in an Oct. 2 corporate post that also defended the company’s data center build-out. He compared the build-out to public benefit projects such as the interstate highway system, and wrote that Amazon understands communities’ “apprehension” about data centers. Still, he wrote, the more than 100 proposed data center moratoriums under construction could sideline the U.S. from the AI race. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman wrote. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.” Amazon isn’t the only hyperscaler trying to make the data center boom easier for host communities to accept. Microsoft pledged in January to cover the electricity and grid costs tied to its facilities, and Meta said it invested more than $550 million in water and wastewater infrastructure in its data center communities. What Amazon is offering Built Together targets common complaints dogging data center projects—that they raise energy bills, strain local infrastructure, and don’t deliver enough lasting benefits to residents. Those concerns have become harder for hyperscalers to ignore. New York imposed a statewide moratorium on new large data centers in July, and opposition spread to major data center markets like Virginia, where only 35% of people said in March that they’d be comfortable with a new facility being built there, according to a Washington Post and Schar School poll. Amazon itself is facing resistance in Loudoun County, Va., where officials are objecting to a proposed 800,000-square-foot data center project on the former George Washington University Virginia Science and Technology campus. Built Together is Amazon’s attempt to answer those objections with more direct benefits for host communities. Amazon said it will cover students’ remaining community college costs after financial aid for certain certificates and associate degrees, including programs in HVAC, fiber optics, and IT, and estimates more than 300,000 students could gain access over five years. The company also said its skilled trades centers plan to train up to 100,000 workers a year for jobs with Amazon and its construction partners by the end of 2028. The company also plans to fund energy efficiency upgrades for more than 30,000 homes and more than 300 schools and community buildings. Local officials and community groups will help steer funding toward projects such as roads, parks, fire equipment, affordable housing, and food assistance. “Working with county officials and trusted community organizations, we will identify the highest-impact investments and provide annual funding with transparent reporting on outcomes,” Garman wrote. “This is not Amazon deciding what communities need—it is Amazon providing resources and letting communities decide.” Amazon is also using the Built Together announcement to push back on some causes of the backlash. Garman wrote that data centers are unfairly blamed for higher electricity bills and water use, and that aging grids are at fault for rising energy bills in some states. “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived,” he wrote. He also said Amazon’s average data center uses less than 13,000 gallons of water per day and said the facilities deliver tax revenue and construction jobs to host communities. In St. Joseph County, Ind., Amazon estimates it will pay more than $3 billion in taxes over the same period, compared with $1.2 million that the land’s previous use would have generated.

artigo.texto: Sistema de armazenamento de energia solar para varanda com duas tomadas de alimentação de reserva: análise do SigenMate 2700 Ultra Sistema complexo de armazenamento para varanda e casa. O SigenMate 2700 Ultra é um sistema de armazenamento tudo-em-um para instalações solares em varandas, oferecendo até 18,8 kWh e 4.000 Wp. A nossa análise revela o desempenho do sistema na prática e onde surgiram problemas. Marcus Schwarten (traduzido por DeepL / Ninh Duy) Publicado 🇺🇸 🇩🇪 ... Veredito do teste do SigenMate 2700 Ultra: Controle rápido, mas também problemas Com base nos nossos testes, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra da Sigenergy oferece uma interessante solução tudo-em-um para sistemas solares de varanda. No nosso teste, gostámos particularmente da elevada potência de entrada fotovoltaica distribuída por quatro MPPTs, da construção de alta qualidade e do assistente de IA na aplicação abrangente. O controlo da injeção na rede também é rápido e preciso - quando a ligação ao contador inteligente funciona. Também nos deparámos com alguns outros problemas menores, mas estes deverão ser corrigíveis com uma atualização de software. No geral, um sistema de armazenamento tudo-em-um mais do que sólido para sistemas solares de varanda, cuja capacidade pode aumentar até 18,8 kWh ao longo do tempo, mas que não oferece qualquer margem para além dos seus 800 W de potência de injeção na rede. Pro Contra Preço e disponibilidade Na Alemanha, o preço de venda recomendado do SigenMate 2700 Ultra é de 1.199 euros (com IVA de 0% na Alemanha). O preço de venda recomendado da bateria de expansão SigenMate BAT 2700 é de 899 euros. Os produtos estão disponíveis diretamente no fabricante, mas também podem ser encomendados em retalhistas como a Amazon ou a Tepto. Com o crescimento dos sistemas solares para varandas e dos pequenos sistemas fotovoltaicos, cada vez mais fabricantes estão a lançar no mercado soluções tudo-em-um que combinam inversores, MPPTs e armazenamento. Além dos nomes habituais, como Anker Solix, EcoFlow e Zendure, existem também soluções de fabricantes menos conhecidos. Entre estas encontra-se o SigenMate 2700 Ultra, que está disponível há alguns meses. A empresa por trás deste produto, a Sigenergy, não é uma recém-chegada, mas até agora tem atuado sobretudo na área dos sistemas fotovoltaicos de maiores dimensões. A nossa análise do SigenMate 2700 Ultra revela como o seu sistema compacto de armazenamento de energia para todos se comporta na prática e como se compara com a concorrência. Specifications Equipamento e instalação: Sistema de armazenamento para sistemas solares de varanda Uma análise das especificações acima mostra que o SigenMate 2700 Ultra tem muito em comum com o Anker Solix Solarbank 3 Pro do ano passado. Também oferece uma capacidade de bateria LiFePO₄ de pouco menos de 2,7 kWh (6.000 ciclos de carga, garantia de 10 anos). Se necessário, esta capacidade pode ser ampliada até 18,8 kWh com seis baterias de expansão BAT2700. Isso deve ser mais do que suficiente para a grande maioria dos lares - não só para sistemas solares de varanda, mas também para armazenamento de energia doméstico. Com uma potência de entrada fotovoltaica de 4.000 W, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra supera até ligeiramente o Solarbank 3 Pro, oferecendo também 4 MPPTs. Isto é vantajoso, pois não só permite ligar até oito painéis solares sem qualquer problema, como também proporciona condições ideais para painéis com diferentes orientações e sombreamento. A potência de saída é limitada a 800 watts, como é habitual num sistema solar de varanda. Além disso, estão disponíveis diretamente no dispositivo duas tomadas de alimentação de emergência com uma potência de saída contínua de 1,400 W e uma potência de pico de 1,800 W. Estas funcionam independentemente da rede elétrica e, por isso, também funcionam durante uma falha de energia (se a bateria estiver carregada). Quando ligado à rede elétrica, é possível atingir até 3,600 W (bypass). Além da entrada solar, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra também pode ser carregado a partir da rede elétrica com uma potência de até 1,400 W. Alguns outros sistemas no mercado oferecem potências máximas de saída e de entrada superiores. No entanto, estas capacidades são suficientes para um sistema solar de varanda. Tudo isto está alojado numa robusta estrutura metálica. A qualidade de construção da unidade que testámos é excelente e transmite uma impressão de produto de gama alta, inclusive em termos de design. Graças à classificação IP66 e à proteção contra corrosão C5-M o sistema está bem equipado para utilização no exterior. Foi concebido para suportar temperaturas entre -20 °C e 55 °C e pode ser aquecido através de uma manta de aquecimento, de acordo com uma programação ou automaticamente, se necessário. No entanto, já gera uma quantidade considerável de calor por si só sob carga. O dispositivo pesa cerca de 29 kg e exige alguma força para o deslocar até ao local de instalação. As duas pegas embutidas à esquerda e à direita facilitam o transporte. As dimensões de 46.0 x 27.5 x 22.5 cm são bastante compactas para um sistema com cerca de 2.7 kWh. Quando combinado com uma ou mais baterias adicionais, a torre torna-se proporcionalmente mais alta. O material de montagem para o fixar a uma parede não está incluído. A embalagem inclui apenas um cabo de alimentação com ficha Schuko, uma chave para desligar os painéis solares e um manual. To get started, simply connect the power cable to the corresponding port on the side of the SigenMate 2700 Ultra and to a power outlet. The system can then be switched on. To generate your own solar power, at least one solar panel must also be connected to the four inputs (MC4 sockets). These are located on the top under a somewhat cheap-looking plastic cover, rather than on the side (as with many competitors). This makes access and cable management easier (the cables run out toward the back). However, the spacing between the individual connectors is quite tight. App & operation: AI assistan

artigo.texto: Empresário transforma negócio de manutenção de maquininhas de cartão em serviços de integração de data centers Com a reestruturação, RGL Solutions passou de uma receita inferior a R$ 500 mil, em 2023, para R$ 18 milhões no ano passado Atualizado Com uma estrutura de 15 colaboradores, que atuam na sede em Barueri (SP), a RGL Solutions experimentou uma virada operacional e financeira expressiva no setor de infraestrutura crítica de tecnologia da informação nos últimos três anos. A empresa, que faturou R$ 465 mil em 2023 durante seu processo de reestruturação, deu um salto significativo ao atingir R$ 17,4 milhões em receita em 2024. No ano passado, registrou R$ 18 milhões em faturamento, movimentando cerca de R$ 40 milhões em transações. Agora, a empresa está estruturando planos de expansão focados em desenvolvimento e sustentação de sistemas baseados em IA. Essa nova frente de soluções é apontada como a alavanca estratégica para atingir uma meta de crescimento de 80% em 2027. Especializada em integração de data centers, redes corporativas e conectividade crítica, a RGL tornou-se parceira estratégica da fabricante chinesa Huawei e assumiu o retrofit completo do data center da fábrica de caminhões e ônibus do Grupo Volkswagen, em Resende (RJ). A projeção para 2026 é alcançar R$ 23 milhões em faturamento. Por trás dessa transformação de modelo de negócio está a trajetória do fundador e diretor-executivo William Cavalcanti. Nascido e criado em Itaquera, bairro humilde da Zona Leste de São Paulo, o empresário iniciou sua caminhada profissional do zero. Formado como tecnólogo em engenharia de automação industrial, ele ingressou no mercado de tecnologia. "Comecei como estagiário numa empresa de meios de pagamento. Honestamente eu nem a conhecia, ainda estava procurando estágio. Então, por acaso, eu consegui emprego nessa empresa. Começamos com um laboratório com quatro pessoas, cinco pessoas, e mirando o que dava para fazer naquela realidade", relembra o executivo. Dificuldade inspirou o empreendedor Cavalcanti ingressou em outra empresa de logística como funcionário, desta vez para montar um centro de reparos dentro da companhia. Lá, ele identificou um gargalo crítico na cadeia de manutenção de terminais de pagamento (máquinas POS) das credenciadoras (empresas responsáveis por credenciar estabelecimentos comerciais para aceitarem pagamentos por cartão e por processar e liquidar essas transações financeiras). Enquanto as devoluções de equipamentos levavam cerca de 45 dias para serem concluídas pelos fabricantes, William idealizou, entre 2007 e 2008, o primeiro laboratório instalado diretamente dentro de um operador logístico. "Nós fomos o primeiro laboratório técnico a ter um centro de reparo dentro do operador logístico. Adotamos uma estratégia e conseguimos reduzir a devolução do equipamento para três dias, diz o empreendedor. Em 26 de agosto de 2010, William fundou, ao lado de um sócio, a empresa batizada originalmente de TOP. A operação iniciou focada na manutenção e logística reversa de terminais POS para gigantes como Cielo e Rede. Em 2012, a companhia fechou um contrato de grande porte com o grupo América Móvil (Claro, Net e Embratel), expandindo sua presença industrial para duas plantas em São Paulo (Cotia e Campinas) e uma no Amazonas, em Manaus. No auge desse modelo, a empresa empregava quase 300 funcionários e recuperava de 150 mil a 200 mil equipamentos por mês. Em 2018, William decidiu vender sua participação de 50% no negócio para o seu sócio. O empreendedor estava em busca de novos desafios. "Vendi as minhas cotas para o meu antigo sócio e segui a vida. Fui fazer outras coisas", conta. Durante esse afastamento, ele fundou um provedor de internet (ISP), implementando mais de 200 quilômetros de rede de fibra óptica e alcançando cerca de 8 mil clientes até vender o negócio, em 2022. Enquanto Cavalcanti conduzia seu novo empreendimento, a antiga empresa enfrentou sérias dificuldades de mercado. Retorno do fundador Com a entrada de concorrentes agressivos e a perda progressiva dos contratos com o grupo América Móvil, a operação original entrou em crise financeira. Procurado para reestruturar a empresa, o empresário selou seu retorno em 28 de outubro de 2022. A repactuação societária envolveu a divisão da operação em dois CNPJs; William assumiu de forma isolada e com 100% do capital o CNPJ original que havia fundado em 2010. "Fui ajustando o que dava para ajustar e assumi os clientes que foram possíveis de recuperar", explica. Com o controle total em mãos, o executivo promoveu uma reestruturação profunda. Transferiu a sede de Campinas para Alphaville, em Barueri, e alterou o nome corporativo para RGL Solutions. Mais do que uma mudança de marca, ocorreu uma pivotagem completa do modelo de negócios. A RGL encerrou as atividades com equipamentos remanufaturados e passou a focar exclusivamente em serviços de TI de alto valor agregado, como redes Wi-Fi 7 corporativas, engenharia de data centers e migração de infraestruturas legadas (com projetos de substituição de tecnologia Cisco para Huawei). "O meu foco foi me dedicar à TI, não mais em equipamento remanufaturado. Nosso forte não é venda de equipamento, nosso forte é prestação de serviço, que é mais rentável", detalha o fundador. Aliada às certificações de qualidade ISO 9001 (e em fase final para a obtenção da ISO/IEC 27001), a RGL mantém uma filosofia de células de trabalho enxutas e de alta produtividade. "Eu sempre procurei ter a quantidade de pessoas suficiente para determinada atividade. Então, geralmente a gente estrutura uma célula para um determinado segmento, amadurece ela, deixa ela redonda antes de expandir. Se eu fosse falar o que é o segredo de sucesso, seria isso", diz o empreendedor.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media Households and the power grid run on alternating current. Batteries — including those in electric vehicles — run on direct current. That AC-DC divide has complicated the prospect of EVs as home backup batteries. Today, almost every commercially available vehicle-to-home (V2H) backup power system in the U.S. requires a pricey DC bidirectional charger: a device that converts direct current from the vehicle to home-ready alternating current. The only exception is Tesla’s. Over the past few years, the major EV and home battery manufacturer has been working out how to get its vehicles to do the job of sending AC power to homes and the grid. Tesla’s Cybertruck has had this ability for more than a year, and on Tuesday, the firm announced it is expanding the capability to its new Model 3 and Model Y EVs — as long as your home has a Powerwall 3 battery, that is. “This is us bringing the whole ecosystem together and allowing our products to complement each other,” said Colby Hastings, head of Tesla Energy’s residential energy business. Instead of relying on a DC bidirectional charger to do the power conversion, AC bidirectional charging does the job with hardware in the vehicles themselves. The Powerwall 3 retails for $8,200 and costs several thousand dollars more to install, but it’s a complete home backup system. The only additional equipment Tesla requires to add between two and three days of additional V2H backup power from an EV battery is its standard Wall Connector charger, which retails for $595. It’s cheaper to set up a Cybertruck for home backup power, since those vehicles don’t require homes to have a Powerwall. Customers simply need to pay for a V2H hardware package that retails for $1,990, plus about $1,800 to $2,200 for installation. Either way, these prices are a good deal compared to the $6,500 to $10,000 and up it typically costs to buy a DC bidirectional charger — a price that doesn’t include a home battery. That’s largely because it’s a lot cheaper to convert DC to AC power within an EV — which already has to convert incoming AC to DC for its battery — than to buy a separate power conversion system that attaches to your house, Hastings said. “We’ve been very focused on what we think is the more long-term scalable pathway,” she said. “That’s what led us to this architecture.” To be clear, Tesla EVs and Powerwall batteries still cost a lot of money. And arguably, Tesla could be seen as something of a latecomer to the V2H game, which other automakers have offered for years with DC V2H backup systems. But in terms of establishing a means for lower-cost AC hardware to turn EVs into home batteries, Tesla’s latest development is a big deal, said Zach Woogen, executive director of the Vehicle-Grid Integration Council. “Many in the industry expect AC bidirectional charging equipment will be economical for customers and manufacturers alike at a lower price point,” he said. “This is an exciting proposition for a technology space that’s been limited by relatively high up-front costs.” Woogen’s group represents EV and charging manufacturers working with utilities and regulators across the country to streamline the use of EVs as backup batteries and as grid assets. The cumulative impact of millions of EVs could be huge. A recent study found that California could get one-third of its grid energy storage needs from tapping just 10% of the 9.7 million EVs it expects to have by the mid-2030s. Automakers have been touting the potential of EVs to back up homes during power outages for years, from the first Nissan Leaf EVs to the discontinued Ford F-150 Lightning. General Motors’ GM Energy business offers home battery and EV charger-power conversion systems that currently retail for just under $12,000 to more than $20,000. Kia markets its EV9 with V2H charging, and electric truck maker Rivian is working on similar capabilities. But beyond Tesla, automakers selling EVs in the U.S. haven’t publicly announced that they have embedded the technology so that the cars can provide AC backup power on their own. That’s partly because adding such tech tacks on complexity and cost to the vehicle manufacturing process. Things get even more complicated when you start talking about sending EV battery power back into utility grids. That’s called vehicle-to-grid, or V2G. Utilities have been running V2G pilot projects for decades, and a handful have started to expand into standard programs that pay customers who let the utility tap their EV batteries. But right now, only California and Maryland have established utility regulations that allow for AC bidirectional charging outside of pilot projects, although other states are working on it. Pacific Gas & Electric, California’s largest utility, has been running V2G pilots for years now and is now testing V2H capabilities with EVs from GM, Kia, Nissan, Polestar, and Volvo using bidirectional DC chargers. But the cost of the gear required for households to sign up has been daunting, said Eli Darby, part of PG&E’s clean energy transportation team. “We’ve had decent participation from DC systems,” Darby said. “But we’ve seen there’s a ceiling to the amount of money customers are willing to spend. The $10,000 to $15,000 it takes to pay for equipment and also installation and interconnection is a barrier.” That’s why PG&E has been working to certify the technology combos that can supply AC power directly from EVs to home chargers, and from there to the grid. So far, “Tesla is the lead product to market,” he said. “We’re technically piloting interconnecting their systems today.” Tesla has been enrolling Cybertrucks in programs with PG&E as well as with Texas utilities CenterPoint Energy and Oncor to tap their battery power to send back to the grid, Hastings said. artigo.texto: Crise energética nos EUA ameaça IA, mas poupa Nvidia e Broadcom Déficit de 34% na energia para data centers até 2028 pode travar a expansão da IA nos EUA, mas as duas maiores fabricantes de chips seguem blindadas, segundo análise do Morgan Stanley. O boom da inteligência artificial criou um problema que dinheiro, sozinho, não resolve: falta energia elétrica. Os bilhões de dólares despejados na construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos esbarram numa infraestrutura energética que não acompanha o ritmo da demanda. E o gargalo começa a redesenhar o mapa de vencedores e perdedores na cadeia de semicondutores. Um relatório do Morgan Stanley publicado nesta segunda-feira estima que os desenvolvedores de data centers nos EUA enfrentarão um déficit líquido de energia de 34% até 2028, o equivalente a 32 gigawatts. Para colocar em perspectiva, isso representa mais do que toda a capacidade instalada de geração eólica do Brasil. O número evidencia que o problema não é marginal: é estrutural. A conclusão central do banco, porém, surpreende pelo otimismo seletivo. Nvidia e Broadcom, as duas maiores fornecedoras de chips de alto desempenho para IA, estão relativamente protegidas contra esse cenário. O risco real recai sobre os elos secundários da cadeia: fabricantes de chips de memória, componentes ópticos, gerenciamento de energia e processadores analógicos. Por que Nvidia e Broadcom escapam do gargalo energético A lógica do Morgan Stanley é relativamente simples. Nvidia e Broadcom têm visibilidade privilegiada sobre a alocação de seus chips, a expansão geográfica dos clientes e a coordenação entre centros de dados, fornecedores e a cadeia de abastecimento de energia. Isso significa que essas empresas conseguem antecipar onde haverá capacidade de instalação e direcionar sua produção de acordo. Na prática, os maiores compradores de GPUs da Nvidia, como Microsoft, Google, Amazon e Meta, são justamente os operadores de data centers com maior poder de negociação junto a concessionárias de energia e governos locais. Esses hyperscalers já garantiram contratos de fornecimento de longo prazo e estão diversificando geograficamente suas operações, inclusive para fora dos EUA. O banco afirmou que não vê os gargalos energéticos colocando em risco as previsões de receita da Nvidia ou da Broadcom para 2027. A análise reforça uma tese que o mercado financeiro já precifica parcialmente: essas duas companhias operam num nível de demanda tão elevado que mesmo restrições de infraestrutura não reduzem a fila de pedidos, apenas redistribuem onde os chips serão instalados. Quem paga a conta: os elos frágeis da cadeia de IA Se a capacidade de produção de chips não puder ser implantada por falta de energia nos data centers, os clientes poderão adiar entregas ou cancelar pedidos. E os componentes mais expostos a esse risco são justamente os que dependem de volumes elevados para manter margens saudáveis. Fabricantes de chips de memória, como Micron e SK Hynix, operam com margens mais estreitas e dependem do ritmo de construção de novos data centers para manter a demanda aquecida. O mesmo vale para fornecedores de componentes ópticos, essenciais para a conectividade entre servidores, e para empresas de gerenciamento de energia e chips analógicos. Como analisamos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a cadeia de semicondutores funciona como um ecossistema integrado, e o atraso num elo propaga efeitos em cascata. O Goldman Sachs também sinalizou restrições crescentes à expansão dos data centers nos EUA, embora com uma leitura levemente diferente. O banco espera impacto limitado no curto prazo, em parte pela resistência política a medidas que freiem investimentos em IA. Já o Morgan Stanley enxerga desafios mais concretos, ligados a mão de obra, fornecimento de energia e entraves regulatórios. O déficit de 32 GW e o que isso significa para investidores O número de 32 GW de déficit projetado para 2028 não é apenas uma curiosidade técnica. Ele tem implicações diretas para quem investe em empresas de tecnologia e infraestrutura. A construção de novas usinas de geração, linhas de transmissão e subestações leva anos. Mesmo com o incentivo bilionário dos governos federal e estaduais, a oferta de energia não se expande na mesma velocidade que a demanda por computação. Esse descompasso já está gerando movimentos concretos. Empresas como Microsoft fecharam contratos para reativar usinas nucleares. Amazon investiu em geração solar e eólica dedicada a seus data centers. Google assinou acordos de compra de energia geotérmica. Como acompanhamos na editoria de finanças, o setor de energia virou talvez o maior beneficiário indireto do boom de IA, com ações de concessionárias e empresas de infraestrutura elétrica acumulando altas expressivas nos últimos 12 meses. Para o investidor, a leitura é que a tese de Nvidia e Broadcom permanece intacta no médio prazo, mas o risco migrou para a segunda e terceira camadas da cadeia. Empresas que pareciam apostas seguras no ciclo de IA, como fabricantes de memória HBM e fornecedores de equipamentos de rede, agora carregam um risco adicional de atraso na implantação que não estava no radar há seis meses. IA e energia: um gargalo que veio para ficar O cenário descrito pelo Morgan Stanley não é temporário. A demanda energética da IA generativa cresce exponencialmente a cada nova geração de modelos. O treinamento do GPT-4 consumiu estimados 50 GWh de eletricidade. Modelos futuros devem demandar ordens de magnitude a mais. E a inferência, o uso cotidiano dos modelos por bilhões de pessoas, adiciona uma camada contínua de consumo que não existia antes. A questão energética, portanto, deixou de ser um risco periférico e se tornou o principal limitador da velocidade de expansão da IA nos Estados Unidos. Países que conseguirem resolver essa equação primeiro, seja por abundância de recursos naturais, seja por agilidade regulatória, tendem a capturar uma fatia desproporcional dos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA.

artigo.texto: ESS, an opportunity for K-batteries Summary The global energy storage system market is rapidly expanding, driven by AI data centers and renewable energy growth. In the first half of 2026, lithium-ion battery shipments for ESS reached 461 GWh, up 71 percent year on year, while the Korean government introduced technology, tax and deployment measures to support the industry. Korean battery companies face strong Chinese competition and intensified price pressure but can pursue opportunities in Europe and North America through local production, supply-chain diversification and compliance advantages. Key Facts - The global ESS market is forecast to reach 1,870 GWh in annual shipments by 2035, roughly twice this year’s level. - The Korean government plans to invest more than 250 billion won in next-generation battery technology, while the industry is expected to invest approximately 8 trillion won through 2030 in manufacturing-process innovation and material localization. - The third ESS Central Contract Market will select project developers for a record-high total capacity of 1,180 megawatts, with successful bidders entering 15-year contracts through the Korea Power Exchange. - Chinese companies accounted for nearly 55 percent of the global ESS market in the first half of 2026, and global ESS supply capacity exceeded actual demand by 288 GWh at the end of 2025. - Europe’s combined renewable-energy and battery facility capacity is expected to rise from 6.3 GW in 2025 to around 35 GW in 2030. A new current is reshaping the global battery market. In the first half of 2026, global shipments of lithium-ion batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) reached 461 gigawatt-hour (GWh), up 71 percent from 270 GWh in the same period a year earlier, according to SNE Research. This represents a remarkable leap for the ESS market, especially compared with the 20 percent year-on-year growth in global battery demand for electric vehicles (EVs), which reached 609 GWh over the same period. Key drivers include rising energy demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, where speed and reliability are critical, and growth in renewable power generation, which requires solutions to address its intermittency. The expansion of AI data centers and the transition to renewable energy are powerful trends unlikely to reverse in the short term. As a result, the global ESS market is forecast to reach 1,870 GWh in annual shipments by 2035, roughly twice this year’s level. The Korean government is also stepping up efforts to develop the domestic ESS industry through a range of policy measures. On the technology front, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced its Battery Industry Technology Roadmap on Sept. 22. The road map’s main elements are to position sodium-ion and solid-state batteries as new growth engines: The government will invest more than 250 billion won in next-generation battery technology development; the country’s three cell manufacturers will collaborate on research and standardization in noncompetitive areas; and the industry as a whole will invest approximately 8 trillion won ($5.97 billion) through 2030 in manufacturing-process innovation and the localization of materials. On the production front, the government has pledged tax support. On Aug. 3, the Ministry of Finance and Economy announced its 2026 Tax Reform Proposal, which introduced a domestic production tax credit to expand local manufacturing capacity in industries of strategic importance to the green transition and economic security. Rechargeable batteries are among the eligible products. On the deployment front, the government is expanding the market through auctions under the Central Contract Market. On Sept. 23, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment announced the third ESS Central Contract Market in which it would select ESS project developers with a record-high total capacity of 1,180 megawatts. By the auction, the Korea Power Exchange competitively tenders the ESS capacity needed to stabilize the grid and enters into 15-year contracts with successful bidders. This is an encouraging development, as it creates substantial new demand for a battery market that has slowed amid moderating growth in EV demand. For K-batteries to build on these policies and strengthen their position, however, they must increase their share of the rapidly expanding global ESS market. This presents both significant challenges and important opportunities. The fact that China has already established a strong lead in the ESS market is a challenge for Korea. The top four companies in the global ESS market in the first half of this year were all Chinese, and together, they accounted for nearly 55 percent of the market. Korean companies have also recorded strong year-on-year growth, but the gap in absolute volume with China remains substantial. Moreover, with global ESS supply capacity exceeding demand — 900 GWh against the actual demand of 612 GWh at the end of 2025 — price competition is intensifying. Competing with Chinese companies, which have maintained operating margins through economies of scale, can seem like an uphill battle. At the same time, several factors create opportunities. First, regional imbalances between battery supply and demand mean that key export markets for Korean companies are likely to face shortages. For example, battery supply in China is expected to exceed demand by about 90 percent in 2030, while Europe is projected to face a supply shortfall of 40 percent. North America is also expected to face a shortage from 2035. This presents an opportunity for Korean companies, which have established production bases in Europe and North America, to increase their market share. Second, in Europe, capacity for facilities combining renewable energy and batteries is expected to rise by more than 450 percent, from 6.3 GW in 2025 to around 35 GW in 2030. In parallel, the region is working to reduce its reliance on battery supply

artigo.texto: Climate experts and other stakeholders yesterday gathered in Abuja for the European Union Climate Dialogues programme ( EUCDs2) for Nigeria’s carbon market roadmap. The event, which focuses on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets Through Robust Monitoring, Reporting And Verification (MRV) Protocols,” brought together government officials, development partners, private-sector operators, investors, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon market must be built on integrity, transparency and credible data, warning that the country would not tolerate practices capable of undermining confidence in carbon credits generated in Nigeria. Represented by the Director, Energy , Transportation and Infrastructure, Mr Michael Ivenso, l she said that the council had issued about 26 million carbon credits so far from projects previously executed in Nigeria, describing the development as evidence of the country’s capacity to participate in international carbon markets. According to her, Nigeria’s objective is to ensure that carbon projects deliver “real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes” while protecting communities, ecosystems and the interests of investors and project developers. The Director-General said the operationalisation of the National Carbon Markets Framework would provide the institutional foundation for a credible carbon market capable of mobilising private capital for clean energy, agriculture, forestry, waste management and other climate interventions. The NCCC boss said a key component of the strategy was the establishment of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry through which every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred or retired in Nigeria would have a digital record. “This will help prevent double-counting and strengthen the integrity of carbon transactions,” she said. She added that Nigeria was also moving towards digital MRV, leveraging remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to improve the accuracy of carbon measurement while reducing the cost and time required for verification. Majekodunmi said effective MRV would also enable regulators to track emissions trajectories, assure buyers that claimed emission reductions were genuine and help communities monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. She called for stronger coordination among federal ministries, state governments, project developers, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. She said the Council was working with relevant stakeholders to ensure that future carbon credit transfers under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were supported by credible national systems. The Director, Federal Department of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, said the forestry sector remained central to Nigeria’s climate response and could become one of the country’s biggest opportunities in the carbon market. She said forests served as carbon sinks and temperature buffers while providing biodiversity, soil protection, water regulation and livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. “We must therefore ensure that carbon-market development supports forest conservation rather than creating pressure for further forest exploitation,” she said. Bawa-Bwari stressed that credible carbon markets could not be built without credible data, particularly in the forestry sector. She said Nigeria needed reliable information on forest cover, degradation, deforestation, biomass and carbon stocks to determine how much carbon was being stored or removed and how those changes occurred over time. She called for continued strengthening of the National Forest Inventory and forest monitoring systems, as well as increased use of satellite imagery, remote sensing and artificial intelligence. However, she cautioned that satellite information must be complemented with ground-based measurements and field verification. The director also called for increased capacity among federal and state forestry institutions to collect and manage forest data. “MRV should not be developed as a stand-alone carbon-market activity. It should build on existing national systems for forest monitoring, greenhouse-gas accounting, REDD+ data, land-use planning and climate reporting,” she said. Bawa-Bwari urged relevant agencies to avoid establishing parallel systems that collect similar information, calling instead for clear institutional responsibilities for the collection, management, validation and reporting of forest-carbon data. On it part, the European Union said Nigeria’s efforts to develop a credible carbon market could help attract much-needed finance for climate action while supporting sustainable economic growth. Mr Jop Weterings, a member of the Task Force on International Carbon Pricing And Marketing Diplomacy at the EU said the bloc had stepped up cooperation with Nigeria on carbon markets over the past year, describing the roundtable as an important milestone in the partnership. The EU said its shared interest with Nigeria was to scale up high-integrity carbon markets capable of strengthening global climate action, channeling resources into Nigerian initiatives and driving sustainable economic growth. It noted that Nigeria’s adoption of the National Carbon Markets Framework had provided an important foundation for building confidence and trust among investors, buyers and other market participants. The EU representative said the focus should now be on operationalising the framework, particularly through strong MRV systems that would ensure carbon credits generated in Nigeria represented credible climate outcomes. artigo.texto: Nigeria is moving to strengthen the credibility and integrity of its emerging carbon market by improving carbon verification and measurement, reporting and verification systems. The National Council on Climate Change is working with the European Union and other stakeholders to operationalise a unified national carbon registry, develop digital MRV systems and establish stronger standards for carbon projects. Key Overview - Focus: Carbon market integrity and verification - Key system: National carbon registry - Technology: Digital MRV, remote sensing, IoT, geospatial data and distributed ledgers - International partner: European Union - Market framework: National Carbon Markets Framework - Priority: High-integrity carbon investments - Key areas: Article 6 cooperation and voluntary carbon markets Nigeria Targets Higher-Integrity Carbon Market Nigeria is seeking to strengthen the credibility of its emerging carbon market as the government looks to attract more private investment into climate action. The National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) has called for stronger carbon verification to ensure that carbon projects generate credible and measurable climate outcomes. The push was discussed during a high-level roundtable on carbon markets in Abuja organised under the European Union Climate Dialogues programme. Government officials, development partners and other stakeholders used the meeting to discuss how Nigeria can operationalise its carbon-market framework and improve the systems used to measure and verify emissions reductions. NCCC Director-General Omotenioye Majekodunmi said Nigeria needs to translate its climate ambitions into tangible, bankable and verifiable actions that can support sustainable economic growth and attract climate finance. Stronger Measurement, Reporting and Verification A central part of Nigeria’s strategy is the development of stronger Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) systems. The NCCC is promoting digital MRV technologies, including remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies. These technologies are expected to improve the accuracy and reliability of emissions data while reducing some of the costs and time associated with verifying carbon projects. The NCCC says effective MRV is necessary for buyers to establish whether claimed emissions reductions are genuine. It can also help regulators track emissions, prevent double-counting and give communities greater visibility over benefit-sharing arrangements. National Carbon Registry Planned Nigeria is also working to operationalise a unified national carbon registry. The registry is expected to create a digital record of carbon credits generated, issued, transferred and retired in Nigeria. This would provide greater visibility over the lifecycle of credits and help reduce the risk of the same emissions reduction being counted more than once. The system is part of the broader effort to create a transparent infrastructure for Nigeria’s carbon market as activity increases. The NCCC also wants to finalise carbon-market regulations, publish sector-specific MRV guidelines and establish local capacity-building hubs to strengthen verification expertise within the country. EU Supports Nigeria’s Carbon Market Development The European Union is supporting Nigeria’s efforts through the EU Climate Dialogues programme. The Abuja roundtable formed part of the second phase of the EU Climate Dialogues, which is focused on supporting Nigeria’s climate and carbon-market development. EU representatives said credible carbon markets require robust systems for transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. The partnership is also intended to help stakeholders align around Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework and develop a roadmap for putting the framework into operation. The EU sees stronger carbon-market systems as a way to support emissions reductions while mobilising investment and encouraging the development of low-carbon economic activities. Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework provides the institutional and regulatory architecture for carbon-market activities in the country. The framework covers domestic and international carbon trading, including Article 6 cooperation, and voluntary markets. It is intended to provide greater clarity for project developers, investors, buyers and regulators while supporting Nigeria’s participation in international carbon markets. The NCCC says the framework can help position Nigeria as a destination for high-integrity carbon investment, provided the country strengthens the systems needed to verify and monitor carbon projects. artigo.texto: Clock ticking for Illinois data center regulation Lawmakers, advocates believe regulations must be approved as soon as possible SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (WAND) – Advocates and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are committed to getting data center regulations across the finish line during veto session. Many believe the POWER Act needs to pass as soon as possible. Illinois has provided millions of dollars in tax credits to data centers since 2019, but Gov. JB Pritzker said AI data centers didn’t exist back then. “What we now see is these hyper-scale massive data centers where they want to take an entire nuclear power plant offline and apply it to a data center that might be many millions of square feet,” Pritzker said. More IL Statehouse Coverage Pritzker said big tech companies need to bring their own clean energy, pay their fair share for power and use closed-loop water systems. The POWER Act could also establish consumer protection and pollution control policies. Some believe local governments should decide where facilities can be located and prevent data centers from being approved within three miles of residential communities. “They’re still on our grid,” said House Minority Leader Tony McCombie (R-Savanna). “They’re still using our energy, and they’re reaping the benefits that are coming to communities. There again, it has to be the community’s decision of whether or not they want them.” The Illinois Environmental Council said communities have been trying to make major decisions about data centers on their own without proper resources. IEC CEO Jen Walling said the POWER Act would ban NDAs for data centers and require full and transparent access to any agreements signed. “I think that this has more political power and urgency behind it in getting things done than anything that I’ve ever seen in Springfield,” Walling said. “I think that people all over the state, bipartisan basis, are pushing legislators to act.” Walling and McCombie note that Illinois will continue to learn new information about data centers, so it is likely multiple plans will need to be passed to address issues that pop up over the next decade. State lawmakers return to Springfield Nov. 17 and only have six days of veto session. They could finalize data center regulations during lameduck session in early January if they fail to pass a bill this fall. Copyright 2026 WAND. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: POSCO Future M signs KRW 1,1 trillion LFP Cathode Material Supply Contract with SK On POSCO Future M (CEO EOM Gi Chen) has signed a large-scale supply contract with SK On for LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cathode materials. Hard on the heels of last month’s long-term agreement to supply 190,000 tons of LFP cathode materials to a Korean battery maker, the company has now secured another major contract as it moves into the LFP market in earnest. POSCO Future M has been working with SK On as a supplier of anode materials and plans to strengthen the partnership further through this contract, its first to supply SK On with cathode materials. The contract also means POSCO Future M now supplies cathode and anode materials to all three Korean battery makers, broadening its customer portfolio and putting its mid- to long-term growth on an even firmer foundation. The contract, signed on the 22nd, is worth approximately KRW 1.1 trillion over three years, from 2027 through 2029, and can be extended by an additional two years upon agreement between the two companies. While LFP batteries have lower power output than ternary batteries such as NCM (nickel-cobalt-manganese) and NCA (nickel-cobalt-aluminum), their strengths lie in competitive pricing and a long lifespan. With power demand recently surging due to the build-out of AI data centers, among other factors, demand for LFP batteries used in ESS is growing to ensure a stable power supply. LFP batteries are also increasingly being adopted in the electric vehicle market, particularly in entry-level models. POSCO Future M is actively responding to customer demand by adding LFP cathode materials to its existing portfolio centered on ternary (NCM and NCA) materials. The company recently completed converting part of its high-nickel cathode material production lines at the Pohang plant to LFP cathode material production, and is set to begin mass-production supply from the end of this year. POSCO Future M plans to continue expanding production capacity by converting more lines as further orders come in. Going forward, the company also plans to produce and supply LFP cathode materials with further improved cost competitiveness and quality by applying a new process that uses lithium from salt lakes in Argentina, drawing on raw material supply chain cooperation across POSCO group. POSCO Future M continues to hold discussions with major battery makers and automakers on supplying cathode and anode materials, backed by a diverse product portfolio and by a supply chain and technological capabilities that can navigate global trade regulations. The company is also stepping up the expansion of its production capacity. Its moves include a KRW 1 trillion long-term supply contract for synthetic graphite anode materials, signed with a global automaker in March this year, and plans to invest approximately KRW 357 billion in a new synthetic graphite anode material plant in Vietnam. A plant to process spherical graphite, an intermediate material for natural graphite anode materials, is under construction at the Saemangeum National Industrial Complex in Jeonbuk and is scheduled to begin trial operation in early 2027, with completion and full-scale mass production planned for the second half of the year. In July, POSCO group announced its future growth strategy, outlining a vision to build a Triple-Core system and become a “national supplier of critical resources.” The system spans industrial resources (steel), strategic resources (such as lithium, cathode and anode materials, and rare earths), and energy resources (LNG and renewable energy). In line with this strategy, POSCO Future M aims to build on its unrivaled technology to strengthen its business competitiveness and expand its markets, and to emerge as a global leader in the cathode and anode materials business, one of the pillars of the group’s strategic resources. artigo.texto: India's battery storage demand to hit 236.22 GWh by FY32, require Rs 3.49 trillion investment: Report Synopsis India's battery energy storage system market is expected to reach 236.22 GWh by FY2031-32. The country will require Rs 3.49 trillion in investments for this growth. Significant advancements in BESS deployment were noted between early and mid-2026. The government is providing extensive support through various initiatives and schemes. These measures aim to enhance project viability and stimulate private-sector participation in the energy storage sector. Furthermore, as of August 2026, 9.08 GWh of BESS capacity was operational, while 79.92 GWh was under construction, with 79.92 GWh under construction, 24.13 GWh awarded, and 63.53 GWh under tendering, taking the total operational and identified project capacity to 176.66 GWh, with the current CEA project pipeline scheduled for commissioning till FY2029-30. In capacity terms, the report noted, this represents approximately "75% of the NEP's projected FY2031-32 requirements, although the identified capacity is at different stages of development and is not yet fully operational." "The share of BESS in India's total energy storage requirement is expected to increase from ~42% in FY2026-27 to ~57% in FY2031-32," it said. The report estimated that India will require around Rs 3.49 trillion in investment in the sector by FY2031-32. Separately, the broader energy storage sector is expected to attract about Rs 4.79 trillion in investments by 2032. The report expects India's BESS market to expand strongly, supported by investments in domestic battery manufacturing, a sizeable project pipeline and government initiatives. Measures including Viability Gap Funding (VGF), the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage and interstate transmission system (ISTS) charge waivers are expected to improve project viability and encourage private-sector participation. The government is also stepping up support for the sector. The Union Cabinet has approved the Rs 1.86 trillion PM-DHARA (PM-Developing Harmonized and Accelerated Renewable-energy Access) Scheme, which includes Rs 500 billion for the deployment of 50 GWh of BESS capacity by FY2032-33, it noted. artigo.texto: Data Center Design in the AI Era The unprecedented performance demands of AI workloads require a reimagined approach to data center design toward fully autonomous operations. October 5, 2026 Sponsored by HPE It wasn’t long ago that organizations thought their data centers would play a less central role in IT service delivery. Virtualized infrastructure, cloud computing, colocation, SaaS applications, and other factors pointed to more computing being done off-premises. But the rapid acceleration of compute-intensive workloads, generative AI, and ever-increasing network complexity is driving organizations to reimagine and, in some cases, completely re-engineer their data centers. The same is true for third-party data centers leveraged by so many organizations, often in tandem with their on-prem facilities. AI training and inference, combined with a rapid swing toward agentic AI, is intensifying pressure on data centers. Even with the impressive advances in compute and storage density, enterprises are realizing that incremental component refreshes cannot solve operational complexity; they require a modern fabric design and shift toward self-driving networks to improve IT agility, increase reliability, and optimize the end user experience. The trends have been exacerbated by huge demands for power and cooling, which data centers have struggled to meet. Research from Uptime Institute notes that 82% of data center operators report their highest-density racks are still below 30 kilowatts, a level unlikely to meet the growing demands of AI-level performance as rack densities increase. New Challenges Force Changes to Data Center Design The harsh reality is that traditional data centers were never designed for the performance, scalability, security, and resilience demands of the AI era. The massive growth in data volumes has created important opportunities for new insights, but also requires a fundamentally different approach to network design. Servers, networks, storage, end-user devices, cloud gateways, applications, security tools, and other sources generate unprecedented amounts of data, making it more difficult for networks to discern whether an alert indicates a potentially serious failure or a minor problem elsewhere. But it’s not just the proliferation of data sources that renders legacy data centers inadequate for the AI era. Traditional data center traffic usually had a fair amount of entropy, making it easier to design for capacity and accommodate occasional demand spikes that could impact network performance. AI has changed that in a big way. Modern AI workloads running on GPUs require deterministic, low-latency, higher-bandwidth networks, and massively scalable storage infrastructure, meaning that both existing and greenfield data centers need to support significantly higher performance. In addition, the traditional siloed approach to IT infrastructure that reflects organizational boundaries rather than end user needs—compute, storage, and networking—has given way to new design principles that promote tighter cross-domain integration for better overall data center and application performance. Shifting the Data Center to Autonomous Operations Although data centers have increasingly embraced automation, the next step is for data center design to progress toward autonomy. Data center personnel are simply too hard-pressed to address the increasing telemetry volume and complexity in real time without tools that provide full-stack, cross-domain visibility across the entire enterprise. AI agents should be an important element in the move toward autonomous operations because they enable lightning-fast assessments, analysis, and decision-making across the full spectrum of infrastructure and data sources. Management should focus not just on automating operations to reduce headcount, but on autonomous operations that improve the quality of application and user experience. The Importance of a Self-Driving Framework AI-era data centers now have the potential for unsurpassed levels of intelligence, autonomous operations, observability, and contextually aware decision-making. This is where self-driving frameworks coordinate data center operations with AI-era requirements. The emphasis has swung decisively away from historically fragmented management frameworks in favor of approaches that collect information from all available sources and put them into an actionable context across infrastructure. A key first step is intent-based networking, which defines the desired state of the network based on operator-intent and continuously validates its conformance to that standard. Problems are identified faster and with greater precision, relieving the data center team of tedious, time-consuming, and often inaccurate triage to avoid failures and downtime. A well-planned and meticulously executed approach to building the right data center architecture helps organizations establish validated topologies, automate deployment, improve visibility, automate remediation, and balance the strengths of AI tools with human experience. artigo.texto: German Sodium-Ion Battery Tech Gains EU Funding Support ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: German startup Revolta AG received €264,200 in EU co-financing for its sodium-ion AC battery project, designed for grid-charging in residential apartments. - Why it matters: This development highlights the growing viability of lithium-free storage solutions that can operate independently of on-site PV generation. - Watch: The impact of new German grid regulations that allow storage systems to arbitrage grid power with reduced levies and fees. Background and Context As the global energy transition accelerates, the development of sodium-ion battery technology is emerging as a critical alternative to traditional lithium-ion systems. German startup Revolta AG has secured significant funding from the German state of Hesse, supported by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), to advance its “Highly Efficient AC Salt Battery” project. This initiative aims to deploy residential-scale storage systems that do not rely on lithium or cobalt, addressing supply chain vulnerabilities and material cost volatility. Key Details The project, which runs from August 1, 2026, to December 31, 2029, involves eligible costs totaling €660,545, with the EU providing a 40% co-financing rate of approximately €264,200. The core innovation lies in the system’s ability to connect directly to the grid, allowing users to charge during periods of low electricity prices and discharge when costs peak. This model is specifically targeted at rental apartments that lack the space or infrastructure for rooftop solar PV installations. Furthermore, the regulatory landscape in Germany has evolved to support this business model. Since October 1, the national grid regulator has implemented rules allowing storage systems to draw power from the grid and feed it back later, benefiting from reduced grid fees and levies. This shift effectively opens a new market segment for storage providers. Beyond Revolta AG, the ERDF is also supporting broader sodium-ion manufacturing, including a €2.52 million grant for a 1 GWh sodium-ion battery plant in Bavaria. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the rise of grid-charging sodium-ion systems represents a shift toward decentralized energy management. While currently focused on the residential sector, the underlying technology—sodium-ion—offers a scalable, safer, and more sustainable alternative for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications. Developers should monitor these advancements as they provide a pathway to integrate storage in locations where solar generation is physically constrained. What Happens Next The industry will closely monitor the performance of these pilot projects as they move toward the 2026 launch window. As India continues to expand its renewable energy sector, the lessons learned from European regulatory frameworks—specifically regarding grid-charging arbitrage and non-lithium storage chemistries—will become increasingly relevant. India’s push for indigenous battery manufacturing under various PLI schemes may eventually incorporate these sodium-ion advancements to diversify the national energy storage portfolio.

artigo.texto: Charleston City Council introduced a slew of bills Monday night, including rules for data centers, a renewal plan for the East End and the reallocation of $300,000 in federal grant money. Data center regulations Bill 8097, written by Councilman Emmett Pepper and co-sponsored by council members Joe Solomon and Frank Annie, would require any data center plan to: Gain Planning Commission and council approval Face a public hearing Sign a community benefits agreement No data center has been proposed in Charleston, but Pepper said the bill is a needed precaution. “The goal is to make sure that if there are going to be data centers that come to the city, they’re developed in a responsible way that is good for the community and will benefit the community,” Pepper said. The bill would require data centers to be built at certain distances from homes and schools, with larger facilities pushed farther away. It covers facilities using up to 89 megawatts. State law bars cities from regulating larger ones. “As we’ve seen around the country, as data centers have gone in places, they are greatly increasing the cost for electric customers,” Pepper said. The bill also caps noise — with $5,000/day fines for noise violations — and requires the data center to have a plan in place to mitigate rising electricity costs and bring jobs into the city. The bill was referred to the Ordinance and Rules committee and the Planning, Streets and Traffic committee. Bill 8096, sponsored by Councilwoman Mary Beth Hoover, would adopt the East End renewal plan that council authorized the Charleston Urban Renewal Authority to draft. The plan would run through 2046. Most of the proposed work is on the streetscape: fixing sidewalks, adding public art and making intersections safer. The plan names no properties for purchase or demolition. It bars taking owner-occupied homes by eminent domain but allows eminent domain on rental properties only as a last resort after public input. The plan sets no price, pointing to tax credits and private investment to cover costs. It has been referred to council’s Urban Renewal and Economic Development Committee. Other bills The council also discussed a few other bills. Resolution 26-112, sponsored by Councilman Joseph Jenkins, would move $300,000 in federal Community Development Block Grant money to demolish a building at 915 Main St. The money would come from completed or canceled projects, including $122,809 from a 2025 ADA curb-cut project and $92,740 from a roof replacement at Sojourner’s homeless shelter, plus leftover contingency money. It has been referred to the Finance Committee. Resolution 26-114, also from Jenkins, would hand a stalled federal pandemic-relief project to Mountaineer Food Bank. In 2022, the city awarded the Partnership of African American Churches $440,000 in American Rescue Plan money to buy and redevelop the former Save a Lot on 748 Virginia St. W. PAAC and the city has not “satisfactorily performed the original project,” according to the resolution. The property has already been turned over to the city, which would then transfer it to Mountaineer Food Bank as a volunteer center where they store and distribute food. The resolution has been referred to the Finance Committee Bill 8099, from council members Solomon and Becky Ceperley, would expand public notice before the city permanently closes a street, alley or other public right of way. People who own property or live within 350 feet would be notified at least 15 days before the Planning Commission’s hearing. Petitioners would also have to name a council member willing to sponsor the closure, and nonprofits could ask the city attorney whether they qualify to receive the land as a donation. artigo.texto: Nvidia e Broadcom se isolam de impacto de crise de energia em data centers dos EUA, diz Morgan Stanley Nvidia e Broadcom estão protegidas da crise energética em data centers nos EUA até 2027, segundo o Morgan Stanley, devido ao forte planejamento e alocação de chips. Contudo, o setor enfrenta um déficit de energia projetado em 34% até 2028, impulsionado pela alta demanda da inteligência artificial. Se a infraestrutura atrasar por gargalos elétricos, fabricantes de componentes secundários, como chips de memória, óptica e analógicos, serão os mais impactados por cancelamentos e adiamentos. Nvidia e Broadcom estão relativamente protegidas contra o agravamento da crise de energia nas centrais de processamento de dados dos Estados Unidos, afirmou o Morgan Stanley em relatório nesta segunda-feira. Porém, qualquer atraso resultante nas implantações de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial pode afetar os fabricantes de chips de memória, componentes ópticos e outros processadores secundários. O banco estimou no mês passado que os desenvolvedores de data centers nos EUA enfrentarão um déficit líquido de energia de 34% até 2028, equivalente a 32 GW. O boom da IA gerou bilhões de dólares em investimentos em data centers, mas as enormes necessidades de computação e eletricidade da IA generativa estão cada vez mais esbarrando nos problemas de fornecimento de eletricidade nos EUA. Tanto Morgan Stanley quanto Goldman Sachs sinalizaram restrições crescentes à expansão dos data centers nos EUA; o GS espera um impacto limitado no curto prazo devido à resistência política, enquanto o MS vê desafios relacionados à mão de obra, energia e política. O Morgan Stanley afirmou que não vê os gargalos colocando em risco as previsões da Nvidia ou da Broadcom para 2027, citando a visibilidade dessas empresas quanto à alocação de chips, à expansão geográfica e à coordenação entre centros de dados, fornecedores de chips e a cadeia de abastecimento de energia. Se a capacidade de produção de chips não puder ser implantada, os clientes poderão adiar entregas ou cancelar pedidos, sendo que componentes de memória, óptica, gerenciamento de energia e analógicos são os mais expostos a problemas de fornecimento, afirmou o Morgan Stanley.

artigo.texto: Suzuki’s newly launched e-Sky relies on BYD’s LFP battery technology while targeting the most affordable position in Japan’s Kei EV market. Suzuki’s newly launched e-Sky has drawn attention for an important detail behind its competitive pricing: the electric Kei car uses battery technology supplied by Chinese automaker BYD. The collaboration has helped Suzuki position the e-Sky as Japan’s most affordable Kei-class electric vehicle. The e-Sky represents Suzuki’s first passenger Kei EV and has been developed specifically for Japan’s compact-car market. Rather than relying entirely on in-house battery development, Suzuki has partnered with BYD to keep production costs under control while offering practical electric range. 26 kWh BYD LFP Battery The Suzuki e-Sky is equipped with a 26 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supplied through the BYD collaboration. Suzuki claims the battery enables a WLTP driving range of up to 310 km. The electric vehicle uses a dedicated EV platform and Suzuki’s own e-Axle drive system. Its compact dimensions measure 3,395 mm in length, 1,475 mm in width and 1,625 mm in height, while the wheelbase stretches to 2,460 mm. BYD Battery Helps Keep Costs Low Battery technology is a key part of the e-Sky’s pricing strategy. The model starts at 2.12 million yen, making it cheaper than several competing Kei EVs before government incentives are applied. Japan’s EV subsidy of 568,000 yen can reduce the effective consumer price to around 1.55 million yen. This puts the Suzuki e-Sky below the subsidised prices of rivals such as the BYD Racco and Nissan Sakura. The e-Sky also weighs approximately 1,030 kg, which is significantly lighter than the BYD Racco. Suzuki’s lower vehicle weight contributes to the model’s claimed driving range despite its relatively compact battery. Suzuki Targets 1,000 Monthly Sales Suzuki is offering the e-Sky in three variants. The entry-level version is primarily aimed at corporate customers and excludes certain equipment, including fast-charging capability, as part of the effort to maintain a lower price. Suzuki is targeting combined monthly sales of around 1,000 units for the three versions. The company’s strong position in Japan’s Kei-car segment gives the e-Sky an established customer base as it expands into electric mobility.

artigo.texto: O mercado brasileiro de sistemas de baterias para armazenar energia elétrica, conhecidos no setor como BESS, vive um boom de vendas puxado por instalações de menor porte em comércios, indústrias, condomínios e residências, segundo reportagem de Luciano Costa no Brazil Journal. Enquanto o leilão federal para grandes projetos segue previsto para dezembro sob incertezas, o segmento encontrou no varejo a via para crescer em ritmo recorde. Conforme levantamento da consultoria Greener citado na reportagem, as vendas e contratações de BESS somaram 730 MWh em 2025, mais do que a soma dos cinco anos anteriores. Nos seis primeiros meses de 2026, foram outros 504 MWh, caminho de um novo recorde histórico. Muitos desses projetos vêm acompanhados de painéis solares em telhados. O CEO da Greener, Marcio Takata, afirmou ao Brazil Journal que o leilão é relevante, mas que o BESS distribuído deve se firmar como um dos principais vetores de flexibilidade da rede elétrica. A trajetória lembra a da geração solar, que decolou com grandes usinas contratadas pelo governo e depois com telhados e miniusinas. Segundo a Aneel, a geração solar distribuída já soma mais de 53 GW no País, contra 23,6 GW das usinas centralizadas. O armazenamento acumulado no Brasil chega a 1,9 GWh, com companhias como WEG e Grupo Moura apostando no segmento. O leilão de dezembro deve contratar pelo menos 2 GW para operar quatro horas por dia, o equivalente a 8 GWh, segundo sinalizações de Brasília, ainda que parte do mercado espere volumes maiores. O Ministério de Minas e Energia também programou certames anuais até 2029 para reserva de capacidade, nos quais as baterias disputarão espaço com termelétricas e hidrelétricas reversíveis. Para André Millions, diretor da Thymos Capital, baterias e hidrelétricas reversíveis são hoje os temas mais quentes do setor. A reserva é considerada importante para a rede absorver a oscilação da geração eólica e solar, mas o certame está sob risco por causa do impasse sobre quem paga a conta dos projetos, conforme fontes do setor ouvidas pelo Brazil Journal. A regra atual divide o rateio entre todas as empresas de geração, o que ameaça levar o tema à Justiça, e o setor pressiona o governo a aprovar um projeto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim que transfere o custo aos consumidores.

artigo.texto: Cindy O’Neil understands the boom-and-bust cycles of industry. Her husband spent years working in Carbon County’s namesake coal mines. In this pocket of central Utah, energy and the economy have long been intrinsically linked, at great sacrifice to county residents. “We’ve had the coal. We’ve dealt, the whole community, with black lung,” O’Neil said. “The explosions, the fires and all the things that came along with it.” But a new industry and type of energy production is about to move near her rural home. And she says it has her and her neighbors even more worried than they were about the dangers that came from their long history with coal. “It’s all descending, these data centers,” said O’Neil, who tracks mysterious new projects in the works and shares updates on Facebook community pages. “They’re setting these things within a couple of miles of homes.” Her latest updates involve a lot of chatter about Valar Atomics, a nuclear startup. The company plans to build a mega-complex of 456 small modular reactors — a still largely untested and unproven technology in the United States — on the vast tracts of Bureau of Land Management land in the county. The project will store radioactive waste, according to a report from National Public Radio, and power an array of industrial activities, including data centers. “Project Beehive” has support from the state of Utah, and will include a square mile of state-owned trust lands. Another data center complex planned for the county, Altigen Energy’s “Jurassic Spark,” will cover hundreds of acres and include a massive natural gas plant. It’s an abrupt shift. Carbon County’s coal mines produced nearly 10 million tons of coal in 2006. But a shift to cheaper energy sources, like renewables and natural gas, along with depleted supplies in the coal seams, sank the region’s main economic engine in just a few decades. Since 2023, not a single pound of coal has been mined in Carbon County. “They say everything’s left us, and if we don’t grab these table scraps we’re not going to get anything,” said O’Neil. “I don’t think our county has to take the table scraps.” None of Carbon County’s new data center plans call for coal. The Utah Trust Lands Administration recently agreed to lease a square mile of its state-owned land for up to 100 years to Valar Atomics. The nuclear startup intends to use that lease to run some of its SMRs, process its uranium TRISO-fuel to feed the reactors, build water desalination, manufacture steel, refine critical minerals — and support data centers. The Valar site is expected to generate $35 million in lease rents over 50 years, according to information the Trust Lands Administration staff presented to its board last month. Revenue collected from the project benefits Utah schools. (The state agency declined to comment on the Valar project.) During that September board meeting, three Carbon County residents who are employed or expected to be employed by Valar spoke in favor of the project. All three of the Carbon County Commissioners also voiced their support. “[We] realize that this topic is a hot button now, along with data centers,” said Larry Jensen, one of the commissioners. “It’s important that you understand that the Carbon County Commissioners are committed to allowing these things to move forward. Even with the pushback — we realize that there are a few in our community who will push back — but the silent majority are the ones that we really represent.” Cheryl Lupo, a longtime resident of the county, balked at that assertion. She is running for a seat on the county commission this year. As an unaffiliated candidate, she had to collect 300 signatures to land on the ballot. She said the opinions she heard during that process were overwhelmingly opposed to data centers and nuclear plants. “People are up in arms,” Lupo said. “Torches and pitchforks. Because they’re not being heard.” Governor Spencer Cox, U.S. Senator John Curtis and other high-ranking Utah officials welcomed Valar to the state earlier this year, allowing it to test its “Ward250” microreactor at the San Rafael Energy Lab in neighboring Emery County. Valar announced it had achieved “self-sustaining criticality” in June – a process where atoms split and maintain a steady fission chain reaction without being fed more neutrons. The company has plans to power a 30-megawatt nuclear-powered AI data center in Emery County, too, in partnership with the computer-chip giant Nvidia. Small modular reactors have yet to be deployed for commercial use in the United States. During last week’s Trust Lands Administration meeting, Mike Nelson, the board’s chair, seemed to acknowledge that the deal with Valar came with some unknowns. “We weren’t always sure what to ask about,” Nelson said, while offering praise for the nuclear startup, “and probably still aren’t sure of everything to ask about because this is a first, right?” Utah has a troubled history with nuclear testing. Lupo’s mother was 38 years old when she died, and Lupo believes the cause was downwind effects from radioactive weapons testing in nearby Nevada during the 1950s. Her mother lived in Carbon County at the time. She believes the fallout caused her grandfather’s death, too. “I will never, ever be a proponent of nuclear,” Lupo said. Even before the proposal to build Valar’s complex started causing a stir, rumors swirled about the possibility of another data center campus in Carbon County. Altigen, a company that builds natural gas-power plants for data centers, has selected an area east of Wellington for its 1,200-acre “Jurassic Spark” project — nearly double the size of the Valar campus, according to meeting minutes from the local Community Economic Development Board. Plans call for building a 250-megawatt gas plant to power the complex initially, but it could eventually produce 3 gigawatts of electricity, according to Jensen.
