artigo.texto: Data Center World estreia com foco em energia e Redata Edição brasileira começa nesta terça-feira, em SP, com debates sobre tributação, capacidade energética, financiamento e conectividade. A primeira edição brasileira do Data Center World começa nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro, no São Paulo Expo, com debates sobre os principais condicionantes para a expansão dos data centers no país. Tributação, disponibilidade de energia, financiamento, conectividade e aumento da demanda computacional estão entre os temas centrais do encontro. Realizado simultaneamente à Futurecom, o evento prevê a participação de mais de 2,5 mil líderes e 300 congressistas. Um dos destaques do primeiro dia será o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). O tema entra na discussão sobre competitividade, atração de investimentos e ambiente regulatório, ao lado dos efeitos do ICMS e de decisões do Confaz sobre a implantação de novos projetos. Oferta de energia concentra debates A disponibilidade de energia aparece como um dos principais fatores para a expansão do setor. O aumento da capacidade computacional exigida por novas aplicações amplia a demanda elétrica dos empreendimentos e afeta decisões sobre localização, escala e continuidade operacional. Os debates vão tratar de oferta efetiva, intermitência, geração, armazenamento e alternativas para reduzir riscos associados ao fornecimento. O crescimento da densidade dos racks também pressiona a infraestrutura elétrica e térmica dos data centers. Esse movimento tem ampliado a discussão sobre novas arquiteturas e sobre tecnologias de refrigeração, incluindo liquid cooling. Financiamento e viabilidade O acesso a capital será outro eixo do congresso. Representantes do Ministério das Comunicações, BNDES, Brasscom e Patria Investments participam de um debate sobre crédito, financiamento e condições para viabilizar novos empreendimentos. A análise de grandes projetos passa também por fatores como localização, custo, latência, segurança e continuidade dos serviços. Esses critérios serão discutidos sob a perspectiva de empresas que contratam infraestrutura de data center. Conectividade e capacidade A conectividade completa o conjunto de fatores que condicionam a expansão do mercado. O congresso terá discussões sobre rotas internacionais, latência e edge computing, relacionando a localização dos data centers ao desempenho das aplicações. O planejamento de capacidade por hyperscalers também estará em pauta, diante da dificuldade de projetar demanda em um ambiente de crescimento acelerado das cargas computacionais. A agenda inclui ainda debates sobre continuidade operacional, preparação para falhas e eventos extremos, além de investimentos e expansão da infraestrutura na América Latina. artigo.texto: South Texas to get $22B power project tied to data center The United States and South Korean governments are working together on a plan that would bring a large gas power plant to La Salle County, Texas, to directly power data centers. Project Star is a $22 billion power project According to the U.S. Department of Commerce, the 6.47 gigawatt combined-cycle gas power plant will be built in Encinal, Texas. The plant will be operated by Related Companies and NextEra Energy Resources, with the first stage expected to come online in 2029 and operate at full capacity in 2032. According to Related Digital, the power plant will be used to power a 5GW data center on an adjacent site, with the remaining power going to the Texas power grid. Related's project page states that the data center project will use a closed loop water cooling system that will use around the same amount of water daily as an office building. The power project is looking for ways to use produced water, water that is a byproduct of oil and natural gas extraction, for cooling. Power plant to bring 170 jobs to the area NextEra said construction on the project is expected to bring 8,400 jobs to the area. Once construction is complete, the power campus is expected to have 170 permanent jobs and the data center will create "hundreds of good-paying permanent jobs." What they're saying: "Project Star demonstrates how energy infrastructure and economic growth can advance together," said John Ketchum, chairman and CEO of NextEra Energy. "By bringing new generation online to serve new demand, we're helping strengthen reliability, support investment and jobs and protect electricity customers." The project comes as part of the implementation of the trade deal between Korea and the United States, announced on July 30, 2025, and the Strategic Investment MOU signed on Nov. 14 of that year. Those efforts aim to enhance cooperation between Korea and the United States in strategic industrial sectors such as energy and artificial intelligence. "I am excited to be working with two world class companies in Related Digital and NextEra Energy to develop Project Star," said Rod Lewis, Founder and CEO of Lewis Energy Group. "This project will bring much needed jobs to South Texas, add new power generation to be available to the state of Texas, and ensure the natural gas produced in the South Texas region provides direct economic benefits to our local communities. As a long-time ranching family and resident of La Salle and Webb Counties, we look forward to working with local communities to create a meaningful and environmentally responsible addition to the local economy." The Source: Information in this article comes from a release from NextEra Energy, the U.S. Dept. of Commerce and Related Digital.

artigo.texto: Telcomp cobra agilidade nas licenças para data centers Entidade relata demora superior à construção de empreendimentos e aponta impasses na regulamentação do Redata como entrave. A demora na emissão de licenças e as pendências na regulamentação do Redata estão entre os obstáculos à implantação de data centers no Brasil, segundo o presidente da Telcomp, Luiz Henrique Barbosa. Durante a abertura do Data Center World, nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro, o dirigente defendeu maior previsibilidade para atrair investimentos e integrar o país às cadeias internacionais de infraestrutura digital. Barbosa relatou o caso de uma associada que aguardou dois anos por uma licença para atravessar uma rodovia no interior de São Paulo. Segundo ele, o prazo foi superior ao necessário para construir o próprio data center. Para o dirigente, situações desse tipo comprometem a segurança jurídica dos projetos. Ele afirmou que investidores estrangeiros comparam as condições brasileiras com as de outros mercados e que o país precisa considerar essa concorrência ao definir regras, tributos e procedimentos de licenciamento. A Telcomp reúne aproximadamente 60 empresas de diferentes segmentos, incluindo operadores de cabos submarinos, satélites, data centers e redes de transmissão de longa distância e metropolitanas. Impasse sobre equipamentos Barbosa também cobrou a conclusão da regulamentação do Redata. Segundo o presidente da Telcomp, há divergências com fabricantes nacionais de equipamentos, preocupados com o alcance dos benefícios para importações. Na avaliação do dirigente, a indefinição mantém investimentos parados. Ele defendeu que o regime seja entendido como uma forma de aproximar a tributação brasileira das condições oferecidas em outros países. No mesmo painel, Walter Wolff, diretor de projetos da Brasscom, afirmou que a regulamentação envolve discussões sobre os equipamentos contemplados e sobre o fornecimento de energia aos empreendimentos. Já o presidente da Equinix, Victor Arnaud, alertou que o detalhamento das regras pode comprometer os resultados do incentivo caso imponha burocracia excessiva aos projetos. Cabos submarinos e segurança jurídica Para exemplificar os efeitos internacionais de decisões sobre infraestrutura, Barbosa citou a proposta de instalação de uma usina de dessalinização na Praia do Futuro, em Fortaleza, nas proximidades de cabos submarinos. Segundo ele, a discussão gerou preocupação entre agentes de outros países porque as conexões que passam por Fortaleza também atendem ao tráfego internacional. O dirigente citou as ligações com a África, a Europa, os Estados Unidos e a Argentina para defender que decisões locais considerem o papel dessas redes. A relação entre data centers e telecomunicações também foi destacada pelo diretor jurídico da Conexis, Bruno Cavalcanti. Ele afirmou que a atração de investimentos em processamento depende de redes de fibra, backbones e conectividade de alta capacidade. Cavalcanti defendeu uma regulação responsiva, com espaço para atuação do mercado, e segurança jurídica para os investidores. Na avaliação do representante da Conexis, regras antecipadas que burocratizem a implantação dos empreendimentos podem prejudicar o crescimento do setor e a competitividade brasileira.

artigo.texto: An industrial park in Irvine, California, may seem an odd spot to show off technology that wouldn’t be out of place in Dune, but that’s what’s happening on a sweltering September morning. The temperature is already over 80 degrees Fahrenheit as the sun rises on a 20-foot-tall, metal-clad machine in the parking lot of Atoco, an Irvine, California-based startup. Engineers open panels to check systems and an iPad that shows a steadily ascending line that reveals the device’s purpose: harvesting water from thin air using special materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs. The materials won Omar Yaghi, the company’s founder, the Nobel Prize for chemistry in 2025, and Atoco has shown they work in prototypes capable of producing gallons of water per day. What’s unique about this iteration of Atoco’s technology is what it doesn’t require. No grid connection or even electricity is needed to grab water from the air at the microscopic level, nor is it required to in turn wring the water out of the materials in a form useful for humans. Instead, all that’s needed is low-level industrial heat. That, Atoco says, makes them a perfect candidate to hook up with AI data centers, which throw off loads of waste heat as servers churn out everything from math proofs to virtual editors while also often requiring massive amounts of water. “We were not really thinking of AI data centers,” four or five years ago, says Atoco CEO Samer Taha. But the massive buildout has created an opportunity for the startup that could allow it to get a step closer to its larger goal of ensuring people living in water-stressed regions have control over an increasingly precious resource. When Yaghi was a PhD student, he says, creating something like MOFs was “every chemist’s dream.” Part of his Nobel-winning work over the past 20 years has been taking theoretical research into the real world, creating a stable molecular structure that links organic material with metal ions. The structure of a MOF looks somewhat “like a jungle gym on a playground,” says Seth Cohen, the dean of the School of Physical Sciences at UC Irvine. MOFs are essentially “molecular sponges—they’re a solid material that’s very, very good at absorbing other molecules,” says Cohen, who is not involved with Atoco. Like a sponge, the materials can also be wrung out using methods including heat to release whatever they’re holding onto. These jungle-gym-like frameworks create open spaces on the microscopic level that can hold an unbelievable amount of material, and small tweaks can yield even more interior space. “The footage of a gram of MOF could cover two football fields,” Yaghi explains. “They can store hydrogen in there to make clean energy, or you could store CO2 in there to make clean air. Or, in this case, you can store water.” Atoco has developed what Taha calls “precision materials” with a specific objective of being able to harvest water, release it, and then do it over again and again. He quips that, as vice president of R&D Benjie Limketkai puts it, the material has to like water but not love it. To succeed commercially, it also has to use as little energy as possible. “The scientists reach a level of precision [where] we really know even the angle of the atom,” in a given material, Taha says. In Atoco’s technology, air passes through the MOF, which has been specially tailored to attract water molecules. Those molecules adhere to the pores. But the material feels completely dry to the touch even when saturated, and squeezing it doesn’t release a single drop. (Taha was kind enough to let WIRED try our hand at it.) Instead, the company relies on heat to release the captured molecules. There are other means of harvesting water. Cohen notes that silica, a popular desiccant, can also pull water out of air, but it doesn’t hold as much moisture and requires you to “heat the heck out of it to get the water back out,” he says. The monolith in the parking lot of the company’s Irvine facility is the culmination of decades of precision development. Atoco’s materials and approach allow its off-grid system to work even when relative humidity is in the teens. The MOFs in the device can harvest and release water with heat as low as 100 degrees Fahrenheit, Taha says. With no data center nearby, Atoco’s team simulated it by piping heat from a source that was around 150 degrees Fahrenheit. A solar panel powers various systems but not the water-harvesting operation itself, making the metal-clad machine eerily quiet. Cars pulling into the adjacent businesses create more of a sonic disruption, but Taha is ready to show the device has been working hard. It’s a little after 9 am, and the temperature is over 90 degrees Fahrenheit when he pushes a button on the side and turns a spigot. Out tumbles a clear stream of water that looks good enough to drink. Unfortunately it’s not on offer for legal liability reasons, though Taha notes it’s the equivalent of distilled water, because Atoco’s MOFs aren’t built to gather air pollution. Tossing it in the bushes, Taha retreats to an air-conditioned conference room where he lays out the company’s vision for its new machine. “Roughly 70 percent of the industrial waste heat is low-grade, unutilized, thrown into oceans or into the air,” he says. “If you convert that waste heat to clean water using our technology, you're talking about trillions of liters of clean water.” Data centers are an increasingly big source of that waste heat, with a single facility capable of pumping out as much heat as tens of thousands of homes. Operators are forced to disperse that heat into the surrounding environment, creating heat islands, while also paying for various types of cooling systems. Many of those cooling systems also rely on water, and some can consume millions of gallons per day. Atoco’s technology would thus address two of data centers’ biggest problems. artigo.texto: A U.K. homeowner says a new 10-kilowatt-hour battery setup sharply reduced peak-time grid use in its first week, offering an early example of how pairing battery storage with rooftop solar can cut electricity costs on a time-of-use tariff. For households dealing with high utility rates and unpredictable weather, that kind of system can provide more control. Here's what to know According to a Reddit post, the setup uses two hardwired Anker Solarbank 4 Pro units stacked for a total of 10 kWh, along with four 410-watt solar panels feeding the MPPT inputs. The household is on Octopus Go, with electricity priced at 8.5p overnight and 30.1p during the day, and the poster said daytime grid imports dropped from roughly 80 kWh before installation to around 15 kWh. Based on those numbers, the poster said the first week delivered a net saving of about £16.50 (~$21.90 USD). They estimated that roughly 65 kWh of electricity that otherwise would have been bought at peak rates was avoided. The panels generated about 40 kWh in total, with around 30 kWh stored in the battery while the household was at work and 10 kWh used directly in the home as it was produced. That meant only about 35 kWh had to be added during the overnight charging window, at a cost of around £3 (~$4). Adding battery storage is one of the best ways to protect your home during outages, save money on energy, and keep more of your solar power available when you actually need it. If you want to explore your options, EnergySage can help you compare home battery storage choices and get competitive installation estimates. More background The post also highlighted the limitations of a modest-sized battery during colder weather. The original poster said, "Two evenings we had the heating on and the stack ran out before 00:30, so those last couple of hours came straight off the grid." They also cautioned that the system could be under more pressure in winter, when solar production is likely to fall. Still, other commenters described similarly strong solar performance. "I generated 174kWh since I had my system installed on September 10th," a commenter wrote. "8 x 495 panels spread 4 east and 4 west. Cannot wait for next summer." Battery storage can also help households rely less on the grid by shifting cheap overnight electricity into the more expensive part of the day and by storing solar power that would otherwise be exported or go unused. What can be done? "40kWh is very good for 4x 410W panels at the end of September," a commenter reacted. "Must have been much more sunny than average back home. It will be interesting to see your data longer term. It's definitely the way to go though." If you're thinking along those lines, EnergySage has teamed up with the electrification brand Qmerit to guarantee you get the best price on home battery storage solutions. Another option is Pila, which offers excellent battery backup choices. Its plug-and-play batteries cost a fraction of a whole-home backup system. Where can I learn more? Home batteries and solar are reshaping how communities manage electricity costs. • In the U.K., a proposal says neighborhood-scale batteries could cut bills by storing cheap power. • In England, residents raised £440,000 for the U.K.'s first community-owned battery to capture excess solar. artigo.texto: Russian internet giant Yandex suspended operations at one of its key data centers on Thursday after a drone strike as Ukraine continues to target the country's infrastructure. The attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan, in western Russia, and affected part of its infrastructure, Yandex said in a statement to CNBC. The data center has stopped operating entirely, and some Yandex services may be unavailable to users, it added. "There are no casualties, and emergency services are on site dealing with the aftermath," Yandex said. Moscow-headquartered Yandex, known as the Google of Russia, provides the country's most widely used search engine. It also developed the region's leading generative AI model, YandexGPT. Although Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the Yandex attack, it has been stepping up its attacks on Russian infrastructure, including energy, over recent months, such as targeting Russian oil refineries, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said are used to "finance the war and the killing of Ukrainians." Ukraine also increased attacks on Russian retail giant Wildberries, a critical part of the consumer infrastructure. Last week, Zelenskyy said the country will double down on its attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes from Moscow designed to force people to leave Kyiv and other cities. Kyiv's power issues Emergency power cuts were enforced in Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, on Thursday due to ongoing Russian air strikes on the country's power grid. Last week, Russia hit key facilities in Kyiv and other major cities across the country, as it looks to destabilize Ukraine's energy foundation ahead of the winter season, threatening heating and other essential services for civilians. In response, Ukraine has been attacking Russia's fuel and energy facilities, with Zelenskyy warning Russian President Vladimir Putin at the United Nations General Assembly in September that Kyiv would make winter painful for Russia if the two sides were unable to come to an energy truce. "Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," Zelenskyy said on Sept. 23.

artigo.texto: Delray Beach, FL, Oct. 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The global Data Center Energy Storage Systems Market is projected to grow from USD 5.17 billion in 2026 to USD 10.48 billion by 2032, registering a CAGR of 12.5% during 2026–2032. Growth is driven by rising AI and hyperscale workloads, increasing data center power demand, renewable energy integration, and the need for resilient and flexible power infrastructure. Key Players: Tesla, Panasonic Holdings, Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, CATL, BYD, Schneider Electric, Vertiv, Eaton, ABB, Siemens Energy, Delta Electronics, Hitachi Energy, Fluence, and Saft. Why This Market Matters Data centers are facing rapidly increasing electricity requirements as AI, cloud computing, and high-performance workloads increase computing density. Energy storage systems provide backup power while also supporting peak-load management, power quality, renewable integration, and grid services. Market Overview The market covers Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), Flywheel Energy Storage Systems (FESS), Supercapacitors, and other technologies, including hydrogen-based storage. ESS applications are expanding beyond conventional backup power toward energy optimization, peak-load management, renewable integration, and grid support. Analyst Perspective The transition toward AI-driven data centers is increasing both power density and power fluctuations. This is creating demand for storage technologies that can provide rapid response, reliable backup, and greater flexibility in managing electricity demand. The emergence of hybrid and multi-technology ESS architectures is also creating opportunities to combine different storage technologies according to specific data center requirements. By Energy Storage Technology — Supercapacitors Grow Fastest Supercapacitor energy storage systems are projected to register the highest CAGR of 16.5% during 2026–2032. Their rapid power delivery and ability to withstand frequent charge-discharge cycles make them suitable for managing short-duration power fluctuations, power quality, and peak-shaving requirements in AI-intensive facilities. By Data Center Type — Cloud & Hyperscale Leads Growth Cloud & hyperscale data centers are expected to record the fastest growth, with a 14.8% CAGR. Increasing AI workloads, cloud adoption, and expansion of large-scale digital infrastructure are increasing requirements for reliable and flexible power systems. By Application — Renewable Integration & Grid Services Renewable integration & grid services is expected to register the highest CAGR of 18.3%. Energy storage enables data centers to manage renewable-energy intermittency, balance electricity supply and demand, and improve overall energy flexibility. Regional Analysis North America — Largest Market North America is expected to account for the largest share of the global market, supported by its established data center infrastructure and strong investments in cloud computing, AI, and digital services. The region's large hyperscale, enterprise, and colocation ecosystem is creating significant demand for reliable power and energy management solutions. Asia Pacific — Fastest-Growing Region Asia Pacific is projected to register the highest CAGR during 2026–2032. Rapid digitalization, expanding cloud and AI infrastructure, and increasing data center construction are driving demand for energy storage solutions across the region. Key Industry Trends AI-driven power demand: Higher computing density is increasing data center electricity requirements. Renewable Integration: ESS is increasingly used to manage intermittent renewable power. Hybrid ESS Architectures: Multiple storage technologies are being combined for different power requirements. Peak-load Management: Energy storage can help manage periods of high electricity demand. Smart Energy Management: AI-enabled monitoring and predictive management are emerging opportunities. Market Dynamics Key Drivers Accelerating investments in AI-driven and hyperscale data centers Expanding ESS adoption across backup, energy optimization, and grid-support applications Key Restraint High upfront capital requirements for ESS deployment Key Opportunities Growing retrofit demand for higher power density and resilience Hybrid and multi-technology ESS architectures Key Challenges Complex ESS integration with existing data center power infrastructure Safety and thermal management across different ESS technologies. Competitive Landscape The market includes major battery, energy-storage, power-management, and data center infrastructure companies. Key Players Tesla Panasonic Holdings Corporation Samsung SDI LG Energy Solution Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. (CATL) BYD Schneider Electric Vertiv Eaton ABB Siemens Energy Delta Electronics Hitachi Energy Fluence Saft Recent Industry Developments June 2026: Schneider Electric launched the ASCO 300 SERIES Multi-Voltage Transfer Switch for backup power architectures. June 2026: Tesla and NatPower initiated the first phase of a USD 5 billion project targeting 25 GWh of Tesla Megapack battery storage in Italy and Britain. March 2026: Panasonic announced plans to expand lithium-ion battery production capacity to address growing demand from data center energy storage and backup systems. March 2026: Samsung SDI expanded its North American ESS business with prismatic battery supplies from its Indiana facility. Strategic Takeaway The USD 10.48 billion opportunity by 2032 reflects the increasing importance of energy storage in modern data center power infrastructure. As AI, hyperscale computing, renewable energy, and power-density requirements continue to expand, opportunities are increasingly centered on BESS, supercapacitors, hybrid ESS architectures, peak-load management, renewable integration, and intelligent energy management.

artigo.texto: A Alibaba Cloud inaugurou seus primeiros data centers no Brasil em São Paulo em agosto de 2026, prometendo reduzir o tempo de resposta de sites e sistemas de pagamento. No entanto, especialistas do Grupo HRZ destacam que a infraestrutura só será útil se integrada a um planejamento completo de CRM, estoque e atendimento, evitando falhas em campanhas de alto volume. A Alibaba Cloud, divisão de computação em nuvem do grupo chinês Alibaba, anunciou em 27 de agosto de 2026 a inauguração dos seus dois primeiros data centers no Brasil, ambos localizados em São Paulo. A chegada dessa infraestrutura aproxima os servidores das empresas e dos consumidores brasileiros, o que pode melhorar significativamente o desempenho de sites, sistemas de pagamento, consultas de estoque e plataformas de atendimento. Essa expansão faz parte do compromisso global de US$ 53 bilhões da companhia com inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem. Com a chegada dos novos data centers da Alibaba Cloud no Brasil, a latência deve cair, mas será que a tecnologia sozinha salva uma operação de vendas instável Especialistas debatem o tema e analisam os desafios de integração de CRM, estoque e e-commerce para aproveitar ao máximo essa nova infraestrutura. - A Alibaba Cloud abriu dois data centers em São Paulo para reduzir o tempo de resposta dos sites brasileiros. - A infraestrutura faz parte de um investimento global de US$ 53 bilhões em inteligência artificial. - Especialistas alertam que servidores rápidos não resolvem falhas de estoque ou atendimento desatualizado. - Campanhas de grande volume, como a Black Friday, exigem estabilidade total de todos os sistemas. - É necessário diagnosticar a operação antes de migrar para garantir que os dados fluam entre canais. Proximidade de servidores reduz tempo de resposta Hugo Silveira, cofundador do Grupo HRZ, holding especializada em crescimento empresarial e estruturação comercial, avalia que a entrada de mais um grande fornecedor amplia as opções para empresas que dependem de sistemas digitais para vender. Ter servidores mais próximos pode diminuir o tempo que a informação leva para ir e voltar. Mas isso, sozinho, não resolve os problemas de uma operação. É preciso analisar o site, as integrações, o estoque, o atendimento e o CRM para entender onde a nova infraestrutura realmente pode trazer ganho, afirma o estrategista. Na prática, essa distância entre o usuário e o servidor influencia a chamada latência, que é o intervalo entre uma ação e a resposta do sistema. Quando um consumidor abre uma página, consulta um produto, tenta finalizar uma compra ou realiza um pagamento, diferentes sistemas precisam trocar informações em poucos segundos. Esse ponto ganha importância em operações que conectam loja física, e-commerce, aplicativo e WhatsApp. O Grupo HRZ atua em projetos nos quais estoque, vendas, CRM e atendimento precisam compartilhar dados para que o consumidor consiga iniciar uma compra em um canal e continuar em outro sem perder o histórico. A Alibaba Cloud informa que sua estrutura em São Paulo conta com duas zonas de disponibilidade. Em termos simples, são ambientes separados, com redes e fontes de energia independentes, criados para reduzir o risco de uma única falha afetar toda a operação. A própria companhia recomenda que as empresas utilizem estruturas próximas de seus usuários quando o objetivo é diminuir o tempo de resposta. Estabilidade é crucial em picos de vendas A capacidade de aumentar recursos rapidamente se torna especialmente importante em períodos que concentram muitos acessos em poucas horas, como Black Friday, lançamentos de produtos e grandes campanhas promocionais. Nessas situações, uma falha pode atingir diferentes etapas da compra, da abertura da página até a aprovação do pagamento. Iury Borges, estrategista de vendas e sócio-diretor do Grupo HRZ, afirma que uma infraestrutura mais próxima pode ajudar, mas precisa fazer parte de um planejamento mais amplo. Uma campanha com milhares de pessoas acessando ao mesmo tempo exige que toda a operação esteja preparada. Não adianta o site responder rápido se o estoque estiver desatualizado, o pagamento apresentar falhas ou a equipe não conseguir atender a demanda. A nuvem é uma peça dessa estrutura, ressalta. O desafio, portanto, não termina na velocidade do site. Sistemas de vendas, estoque, CRM e atendimento precisam trocar informações de forma organizada. Quando essa comunicação funciona, a empresa consegue atualizar a disponibilidade dos produtos, identificar a origem das compras e manter o histórico do consumidor ao longo do relacionamento. João Vinas, engenheiro e sócio do Grupo HRZ, onde atua em projetos de CRM, automação comercial e inteligência artificial aplicada a vendas, afirma que a migração para uma nova infraestrutura deve começar por um diagnóstico. O varejista precisa saber onde seus dados estão armazenados, quais sistemas dependem uns dos outros, quais serviços estão disponíveis no Brasil e quanto uma mudança custaria. Só depois desse levantamento é possível saber se a migração faz sentido, aponta. Privacidade de dados e diagnóstico prévio A presença dos servidores no Brasil também pode ser considerada por negócios que desejam manter parte do processamento de informações no território nacional. Isso, porém, não substitui as demais obrigações de proteção de dados. A Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados estabelece responsabilidades para empresas que coletam e utilizam informações pessoais, enquanto transferências internacionais seguem regras específicas da Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados. Antes de trocar de fornecedor ou transferir sistemas, a recomendação é medir o desempenho atual. O primeiro passo pode ser verificar, principalmente pelo celular, quanto tempo uma página de produto leva para abrir, como o checkout responde e em quais pontos o consumidor encontra demora. artigo.texto: O projeto em Abu Dhabi combina painéis fotovoltaicos e armazenamento em baterias de escala gigante para superar a intermitência do sol e alimentar data centers de inteligência artificial sem parar. Como a luz do sol consegue gerar eletricidade durante a noite inteira? Você já percebeu como uma luminária solar de jardim se apaga poucas horas após o anoitecer? Em uma rede elétrica industrial, essa oscilação causaria apagões imediatos em fábricas e servidores de computadores. Para evitar falhas, o sistema usa uma técnica de superdimensionamento de captação combinada com armazenamento imediato, chamada de geração ininterrupta Round-the-Clock (RTC). A usina gera 5,2 GW em horário de pico, volume mais de cinco vezes superior à capacidade de entrega contínua. Esse excedente diurno carrega um sistema de armazenamento em baterias BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) de 19 GWh, quantidade suficiente para abastecer centenas de milhares de casas por uma noite inteira. Assim, a energia flui de forma estável para a rede sem depender de usinas a gás. Qual é o tamanho e a capacidade do maior complexo solar e de baterias do mundo? Projetado pela estatal Masdar e pela concessionária EWEC com investimento de US$ 6,1 bilhões, o complexo reúne números inéditos na engenharia de energia global. Capacidade fotovoltaica total: 5,2 GW em corrente contínua instalados em painéis de alta eficiência no deserto de Abu Dhabi. - Armazenamento em baterias: capacidade nominal de 19 GWh em módulos de íon de lítio acoplados à rede. - Fornecimento contínuo garantido: entrega firme de 1 GW de potência limpa sem interrupção 24 horas por dia. - Aporte financeiro: orçamento fechado de US$ 6,1 bilhões com consórcio bancário internacional. - Previsão de operação: início de funcionamento comercial programado para o ano de 2027. Como o sistema gerencia a oscilação entre o dia e a noite na prática? Durante as horas de sol forte no deserto, os 5,2 GW de painéis solares produzem energia máxima. Os inversores centrais direcionam 1 GW direto para a rede elétrica e enviam os 4,2 GW restantes para carregar os bancos de baterias em contêineres climatizados. Quando o sol se põe, o sistema de controle inteligente chaveia a fonte em milissegundos sem deixar a voltagem cair. As baterias assumem a descarga e mantêm a transmissão de 1 GW até o alvorecer seguinte, garantindo fornecimento ininterrupto para infraestruturas críticas. Onde assistir aos detalhes do projeto gigawatt de energia solar e baterias? Engenheiros da empresa estatal Masdar e da parceira construtora PowerChina detalharam os desafios de erguer uma infraestrutura desse porte no clima desértico. A instalação exige milhares de rastreadores solares e estruturas de climatização para evitar o superaquecimento dos módulos de bateria. O vídeo oficial de apresentação mostra a maquete técnica, o canteiro de obras e a arquitetura do sistema elétrico que vai abastecer os novos data centers de inteligência artificial da região. Abaixo, um vídeo do canal oficial da Masdar que aprofunda o tema: Quais normas internacionais garantem a segurança de baterias em escala de gigawatt? Projetos de armazenamento em baterias deste porte precisam cumprir rigorosos padrões globais de segurança contra incêndios e gerenciamento térmico, como as normas IEC 62933 para sistemas BESS e a NFPA 855 para prevenção de riscos em baterias de íon de lítio. Além disso, a conexão com a rede de alta tensão segue a norma IEEE 2800, garantindo que as baterias consigam estabilizar a frequência e a voltagem do sistema elétrico sem causar oscilações no grid nacional. Quando é necessário contratar um engenheiro eletricista especializado em energia renovável? Seja para projetar um parque solar comercial ou instalar um sistema de baterias industrial, é fundamental contar com um engenheiro eletricista ou um especialista em sistemas de energia para dimensionar a carga e a proteção contra surtos. Projetos de armazenamento envolvem alta densidade energética e riscos térmicos que não permitem improvisos. Uma avaliação técnica incorreta pode resultar em curtos-circuitos, perda de eficiência das células de bateria ou desaprovação junto à distribuidora de energia local. Contexto importante: Este artigo é informativo. Para projetos estruturais e elétricos locais similares, recomenda-se avaliação de engenheiro eletricista ou especialista em engenharia de energia, especialmente em contextos de risco de sobrecarga, aquecimento térmico ou integração com a rede elétrica.

artigo.texto: Nevada data centers promise big power demand. Who will pay the bill? As Nevada faces unprecedented demand for electricity from the data center industry, developers are pushing back against some of NV Energy’s proposed safeguards designed to prevent the cost of serving their projects from shifting to other customers. But as the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada weighs agreements with future data center customers, confidentiality claims and redactions are preventing the public from seeing project-specific information needed to determine whether those safeguards are sufficient. Many data center developers currently seeking electric service from NV Energy are requesting 300 to 500 megawatts of electricity, six to 10 times the roughly 50 megawatts a major casino or mine might use, said Shawn Elicegui, NV Energy’s senior vice president of regulatory and resource planning. “What we see from data centers is unprecedented,” Elicegui said in a recent interview. “There’s really nothing comparable to data center load.” Unlike most customers — such as households or small businesses, which typically receive a monthly bill based largely on how much electricity they use — data centers typically commit in advance to how much power they expect to need. If they take service under terms approved by the PUC, they can be required to make minimum payments based on those commitments, even if they ultimately use less electricity. The stakes are significant. NV Energy’s plans for future electricity needs account for the enormous demand expected from data centers and other large customers, as well as the infrastructure needed to serve them. If a data center ultimately uses less power than expected, the utility could be left with costs it expected the large customer to help cover, potentially shifting some of those costs to other ratepayers. NV Energy wants some of its largest new customers to pay minimum charges tied to at least 90 percent of the power demand and energy use they sign up for. At least one data center developer, however, wants that minimum set at 70 percent, according to PUC regulatory filings. The disagreement is a test of NV Energy’s promise that Nevada’s growing data-center industry will pay the costs it creates rather than shift them to other customers. Guardrails — but not enough information to test them A Las Vegas Review-Journal investigation found several guardrails in regulatory filings designed to support NV Energy’s repeated promise that data centers will pay their own way. They generally include proposed minimum payments, charges for new generation, financial guarantees and penalties if a customer leaves early. But simply having those protections does not show whether they are sufficient to prevent the costs of serving data centers from shifting onto other ratepayers, energy and utility-regulation experts told the Review-Journal. Sarah Wang, a researcher who studies massive customers called large loads, said regulators can calculate the minimum revenue a customer must provide and compare it with the costs the utility would not otherwise incur. “Without modeling, or some set of calculations, it’s really hard to figure out what 70 percent or 90 percent really mean,” said Wang, a senior associate at energy policy research organization RMI. Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the key question is whether the service agreements between utilities and data center developers cover all the infrastructure costs created by the new demand, rather than only some of them. “I believe that large loads should be required to pay for 100 percent of the incremental costs,” Peskoe said. Utilities around the country are confronting similar questions as they plan new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure to accommodate rapidly growing data center demand. New large-load customer rules increasingly use minimum payments, long-term contracts, financial guarantees and exit charges to reduce the risk that other customers are left paying for infrastructure built for projects that arrive late, use less power than expected or never fully develop. The Review-Journal examined proposed agreements between data center customers and NV Energy, utility testimony and power plans, and submitted multiple public records requests to the PUC. The public filings and records obtained for several data center projects the newspaper reviewed do not contain enough project-specific information to compare the minimum revenue those data centers would provide with the costs NV Energy would not otherwise incur — and determine whether any of those costs could shift to other ratepayers. What 90 percent vs. 70 percent really means The minimum-billing dispute is playing out in a pending commission case over proposed large-load electric service agreements between NV Energy and industrial real estate company Prologis for at least one data center project under development in North Las Vegas. The agreements would govern how NV Energy supplies data centers’ enormous power needs. Prologis argues that a 70 percent minimum better reflects how data centers actually operate, saying their electricity use does not consistently reach 90 percent of capacity in every billing period and can vary as tenants move in. Prologis did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Wang said a 70 percent minimum could recover all new costs incurred by a customer if the underlying rates, direct cost assignments, contract terms and exit provisions enable a utility to collect sufficient revenue. The reverse, she said, is also possible: Even requiring minimum billing at 100 percent of contracted demand would not guarantee full cost recovery if the rates or the way costs are assigned are inadequate. The goal, Wang said, should be 100 percent recovery of the total cost to serve — both the properly assigned new costs and the large customer’s share of existing infrastructure it uses. (NYSE: VSH) announced that the company will showcase its latest passive component technologies, semiconductors, and reference designs at The Battery Show North America 2026, taking place October 12–15 in Detroit (Booth 4807). At the event, Vishay will highlight solutions that address key design challenges in battery management, protection, and high voltage power conversion for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. artigo.texto: Three-year agreement to supply 60 GWh energy storage systems aims to accelerate global industrial-scale deployment of sodium-ion technology. Continue reading On Tuesday morning, Zsolt Tárkányi, a member of the National Assembly from TISZA, published seven pages of documents on social media regarding the agreement signed for the Chinese battery factory in Debrecen (eastern Hungary), Világgazdaság reported. The tone of the post suggests that this politician strongly disapproves of what the Orbán government promised the world’s largest battery manufacturer to persuade it to build its next plant in Hungary. However, upon reviewing the letter of intent, no glaringly unusual promises can be found in it; rather, it can be concluded that the previous FIDESZ-KDNP-led cabinet sought to make a good offer to the Chinese side. This is, of course, no coincidence, since when this agreement was reached, CATL was considering a massive investment totaling 7.3 billion euros to build a battery manufacturing plant with an annual capacity of 100 GWh. The Hungarian government, for its part, expressed its intention to support the implementation of the planned investment in Hungary at the priority site in Debrecen that CATL was considering. This is because the Chinese side had previously considered Hungary as a potential investment location after deciding to expand its manufacturing presence outside of China. The fact that CATL ultimately chose Debrecen was by no means a foregone conclusion, as several European countries—including Western ones—were competing for the project. In other words, the Orbán government’s proposal deserves to be evaluated from this perspective: it fought hard to win the Chinese company’s favor in a highly competitive situation, securing a commitment to invest more than 2,600 billion forints here. Hungary may have caught the attention of the Chinese because, by that time, it had already become one of the most attractive destinations for direct foreign investment (FDI) by major battery manufacturers. According to the Orbán government’s view, the related large-scale investment projects contribute significantly to the country’s economic development. In addition, they have a substantial impact on long-term employment, technology transfer, and cluster effects, as well as stimulating industrial and technological development. It is a fact that, thanks to FDI, Hungary’s innovation performance has improved rapidly and significantly in recent years. Zsolt Tárkányi, however, focuses not on this but on the fact that the Chinese investment was granted VIP status. In reality, though, this simply refers to a completely standard category. The point is that with the establishment of the Debrecen Southern Industrial Park in 2015, Debrecen committed itself to attracting future industrial investments to boost economic growth in the region and in Hungary. To support the development of the Industrial Park, the Orbán government designated existing and future investments in the Industrial Park as projects of priority importance to the Hungarian economy. This is what the “VIP Status” referred to in the recently published cooperation agreement signifies. The Orbán government was aware that CATL’s potential investment and other industrial developments in the priority region would pose infrastructure challenges. Therefore, as a prerequisite, it ensured that adequate public utilities would be developed and made available to all investments in the region. It decided to provide funding for the existing utility infrastructure and the utility development program in the area where CATL plans to carry out its project. The Chinese side had already indicated its potential utility needs—including water, gas, wastewater, and electricity—in this document, but Zsolt Tárkányi redacted these details. It was also put in writing that the Hungarian government would do everything in its power to ensure that airlines establish regular flights between Debrecen and China, either directly or with layovers in Türkiye or the United Arab Emirates. As is the case with many other major investment projects, the government at the time would also provide other (including non-financial) support in connection with the CATL plant, such as Tárkányi took particular issue with the fact that CATL had been promised tax breaks on several counts. Specifically, the development tax credit would have entailed a reduction of up to 80% of the corporate income tax (CIT) liability for a maximum of 13 tax years, subject to European Union approval once the national threshold was exceeded. However, based on the document, cash grants for innovation would also be available for innovation projects, covering up to 25% of the costs. At the same time, it is important to emphasize that the published letter of intent cannot be considered legally binding. It also states that any transaction between the parties remains subject to the conclusion of a final, written, and signed agreement(s), as well as approval by CATL’s general meeting, the relevant Chinese government authorities, the Hungarian government, and the European Commission. artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Virtual Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline By Canary Media This article is part of the series “Power Struggle: Building Clean Energy in Rural America.” Read more. The soil in northwest Iowa is so fertile it’s referred to as “black gold.” “It’s incredibly rich, wonderful topsoil from thousands of years of silty deposits from the Missouri River,” said Luke Seaberg, a researcher at Iowa State University’s extension program. So rich that some counties restrict development on land that scores especially high on the state’s official Corn Suitability Rating. The Smith family has been farming that soil for six generations in Cherokee County, population 11,000. But the corn market has been depressed lately, prompting the three Smith brothers to consider other uses for a 160-acre parcel, 10% of their farmland. Looking at rising beef prices and the region’s ballooning energy demand, they landed on an idea: Graze cows amid rows of solar panels. “We’re trying to diversify into another revenue stream. The cattle business is really good right now, and grain has been not as good,” Mark Smith told me over the phone, as he drove across the state for his son’s high school football game. “With solar, we can put cornfields back to pasture. Solar revenue plus cattle revenue makes it work.” But to loft the solar panels up above the butting heads of grazing cattle costs more than a regular solar installation; indeed, this type of agrivoltaics only recently entered commercial-scale use, at a 40-acre, 3-megawatt site in Tennessee developed by Silicon Ranch. To mitigate the extra cost, the Smiths want to pair 30 megawatts of cattle-friendly solar capacity with a 25-megawatt/100-megawatt-hour battery composed of modular containerized units covering about an acre and a half. The Smith brothers’ desire to install batteries on their land, though, set them on a collision course with local authorities. When the county supervisors heard of the plan, they approved an indefinite moratorium on March 24, blocking any battery projects in the county. Similar bans are popping up around the country as communities grapple with the real and perceived risks of lithium-ion batteries, which rose from obscurity over the last decade and now constitute the largest source of on-demand power getting built in the U.S. In many counties, this story ends with the battery moratorium, stymieing new emissions-free power capacity at a time when everyone from climate advocates to AI giants to the Trump administration wants to see more batteries get built. But the Smiths found an ally in Supervisor Shane Bellefy, the lone vote against the moratorium. Together, they set out to flip the county back to a place that lets landowners decide what to do on their acreage. Within just five months, they succeeded. Iowa subscribes to the “home rule” philosophy, whereby the state constitution leaves many decisions up to city or county governments, Seaberg said. But even those local authorities typically take a hands-off approach. The state’s “right to farm” law blocks local governments from regulating what landowners choose to grow or raise on their farmland. Some rural counties don’t even have a zoning code. “Your nearest neighbor might be 5 or 10 miles down the road,” Seaberg explained. “The general policy of county supervisors was, folks can do what they want to do with their land.” That attitude started to shift after the onshore wind boom came to Iowa in the early 2000s. The state has since added 13 gigawatts and remains the nation’s top state for share of wind energy produced. But in some rural counties, the nonexistent zoning code enabled a frenzy of development that “left a bad taste in their mouths,” Seaberg said. Now some counties have added land use regulations — but only for wind and solar. In Cherokee County, an earlier proposed 900-acre solar project prompted the supervisors to throw up a solar moratorium last year. But they subsequently worked through their concerns with the technology and adopted an ordinance allowing large-scale solar, with some restrictions. The March 2026 battery moratorium, though, would block the Smiths’ project, jeopardizing tens of millions of dollars in financing that the developers had lined up from investment banks. The Smiths might have had a case to challenge the moratorium on procedural grounds, since it passed without the usual multiple readings and lacked a specified time frame. But instead, they opted for persuasion. After the moratorium was approved, it fell to the county zoning board to compose a long-term ordinance to govern battery development. That body held a public meeting in May where the Smiths testified about their plans. The family also invited Seaberg to answer the community’s questions about battery technology based on Iowa State University’s independent research. The Smiths explained what they wanted to build on their land in partnership with energy developer Nomad Infrastructure. The Indiana-based firm has considerable experience constructing solar and battery projects, and one brother, Thomas Smith, works there as an engineer. They had gotten permission from the local rural electric cooperative, Mark Smith noted, to transmit the generation over the wires and sell it in the broader regional grid, run by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator. The MISO grid has very high rates of wind and solar production, but batteries are just starting to proliferate there. Meanwhile, data center expansion is driving up electricity demand in the region to never-before-seen heights, making for auspicious conditions to sell on-demand power from a battery. Bellefy, who works as a banker, pitched his fellow supervisors on the economic potential of allowing the project to move forward. The Smith installation would involve investing upwards of $80 million, which could generate $60,000 to $80,000 in new county tax revenue annually, Bellefy estimated. “Land in Iowa is our

artigo.texto: Em uma manhã ensolarada de agosto, Bob Clark visita o novo Obama Presidential Center, no Jackson Park, zona sul de Chicago. Fundador da gigante da construção Clayco, ele ajudou a erguer o complexo, avaliado em US$ 850 milhões (R$ 4,23 bilhões). Clark faz uma rápida inspeção no “Obamalisk”. É assim que chama, carinhosamente, a torre central de oito andares, feita de granito, vidro e concreto. Depois, cumprimenta Valerie Jarrett, ex-assessora sênior da Casa Branca e atual CEO da Obama Foundation. A visita é rápida. Clark entra no banco traseiro de um Escalade branco e segue pela Lake Shore Drive. O destino é outro de seus projetos, que pode ter uma importância ainda maior para Chicago e para o mundo. Às margens do Lago Michigan, o “Quantum Shore” ocupa uma área onde funcionava uma fábrica da U.S. Steel. Quando for inaugurado, no fim de 2027, será um dos maiores campi de computação quântica dos Estados Unidos. Entre os ocupantes estarão a IBM e a PsiQuantum, empresa de Palo Alto, na Califórnia. A companhia pretende construir no local um computador quântico de 1 milhão de qubits. Uma máquina desse porte teria uma capacidade difícil de imaginar. Poderia quebrar os tipos tradicionais de criptografia que protegem grande parte dos computadores — e das contas bancárias — do mundo. No futuro, também poderia acelerar o aprendizado de sistemas de inteligência artificial. Isso ocorreria por meio da redução do tempo de treinamento de determinadas arquiteturas complexas de aprendizagem profunda. O Quantum Shore é um empreendimento complexo — e caro. A primeira fase está sendo desenvolvida pela CRG, subsidiária imobiliária de Clark, em parceria com o escritório do Meio-Oeste da gigante imobiliária Related Companies. O projeto custará US$ 12 bilhões (R$ 59,76 bilhões). Desse total, US$ 500 milhões (R$ 2,49 bilhões) serão aportados pelo estado de Illinois. Os bits quânticos, conhecidos como “qubits”, são extremamente sensíveis às condições ambientais. Por isso, a estrutura terá uma instalação criogênica. Ela fornecerá hélio e nitrogênio líquidos super-resfriados aos computadores. “A única maneira de estabilizar o chip é mantê-lo mais frio do que o espaço sideral”, diz Clark, enquanto guindastes de 550 toneladas passam pelo local. A complexidade da obra impressiona até mesmo o empresário. Ele se lembra de quando o CEO da PsiQuantum lhe disse que projetaria um edifício que iria “mudar tudo”. O negócio Clark, de 67 anos, parece adequado para comandar um projeto dessa dimensão. Ele constrói data centers desde a década de 1980. Somente no ano passado, concluiu 16. Outros 77 estão em andamento em 13 estados americanos. Os centros de dados devem responder por 75% da receita de quase US$ 12 bilhões (R$ 59,76 bilhões) da Clayco em 2026. A expansão do segmento deve ajudar a companhia a elevar o faturamento em 43% na comparação com 2025. “Trabalho no setor de data centers durante a maior parte da minha carreira, mas nunca teria imaginado o que está acontecendo hoje”, afirma. Quando Clark começou, há quatro décadas, um data center era algo bem mais simples. Eram apenas algumas salas de computadores instaladas nos fundos de um banco. Hoje, o cenário mudou. Sediada em Chicago, a Clayco ergue estruturas que equivalem a cidades autossuficientes de bilhões de dólares. Elas praticamente não têm presença humana e podem abrigar 100 mil ou mais das GPUs mais avançadas do mundo. Entre os clientes estão Amazon, Microsoft e Oracle. Para construir esses complexos com eficiência e em grande escala, a Clayco controla suas próprias empresas de arquitetura, concreto, compras e logística. É uma máquina criada para alimentar as máquinas insaciáveis da inteligência artificial. Corrida dos data centers Os gastos dos Estados Unidos com a construção de data centers mais do que triplicaram desde 2023. Neste ano, devem chegar a US$ 75 bilhões (R$ 373,5 bilhões), segundo dados do Census Bureau. O montante nem sequer inclui a compra dos computadores. Esses equipamentos podem representar 40% do custo total de um projeto. Jeff Blau é CEO da Related e parceiro de Clark no Quantum Shore. Os dois também trabalham em um data center de US$ 1,2 bilhão (R$ 5,98 bilhões) para a CoreWeave, em Cheyenne, no Wyoming. Segundo Blau, a forte demanda por centros de dados, somada aos juros elevados, tirou espaço de muitos outros grandes projetos de construção. “Isso não tem precedentes. Nunca tivemos algo com uma demanda tão forte e, ao mesmo tempo, em uma escala tão grande”, afirma. A Related Digital, comandada por Blau, tem US$ 55 bilhões (R$ 273,9 bilhões) em projetos de data centers em desenvolvimento. Para as construtoras, é uma ótima notícia. Quase 1.300 data centers já estão em funcionamento nos Estados Unidos. Essas colmeias de concreto e aço consomem aproximadamente 70 milhões de galões de água por dia. Também precisam de um fornecimento constante de 62 gigawatts de energia. Para efeito de comparação, a cidade de Nova York utiliza, em média, seis gigawatts. E a expansão está longe de terminar. Outros 2.142 centros estão planejados ou em construção, segundo a empresa de inteligência em infraestrutura Cleanview. Sem medo de uma bolha O boom da IA também tornou Clark muito mais rico. Seu patrimônio líquido quadruplicou nos últimos três anos e chegou a US$ 7 bilhões (R$ 34,86 bilhões). A fortuna garantiu ao empresário uma estreia na lista Forbes 400 deste ano. Ele aparece na 245ª posição. Mas a expansão dos data centers também trouxe outro efeito: uma oposição cada vez maior. Uma pesquisa recente do Annenberg Public Policy Center mostrou que 61% dos americanos são contrários à construção dessas instalações em suas comunidades. Quatro meses antes, eram 49%. Segundo o Data Center Watch, projetos avaliados em US$ 18 bilhões (R$ 89,64 bilhões) foram bloqueados. Outros US$ 46 bilhões (R$ 229,08 bilhões) em construções sofreram atrasos. Clark não se intimida com a reação. Prefere manter o foco nos resultados. “Não vemos nenhum sinal de alerta no horizonte”, afirm

artigo.texto: Reduce emissions to 'profit': New opportunities from the carbon market. (CLO) Officially operational from the end of June 2026, the carbon exchange in Vietnam is considered a significant step towards a low-emission economy. Although the market is still in its nascent stages, Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung - Director of VinaCarbon Investment Fund - believes that Vietnam has sufficient potential to transform emission reduction into a real source of economic value, attracting large capital flows into forestry, clean energy, and agriculture. The carbon exchange in Vietnam officially began operations at the end of June 2026. To date, the number of products and transactions on the market remains quite limited. However, the potential for development is considered significant as Vietnam is accelerating its emission reduction goals, promoting green transitions, and gradually improving the legal framework for the carbon market. Regarding this issue, a reporter from the Journalists and Public Opinion Newspaper had a private interview with Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung, Director of VinaCarbon Investment Fund, about the prospects of the carbon market in Vietnam. The Vietnamese carbon market has many favorable conditions for strong growth. + Sir, the official launch of the carbon exchange in June 2026 is considered the starting point for the carbon market in Vietnam. From an investment perspective, how do you view the opportunities and growth potential of this market in the coming years? - It can be said that the Vietnamese carbon market has many favorable conditions for strong development, especially given that our country is in a favorable position thanks to the convergence of four factors: international demand, natural supply, legal framework, and international institutions ready to cooperate. The pilot operation of the domestic carbon exchange, despite its limited number of products and transactions, is a significant step forward, as it lays the foundation for a transparent market, moving towards a low-emission economy and fulfilling Vietnam's climate commitments. The potential for growth in Vietnam's carbon credit market stems primarily from demand. Domestically, the need to reduce emissions and transition to green is being concretized through quota mechanisms, starting with high-emission industries such as thermal power, steel, and cement, and will be tightened to more industries in the future. Globally , the trend of greening supply chains is gaining momentum, with many new requirements for reducing emissions. From the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for Aviation (CORSIA), the net-zero commitments of multinational corporations, to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), exporting businesses are being forced to manage their emissions more tightly. This creates a significant demand for high-quality and integrity carbon credits in the future. To meet that demand, Vietnam has potential supply sources in many sectors such as agriculture , renewable energy, waste management, and especially forestry, where there are clear and sustainable advantages. Vietnam has a large forest area, with planted forests accounting for a significant proportion, along with years of experience in forest management and established forest product value chains. Furthermore, forest carbon already has its own legal framework. Projects for forest protection, restoration, and sustainable management can both generate substantial emission reductions and support community livelihoods if appropriate benefit-sharing mechanisms are in place. And because forests are a long-term asset, with project cycles spanning decades, forestry is also best suited to the medium- and long-term development narrative of the market. However, having both supply and demand is not enough, because a market can only develop sustainably when it has the necessary infrastructure. In just about a year and a half, Vietnam has built almost the complete "framework" necessary for a carbon market, from a domestic emissions trading mechanism, an official exchange, a national registration system, to regulations for transferring credits internationally and a separate decree on forest carbon. Furthermore, Vietnam has also established bilateral cooperation channels with Japan and Singapore. In summary, Vietnam has all the necessary conditions for carbon market growth in the coming years. However, the pace of development will depend on the completeness of the legal framework and trading infrastructure, the quality and integrity of the credits, and the ability to meet international standards. You may also like + In your opinion, what are the biggest difficulties and challenges hindering the development of Vietnam's carbon credit market, in terms of credit supply, credit quality, trading mechanisms, and the ability of businesses to participate? - The biggest challenge currently is the limited supply of high-quality carbon credits. Generating a carbon credit requires a relatively long and expensive process, from project development and evaluation to registration, making it generally difficult for investors to access. Furthermore, buyers of carbon credits are becoming increasingly demanding regarding quality. Criteria such as complementarity, risk of reversal, and risk of double counting are receiving more attention. Therefore, the market will tend to prioritize credits certified by reputable standards. This requires Vietnam to improve its measurement, reporting, and assessment capabilities, while gradually harmonizing domestic standards with international practices. Another challenge lies in the legal framework and market infrastructure. Regulations, credit standards, data systems, and supervisory mechanisms still need further improvement to increase transparency, build confidence, and reduce uncertainty for investors. artigo.texto: ESS, an opportunity for K-batteries A new current is reshaping the global battery market. In the first half of 2026, global shipments of lithium-ion batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) reached 461 gigawatt-hour (GWh), up 71 percent from 270 GWh in the same period a year earlier, according to SNE Research. This represents a remarkable leap for the ESS market, especially compared with the 20 percent year-on-year growth in global battery demand for electric vehicles (EVs), which reached 609 GWh over the same period. Key drivers include rising energy demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, where speed and reliability are critical, and growth in renewable power generation, which requires solutions to address its intermittency. The expansion of AI data centers and the transition to renewable energy are powerful trends unlikely to reverse in the short term. As a result, the global ESS market is forecast to reach 1,870 GWh in annual shipments by 2035, roughly twice this year’s level. The Korean government is also stepping up efforts to develop the domestic ESS industry through a range of policy measures. On the technology front, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced its Battery Industry Technology Roadmap on Sept. 22. The road map’s main elements are to position sodium-ion and solid-state batteries as new growth engines: The government will invest more than 250 billion won in next-generation battery technology development; the country’s three cell manufacturers will collaborate on research and standardization in noncompetitive areas; and the industry as a whole will invest approximately 8 trillion won ($5.97 billion) through 2030 in manufacturing-process innovation and the localization of materials. On the production front, the government has pledged tax support. On Aug. 3, the Ministry of Finance and Economy announced its 2026 Tax Reform Proposal, which introduced a domestic production tax credit to expand local manufacturing capacity in industries of strategic importance to the green transition and economic security. Rechargeable batteries are among the eligible products. On the deployment front, the government is expanding the market through auctions under the Central Contract Market. On Sept. 23, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment announced the third ESS Central Contract Market in which it would select ESS project developers with a record-high total capacity of 1,180 megawatts. By the auction, the Korea Power Exchange competitively tenders the ESS capacity needed to stabilize the grid and enters into 15-year contracts with successful bidders. This is an encouraging development, as it creates substantial new demand for a battery market that has slowed amid moderating growth in EV demand. For K-batteries to build on these policies and strengthen their position, however, they must increase their share of the rapidly expanding global ESS market. This presents both significant challenges and important opportunities. The fact that China has already established a strong lead in the ESS market is a challenge for Korea. The top four companies in the global ESS market in the first half of this year were all Chinese, and together, they accounted for nearly 55 percent of the market. Korean companies have also recorded strong year-on-year growth, but the gap in absolute volume with China remains substantial. Moreover, with global ESS supply capacity exceeding demand — 900 GWh against the actual demand of 612 GWh at the end of 2025 — price competition is intensifying. Competing with Chinese companies, which have maintained operating margins through economies of scale, can seem like an uphill battle. At the same time, several factors create opportunities. First, regional imbalances between battery supply and demand mean that key export markets for Korean companies are likely to face shortages. For example, battery supply in China is expected to exceed demand by about 90 percent in 2030, while Europe is projected to face a supply shortfall of 40 percent. North America is also expected to face a shortage from 2035. This presents an opportunity for Korean companies, which have established production bases in Europe and North America, to increase their market share. Second, in Europe, capacity for facilities combining renewable energy and batteries is expected to rise by more than 450 percent, from 6.3 GW in 2025 to around 35 GW in 2030. In parallel, the region is working to reduce its reliance on battery supply chains from any one country. For example, it is preparing an Industrial Accelerator Act that would encourage greater use of components and batteries manufactured within Europe when awarding public procurement contracts and subsidies. Korean battery companies are well positioned to benefit, as they already have a substantial manufacturing footprint in Europe. Third, the U.S. market is also opening up significant opportunities for Korean companies. ESS demand is growing rapidly as AI data centers proliferate, while U.S. policies to reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains are being strengthened. artigo.texto: SEATTLE — Amazon.com Inc. is pledging $1 billion or more over five years to communities where it builds and operates data centers. The company last week unveiled the “Built Together” investment framework for communities where the tech giant operates data centers across the United States. The increased investment will fund free community college for local residents, energy upgrades for homes and businesses, job training and protecting local water resources, the company said. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run,” Matt Garman, chief executive officer for Amazon Web Services, wrote in an October 2 post. “The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so.” Amazon is a leading player in the tech industry’s massive AI buildout that relies, in part, on finding communities willing to host data centers. Garman noted that there are more than 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the United States. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race,” he said, “and the consequences would last generations.” Added Garman, “There are clearly areas in which the technology and energy industries can be doing better (along with their government partners) but just like in the past when the country has banded together to accomplish something that’s critical for our national security and economic prosperity — we should approach this as a long-term mission that the private and public sectors pursue together.” Amazon said it is responding to apprehension over the data center buildout by codifying a series of tenets in what the company is calling its “Amazon Data Center Commitment.” The company commits to “protect and enhance communities,” “provide jobs and economic opportunities,” “engage communities,” and “build and operate responsibly.” Submit Your Press Release Have news to share? artigo.texto: Reduzir emissões para 'lucrar': Novas oportunidades no mercado de carbono. (CLO) Oficialmente operacional a partir do final de junho de 2026, a bolsa de carbono no Vietnã é considerada um passo significativo rumo a uma economia de baixas emissões. Embora o mercado ainda esteja em seus estágios iniciais, o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung, Diretor do Fundo de Investimento VinaCarbon, acredita que o Vietnã tem potencial suficiente para transformar a redução de emissões em uma fonte real de valor econômico, atraindo grandes fluxos de capital para os setores florestal, de energia limpa e agrícola. A bolsa de carbono no Vietnã iniciou oficialmente suas operações no final de junho de 2026. Até o momento, o número de produtos e transações no mercado permanece bastante limitado. No entanto, o potencial de desenvolvimento é considerado significativo, visto que o Vietnã está acelerando suas metas de redução de emissões, promovendo a transição para energias limpas e aprimorando gradualmente o arcabouço legal para o mercado de carbono. A respeito desse assunto, um repórter do jornal Jornalistas e Opinião Pública realizou uma entrevista particular com o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung, Diretor do Fundo de Investimento VinaCarbon, sobre as perspectivas do mercado de carbono no Vietnã. O mercado de carbono vietnamita apresenta muitas condições favoráveis para um forte crescimento. Senhor, o lançamento oficial da bolsa de carbono em junho de 2026 é considerado o ponto de partida para o mercado de carbono no Vietnã. Do ponto de vista de investimento, como o senhor vê as oportunidades e o potencial de crescimento desse mercado nos próximos anos? Pode-se afirmar que o mercado de carbono vietnamita possui muitas condições favoráveis para um forte desenvolvimento, especialmente considerando que o país se encontra em uma posição privilegiada graças à convergência de quatro fatores: demanda internacional, oferta natural, arcabouço legal e instituições internacionais dispostas a cooperar. A operação piloto da bolsa de carbono doméstica, apesar do número limitado de produtos e transações, representa um avanço significativo, pois estabelece as bases para um mercado transparente, caminhando rumo a uma economia de baixas emissões e cumprindo os compromissos climáticos do Vietnã. O potencial de crescimento do mercado de créditos de carbono do Vietnã decorre principalmente da demanda. No âmbito interno, a necessidade de reduzir as emissões e fazer a transição para energias limpas está sendo concretizada por meio de mecanismos de cotas, começando com indústrias de alta emissão, como energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento, e será estendida a mais setores no futuro. Globalmente , a tendência de tornar as cadeias de abastecimento mais ecológicas está ganhando força, com muitos novos requisitos para a redução das emissões. Do Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação (CORSIA), aos compromissos de emissões líquidas zero das empresas multinacionais, ao Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) da União Europeia, as empresas exportadoras estão sendo obrigadas a gerenciar suas emissões com mais rigor. Isso cria uma demanda significativa por créditos de carbono de alta qualidade e integridade no futuro. Para atender a essa demanda, o Vietnã possui fontes de suprimento potenciais em diversos setores, como agricultura , energia renovável, gestão de resíduos e, principalmente, silvicultura, onde existem vantagens claras e sustentáveis. O Vietnã possui uma vasta área florestal, com florestas plantadas representando uma proporção significativa, além de anos de experiência em gestão florestal e cadeias de valor de produtos florestais já estabelecidas. Além disso, o carbono florestal já possui seu próprio marco legal. Projetos de proteção, restauração e gestão sustentável de florestas podem gerar reduções substanciais de emissões e apoiar os meios de subsistência das comunidades, desde que existam mecanismos adequados de compartilhamento de benefícios. E como as florestas são um ativo de longo prazo, com ciclos de projetos que se estendem por décadas, o setor florestal também se adapta melhor à narrativa de desenvolvimento de médio e longo prazo do mercado. No entanto, ter oferta e demanda não é suficiente, pois um mercado só pode se desenvolver de forma sustentável quando possui a infraestrutura necessária. Em apenas um ano e meio, o Vietnã construiu praticamente toda a "estrutura" necessária para um mercado de carbono, desde um mecanismo doméstico de negociação de emissões, uma bolsa oficial, um sistema nacional de registro, até regulamentações para a transferência internacional de créditos e um decreto específico sobre carbono florestal. Além disso, o Vietnã também estabeleceu canais de cooperação bilateral com o Japão e Singapura. Em resumo, o Vietnã possui todas as condições necessárias para o crescimento do mercado de carbono nos próximos anos. No entanto, o ritmo desse desenvolvimento dependerá da completude do arcabouço legal e da infraestrutura de negociação, da qualidade e integridade dos créditos e da capacidade de atender aos padrões internacionais. Você também pode gostar + Na sua opinião, quais são as maiores dificuldades e desafios que impedem o desenvolvimento do mercado de créditos de carbono do Vietnã, em termos de oferta de crédito, qualidade do crédito, mecanismos de negociação e capacidade das empresas de participar? O maior desafio atualmente é a oferta limitada de créditos de carbono de alta qualidade. Gerar um crédito de carbono requer um processo relativamente longo e caro, desde o desenvolvimento e avaliação do projeto até o registro, o que geralmente dificulta o acesso para investidores. Além disso, os compradores de créditos de carbono estão cada vez mais exigentes em relação à qualidade. Critérios como complementaridade, risco de reversão e risco de dupla contagem estão recebendo maior atenção. Portanto, o mercado tenderá a priorizar créditos certificados por padrões reconhecidos.
