artigo.texto: Good morning. Andrew Nusca here, back in action after a week in New York for our inaugural AIQ Summit about putting AI to work in large companies. (Many thanks to Alexei Oreskovic for steering the ship while I was away.) Miss the AIQ festivities? No sweat—you can watch the entire thing here or view a session of your choosing here. If you’re in the business of deploying AI in the enterprise, there are lots of good insights to be had. And today’s tech news? Well, let’s get right to it. —Andrew Nusca Thoughts? Suggestions? Hot tip? Drop me a line. THE BIG STORY Meta is building one of the world’s biggest undersea cable networks While data centers dominate headlines amid mounting local opposition over electricity bills, water use, and zoning fights, Meta has been expanding its infrastructure somewhere far less visible: the bottom of the ocean. On Sept. 21, the company announced Petal, a roughly 4,300-mile subsea cable connecting the U.S. and France. Meta says the cable, expected to enter service in 2029, will be the first to deliver petabit-scale capacity across an ocean—double what today’s most advanced transoceanic cables can handle, thanks to “two-core fiber” that fits two light paths inside each strand. Projects like this rarely make headlines in an industry fixated on AI models and apps, but they’re what make those products run. Products like Meta’s personal AI agent Muse depend on moving enormous volumes of data between its data centers and its users around the world. Subsea cables aren’t new territory for Meta, which is now valued at roughly $1.85 trillion. The company has spent the past decade building its presence on the seafloor and says it has invested in more than 20 subsea cable projects. Taken together, those projects touch every continent except Antarctica. The most ambitious is Project Waterworth, announced in February 2025. Meta says the system will stretch more than 31,000 miles, longer than the Earth’s circumference. It will connect the U.S., Brazil, South Africa, India, and other regions across five continents. Meta hasn’t built all of this alone. Petal is being developed with Japan’s NEC and Sumitomo Electric Industries, and French telecom Orange is handling the landing on France’s Atlantic coast. Meta has even partnered with rivals: The MAREA cable between Virginia and Spain, completed in 2017, is jointly owned with Microsoft and telecom company Telxius. These projects don’t come cheap. TechCrunch estimates that the Waterworth project could top $10 billion. —James LaForge THE BLIND BOX “Just because you are using AI, that is not a proxy for your productivity or you doing a good job at work.” THE RUNDOWN —Trump forms “Super Intelligence Force” led by National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. —OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” —Meta's Muse compiles “a page for every person in the user's life,” per Wired. —Firmus IPO: Investor demand far exceeds the offer size, one of Australia's largest. —Schneider Electric may buy PTC, the U.S. engineering software firm, for $20 billion. —Apple CEO John Ternus is in the design studio “several times per week,” per Bloomberg. —McKinsey: AI and automation will eliminate 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 but add 41 million elsewhere. —U.K. neobank Monzo may sell a 15% stake to CVC and Advent after a Nubank deal fell apart. artigo.texto: Cygni Energy and Indus Towers will explore BESS manufacturing capacity of up to 1.5 GWh for telecom applications The companies will evaluate higher-capacity and emerging battery technologies for telecom infrastructure Cygni currently operates a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS facility in Hyderabad and plans to expand its overall capacity beyond 10 GWh Indian energy storage manufacturer Cygni Energy and telecom infrastructure company Indus Towers have joined hands to explore up to 1.5 GWh of battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing in India to serve telecom infrastructure. The duo has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) and plans to establish manufacturing capacity to meet the ‘evolving energy requirements’ of telecom infrastructure in India. The partnership will also evaluate advanced battery technologies for telecom applications. Formed by the merger of Bharti Infratel Limited and Indus Towers, Indus Towers Limited had over 267,611 towers and 432,250 co-locations as of June 30, 2026. It is present across 22 telecom circles. While Cygni's official statement does not reveal details about the MoU, telecom companies have been exploring energy storage as a backup power strategy to improve operational efficiency. According to Battery Council International (BCI), batteries can help provide stable power for data centers and telecom systems. Incubated at IIT Madras, Cygni Energy develops energy storage products for telecom, stationary energy storage, mobility, and other applications. Its battery portfolio currently includes 100 Ah solutions and could expand to higher-capacity systems, including 314 Ah. “We plan to develop capacity of up to 2 GWh, while building a portfolio that can evolve from today’s 100Ah solutions to higher-capacity 314Ah systems and emerging battery technologies,” said Cygni Energy Founder & CEO Venkat Rajaraman. In 2025, Cygni Energy opened a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS Gigafactory in Hyderabad’s Maheshwaram, with plans to scale it up to exceed 10 GWh in the future. “Our ambition is to combine scale, reliability and Indian engineering to create future-ready energy storage solutions that can evolve alongside India’s rapidly expanding digital infrastructure,” added Rajaraman. According to Crisil, India could see up to 50 GWh of BESS installations by FY2028 as the technology helps improve power availability during peak demand. However, reducing reliance on overseas suppliers remains important to limit exposure to global supply disruptions and procurement uncertainties (see Crisil Projects India To Add 50 GWh BESS Capacity By FY2028).

artigo.texto: Frederico prevê regulamentação do Redata até o fim do ano Ministro das Comunicações diz que pendência está concentrada na questão energética e diverge da estimativa de seis meses apresentada pelo governo paulista O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, afirmou nesta terça-feira, 6, que o governo trabalha para concluir até o fim de 2026 a regulamentação do Redata, regime tributário destinado aos investimentos em data centers. A declaração foi dada a jornalistas durante a Futurecom 2026, em São Paulo, após o vice-governador paulista estimar que o processo poderia levar aproximadamente seis meses. Segundo Frederico, a etapa considerada mais difícil — a aprovação do regime pelo Congresso — já foi superada. Agora, disse, restam questões de regulamentação. “A questão da regulamentação agora são ajustes finos”, afirmou. Segundo ele, “com relação à infraestrutura digital está resolvido” e permanece em discussão a questão energética. “A expectativa é que sim, a gente consiga resolver até o final do ano.” A declaração estabelece uma diferença de expectativa entre o governo federal e o paulista sobre o calendário necessário para que o regime possa produzir efeitos sobre novos investimentos. São Paulo trabalha com prazo maior Pouco antes, o vice-governador de São Paulo havia afirmado que a regulamentação poderia levar cerca de seis meses e associado a conclusão desse processo ao avanço da discussão estadual sobre ICMS. No discurso de abertura, ele disse que São Paulo pretende acompanhar a regulamentação federal para posteriormente adequar a legislação estadual, “principalmente em tópicos do ICMS”. Questionado pelos jornalistas sobre essa diferença de calendário, Frederico sustentou a possibilidade de concluir o processo ainda em 2026. O ministro não anunciou, entretanto, uma data para publicação dos atos nem detalhou quais instrumentos normativos ainda serão necessários. Também questionado sobre a possibilidade de os efeitos do Redata perderem relevância diante da entrada em vigor de etapas da reforma tributária, Frederico afirmou que o governo está concentrado no efeito econômico final para os investidores. “O que vale no final do dia é qual é o benefício que toda essa solução vai trazer ao investidor. Se vai ser o Redata ou se vai ser reforma tributária, o importante é a gente discutir o benefício”, disse. Governo discute regulamentação entre ministérios Frederico afirmou que o Ministério das Comunicações mantém discussões com outras áreas do governo, citando Minas e Energia, Casa Civil e outros ministérios envolvidos no tema. Questionado se algum projeto poderia utilizar os benefícios ainda em 2026, respondeu que o governo trabalha para acelerar as definições no período posterior às eleições. A regulamentação também apareceu no discurso oficial do ministro na abertura da Futurecom. Na ocasião, Frederico afirmou que o governo trabalha para dar previsibilidade ao setor produtivo e evitar a perda de investimentos. O Redata também foi citado pelo vice-governador paulista e pelo deputado federal e ex-ministro das Comunicações Juscelino Filho durante o evento, indicando convergência entre União, governo estadual e Congresso quanto à utilização do regime como instrumento de atração de data centers. A diferença está, neste momento, no calendário e nas etapas complementares necessárias para que os incentivos sejam operacionalizados. ICMS será próxima frente O ICMS aparece como uma dessas etapas. Como o tributo é estadual, sua eventual redução depende de decisões dos estados e das regras aplicáveis à tributação estadual. O governo paulista afirmou que pretende atuar nessa frente, mas depois de conhecer a regulamentação federal. Além da tributação, autoridades presentes à Futurecom relacionaram a expansão dos data centers à disponibilidade de energia, redes de fibra óptica, cabos submarinos e infraestrutura de conectividade. Frederico afirmou que data centers dependem de uma rede capaz de transportar os dados processados e armazenados. Essa combinação entre incentivos tributários, energia e telecomunicações deverá determinar a capacidade do Redata de efetivamente destravar novos projetos.

artigo.texto: Just outside Toledo, Ohio, Meta is building an $800 million data center campus. Annually, the data center will use only as much water as two full-service restaurants using a technology known as a closed-loop system. The Great Lakes region offers an unmatched set of resources ripe for data center development, including an abundance of fresh water for cooling; longer, colder winters than the South or Sunbelt; and former industrial lands ready for redevelopment. But in Illinois, a polarizing data center debate has heated up in recent weeks. I agree with Gov. JB Pritzker’s recent statement at New York’s America is All in Conference. When asked whether we should be welcoming data centers into Illinois, he said that we need to ensure that data centers are bringing their own energy, and they are using their own closed-loop water systems. There are still very valid public concerns about letting these data centers develop projects untethered to government accountability. I hear them weekly on the campaign trail from Chicagoans who voice concern that we could damage Lake Michigan by exploiting its resources too heavily and that our electricity bills could skyrocket. I have two solutions for those main two concerns. Regarding the first concern — water usage — many Chicagoans I speak with hear “data center” and picture a server farm drinking up the lake. My vision is to build a massive geothermal heat sink coil system in Lake Michigan. This system is closed loop and filled with liquid coolant. This loop would be miles, perhaps tens or hundreds of miles, long and coiled far offshore at or near the bottom of the lake (the deeper, the better, as it’s colder). This system would consume water over time, thus taking a data center’s water consumption to virtually zero. The second concern I have heard is that with this new architecture, we would cook the lake. But Lake Michigan holds about a quadrillion gallons of water, so adding data centers is like setting a sealed coffee thermos in a swimming pool — it wouldn’t change. From a thermodynamics perspective, even with miles of coils and loops constantly cooling themselves in Lake Michigan, we likely could not even marginally increase the temperature or create an environmentally noticeable impact. But “it’s fine, trust me” is not good enough for a lake this city drinks from, so I propose a water and environmental study before a single pipe goes in, with the results and data published where anyone can read it. On top of closed-loop infrastructure at the bottom of the lake, data centers should have windows. It may sound basic, but right now, data center construction typically creates hard cases of primarily concrete with no ability to leverage the outside cold air. They are basically heat-trapping boxes, and, as we now know, they produce a massive amount of heat. When a house is hot, open the windows. When a data center is hot, open the windows. Chicago’s cooler fall, chilling winter and brisk spring climates all lend themselves to a basic idea of circulating cold air into the data center itself and hot air out. With windows open, they essentially have natural air conditioning three-quarters of the year. The marginal cost to put in windows and natural cooling systems in northern and colder climates such as Chicago far outweighs the risk of continuing to use billions of gallons of water and energy to sustain these operations. The potential savings are not marginal; they are massive. Cornell University has cooled its campus from a Finger Lake for 25 years and reports saving roughly 85% of the energy conventional refrigeration would burn. Toronto has cooled more than a hundred downtown buildings with Lake Ontario since 2004, saving about 90,000 megawatt hours a year, enough to power a town of 25,000 people. Its system is nearly full, and it is spending $100 million to expand it. A massive, closed-loop coil system in Lake Michigan could cool much more than data centers; it could provide air conditioning and cooling for hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of households and buildings across the city as climate change increases the overall temperature throughout the year. None of this is theoretical anymore because the demand is already here. Chicago’s data center vacancy rate is under 2%. There is not a single block of 5 megawatts or more available to lease anywhere in this market, and developers asking ComEd to connect new projects are being told 2032 and beyond, which is why they are now buying land based on where the power is rather than where they want to be. The real question is whether we shape our response or let it shape us. We are constantly told we have to pick. Jobs or the lake. Investment or affordable power bills. The artificial intelligence economy or the environment. I have never accepted that framing, and my entire plan for Chicago when I am mayor argues against it. This is not a “this or that.” It is both creating more jobs while protecting the lake and environment. Chicago has an answer, and it is sitting a few miles off Michigan Avenue at the bottom of the lake. Joe Holberg is a Chicago mayoral candidate. He was a math teacher on the West Side, then a small business owner and entrepreneur helping Chicagoans work toward financial goals. artigo.texto: Developers have legitimate business interests to protect. Minnesotans deserve a meaningful say in projects that could reshape their communities. In my hometown of Inver Grove Heights, a proposed data center has generated intense public debate. City Council meetings have been packed with concerned residents who feel left out of the process, and the city enacted a one-year moratorium before ultimately exempting the proposed project amid litigation. The tension is only increasing across Minnesota, and now we are throwing secrecy into the mix. Across our state, data-center developers and tech companies have asked local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements. In Pine Island, discussions surrounding the development now known as “Project Skyway,” which involves Google, began in late 2023. Residents were not let in on those discussions until September 2025, only months before city approval, leaving little time for public input on this major project. In Hermantown, an NDA prevented city officials from sharing information about Google’s proposed 1.8-million-square-foot data center until a Data Practices Act request finally brought the information to light. To be clear, businesses have legitimate reasons to seek confidentiality, but within reason. Revealing the identity of a prospective developer can fuel land speculation. And businesses considering multiple sites understandably do not want competitors learning every detail of their plans, but that still leaves a question: Why have NDAs become so prevalent in data-center development? “There should be 100% transparency with the public,” said Rep. Drew Roach (R-Farmington), co-author of HF 4077. Both Republican and DFL lawmakers have backed measures aimed at limiting their use. Interestingly, Minnesota law already protects legitimate business secrets. Under the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, Minn. Stat. § 13.37, legitimate trade-secret information held by the government is already protected from public disclosure. The real problem here is that these NDAs go much further. They tend to prevent members of the community from participating in decisions about massive projects coming into their own neighborhoods until the process is already almost wrapped up. Whether that is the intention or not, it sure looks that way to the people being stonewalled. Developers may think these NDAs are helping them get projects built. But the secrecy may actually be doing the opposite, turning communities against them. That is never a good idea here in Minnesota. Imagine discovering that your local government had been discussing a big, intrusive development planned for your backyard for years, and officials agreed not to tell you about it until the process was already nearing the final signature. Even people who support data centers have to wonder: Why all the secrecy? What else are they hiding? It’s not a good look, and it is costing these developers what little support they may have had. Secrecy creates suspicion. Suspicion creates questions. Leave those questions unanswered long enough, and you may be surprised by how hard the people of the North Star State will push back. Some Minnesota lawmakers have gotten the message. HF 4077 would restrict local governments from signing NDAs that keep information about these development projects from the public. Of course, information already protected by state or federal law would remain protected. The bill has bipartisan authors, although some lawmakers remain hesitant about the extent of these restrictions. It’s a tough spot for lawmakers. They have to find a way to keep communities from being shut out of monumental decisions while also respecting free enterprise and rightful business interests. As tempting as it may be to target data centers, the same transparency rules should apply to every industry. They must protect developers from government overreach, and they must protect the people of these communities from being kept in the dark. The debate over where that balance should be drawn is just getting started. I am not calling for our state to be especially hostile toward data centers, but I understand why that hostility is growing. If developers believe in these projects, why hide the details? We have simple questions: How will they affect our water supply? What about our power grid? How much noise will they create? Too often, we aren’t getting answers. We as Minnesotans welcome entrepreneurship, but we also demand the opportunity to judge these projects on their merits. Transparency is all we are really asking for. AJ Gubash is a Minnesota legal professional working in nonprofit public-interest law, a graduate legal studies student at Hamline University, and a candidate for the Minnesota House of Representatives.

artigo.texto: Scale Microgrids, the corporation behind Nodaway County’s proposed data center project, is partnering with another company to operate the facility, though that end user is not yet known. While the Nodaway County Commission said the company is close to announcing the details of the partnership, not everyone is so sure this is true. Missouri allows data center developers in the state to receive tax exemptions on their facilities. Scott Wilson is an independent candidate running for Nodaway County presiding commissioner this November. He said he feels like Scale Microgrids is waiting for the commission to give the company a tax abatement before the public receives more information. Last week, Wilson took these concerns to a Nodaway Says No informational meeting in Graham, Missouri, which saw around 100 attendees. He said he feels apprehensive about how a hyperscale data center could affect environmental safety and the local ecosystem. “There’s a lot of different ways that people talk about it, and a lot of the people, the citizens, have had to try to prove to the commissioners that the things that are being said are actually true, and I don’t know that that’s a 100% fair way to do it,” Wilson said. “It would seem more like that data center developer and the commissioners would have to prove to the citizens that it is safe, not the citizens having to prove to them that it’s not safe.” He said he has heard many people talk about the impact data centers have on livestock due to the sound pollution it causes. Particularly, he heard it can reduce reproduction and increase stillbirths in cattle populations. Cows are not the only animals at risk. Horses, sheep — and even insects — are sensitive to sound. “They’ve talked about the bees, and they communicate with sound, and they can’t hear this,” Wilson said. “Someone mentioned just the other day, it’s like being at a loud party, and they can’t figure out what’s going on, so they can’t even get back to their hives, and it could drive the wildlife out of that area,” Wilson said. Nodaway County, he said, has a lot of land that is tilled up and farmed. He said adding a data center into such an agriculture region feels invasive — both to people and animals. “They talk about a heat dome…I think someone said it could raise the temperature within six miles of 16 degrees, like, average four to 16 degrees, just because of the massive amounts of concrete and all the cooling systems,” Wilson said. Another major concern for many residents is water. Scale Microgrids will need at least 1.5 million gallons of water to operate its facility, but not all residents see how it is feasible. “Of course, the river, if they suck too much water, they’re going to run the river lower than it already is at times,” Wilson said. The water Scale Microgrids uses would routinely filter through the 102 River every three years. However, many data centers add synthetic compounds — known as forever chemicals — into their water supplies. These can take hundreds or thousands of years to break down, and they are harmful to the ecosystem, according to the World Economic Forum. The Missourian reached out to the Nodaway County Public Water Supply District No. 1, which would supply water to the data center, and received a message in response. “When the project particulars are agreed to by all entities public and private maybe we could give a story with background on the whole thing,” the message said. “However since the district is in the middle of contract negotiations with suppliers and customers, we really say can’t speak to much.” Along with water stress and rising temperatures, emitted light from the facility can also be an issue, as it can disturb humans and confuse animals. People living within a half-mile of Scale Microgrids’ project, called White Cloud Acres, may be most heavily affected by the light. “They say that the critters need to have time at night to where they know it’s night and day, and if the lights are on all the time, it bothers them, but some of this can be mitigated,” Wilson said. “They can have different dimming type of lights or different ways to help all these problems along the way, but again, all that costs more for the developer, and it makes the return on investment less, but that really shouldn’t be our problem.” He said officials at hand should strive to make the best decision possible regardless of money. “I believe that the commissioners should strive to make this as safe as possible, and it doesn’t really matter what the developer’s return on investment is,” Wilson said. “If it doesn’t work out for them, it just doesn’t work out.”

artigo.texto: [Photo: MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND CLIMATE CHANGE/ FACEBOOK] Fiji has launched a five-year $5.2 million plan aimed at preparing the country to enter international carbon markets by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan was launched yesterday during the opening of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan sets out the regulatory, technical and institutional systems Fiji needs before its first international carbon trade under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. It focuses on sectors including energy, transport, agriculture, waste and forestry, with strong emphasis on forests, mangroves, wetlands and other nature-based solutions. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu says carbon markets must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners.” The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre, with provisions for fair benefit-sharing, social and environmental safeguards and Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Fiji will also establish a Fijian Transactional Registry and a National Carbon Market Inter-Agency Technical Working Group to manage and track carbon market activities. The Government will use the plan to engage development partners, donors and potential carbon buyers to secure the finance and technical support needed for implementation. Conservation International says the plan could help Fiji attract high-integrity carbon finance while protecting ecosystems and supporting resilient livelihoods.

artigo.texto: Tighter data center rules on Fort Smith Board agenda The Fort Smith Board of Directors is set to vote Tuesday (Oct. 6) on an ordinance that would give the city more oversight of any planned data center development within the city. The ordinance, if approved, also would require more information from utilities about energy availability and potential energy load. Board members on Aug. 11 asked city staff to craft new rules or amend existing rules around water use, zoning and other areas to discourage data center construction in the city and the metro. According to the city, there are no known data centers being considered in the Fort Smith metro. Tim Allen, president and CEO of the Fort Smith Regional Chamber of Commerce, said chamber staff are ânot actively working a data center project.â There are five large announced data center projects in the state. The facilities are either planned or in some stage of construction in Clarksville, Conway, Little Rock, Pulaski County, and West Memphis. The proposed ordinance the board will consider Tuesday would require a development plan review by the Planning Commission and then full board approval of a data center project in the cityâs industrial zoning districts. The ordinance also would require an eight-foot opaque wall surrounding the property, 500 feet setbacks from each property line, and âletters from applicable public utilities regarding capacity and proposed load.â The cityâs Planning Commission voted unanimously for the proposed ordinance, according to a memo from Deputy City Administrator Maggie Rice. The ordinance does not include any language about water rates and access to the cityâs regional water system. At the Aug. 11 board study session, Director Kevin Settle suggested the city consider significantly higher water rates for data centers. Settle also said he would support language that gives the board authority over certain water connections outside city limits. âTo me, the water, Iâve said many times, is our commodity, and we should be able to choose what is the price for it,â Settle said at the Aug. 11 meeting. BACKGROUND Arkansas officials, with support from Gov. Sarah Sanders, have restricted local government actions on data centers. Arkansas Act 851 of 2023 prevents local governments from banning data center development. The law does not prevent local governments from adopting rules that create delays or significant restrictions with data center projects. The cities of Fayetteville and Little Rock have approved more stringent data center development rules. The development of data centers nationwide and in Arkansas has become controversial, with pushback often resulting from local grassroots efforts. Concerns include the potential for massive water use, rising utility rates, excessive noise, and groundwater pollution. The state of New York recently implemented a one-year moratorium on data center construction. According to reporting from CNBC and other outlets, more than 500 local governments nationwide have enacted bans, moratoriums, and other restrictions on data centers. âData centers sit at the intersection of economic development, energy policy and state fiscal health,â according to a report from the National Conference of State Legislatures. âWhile 38 states currently offer dedicated tax incentives to attract data centers, lawmakers across the country are working to balance economic development priorities with sustainable development goals. These capital-intensive projects can generate significant tax revenue for localities, yet data centers also contribute to surging energy demand across the country.â

artigo.texto: Battery Energy Storage Trends: Shorter PPAs and Market Growth ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: Battery energy storage developers are pushing for shorter PPA tenures, while the MNRE updated ALMM List-II to 37,394 MW and Chhattisgarh approved a ₹2.98/kWh tariff for a 125 MW/500 MWh BESS project. - Why it matters: Shorter, more flexible PPAs are essential for the bankability of BESS projects, which currently face rigid 20-25 year contract structures similar to solar and wind. - Watch: Further regulatory shifts regarding transmission charges for open access customers and the progress of upcoming pumped hydro and solar tenders. Background and Context The Indian energy storage market is undergoing a significant evolution as stakeholders call for more flexible contractual frameworks. While solar and wind projects have traditionally relied on 20-25-year Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), battery energy storage developers are increasingly advocating for shorter tenures to better align with the operational lifecycle of battery technology. This shift is critical as the country integrates larger volumes of variable renewable energy into the grid. Key Details Regulatory activity remains high across the sector. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) has revised its standardized nomenclature for solar cells under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II. The 11th revision has expanded the total enlisted capacity to 37,394 MW, mandating that module model numbers clearly identify the country of origin for both cells and modules. In the storage segment, the Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission (CSERC) has set a benchmark by adopting a tariff of ₹2.98 (~$0.031)/kWh for a 125 MW/500 MWh standalone battery energy storage system. Meanwhile, in Karnataka, Sumitomo Corporation has committed to investing in a 500 MW solar and wind project with a co-located 200 MWh BESS, being developed by Hero Future Energies in Bidar. Other notable developments include the rejection of MP Power Transmission Company’s petition on transmission charges by the Madhya Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission, and NTPC Renewable Energy’s call for bids for interstate transmission system-connected pumped hydro projects. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the push for flexible PPAs signals a maturing market where risk-sharing is becoming more sophisticated. The standardization of ALMM nomenclature provides greater transparency in the supply chain, which is vital for procurement planning. Furthermore, the adoption of competitive tariffs for BESS projects suggests that storage is becoming increasingly cost-competitive, opening new avenues for large-scale infrastructure projects. What Happens Next The industry is closely watching the outcome of the NTPC Renewable Energy pumped hydro tender, with bids due by November 3, 2026. As the India renewable energy sector continues to scale, the interplay between regulatory policy, such as the ALMM updates, and commercial innovations in PPA structures will define the next phase of growth for developers and EPC firms alike.

artigo.texto: Director-General, National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi, has called for a stronger carb on verification to enhance the credibility and integrity of Nigeria’s carbon market. Majekodunmi, who was represented by Mr Michael Ivenso, Director, Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, NCCC, made the call at an NCCC/European Union Climate Dialogues High-Level Roundtable on carbon markets in Abuja on Tuesday. Majekodunmi said Nigeria must turn its climate ambition into tangible, bankable and verifiable action to support sustainable economic growth and attract climate finance. She said Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework had established the institutional and regulatory architecture required to govern carbon activities, including Article 6 cooperation, voluntary markets and national oversight. She said the NCCC was operationalising a unified national carbon registry while promoting digital Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) through remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to enhance accuracy. The director-general called for stronger collaboration among government agencies, private developers, financial institutions, development partners, civil society and academia to establish bankable projects and strengthen local verification capacity. Majekodunmi said priorities included finalising carbon market regulations, publishing sector-specific MRV guidelines and establishing local capacity-building hubs to position Nigeria as a destination for high-integrity carbon investments. Jop Weterings, Policy Professional and Team member at the DG CLIMA’s Task Force on International Carbon Pricing and Markets, European Commission, said the EU adopted legally binding target to cut emissions 40 per cent by 2040. Weterings said the target includes at least 85 per cent domestic reductions and up to five per cent high-quality international carbon credits under Article 6, from 2036. He said quality, transparency and robust accounting were essential to scaling carbon markets, and urged stronger methodologies, fair transactions, equitable benefit-sharing and national strategies protecting domestic climate priorities. Weterings said that EU support for carbon pricing and international markets was increasing, while cooperation with Nigeria offered opportunities to operationalise its framework and strengthen high-integrity markets. Mrs Halima Bawa-Bwari, Director of Forestry, Ministry of Environment, urged Nigeria to strengthen forest inventories, monitoring systems, remote sensing, satellite technology and artificial intelligence for carbon monitoring. Bawa-Bwari said satellite information should complement ground measurements and field verification, while forestry institutions require stronger capacity to collect, manage and utilise reliable data for carbon markets. She called for coordinated, transparent and independently verifiable forest-carbon data, warning against parallel systems and stressing clear responsibilities, accountability, technical credibility and stakeholder partnership for high-integrity markets. Ms Yolanda Jose, Head, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, said that credible carbon markets require robust systems ensuring transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. Jose said Nigeria’s adoption of its National Carbon Markets Framework established a structured legal and institutional sytem for domestic and international carbon trading under relevant climate agreements. She said the EU Climate Dialogues roundtable would align on operationalising Nigeria’s framework, strengthen MRV practices, mobilise investment and support Nigeria’s low-carbon development pathway. Mr Huzi Mshelia, Country Facilitator, Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) partnership said robust MRV systems were essential for building trust and investor confidence, welcoming the dialogue’s convergence of stakeholders to establish common national standards and understanding. He stressed partnership among NCCC, Finance, Budget and National Planning institutions, ensuring climate actions align with development priorities, while technical support strengthens Nigeria’s MRV system globally.

artigo.texto: The e SKY, Suzuki’s first electric kei car, is expected to undercut BYD’s Racco as Japan’s cheapest mini EV, starting at around $13,500. Suzuki launches its first mini EV using BYD batteries Suzuki is entering Japan’s competitive electric mini car segment with the e SKY set to launch on November 16. The e SKY will start at around 2.12 million yen, or about $13,500, according to Nikkei, making it the lowest-priced EV in its class. BYD currently holds the title with the Racco EV priced from 2.145 million yen ($13,600). Suzuki said the e SKY offers a WLTC driving range of up to 310 km (192 miles) and a “class-leading” AC energy consumption rating of 97 Wh/km. Suzuki developed a dedicated kei EV platform and electric drive system for the e SKY to optimize efficiency. Interestingly, Suzuki’s mini EV uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries supplied by BYD’s battery unit to cut costs. Government subsidies have yet to be announced, but if it qualifies for the same 568,000 yen subsidy as its commercial kei EV, the e-Every, the e SKY would cost about the same as the Spacia. The Spacia is Suzuki’s most popular gas-powered kei car. It starts at 1.53 million yen, or slightly under $10,000 in Japan. BYD’s cheapest Racco 200 model uses a 22.4 kWh LFP battery, providing a WLTC driving range of 210 km (130 miles). High-priced trims, including the Racco 300 Plus and Premium models, use a larger 35.84 kWh battery with a range of up to 320 km (199 miles). BYD said it was the first kei EV to offer over 300 km range. BYD’s Racco and the Suzuki e SKY will be more affordable and offer a longer driving range than the Nissan Sakura, which starts at ¥2,448,600 ($15,000). BYD aims to sell 10,000 Racco models by the end of 2026. In its first two weeks on the market, BYD’s mini EV secured 1,000 orders. On Monday, BYD Japan also celebrated reaching 10,000 domestic cumulative registrations.

artigo.texto: Dear editor, “No Data Center” signs proliferate in Monticello and Wright County, and for good reason. That is worth considering alongside the legitimate questions Minnesotans are raising about data centers. When you vote, consider whether Emmer’s position on data centers reflects your priorities and concerns. Emmer’s opponent, Doug Chapin, confirmed that he is not taking crypto or data center lobby money. By the end of this election cycle, Chapin’s campaign says he will have held 20 or more in-person town halls. Emmer’s last documented in-person town hall was in August 2023. Chapin is visible in his district and listening to the people he hopes to represent. Tom Grue Monticello

artigo.texto: ROX Capital Launches Gulf Energy Storage Platform ROX Capital has launched a platform to develop utility-scale and commercial energy storage projects in Gulf. October 06, 2026. By EI News Network ROX Capital Group has launched the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform to develop utility-scale and commercial energy storage projects in the UAE and Oman, as the Gulf region expands its large-scale solar capacity. The UAE-based real assets investor and developer said that the platform will assess multiple energy storage technologies, including vanadium redox flow batteries, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and sodium-ion batteries. It will also evaluate long-duration energy storage technologies such as CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage. ROX said that it will partner with selected technology providers based on their track record in deploying large-scale storage projects, expertise in long-duration energy storage, financial and operational capabilities, and ownership or control of core technology intellectual property. The platform will prioritise technology providers offering bankable systems, established manufacturing capabilities, long-term technical support, performance guarantees and warranties, according to the company. ROX and its technology partners will participate in upcoming energy storage tenders in the UAE and Oman. The platform will also examine opportunities for local assembly and manufacturing in the region where commercially viable. Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group, said the Gulf’s growing deployment of large-scale solar projects was increasing the need for energy storage to make renewable power available after sunset and during periods of peak electricity demand. Antony said that no single storage technology would be able to address all energy storage requirements in the region. The platform will therefore seek to match different technologies with the specific requirements of individual projects while also exploring opportunities for local manufacturing. ROX said that lithium-ion batteries will remain an important part of the Gulf’s energy storage mix, but regional conditions could create demand for a wider range of technologies. High summer temperatures in the Gulf can increase cooling requirements for battery systems, while power systems with a high share of solar generation require longer-duration storage to supply electricity after sunset. Against this backdrop, ROX said that technologies including vanadium flow batteries, CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage and thermal storage could complement lithium-ion systems in the Gulf market. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Voters in eight states have faced, or are soon to face, local ballot measures over data center development, as the infrastructure powering AI becomes an increasingly important issue in the midterm elections. According to the latest Ballotpedia count, at least 39 measures have been scheduled across California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin. Of those, 35 will be decided during the November 3 general election, while four were put to voters earlier in the year. The proposals range from outright bans on new data centers to advisory questions supporting the development. Others would require voter approval, introduce zoning protections or place conditions on companies receiving tax incentives. Data centers have become a major midterm issue because of concerns about their demands on electric grids, water supplies and land, as well as questions about tax breaks and whether residential customers could be left paying for infrastructure upgrades. At the same time, supporters argue that the facilities are essential to America’s AI ambitions and can generate construction work, investment and local tax revenue. The debate is affecting midterm races, even when data centers don’t appear directly on the ballot. Candidates are increasingly being judged on whether they do or don’t support tax incentives or projects, or whether they have or haven't called for restrictions and greater protections for ratepayers. In Ohio, for example, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has sought to make Republican Senator Jon Husted's role in the growth of the state's data center industry a central campaign issue, arguing that Husted was a leading advocate for the projects during his time as lieutenant governor. Brown told the Statehouse News Bureau in August: "I've made clear from the beginning that Jon Husted is the point man for these 230 or 240 new data centers in Ohio," labeling him “the face of data centers in Ohio.” During his time in office, Husted did publicly celebrate projects from technology companies including Google and Amazon Web Services, arguing that they would help establish Ohio as the "tech capital of the Midwest" and strengthen the state's role in the AI economy. More recently, however, Husted has emphasized consumer protections around data center growth, introducing the Ratepayer Protection Act, which seeks to ensure large electricity users such as data centers pay for the infrastructure needed to serve them rather than shifting costs onto households and small businesses. That evolution is reflected in Newsweek's AI Policy Scorecard, an interactive tool that evaluates where members of Congress stand on AI-related issues including regulation, data centers and energy, jobs and the economy, safety and privacy, and national security. Lawmakers are ranked from "AI Skeptic" to "AI Booster" based on their voting records, legislation, and public statements. While Brown continues to focus on Husted's previous support for bringing data centers to Ohio, the scorecard currently categorizes Husted as a "Lean Skeptic" on data centers and energy, indicating a more cautious approach to large-scale expansion and its impact on communities and utility customers than lawmakers classified as "boosters." Here are all 39 measures tracked by Ballotpedia, including the 35 scheduled for November and four decided earlier in 2026. California Voters in Alhambra will settle on a measure that would prohibit data centers within the city. It’s one of the most straightforward measures on the November ballot, as it simply asks residents whether the facilities should be banned rather than regulated through additional conditions. A second California measure has already been decided. In June, 88 percent of voters in Monterey Park supported a policy that amended the city’s land-use framework to prohibit data centers. Florida In Edgewater, voters will consider an amendment prohibiting new data centers from being approved, built, expanded, or operated within the city. The measure goes beyond preventing new projects by also addressing the expansion and operation of data center facilities, giving voters a broader choice over how they want the industry to operate within the community going forward. Illinois Seven measures are being put before Illinois voters, although several are advisory and would communicate residents’ preferences rather than automatically changing local law. In Bloomington, voters will determine whether to advise the city to impose a moratorium on the construction of large-scale data centers. Four measures are concentrated in Madison County. Voters in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki, and Venice will be asked whether officials should permit the construction and operation of new data centers. In Joliet, in Will County, voters will consider an advisory question asking whether the city should approve the construction of AI data centers. Meanwhile, voters in Morgan County will decide whether to advise county officials to impose restrictions on the construction and operation of data centers. Together, the Illinois measures show that not every data center vote is designed to block development: Five ask whether officials should support or permit projects, while two seek a moratorium or additional restrictions. Kansas Three Kansas cities will vote on proposed data center prohibitions. In El Dorado, an initiative would prohibit the construction of “high-impact” data centers, as well as certain Type 2 and Type 3 battery energy storage systems. Voters in Emporia will also consider a measure prohibiting the construction of high-impact data centers within the city. In Ottawa, the proposed ban is tied to electricity consumption. It would prohibit data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power, a threshold also used by several measures in Ohio. (NASDAQ:CSIQ) said its energy storage subsidiary, e-STORAGE, has signed an agreement to supply and commission a 100 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system for OX2's Muswellbrook Solar Farm and Battery project in New South Wales, Australia. The agreement also includes a 20-year long-term service arrangement covering hardware, software and system performance. Project Located at Former Coal Mine Site The Muswellbrook project is located approximately 2.5 kilometres east of Muswellbrook on land at a former coal mine within the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. Once operational, the battery system will support a long-term hybrid power purchase agreement that OX2 has signed for the project. "Australia's energy transition is being decided in regions like the Hunter, where storage now has to carry the load that retiring coal once did. artigo.texto: A WEG prepara uma expansão industrial de US$ 165 milhões na América do Norte, com novas estruturas no México e nos Estados Unidos e uma meta de multiplicar por cinco sua capacidade global de geradores até 2030. A brasileira WEG anunciou um plano de investimento de US$ 165 milhões, aproximadamente R$ 840 milhões pela conversão divulgada pela própria companhia, para ampliar a fabricação de geradores na América do Norte. O projeto será executado em duas fases e pretende elevar a capacidade global da empresa dos atuais 10 para cerca de 50 geradores por dia, avanço relacionado ao aumento da demanda por infraestrutura crítica nos Estados Unidos, especialmente para data centers. Anunciada em 28 de setembro de 2026, a expansão combina uma nova operação no México e a construção de outras duas instalações industriais na América do Norte. A primeira etapa deverá entrar em operação já no segundo trimestre de 2027, enquanto a segunda está prevista para ser concluída até 2030. - Gigante chinesa prepara fábrica de R$ 200 milhões em Minas Gerais para dobrar produção de cabos ópticos - Brasil pode perder empregos e valor da sucata porque Repetro facilita operação de plataformas, mas deixa desmantelamento e reciclagem fora da mesma lógica tributária - Fábrica de semicondutores no RS recebe R$ 84,86 milhões para produzir memórias avançadas usadas em smartphones e inteligência artificial - Após 64 anos no Rio, Limppano investe R$ 50 milhões para ampliar fábrica, comprar novas áreas e modernizar produção O investimento ocorre enquanto grandes centros de processamento de dados ampliam a demanda por equipamentos capazes de sustentar operações que não podem ficar sem eletricidade. No caso da WEG, os geradores são destinados a aplicações críticas e podem integrar sistemas de energia de emergência e continuidade de fornecimento. O próprio presidente da companhia, Alberto Kuba, relacionou recentemente o movimento à aceleração desse mercado. Em entrevista à Exame, o executivo afirmou que a empresa “não imaginávamos que teria esse boom”, ao comentar o ritmo da demanda associada aos data centers. México receberá primeira etapa da expansão A expansão começará no México. Dos US$ 165 milhões previstos, US$ 24 milhões serão destinados à compra e adaptação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual Parque Industrial de Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula. A nova estrutura será voltada à montagem de geradores e deverá começar a operar no segundo trimestre de 2027. A escolha do local aproveita uma presença industrial que a WEG já mantém no município mexicano. Em janeiro de 2025, a companhia havia inaugurado a ampliação de uma fábrica de produtos de automação em Atotonilco de Tula, com aproximadamente 4,9 mil metros quadrados de área construída. A estrutura passou a concentrar atividades de produção, engenharia, projetos de painéis e treinamento. Segunda fase concentra US$ 141 milhões No novo projeto de geradores, porém, a maior parte dos recursos ficará para a segunda fase. A WEG prevê desembolsar US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais em território norte-americano. Até o anúncio, a empresa ainda não havia definido publicamente onde essas duas unidades serão construídas. Essa segunda etapa terá uma configuração mais verticalizada. Em vez de concentrar a operação apenas na montagem, as novas fábricas deverão incorporar processos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças. Segundo a WEG, a internalização dessas etapas busca aumentar a eficiência operacional e a competitividade da produção. O projeto também reduz a quantidade de processos industriais que precisam ser executados fora da nova estrutura antes da montagem final dos equipamentos. A diferença de escala entre as duas fases aparece também na distribuição dos investimentos. Os US$ 141 milhões previstos para a segunda etapa representam aproximadamente 85% dos US$ 165 milhões anunciados para todo o programa de expansão. Capacidade global pode saltar de 10 para 50 geradores por dia Quando o projeto estiver concluído, a mudança deverá ser significativa na capacidade industrial da companhia. Hoje, a WEG informa capacidade global de aproximadamente 10 geradores por dia. Até 2030, a previsão é alcançar cerca de 50 unidades diárias, considerando as fábricas localizadas no México, Estados Unidos, Brasil e China. Isso representa uma capacidade cinco vezes maior que a atual. O número, contudo, deve ser entendido como capacidade global de fabricação prevista depois da conclusão da expansão, e não como produção efetivamente realizada hoje ou como volume destinado exclusivamente aos data centers. A WEG também não informou que todos os 50 geradores diários serão produzidos nas novas instalações da América do Norte. A projeção considera o conjunto das operações da companhia nos quatro países citados. Expansão está ligada ao negócio incorporado com a Marathon O movimento industrial está ligado à Marathon, marca incorporada ao portfólio da WEG após uma aquisição anunciada em setembro de 2023. Na ocasião, a companhia brasileira fechou a compra dos negócios de motores elétricos industriais e geradores da Regal Rexnord por US$ 400 milhões, operação que envolveu as marcas Marathon, Cemp e Rotor. A transação trouxe para a WEG aproximadamente 2.800 funcionários e dez fábricas distribuídas por sete países: Estados Unidos, México, China, Índia, Itália, Países Baixos e Canadá. Também foram incorporadas estruturas comerciais em outros mercados. Três anos depois, a companhia associa diretamente os novos US$ 165 milhões ao crescimento desses negócios. João Paulo Gualberto da Silva, vice-presidente da Unidade de Energia da WEG, afirmou no anúncio que a expansão aumenta a capacidade produtiva e reforça a integração das operações incorporadas com a Marathon. artigo.texto: What does the data say about data centers? People everywhere are talking about data centers, the high-tech facilities that house our nations growing digital infrastructure. Illinois is a Top 10 state for data centers, with a history dating all the way back to the 1970s, initially as a central repository to meet the technology needs of state agencies. More recently, however, data centers have become the foundation of a global technology race in the private sector, housing large computer servers, storage, and networking equipment necessary to support cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI). In Illinois, they comprise 7% of total electricity demand (and climbing). Many rely on water for cooling. And new data centers often come seemingly out-of-nowhere, as major technology companies use of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with elected officials instead of committing to public transparency. All of which has contributed to a public backlash against construction of these facilities that is playing out in statehouses and electoral campaigns around the country. Developments have been canceled or postponed, and Gov. JB Pritzker paused Illinois tax exemption for data centers. But data centers now are a fixture of the modern economy. Understanding their costs and benefits and identifying the guardrails needed to mitigate risk to our communities is of paramount importance. It is with these factors in mind that the Illinois Economic Policy Institute and the Project for Middle Class Renewal at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign recently undertook the most robust analysis of Illinois data centers to date. Specifically, we looked at 75 completed and ongoing projects and related reports culled from state, county, and industry data, and integrated industry-standard economic modeling to forecast potential impacts of $57 billion in planned data center projects across our state over the next decade. Here’s what we found. First, data centers mean jobs. More than 120,000 of them over the next 10 years, to be exact. About a third of these will be in skilled construction occupations or IT, engineering, and operations jobs that pay well into the six figures, and the other two-thirds in the supply chain or as a result of related increases in consumer spending across the economy. This investment will grow the Illinois economy by $5 billion a year during the construction phase, and about $2 billion per year thereafter. The facilities would also mean $300 million in new property tax revenue going to local communities each year nearly two-thirds of which will support public schools. When it comes to protecting communities from potential costs, the picture is more complex. By 2035, new data centers could use the same electricity as 4.5 million Illinois homes. Without any sort of requirements that data centers produce or otherwise offset their power demands, this would increase average Illinois household electric bills by $12 per month. Water resources can also be strained, unless new data centers use the air-cooling or closed-loop systems which recycle water instead of constantly drawing on new resources that are becoming commonplace. In both cases, there are tools available to policymakers to mitigate the risk and ensure responsible development of data centers. First, they can be required to pay for 100% of their energy, transmission, and interconnection costs and to use closed-loop or air-cooling systems to reduce water usage. The currently suspended sales tax exemption could be reformed to promote stronger energy and environmental standards, rewarding only those facilities that install Illinois-based clean energy. New data centers can be required to have battery storage. And policymakers can improve public disclosure around energy usage, water usage, and contact with elected officials. Even though the data on data centers shows they can be a net positive for our economy and our communities, there is a trust deficit. With commonsense guardrails, Illinois can modernize our energy system, protect workers and ratepayers, and improve transparency around an industry that too many people believe has been operating in the dark. Frank Manzo IV, MPP is an economist at the nonpartisan Illinois Economic Policy Institute.

artigo.texto: Following major purchases in recent months by tech billionaires, Oakland is putting a pause on data center development in the city. The Oakland City Council on Tuesday unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on building the controversial facilities, giving leaders more time to create a regulatory framework for appropriate uses that protect workers, the power grid and environmental resources. As author of the legislation, Councilmember Carroll Fife said the moratorium is “prudent and critical” at the local level. “Given advancements in technology, the City reasonably anticipates that absent this moratorium, applications for data centers will be submitted under existing regulations before the City can complete the necessary study and adopt regulations,” a policy analysis from Fife’s office states. With the number of data centers growing nationally, so have concerns about the resources they generally require for operation. In 2023, data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity, about 4% of total U.S. consumption that year, according to a 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report. Data centers are expected to consume up to 12% of all available electricity in the country by 2028, the report stated. Because data center servers require a cooling system, some of the larger facilities can use as much as 5 million gallons of water per day – equivalent to more than seven Olympic-sized swimming pools, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute. In response, hundreds of municipalities across the U.S. have announced moratoriums – sometimes even outright bans – on data centers until they can properly regulate them. In the Bay Area, Richmond and San Francisco each recently approved a pause on data center developments. “It’s a real testament to the power of the people organizing and what we can achieve against these big tech companies,” said Adi Varshneya, an organizer for the Party for Socialism and Liberation, one of the key groups against data centers in Oakland. “Thousands have signed petitions, hundreds have been volunteering and sharing online with their community network.” Oakland’s pause comes as major companies this summer announced plans to invest in the city, sparking public outcry for increased action at City Hall. The Behring Company is seeking to create a 20,000-square-foot data center at the former Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory supercomputer site at 415 20th St. Jeff Bezos’ artificial intelligence startup Prometheus leased a 100,000-square-foot space in West Oakland. Tesla leased a 40,000-square-foot facility in West Oakland for potential robotics and manufacturing work. Many residents who spoke during public comment on Tuesday urged the council to go further than the moratorium. “What we’d like to see is a ban on data centers,” said Quanah Parker Brightman, executive director of United Native Americans, an Indigenous civil right organization promoting decolonization. “We have an opportunity here today to start that process.” Some residents, however, did not view data centers as a negative for the city. Oakland resident Andrea Ingram said AI data centers are simply the next major innovation, much like electricity. She said the city should consider the tax revenue benefits the facilities could provide as Oakland faces a structural deficit exceeding $100 million. “We need the data centers. We need every form of modern science and technology and industry that we can get” Ingram said. “Oakland is good at driving those things out of the city, and then we turn around and ask why we can’t give a raise to city workers.”

artigo.texto: By PACNEWS Fiji has launched a FJD$5.2 million (US$2.6 million) five-year plan to develop its carbon market and position the country to undertake its first international carbon trade by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan 2026–2030 was launched by the Government on the opening day of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan, developed by the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change in collaboration with the Ministry of Forestry and Conservation International, sets out the systems and frameworks Fiji needs to participate in international carbon markets. Carbon markets allow verified reductions in greenhouse gas emissions to be traded, creating opportunities for Fiji to attract climate finance for projects that reduce emissions and protect natural ecosystems. The Government said the plan could help attract new investment into renewable energy, sustainable forestry, waste management and the protection of forests, mangroves and other ecosystems. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu said Fiji’s carbon market must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners,” Bulitavu said. The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre of Fiji’s carbon market development, with a focus on fair benefit-sharing, safeguards and resilient livelihoods. The Government said the framework would prepare Fiji to access emerging sources of climate finance while ensuring communities and resource owners share in the benefits. It has also called on development partners to support implementation of the plan. The plan forms part of Fiji’s broader efforts to mobilise climate finance and strengthen its capacity to respond to climate change while protecting the country’s natural ecosystems.

artigo.texto: A Motorola anunciou nesta terça-feira (6) o lançamento do novo Moto G37 para o mercado brasileiro, focado em apresentar características mais básicas ao mercado de entrada. O novo aparelho da companhia traz um conjunto de câmeras suficiente, com principal de 50 MP, e bateria para 43 horas, mas pouca memória RAM. Com características mais básicas, o Moto G37 aposta em uma tela HD+ e tamanho de 6,7 polegadas. O painel é simples, de LCD, com taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho máximo de 1.050 nits, mas sem grandes funcionalidades além da profundidade de cores em 8-bits. Em termos de bateria, a fabricante explica que a capacidade do componente é de 5.200 mAh, proporcionando uma autonomia de 43 horas. Vale notar que no site estrangeiro da companhia esse número vai para 63 horas. Já o carregador é padrão de 20W. Câmera de 50 MP e chip MediaTek Por ser um produto bem inclinado ao mercado de dispositivos de entrada, o Moto G37 possui um conjunto traseiro de câmeras bem básico, mas aparentemente suficiente. Esse sensor principal trabalha com resolução de 50 megapixels, mas acompanha um sensor de ambiente dois em um. - Quando o assunto são as especificações internas desse celular, o chip escolhido pela Motorola é o Dimensity 6300, da MediaTek; - A plataforma foi lançada no fim de 2024, fabricada em um processo de 6 nanômetros e compatível com a rede 5G; - A parte mais complicada é o fato de esse aparelho ter somente 4 GB de memória RAM, embora a marca cite os 8 GB de memória virtual; - Além disso, há opções de 64 GB ou 128 GB para o armazenamento interno, mas há compatibilidade com cartão microSD para expansão de até 1 TB; - O modelo possui certificação militar MIL-STD 810H e proteção IP64 contra respingos d’água e poeira; - As possibilidades de gravação incluem resolução 2K a 30 fps na frontal e traseira; - Por ser um modelo de entrada, a conexão de 3,5 mm para fone de ouvido está disponível; - Tecnologias como o Gemini e o Circule Para Pesquisar são integradas ao aparelho. O novo Motorola Moto G37 já pode ser oficialmente adquirido no mercado brasileiro, através do site da fabricante, pelo preço de R$ 899 na versão de 64 GB e R$ 1.079 na variante de 128 GB. É possível adquirir o produto nas cores grafite, azul turquesa, azul náutico e rosa com certificação Pantone. Ficha técnica - Tela: LCD de 6,67 polegadas, resolução HD+ (1604 x 720), taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho de até 1.050 nits - Processador: MediaTek Dimensity 6300 (octa-core de até 2,4 GHz, 6 nm) - Memória RAM: 4 GB LPDDR4X (expansível via RAM Boost) - Armazenamento interno: 128 GB (expansível via cartão microSD de até 1 TB) - Câmeras traseiras: 50 MP (f/1.8, PDAF, Quad Pixel) e sensor 2 em 1 de luz ambiente e detecção de cintilação - Câmera frontal: 8 MP (f/2.0) - Gravação de vídeo: até 2K a 30 fps (frontal e traseira) - Bateria: 5.200 mAh com carregamento TurboPower de 20 W e recarga reversa com fio de 6 W - Sistema operacional: Android 16 - Construção e durabilidade: vidro frontal Gorilla Glass 7i, proteção IP64 contra poeira e respingos d’água, e certificação militar MIL-STD-810H - Áudio: alto-falantes estéreo com Dolby Atmos e entrada P2 (3,5 mm) para fone de ouvido - Conectividade: 5G, Wi-Fi dual-band (2,4 GHz e 5 GHz), Bluetooth 5.4, NFC e porta USB-C 2.0 - Segurança: leitor de digitais na lateral e reconhecimento facial - Dimensões e peso: 166,23 x 76,50 x 7,85 mm; 191 g Compre o Moto G37 - Moto G37 de 128GB por R$ 1.079,10 no site da Motorola - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 899,10 no Magazine Luiza - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 999,00 na Amazon - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 999,00 no Mercado Livre Por falar em produtos, a Motorola lançou os novos Moto Watch Ultra recentemente no Brasil com especificações bem robustas. artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Cost of living, immigration, water and data centers were among the issues debated Wednesday night by candidates for Arizona’s Congressional District 1. Presented in partnership with Clean Elections, the Citizens’ Clean Elections Commission and the Arizona Media Association, the event offered a stark contrast between the two major party candidates: the Republican, Thomas “Jay” Feely IV, and the Democrat, Dr. Amish Shah. The race for the open seat is widely regarded as one of the competitive contests that will help determine which party takes control of the U.S. House in the Nov. 3 midterm election. "On my side, I believe in limited government, in lower taxes, in individual liberties," Feely said during the debate, which streamed live from Sneaky Big Studios in Scottsdale, Ariz. "Shah and Democrats believe in bigger government, government solutions, more government intrusion and higher taxes." Shah, an emergency room physician and former state legislator, emphasized his hands-on experience treating patients and working across the aisle. Shah said that will be needed to help Arizonans. "Gas is high. Diesel is even higher," said Shah. "We're talking about groceries, people looking at a box of cereal and having to put it back." Shah added that the increased cost of energy from the conflict in Iran is a big reason for today’s prices. "What we say in the Emergency Department is, 'Let's stop the hemorrhage,' " said Shah. "Let's stop making this worse so we can end the war." Feely, a former NFL player, broadcaster and financial adviser, countered by pointing to historical inflation rates, arguing that excessive federal spending fueled the current economic climate. He suggested actions to help people earn more money. "When you put more money into people's pockets, it helps them to deal with inflation," said Feely. "No. 2, stop printing money." When it comes to healthcare access and the cost of treatment, Shah expressed deep concern over hospital financial strains and patient debt. "I have to treat those people because Ronald Reagan signed EMTALA [Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act] in 1986, which I happen to agree with, which says that everybody who comes to an Emergency Department has to get seen and has to get treated," said Shah. "It's the moral thing to do. And I agree with it. But that care isn't free. Somebody has to pay that." Feely criticized past healthcare reform laws for empowering large insurance companies at the expense of individual consumers. Advocating for transparent, market-driven changes, Feely pushed for things such as price transparency. “It’s the only industry where you do not know what something costs before you go in there and then you take advantage of it,” said Feely. “You have to have that.” Border policy and national security formed another critical point in the debate, particularly regarding how immigration intersects with federal safety nets and public resources. Focusing heavily on enforcement, Feely argued past policy changes wrongfully extended government benefits to noncitizens. While agreeing on core limitations regarding public assistance, Shah emphasized practical enforcement and criticized blanket administrative maneuvers. “I don’t think illegal immigrants should be on Medicaid.” Still, Shah disagreed with methods such as rigid work requirements, arguing that states that tried this created administrative waste rather than practical solutions. The candidates agreed on Arizona's need for an adequate water supply. They discussed the Colorado River - a key source for water supplies, irrigation for agriculture and recreation in the Southwest - and a federal plan requiring Arizona, Nevada and California - the lower basin states - to make cuts in their usage. The plan, developed by the Bureau of Reclamation, doesn't require cuts of the upper basin states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming. If federal cuts need to be made, upper basin states and the lower basin states should make those cuts equally, Feeley argued. "Water impacts everything,” the Republican candidate noted. “It impacts our ability to have more housing. It impacts our ability to bring industry here." Feely then pushed for innovative solutions and regional cooperation. "When you talk about desalination, when you talk about new farming practices, Arizona has done a really good job of conservation,” he said. “We should have a desalination plant. We should look at all the measures that we can do to make sure that we are water-independent.” Shah, whose first vote in the Legislature was for a drought contingency plan, said Arizonans should “fight like hell for every drop” of water. "Thinking outside the box while I was in the state Legislature again, a lot of the Republicans were talking about desalination,” the Democratic candidate said. “So I'm glad we agree also that this is something that can be done. We're talking about a study committee right now to look at that and buying up water rights while we help build desal plants elsewhere." Near the end of the debate, the candidates were asked about data centers. It was a timely question, with many states and cities expressing concern about data centers using too much water and electricity. Supporters downplay the concerns. Shah said the U.S. is going to need data centers because artificial intelligence is coming. "I just don't want them in CD1, our district here,” he said. “The reason I say that is because, again, I'm fighting for the voters and making sure that their wishes are what is paramount here." In contrast, Feely has framed data center development as vital for technological competitiveness against China. He added that data centers benefit Arizona’s economy. “Right now in the state of Arizona, data centers bring in $27 billion to our GDP. artigo.texto: I’ll admit that I’m the Computer Village Idiot when it comes to using technology like personal computers and smartphones; I still struggle. And I’m in over my head trying to figure out this whole AI (artificial intelligence) thing that some Anthropic research experts believe could ultimately destroy mankind. Are you thinking about artificial intelligence? AI is in the news everywhere these days, and the subject of AI data centers popping up in one’s town or city is enough to freak out most people. There are many unknowns about artificial intelligence, and we need to learn as much as we can about this new technology. Here in the Granite State, there are multiple traditional data centers, but they aren’t the same as AI data centers. There’s often confusion about the two, and unfortunately, AI has become the catch-all term for modern tech infrastructure. For instance, data center space is available for lease in Nashua Technology Park off Exit 1 near the NH/MA border. The campus offers dedicated data center space equipped with heavy-duty corporate infrastructure, but it lacks the capacity and available land for a huge hyperscale or large-scale AI build. And the same could be said for my city’s Millyard Technology Park in the historic district. The tech park leases general office space to companies of all sizes under one roof, featuring “software firms, various service businesses, more than one corporate headquarters, and a few computer hardware companies,” its website says. I know of no AI data center proposals in Nashua, and that’s good news to me. However, a warehouse-sized data center using 40 acres of land on Old Turnpike Road was proposed for the town of Nottingham last May. Residents were up in arms, blasting Granite State developer Tom Moulton. He later withdrew his application because of heavy community opposition. Nottingham residents recently voted overwhelmingly on a 12-month moratorium on any data center development within town limits. That enormous proposal wouldn’t sit well with most people. Massive data centers consume tons of energy, thereby placing a significant strain on water infrastructure and the power grid. These facilities are also seen as a threat to residents’ income, quality of life and the environment. In Bow, residents have come out fighting hard against Granite Shore Power, which owns the shuttered Merrimack Station. The owners had filed a request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to discuss connecting a 350-megawatt project to the regional power grid for a potential hyperscale AI data center. No data center development proposal has been submitted to the town yet, but that was enough to draw outraged locals to the Bow municipal building. Some of us also wonder about the harm AI could do to the journalism industry. Generative AI is considered a time-and-money-saving newsroom tool that can handle diverse data types like documents, videos and social media at speeds unmatched by traditional processing. But it could also eliminate jobs. However, AI has limitations and cannot replace human reporting, as Mike Reilley explained in an essay for the Red Line Project. Reilley is a University of Illinois Chicago digital journalism professor and an expert in artificial intelligence and data visualization within newsrooms. “Specifically, AI cannot: physically enter a courtroom or interview a defendant behind bars; cultivate trust with a whistleblower; brave the front lines of a war zone; provide the critical thinking, original reporting and smart editorial judgment that humans do.” Innovation should always be welcomed with responsibility. On that note, here’s to a free press!
