artigo.texto: Trending VANDALIA, Ohio --- President Donald Trump defended data centers that power artificial intelligence projects but have become a contentious campaign issue nationwide, as he took his midterm tour to Ohio this weekend to insist his party will keep its majorities in Congress despite steep political headwinds. Trump took several minutes during his campaign rally in southwestern Ohio near Dayton late Saturday night to promote his administration's action on data centers, saying he was seeking to ensure they "benefit local communities" and praising Republican Sen. Jon Husted for an ill-fated attempt to push forward legislation on the issue. "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China," Trump said, repeating his defense of data centers that he had made before. The massive warehouse campuses generating energy for AI projects have become a toxic political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies. It's become especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centers to Ohio when he served as lieutenant governor. Trump is embarking on what he says will be a 32-day blitz ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, hitting the deep red states of Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama last week before pivoting to Ohio, a battleground state once again that's home to one of the top-tier Senate races this cycle. Husted -- who was appointed to fill the Senate vacancy left by now-Vice President JD Vance -- is running to win the seat outright. There is likely no path to a Senate majority for Democrats without flipping Ohio, where former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the Senate after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno two years ago. Polls show that race is extremely tight. Since last year, Democrats have listed Ohio, along with states such as North Carolina and Maine, as key races to win control of the Senate. And this past week, the head of the Senate GOP's campaign arm said Ohio is among 10 battleground races that are "within striking distance." "The good news for us is that Jon Husted is a closer," Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told reporters. "We're seeing the gap that was there between the two candidates, which was just a few points, now it is right at a dead-even race. So this is as tight as ticks, as we say in South Carolina." DATA CENTERS At his rallies, Trump has been trying to convince voters that the economy is better than they feel it is, even though polls show Americans are frustrated with the way he's handled it. The high cost of living, including gas prices elevated by Trump's war on Iran, is a top issue in the Dayton area, too. And just days before Trump's rally, nearly 1,400 people were laid off from a truck factory in nearby Springfield. "Your state is booming. Every -- I hate to say it -- every state is booming," Trump said Saturday. "They're all booming." Trump's rally comes as Republicans worry that Husted's campaign has failed to adequately catch fire with voters in the state. Brown and allied groups have hammered Husted for his data-centers role, and the NRSC has pinpointed it as a political vulnerability. The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats. "You got to remember, Sherrod Brown was for data centers, and Jon Husted is for data centers being responsible," Scott told reporters this week. "If a community doesn't want them, he doesn't want them either." But Trump has become one of data centers' most vocal proponents, shrugging aside voter concerns and arguing that the U.S. cannot cede advancements in AI to China. "Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio," Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump's visit. "Now, he's making Ohioans foot the bill." Brown's campaign also has hammered Husted for donations he's received from retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Husted has donated remaining Wexner contributions to an anti-human trafficking charity. There were several Epstein-themed signs outside the Vandalia school where the rally was being held, as more than a hundred protesters lined the road with a slew of anti-Trump and anti-Husted signs. But inside the school's gymnasium, the boisterous crowd -- decked out in red "Make America Great Again" hats and "Trump 47" jerseys -- greeted each Republican candidate enthusiastically as they awaited the president's arrival. From the stage, Husted said the state had been through "hard times," noting his dad had worked at a factory that closed down. But he said Republicans in the state had turned it around. "We now have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate we've ever had in the history of Ohio," he said. Meanwhile, in the governor's race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director. A wealthy biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate, Ramaswamy's star appeal among conservatives led to quick backing by Ohio Republicans and hopes of an easy victory in the Republican-dominated state. However, despite a massive fundraising lead and more than $12 million spent in campaign advertising, he is now locked in a close fight with Acton with weeks to go until Election Day. "I'm so grateful to this state and to this country for giving a kid like me opportunities that would not have been available to my family in any other country on planet earth," Ramaswamy said at the rally ahead of Trump's arrival, as he underscored the American dream for his Indian immigrant family.

artigo.texto: BYD unveils interior of its third-generation Tang EV BYD has officially unveiled the interior of its third-generation Tang. Lu Tian, General Manager of BYD’s Dynasty Series Sales Division, released the official images today with two new interior colour schemes: Dune Beige and Amber Brown. The interior design features a “Star Ring” display and a panoramic glass roof. BYD has utilised fine leather upholstery with diamond-quilted stitching. The cabin has integrated ambient lighting that runs throughout the dashboard and door panels. The third-generation Tang is also known as the 8 Series Tang, and joins the Tang L and the larger 9 Series Da Tang (Great Tang) in BYD’s domestic SUV family, while overseas markets have used the Atto 8 and Sealion 8 names for related models. Exterior and Dimensions The third-generation Tang continues the evolution of BYD’s “Dynasty” design language. The front fascia is dominated by a full-width LED light bar and air intakes. The side profile features a floating roof design and semi-concealed door handles. Customers can choose between 20-inch and 21-inch wheels. Vehicle Dimensions: - Length: 5,045 mm - Width: 1,980 mm - Height: 1,760 mm - Wheelbase: 2,950 mm Performance and Technology Under the hood, the new Tang is powered by a TZ205QYD electric motor, delivering a maximum power output of 300 kW (402 hp). The vehicle is equipped with BYD’s second-generation Blade Battery, available in two capacities: 88.682 kWh and 105.792 kWh. Depending on the configuration, the model offers CLTC-rated pure electric ranges of 730 km (591 km WLTP), 830 km (672 km WLTP), and 850 km (689 km WLTP). The vehicle also supports BYD’s flash-charging technology. The third-generation Tang features the DiSus-A intelligent air body control system, which includes dual-chamber air suspension and intelligent road-surface preview technology, allowing the vehicle to adapt rapidly to changing road conditions. Additionally, the SUV is equipped with the “God’s Eye B” intelligent driving assistance system.

artigo.texto: Veja o resumo da notícia - Pastores no Quênia processam organização local por redesenhar rotas de pastoreio para gerar créditos de carbono. - A medida, que visa sequestrar carbono, restringe o acesso dos rebanhos a pastagens tradicionais e afeta o modo de vida local. - Netflix, Meta, British Airways e Beiersdorf estão entre as empresas que compram esses créditos de carbono. - A ação judicial questiona a legitimidade do consentimento das comunidades e a distribuição dos valores arrecadados. - O caso levanta debate sobre a qualidade dos offsets climáticos e o impacto social em territórios tradicionais. - No Brasil, dilemas semelhantes surgem em projetos de crédito de carbono na Amazônia, com comunidades cobrando participação. - A disputa expõe a assimetria de poder entre o mercado global de carbono e as comunidades que habitam as áreas afetadas. Os pastores que há gerações conduzem o gado pelas mesmas rotas no norte do Quênia afirmam que perderam o controle prático sobre a terra quando uma organização local passou a redesenhar o pastoreio para gerar créditos de carbono vendidos a empresas ocidentais, entre elas a Netflix e a Meta. A revolta virou processo judicial em torno da área do reservatório natural de Biliqo Bulesa, uma reserva a algumas centenas de quilômetros a nordeste de Nairobi, a capital queniana, território usado por comunidades de pecuaristas desde tempos imemoriais. Segundo os autores da ação, o Northern Rangelands Trust, conhecido pela sigla NRT, teria começado a transformar o manejo do solo sem o consentimento pleno das famílias que dependem daquelas pastagens, e o resultado imediato é a restrição de caminhos por onde o rebanho sempre circulou. A reportagem do NOS descreve o mal-estar como consequência direta de um esquema em que companhias pagam para, no papel, reduzir a própria pegada de dióxido de carbono enquanto a organização queniana “fabrica” os créditos ao impedir que o gado paste em trechos determinados, permitindo que a vegetação cresça mais e armazene mais carbono. Os pastores cobram transparência sobre os valores exatos arrecadados e dizem que a entidade passou a exercer poder excessivo sobre o modo de vida que sustenta suas famílias. O mecanismo em disputa é o crédito de carbono, instrumento pelo qual cada tonelada de dióxido de carbono que deixa de ir para a atmosfera ou que é capturada pode ser convertida em um comprovante negociável. Países e empresas usam esses comprovantes para cumprir metas climáticas ou para compensar emissões difíceis de cortar na própria operação. O vendedor, seja governo ou organização, não pode mais contabilizar aquele volume para as próprias metas depois de repassar o crédito, mas recebe dinheiro pela transação. No projeto queniano, um dos maiores do mundo nesse formato de pastagens, a lógica central é ajustar rotas tradicionais de pastoreio para que plantas voltem a crescer com menos pressão do gado, produzindo biomassa maior e, com ela, mais sequestro de carbono. Netflix, Meta, British Airways e Beiersdorf figuram entre os compradores que repassam recursos à organização local e, em troca, contabilizam uma emissão menor em seus balanços climáticos. Para os pastores, o que aparece como solução climática no exterior se traduz em perda de acesso a áreas de pasto, incerteza sobre renda e a sensação de que a terra ancestral foi convertida em ativo financeiro sem que as comunidades tivessem voz decisória sobre o desenho do projeto. Como o crédito de carbono transforma pastagem em ativo negociável para big tech Na prática cotidiana, o rebanho precisa se deslocar conforme a chuva, a seca e a regeneração do capim, e qualquer redesign de rotas que feche corredores históricos obriga os pastores a alongar jornadas, concentrar animais em faixas menores ou aceitar pastos de pior qualidade. O NRT argumenta, no desenho do programa, que a regeneração controlada aumenta a capacidade de armazenamento de carbono das pastagens e, portanto, gera créditos legítimos. Os herdeiros da tradição pastoril respondem que a transformação ocorreu sem autorização clara e que a organização lucrou milhões com a venda desses créditos enquanto as famílias ficaram sem informação detalhada sobre valores, contratos e distribuição de benefícios. A exigência judicial de abertura dos números não é apenas contábil: trata-se de saber se a compensação financeira chega de fato a quem perdeu flexibilidade de manejo e se o preço pago pelas empresas cobre o custo social de alterar um sistema de subsistência construído ao longo de gerações. A tensão cresce porque o mesmo solo que alimenta o gado passa a ser lido, nos relatórios corporativos de tecnologia e aviação, como sumidouro de carbono capaz de limpar parte da imagem climática de plataformas de streaming, redes sociais e companhias aéreas. Empresas de tecnologia e de entretenimento digital operam cadeias globais de data centers, deslocamentos de equipes e produção audiovisual com pegada energética elevada, e a compra de créditos aparece como atalho para metas de neutralidade anunciadas em relatórios anuais. No caso queniano, o atalho passa por uma paisagem semiárida onde a sobrevivência depende da mobilidade do rebanho. Quando a organização gestora limita o pastejo para maximizar o crescimento vegetal mensurável, o indicador de carbono sobe e o crédito se valoriza, mas o pastor vê encolher a margem de manobra que sempre usou para enfrentar secas. A ação judicial em torno de Biliqo Bulesa coloca em xeque não só a legitimidade do consentimento, mas o próprio modelo de governança em que uma entidade intermediária concentra poder de redesenhar o território e negociar com compradores internacionais. Os pastores afirmam que essa concentração altera regras de uso da terra e de convivência entre clãs e famílias, porque quem controla o mapa do pastoreio controla, em última instância, o calendário da sobrevivência. artigo.texto: 2 min leitura Mercado Voluntário de Carbono alarga projetos florestais Duas novas metodologias juntam-se à de Novas Florestações, aumentando as oportunidades para projetos de sequestro de carbono em Portugal. Carbono azul e pradarias marinhas vão seguir-se, 06 Out 2026 - 07:45 2 min leitura O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passa a contar com três metodologias para projetos florestais, abrindo novas oportunidades à mobilização de investimento privado para o sequestro de carbono e a gestão sustentável da floresta. Foram aprovadas duas novas metodologias de carbono dedicadas à Reflorestação e à Gestão Florestal Melhorada, que se juntam à metodologia já existente para Novas Florestações. As novas metodologias permitem abranger um conjunto mais diversificado de intervenções florestais, reforçam o potencial de geração de créditos de carbono em Portugal e incentivam práticas de gestão sustentável com benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática. Ao alargar as metodologias disponíveis, reforçamos a credibilidade e a capacidade de crescimento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono e mobilizamos financiamento privado para projetos que contribuem simultaneamente para a neutralidade carbónica, a valorização do território e a resiliência das nossas florestas”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, numa nota enviada às redações. Atualmente, o MVC conta com dois projetos registados na tipologia de Novas Florestações e um terceiro projeto está em fase de validação inicial. Estão ainda disponíveis 977 créditos de carbono para venda, a plataforma conta com 29 utilizadores registados e existem 10 verificadores qualificados para assegurar a validação inicial e a verificação periódica dos projetos, segundo o ministério. “O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono está a ganhar escala e maturidade. Depois das metodologias florestais, estamos já a trabalhar em novas abordagens para valorizar o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, para colocar também os ecossistemas costeiros no centro da ação climática e da valorização do capital natural”, acrescenta a ministra.

artigo.texto: Battery energy storage is moving from a supporting role in the energy transition to one of its central pillars. IDTechEx puts figures on that shift in its newly updated report Batteries for Stationary Energy Storage 2027–2037, forecasting that the global lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) market will reach $135 billion by 2037, with cumulative installations exceeding 10.5 TWh worldwide. It traces this growth to the rising share of renewables in electricity grids, new demand from data centre build-out and a shift in policy from headline storage targets towards bankable revenue frameworks and more sophisticated routes to market. A rapid shift in battery demand Lithium-ion remains the dominant chemistry for stationary storage, supported by broad availability, falling costs and steady performance gains. Total lithium-ion battery demand continues to climb, but the application mix is changing quickly. Electric vehicles still account for the largest share of global demand, although their portion fell from 84 percent in 2023 to 78 percent in 2025, while the BESS share rose from 10 to 19 percent over the same period. Policy shifts in the EV market have contributed to this change, but the main driver is the faster growth of stationary storage as grids integrate more variable renewable generation and require greater flexibility. AI turns storage into a multi-revenue asset for industry Within lithium-ion, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) continues to extend its lead over nickel manganese cobalt (NMC), reflecting lower cost, longer cycle life and better thermal stability. Sodium-ion is also gaining ground as developers improve performance and cut production costs, but LFP is expected to remain the chemistry of choice for most BESS applications over the forecast period. Deployments triple in two years IDTechEx estimates that annual global Li-ion BESS deployments across grid-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential segments rose from 92 GWh in 2023 to 318 GWh in 2025, an increase of more than threefold. China accounted for 58 percent of 2025 deployments at 183 GWh, with the United States contributing 57 GWh, or 18 percent. China is likely to retain its lead over the coming decade, supported by intense domestic competition, growing grid flexibility requirements and expanding LFP cell and BESS manufacturing capacity. The US market, by contrast, is being reshaped by industrial policy aimed at reducing reliance on Chinese cells and systems. That policy is accelerating the localisation of the domestic supply chain, with several players expanding LFP cell and BESS manufacturing capacity in the country, while most Chinese suppliers have scaled back or exited the market. Beyond the two leaders, countries previously absent from the global top tier are now entering it at scale. Saudi Arabia emerged as the third-largest market in 2025, boosted by several gigawatt-hour-scale projects, and Chile also broke into the top ten. IDTechEx expects more countries to follow, with leading suppliers already securing projects of several hundred megawatt-hours up to gigawatt-hour scale in markets where deployment had previously been limited. Europe scales up through policy and procurement Europe is emerging as one of the most dynamic regions in the global BESS market, with the report covering Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Spain and Poland in detail. Two policy schemes stand out. The UK’s cap-and-floor framework for long-duration energy storage is designed to unlock projects that struggle to secure financing on merchant revenues alone, while Italy’s MACSE auction establishes a central procurement route for large-scale storage. Europe hits 100 GWh as utility-scale takes over the storage market Beyond these schemes, Germany continues to anchor Europe’s residential and commercial storage segments, and markets such as Bulgaria, Spain and Poland are moving quickly from early projects to structured pipelines. Together, these developments are shaping Europe into a region where storage deployment is increasingly underpinned by predictable revenue mechanisms rather than merchant exposure alone. Procurement, revenue models and bankability The same shift is under way well beyond Europe. Governments and system operators are moving beyond headline targets towards mechanisms that can carry large waves of BESS projects through tendering and commissioning. Examples include Australia’s Capacity Investment Scheme and the New South Wales Long-Term Energy Service Agreements, as well as state-backed tenders in the Middle East. Overstated battery availability puts investor returns at risk Project financing is also becoming more sophisticated. Revenue floors, capacity contracts, tolling agreements and stacked revenue models combining arbitrage, ancillary services and capacity payments are improving bankability and enabling a broader pipeline of projects to secure investment. In the residential segment, subsidies continue to play a decisive role, as shown by the strong uptake under Australia’s Cheaper Home Batteries Program. When such schemes are phased out, however, activity can drop quickly. Technology trends: larger cells, denser systems At the technology level, developers are increasingly launching containerised grid-scale systems built around higher-capacity cells, with a growing number of units rated at 6.5 MWh or more. Larger cells can improve system-level energy density by reducing the number of cells, interconnections and casings per megawatt-hour, allowing a greater share of the container to be occupied by active battery material. The approach also simplifies manufacturing and can lower project-level costs, as fewer units are needed for a given site capacity. Although energy density has traditionally mattered less for stationary storage than for EVs, it is becoming a point of differentiation. artigo.texto: MONTGOMERY, Ala. – The Alabama Public Service Commission unanimously adopted a procedure Tuesday allowing automatic approval of Alabama Power’s contracts with large load data centers if the commission fails to take a vote within 90 days of submission. Chief Administrative Law Judge Luke Bentley had recommended that the PSC adopt a policy requiring a vote on every large load data center contract but did not include a time window for a vote, which is standard for PSC procedures. Following legislation, the PSC defines large load data centers as facilities that require 150 megawatts or more of electricity and operate on one piece of land. Commissioners Chris Beeker and Jeremy Oden expressed concerns about contracts potentially falling through because of the PSC not acting in a timely manner. Oden called the automatic approval procedure a “consequence” for the PSC not voting. “I want the commission to vote, but then again, I understand if they do not vote, then it’s not on the company and it’s not on the data center. It’s really and truthfully back on the commission …” Oden said. “Saying, ‘Well, since we just didn’t bring it up and vote, it’s gone,’ I don’t think that’s a good move, I don’t think it’s a good economic presentation for the state if we do that.” Though she ultimately introduced an amendment setting up an automatic approval in the case of the PSC’s inaction, PSC President Cynthia Almond said she felt strongly that the commission should take a public vote on data centers because of the public’s concern about the massive facilities that power artificial intelligence. She included the 90-day window for voting in her amendment. “We should not follow the ‘deemed approved’ process that we’ve been following for a number of years,” Almond said. “The current (rate) FCR deals with industry that is one megawatt or greater, and we’re talking about industry now that is at least 150 megawatts, and those are some of our smaller data centers. So these are just to me different animals, and it should be a very public process that we go through.” Data centers previously fell under the general rate flexible contract rate docket – rate FCR – like all commercial and industrial customers with accounts of at least one megawatt. The rate FCR for data centers temporarily had a turnaround time of 45 days, up from the standard 10, while the commission established new procedures. Under Almond’s amendment, the commission is supposed to vote on the contracts within 90 days. If it doesn’t, the contract will automatically be approved. The new procedure does not mandate a public hearing about proposed data center contracts. Tuesday’s vote came after a monthslong general proceeding seeking input from members of the public about how the commission should evaluate Alabama Power’s contracts with data centers. Legislation requiring data centers to pay for the additional electricity they need and refining the longstanding public interest standard sparked the proceeding. Nineteen people and organizations submitted initial comments in the proceeding, while 10 offered reply comments, Bentley said. The newly approved procedure for evaluating contracts also establishes specific reporting requirements for Alabama Power and its data center customers, including a public petition naming the entities behind the facility, its maximum electric capacity and the municipality or county where the center will be. Alabama Power, the state’s largest utility, will now also be required to submit a full copy of its contracts to the PSC and the attorney general’s office. This submission will be confidential. The company must also include in the confidential submission an estimate of impacts on other customers’ costs, how much revenue the project would generate for the company and the cost of the incremental capacity required. It also has to provide a detailed explanation of how the contract meets the public interest standard expanded in Senate Bill 270. That legislation, which established that data centers are in the public’s interest only if they “promote positive benefits” to other customers, went into effect Oct. 1. Lowering the cost for other customers, increasing the efficiency of the power system and contributing to economic growth in the community where a data center is located are examples of positive benefits the bill lays out. The new procedure also forbids the utility from informally submitting information to the PSC or attorney general’s office before filing the public petition. Alabama Power told Alabama Daily News that it is committed to complying with all applicable regulatory requirements, including the one approved Tuesday. “Alabama Power will continue to require large load data center customers to pay the full cost to serve their energy needs, so costs are not shifted to existing customers,” the company said in a statement. “Alabama state law affirms that same standard and the Alabama Public Service Commission approves contracts that meet that standard while promoting positive benefits for other customers.” Though Energy Alabama and the Southern Environmental Law Center celebrated some of the new transparency requirements created by the PSC on Tuesday, the advocacy groups said in statements that they wished the commission had done more to loop the public into its future decision-making. artigo.texto: A Navitas Semiconductor (NASDAQ:NVTS) e a Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) desenvolveram em conjunto um projeto de referência de 800V CC para 6V CC para aplicações de alimentação de racks de data centers com inteligência artificial, anunciaram as empresas em 5 de outubro de 2026. A plataforma combina os controladores de sinal digital dsPIC33AK da Microchip e o dispositivo de criptografia TA100 com os dispositivos de potência de nitreto de gálio GaNFast da Navitas. O projeto está alinhado com o padrão Open Compute Project 800V DC e combina estágios de conversão de 800V DC para 50V DC e de 50V DC para 6V DC em um único conversor. O projeto visa atingir uma eficiência máxima de 96% Segundo as empresas, a plataforma de referência visa uma eficiência máxima de até 96% em plena carga, uma frequência de comutação de 1 MHz e uma densidade de potência de 2.100 watts por polegada cúbica. O lado primário utiliza 16 FETs GaNFast Navitas NV6034 de 650V em uma topologia de meia ponte empilhada. A família de controladores dsPIC33AK256MPS306 da Microchip inclui um núcleo de 32 bits de 200 MHz, moduladores de largura de pulso de alta resolução de 78 picossegundos e conversores analógico-digitais de 12 bits operando a até 40 MSPS. Os controladores também são compatíveis com algoritmos de criptografia pós-quântica do pacote Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0. O dispositivo TA100 CryptoAuthentication da Microchip oferece funções de segurança baseadas em hardware, incluindo inicialização segura, geração de código de autenticação de mensagens, atualizações de firmware confiáveis e suporte a Transport Layer Security (TLS). “À medida que o ecossistema avança em direção a sistemas de alimentação de rack de alta tensão, os desenvolvedores precisam de componentes básicos comprovados que ajudem a reduzir o risco de projeto e acelerar a inovação”, disse Joe Thomsen, vice-presidente corporativo da unidade de negócios de controladores de sinal digital da Microchip. Plataforma de referência será apresentada em outubro As empresas planejam apresentar a solução no evento OCP da Microchip em San Jose, Califórnia, agendado para 12 a 15 de outubro de 2026. artigo.texto: Utah Survey Uncovers Why Residents Oppose New Data Centers LOGAN — A new Utah State University statewide survey examines Utah residents’ views on data centers. The results indicate that 75.8% of respondents oppose or strongly oppose building new or additional data centers in Utah. The survey offers insights about what drives this opposition. The findings appear in the first executive summary from a broader research project led by Gina Gilson, Stacia Ryder, and Jessica Schad of USU’s Community and Natural Resources Institute (CANRI). The project will examine data centers’ water and energy demands, Utah residents’ views on data centers, and generate information that could help state and local leaders evaluate proposed development. The August 2026 survey gathered responses from nearly 900 Utah residents and is representative of the state adult population. “We are excited to share some of the initial results from our statewide survey on data centers,” said Schad, CANRI director and administrator of the survey. “One of the most important findings in my view is that public participation in decision-making processes is nearly as important as the amount of energy and water projects consume, meaning that government and business leaders may want to consider how they can engage communities throughout the planning process.” The results show that water and energy use, location, and opportunities for public participation are important considerations for residents evaluating data center projects. The survey predominantly measured reported views of hypothetical project features; it only asked about whether residents support or oppose the Stratos data center in Box Elder, which 60.7% strongly opposed. More than half of respondents (57.2%) strongly oppose data center development, and opposition rises when proposed projects are closer to where respondents live. Residents’ responses also vary with the characteristics of a proposed project. Asked how specific features would affect their views of a data center within 3 miles of home, 54.1% said usage of recycled or other non-potable water would make them more likely to support it. Renewable energy infrastructure had a similar effect for 51.2%, while 43.4% said a project that built or paid for new energy infrastructure would increase their likelihood of support. By comparison, 61.3% said using nonrenewable energy would make them more likely to oppose a local project. The use of nuclear energy increased the likelihood of opposition for 41.4%. Responses to a proposal for public reporting of annual water and energy use were more mixed. “Similar to what we have seen in the context of other energy infrastructure project siting processes, like for shale gas, residents in our survey indicate the continued importance of processes creating avenues for meaningful community participation in these decision-making processes,” said Ryder, assistant professor of sociology. "Additionally, the type of energy and water used to support data centers matters to residents, as respondents were likely to respond more positively to the use of renewable energy and recycled or non-potable water. These are important considerations for shaping planning and public reception." Gilson, assistant professor of environment and society and interim director of USU’s Center for Colorado River Studies, said: “Our survey findings underscore the concern that Utahns feel about our water resources. I think it’s important for us to better understand where the water comes from, how much water is used on-site, and how much is used to generate the electricity that powers data centers. Our research will gather information to help answer these questions." The survey is one part of an ongoing project. CANRI researchers also want to examine public documents and media coverage to assess what information is available about data centers’ water and energy use, and to interview policymakers, developers, community leaders, and residents of select Utah communities affected by data center development. A follow-up survey in 2027 is planned to assess whether residents’ views change over time. To learn more, read the executive summary: https://artsci.usu.edu/canri/projects/data-center-development-in-utah. artigo.texto: Oakland City Council approves 45-day moratorium on new data centers OAKLAND, Calif. - The Oakland City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to place a 45-day temporary moratorium on all new data center development across the city. Oakland Enacts Temporary Moratorium on Data Center Construction The urgency measure, sponsored by Councilmember Carroll Fife, pauses new approvals to allow city leaders time to study the potential environmental and operational impacts of data centers on local water supplies, electrical grids, and air quality. Before the vote, protesters rallied outside Oakland City Hall to demand a pause on data center developments, expressing concerns over natural resource consumption. Inside council chambers, community members and activists offered mixed testimony on the proposal. Opponents of data centers highlighted the massive water demands required for cooling systems. "My concern about it being in Oakland is that we have limited water from the Mokelumne River, and that’s in the Sierra Nevada, and we’re already taking up to 60 to 70 percent of that river out of the river," said Dr. Elizabeth Dougherty. "If we increase water use here, that would take more and more out, so what would be impacting not just our ecosystem, but also up river in the Sierra Nevada." Other residents voiced fears regarding daily utility volume, with one speaker noting that "a large data center can use up to 5 billion gallons of water a day," while another called on the council to implement a permanent ban. Conversely, supporters urged the council to reject the moratorium, emphasizing the economic potential and job creation tied to technology infrastructure. "I oppose the moratorium on data centers," one resident told council members. "Data centers will bring jobs. They will not take jobs away," another resident added. Concerns Over Non-Disclosure Agreements and Downtown Proposal Councilmember Fife, who proposed the moratorium, has criticized developers for using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to shield specific project details from city officials and the public. The vote followed growing scrutiny over plans announced by Behring Companies to convert the ground floor of a building near 20th and Franklin streets in downtown Oakland into a data center. The developer stated that the other floors of the facility would serve as office space for artificial intelligence research. Mayor Barbara Lee noted that the pause would provide necessary time for public engagement. "This is a moment to have the public weigh in, and the public will be able to weigh in during this 45-day moratorium to see exactly what people here in Oakland want," Mayor Lee said. Next Steps and Public Forum The 45-day moratorium takes effect immediately. City officials will use the interim period to analyze policy options and development standards for future data center projects. Councilmember Fife has scheduled a community conversation for Oct. 24 at 10 a.m. at the Beth Eden Baptist Church at 1183 10th Street in West Oakland to allow residents to further discuss the future of data centers in the city.

artigo.texto: Hallam Village Board approves zoning rights for data center HALLAM, Neb. (KOLN) - The village of Hallam is now one step closer to getting a data center. The village board approved zoning rights in a vote on Monday. It was about an hour of discussion between board members, the public, and a representative from Crusoe Technologies, who signed a special permit alongside Monolith Materials back in July to get the data center plan started. People had questions about fire safety and noise, but Steve Buster, a Crusoe Technologies representative, said they have a fire plan just in case something does happen. A handful of people from Hallam were invited to a data center to help calm worries about excessive sounds. Even though there wasn’t much drama during the vote, some weren’t happy with the decision. “Well at first I thought that’s okay, you can just move somewhere but everywhere you look they are fighting data centers,” said a woman at the discussion. “So where will you move where there won’t be another data center.” While a number of people were disappointed, a reporter said about half the room applauded when the zoning rights were approved. Information on when the data center will be built has yet to be released. Stay connected to 1011now.com for updates on this story. artigo.texto: Três carros para comprar com valor do novo BYD Sealion 7 O BYD Sealion 7 tem 531 cv de potência, 70,3 kgfm de torque e roda 360 km de autonomia com uma carga completa A BYD lançou um novo modelo elétrico para o mercado brasileiro chamado de Sealion 7. O SUV 100% elétrico tem mais de 4,80 metros de comprimento e desempenho de esportivo. Com preço de R$ 339.990, a reportagem da CNN Brasil separou algumas opções de carros para comprar com esse valor. O BYD Sealion 7 tem 531 cv de potência, 70,3 kgfm de torque e pode rodar 360 km com uma carga completa. Com essa mecânica, o SUV atinge os 100 km/h em 4,5 segundos e a velocidade máxima é de 215 km/h. Com esse valor do SUV, uma opção semelhante é o Volvo EC40. O modelo da marca sueca parte de R$ 334.950. A configuração perde na potência, que conta com 238 cv e acelera de 0 a 100 km/h em 7,3 segundos. A vantagem fica por conta da autonomia. Segundo o Inmetro, o Volvo EC40 pode rodar 385 km com uma carga completa, superando o número do BYD Sealion 7. Em termos de tamanho, contudo, a vantagem fica para o modelo chinês. Um outro SUV chinês que é posicionado no mesmo patamar do Sealion 7 é o GAC Hyptec HT. Com preço de R$ 314.990, o modelo entrega mais autonomia elétrica. Na versão Elite, de entrada, são 431 km de autonomia elétrica com uma única carga. O SUV da GAC também é superior em algumas dimensões. Tem 4,93 metros de comprimento (+10 cm), 1,92 de largura e 2,93 metros na distância entre os eixos. O porta-malas tem 670 litros — O BYD tem 500 L. Com R$ 10 mil a mais no bolso, uma outra alternativa é o Chevrolet Equinox EV. O SUV elétrico tem 304 cv de potência (menos que o Sealion 7), mas ganha com grande vantagem no alcance elétrico. Segundo dados do Inmetro, o Equinox EV consegue rodar 443 km com uma única carga de bateria completa. Com os 443 quilômetros de autonomia, a velocidade de recarga é de até 22 kW (AC) e 150 kW (DC). Em apenas 10 minutos nesta última, o motorista pode somar 130 km de autonomia. No porte, o Equinox é bem semelhante ao Sealion 7. São 4.840 mm de comprimento, 1.954 mm de largura, 1,64 metro de altura e 2.336 kg. O entre-eixos tem 2,95 metros.

artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons shares hit a day high of Rs 226.99 on 5 October, up 1%, after the firm won a Rs 100 crore battery storage order in Uttarakhand. The company told exchanges about the win at around 13:30 pm. Jupiter Wagons, better known for building railway wagons, landed the job through JEM Energy, its clean energy arm. Madhav Infra Projects Limited is its partner on the project. The customer is Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL). The project is essentially a giant battery. It stores electricity when demand is low and sends it back to the grid when demand peaks. The system is rated at 41 MW and can hold 102.5 MWh of energy. Jupiter and its partner will supply and set it up, and the work is worth about Rs 100 crore. The two firms won by quoting the lowest price in a competitive bidding round run by UPCL. It is JEM Energy’s first project in Uttarakhand. This is not the only recent win. In August 2026, the company also received a formal award letter from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited. That job is a 50 MW/200 MWh battery project at the Jeerat substation in North 24 Parganas. Managing Director Vivek Lohia called both wins important steps in turning JEM Energy into a bigger business. Jupiter Wagons still aims to build a battery storage order book of about Rs 1,000 crore by FY27. Lohia also said the electric mobility arm, Jupiter Electric Mobility, should start making an operating profit in the October to December quarter of FY27. He expects it to turn profitable overall by FY28. The orders follow the Union Cabinet’s approval of Green Energy Corridor Phase-III, which includes 50 GWh of battery storage. The early rally did not hold. Jupiter Wagons closed at Rs 223.44 on the NSE, down 0.22%, after swinging between a low of Rs 218.61 and its high of Rs 226.99. artigo.texto: COLORADO SPRINGS, Colorado — Billions of dollars in data center construction are generating significant insurance demand, but a growing challenge for insurers is the accumulation of exposures rather than a broad shortage of capacity, insurance executives say. Most projects can obtain the property and builders risk capacity they need, but insurers and reinsurers must track overlapping construction, operational property, equipment and power exposures, they said. The executives spoke this week at the Insurance Leadership Forum, sponsored by the Council of Insurance Agents & Brokers. The boom has sparked public opposition in some states over concerns about electricity and water use and the effect on local communities, prompting proposals to restrict or pause some developments. Despite the pushback, insurance executives at the conference generally described data centers as a major growth opportunity for the industry. Thousands of data centers are expected to be developed globally, with many projects valued between $3 billion and $5 billion, said Ryan Barber, New York-based global head of property at Aon. There is ample capacity for projects of that size, which are generally highly engineered and attractive property risks, he said. “We’ve done placements now with limits as high as $8.5 billion, and that was over a year ago; we could probably do placements in excess of $10 billion now,” Mr. Barber said. Aon is developing an operational property insurance facility for data centers. Aon estimates data centers could generate more than $100 billion in new insurance premiums over the next five to 10 years, he said. But rapid development is creating accumulation issues as large campuses are built in phases, leaving insurers with builders risk and operational property exposures at the same site, Mr. Barber said. Other exposures can include high-value computer equipment and dedicated power generation, increasing the potential for insurers and reinsurers to accumulate exposures to the same projects. “The biggest struggle right now for insurers and reinsurers, for that matter, is to just track and understand the accumulation of risk that they’re taking on from these data centers,” Mr. Barber said. Managing aggregation is also an important consideration in site and insurer selection, said Pat Donnelly, Chicago-based head of risk and broking for North America at Willis. Some insurers can provide coverage across several phases of a development, while others prefer individual segments, he said. Insurers must consider those exposures alongside property risks already on their books, said Marc Orloff, Boston-based president of global risk solutions North America at Liberty Mutual. “We all write a lot of property already … so it’s all about managing tolerances. How much of our exposure do we want? How much volatility do we want on our balance sheets?” he said. Concentrations of expensive data centers in areas exposed to severe convective storms add to the uncertainty, Mr. Orloff said. Property and business interruption capacity remains plentiful for most projects, but capacity in other lines is more constrained, said Marc Kunney, San Francisco-based chief client officer at EPIC Insurance Brokers & Consultants. “Where some of the challenges are is on the professional liability, which is a much more limited marketplace,” Mr. Kunney said. The construction boom is generating substantial premium, but not all of the revenue will recur once projects are completed, Mr. Orloff said. Operational property coverage may generate lower premium volumes, while builders risk premium will decline if construction slows, he said. “It’s not a recurring revenue stream,” Mr. Orloff said.

artigo.texto: Fayette County residents push back on data center zoning plan Opponents call for extended moratorium, stricter limits on hyperscale facilities LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Fayette County residents voiced opposition Tuesday to hyperscale data centers and current zoning recommendations put forth earlier this year by the planning commission. “I expect for my council, my representatives to represent me. Not big industry,” one resident said. Opponents cite risks, demand moratorium extension Opponents said that if the draft moves forward, anticipated noise, water, energy, financial and air quality impacts will put communities at risk. Those opposed overwhelmingly demanded a two-year extension of the moratorium and a complete ban of centers larger than 25 megawatts if evidence discovered in those two years points to negative impacts. “Other safety critical industries such as transportation, energy, medicine and weapons are regulated and monitored. AI needs to be treated the same,” one speaker said. Other demands included a cap on data center license issuances, incentives to use lower carbon emission fuels, cutting the decibel limit to 25, and changing zoning rules to limit a center by its utility intake rather than square footage. Some also called for a one-year extension of the data center moratorium. Some see economic opportunity Others in attendance Tuesday said they see AI and data centers as drivers of economic growth in the future and do not wish to jeopardize it. “Data infrastructure is critically important. Data technology, having that infrastructure here is as essential to economic development today as sites and buildings, as water and sewer, and broadband capacity,” one speaker said. Developer addresses concerns Several speakers noted data center developer DART Point’s recent acquisition of more than 300,000 square feet of property to create a data center campus. A DART Point representative addressed resource-based concerns. “We’re not a threat on the noise factor, the water system we use will be a closed loop system, and the power, we already have it,” the representative said. Urban County Council members said they will continue discussions on data centers at the next meeting, including where any potential projects could be developed and how the data centers would be used. The possibility of a one-year extension of the moratorium will also be discussed. Copyright 2026 WKYT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Data center moratorium vote postponed after fight, protests MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) — Chaos ensued during Tuesday night’s data center moratorium vote by the city council in Memphis, Tennessee. More than 100 people showed up to the meeting to hear the outcome on the proposed ordinance. “This is just a total hazard. We’ve basically been invaded by strangers, by people that have gotten paid, and they have not communicated with us in any way,” said Amber Lowe, a local community member. “This is hurtful, and I’m rethinking where I need to be living at.” The decision to delay the vote until Oct. 20 led to a fight breaking out in the lobby and tense exchanges among city council members. A fight between two women spilled into the lobby, with punches thrown while protesters chanted inside the meeting. One woman had her hair pulled and was slapped seconds later. Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton was pulled out of the meeting after arguing with protesters and council member JB Smiley. “You could’ve came to see me like I asked you to... I ain’t no coward; you pipe down, baby, I clap back,” Cooper-Sutton said. The city council halted the meeting amid the turmoil and subsequently delayed the vote. Crowds chanted “this is our city” and “show me what democracy looks like” as the demonstration moved from the chamber into the halls of the building. Protesters said they are not done pursuing the issue. Memphis police were called to the disturbance at city hall, but a department spokesperson says no one was detained and no one was harmed. artigo.texto: Verso Energy inaugurates a 6 MW battery at its floating solar site The energy company commissions a 6 MW / 12 MWh system at Gueugnon, paired with a 23.1 MWp floating park. It is also starting a 23 MW / 46 MWh battery in the Marne. Verso Energy has inaugurated a 6 MW / 12 MWh battery storage system at its floating solar site in Gueugnon. According to the company, the installation stores electricity produced during the sunniest hours, when the grid cannot absorb everything, and releases it later. Verso Energy is simultaneously starting construction of a 23 MW / 46 MWh battery at VÃ©signeul-sur-Marne, in the Marne department. The Gueugnon site, launched in July 2025, includes a 23.1 MWp floating photovoltaic park. Huawei supplied the batteries, while CEME and Bouhet TP carried out the construction. According to Verso Energy, combining panels and batteries makes it the largest hybrid floating solar plant in France. Other players are developing comparable projects, such as Nala Renewables, which started construction of a 125 MW/250 MWh battery storage project in Finland, or EDF and NYPA, which are partnering to develop 240 MW of solar in New York. A grid that cannot absorb everything At peak sunshine, the Gueugnon plant can produce more electricity than the grid can absorb, the company says. Until the reinforcement planned by Enedis in 2028, the battery stores the midday surplus instead of dissipating it, then feeds it back later. Total investment, covering the solar plant and the batteries, stands at about â¬27 million. Company Huawei: company profile Verso Energy presents these solutions as flexibility tools, meaning the ability to shift electricity production or consumption over time. They would help balance the power system as new uses grow, including data centers, mobility, heat pumps, and hydrogen and synthetic fuel plants. Storage, a segment gaining speed for Verso Energy Battery storage has become a priority for the company, which has been accelerating in this segment since 2025. The VÃ©signeul-sur-Marne project, acquired in late 2025, is nearly four times more powerful than the Gueugnon one. Verso Energy operates these batteries with its own teams, which run the facilities and market the stored electricity, an activity known as "aggregation". The batteries are monetized in two ways: by selling electricity when demand is highest, and by providing grid services, notably maintaining the balance between production and consumption at all times. "The commissioning of this battery in Gueugnon shows our ability to combine solar production and storage, and to turn a grid constraint into an opportunity," says Antoine Huard, chief executive and co-founder of Verso Energy. He adds that this know-how should allow the company's future hydrogen and synthetic fuel plants to become flexibility tools, able to adapt their consumption to grid needs. The company also says it is leading the development of eight e-fuel production units in France and Finland, and reports 2 GW of renewable energy projects in development, under construction or in operation. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: An ambitious ETS can strengthen European competitiveness The Commission’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) proposal maintains the pathway towards decarbonisation by 2050 but risks slowing down industrial renewal in Europe. Co-legislators should keep the supply of allowances in check to enable frontrunner investments in decarbonisation. In her State of the European Union speech, President Ursula von der Leyen correctly noted that our dependence on fossil fuels has led to over 90 billion euros in additional costs, “without a single molecule of energy added”. A large part of that amount flowed outside of Europe. She also set out the alternative: an electrified Europe that could cut the fossil fuel import bill by 260 billion euros a year. She also reiterated her support for the EU’s climate targets, which are the basis for flagship energy and climate legislation of this mandate: namely, the revision of the EU Emissions Trading System, which the Commission adopted in mid-July this year. It’s not just the destination that matters The Commission’s proposal does indeed align the ETS with the EU’s emission reduction target. But in addition to the destination, the journey there matters: the Commission’s proposal and the alternative option included in the Parliament’s draft report would increase the volume of allowances released by roughly 30–40 percent between 2030 and 2040. Furthermore, free allocation would continue for several years longer. These changes would weaken the incentives for the deployment of clean technologies in Europe. In practice, a significantly less ambitious trajectory for cutting emissions would affect European companies investing in the development of clean technologies and production of near-zero emissions materials. Manufacturers like Metso, Andritz and Valmet provide state-of-the art solutions for industrial processes such as clean steelmaking and hydrogen production. Metal producers such as SSAB, Outokumpu and Boliden offer low-carbon metals for customers globally, with plans to go even further. Furthermore, all of this is supported by a strong grid technology sector, whose ranks include companies like ABB and Prysmian. In many of these sectors, European companies remain global leaders and the EU, with ambitious policies like the ETS, has built an excellent environment for deploying their technologies. A large number of countries and regions are following Europe’s example, with the share of global emissions covered by carbon pricing on the rise. The IEA estimates the global market for clean technologies to grow rapidly from the current 1.2 trillion to 2–5 trillion USD by 2035. There is also significant untapped potential in the market for near-zero emissions materials such as clean steel, that will, according to the IEA, remain unrealised without a strong policy push. Taking a giant leap requires trust To take the next step in decarbonisation, gradual change is not enough: we need frontrunner investments in ground-breaking technologies, such as steelmaking based on clean electricity and hydrogen. Trust in the system is crucial for turning plans into reality: the ETS works not only because it encourages companies to cut emissions here and now but also in the long run. That helps companies plan long-term and make investments in innovative new technologies instead of only making their existing processes more efficient. Keeping the increase in in the volume of released allowances more modest than in the Commission’s proposal is important for securing that trust. Similarly, sticking to the previously agreed timeline for phasing out free allocation is crucial. Putting revenues to work The ETS does come with costs. But unlike the money spent on imported fossil fuels, ETS revenues stay in the coffers of the EU and the Member States. Yet only around 5 percent of them are currently channelled back to industry to speed up decarbonisation. This needs to change: smarter use of the revenues and free allocation can help kickstart the switch to clean steelmaking, fuels and feedstocks. The need to develop and tune the EU ETS has been part and parcel of the journey from the beginning. The revision of the ETS is an opportunity to prove that we can also persist, by holding the agreed course on the cap and free allocation, and by putting the system’s own revenues to work. In doing so, we can also show that climate action and competitiveness can go hand in hand. TIF recommendations for the revision of the EU ETS - Align the cap with the 90 % emissions reduction target while keeping the cumulative number of issued allowances in check: an ambitious LRF in the early 2030s is crucial for achieving this goal. - Ensure that the revenues collected are channelled back to the sectors affected by the EU ETS - Shape free allocation into an instrument for speeding up the decarbonisation in Europe, especially in energy-intensive industry - Allocate EU funding to projects based on excellence - Include a broad range of permanent carbon removal technologies in the EU ETS

artigo.texto: Data centers face a sweeping new power regime Lawmakers are considering forcing data centers to shoulder new costs and restrictions while speeding up the energy infrastructure needed to power the AI boom. Why it matters: The bipartisan legislation, unveiled last week, represents the most aggressive response yet from Washington to data centers amid growing backlash over their energy and environmental impacts. Driving the news: The provisions are part of broader Senate legislation aimed at speeding up permitting for energy — but make no mistake: The data-center measures are significant and would go far beyond Washington's largely voluntary efforts to date. - The bill's sponsors say it would accelerate energy development while ensuring data centers pay their share of grid upgrades. "I don't think we've seen it before," said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, about the proposed additional costs and restrictions. - "But I don't think we've seen growth that's comparable to data centers today, and I certainly don't know any industry whose electricity usage has captured so much political attention." Between the lines: For tech companies, the bill cuts both ways. Congress would make it easier to build the energy infrastructure they need while erecting a sweeping framework aimed at keeping other electricity customers from footing the bill. "Just to be candid, having some teeth on data center accountability and ratepayer protection is just table stakes to getting a deal done," said Jane Flegal, a former White House official under President Biden and now a senior fellow at the nonprofit Searchlight Institute. The big picture: Congress has been talking about overhauling permitting for years. The AI boom has given lawmakers an urgent reason to finally act: America suddenly needs enormous amounts of new power infrastructure, fast. - Faster approvals for power plants and transmission lines could directly benefit data centers struggling to secure enough electricity for their expansion. How it works: The bill reaches into virtually every part of the relationship between large data centers and the electric grid. - Data centers would be required to pay both their share of the existing transmission network and the incremental transmission costs needed to serve them, reversing a decades-old federal pricing policy that generally prevents charging both. This is the biggie, but it doesn't stop there. - New data centers of at least 20 megawatts would have to bear the incremental costs they impose across the power system, including generation, storage, transmission and distribution. - Regulators at both the federal and state levels could charge large data centers even more than those incremental costs — and use the excess to reduce other customers' bills. - Data centers would remain on the hook for infrastructure costs even if they stop buying electricity before those costs have been recovered. Utilities would also have to secure financial guarantees before building infrastructure to serve them, protecting ratepayers if projects don't materialize. Zoom in: States are already moving aggressively to protect ratepayers, with dozens of policies pending or in place across more than half the states aimed at making data centers shoulder more of the costs of serving them. - The bill would explicitly give states wide latitude to go further, including treating data centers less favorably than other large industrial customers, competitively allocating access to electricity and requiring them to secure new power supplies or accept limits on electricity use. What they're saying: Not much publicly, yet. The Data Center Coalition, which represents companies across the industry, said it is still reviewing the legislation. - Microsoft, Google and Nvidia declined to comment, while Meta didn't respond to a request for comment. - Amazon energy policy director Craig Sundstrom said the aging grid and slow permitting are putting pressure on electricity costs, adding that the bill "could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster." The intrigue: One tech industry official called some provisions an "unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment" for a single industry. - The official, who spoke anonymously to discuss industry deliberations, said tougher grid-connected requirements could encourage some developers to build more power systems completely off-grid instead — potentially undermining the overarching purpose of the bill. The other side: Travis Fisher, a former Trump White House energy official now at the libertarian Cato Institute, said he has "mild support" for the approach despite concerns about setting a discriminatory precedent. - He said the provisions "break new ground" at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission but are consistent with the White House's ratepayer-protection pledge many of the largest data center companies have already signed. What we're watching: Flegal said she would be "incredibly surprised" if tech companies ultimately oppose the broader package. What's next: With the Senate out of town ahead of the midterm elections, lawmakers and stakeholders have plenty of time to push for changes before a possible lame-duck debate. AI is moving fast. CleanChoice Energy has secured more than US$166 million in financing for two solar photovoltaic projects in the US Northeast, the Dolan project in New York at roughly 27MW and the Kylertown project in Pennsylvania at roughly 28MW. The package included a US$105 million construction loan from Investec Bank, which acted as lead arranger, green loan structuring agent and collateral agent. BHI, the US branch of Bank Hapoalim, BM and Stifel Bank served as coordinating lead arrangers. Advantage Capital supplied a US$61 million tax equity commitment for the portfolio. Both projects are expected to reach commercial operations in 2027. Separately, distributed energy company Maxwell Power has closed an US$800 million investment from private equity firm Fairtide Partners to acquire battery storage and solar PV power projects. The deal follows investments of US$250 million and US$750 million in 2024 and June 2026, lifting Fairtide's total commitment to US$1.8 billion for projects developed by Maxwell. Maxwell said it has helped its consumer and small commercial customers achieve US$100 million in future energy savings so far this year. The company also relocated its headquarters from San Diego, California, to Salt Lake City, Utah, a move it described as fulfilling a promise to Utah Senator John Curtis. In a third transaction, independent power producer Lydian Energy and infrastructure asset manager Infranity agreed on a US$300 million holding company credit facility intended to support expansion of Lydian's 6GW portfolio of solar PV and utility-scale battery energy storage systems. The bespoke facility is based on Lydian Energy's existing operating and construction-ready assets and is designed to give the company added flexibility to accelerate build-out of its business pipeline. Lydian said the financing will help it advance projects from development through construction and retain ownership of operating assets. Lydian Energy is backed by Exelsior Energy Capital. Sacha Kamp, global head of debt investment at Infranity, characterized the transaction as resting on a portfolio of high-quality contracted projects and a strong pipeline of energy infrastructure assets developed and owned by Lydian, adding that the support of an experienced and committed sponsor provides a foundation for long-term growth. artigo.texto: FREELANDER Details Powertrain, Battery and All-Terrain Technology for International Left-Hand Drive FREELANDER 8 Source: GlobeNewswire ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates, Oct. 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- FREELANDER has detailed the powertrain, battery, chassis and all-terrain technology of the international left-hand drive variant of FREELANDER 8, following its unveiling at the brand’s Global Brand Launch in Abu Dhabi on 29 September 2026. Developed for a wide range of driving conditions, FREELANDER 8 brings together premium quality, everyday comfort and all-terrain capability. Its electrified powertrain, adaptive chassis and intelligent terrain management are designed to support journeys ranging from urban commuting to demanding off-road environments. The figures in this release apply to the Middle East market model only; specifications vary by market and trim level. 460 kW hybrid powertrain and 110 km of all-electric range The Middle East market model combines a 2.0T Dedicated Hybrid Engine with a 34.12 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and dual-motor all-wheel drive. The system delivers up to 460 kW of peak power and 662 N·m of peak torque, with 0–100 km/h acceleration in 5.8 seconds. With a full tank and a fully charged battery, FREELANDER 8 delivers a total range of 886 km and an all-electric range of 110 km, both measured on the combined cycle. Actual range varies with driving conditions and use. The battery supports 11 kW AC charging and DC fast charging from 20% to 80% in 20 minutes or less. Dual-chamber air suspension and Continuously Controlled Damping The chassis combines dual-chamber air suspension with Continuously Controlled Damping (CCD), offering a maximum ground clearance of 266 mm. Adjustable ride height and damping help the vehicle respond to changing road conditions, supporting ride comfort on paved roads and clearance over uneven terrain. The All-Terrain Dual Lock System, combining a Virtual Central Differential Lock and an Electronic Limited-Slip Differential (e-LSD), manages torque distribution to help maintain traction on low-grip surfaces and during cross-axle conditions. Nine modes bring powertrain and chassis control together The i-ATS (Intelligent All-Terrain System) offers nine modes: seven terrain programmes, including Sand Mode, plus Smart Mode and Expert Mode. Working with the electrified powertrain and chassis, it helps the driver adapt to changing surfaces. Under the relevant test conditions, FREELANDER 8 can pass an 800 mm cross-axle test, climb a 70% gradient, equivalent to approximately 35 degrees, and wade through water up to 900 mm deep. These capabilities support driving across environments including sand, rough ground, steep slopes and water crossings. Off-road and wading capability remains subject to the vehicle’s operating limits and appropriate driving conditions. International roll-out begins in left-hand drive markets The Middle East is FREELANDER’s strategic starting point for international expansion. The roll-out will proceed in stages, beginning with left-hand drive markets before expanding to right-hand drive and EU specification markets. The international left-hand drive variant will make its dynamic debut at the 2026 Chery International User Summit in Wuhu this October. About FREELANDER FREELANDER is a British Premium Intelligent All-Terrain Brand, jointly developed by JLR and Chery. JLR owns the FREELANDER brand and has established a dedicated FREELANDER Design Hub that leads its design. Chery provides advanced intelligent technology and a top-tier global supply chain. The brand is supported by a strong global foundation, including more than 5,000 employees, five strategic hubs, and fully integrated capabilities spanning design, R&D, manufacturing, and global operations. artigo.texto: Amazon Commits $1 Billion to US Data Center Communities Amid AI Backlash - Amazon will invest more than $1 billion over five years in US communities hosting its data centers, targeting education, workforce training, energy affordability and water preservation. - AWS says it is 75% of the way toward its 2030 water-positive goal, as scrutiny grows over the electricity and water demands of AI infrastructure. - More than 100 data center moratoriums are under consideration across the US, raising political and investment risks as technology companies accelerate AI infrastructure spending. Amazon is committing more than $1 billion over five years to communities hosting its US data centers. The investment comes as the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure faces growing resistance over energy costs, water consumption and local impacts. Amazon Web Services will direct the funding through its new Built Together framework. It will support education, job training, energy affordability, water preservation and other community priorities. The initiative adds a community investment component to one of the largest private infrastructure expansions underway in the United States. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025. Large projects or expansions are now underway across several states, including Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia and Mississippi. AI growth collides with local infrastructure concerns Data centers provide the computing capacity required to train and operate AI models. Their rapid expansion has also intensified questions about who bears the infrastructure costs. Communities across the US have raised concerns about electricity demand, utility bills, water use and pressure on local infrastructure. More than 100 data center moratoriums are currently being considered nationwide, according to Amazon. That opposition creates a growing governance challenge for technology companies and policymakers. It also adds a political dimension ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. AWS CEO Matt Garman framed continued construction as an economic and national security priority. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it,” Garman said. Amazon compared the current expansion of digital infrastructure with the construction of the US interstate highway system. However, the company stressed one major difference. Private companies, rather than taxpayers, are financing much of today’s infrastructure buildout. AI infrastructure is increasingly tied to healthcare, education, financial services, cybersecurity, defense and scientific research. That broadening role has strengthened the case for investment while increasing scrutiny of its environmental footprint. RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Adds 50+ Mercedes Electric Trucks in Germany Water and energy move higher on the agenda Amazon’s investment framework seeks to address some of the most contentious environmental issues surrounding data centers. AWS has committed to becoming water positive across its data center operations by 2030. The company said it is now 75% of the way toward that goal. Water positive means returning more water to communities than its operations consume. The commitment has become increasingly relevant as new data centers expand into regions facing competing demands for water and electricity. Energy affordability is another focus of the $1 billion program. Rising data center demand has prompted questions about grid investment and whether households could face higher costs as utilities build infrastructure to serve large technology customers. For Amazon, addressing those concerns has become part of maintaining community support for continued expansion. Community acceptance becomes an investment risk The scale of proposed data center development means community relations are moving from corporate philanthropy into core infrastructure strategy. Moratoriums, permitting disputes and public opposition can delay projects and raise development costs. They can also complicate the long-term power procurement and grid planning needed to support AI investment. Amazon’s Built Together framework gives communities a role in determining how funds are allocated. That approach could help companies align investments with local concerns rather than applying a uniform national model. For executives and investors, the broader issue extends beyond Amazon. AI growth depends on physical infrastructure that requires land, power, water and political approval. The next phase of the AI investment cycle will therefore depend on more than access to capital and computing technology. Developers will need credible plans for resource use, community benefits and energy affordability. As governments compete for leadership in AI, those local constraints are becoming part of the global race for digital infrastructure. The companies that manage them effectively may gain an advantage in securing the permits, power and public support required for continued expansion.
