artigo.texto: The voluntary carbon market (VCM) continued to move away from a volume-driven model in the third quarter of 2026, with carbon credit retirements falling even as buyers spent more on the credits they purchased. - Carbon credit retirements reached 30.6 million in Q3 2026, down 9% from 33.7 million a year earlier, according to carbon market data provider Sylvera. However, the value of those retirements rose to $211.8 million from $190.6 million in Q3 2025. The difference points to a market where buyers are becoming more selective. The report reveals that the average price paid for a retired credit climbed to $6.92 in Q3, compared with $5.66 a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, the average reached $6.12, up from $5.40 during the same period in 2025. The trend also builds on what Sylvera identified earlier this year. In the first half of 2026, retirement volumes were down 9% year over year, while market value increased. By the end of Q3, however, cumulative retirements had edged above 2025 levels at 130.3 million credits, compared with 129.1 million through the first three quarters of last year. Meanwhile, year-to-date retirement value reached $798 million, 14% above the $697.3 million recorded a year earlier. Quality Is Taking a Bigger Role in Carbon Credit Pricing The strongest signal from the latest data comes from the widening gap between higher- and lower-quality credits. Credits rated BBB or higher represented only 18% of rated retirement volume in Q3. Yet they generated 42% of rated market value. This suggests buyers are willing to pay significantly more for credits that meet stronger quality expectations rather than simply purchasing the cheapest available supply. The premium becomes even clearer across individual project categories. - For afforestation, reforestation and revegetation (ARR), BBB+ credits averaged $23.47 per tonne in Q3, compared with $12.80 for credits rated BB or below. Improved forest management (IFM) showed a similar divide. BBB+ IFM credits reached $21.07, while lower-rated credits averaged $12.79. - REDD+ also saw a sharp quality-driven price difference. BBB+ REDD+ credits averaged $7.75 in Q3, up 58% from $4.90 a year earlier. Lower-rated REDD+ credits increased from $2.70 to $3.56 over the same period. As a result, the REDD+ price gap between the two quality groups nearly doubled from $2.20 to $4.19. The trend suggests that buyers are not abandoning nature-based credits altogether. Instead, they appear increasingly willing to distinguish between projects based on perceived quality. - RELATED: Carbon Credit Prices Explained: What Determines the Value of a Carbon Credit? - LIVE PRICES: Carbon Credit Prices Today 2026 | Live Chart, EU ETS & VCM Renewables Still Dominate, But Their Market Position Is Changing Renewable energy projects accounted for 41% of Q3 retirements, giving them the largest share among project categories. However, Sylvera cautions that the increase in market share does not represent renewed growth in renewable credit demand. Renewable retirements totaled 40.7 million credits during the first nine months of 2026, roughly unchanged from the same period in 2025. That remains far below the 77.1 million credits retired during the first three quarters of 2022. Full-year renewable retirements peaked at 99.7 million in 2022 before falling to 49.3 million in 2025. The quality issue is particularly important here. Sylvera does not rate renewable projects above C because many grid-connected renewable projects face additionality concerns. As a result, renewables accounted for 76% of B/C/D-rated retirement volume in Q3. That helped push the share of B/C/D-rated credits across the entire retirement market to 66.1%, the highest level since Q3 2023. In other words, renewable credits continue to provide substantial market volume, but their presence also weighs on the overall quality profile of retirements. REDD+ Demand Normalizes While Agriculture Gains Ground REDD+ accounted for 18% of Q3 retirements, down sharply from 38% in Q2. However, the comparison needs context because Q2’s unusually high share was largely driven by one major retirement. Beyond that temporary spike, REDD+ demand appears relatively stable, with retirement activity spread across Colombia, Brazil, Cambodia, Peru, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Agriculture was a more notable growth area. Its share of retirements increased from 2.55% to 7.82%, while retirement volume more than doubled. Energy and utility companies played an important role in that shift, with agriculture representing 28% of their Q3 retirement mix, compared with 6.8% a year earlier. This diversification matters because the market is gradually moving beyond a small group of traditional project categories. Buyers are showing greater interest in credits tied to agriculture, forest management, and other project types where measurable climate and environmental benefits can support stronger pricing. Corporate Buyers Are Still Active Despite the overall decline in quarterly retirement volumes, major corporate buyers continued to transact at scale. Yamato Transport and Corpay each retired about 2 million credits in Q3, making them the largest retirees during the quarter. Primax Colombia followed with just over 1 million. For the first nine months of 2026, Eni remained the largest retiree with nearly 9 million credits. TASC, Organización Terpel, Engie and Lenovo also ranked among the largest buyers. At the same time, Shell’s retreat remains significant. The company retired only about 496,000 credits through the first three quarters of 2026, compared with roughly 7 million during the same period in 2025. Sylvera first highlighted the decline in its Q2 report, and the latest numbers suggest the pullback has continued. artigo.texto: Pennsylvania governor candidates debate data centers and education Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity debated key issues, including data center development and education, during a gubernatorial debate at the state Capitol in Harrisburg. Video above: Top news stories, weather forecast. Candidates clash over data center development The development of large data centers has been a major political topic this year, with Shapiro and Garrity expressing differing views on the issue. Shapiro defended his decision not to implement a moratorium, instead using an executive order to protect communities. "If a local community does not want that data center to be built in its community, it will not be built. That policy won't even be heard. That proposal won't even be heard by the Commonwealth when it comes to permitting," Shapiro said. Garrity, who earlier this year called for a pause on hyperscale data center development, did not commit to a specific timeline but emphasized collaboration with stakeholders. "Real leaders don't need that long of a pause. You get all the stakeholders around the table and you find out what you need to protect ratepayers and protect communities. So as long as it takes," Garrity said. Education funding and achievement take center stage Education funding and student achievement were also key topics during the debate. Garrity stressed the importance of ensuring students meet academic benchmarks. "By the third grade, your child needs to be able to read, and if they can't, there are a lot of steps you can take to make sure that they're not falling behind. They need to stay at that grade level. By the time they get to the eighth grade, they need to read and do math at grade level," Garrity said. Shapiro highlighted public school investments during his term and expressed support for both public education and private school vouchers. "It is not an either-or... either we invest in public education or we make those investments in educational opportunities. It's both/and. I want to see investments in public schools like we have done, and I'm open to seeing the Democrats and Republicans come together to be able to provide that opportunity," Shapiro said. Budget challenges ahead Shapiro also addressed his veto of lifeline scholarships during his first year in office, explaining that it was due to lawmakers not having a deal in place that would have upheld the state budget. The candidates are expected to share their thoughts on budgeting challenges in what could be a tighter year for Pennsylvania’s savings.

artigo.texto: BYD puts battery cells directly in cooling liquid in new patent BYD has filed an invention patent application describing a battery cabinet that separates its electrical equipment from a lower compartment where cell modules are submerged in dielectric fluid. The design centres on a relatively simple question with significant consequences for an immersion-cooled battery system: how do electrical connections cross the boundary between a dry compartment and a liquid-filled one? Published by the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) on October 5, 2026, as CN 122868832 A, the application covers battery cabinets and energy storage equipment. Filed in March 2025, it describes a two-chamber enclosure in which the cooling medium surrounds the cell modules while electrical equipment remains outside the liquid volume. Why immersion cooling changes the battery enclosure Many contemporary battery systems use indirect liquid cooling. Coolant circulates through aluminium cold plates positioned against the battery modules, with heat passing through the cell casing and intervening materials before reaching the coolant. Immersion cooling changes that arrangement. Instead of bringing coolant to a separate cooling plate, the battery modules sit directly in a non-conductive dielectric fluid. Heat can therefore transfer from the wetted surfaces of the modules directly into the surrounding fluid. The arrangement shortens the thermal path between the battery and the cooling medium, but it also changes the enclosure problem. The liquid must be contained, while electrical components and connection points that are not intended to operate in the fluid must remain isolated from it. That boundary is where BYD’s patent application focuses. Production battery systems still rely on indirect cooling. The distinction is easier to see against BYD and CATL’s existing production architectures. BYD’s MC Cube energy storage system integrates Blade batteries using its cell-to-system architecture, while the MC Cube-T specifies liquid cooling. CATL’s EnerOne and EnerC storage systems likewise use liquid cooling, with cooling plates positioned outside the battery modules. CATL’s Qilin passenger-vehicle battery uses a different packaging arrangement, integrating a liquid-cooling plate into a multifunctional interlayer positioned between adjacent cells. These systems keep the cooling medium in a defined thermal path rather than surrounding the battery modules directly. BYD’s new filing describes another arrangement: the cell modules occupy the liquid-filled chamber itself, while electrical equipment is kept in a separate dry chamber. The resulting engineering problem is not simply how to transfer heat. It is how to maintain an electrical connection across a liquid-tight boundary. BYD routes the connections through the top CN 122868832 A divides the cabinet into two isolated chambers: - Chamber 1: An upper dry compartment containing electrical equipment components. - Chamber 2: A lower liquid compartment containing cell modules submerged in dielectric fluid. The connection between the two chambers is routed through the upper portion of the liquid compartment. Rather than bringing the electrical and signal leads through the floor or side walls of the wet chamber, the design directs them upward before they enter the dry compartment. Location matters because hydrostatic pressure increases with liquid depth. A sealing interface positioned higher in the chamber therefore experiences less hydrostatic pressure than an equivalent interface positioned deeper in the liquid. The electrical equipment remains outside the liquid volume while maintaining the connection to the submerged battery modules. In other words, the filing does not rely solely on the fluid’s cooling dielectric properties to separate the battery’s thermal and electrical environments. It also uses the cabinet’s physical layout to keep the electrical connection points above the main liquid volume. The filing is about a cabinet, not a new vehicle battery The application covers battery cabinets and energy storage equipment and does not identify a passenger vehicle application. It specifies dielectric fluid, including hydrocarbon- or ester-based formulations, rather than standard liquid coolant. The filing therefore describes an immersion-cooled stationary battery enclosure with a dry electrical compartment and a wet battery compartment. That distinction matters because a patent application is not evidence that the architecture has entered production. The application remains under substantive examination, and BYD has not announced commercial production plans for the design. For now, CN 122868832 A documents an enclosure architecture and a specific way of routing electrical connections through the boundary between its dry and liquid-filled sections.

artigo.texto: Old Town became the second Greater Bangor community to pass a short-term ban on data centers Monday. The six-month ban, which outlaws the development of data centers in the city’s industrial zones, is retroactive to Sept. 8, when the Old Town City Council first discussed the possibility of a ban. Data center developments are already not allowed in other zones, according to the city’s land use ordinance. Communities across Maine have passed moratoriums, or temporary bans, on data center developments this year due to the limited knowledge of how they will affect municipalities. The bans, which are generally set to last six months, give towns time to learn about the technology and draft laws to regulate its development. The Old Town City Council passed the ban unanimously at its Monday meeting. Due to extensive conversation about a possible ban during a September meeting, discussion on the ban Monday lasted for about one minute. “I think that our conversation last time was pretty substantial and overarching, and as previously stated, it gives us plenty of time to adequately assess the risks and benefits and pros and cons of all that this super complex, super new thing entails,” Councilor Zachary Wyles said. Residents reached out to councilors before the ban was proposed to say they didn’t want a data center to come to Old Town. Old Town could be a desirable location for a data center because of its history with businesses like Nine Dragons Paper and Old Town Canoe, and its industrial zones, Council President Christian Pushor said at the Sept. 8 meeting. Councilors previously said a long-term ban in the form of zoning changes would be sent to a public referendum to allow voters to decide. The next possible election date would be June 2027. The six-month ban is set to expire in March, but an extension to June could be approved. “I feel like this is such a hot topic that I would like it to go to the public instead of relying on people who have the time and energy to contact us,” Councilor Katrina Wynn said on Sept. 8.

artigo.texto: 43 proposed power plants needed to fuel data centers listed across NEPA PHILADELPHIA (WOLF) — A new environmental report warning about Pennsylvania’s expected growth in natural-gas power generation comes as proposed power plants are already listed across much of northeastern and central Pennsylvania. PennEnvironment Research & Policy Center and Frontier Group project Pennsylvania could add 4.4 gigawatts of natural-gas capacity by the end of 2030, an increase of nearly 15% over the state’s existing gas footprint. The groups say growing demand from data centers is a major driver behind the proposed expansion. A separate Track Data Centers listing provided to FOX56 identifies 43 proposed power plants across the station’s coverage area. Lackawanna County has the largest number, with 15 proposals and 4.8 gigawatts of listed capacity. Luzerne County has nine proposals and 4.3 gigawatts of listed capacity. Three plants are listed in each of Carbon, Northampton and Schuylkill counties. Carbon County’s listed capacity is 350 megawatts, while Northampton and Schuylkill counties each have 1.2 gigawatts listed. Bradford, Monroe and Union counties each have two proposed plants. Listed capacity is 248 megawatts in Bradford County and 300 megawatts in Union County; no capacity figure was listed for Monroe County. One proposed plant is listed in each of Columbia, Lycoming, Montour and Wayne counties. The listed capacity figures total nearly 12.4 gigawatts in the counties where capacity was provided. The database listings may cover projects with different timelines and scopes than the statewide projections cited in PennEnvironment’s report. PennEnvironment says new gas plants can operate for 25 to 30 years and has called for a moratorium on new data centers, arguing that the projects could increase air pollution and long-term greenhouse-gas emissions. The organization’s conclusions and policy recommendations reflect its environmental advocacy position.

artigo.texto: Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) delivered more vehicles than Wall Street expected in the third quarter of 2026, giving investors a reason to turn more positive on the electric vehicle maker’s near-term outlook. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, beating the company-compiled analyst consensus of 461,974. Deliveries also rose 1.3% from 480,126 vehicles in Q2. However, they remained 2.1% below the 497,099 vehicles delivered in Q3 2025. The stronger-than-expected result helped Tesla stock rebound. Shares closed at $370.59 on October 2, up 4.7% in the session. Reuters reported that the stock gained more than 5% earlier in trading after the delivery figures were released. Still, Tesla faces a growing challenge from Chinese EV giant BYD. BYD’s battery-electric vehicle sales continued to pull further ahead of Tesla during the quarter. Tesla Q3 Deliveries Beat Estimates Tesla’s Q3 delivery result came in well above the latest company-compiled consensus. Analysts surveyed by Tesla had expected 461,974 deliveries, with a median estimate of 463,406. Tesla ultimately delivered 486,532 vehicles, exceeding the consensus by about 24,600 vehicles. The Model 3 and Model Y remained the company’s main volume drivers. Tesla delivered 478,237 Model 3/Y vehicles during the quarter, compared with just 8,295 deliveries across its other models. Production, meanwhile, reached 464,391 vehicles. Tesla also deployed 13.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage products during Q3. That figure was below the 15.9 GWh analyst consensus, highlighting that Tesla’s energy business remains an important part of the company’s broader growth story. The delivery beat is significant because analysts had entered the quarter expecting a decline. FactSet estimates cited by MarketWatch had pointed to roughly 461,000 vehicles, or a 7% year-over-year decline. Instead, Tesla limited the decline to about 2%. Tesla vs. BYD: The EV Gap Is Growing Despite Tesla’s better-than-expected quarter, its competition with BYD is becoming more intense. BYD sold 762,478 battery-electric passenger vehicles during Q3, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. That was up nearly 31% from a year earlier and 37% from Q2. As a result, BYD sold about 275,946 more battery-electric vehicles than Tesla during the quarter. The comparison needs some context. Tesla reports deliveries of its vehicles, while BYD sells both battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids under its broader new-energy vehicle category. BYD sold 1.32 million new-energy vehicles in Q3, including both types. Total NEV sales rose 18.8% year over year. BYD also recorded 463,561 new-energy vehicle sales in September alone, its strongest monthly result of 2026. Overseas passenger vehicle and pickup shipments jumped 153.9% year over year to 179,877 in September, Reuters reported. This international expansion could become increasingly important for the global EV market. It also shows how competition is moving beyond traditional EV strongholds as Chinese manufacturers expand into overseas markets. Sustainability Remains a Key Part of Tesla’s Story Tesla’s delivery numbers also matter from a sustainability perspective because more EV sales can accelerate the shift away from gasoline-powered vehicles. The International Energy Agency said global electric car sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, with EVs accounting for one in four new cars sold worldwide. China remained the largest EV market, accounting for six out of 10 electric cars sold globally. - Tesla says its products helped avoid 37 million metric tons of CO₂e emissions in its 2025 Impact Report. The company’s sustainability strategy also extends beyond vehicles to battery storage, solar energy, and its supply chain. The company also highlighted the emissions benefit of its electric vehicles over their operating lives. It estimates that one Tesla vehicle can avoid about 32 metric tons of CO₂ emissions over its lifetime compared with a comparable gasoline-powered vehicle. However, the actual benefit varies by factors such as electricity generation, vehicle efficiency, and driving patterns. However, EV growth does not eliminate the environmental impact of manufacturing. Batteries require minerals such as lithium, nickel, graphite, and other materials, while vehicle production and electricity generation also create emissions. That makes the growth of energy storage particularly relevant. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of storage products in Q3, while the company-compiled analyst consensus had expected 15.9 GWh. Large-scale batteries can help integrate renewable power into electricity systems by storing electricity when supply is high and releasing it when demand rises. Can Tesla’s Q3 Delivery Beat Support Its Stock? Tesla stock entered October under pressure after a volatile year. Shares closed at $370.59 on October 2, although the latest delivery beat provided some relief. Investors are now looking beyond vehicle sales. Tesla’s valuation increasingly depends on its plans for robotaxis, AI, robotics and energy storage, while its automotive business remains critical to funding those investments. Tesla will report its full Q3 financial results on October 21. The earnings report should give investors a clearer view of vehicle margins, revenue, cash flow, and spending on its next-generation businesses. For now, the delivery beat strengthens Tesla’s near-term position. However, BYD’s growing lead in battery-electric vehicle sales highlights the competitive pressure facing Tesla as global EV adoption accelerates. The longer-term sustainability opportunity remains significant, but Tesla must balance EV growth with improving manufacturing efficiency, battery supply chains and the emissions impact of its operations.

artigo.texto: Springfield, IL-(Effingham Radio)- As more Illinois municipalities weigh moratoriums on data center construction, Gov. J.B. Pritzker is pressing state lawmakers to pass uniform regulations – despite light pushback from some who view the proposed rules as potentially misguided. The Illinois General Assembly failed to pass legislation to further regulate data centers statewide through the POWER Act before the end of the spring session on June 1. Pritzker said recently he’s not concerned about getting short-term solutions passed sooner than when state lawmakers return to Springfield. Pritzker noted there isn’t always transparency for communities when a data center project is being pitched in a locality. State Rep. Jeff Keicher, R-Sycamore, said data center non-disclosure agreements aren’t much different from privacy measures put in place when others buy a property, but there should be transparency after that. He also said there’s been benefits in his district including significant decreases to the property tax levy – though he acknowledged there are bad actors in the space. Lawmakers are set to return to Springfield for a six-day veto session from Nov. 17-19, and Dec. 1-3. The legislature is expected to return to bills that didn’t pass in May, such as the Power Act. artigo.texto: Champaign County residents voice opposition to potential data centers The county could vote on an ordinance before the moratorium is lifted in April CHAMPAIGN, Ill. (WAND) — The repeated message heard from Champaign County residents — they don’t want a data center in their backyard. “Letting this data center come and be here in our county would detrimentally affect all businesses, and that would just be a problem for the continued survival of us as people,” said one community member during public comment. After Mahomet’s recent rally against potential data center additions, Champaign residents said they don’t want the same situation playing out in their community. “I really just wanted to reiterate how important this was before — how close things got with Mahomet,” said another resident. “That’s very scary for everyone, and I really think it lit a fire in the community to make this ordinance have as much teeth as possible.” Some board members also shared their own insight on the potential addition. “We can still cover a substantial amount of Champaign County, and other counties will look to us just like we look toward Aurora,” said Prairie Rivers Network Director of Climate Policy Andrew Rehn. “I think we have a chance to be a leader here.” No decisions were made during the meeting, but this won’t be the last chance for the public to weigh in. “Let’s just think big on this and make it as tough as possible for any data center to be built here. Thank you,” said one resident. Copyright 2026 WAND. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: IMPERIAL — As part of their bus tour across 28 states, conservative non-profit organization Humans First stopped at Eager Park in Imperial to spread their message against an “unaccountable AI buildout” on Friday, Oct. 3. Despite the nationwide bus tour being called “AI Data Center Revolt,” Kylie Jane Kremer, Senior Advisor for Humans First, said the movement is not anti-AI or anti-AI data centers, but rather “America first.” “We’re definitely not anti-data center, we’re not anti-AI; we’re not anti-tech, as I said. We believe we can do this in a way that is transparent and lets communities know what they’re getting into and what’s involved,” said Kremer. For Humans First, communities facing AI data center proposals should be the ones with the authority to welcome or reject the projects while having full transparency from the project developers and local officials. “If these data centers are so great, if they’re going to bring so many jobs and be so powerful in these communities and be this economic boom, why are they not being transparent?” said Kremer. ”Shouldn’t they be able to sell this to the American people very easily and tell them all the facts? Because if they’re so great, it should be an overwhelming yes. But they know that that’s not the truth, that these are not great for communities.” “People don’t want them, and so that’s why they’re having to go about it in sneaky ways where they’re doing NDAs, payouts, and that sort of thing,” explained Kremer. The bus tour transporting the Humans First team began their cross-country trip with stops at 35 different cities in Austin, Texas, and going as far east as Washington, D.C. The tour then made its way toward the West Coast, where it will reach San Francisco as its final stop on Monday, Oct. 5. Kremer explained that each city the Data Center Revolt bus tour stopped at was at different stages of an AI data center project, but their goal to elevate community voices and make them engaged stayed the same. Some cities face an uphill battle when it comes to opposing AI data centers, such as Jonesburg, Missouri, one of the stops made by Kremer and her team. Jonesburg is located in rural Montgomery County, which currently has two data centers under development, despite local opposition. “It’s a town of, I think, 640 people. They have roughly an $18 million county budget annually. Google and Amazon are going there and bringing two massive hyperscale data centers over $25 billion,” explained Kremer. “How does a town of 640 people with an $18 million annual budget even begin to fight that? So we went there; it’s about generational land, farmers, communities that really matter just like here in Imperial.” Tom Gaitens, Senior Advisor for Humans First, praised Imperial for their success in opposing the hyperscale AI data center proposed in Imperial County, which, if built, would be the largest data center in the state. “What you did here needs to be echoed around the country. What you did here, you’re heroes. You found out the process late in the game, and they tried to hide it from you,” said Gaitens. “They did not want to disclose this information in public hearings and allow you to see what your neighbors were going to be doing, but you are the heroes who stood up, faced this giant, a $10 billion giant, and you held it at bay.” Local opposition against data centers has been an issue that Democrats and Republicans find common ground on, with Kremer noting that the issue affects local communities as a whole, bringing them together against a common cause. Kremer stressed the importance of staying engaged in creating opposition to data centers, and despite meaningful victories, the issue of data centers is far from over. “We’re seeing time and time again that communities have wins, and then the people get complacent or, you know, have this victory and they kind of take a break from it. What happens when people let their guard down is that the big tech companies come back with bigger lawyers, smarter about the process,” said Kremer. “We are on track to have over 10,000 data centers in the United States by 2030. And right now we’re just roughly over 5000, so that will be doubling it. So this issue is not going away; it’s not just temporary, this is a long-term play that people need to remain engaged in,” explained Kremer.

artigo.texto: Demand for artificial intelligence data centers will continue to push shares of Vertiv higher, according to BMO Capital Markets. The firm initiated coverage of the stock on Sunday with an outperform rating and $329 price target, which implies roughly 30% upside from Friday's close. The company provinces digital infrastructure and hardware for data centers and other facilities, with data centers making up about 85% of its revenue, said analyst Daniel DiCicco. He called Vertiv a "premium data center play" that has already run up more than 900% in the last five years. Shares have pulled back from their peak in May and now offer an attractive entry point, he said. "Vertiv is well positioned as data centers are increasing in scale and intensity (more power to the rack) and demand for resilience and speed to deployment continues to increase," DiCicco wrote in a note to clients. VRT YTD mountain Vertiv year to date There are more than 4,700 data centers in the United States — and the number is growing . Some $6 billion was spent on land purchases in the U.S. for future data centers in the first half of 2026, according to commercial real estate firm Avison Young. That's a 79% increase from last year, the firm found. Vertiv's management has estimated that its $75 billion total addressable market is increasing 16% to 18% a year, with data centers growing 18% to 20% annually, DiCicco said. However, the company's long-term growth forecasts could be conservative, he noted. Plus, Vertiv has a full suite of offerings. The current rate for data center content is $3.25 to $3.75 per megawatt, but innovation, standardization, service growth and integrated systems can all push that higher, DiCicco pointed out. "VRT has positioned itself as one of the few providers capable of delivering a fully integrated power and thermal management solution across the entire data center," he said. Shares of Vertiv are up nearly 56% year to date. — CNBC's Tobias Burns contributed reporting.

artigo.texto: San Francisco approves, other cities consider bans and reviews on data center growth SANTA CLARA, Calif. - As artificial intelligence and digital services rapidly expand, several California local governments are stepping back to evaluate the footprint of data center development in their communities. Cities across the Bay Area and Southern California are considering pauses or reviewing long-standing policies to address rising concerns over energy demand, water usage, and environmental impacts. High demand prompts policy evaluation The City of Santa Clara stands as one of California's primary data center hubs. Despite its population of roughly 133,000 residents, Santa Clara currently hosts 56 data centers, with two additional projects in development. The industry has proven highly lucrative for Santa Clara, contributing $35 million annually in taxes directly into the city's general fund. However, high power demand prompted the city's municipal utility, Silicon Valley Power, to stop accepting new data center applications in 2023. Santa Clara officials are launching a year-long interdepartmental review of environmental, water, power, and quality-of-life impacts before updating local development rules. Regional moratoriums and community pushback Local perspective: In Oakland, City Council members are considering a 45-day temporary moratorium on new data center construction. Protesters gathered at Oakland City Hall ahead of a council vote scheduled for Tuesday night to voice concerns about local neighborhood impacts, high water consumption, and energy efficiency. Similarly, San Francisco supervisors unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on data center approvals, declaring an immediate threat to public health, safety, and welfare without comprehensive regulations in place. Supervisor Shamann Walton noted the pause allows the city time to study energy, water, air quality, land use, and community effects. Meanwhile, Southern California is taking a similar approach. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors received a proposal to permanently ban massive "hyperscale" data centers—frequently built to support resource-intensive AI workloads—while leaving allowances for smaller operations.

artigo.texto: Denver is taking its next step toward deciding where data centers can operate — and under what conditions — as concerns mount over their demands on electricity, water and surrounding neighborhoods. Mayor Mike Johnston and three Denver City Council members announced Wednesday the selection of 26 people to a working group tasked with developing recommendations for regulating the facilities. Recommended Stories “It will be Denver — not corporations — that decide if and how data centers may operate in our city,” Johnston said in a statement. “This group brings together people with different perspectives to help us get this right: setting clear rules, protecting Denver’s resources, and putting the interests of Denverites first. Let’s get to work.” The working group is comprised of wide swath of individuals representing utility, academia, healthcare and air quality as well as community members. The group is expected to create policy suggestions. Among those serving are Ean Thomas Tafoya, with GreenLatinos; Rev. Terrance D. Carroll, former speaker of the Colorado House of Representatives and Melissa Almond of Xcel Energy. More than 250 people applied, according to the mayor’s office. The first meeting is expected to be held Friday, with sessions streamed in English and Spanish. The community is encouraged to submit questions and comments. Privately owned, a data center houses IT infrastructure for building, running and delivering computer applications and services. It also stores and manages the associated data. Data centers date back to the 1940s with the U.S. military and one of the world’s first digital computers, which was developed at the University of Pennsylvania during World War II and required a dedicated space to house the machines. With the advent of microcomputers in the 1990s, data centers today dramatically reduce the amount of space required for IT operations. These microcomputers filled mainframe computer rooms, or servers, that became today’s “data centers.” The Denver metro area has 54 data centers, according to the Data Center Map. Nearly 2,800 data centers are planned or under construction nationwide, according to a 2025 American Edge Project report, which identified another 4,149 already operating. Fueled by America’s AI boom, the rapid expansion of data centers has drawn comparisons to the railroads of the 19th century, highways of the 1950s and broadband of the 1990s — even earning the description of a “modern-day Moonshot moment.” Dan Diorio at the Data Center Coalition said data centers are a positive investment for communities, adding that data center success goes hand-in-hand with the success of the community it’s built in. “It matters how a company responds, and overwhelmingly you’ll find good actors in this space,” he said about community concerns. “Transparency and trust matter.” But public opposition to data centers is mounting because of the water and electricity demands and other strains associated with them. More Americans believe data centers have a negative effect on the environment, energy costs and the quality of life than say they have a positive impact, according to a Pew Research Center poll earlier this year. In May, the Denver City Council unanimously voted to impose a one-year moratorium on permits and site development applications for data centers. Data centers permitted before May of this year are not subject to the moratorium. Other cities are also pushing back. Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman has said that the proposed Trident Data Center near Green Valley Ranch “must be stopped.” And the 170,000-square-foot CoreSite DE3 data center in Denver’s Elyria-Swansea neighborhood has sparked fierce protests from residents who have complained about the lack of notification prior to the city approving the project. Johnston’s working group also includes representatives from Globeville, Elyria and Swansea. “We will take our time and use this opportunity to ensure we are establishing protections for our communities and resources today and in the future,” Councilwoman Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez said in a statement. “I am grateful to the people who took the time to apply and are going to devote additional time and expertise to this process.” Reporters Deborah Grigsby and Kyla Pearce contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Data centers pedem redução de 90% do ICMS para equipamentos Brasscom relata resistência dos estados à proposta discutida no Confaz; entidades também cobram regulamentação do Redata. As entidades do setor de data centers negociam com o Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) uma redução de 90% do ICMS sobre equipamentos contemplados pelo Redata. Segundo Walter Wolff, diretor de projetos da Brasscom, a proposta enfrenta resistência dos estados e busca complementar os incentivos federais do regime. A discussão foi apresentada durante a abertura do Data Center World, nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro. De acordo com Wolff, o setor trabalha com uma lista de 25 equipamentos, concentrada em eletrônicos. A relação está em discussão com outras associações, incluindo representantes dos fabricantes brasileiros. O dirigente explicou que o foco da negociação está nos equipamentos de tecnologia, sem abranger toda a infraestrutura física dos empreendimentos. A Brasscom defende que o tratamento estadual acompanhe os benefícios federais para aumentar a competitividade do Brasil na disputa por projetos. Na avaliação de Wolff, a negociação deve considerar a concorrência com outros países pela instalação de data centers. A Conexis também participa da mobilização. Seu diretor jurídico, Bruno Cavalcanti, afirmou que a entidade assinou, com outras associações, um manifesto dirigido ao Confaz. “Não existe um Redata completo sem esse endereçamento do tema no Confaz”, declarou. Regulamentação ainda em discussão Além do ICMS, as entidades aguardam a regulamentação do Redata. Wolff afirmou que a expectativa é concluir essa etapa nas próximas semanas, mas reconheceu os obstáculos nas negociações. “Tem sido uma discussão extremamente difícil”, disse o dirigente da Brasscom. Segundo ele, as condições de fornecimento de energia aos data centers estão entre os assuntos discutidos. A definição dos equipamentos beneficiados também permanece pendente. Renan Lima Alves, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), explicou que a lista de classificações fiscais dos produtos ainda precisa ser divulgada, assim como os procedimentos para apresentação de pedidos de inclusão. Alves destacou a dificuldade de aproveitamento dos créditos tributários da aquisição de hardware na prestação dos serviços. Por isso, a entidade considera o tratamento do ICMS parte relevante da política de redução dos custos de implantação. Wolff também apontou a previsibilidade dos benefícios para os próximos cinco anos como um elemento importante para decisões de investimento de longo prazo. Incentivo à transferência de processamento Para o presidente da Equinix, Victor Arnaud, a combinação entre regulamentação do Redata, tratamento dos tributos estaduais e compatibilidade com a reforma tributária determinará as condições de aplicação do incentivo. O executivo identificou como oportunidade imediata a transferência para o Brasil de cargas de processamento que atendem ao mercado brasileiro, mas estão hospedadas no exterior. Segundo ele, a redução da diferença de custos pode estimular empresas a manter esses dados em território nacional. Arnaud ressaltou, porém, que a demanda por data centers já cresce independentemente do regime. Na avaliação do executivo, os incentivos podem ampliar esse movimento e melhorar as condições de atração de novos projetos.

artigo.texto: New battery chemistry could help lithium-sulfur batteries store more energy Lithium-sulfur batteries are an experimental alternative to today’s lithium-ion batteries that could store considerably more energy for their weight but have proved difficult to make durable and practical. Now, researchers at Vanderbilt University and the University of Maryland have demonstrated a new approach that could push their energy-storage potential further. In a study published in Nature Energy, the team developed a battery chemistry that allows sulfur to participate in an additional energy-storing reaction. The result is a sulfur-based battery that operates at a higher average voltage while also storing more charge. De-en Jiang, the H, said: The traditional way of thinking about lithium-sulfur batteries leaves some of sulfur’s redox power untapped, Eugene McBrayer Professor of Chemical Engineering and Professor of Chemistry. He is also a co-corresponding author of the study. “We wanted to see whether we could expand sulfur’s redox capability and use it to store more energy.” Getting more energy out of sulfur Sulfur has long attracted battery researchers because of its abundance and lower cost. Plus, it can store far more charge by weight than the materials commonly used in lithium-ion battery cathodes. The challenge has been that most lithium-sulfur batteries operate at a relatively low voltage. And the amount of energy a battery can store depends on both how much charge it holds and the voltage at which it operates. The researchers found a way to improve both functions. In a conventional lithium-sulfur battery, each sulfur atom can exchange two electrons as the battery charges and discharges. The new system extends that chemistry by introducing chlorine, allowing sulfur to exchange a third electron. That additional reaction also takes place at a higher voltage. In laboratory tests, the new chemistry increased sulfur’s charge-storage capacity by about 58% and raised the battery’s average operating voltage from about 2.05 volts to 2.54 volts compared with standard lithium-sulfur chemistry tested under the same conditions. The combination of the higher charge-storage capacity and the higher voltage allowed one kilogram of sulfur to store more than 1,700 watt-hours of energy in their experimental cell. Designing an electrolyte to make it work Making the new reaction reversible presented another challenge. The team needed chlorine to interact with sulfur during charging without allowing the resulting sulfur-chlorine compound to travel through the battery and react with its lithium-metal electrode. Researchers used molecular simulations to understand how lithium and chloride ions behave inside different electrolytes. Those calculations led to the design of an electrolyte in which chloride remains available to react with sulfur. The team also selected an electrolyte in which the sulfur-chlorine reaction product does not readily dissolve. That helps keep it where it belongs—inside the battery’s positive electrode—so the reaction can be reversed when the battery discharges. Experiments using several different spectroscopy techniques confirmed that sulfur repeatedly moved through the newly accessible chemical state as the cells were charged and discharged. An early demonstration The researchers ultimately built a small, single-layer pouch cell to show that the chemistry could work outside the coin cells commonly used for early battery experiments. The pouch cell retained 78% of its initial capacity after 100 charging cycles. Considerable work remains before the approach could be used commercially. The prototype uses a lithium-metal electrode, relatively modest amounts of sulfur and more electrolyte than would be desirable in a commercial battery. But Jiang said the larger significance is the possibility of expanding the chemistry available to sulfur batteries rather than simply improving the conventional reaction. The researchers estimate that, after accounting for major battery components rather than the electrode alone, the approach could enable a stack-level specific energy of 477 watt-hours per kilogram, about 37% higher than the conventional lithium-sulfur system used for comparison in the study. artigo.texto: Large-scale battery storage, life extension for Lepreau and new nuclear feature in N.B. Power’s latest plan Ramp-up of wind, solar and gas combustion turbines also figure in utility's future N.B. Power’s latest plan is calling for large-scale battery storage in the province by 2035. The utility released a new integrated resource plan on Monday, replacing a 2023 version of the plan that was criticized as out-of-date during hearings on the proposed 500-megawatt Tantramar gas plant earlier this year. The plan is N.B. Power’s roadmap for making sure it can meet energy demand over the coming decades. It calls for 500 megawatts of battery storage in the province in the next decade and also for an extension of life for the Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station that would take it beyond its estimated expiry date in 2045. The plan also calls for big build-outs of wind and solar generation, an expansion of gas turbine generation, and the possible addition of new nuclear generation on the Point Lepreau site. 'Final throes' of analysis on battery proposals Brad Coady, the utility's chief commercial officer, said he’s “hopeful that we can get to a battery here in the short run.” N.B. Power issued requests for proposals for 50-megawatt battery storage projects in 2023 and in 2025, but the utility has yet to build a large-scale project. The batteries allow energy to be saved up and used during peak times. Coady said the utility is “in the final throes of doing the analysis at our latest call for proposals.” According to the new resource plan, the first 500 megawatts of battery storage development is cost-competitive with combustion turbine technology, such as the Tantramar gas and diesel plant. But Coady said the proposals he has seen in response to N.B. Power’s December 2025 request for proposals would require government subsidies. “Based on the bids and offers that were submitted, they're not great without government help,” said Coady. “So we're working very closely with our federal government to say, 'Can we make these cost effective solutions for New Brunswickers?'” Nuclear decision has public policy angle The 2023 version of the plan named small modular nuclear reactors as a critical part of N.B. Power’s future. The 2026 plan takes a more technology-agnostic approach, which “could include large nuclear or could include small modular nuclear,” said Coady. The plan explores the possibility of adding 750 megawatts of new nuclear capacity at the Point Lepreau site by 2039 or 2040. It also calls for either another new nuclear project or the refurbishment of Point Lepreau in 2045. Coady acknowledged the conversation over nuclear power would go beyond the scope of N.B. Power’s plan. “The decision for a future nuclear plant in New Brunswick is also going to have to be a pretty strong public policy angle,” said Coady. While the utility does not include a new nuclear plant in its “base case," said Coady, it does identify “the amount of utility it brings the power system.” Lepreau costs, especially when it's down Coady acknowledged that repairs to Lepreau have been driving increased debt with N.B. Power in recent years. But he noted those investments are expected to pay off for the next 20 years. “I'd argue the larger driver to our debt is actually when [Lepreau] doesn't produce the electricity that we depend on it for,” said Coady, “and we have to turn to more expensive sources.” In addition to proposed nuclear and battery capacity, the plans also calls for big increases to wind and solar generation and more gas turbine projects. “I often describe the power system much like an orchestra,” said Coady, “and we need all parts of that orchestra performing the tune or we're not going to sound very good at the end of the day.”

Those opposed created a Facebook group “Newport Twp. SAY NO TO DATA CENTERS.”

artigo.texto: On Monday, 5 October, the European Commission published the price for the third quarter of 2026, which will be used to calculate the charges for importers whose products are subject to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The cost of 1 metric tonne of CO₂-equivalent emissions stood at €82.32. This information was revealed in updates on the European Commission’s website. By way of comparison, the price in the first quarter was €75.36, and in the second quarter €75.28 per metric tonne of embedded emissions. In other words, over the course of three months, the cost of atmospheric pollution on the European market rose by almost 10 per cent. Link to the EU ETS To determine the average quarterly price for the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), the EU uses the average price of emission allowances within the EU ETS. In this way, the EU seeks to maintain a balance between what European producers and importers pay for emissions, in order to achieve what the EU considers to be a fair environmental burden on businesses. For 2026 — the first year in which the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) will be fully operational — prices will be set on a quarterly basis. From 2027 onwards, the European Commission will publish the price of these allowances on a weekly basis. The sale of certificates under the CBAM scheme will begin on the central platform in February 2027. As a reminder, emissions calculations under the CBAM are carried out either using standardised values or actual figures. The former are usually higher than the latter, but the latter must be verified by accredited verifiers. Ukraine, which is not yet a member of the EU, is entitled to apply to the national accreditation body of any EU country. The Ministry of Economy has agreed on such cooperation with the Swedish body SWEDAC. A company from Greece was the first in the world to receive accreditation for verifying CBAM emissions. Experts noted a curious approach — granting the accrediting body the authority to assess emissions across all industrial sectors covered by CBAM. Also in September, the European Parliament extended the scope of the emissions trading scheme to include derivatives. Due to the CBAM, Ukraine has already lost more than half of its exports of certain types of products, as industry, which is trying to operate under wartime conditions, is unable to cope with the additional financial pressure.

artigo.texto: Alarm.com Extends Intelligent Video Protection to More Entryways with New Battery-Powered 781B Wire-free video doorbell brings intelligent video, relevant alerts, and proactive deterrence to entryways where traditional doorbells aren't practical TYSONS, Va.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 6, 2026-- Alarm.com (Nasdaq: ALRM), the leading platform for intelligently connected properties, today announced the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell, giving homeowners and businesses a new way to bring video security to entryways throughout their properties. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261006740792/en/ Alarm.com announces the release of the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell (ADC‑VDB781B). The 781B combines a rechargeable battery, Wi-Fi connectivity, and intelligent video capabilities in a doorbell designed for locations without existing doorbell wiring. Customers can install the 781B at a front door, side door, back door, detached garage, gate, shed, or other entryway where running new wiring may be impractical. As part of the Alarm.com platform, the doorbell works alongside the broader connected property system, unlocking a range of intelligent features that go beyond basic video coverage. "The 781B brings intelligent video, proactive deterrence, and connected actions to more entryways," said Dan Kerzner, President of Platforms Business at Alarm.com. "It gives our service providers another strong wireless option for delivering comprehensive video coverage across a property." Intelligent Awareness at More Entryways A square 1:1 view captures visitors from head to toe, while Advanced Video Analytics can identify people, animals, vehicles, and packages to help deliver more relevant alerts. As the first Alarm.com battery video doorbell to offer animal and vehicle detection, the 781B helps customers distinguish different types of activity around their property. Familiar Face Analytics can recognize up to five familiar people and support customized notifications, while Package Alerts help customers stay aware of deliveries and removals of packages. When a response is needed, customers can interact with visitors remotely through crisp two-way audio and Call Screen Actions, allowing them to unlock doors, turn on lights, and more through the Alarm.com platform without leaving the doorbell screen. For unwanted visitors, Perimeter Guard® combines attention-grabbing lights and audio alerts with the ability to trigger connected lights throughout the property. AI Deterrence can also deliver AI-generated verbal warnings when a person is detected at the door. Flexible Protection Without Doorbell Wiring The 781B is designed to make video protection possible in more locations without requiring an existing doorbell power source. Its battery-powered, Wi-Fi-connected design allows customers to install the doorbell where traditional wired models may not be an option without requiring connection to a hub or base station. Specially designed Energy Saver Video Analytics help conserve battery power during periods of inactivity. When it's time to recharge, the removable battery can be swapped out, or customers can use optional wiring for continuous trickle charging. The removable universal rechargeable battery is also compatible with the Alarm.com Volt Series™ V731B Battery Camera, giving customers a common battery solution across compatible devices and a simpler way to expand battery-powered video throughout a property. Designed for Everyday Security From monitoring a side entrance to keeping an eye on packages delivered near a garage, the 781B extends the role of the video doorbell beyond the front door. Customers can see activity, communicate with visitors, and respond to unexpected activity from the Alarm.com platform, wherever the doorbell is installed. The 781B also supports Bluetooth® Enrollment, designed to make device setup faster and easier for service providers. Availability The 781B is compatible with a range of Alarm.com residential and commercial video service packages, with feature availability varying by service package. To learn more about the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell, visit www.alarm.com or contact an Alarm.com service provider. About Alarm.com Alarm.com is the leading platform for intelligently connected properties. Millions of homeowners and businesses rely on Alarm.com’s technology to secure, monitor, and manage their environments from anywhere. Our comprehensive suite of solutions—including security, video surveillance, access control, active shooter detection, intelligent automation, energy management, personal safety and awareness, and fire—is delivered exclusively through a trusted network of thousands of professional service providers and commercial integrators across North America and worldwide. Alarm.com’s common stock is traded on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ALRM. Alarm.com delivers serious security for serious people. To learn more, visit www.alarm.com. artigo.texto: Physical AI’s bottleneck shifts from what robots can do to whether factories trust them AI is moving beyond the data centers where models are trained and onto factory floors where machines must handle constant change. But traditional industrial robots work behind a cage, repeat a single task and were never designed for the complexities of today’s market. Manufacturers now want general-purpose machines that can switch tasks and improve as processes evolve. The hard part is deploying it, according to Adrien Gaidon (pictured, right), co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics Inc. “If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon said. “What we do is we do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.” Gaidon and John Mancuso (left), vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc., spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante at Fully Connected, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how cloud infrastructure, simulation and human assistance help robots learn and adapt on factory floors. (* Disclosure below.) Physical AI moves from data centers to the factory floor Walden spun out of Toyota Research Institute in January 2026 and launched with $300 million in July to put general-purpose robots to work in manufacturing. Its robots have worked full production shifts alongside people since May. They handle machine tending, parts kitting, and subassembly, tasks manufacturers had either failed to automate or never tried, Gaidon explained. “There’s half a million open positions for machinists in the U.S. because it’s a hard job and it requires skills,” Gaidon said. “But part of that job does not require the craft or the human creativity.” Getting a robot to that point takes serious compute long before it reaches a production line. CoreWeave, which has been betting on physical AI, also brings mechanical engineers and robotics experts into customer engagements alongside its infrastructure, Mancuso explained. “In the end, before a model is ever going to do something in the physical world, it’s going to have a tremendous amount of simulation that happens in the virtual world,” Mancuso said. “We’re providing the infrastructure.” But while simulation in data centers can make a robot useful, but it can’t make it perfect. Walden pairs autonomous robots with remote human assistants. The setup is comparable to automated looms of 120 years ago, when one person oversaw 40 machines, Gaidon noted. “Our robots are autonomous, but they know how to call for help,” Gaidon said. “They know when they need some assistance – and that assistance feeds the most valuable data to improve over time.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of Fully Connected: (* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Fully Connected 2026 event. artigo.texto: Fisk Electric Awarded $24 Million Data Center Electrical Project, Expanding Prefabrication Capabilities in Houston LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 6, 2026-- Tutor Perini Corporation (NYSE: TPC) (the “Company”), a leading civil, building and specialty construction company, announced today that its subsidiary, Fisk Electric Company (“Fisk”), has been awarded an electrical services contract for a confidential data center customer in Houston, Texas. The contract value is approximately $24 million. Fisk’s scope of work includes prefabrication and assembly of modular containment systems and related electrical infrastructure, including liquid-cooled components and piping, for a new ground-up data center. These units will be built at Fisk’s new 75,000-square-foot prefabrication/manufacturing facility in Houston. This new emerging prefabrication market is in high demand due to the nationwide shortage of electricians, enabling Fisk to increase its prefabrication work when serving as the prime electrical contractor supporting data center owners, developers, and general contractors in refining offsite manufacturing to ensure schedules are met with the limited resources available nationwide. Electrical construction work is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 with substantial completion anticipated in the first quarter of 2027. The contract value will be reflected in the Company’s backlog for the third quarter of 2026. About Tutor Perini Corporation Tutor Perini Corporation is a leading civil, building and specialty construction company offering diversified general contracting and design-build services to private customers and public agencies throughout the world. We have provided construction services since 1894 and have established a strong reputation within our markets by executing large, complex projects on time and within budget while adhering to strict safety and quality control measures. We offer general contracting, pre-construction planning and comprehensive project management services, and have strong expertise in delivering design-bid-build, design-build, construction management, and public-private partnership (P3) projects. We often self-perform multiple project components, including earthwork, excavation, concrete forming and placement, steel erection, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC), and fire protection. artigo.texto: Renesas Expands GaN Portfolio with First Low-Voltage GaN FETs for AI Data Centers and Robotics New 100V E-mode GaN Advanced Power Transistor Family Delivers Higher Power Density and Industry-Leading Figure-of-Merit Performance TOKYO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 6, 2026-- Renesas Electronics Corporation (TSE:6723), a premier supplier of advanced semiconductor solutions, has expanded its GaN portfolio into low-voltage applications with its first family of 100V enhancement mode (E-mode) GaN-based discrete power transistors. The RTP100E005G1FL, RTP100E2P6G1FL, RTP100E1P8G1FL-DSC and RTP100E1P2G1FL-DSC low-voltage GaN FETs deliver ultra-fast switching speeds and enhanced thermal performance in efficiency-critical, high power density applications, including AI data centers, humanoid robotics, factory automation and industrial motor drives, power tools and solar microinverters. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261006989457/en/ The new GaN FETs achieve industry-leading hard- and soft-switching figure-of-merit (FOM) performance, delivering up to 35% lower hard-switching FOM and up to 63% lower soft-switching FOM than comparable GaN devices. The low-voltage GaN devices also maintain a silicon-compatible footprint that allows for easy adoption into existing designs. Power converters in today's data centers generally operate at switching frequencies of a few hundred kilohertz. But as AI servers and industrial infrastructure transition to 800 VDC power distribution and 48V bus architectures, many converter stages are moving toward megahertz-class switching to shrink magnetics, increase power density and improve overall efficiency. Using low-voltage GaN in 800V high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power architectures simplifies power conversion design, significantly reducing passive component size, switching losses and cooling requirements. At the system level, this translates to better efficiency, fewer thermal management requirements and lower energy and BOM costs. Broad GaN Portfolio Yields Greater Efficiency, Power Density and Design Flexibility Built on Renesas’ recently expanded low-voltage E-mode GaN technology platform, this new transistor portfolio features ultra-fast GaN switching with low total gate charge (Qg) and output charge (Qoss) to minimize the overlap between voltage and current. It reduces energy lost in each conversion cycle across AI power supply units, motor drives and DC-DC power stages. The devices also offer zero reverse recovery (Qrr = 0), which eliminates energy losses for immediate switching efficiency gains. Fast switching increases power density and yields higher frequency operation by shrinking PCB footprint and reducing the size of magnetic and passive components, while low RDS(on) improves operating efficiency by curtailing conduction losses. Available bottom- and dual-side cooling configurations provide added heat dissipation and design flexibility. Depending on application requirements and power-conversion architecture, the low-voltage GaN devices can achieve up to 40–70% lower switching losses and up to twice the power density at the system level. The new GaN transistors are offered in multiple standard MOSFET-compatible packages, allowing customers to quickly migrate from silicon MOSFET layouts for faster design implementation without significant PCB rework. The package options, combined with a wide RDS(on) range (5 mΩ-1.2 mΩ), enable designers to scale across power levels and applications, including synchronous rectification, multiphase buck conversion and motor drives. "Customers adopting next-generation GaN technology for AI servers, robotics, industrial motor drives and renewable energy systems are looking for ways to deliver more efficient power conversion performance from increasingly compact systems,” said Akhil Nair, Senior Director, Low-Voltage GaN at Renesas. "Our low-voltage GaN family delivers the efficiency, switching performance and power density designers expect from GaN while making it significantly easier to transition from existing silicon MOSFET designs.” High GaN Performance in Silicon-Compatible Footprints The new GaN family is built on E-mode (normally off) GaN technology, which offers the performance advantages of GaN in a convenient silicon-compatible footprint. This helps designers capture the efficiency and power benefits of GaN and simplifies migration from existing silicon-based designs. Key features of the new low-voltage GaN family - 1 to 3% higher efficiency over silicon-based designs, eliminating Qrr loss - Drastic 40 to 70% reduction in switching losses - Doubled power density by reducing switching energy per cycle and supporting high frequency operation - Smaller system footprint with higher switching frequency reducing magnetics size and lowering overall system losses - Optimized thermal management reduces fan and active cooling requirements, cutting system complexity and BOM cost Additionally, with its lower total energy consumption per power stage, the new GaN family helps designers meet sustainability objectives. This is achieved by reducing the size of fans required for thermal and airflow management, enabling the use of smaller magnetics and shrinking overall PCB footprint, which contributes to AI data center and industrial energy efficiency targets. Availability The new low-voltage GaN power transistors are available now in FCLGA and FCLGA-DSC packages, along with corresponding evaluation boards. More information about these devices and development tools is available at: renesas.com/lv-gan-fets. Winning Combinations The new low-voltage GaN FETs can be easily integrated with other Renesas power reference designs, including a 6 kW 800V to 48V DCX LLC solution and industrial DC Servo platform. artigo.texto: The electric vehicle revolution has a hidden Achilles’ heel, and it is not the batteries themselves but the fragile web of companies that mine, refine, and ship the minerals inside them. A new study published in iScience has mapped the entire firm-level supply network of the lithium-ion battery industry and stress-tested it against shortages of lithium, cobalt, and nickel. The results reveal a system that is far more vulnerable than its headline market size suggests, with losses cascading through unexpected pathways and recovery depending less on direct suppliers than on a handful of shared corporate hubs. The research team, led by Xuena Liu and Haibin Liu, constructed a multilayer supply chain network centered on nine of the world’s dominant battery manufacturers, including CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, SK Innovation, CALB, Samsung SDI, Gotion, and EVE Energy. Using the FactSet Revere database of interfirm supply relationships, supplemented by corporate disclosures and stock-market volatility data, they built a directed, weighted network spanning mineral extraction, intermediate materials, battery assembly, electric vehicle manufacturing, and recycling. The timing could hardly be more pressing: global electric vehicle battery demand reached 950 gigawatt-hours in 2024 and is projected to exceed 3 terawatt-hours by 2030, while the International Energy Agency expects electric vehicles and energy storage to account for more than 90 percent of future lithium demand. The network’s anatomy alone tells a striking story. All nine manufacturer-centered networks follow power-law degree distributions, meaning a few hub firms dominate connectivity while most firms maintain only a handful of relationships. The commodity trader Glencore, the Australian lithium producer Pilbara Minerals, and the Chinese materials firm CNGR each maintain business relationships with seven to nine core battery makers, forming what the authors call cross-layer super-hubs. Meanwhile, most shared nodes connect to only two manufacturers. The networks led by Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution are strongly correlated with each other and with Panasonic’s, implying that a shock at a shared supplier could transmit simultaneous damage across multiple corporate ecosystems. By contrast, the SK Innovation- and Gotion-led networks show slightly negative correlations, hinting at potential substitutability at certain supply nodes. When the researchers simulated shortages of increasing intensity, from 10 percent to a complete cutoff of supply, lithium emerged as the most damaging mineral by a clear margin, with network losses ranking lithium above cobalt above nickel under every scenario. This asymmetry reflects chemistry as much as geology. Lithium is an indispensable element in every lithium-ion battery, whereas cobalt is progressively being engineered out of newer cathode designs, and nickel benefits from abundant resources and diversified supply. At a shortage intensity of 0.9, the CATL-dominated network suffered losses of 1171.42 under lithium scarcity, compared with 909.05 for cobalt and 918.45 for nickel. The BYD-led network fared worst of all under lithium stress, reaching 2587.49, a consequence of its enormous lithium iron phosphate production volumes and vertically integrated business model. Manufacturer-level losses varied dramatically, defying any simple ranking of corporate might. CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, recorded the highest losses across all three minerals, ranging from roughly 130 to 160 under lithium shortages, a pattern the authors attribute to its simultaneous operation of both LFP and high-nickel NMC pathways, which broadens its mineral exposure and concentrates its supplier base. SK Innovation’s network proved exceptionally vulnerable to nickel because its product portfolio is dominated by high-nickel NCM811 cells, while EVE Energy’s cobalt-containing cathode materials and stringent certification requirements concentrated its dependence on upstream refining hubs. Panasonic, by contrast, recorded the lowest losses and responded only weakly to changes in shortage intensity, reflecting its comparatively low structural exposure. Tracing exactly where the damage came from produced some of the study’s most actionable findings. Under cobalt shortages, a single firm, Glencore, accounted for between 73.43 and 92.75 percent of CATL’s attributed losses, a near-single-source structure in which one disruption could rapidly amplify risk downstream. Nickel losses for CATL were dominated by Glencore and the Indonesian producer Trimegah Bangun Persada, the latter reflecting the localized supply concentration fostered by Indonesia’s nickel ore export ban. Lithium losses were far more dispersed, spread across Tianqi Lithium, Ganfeng Lithium, Yahua, and Albemarle. Path analysis of a total Tianqi Lithium shortage showed that two pathways, a direct cross-chain link to BYD and a long cascade through the midstream materials firm BTR, together accounted for roughly 70 percent of BYD’s total impact, with the cathode makers Hunan Yuneng and Ronbay emerging as the most frequently traversed intermediary nodes. Perhaps the most surprising result concerns how the industry recovers. The researchers decomposed recovery into three mechanisms: direct restoration through existing supply relationships, indirect recovery through shared nodes that connect multiple manufacturer networks, and recovery through newly established supply links. Indirect recovery dominated overwhelmingly, contributing 70 to 74 percent of total recovery, followed by new links at 15 to 18 percent, with direct recovery contributing a mere 10 to 12 percent. In other words, when a mineral shortage strikes, battery makers do not primarily heal through their own contracted suppliers; they heal through the network’s hidden cross-connections, as shared suppliers reallocate resources across tiers. artigo.texto: Hillsboro weighs two-phase data center limits as moratorium continues HILLSBORO, Ore. (KATU) — Hillsboro City Council took a first look Tuesday at new limits on data centers. The city is working on a two-phased plan while a 120-day moratorium is in place. Phase one would ban data centers in most zones, caps acreage in two industrial zones, and keeps them a thousand feet from schools. PAST COVERAGE | Hillsboro pauses new AI data centers. What's next over the next 120 days? Phase 2 of the plan would set building rules for data centers in Hillsboro including height limits, setbacks, green building requirements, and buffers from parks and natural areas. Hillsboro resident Britt Holloway spoke at the meeting about this phase, and what it could mean long term. “We need to evaluate power demand, water use, noise, emissions, and impacts on nearby farms and neighborhoods. Keep in mind that well-designed facilities can minimize a lot of these impacts. However, poorly-designed facilities are often resulting in cost-cutting measures, which can create an exponentially increasing burden for residents,” Holloway said.
