artigo.texto: RALEIGH, N.C. (WTVD) -- The Raleigh City Council voted 7-1 on Tuesday to approve a six-month moratorium on new data center development, a move city leaders say will provide time to study potential effects and develop regulations for the rapidly growing industry. The temporary pause applies to data centers with footprints exceeding 10,000 square feet. City officials said Raleigh's current regulations do not include standards specifically tailored to large-scale data centers. The decision followed public debate both outside and inside council chambers, where community advocates argued the moratorium does not provide enough time to fully evaluate potential effects on utilities, communities, and the environment. "There's a lot that the city does not know. Can it get all this information in six months? That becomes a really big question," said Rania Masri of the North Carolina Environmental Justice Network. During the council meeting, advocates continued to express concerns about the scope and duration of the pause. "This moratorium doesn't have a conditionality about it. It's simply time. So in six months, whether or not the city can do what it says it's going to do, the moratorium ends," Masri said. Supporters of a longer pause said more time is needed to address unanswered questions about the effect of data centers on Raleigh communities. "What is the harm in giving Raleigh more time? We have a city, a new half a million people, and there's still a massive knowledge gap about what the center for in our communities. And somehow, six months is enough. We're asking for 32 months," said Raleigh resident Zainab Baloch. The moratorium is intended to give city staff time to study the effects of data center development and determine whether additional regulations are needed. Residents also voiced concerns about whether six months would allow for meaningful public engagement and long-term planning. "Six months is not enough time to make decisions that impact not only the major decisions, but also their lifetimes and future generations. The people of our city, especially those in southeast Raleigh, deserve to have a policy and a vision of all of the nations around the data centers. And this period will not allow that to happen," said Raleigh resident Anusha Yadav. Councilwoman Christina Jones, the lone dissenting vote, said she had concerns about the structure of the moratorium and the challenges it could present. "When you were watching different municipalities extend their moratoriums having longer ones. It's something that we are in the defensive mode to begin with, and so for me not having those laid out at this moment or voting on the moratorium is where I'm struggling to get there," Jones said. Duke Energy said data centers account for less than 1% of total peak electricity demand, but that figure is projected to rise to 13% of sales by 2030. The utility said it has been involved in discussions with Raleigh leaders about managing future growth. Lee Freedman, a Duke Energy spokesperson, said the company is focused on balancing expansion with reliability for customers. "That means protecting reliability and making sure customers benefit and not subsidize growth -- so we're working with city staff to educate them, educate council members, and if this moratorium does pass, we will continue working with them," Freedman said. Freedman also said projects under development are expected to provide financial benefits in the future. "We're talking about billions of dollars in bill relief beginning in about 2029 when the new data centers start going online in North Carolina," he said. Dustin Winkler, an AI enablement engineer and owner of the consulting company AWACS.AI, said data centers are essential to his work helping enterprise teams integrate AI technology into their operations and build applications. "I don't know where I pull from, just like no one else does," Winkler said of the network of data centers that support AI services. Despite relying on those facilities professionally, Winkler said he supports a temporary pause to assess potential effects. "It is something that can be hard to reconcile," he said. "I think it's good to take a pause and make sure that we don't limit ourselves and to what kind of a technology expansion that we want. But we also are careful about our area. Make sure that it's not overtaxed." The City said it is aware of eight data centers within Raleigh city limits, most of which are smaller-scale facilities. City officials said Raleigh does not have a hyperscale data center within its jurisdiction. There are eight hyperscale data centers in North Carolina, with others under construction. Amazon is building a $10 billion data center and AI campus in Richmond County. Raleigh Mayor Janet Cowell said city leaders are seeking a balanced approach that encourages innovation while addressing community concerns. "We want to have a very rational, careful approach that protects individuals who live in Raleigh and still be known as a tech-right, innovative city," she said. The moratorium takes effect immediately and is scheduled to continue through April. City leaders said they plan to provide nearly a dozen opportunities for public comment as they work toward developing a city ordinance. Advocates, however, said they are seeking a broader conversation about data center development in Raleigh.

artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: quem vai construir, operar e crescer com eles? Em artigo à CNN Infra, Léo Oliveira explica como infraestrutura de data centers deve transformar o investimento em capacidade local no país A chegada de um data center deve levar quem lidera empresas e políticas de desenvolvimento a pensar em como transformar esse investimento em oportunidades para as pessoas e os negócios da região. Com a sanção do Redata, o Brasil reforça sua aposta na atração de data centers. Energia, conectividade e equipamentos estão no centro dessa agenda, mas a preparação das regiões para construir, operar e prestar serviços a esses empreendimentos também precisa fazer parte do planejamento. Quem vai transformar o investimento em capacidade local? Como CEO de uma plataforma de IA, Executivo de RH e Líder, vejo três prioridades. A primeira é preparar pessoas antes da inauguração, considerando que construção, operação e manutenção exigem competências diferentes. O plano de formação deve acompanhar o cronograma e prever os profissionais necessários na obra, na entrada em operação e nos anos seguintes. É preciso um planejamento rigoroso para estabelecer vagas temporárias, permanentes e explicar quais caminhos de qualificação permitem transitar entre essas etapas. Empresas, escolas técnicas e universidades devem organizar essa preparação a partir das demandas concretas. As empresas devem sinalizar as competências e os prazos para que as instituições de ensino avaliem como preparar os profissionais com antecedência. Quem já trabalha também precisa encontrar caminhos para ampliar sua qualificação através de cursos, formações e trocas para se manter relevante. Que oportunidade terá o jovem que mora perto desse investimento? Ele precisa saber quais profissões serão necessárias e encontrar condições para conciliar formação, deslocamento e renda. Os programas devem considerar essas questões para que as pessoas consigam frequentar o curso, concluir os estudos e disputar uma vaga. A segunda prioridade é criar condições para que empresas brasileiras participem da cadeia de fornecedores desses projetos. Os empreendedores precisam informar quais serviços pretendem contratar na região e os requisitos técnicos e de segurança que serão exigidos, permitindo que empresas locais se preparem para disputar contratos. Pense em uma empresa regional de manutenção elétrica interessada em atender um data center. Ela precisará conhecer as exigências da operação, qualificar profissionais e demonstrar que consegue cumprir os padrões do contratante. Um programa de desenvolvimento de fornecedores pode apoiar essa preparação, com critérios claros e sem garantia de contratação. Essa conexão pode ampliar a competência de empresas locais e abrir mercados para seus serviços. Cabe aproximar universidades e empreendimentos para pesquisar soluções para a operação. O desenvolvimento que buscamos inclui conhecimento que permaneça na região e possa ser utilizado em outros negócios. A terceira prioridade é trazer o RH e a liderança para o planejamento desde o início. Se a formação necessária leva mais tempo que o previsto para contratar, o projeto precisa reconhecer esse descompasso. Quem vai formar os gestores, organizar o trabalho e acompanhar os resultados? Essas decisões precisam estar presentes quando os investimentos e os prazos são definidos. O RH pode contribuir com o diagnóstico de competências, a formação, os caminhos de carreira e se antecipar conhecendo o negócio. As lideranças precisam traduzir a estratégia em responsabilidades, recursos e condições de execução. Essa construção exige muita articulação entre operação, finanças e compras, instituições de ensino técnico e superior, governos, lideranças locais e movimentos sociais. A articulação precisa ter responsáveis, prazos e compromissos claros. Governos podem coordenar ações de qualificação e acesso em parceria com instituições de ensino técnico e superior. Lideranças locais e movimentos sociais ajudam a identificar barreiras de transporte, renda e informação, enquanto as empresas devem explicitar suas demandas e os critérios de seleção. Essa pode ser uma chance de ampliar o emprego e desenvolver essas regiões, abrindo caminhos para as profissões do futuro. O legado que devemos buscar inclui profissionais mais preparados e empresas locais mais capazes de inovar. Quando os data centers estiverem operando, o que os brasileiros estarão mais preparados para fazer, criar e liderar? Léo Oliveira é fundador e CEO da Humanos & Inteligência Artificial*

Carbono azul e pradarias marinhas vão seguir-se, O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passa a contar com três metodologias para projetos florestais, abrindo novas oportunidades à mobilização de investimento privado para o sequestro de carbono e a gestão sustentável da floresta. Foram aprovadas duas novas metodologias de carbono dedicadas à Reflorestação e à Gestão Florestal Melhorada, que se juntam à metodologia já existente para Novas Florestações. As novas metodologias permitem abranger um conjunto mais diversificado de intervenções florestais, reforçam o potencial de geração de créditos de carbono em Portugal e incentivam práticas de gestão sustentável com benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática. Ao alargar as metodologias disponíveis, reforçamos a credibilidade e a capacidade de crescimento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono e mobilizamos financiamento privado para projetos que contribuem simultaneamente para a neutralidade carbónica, a valorização do território e a resiliência das nossas florestas”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, numa nota enviada às redações. Atualmente, o MVC conta com dois projetos registados na tipologia de Novas Florestações e um terceiro projeto está em fase de validação inicial. Estão ainda disponíveis 977 créditos de carbono para venda, a plataforma conta com 29 utilizadores registados e existem 10 verificadores qualificados para assegurar a validação inicial e a verificação periódica dos projetos, segundo o ministério. “O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono está a ganhar escala e maturidade. Depois das metodologias florestais, estamos já a trabalhar em novas abordagens para valorizar o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, para colocar também os ecossistemas costeiros no centro da ação climática e da valorização do capital natural”, acrescenta a ministra.

artigo.texto: Wisconsin is preparing for a massive expansion of data centers. Billions of dollars are flowing into new facilities, which could sharply increase the state’s electricity demand. At the same time, families across Wisconsin are struggling to afford something much more basic: child care. Child care costs in Wisconsin have climbed beyond what many families can afford. In 2026, full-time infant care at a center costs an average of $17,400 a year — equal to 22% of Wisconsin’s median household income and more than a year of in-state tuition at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The problem extends beyond cost. Wisconsin’s child care workforce declined by more than 26% between 2010 and 2022. Child care workers in 2022 earned a median annual wage of $26,333, ranking 13th lowest among 546 occupations, according to a 2023 Forward Analytics report. This is not just a problem for parents. It’s a drag on the economy. When families cannot find reliable care, parents may reduce their hours, turn down jobs or leave the workforce. When providers cannot afford to retain workers, classrooms close and families lose options. Wisconsin has already seen what targeted investment can accomplish. Child Care Counts supported 5,762 programs, 75,740 educators and more than 430,000 children. It also helped the early childhood workforce grow by roughly 17%, according to the Wisconsin Early Childhood Association’s Center for Policy, Research, and Engagement. But that funding was temporary, and about one-quarter of providers could close or significantly reduce services without continued support. We cannot keep treating child care as a temporary crisis. Like roads, power lines and broadband, child care is infrastructure that allows the economy to function. That is why Wisconsin needs a Wisconsin Public Child Care Act to create a permanent child care trust fund that would make care more affordable and stabilize providers while supporting private, nonprofit, family-based, tribal and in-home programs. Regional child care councils would help tailor investments to local needs. A permanent program also needs a permanent funding source. Wisconsin’s growing data center industry provides an opportunity. A 2026 UW-Madison Extension analysis identified more than 4,500 megawatts of potential electricity demand from major current and planned data center projects across the state. The Public Service Commission projects Wisconsin’s peak electricity demand could rise from 14.2 gigawatts in 2026 to approximately 20 gigawatts by 2032, a roughly 40% increase. Wisconsin already offers significant tax incentives to attract data centers. The Legislative Fiscal Bureau estimates the state’s data center sales and use tax exemption could result in more than $2 billion in forgone tax revenue from data centers that come to the state. If Wisconsin is willing to invest billions to attract these projects, it should also ask them to invest in the workforce they rely on. Rather than treating data centers and child care as competing priorities, Wisconsin should connect them. The largest facilities could pay a modest assessment based on electricity capacity. At an illustrative $50,000 per megawatt, 2,000 megawatts of qualifying capacity could generate approximately $100 million annually for child care. That revenue would increase as more data centers go online. This is not an anti-business proposal. Data centers depend on Wisconsin’s roads, energy systems, communities and workforce. That workforce depends on child care. Wisconsin should welcome economic development while ensuring the public shares its benefits. A small contribution from the state’s largest data centers could help families afford care, stabilize providers, improve child care worker compensation and expand access in communities facing shortages. Wisconsin should not have to choose between technological investment and working families. We can build the data centers of the future while investing in the child care system that allows Wisconsin’s economy to function. Child care is essential infrastructure. Wisconsin should fund it accordingly. Connie Acuahuitl is a University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee student. She recently completed a fellowship with the Roosevelt Institute, which “champions new ideas and new leaders to make our economy and democracy work for the many, not the few.” She also interned at Caring Across Generations, whose mission is to “change our culture and policies in America to value and support caregiving.” Originally published by Wisconsin Watch.

artigo.texto: A CPFL (CPFE3) sinalizou, em seu Investor Day, que pode disputar espaço no segmento de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês), com foco nos próximos leilões desenhados para a tecnologia. A informação consta de relatório do Safra sobre o evento, realizado na terça-feira (6) com a participação do CEO, Gustavo Estrella, do CFO, Kedi Wang, e de outros executivos. Apesar do tom construtivo, o banco manteve recomendação neutra para as ações da companhia, com preço-alvo de R$ 58,70 para os papéis CPFE3. A avaliação do Safra se baseia principalmente no valuation: segundo o relatório, a CPFL negocia a uma taxa interna de retorno (TIR) real implícita de 10,9%. Para a gestão da CPFL, o avanço tecnológico no segmento de armazenamento, a maior demanda por esse tipo de solução e o crescimento das fontes intermitentes de energia ampliam a necessidade de capacidade de potência. A companhia poderá avaliar oportunidades nos leilões previstos para o setor. Os executivos também destacaram vantagens estruturais da área de atuação da CPFL para atender data centers, como a proximidade dos mercados de maior demanda e uma infraestrutura mais robusta. Segundo o Safra, o armazenamento por baterias e a autoprodução podem se expandir para sustentar o maior consumo de eletricidade no futuro. Preparação para o El Niño e agenda regulatória A companhia concentrou seus investimentos dos últimos anos em robustez da rede, resposta rápida e restabelecimento ágil do serviço. A exposição à Região Sul, afirma a gestão, ajudou a entender os desafios de eventos climáticos extremos. O cenário de incerteza climática é tratado como base, com variações conforme a intensidade de cada El Niño. Neste ano, as ocorrências foram resolvidas de forma satisfatória por meio de monitoramento e automação. Na regulação, a CPFL espera desdobramentos positivos na agenda do próximo ano para as distribuidoras, incluindo temas como perdas, atualização da base de inadimplência e recálculo do componente Pd. A empresa também poderia se beneficiar de um eventual reconhecimento dos investimentos em medidores inteligentes, dada a eficácia comprovada no controle de perdas. Na geração, a administração avaliou como positivos os avanços da Consulta Pública 45/2019, que distribui o ônus do curtailment (corte de geração) entre usinas eólicas e solares e, após um ano de teste, hidrelétricas com capacidade de geração vertível. A companhia vê o movimento como um passo para estabilizar o segmento. Crescimento e dividendos O principal vetor de crescimento segue sendo o investimento nas concessões de distribuição. A companhia deve manter sua política de payout e buscar oportunidades nos segmentos em que já atua, incluindo os próximos leilões, inclusive de armazenamento. Em distribuição, também pode avaliar oportunidades de mercado, com disciplina de capital e atenção a risco e retorno. Para o Safra, o evento transmitiu uma perspectiva positiva para o setor, com sentimento favorável em relação à agenda regulatória do próximo ano e reforço do compromisso da CPFL com a disciplina de capital. artigo.texto: Data center como obrigação reflete novo ecossistema de telecom, avalia Anatel Nilo Pasquali diz que consulta sobre 6 GHz abre discussão sobre novos compromissos de infraestrutura; agência pretende manter modelo que prioriza investimentos em vez de arrecadação A Anatel pretende discutir se investimentos em data center e outras infraestruturas digitais podem integrar os compromissos associados a futuras licitações de radiofrequência, que já aparece na consulta de futuros leilões relacionados à faixa de 6 GHz. Segundo o superintendente de Planejamento e Regulamentação da agência, Nilo Pasquali, esse é um movimento natural, diante das mudanças do ecossistema de infraestrutura digital. Ele participou de painel na Futurecom 2026, nesta terça-feira, 6. Pasquali afirmou que a inclusão de data centers na discussão não representa uma mudança abrupta de atribuições da agência, mas uma consequência da integração crescente entre telecomunicações e outras infraestruturas digitais. “Eu acho que não é uma mudança, eu acho que é uma maturidade da agência, por conta das discussões dos últimos anos”, afirmou. Segundo ele, as antigas divisões entre os segmentos deixaram de refletir o funcionamento do mercado. “A gente está agora em um ambiente digital. A gente não está mais naquele momento de divisão das cadeias, as estruturas bem divididinhas, todo mundo no seu quadrado. Quando a gente está falando de ecossistema digital, a gente está falando de telecom e mais uma série de outras coisas também.” Pasquali confirmou que a proposta submetida à consulta pública leva os data centers para a discussão sobre os compromissos associados ao espectro. O superintendente ressaltou, porém, que a proposta está em consulta e pode ser modificada. Segundo ele, essa é justamente a finalidade do processo: avaliar se a formulação faz sentido, se deve permanecer como apresentada ou se precisa de outro desenho. A discussão acontece no contexto da Consulta Pública nº 37, que trata da faixa de 6 GHz. Conectividade continua pendente Pasquali ressalvou que a incorporação de novas infraestruturas aos compromissos não significa que o problema tradicional de cobertura esteja resolvido. “O Brasil não acabou de conectar o país”, afirmou. Segundo ele, ainda existem áreas identificadas nos levantamentos da agência que demandam expansão das redes. A diferença é que a Anatel considera necessário começar a observar simultaneamente outras estruturas que compõem o ecossistema digital. “Tem que se começar a olhar para as outras infraestruturas que também fazem sentido, que compõem esse ecossistema e começam a contribuir para colocar o Brasil no futuro”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: Memphis mayor defends data center benefits ahead of moratorium vote Leaders speak ahead of highly anticipated vote MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Memphis Mayor Paul Young said his goal is to make the city better by accommodating everyone as data centers continue to be an issue for some Memphians and surrounding cities. The comment comes a day before a critical vote on a data center moratorium. “We must do it in a way where our people are protected; I think that’s really important. They need to have confidence they’re protected,” Young said. Addressing community concerns “That’s part of governance; governance is finding a way to address the potential negatives and harms that could be brought to the community and find a way to maximize the potential benefit to the community,” Young said. Groups like Memphis Community Against Pollution (MCAP) have laid out what the negatives are: - Air pollution - Nearby residents dealing with noise complaints - Effects on the water supply - Rising energy prices Tax revenue from data centers Young said significant tax dollars are generated by projects like data centers. He said Memphis is the only city with an ordinance requiring data centers to pay full taxes, with 25% of those taxes going back to the community most adjacent to them. Young said SpaceXAI alone generated $54 million between the city and county this year. He gave a comparison to help people understand the scale: “That’s the equivalent of 12,400 units of housing built in our city at $300,000 each,” Young said. The initial vote was supposed to happen September 15, but Councilman JB Smiley Jr., the ordinance’s leading sponsor, says the council wanted to factor in more community concerns. “One of the things that I heard consistently from the community is, ‘What about us? You can create laws, but you’re not talking to us,’” Councilman Smiley told Action News 5. While the council is speaking to various experts, Sarah Houston, executive director of Protect Our Aquifer, says they should also prioritize lifting up the voices of local organizations on concerns about the data centers, since they’re the ones on the ground. “There’s been a lot of confusion and a lot of listening to people with fancy titles,” says Houson. “The reality is there’s a lot of expertise in the Memphis community that city council members really need to lean on and really need to listen to.” Smiley says he believes the council likely has six votes for the moratorium and four against it, leaving the remaining three councilmembers to decide its fate. He says the point of a temporary moratorium is not necessarily to shut the door on the industry, but to make sure the city understands what it’s getting into before moving forward. “What I don’t want to happen is we allow 20, 30 more data centers to come in and in a year’s time, data centers stop being the hot thing and we have 30 empty buildings,” says Smiley. artigo.texto: Battery demand for stationary energy storage (ES) is set to grow as the penetration of renewable energy sources (RES) within electricity grids increases, alongside new demand created by data center build-out. Policy is also shifting from simply setting storage targets towards creating bankable revenue frameworks and increasingly sophisticated routes-to-market for battery energy storage system (BESS) deployment. As shown in IDTechEx's newly updated market report "Batteries for Stationary Energy Storage 2027-2037: Markets, Forecasts, Players, Technologies, Policy, and Projects", the global Li-ion BESS market will reach US$135B in value by 2037. Li-ion battery demand shifts across sectors Li-ion batteries (LIBs) continue to dominate the stationary battery energy storage system (BESS) market, driven by their wide availability, low cost and improvements in performance. While total cross-sector LIB demand has continued to increase, the application mix has shifted. EV batteries still dominate global demand, but their share decreased from 84% in 2023 to 78% in 2025, while the share attributable to BESS applications increased from 10% to 19%. Policy-driven changes in the EV market have contributed to this shift, alongside much faster growth in BESS demand as electricity grids integrate greater volumes of renewable energy and require increasing levels of flexibility. Li-ion BESS demand by country and key drivers IDTechEx estimates that annual global Li-ion BESS deployments increased by more than 3x between 2023 and 2025 across grid-scale, commercial and industrial (C&I), and residential sectors. This is equivalent to 92 GWh deployed in 2023 and 318 GWh in 2025. China and the US represented 58% and 18% of deployments in 2025, respectively, highlighting China's continued lead in the global market. The US BESS market is increasingly being shaped by industrial policy and efforts to reduce dependence on Chinese cells and BESS technologies. Critically, countries not previously prominent in the global BESS market have emerged within the top 10 by GWh deployed, including Saudi Arabia and Chile. IDTechEx would expect more countries to enter the market at significant scale. Key drivers facilitating BESS growth across both established and emerging markets include a growing number of procurement frameworks, routes-to-market and increasingly sophisticated financing structures that improve project bankability and help BESS projects secure investment. Examples include Australia's Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS), New South Wales' Long-Term Energy Service Agreements (LTESAs), Italy's MACSE, state-backed Middle Eastern tenders, and the UK LDES cap-and-floor framework. Future challenges, pricing, and technology trends While many future projects are being facilitated by government-backed procurement and revenue-support frameworks, often administered by regulators, system operators or designated procurement bodies, grid connection queues are emerging as a key bottleneck. Project delays and attrition may therefore be expected, while an increasingly competitive BESS developer landscape is also making it more difficult for new entrants to penetrate the grid-scale market at scale. Developers with proven utility-scale experience, strong local execution capabilities and demonstrable bankability are increasingly winning significant projects. Further upstream, raw-material prices and policy changes may also create uncertainty. China's reduction in and eventual elimination of its battery export VAT rebate could affect future cell and BESS pricing. This has encouraged some front-loading of battery production and exports and, alongside other factors, contributed to higher lithium carbonate prices in early 2026. If such prices are sustained, they could place upward pressure on cell and BESS prices, weaken project economics and increase margin pressure across the containerized Li-ion BESS supply chain. At the technology level, many players are launching containerized grid-scale BESS technologies using increasingly high-capacity cells, contributing to a growing number of systems with capacities of 6.5 MWh or greater. Higher capacity cells can improve system-level energy density by reducing the number of cells, interconnections and casings required per MWh, allowing a greater proportion of the container to be occupied by active battery material. This can also bring project-level cost benefits, as fewer BESS units are required to achieve a given site capacity. However, these designs create additional thermal management requirements and can introduce transportation weight constraints, contributing to new system-level design trends. --- Conrad Nichols, Principal Technology Analyst, IDTechEx.

MONTGOMERY, Ala.—The Alabama Public Service Commission approved a new set of rules for future data center projects Tuesday that require more transparency and disclosure from data center companies and public votes by the PSC for data center approval. But they leave in place what critics call a “disappointing” provision allowing for approval by default of large data center projects if the commission does not schedule a vote on them. Under the new rules, Alabama Power will have to release public summaries of data center contracts that include the name of the company the utility is contracting with, along with parent entities, where the project is located and the maximum amount of electricity the project could use. Unredacted versions of those contracts would be reviewed by the commission and the Alabama Attorney General’s Office to ensure the projects are “consistent with the public interest.” PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond said the new procedures will help keep the public better informed about data centers that may be developed. “Currently, the redacted [public] filings of Alabama Power pretty much blacks out most everything that you might find important,” Almond said. “And so we required certain information in the filing that is not currently required.” Currently, data centers undergo the same approval process as any other large industrial site, which does not require a separate vote by the commission. The new rules would change that for the massive server farms, many of which sprawl across dozens, even hundreds, of acres and use as much electricity as cities. “To me, it was important, because of the size of the data centers and the amount of energy they’re using and all the public concern about data centers, that we take a public vote on data center contracts,” Almond said. Despite Almond’s support for public votes on data centers, the final version of the new rules includes a provision that could allow projects to be approved by default without a vote by the commission. The rules say that the commission “shall” vote on each new data center project larger than 150 megawatts, but a late amendment stated that if the commission failed to vote on the contracts within 90 days, those projects would be approved by default. Data center contracts will also have to include more financial details showing that the facilities are paying all the costs they incur, including whatever new infrastructure may be required. The new rules were drafted in response to an Alabama law passed this year requiring stronger data-center disclosures. The commission order instructs Alabama Power to create a new rate schedule for data centers complying with the terms of the order within 10 days, with the changes to take effect not less than 30 days after that. Alabama Power, through a spokesman, said it was committed to following all regulatory requirements, including the new data center rules. “Alabama Power will continue to require large load data center customers to pay the full cost to serve their energy needs, so costs are not shifted to existing customers,” the company said in a statement after the PSC adopted its new rules. “Alabama state law affirms that same standard and the Alabama Public Service Commission approves contracts that meet that standard while promoting positive benefits for other customers.” Critics point to potential loophole The default approval provision was first introduced by Commissioner Chris Beeker III, who said it would spur the commission to take timely action on submitted contracts. “We don’t have anything specific in this verbiage that says when we will take it to a vote,” Beeker said. “That’s what I’m trying to kind of right. So it’s deemed approved unless you want to disapprove it.” Almond responded that she understood Beeker’s position but said it was important for the PSC to vote publicly on each proposal. “I feel strongly that we should take a public vote as a commission on data centers, and we should not follow the deemed approved process that we’ve been following for a number of years,” Almond said during the meeting. Commissioner Jeremy Oden said he understood both points of view. After about 20 minutes of discussion among the commissioners and Luke Bentley, the PSC’s administrative law judge, the commissioners agreed to an amendment that included the 90-day deemed approval provision. Currently, data center contracts submitted to the PSC for approval are deemed approved unless the commission takes action within 10 days of receiving them. The new rules essentially extend the deemed-approved period to 90 days. The Southern Environmental Law Center said in a statement that the default approval provision was “a blow for data center accountability.” The SELC also notes that the new rules do not call for public hearings or other opportunities for the public to comment on data center proposals. “I am hopeful this is only the beginning of a deeper conversation about how to protect Alabama Power customers from the costs and risks of the data center boom,” Jaclyn Brass, an attorney in SELC’s Birmingham office, said in a news release. “It’s disappointing the commission would not commit to taking public votes on all contracts,” Brass said. “However, requiring Alabama Power to disclose basic information about these contracts, including the name of the data center and the maximum contracted electric capacity, are all important steps toward greater transparency.” Daniel Tait, executive director of clean energy advocacy group Energy Alabama, said data center contracts are unique in their requirements and the commission should vote publicly on them. “Ninety days is better than ten, but silence still counts as yes,” Tait said in a news release. “A contract this big should never t

artigo.texto: Escobar: Fort Bliss data center to shrink, shift site and use brackish water EL PASO, Texas (KFOX14/CBS4) — Changes to a planned data center at Fort Bliss are being touted as progress by U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, who said the Army and the Carlyle Group appear to be responding to community concerns even as key issues remain unresolved. On Monday, Escobar released a statement describing what she called “positive developments” about the project, including a smaller footprint, the use of brackish water and a move away from residential areas. She said the facility will still be located close to neighborhoods and that she will continue pushing for a different location. Escobar also said she remains concerned the data center will rely on gas-generated power. RECOMMENDED: Proposed Fort Bliss data center could use more power than all of El Paso Below is Escobar's full statement: "Today, the Army and Carlyle Group held a meeting of El Paso community stakeholders to discuss the latest updates on the Fort Bliss data center. "Since March, when my team and I first learned of this project, we have asked that the public and local representatives be kept in the loop and be allowed to voice their concerns and ask questions. I’m grateful to the Army and Carlyle for their continued engagement. "I’ve consistently had a number of requests, including that they: - Move the data center far away from any neighborhood; - Preserve our water; - Use renewable energy for the electrical generation; - Be transparent and accountable. "Today we learned that the location of the data center has indeed been moved, but it is still too close to residential areas. Close proximity to homes is not acceptable, and I will continue to advocate for a different location. "We also learned that their water use will likely be of brackish water that will be sent to the Kay Bailey Hutchison Plant for desalination, which I see as a positive development. And while the scale of the data center has also been reduced, they are still on track to utilize gas generation for their power needs. The gas generation for power remains an additional serious concern. We must protect our community’s air quality, and I will continue to push for the use of renewable energy. "As more information becomes available, my team and I will continue to keep the community updated." artigo.texto: YOU.ON e HyperStrong firmam acordo para leilões de baterias Parceria busca unir as capacidades das empresas para disputar projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias no Brasil SBT News Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias da Hyperstrong instalados na Europa Foto: Hyperstrong As empresas YOU.ON Energia e HyperStrong International USA Corp. anunciaram nesta terça-feira (6) a assinatura de um acordo vinculante para atuar conjuntamente nos Leilões de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (LRCAP 2026), previstos para ocorrer no Brasil. O acordo foi firmado no fim de setembro. A parceria prevê cooperação exclusiva entre as empresas nos dois leilões previstos no LRCAP 2026, identificados como Leilões A e B. O objetivo é integrar as capacidades das duas companhias para disputar oportunidades de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de grande escala no país. Para o Leilão A, a YOU.ON obteve credenciamento junto ao Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e está avançando no processo para obter o código de identificação CFI. Acompanhe o SBT News nas TVs por assinatura Claro (586), Vivo (576), Sky (580) e Oi (175), via streaming pelo +SBT,Site e YouTube, além dos canais nas Smart TVs Samsung, LG e Roku. Segundo Martin Ding, presidente da HyperStrong, o acordo amplia a atuação da companhia no mercado brasileiro e combina sua experiência em sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) com a presença local da YOU.ON. “Estamos muito satisfeitos em anunciar que assinamos um acordo vinculante com a YOU.ON para trazer soluções de armazenamento de energia de última geração ao Brasil”, afirmou. O presidente da YOU.ON Energia, Giorgio Seigne, disse que a parceria combina a capacidade local de engenharia, prestação de serviços e assistência técnica da empresa com a tecnologia e os produtos da HyperStrong. “Essa união nos posiciona para oferecer soluções integradas, competitivas e financiáveis para os Leilões do LRCAP 2026, contribuindo para o avanço do armazenamento de energia no Brasil”, afirmou. Fundada em 2011, a HyperStrong integra sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias e tem ações listadas no STAR Market da Bolsa de Valores de Xangai desde janeiro de 2025. Sua capacidade instalada acumulada superava 70 GWh em agosto de 2026, distribuída em mais de 400 projetos. A YOU.ON é uma empresa brasileira especializada em sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A companhia atua em projetos residenciais, comerciais, industriais, de agronegócio e de grande porte para o setor elétrico. O acordo entre as empresas representa o primeiro passo de uma integração para a atuação conjunta em novas oportunidades de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de grande escala no Brasil. artigo.texto: By Chuks Oyema-Aziken Nigeria has reaffirmed its commitment to developing a credible and transparent carbon market capable of attracting climate finance and supporting sustainable economic development. This was disclosed at a High-Level Roundtable on Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV), held in Abuja on Tuesday, under the European Union Climate Dialogues Programme. Speaking on behalf of the Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs. Omotenioye Majekodunmi, the Director of Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, Michael Ivenso, said Nigeria was determined to turn its climate ambitions into tangible and bankable investments. Ivenso said climate action under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration was being viewed as an economic opportunity, particularly in clean energy, agriculture, forestry, waste management and clean technology. He said carbon markets could provide an important avenue for mobilising private capital, but stressed that their credibility would depend on reliable data, transparency and effective verification. According to him, Nigeria would not accommodate carbon markets that encourage greenwashing, insisting that carbon projects must deliver real, additional and permanent emissions reductions. He identified the National Carbon Markets Framework as a major step towards establishing a structured regulatory and institutional system for carbon-market activities in Nigeria. Ivenso said the NCCC was also working towards an integrated national carbon registry that would track carbon credits generated, issued, transferred and retired in the country, thereby helping to prevent double counting. He added that Nigeria was promoting digital MRV through remote sensing, geospatial information, IoT sensors and other technologies to improve accuracy and reduce verification costs. Representing the EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms. Yolanda San Jose said the roundtable was coming at an important time as countries increasingly sought practical ways to translate climate ambitions into action. She said carbon markets were becoming important instruments for supporting emissions reduction, mobilising finance and encouraging investment, but stressed that they must be supported by credible systems that guarantee transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. San Jose commended Nigeria for adopting its National Carbon Markets Framework, describing it as an important foundation for confidence, trust and effectiveness in the country’s emerging carbon market system. She said the framework would help align Nigeria’s climate targets with its broader development priorities while creating an enabling environment for investment in a low-carbon economy. She explained that the EU Climate Dialogues programme was supporting discussions aimed at aligning stakeholders around the framework and developing a practical roadmap for its implementation, with MRV serving as a critical pillar. Also speaking, Director of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, stressed the importance of forests to Nigeria’s climate response, calling for stronger forest monitoring, satellite technology, ground verification and institutional capacity to ensure a high-integrity carbon market.

artigo.texto: Wartsila Launches Valo Joint Venture with RCT Solutions for Energy Storage According to ESS News, Finnish technology group Wartsila has shifted its worldwide energy storage operations into Valo, a joint venture it co-owns on an equal basis with German engineering firm RCT Solutions. The company anticipates that the new entity will post losses during 2026 before returning to profitability near the close of 2027. Valo, characterized as a utility-scale battery energy storage system integrator encompassing Wartsila's Energy Storage operations, commenced on Oct. 1 following the completion of the joint venture between the two owners. Valo starts with over 20 GWh spanning more than 130 projects globally. Peter Fath, who formerly served as chief executive of RCT Solutions, heads the new venture as chief executive, while Luke Witmer holds the position of chief technology officer. Wartsila disclosed the transaction on June 15, stating it would hand over net assets amounting to under 5% of its total net assets. Finalization hinged on regulatory clearances and securing a financing package. Additional investors could enter at a later stage, possibly reducing the stakes of the two founding shareholders, and the joint venture will gain from project guarantees Wartsila has already provided on ongoing projects, according to the Helsinki-based group. Wartsila further indicated that the joint venture would operate at a loss in 2026 owing to weak recent order intake and transformation expenses, primarily a write-down of capitalized research and development. It projected the effect on its full-year 2026 operating result at EUR40 million to EUR50 million, or $45.2 million, contingent on when closing occurs. The company expressed expectations that the joint venture would deliver positive results near the end of 2027, and its Oct. 1 closing release restated the anticipated 2026 loss. Wartsila noted that the energy storage business represented its smallest segment, employing roughly 480 people. It recorded net sales of EUR694 million in 2025 with an operating margin of 3.3%, finishing the year with an order book valued at EUR719 million. Wartsila stated that RCT Solutions, established in 2012, has overseen the engineering and creation of multiple battery and solar manufacturing plants across the globe, and that one RCT entity has served as a crucial supplier to Wartsila Energy Storage for several years. It added that RCT also offers a chance for vertical integration via an existing integrated battery energy storage system manufacturing effort in the United States in the near term. Neither company has disclosed the project's name. Wartsila initiated a strategic review of the business in October 2023 and concluded it in March 2025 by separating storage into a distinct reporting segment with its own financial objectives. Following the joint venture agreement, it reclassified the unit as discontinued operations, and it will now report its stake as a share of result in associated companies. At the time it began the review, Wartsila reported net sales of EUR983 million for the business on a 12-month rolling basis through the end of the third quarter of 2023. The targets established in March 2025, low double-digit annual organic growth and an operating margin of 3% to 5%, are no longer applicable after the joint venture agreement. - 1. artigo.texto: Supercapacitors charge in seconds and batteries store vast amounts of energy, but no single device has ever managed to do both at once. A team of researchers from India, China, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Thailand now reports a promising step toward closing that gap. In a study published in the Journal of Materials Science, the group synthesized petal-like nanostructures of bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3) and demonstrated that these flower-shaped particles can serve as the workhorse positive electrode in a supercapattery, an emerging hybrid device that combines the battery-like ability to store large amounts of charge with the supercapacitor-like ability to deliver it rapidly. The work stands out not only for its impressive performance numbers but also for the depth of its explanation: the team paired meticulous electrochemical experiments with density functional theory (DFT) simulations to reveal, atom by atom, why the device works best in one particular electrolyte. The choice of material is deliberate. Bismuth sulfide is an earth-abundant, environmentally benign semiconductor that has attracted growing attention as an electrode material for energy storage. Its layered orthorhombic crystal structure, built from covalently bonded Bi2S3 ribbons held together by weaker van der Waals forces, offers open channels along which ions can migrate, making it naturally suited to intercalation-based charge storage. Previous studies have produced Bi2S3 in the form of nanorods, nanowires, nanoflowers and nanoflakes using solvothermal, chemical bath and spray methods, and several groups have reported respectable supercapacitor performance from composites that pair the sulfide with graphene, carbon nitride or nickel foam. What has been missing, the authors argue, is a systematic understanding of how the electrolyte itself, not just the material, controls the charge storage process. To build their electrode material, the researchers turned to hydrothermal synthesis, a technique that grows crystals from aqueous precursors inside a sealed, heated vessel. Under the right combination of temperature, time and precursor chemistry, the reaction self-assembles Bi2S3 into petal-like nanopetals, which the team abbreviates BSNP. This flower-like architecture is more than aesthetic. The petals create a high surface-area scaffold with abundant exposed active sites, short diffusion pathways for ions and open voids that accommodate the volume changes that occur as charge is stored and released. Such morphological engineering is a central strategy in modern electrode design, because electrochemical reactions happen only at surfaces and interfaces; the more accessible surface a material presents to the electrolyte, the more charge it can store and the faster it can deliver it. The heart of the experiment is a comparison across three alkaline electrolytes: 2 M solutions of lithium hydroxide (LiOH), sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and potassium hydroxide (KOH). All three contain the same charge-carrying hydroxide ion, but they differ in the size and hydration behavior of their cations, and those differences ripple through every aspect of electrode kinetics. When the team tested BSNP as the positive electrode in each solution, the results were striking. In 2 M KOH, the nanopetals delivered a gravimetric capacity of 797.9 coulombs per gram at a scan rate of 1 millivolt per second, outperforming the same material in LiOH and NaOH. In other words, simply swapping the electrolyte cation from lithium or sodium to potassium unlocked a substantially larger fraction of the material’s theoretical storage capability. Why would potassium ions give bismuth sulfide an edge? The answer, the researchers show, lies in the electronic and ionic interplay at the material’s surface. Using DFT calculations, they probed how hydroxide species interact with the Bi2S3 lattice under each electrolyte condition. Orbital hybridization analysis revealed favorable overlap between the electronic states of the surface and the adsorbed species in the KOH case, while Bader charge analysis quantified the electron transfer between them. Charge density difference maps and electron localization function analysis visualized where electrons accumulate and deplete during adsorption, painting a consistent picture: the potassium-containing environment promotes stronger, more favorable electronic coupling at the Bi2S3 surface, which lowers the energetic barriers for the redox reactions that store charge. This computational evidence aligns neatly with the electrochemical data, giving the performance claims a mechanistic foundation rather than leaving them as empirical observations. Kinetic analysis added another layer of insight. Applying Dunn’s method, a widely used technique that separates the capacitive (surface-controlled) and diffusion-controlled contributions to charge storage from cyclic voltammetry data measured at different scan rates, the team confirmed that diffusion-dominated processes govern the behavior of the BSNP electrode. That finding matters because it places the material firmly in the battery-type category rather than the purely capacitive one. Battery-type electrodes store charge through faradaic reactions, in which ions insert into the crystal lattice and electrons transfer to or from the metal centers, allowing much more charge to be packed per gram than in the electrostatic double-layer storage that characterizes carbon-based supercapacitor electrodes. It is precisely this battery-like positive electrode, paired with a capacitive negative electrode, that defines the supercapattery architecture. To prove the concept at the device level, the researchers assembled an asymmetric supercapacitor (ASC) in which the BSNP nanopetals served as the positive electrode and activated carbon, a classic high-surface-area capacitive material, served as the negative electrode. artigo.texto: Tuesday night’s Urbana City Council meeting lasted about four and a half hours, wrapping up around 10:30 p.m., with much of the meeting focused on a pending agreement involving Thor Equities and a proposed data center. Approximately 30 people addressed council during the meeting, with speakers raising concerns about the proposed settlement and a potential data center development. The proposed facility could include approximately two million square feet and would be located within the Urbana city limits along South U.S. 68. While individual comments varied, several common themes emerged. Speakers questioned whether the decision should remain a local one and raised concerns about the proposed agreement and its potential long-term effects. Some speakers said, “This should be a local choice,” “No man can serve two masters,” and “We cannot be bought.” Others described the proposal as a potential “buyout,” questioned what price Urbana could be bought for, and warned that once the city “opens Pandora’s box,” it may not be able to close it. Some members of the public also raised the possibility of recalling the entire city council. The comments followed a recent public letter released by Urbana Mayor Bill Bean regarding the proposed data center agreement. Community member Brad Winner Jr. urged council members to carefully consider any proposed settlement and asked why the matter is being handled through an executive session. The letter also raises concerns about the financial incentives that could be associated with the proposed data center, including possible cash, infrastructure, and other financial commitments. Winner alleged that the city administration and developers have been working on the project for some time and questioned the extent to which council members and the public have been informed. He also raised concerns about additional pending litigation involving property rights and affected citizens, and questioned whether approving a settlement could result in what was described as “trading one lawsuit for another.” Council Approves EMS Equipment Funding Also during Tuesday night’s meeting, Urbana City Council unanimously approved additional funding for EMS equipment replacement and service agreements. Last year, council approved a $150,000 capital allocation for three critical pieces of emergency medical equipment manufactured by Stryker. Those include a LUCAS 3 mechanical CPR device, a LIFEPAK 35 monitor and defibrillator, and a Power-PRO 2 powered ambulance cot. The equipment is used on Urbana’s frontline emergency response vehicles, including Engine 1, Medic 1 and Medic 2. According to information presented to council, the equipment currently in service includes previous-generation models that have reached, or are approaching, the end of their manufacturer-supported life cycle. The department also explained that a Medic 1 accident in late 2025 changed some of the original equipment replacement priorities. The city has since received a new chassis and a new Stryker Power-PRO 2 cot for Medic 1. The legislation approved Tuesday authorizes a purchase order of $108,464.98 to Stryker Medical for a replacement Power-PRO cot loading system and a service agreement covering the department’s Power-PRO cot loading systems. The new cot loading system will be installed in Medic 2. The service agreement provides seven years of coverage, including parts, labor, travel, per diem, maintenance, and battery service. City officials said the agreement will provide more predictable maintenance costs and help ensure the equipment remains operational and supported throughout its service life. The expense will be paid from the Police and Fire Capital Improvement Fund and is included in the 2026 budget. The council’s approval of the additional EMS funding and service agreement was unanimous. No Action Taken on Pending Litigation Toward the end of Tuesday night’s meeting, council members entered executive session for pending litigation. The executive session lasted more than an hour. Council members eventually returned to the public meeting and told those who remained that no action would be taken at this time regarding the pending litigation. Council members said they want to gather additional information so they can make an educated and informed decision. The next Urbana City Council meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at 6 p.m., where it’s expected to be decided at that time.

artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – Indonesia is pushing ASEAN to make its emerging carbon pricing systems more compatible as countries across the region develop different national approaches amid growing pressure from carbon-related trade measures and international markets. Mari Elka Pangestu, Indonesia’s Special Envoy for International Trade and Multilateral Cooperation and Co-Chair of the Green Investment Principles (GIP) ASEAN, said ASEAN countries were no longer debating whether carbon pricing was needed, but how their systems could work together. “We are no longer now talking about whether we need carbon pricing. We know we do need it, but we need to figure out how we should be doing it, whether as each country or as ASEAN as a region,” Mari said at the GIP ASEAN research dissemination of The Emerging Carbon Pricing Landscape in Southeast Asia in Jakarta on Monday (Oct. 5, 2026). She said ASEAN countries had made progress in developing carbon pricing systems over the past decade, with each country pursuing a different model based on its own circumstances. Singapore has established a carbon tax and recently raised the price to US$45, while Indonesia and Vietnam are developing emissions trading systems. Thailand has focused on international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, while Malaysia is moving from voluntary toward compliance carbon markets. Indonesia is also moving to implement sectoral regulations under Presidential Regulation No. 110/2025 on carbon economic value. Mari said the country had made progress on its carbon registry and forestry regulations, while energy-sector regulations were also being prepared. She identified forestry and energy as two key sectors for Indonesia’s carbon market, with further sectoral regulations expected for agriculture, marine and fisheries, and industry. Market Access Mari said differences in national systems were natural given the varying economic conditions of ASEAN countries. However, developing carbon markets in isolation could create risks if rules become disconnected, data are misaligned and carbon prices differ significantly. “This learning by doing, of course, comes with risks if we are developing our systems in isolation with disconnected rules, misaligned data, and very different price levels,” she said. Such fragmentation could make it harder for countries to trade carbon assets, attract investment and gain recognition from international partners, she added. The pressure to improve compatibility is also coming from international trade measures, including the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), as well as green standards and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Mari said businesses, particularly exporters, were increasingly aware of the need for carbon pricing as they face growing climate-related requirements in international trade. “Being competitive today means sustainability. You have to be part of a sustainable supply chain,” she said. She said the EU CBAM and similar measures being developed elsewhere could increasingly affect how carbon pricing is linked to international trade. “If we do not price our own carbon, others will price it for us, and the revenue will go to their budgets, not ours,” Mari said. GIP ASEAN Study The research dissemination was organized by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), which has served as the secretariat of GIP ASEAN since its inception in 2023. The GIP ASEAN chapter seeks to connect research and policy recommendations with financial institutions, governments, investors and other stakeholders to support Southeast Asia’s green transition. Yose Rizal Damuri, Executive Director of CSIS, said the research presented at the event examined carbon pricing in Southeast Asia and its implications for the region. Carbon pricing, he said, should not be viewed solely as a mechanism for carbon markets, but also as a way to translate sustainability principles into economic activities, including investment and emissions reductions. “When we’re talking about carbon pricing, we have to look at also on how to translate this carbon pricing into real investment and also to emission reductions, to internalize the carbon price into our economic activities,” he said. The study also highlighted the importance of ASEAN cooperation while recognizing differences in economic structures and levels of readiness among member states. Yose said regional cooperation should focus not on creating a uniform carbon pricing mechanism, but on reducing uncertainty and improving interoperability among national systems. “It will reduce uncertainty for business and investors while also strengthening their confidence in carbon market and also in internalizing the carbon price into their decision,” he said. ***

artigo.texto: Letter to the editor: Data centers represent opportunity for region Published 12:00 am Thursday, October 8, 2026 I’ve been a union electrician for most of my working life, and I’ll tell you what that has meant: good wages, real benefits, and the ability to raise a family in southern Ohio without having to leave to do it. Not everyone has been that lucky: I’ve watched too many skilled tradespeople in this region pack up and drive hours away to find work that should exist right here. That’s why I’ve been paying close attention to the growth and development of data centers. These facilities require hundreds of skilled electricians working for years on a single campus. Once operational, they need licensed electrical staff on-site permanently. This isn’t temporary work, either, as some critics like to suggest. It’s the kind of sustained, high-skill employment that builds careers and keeps families rooted in their communities. Rural Ohio has a deep bench of talented tradespeople. What it has lacked is enough local work to keep them here. When a young electrician finishes their apprenticeship in Lawrence or Scioto County today, the honest answer too often is that the best opportunities are somewhere else. That shouldn’t be the case. As the owner of SJS Electric, I think about this practically. More large-scale electrical projects in this region mean more opportunities for local contractors, more hours for local workers, and more investment in the skilled trades pipeline that our communities depend on. It means apprentices have a reason to stay. I’m not asking anyone to take this on faith. I’m asking Ohio’s leaders to look seriously at what this industry offers to working people in parts of the state that have been waiting too long for this kind of opportunity. The work is here. Let’s make sure the workers are too. Steve Sydow Ironton

artigo.texto: Power U.S. Battery-Power Kickoffs Hit $3.2 Billion in September Industrial Info Resources is tracking 11 standalone U.S. BESS projects that were scheduled to kick off in September, totaling US$3.28 billion of investment Released Monday, October 05, 2026 Written by Jesse Broehl, Editor-in-Chief, Breaking Energy News (BEN), IIR Intelligence, (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Eleven standalone BESS projects were scheduled to break ground across the U.S. in September, representing $3.28 billion in combined investment and 2,236 MW of capacity. BESS Ranks Third Among Power Plant Types for September Sixty power generation projects in the U.S. are scheduled to break ground this September, representing a total investment value (TIV) of $16.8 billion and roughly 18,083 megawatts (MW) of capacity across 10 fuel categories. Standalone battery energy-storage systems (BESS) rank third among power plant types this month for total investment, and it trails only solar in project count. Rarely built a decade ago, BESS plants are a rapidly growing market. According to Industrial Info Resources data, 11 standalone BESS projects are scheduled to break ground across the U.S. in September, representing $3.28 billion in combined investment and 2,236 MW of capacity. This story focuses on project starts in the BESS sector for September. For a look at all generation types of plants kicking off, see this accompanying overview news story by IIR Energy. Solar focus is here and natural gas here. See this data compilation for the full list of projects, all generation sources for September. Multiple Enabling Factors Drive Fast-Growing BESS Market BESS's success is driven by multiple factors: battery costs have drastically fallen, making the plants more cost-effective to build. According to BloombergNEF's annual Lithium-Ion Battery Price Survey, overall, battery pack prices have fallen 93% since 2010 -- from roughly $1,436 to $1,474 per kWh (in real 2025 dollars, per BNEF's own inflation-adjusted figures) down to $108 per kWh in 2025. Policy also has been a key factor. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) provided for the first time tax credits for standalone BESS, which before had been limited to co-located with solar. After U.S. elections in the fall of 2024 ushered in a second Trump Administration and full Republican control of Congress, wind and solar tax credits were phased out while the credits for BESS were left intact. Eleven Battery Storage Projects, 2,236 MW of Capacity Texas hosts the largest project (the 1,043-MW Zeus Armstrong BESS), while California and New Mexico each host multiple smaller projects. Minnesota, Indiana and Michigan each have one project. Every one of the 11 projects is new construction; as with solar, there is no refurbishment or life-extension activity in this category, consistent with battery storage being a fundamentally newer technology at utility scale. Ownership skews heavily nonutility, similar to solar: Nine of the 11 projects, representing $2.91 billion, are developed by nonutility/IPP entities. Only two projects are utility-owned--and, notably, both belong to the same company, Xcel Energy. Some notable projects and ownership or offtake structure include: Zeus Armstrong BESS Unit Addition (Claude, TX): At 1,043 MW and $1.57 billion, this is the largest battery-storage project in the September pipeline, and the largest planned standalone battery project in Texas overall, according to third-party interconnection-queue tracking. The project, developed by Zeus Renewable Energy Development, sits in Armstrong County, Texas -- the same county as this month's Claude Armstrong Phase I solar project profiled in IIR Energy's accompanying solar coverage for September planned starts. Armstrong County is also home to a major Crusoe Energy AI data center campus with Google as an anchor tenant, part of Google's broader $40 billion Texas AI infrastructure buildout. Becker Sherco BESS (Clear Lake Township, MN) and Shakopee Blue Lake BESS (Shakopee, MN): These two projects, together worth $549 million, are both pieces of a single, coordinated Xcel Energy clean-energy transition plan. Xcel filed a proposal with Minnesota regulators in October 2025 to double battery storage capacity at its retiring Sherco coal plant in Becker to 600 MW -- Minnesota's largest power plant, scheduled for full coal retirement by the end of 2030 -- while separately adding 135.5 MW of storage at its Blue Lake facility in Shakopee. Both projects reuse existing grid interconnections from the coal and gas infrastructure already on site. The following charts show all 11 projects in two charts, ranked by TIV value and by MW installed capacity. See this data compilation for the full list of all projects, all generation sources for September. Source: IIR Energy Key Takeaways - Standalone battery energy storage (BESS) ranks third among power plant types this month for total investment level. - Eleven standalone BESS projects are scheduled to break ground across the U.S. in September, representing $3.28 billion in combined investment and 2,236 MW of capacity. - The reason for BESS's success is driven by multiple enabling factors: Costs have fallen 93% since 2010. Tax credits for BESS were added in 2022. When wind and solar tax credits were phased out by Congress in 2025, the credits for BESS were left intact. - Texas hosts the single-largest project (the 1,043-MW Zeus Armstrong BESS), while California and New Mexico each host multiple smaller projects. artigo.texto: Rethinking WUE: Data Center Water Strategy Beyond The Facitily As AI reshapes data center cooling, improving water usage effectiveness requires a system-level view. October 5, 2026 Water has always served a strategic role in hydronic applications. It carries thermal energy more efficiently than air, making it well-suited for applications where precise thermal management is critical. Today, that includes AI data centers, where rising computing densities are creating unprecedented cooling demands. But as data center development accelerates, the conversation around water is changing. Water is no longer merely a cooling input – its availability, quality and infrastructure capacity have become important considerations for siting, permitting, resilience and community alignment. That makes water usage effectiveness (WUE) an increasingly important metric, but also one that needs to be considered in context. Water as a strategic resource Liquid-based cooling isn't new. Data centers have used water for decades to absorb and remove heat generated by IT equipment. What is changing is the scale and concentration of that heat. AI and high-performance computing are driving higher rack densities that challenge traditional air-cooling approaches. As a result, direct-to-chip liquid cooling and other liquid-based architectures are moving closer to the heat source, where they can efficiently capture heat from CPUs and GPUs. Closed-loop hydronic systems can also recirculate fluid rather than continuously consuming makeup water. Together, these approaches create opportunities to reduce reliance on evaporation and improve facility-level WUE. But there's an important distinction: Using water more efficiently inside a data center doesn't necessarily tell the whole story. Look beyond WUE alone Every cooling architecture involves trade-offs. A closed-loop system, for example, may significantly reduce on-site water consumption, but the heat still has to go somewhere. Depending on the heat rejection strategy, reducing water use can increase electrical demand. Conversely, evaporative cooling can reduce cooling energy under the right conditions while consuming more water. That’s why WUE shouldn't be considered separately from power usage effectiveness (PUE). Water and energy use are closely connected, and the electricity powering a data center can carry its own water footprint depending on the regional generation mix. A cooling strategy that reduces water consumption on-site but requires more electricity may simply shift some of that water demand upstream rather than eliminate it. Liquid cooling adds another factor. Moving liquid closer to high-density computing equipment provides an effective way to manage concentrated heat loads, but liquid cooling alone doesn't determine overall water consumption. Operators and designers still need to consider the complete thermal chain, including pumping, heat exchange, heat rejection and the energy required to operate the system. The objective isn't simply to drive one metric lower. It's to find the appropriate water-energy balance for the site. That balance will look different from one data center to another. Climate, water availability and quality, workload, rack density, grid characteristics, utility capacity and local infrastructure can all influence the appropriate cooling strategy. A data center in a water-stressed region with available electrical capacity may require a different approach than a facility where water is abundant but the grid is constrained. That's where system-level thinking comes in. Instead of starting with a specific cooling technology, project teams should consider the outcomes the facility needs to achieve and consider the complete water cycle: - Where will water come from? - What quality is required? - How will it be treated and moved? - How efficiently can it be reused? - How will heat be rejected? - What happens to the water before it leaves the facility? Advanced treatment technologies can expand opportunities to use reclaimed or alternative water sources while maintaining the quality required for reliable cooling, while digital monitoring can provide visibility into water quality, flow, equipment condition and changing system performance. Meanwhile, heat recovery may create opportunities to put captured thermal energy to beneficial use rather than simply rejecting it. Collaboration outside the facility matters, too. Early coordination with water and wastewater utilities can help data center developers understand local constraints, evaluate reuse opportunities and identify infrastructure investments that strengthen long-term water resilience. Design WUE into the system As AI infrastructure scales, water strategy can no longer be something addressed after the cooling architecture is already established. While WUE provides an important measure of progress, the bigger opportunity is understanding what sits behind the metric. Water source, treatment, hydronics, cooling, monitoring, reuse, discharge and even community infrastructure are all interconnected. The goal isn't simply to use less water. It's to manage water and energy together in a way that supports thermal performance, uptime and responsible growth. For the next generation of data centers, that broader view may be the most effective way to make every drop – and every watt – count. About the Author: Steven Lucente is a business development manager for Xylem’s Applied Water business, where he leads data center business development and turns customer infrastructure challenges into scalable growth strategies and win-ready solutions.
