artigo.texto: Politics & Government Operations Suspended At 2 East End Battery Storage Facilities: Romaine "Operations must cease until changes are made that will protect our drinking water." EAST HAMPTON, NY — Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine announced Monday that NextEra Energy had agreed to suspend operations at two battery energy storage facilities on the East End: the facility at Cove Hollow Road in East Hampton and the facility in Montauk near Fort Pond. Both facilities are jointly owned by NextEra Energy and National Grid. "Less than 24 hours after the town board unanimously authorized litigation to shut down the East Hampton and Montauk battery storage facilities, NextEra has temporarily shut both facilities down," East Hampton Town Supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez said. "This is the action we demanded, and I am pleased that NextEra responded swiftly to my September 29 letter and the town board’s action. The board had authorized litigation, retained counsel and taken the steps necessary to go to court to secure this shutdown. I am pleased that NextEra acted before litigation had to be commenced." Find out what's happening in East Hamptonfor free with the latest updates from Patch. She added: "The town will hold off on commencing litigation while counsel reviews the agreement. The town retains all of its legal rights should NextEra fail to follow through on removing all NOVEC 1230 from both facilities and ensuring appropriate fire safety and environmental measures are in place." The suspension, Romaine said, follows weeks of discussions between Suffolk County and NextEra. Find out what's happening in East Hamptonfor free with the latest updates from Patch. NextEra did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Patch. Under the arrangement, NextEra will suspend operations at both sites and remove the Novec 1230 fire suppression agent from both facilities by about October 9, Romaine said. "We are very grateful that this agreement has been reached," said Romaine. "The 2023 fire at the East Hampton BESS location, and the consequent contamination of the site and surrounding areas, prove that the operations must cease until changes are made that will protect our drinking water." The State Department of Environmental Conservation has determined that when water was applied to the East Hampton facility during a May 2023 fire, it mixed with Novec 1230 and broke down into PFPrA, a short-chain "forever chemical," which has since been detected in drinking water in the surrounding area, Romaine said. Two Suffolk County Water Authority wells have been taken offline, he added. The county has drilled monitoring wells to investigate the contamination and supports the Water Authority's litigation against NextEra, he said. In July, Romaine and East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen sent letters to the chief executives of NextEra Energy and National Grid urging them to suspend operations at the East Hampton facility until the investigation is completed, he said. "We need a remediation plan immediately, one approved by the DEC, so the hard work of cleaning the site can begin," said Romaine. "The community did not know for years that the 2023 fire had left behind PFPrA. They should not wait any longer for the situation to be addressed." In August, the Town of East Hampton formally directed East Hampton Energy Storage Center, NextEra Energy and National Grid to take six specific actions, at their sole expense, to address fire-water containment and other safety concerns at the battery energy storage facility on Cove Hollow Road. The demands include new engineering controls capable of containing all fire water and runoff, a revised emergency and safety plan, complete and certified technical information, a hazardous-waste management plan and an independent study of whether the facility remained necessary for the East End electric grid. The action followed questions raised by the May 2023 battery fire and came as state and county agencies continued an investigation into PFPrA and other PFAS contamination near the Suffolk County Water Authority’s Bridgehampton Road Wellfield. No source had been determined, town officials said. Earlier this year, the Water Authority detected PFPrA at the wellfield, removing three wells from service and limiting a fourth to emergency use, town officials said. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation is currently sampling the battery storage property, town officials said. The Suffolk County Department of Health Services is also conducting groundwater sampling and testing private drinking-water wells in the area. The county has identified 26 homes in the area that are not connected to public water; results are not yet available for all of those wells, and several have not yet been sampled, town officials said. When the facility was reviewed in 2017 by the town’s planning board, the town relied on technical information provided by the applicant stating that no liquid within the battery cells could spill and that the only hazardous spillable liquid at the site was oil contained in the transformers and inverters, town officials said. The approved plans therefore included containment for that oil, but not a permanent system capable of capturing the fire-suppression water generated during the May 2023 battery fire, which the Water Authority alleges exceeded 2.2 million gallons, officials added. The town required the companies to: - Submit a revised emergency and safety plan for town approval explaining how the facility would respond to a worst-case battery fire, contain all fire-suppression water and promptly notify the town and emergency agencies. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr. e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA A diretoria da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) aprovou nesta terça-feira (6) a abertura de consulta pública sobre o rateio do encargo que vai custear a contratação de baterias via leilão. A proposta da área técnica é ratear os custos entre todos os geradores conforme a flexibilidade oferecida ao sistema. Desta forma, as usinas intermitentes, que não geram de forma firme, devem pagar 100% do encargo. Já os geradores que são mais flexíveis devem pagar menos, entre 75% e 25% do encargo. Assim, usinas eólicas, solares e nucleares pagariam mais, as térmicas um pouco menos e hidrelétricas, o menor patamar. A MMGD (Micro e Minigeração Distribuída), a princípio, não entraria no rateio. Também será discutida na consulta uma proposta do ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) para que o encargo seja reduzido no caso de fontes que entreguem mais potência na ponta de carga – janela em que a geração solar cai e o consumo aumenta, exigindo resposta rápida do sistema. As contribuições poderão ser enviadas até 9 de novembro, e, com isso, a conclusão do processo deve se dar após a realização do primeiro leilão de baterias, marcado para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro.

Battery Storage Project Denied State Incentives Maryland regulators have denied state financial credits for the proposed 500-megawatt Oystercatcher battery storage project in White Hall. WHITE HALL, MD — Regulators denied state financial incentives for a controversial battery energy storage project proposed for northern Harford County after determining it was not cost-effective for Maryland ratepayers. Harford County officials have raised other concerns, including the project's proximity to Deer Creek, a tributary to the Susquehanna River. The facility would sit on approximately 71 acres. The mostly forested site identified for the facility already hosts Baltimore Gas & Electric’s Conastone Substation, located in the northwestern corner of Harford County. A representative from Tenaska, the company developing the project, said that the facility would be located at least 600 feet from the waterway, and that most of the 70 acres would remain forested. However, the state's decision does not kill the proposed Oystercatcher Energy Storage System, which would be built along Norrisville Road in White Hall next to Baltimore Gas and Electric's Conastone Substation. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced Oct. 1 that it had declined to award Energy Storage Capacity Credits to the 500-megawatt Oystercatcher project during the first round of the state's energy storage procurement program. The credits provide financial support intended to protect qualifying energy storage projects from fluctuations in electricity grid prices. Tony Ruffin, a PSC spokesperson, told The Baltimore Sun that Oystercatcher's developers can still move forward with the Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity process, which the project would need before it could be built. They would have to do so without the financial benefits provided through the Energy Storage Capacity Credit program. The PSC cited the project's lower ranking, lack of cost-effectiveness, and potential ratepayer impacts in declining to award the credits. A cost-benefit analysis prepared by Power Advisory LLC also found the project's projected economic benefits did not match its costs. The analysis redacted some financial information. The proposed lithium-ion battery facility could store up to 500 megawatts of electricity for six hours and connect to BGE's Conastone Substation. According to the PSC, battery storage facilities can help stabilize the electric grid by storing electricity and releasing it when demand requires. Harford County Executive Bob Cassilly has been among the project's most vocal opponents, raising concerns about potential environmental and public safety risks, including the facility's proximity to Deer Creek. "The proposed location raises significant environmental and public safety concerns, particularly in the event of a fire or other incident," Cassilly wrote in a May 15 petition to intervene. Residents also opposed the project during a July 30 public comment hearing. The PSC said there needs to be "continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County" if developers decide to continue pursuing the project. “Environmentally, you would struggle to find a worse site for this project,” said Jennifer Wilson, a resident who said at the public hearing that her children attend the nearby Norrisville Elementary School. In an interview with Maryland Matters, Cassily said the beloved creek, a favorite kayaking spot for him and his family, lies downhill. He said he worries firefighters would have trouble fighting any blazes at the site nestled behind the substation, and that any firefighting chemicals, or chemicals contained within the battery facility itself, would flow into the river. “If anything goes wrong with this thing, it goes right down into the Deer Creek,” Cassilly said. “This is a cherished waterway that feeds the water supply.” Lee Hine, who lives about a half mile from the proposed project, said at the public hearing that he was surprised by its location, given the hilly terrain and the area's status as a prized natural area. “The watershed is a prime aspect of why we all moved to this area. It’s a natural preserve here,” Hine said. “I’m trying to understand why we’re not looking for ‘brown ground’ facility areas — or at least flatter areas. This is a mountain. We live on a mountain.” Despite denying Oystercatcher financial support in the first round, regulators have not closed the door on the project. Oystercatcher was one of five projects that initially sought financial support through a program established under Maryland's Next Generation Energy Act. Two of the five applicants later withdrew. The PSC ultimately conditionally selected the 400-megawatt Chalk Point Storage Project in Aquasco in Prince George's County and the 40-megawatt Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in Barton in Garrett County. Together, the two projects would provide 440 megawatts of storage capacity, well short of the 800 megawatts sought during the first round. The projects would operate with four-hour storage durations under flat, 15-year award terms, subject to PSC conditions and additional approvals. The commission estimated the two selected projects would cost a typical Maryland residential customer about 7 cents per month combined. artigo.texto: Delphos City Council approves 18-month data center moratorium DELPHOS, Ohio (WLIO) — Delphos is joining other cities in the area that are putting a hold on new data centers. Delphos City Council voted Monday night to impose an 18-month moratorium on data centers and renewable energy projects. Each of the Ohio gubernatorial candidates has plans for data centers moving forward in the state. Delphos officials want to wait and see what Ohio lawmakers do to shape how new data center projects are addressed in the state. Council also appointed Doug Mullenhour as mayor to replace Andre McConnahea, who resigned in August. Mullenhour previously served as Delphos mayor from 2020 to 2024 and said he is glad to be back in the mayor’s seat. “Delphos is a great place to live and raise a family. I’ve done that here and we’ve made a lot of progress in the last past years and I just wanted to come back and make sure we get that progress momentum keep it keep it going. We got a safety service building to get built and we got a canal to keep pushing through to try to get it cleaned up and some development going down there. So, there’s a lot of things in the fire” says Doug Mullenhour, Delphos Mayor. During its next meeting, council will vote on a tax abatement agreement that would help establish a pharmacy in the city. artigo.texto: Four EV battery stocks with strong future roadmap New Delhi, Oct. 7 -- India's electric-vehicle (EV) revolution is creating opportunities well beyond vehicle manufacturers, with batteries emerging as a critical part of the ecosystem. As EV adoption increases, demand for lithium-ion cells, battery packs, advanced energy-storage systems and critical battery materials is expected to grow substantially. Indian companies are therefore investing in new battery technologies, manufacturing capacity, and supporting infrastructure to reduce dependence on imports and capture a larger share of this emerging market. In this editorial, we examine four listed companies with significant battery-related ambitions and clearly defined roadmaps. Their businesses span EV batteries, advanced battery technologies, and key materials used in battery manufacturing. This is not a stock recommendation. Exide Industries is one of India's largest battery companies, with more than seven decades of operating history. Its core business remains lead-acid storage batteries, but it's now investing heavily in lithium-ion technology, creating a second growth platform. Exide Energy Solutions, a wholly owned subsidiary, is engaged in lithium-ion cells, modules and battery packs, with applications across electric vehicles and stationary energy storage. The company's new plant is progressing rapidly. At the Bangalore gigafactory, equipment across all four production lines has been delivered, installed, and is fully operational. The company's first NCM cylindrical line has commenced customer sample deliveries. The LFP prismatic line has also started sample supplies for three-wheeler and telecom applications. Management says it has completed key certifications and testing requirements, including multiple BIS standard registrations. They expect revenue contribution from the Bengaluru plant to commence during FY27. According to the company, Exide is building a genuinely Indian advanced chemistry cell platform, with multiple chemistries, multiple form factors, strategic sourcing partnerships for raw materials, automation-led manufacturing, and a global technology partnership. The company's lithium-ion modules and packs are designed for two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles and commercial vehicles, among other applications. On the financial front, the company reported revenue of Rs.5,528.4 crore for Q1 FY27 vs Rs.4,695.1 crore year-on-year. Net profit at Exide Industries was Rs.350.7 crore vs Rs.274.2 crore on-year. Q1 FY27 saw broad-based growth across Exide Industries' key businesses. The automotive OEM business marked its third consecutive quarter of 25% year-on-year growth. According to the management, this reflected sustained momentum in automotive OEM demand and our strong position across key vehicle platforms. Home inverters and solar also grew over 20% on-year, aided by strong summer demand and focused market initiatives. Solar achieved its highest-ever quarterly revenue of Rs.400 crore plus. Industrial Infrastructure, excluding telecom, maintained its double-digit growth trajectory, supported by industrial UPS and traction business. However, management said government tenders remained muted during the quarter, though they expect them to pick up in the second half. The exports business, on a low base after five consecutive quarters of decline, grew revenue by more than 20%. The company says that it continues to closely monitor the evolving global macro environment, as the global situation remains volatile. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility, formerly Amara Raja Batteries Ltd, is one of India's largest manufacturers of lead-acid batteries. The company changed its name in 2023 to reflect its broader vision to lead India's energy transition in the energy and mobility space by providing comprehensive energy solutions. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility has strong brands like 'Amaron', 'PowerZone', 'Quanta', and exports to 70 countries. The company has evolved considerably over the last few years. While the lead acid battery business continues to hold a strong position across automotive and industrial applications, it now extends beyond its traditional areas of operation. Investments in battery packs, cell technologies, energy storage solutions, recycling and power electronics have broadened its presence across the energy and mobility landscape. The company has manufacturing infrastructure that has 1.5 GWh of EV battery pack capacity. Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies (ARACT) is leading initiatives across lithium-ion cell manufacturing and next-generation energy storage technologies. The business is supported by manufacturing infrastructure, R&D capabilities, strategic partnerships and a phased scale-up roadmap aligned to evolving market requirements. The new energy business has a capex plan of Rs.9,500 crore for setting up a Giga Corridor in Telangana. The net profit for Q1 FY27 was Rs.190.9 crore vs Rs.164.8 crore on-year. The new energy business grew by more than 70%, recording revenue of around Rs.209 crore. artigo.texto: Europe’s solar and battery storage sectors supported nearly one million jobs in 2025, highlighting the growing contribution of clean energy to the European Union’s economy. According to the latest industry assessment, solar photovoltaics and battery energy storage systems (BESS) together provided approximately 982,000 full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs across the EU. Solar PV accounted for the largest share with 874,000 FTE jobs, while BESS contributed 108,000 FTEs. Battery storage employment was assessed separately for the first time in the report. Solar employment grew by 1% during the year, twice the pace of overall EU employment growth. Indirect employment across supply chains represented 56% of the total workforce, while direct jobs accounted for the remaining 44%. Strong deployment of renewable energy and storage capacity was the primary driver behind this employment growth. The EU installed 69 GW of new solar capacity and 27 GWh of battery storage in 2025. Deployment activities generated around 742,000 solar FTE jobs, representing 85% of total solar employment. For battery storage, deployment accounted for approximately 90,000 FTE jobs, or 84% of the sector’s total workforce. Operations and maintenance activities also recorded significant employment gains. Solar O&M supported a record 78,000 FTE jobs, while battery storage operations and maintenance contributed another 8,000 FTEs. The increase reflects the expanding installed base of solar and energy storage projects across Europe. However, manufacturing continued to face challenges from strong international competition, low factory utilization and plant closures. Solar manufacturing supported only about 37,000 FTE jobs. Inverter production dominated this segment, accounting for around 90% of solar manufacturing employment. Battery manufacturing supported approximately 64,000 FTE jobs across the broader battery industry. However, only about 7,000 of these jobs were directly linked to stationary energy storage, as electric vehicles continued to account for the majority of battery manufacturing activity. Germany and Spain emerged as the largest solar employment markets in Europe, each supporting nearly 165,000 FTE jobs. Italy followed with approximately 85,000 FTEs. Together, the three countries represented nearly half of total solar employment in the EU. Utility-scale solar projects also overtook rooftop installations for the first time, accounting for 50.2% of solar jobs. Large projects in Spain, Germany, Italy and Romania contributed significantly to this shift. By 2030, the EU solar workforce is projected to decline by 12% to around 766,000 FTEs. The decline is expected to reflect greater industry productivity and market maturity rather than a contraction of solar power. Annual installations are projected to stabilize at around 70 GW under the medium scenario. Deployment-related employment could fall by 22%, while O&M jobs are expected to increase to 109,000 FTEs. Manufacturing employment could reach 49,000 FTEs if planned projects are completed, while decommissioning and recycling jobs could nearly double to 30,000 FTEs. The report recommends stronger access to training funds for SMEs, updated vocational education covering digital technologies, smart grids and storage, and implementation of installer measures under RED III. Apprenticeships, new career pathways and reskilling programmes for former fossil-fuel workers are also expected to help Europe maintain a skilled workforce for its clean energy transition. artigo.texto: Independence council restricts future data centers after Nebius backlash INDEPENDENCE, Mo. (KCTV) - The Independence City Council voted 6-0 Monday to approve restrictions on future data center development, following a push by opponents of the Nebius AI data center project. The new rules will not affect the Nebius facility, a hyperscale data center on 400 acres at Highway 79 and Little Blue Parkway that broke ground in May. The project drew opposition earlier this year after the previous council approved tax breaks for the company. Voters later removed two city councilors who supported the project and recalled another. Under the new rules, the city council must approve “major” data centers before they can be built. Major data centers are defined as those with electrical loads greater than five megawatts. The city’s amendment to its development ordinance also sets specific requirements, including how far such facilities must be from homes. Councilman Brice Stewart, the only remaining council member who voted against the Nebius incentives, said large-scale data centers were not anticipated when the city’s code of ordinances was last updated in 2022. “The Nebius data center, everything was zoned. They could just come in, buy the land and open the data center,” Stewart said. A planning commission report on the proposed changes said large data centers differ from traditional industrial development, citing “substantial electrical demand, water consumption backup, power generation noise from mechanical equipment, large building, footprints, visual impacts, and potential compatibility, concerns with nearby residential neighborhoods, and community facilities.” The revisions include the following requirements for major data centers: - Generator testing is limited to normal weekday business hours, no more than 10 hours per month, with required sound attenuation and generator testing records. - Closed-loop cooling systems, or similar technologies that use less water than other systems, are required. - Architectural design standards are required that are “intended to reduce their appearance of large uninterrupted building walls.” - A 1,000-foot setback, measured property-line to property-line, is required from residential areas, schools, parks, playgrounds, daycares, nursing homes, hospitals and places of worship. The setback was amended from an initially proposed 500 feet before passage Monday. Resident Daniel Morehead told the council Monday that the city has failed to enforce its current rules on light and noise at the Nebius construction site. “Several of the residents have had to find alternative ways to even exist, most of them moving to their basements, finding other locations with lower noise emissions, just so they can get some sleep,” Morehead said. The new restrictions for major data centers are part of a broader set of changes that create a tiered framework with different rules for smaller facilities. A related set of rules was also created for battery energy storage systems. A six-month moratorium on new data centers, passed by the council in July, remains in effect through Jan. 2, 2027. artigo.texto: America is hopelessly divided along party lines. That’s a stubborn fact, we’re told, and the polling bears it out: Democrats dislike Republicans and Republicans dislike Democrats, in almost precisely the same proportions. But every election produces surprising coalitions that defy entrenched partisanship. In these midterms, left and right have found something so commonly loathed that politicians across the country are flip-flopping in real time. Mother Jones has been tracking the backlash to data centers on the ground long before the water-guzzling behemoths became the country’s bête noire. The AI boom, with its insatiable need for computing, has unleashed a power grab by tech billionaires. “Data centers have replaced megayachts as the preferred theater of oligarchic status signaling,” national correspondent Tim Murphy wrote in his big Mother Jones investigation into hyperscale data centers and the communities they land on. “Oligarchy is now more than an idea; it is a place.” On today’s episode of Stress Test, Tim joins host Garrison Hayes to discuss how data centers—and other AI-boom technologies, like Flock cameras—have upended political fortunes and ripped up the partisan playbook ahead of November’s vote. “It’s maybe the single most toxic issue in the midterms this side of, you know, gas prices,” Tim tells Garrison. “It’s like a three-to-one opposition among voters. Nobody wants data centers. Everybody’s fired up about it.” Take Texas. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott promoted the state as a place where companies could build almost anything. Then rural and suburban communities got the facilities, and the gas plants that power them, in their backyards, along with strained water supplies, pollution, and rising utility bills. “People are complaining about what they have to live next to,” Tim says. “And it just builds and builds and builds.” Under pressure (and running for reelection), Abbott made a stunning reversal, announcing steps that amount to a moratorium. And he’s not the only one feeling the heat. So what changed? Data centers used to be half the size of an Amazon warehouse; now they’re measured in “multiples of Manhattan,” says Tim, who explains how we got here and what to expect next. He heads back to Texas in the coming weeks, and we’ll follow what he learns right up to Election Day. For more, read Tim Murphy’s road trip through the towns living in the shadow of the AI boom: “How the American Oligarchy Went Hyperscale,” from our May+June issue. artigo.texto: Um carro elétrico da BYD foi usado pelo Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Paraná (TRE-PR) para manter as urnas eletrônicas em funcionamento em Salto de Lontra, no interior do estado, depois que um temporal interrompeu o fornecimento de energia no cartório durante o primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. O veículo, cujo modelo não foi informado, foi conectado à estrutura do local por meio da função V2L (Vehicle to Load). O recurso permite que o automóvel libere parte da carga da bateria — em geral entre 30 kWh e 60 kWh — em tomadas comuns, com o auxílio de adaptadores, e sustente aparelhos de baixo consumo por horas. A tecnologia vem de série em modelos como o Dolphin Mini, da BYD, e o EX2, da Geely. Situações semelhantes ocorreram em Francisco Beltrão e Umuarama, também no Paraná, onde a queda de energia foi contornada com a lanterna de celulares ou com a carga própria das urnas. Em Goiás, um policial militar recorreu a um inversor de voltagem para ligar a urna à rede elétrica de um automóvel.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no EPE adia estudo de data centers no RS para dezembro Publicado 06/10/2026 • 18:17 | Atualizado há 13 horas KEY POINTS Informe trimestral reorganiza 47 estudos de transmissão: nove estão concluídos, 28 em andamento e dez ainda serão iniciados. Alterações de prazo não significam atraso automático em obras. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) atualizou o calendário da Programação de Estudos da Transmissão de 2026. O informe trimestral de setembro reúne 47 análises: nove finalizadas, 28 em andamento e dez ainda por iniciar. Uma das mudanças alcança o estudo sobre o atendimento a grandes cargas de data centers no Rio Grande do Sul. A conclusão, antes indicada para agosto, passou para dezembro de 2026. O trabalho examina a integração dessas cargas à rede de transmissão; a nova data é do estudo e não representa, isoladamente, adiamento de um empreendimento privado ou de uma obra específica. Também foi ampliado o horizonte do estudo de compensação dinâmica de potência reativa no Sistema Interligado Nacional, de dezembro de 2026 para abril de 2027. A análise sobre controle de tensão no Norte foi dividida em duas partes: a primeira segue para outubro de 2026 e a segunda, incorporada agora à programação, tem término previsto para fevereiro de 2027. A segunda parte do trabalho do Norte está associada à consulta tecnológica da EPE sobre recursos avançados para controle de tensão e suporte dinâmico, aberta até 31 de dezembro. A separação indica que o planejamento pretende incorporar respostas do mercado antes de fechar a recomendação tecnológica. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Na comparação com junho, três estudos passaram à condição de finalizados: atendimento à região da Grande Vitória, à região de Sorocaba, Indaiatuba e entorno e ao sul do Rio Grande do Sul. A finalização do estudo significa conclusão da análise técnica e não equivale a licenciamento, contratação ou entrega das instalações recomendadas. Outros cronogramas foram estendidos. Entre eles estão as análises da ilha do Marajó, da interligação Acre–Rondônia–Mato Grosso, do noroeste de Minas Gerais e de regiões de Campinas e Curitiba, agora apontadas para dezembro. Trabalhos no Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Minas Gerais, Paraná e Rio Grande do Sul também receberam novos marcos entre outubro de 2026 e fevereiro de 2027. O documento funciona como instrumento de transparência do planejamento. Os estudos podem recomendar novas linhas, subestações, transformadores, compensadores ou soluções operativas; depois, cada alternativa ainda precisa percorrer decisões setoriais, autorização ou leilão, licenciamento, contratação e implantação conforme o caso. Para transmissoras, grandes consumidores, fabricantes e financiadores, a atualização ajuda a identificar quando soluções técnicas deverão ficar maduras para as etapas seguintes. Os pontos de controle são as entregas previstas para o último trimestre de 2026, a conclusão da consulta tecnológica e a publicação dos relatórios finais com recomendações e estimativas de investimento. 🔷 Canal 562 ClaroTV+ | Canal 562 Sky | Canal 592 Vivo | Canal 187 Oi | Operadoras regionais 🔷 TV SINAL ABERTO: parabólicas canal 562 🔷 ONLINE: www.timesbrasil.com.br | YouTube 🔷 FAST Channels: Samsung TV Plus, LG Channels, TCL Channels, Pluto TV, Roku, Zapping | Novos Streamings

artigo.texto: The Baldwin County Commission passed a 180-day moratorium on all rezoning requests, new data centers and renewable energy projects within zoned areas. Commissioner Jeb Ball said the county has received many rezoning requests, and without a planning director or an updated master plan, he believes it's best to let the incoming commission and a new planning director decide future rezoning cases. "The moratorium will actually be enacted after we leave this meeting today. Is it going to cause some backlashes and rifts? It probably will. Don't care," Ball stated. "It's needed for mainly our staff and for the citizens of this county just to slow down a minute and catch our breath, let the new commission get a planning director in place, let them get the master plan set up and then if they feel like they're ready to go, the new commission can always undo the moratorium." RELATED: Foley puts six month moratorium on data centers to update ordinances, evaluate capacity Ball hopes developers will have time to consider more plans before presenting them to the new commission. "It shouldn't be controversial," he added. "It shouldn't be going against everybody's will around the area and stuff like that, and that's what this master plan, once it's solidified and a new planning director are going find." There are currently exceptions to single-family residential building permits on existing, individually owned lots that do not require a change in zoning or special exception approval. Exceptions also exist for previously approved renewable energy projects and data centers. "I don't disagree with the moratorium. The staff-they're going to get hit harder too once this 180 days is up and there's going to be a lot of rezoning cases coming in front of them," Commissioner Matt McKenzie voiced. "This helps out. I really appreciate it and I know the developers will be upset, but like I said earlier, when do we ever listen to developers?" Commissioner Billie Jo Underwood, who will serve on the next commission, believes the moratorium will allow for smarter preparation for growth as the master plan is updated. "I understand that master plans are just a guide. They're not statutory. But we're being asked more and more to put the brakes on things," Underwood said. "This is not about putting brakes on development at all. It's about making sure we have the proper framework in place to guide the development that is continuing to come." Underwood is unaware of any data center plans for Baldwin County but wants the commission to be prepared as the demand for data increases nationwide. The moratorium was imposed upon passage. artigo.texto: City Beats Follow Us on Google October 6, 2026 by Franca Ochigbo, Abuja Climate Change: Stakeholders urge FG to harmonise policies, boost carbon trade The Director General, National Council on Climate Change, Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi, in partnership with Climate Change stakeholders, have called on the federal government and regulatory agencies to harmonise policies on climate change, while urging Fiscal and monetary authorities to provide clarity on taxation, foreign exchange rules and investment incentives for carbon transactions and optimisation of domestic benefit retention. The DG made the call during a High-Level Roundtable on Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) in Abuja, calling on Private Sectors and Project Developers to build a robust, bankable pipeline of high-integrity projects. She urged the private sector and developers to align their methodologies with Nigeria’s national baseline criteria and also prioritise community impact alongside financial returns, noting that from Policy Intent to Market Delivery Nigeria stands at a pivotal juncture in its socio-economic journey. According to her, “This gathering is under the auspices of the European Union Climate Dialogues programme; it is to address one of the most vital policy imperatives of our generation, which is turning Nigeria’s climate ambition into tangible, bankable, and verifiable action. Through initiatives such as the EU Climate Dialogues, we continue to foster the critical institutional momentum required to transition our climate commitments into sustained economic growth. “This is to power clean energy transitions, restore degraded lands, modernise agriculture, improve waste management, and expand clean technology access across our 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, climate finance at scale is indispensable with global carbon markets presenting one of the most promising avenues to mobilise this private capital”. She added that carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits. A carbon market without rigour is merely an exercise in greenwashing a scenario that Nigeria will not accommodate. The goal is straightforward: Nigeria’s carbon projects must deliver real, additional, and permanent mitigation outcomes that benefit the communities, protect its ecosystems, and deliver fair value to project developers and investors alike. Speaking, the Director of Forestry, Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, noted that the forestry sector is central to Nigeria’s climate response because forests are carbon sinks, temperature buffers, reduce natural disaster risks, important sources of livelihoods, primary food and pharmacy sources, among others. artigo.texto: Trending With the November midterm elections approaching, environmental and community advocates gathered at the Capitol Rotunda in Harrisburg Tuesday to protest the impacts of hyperscale artificial intelligence data centers and urge their fellow Pennsylvanians to become more civically engaged. The demonstration was organized by several advocacy groups, including the Better Path Coalition, a grassroots organization that advocates for clean, renewable energy and government policies that prioritize public health. Attendees were encouraged to sign constituent letters representing different subgroups. Organizers said the letters are intended to show lawmakers and other decision-makers opposition to the expansion of data centers while giving frustrated voters a way to engage with elected officials. Organizers said they hope that engagement will motivate voters to participate in the November elections, even if they are angry with the elected leaders on either side of the aisle. "What we're doing is launching the campaign today to encourage people to write constituent letters so that we can send them to not only the governor and our legislators, but anyone who is making decisions about data centers," said Karen Feridun, co-founder of the Better Path Coalition. "I know a lot of people are really angry because they're not seeing an alternative ... sometimes I worry that people might stay home on Election Day." The letters represented a range of concerns, including artists worried about how generative AI could affect their work, parents and guardians concerned about the effects of data centers and AI on children, health care professionals focused on potential impacts to physical and mental health and faith leaders seeking to protect God's creation and marginalized communities, according to Better Path. Though organizers said the event was not intended to rally behind a particular candidate, some attendees held signs that read "Senator Katie Muth: Write-In for Governor." Muth, a Democrat from Montgomery County, introduced Senate Bill 1349 in June. The legislation would impose a three-year moratorium on hyperscale data center development. Speakers criticized Democrat Gov. Josh Shapiro for initially "rubbing elbows" with Amazon Web Services (AWS) executives before calling for greater scrutiny of the data centers supporting AI development. AWS operates hundreds of data center facilities worldwide, though the company does not publish an official count. "Pennsylvania lawmakers, particularly Governor Shapiro, put communities across the state in a very difficult position when it came to hyperscale data center development," said Stuart Day, co-founder of Ohio Valley Allies. "The governor enthusiastically promoted the AI and data center boom, supported these companies, pushed fast track permitting and talked about Pennsylvania working at the speed of business, but while he was cheerleading for this industry, communities -- real communities like mine -- were burdened with figuring out the consequences in real time." Shapiro's administration has sought to regulate that infrastructure through its GRID standards, which set requirements for data centers related to energy, environmental protections and community engagement. A subsequent executive order signed in August requires developers to meet those standards as part of the state permitting process. Speakers at the rally raised concerns about the long-term environmental and health impacts of data centers and what their expansion could mean for future generations. "Communities across the state see the horrific consequences of these data centers on our health, including air pollution, which damages the heart and the lungs, and light pollution, which does not sleep and leads to chronic stress," said Parker Studebaker, director of the Phoenixville Liberation Center. The speakers urged lawmakers to prioritize the health and interests of Pennsylvania communities over the economic incentives driving data center development. "Our parents are not just numbers in the study. Our children are not just a profit margin. Our friends and neighbors are not just a check to be cashed," said Anneke van Rossum, advocacy and advancement coordinator at the Delaware Riverkeeper Network. "I'm tired, but more than anything, I'm angry. The people are angry, and we are not going to let them get away with it this time." Lawmakers advanced several bills last week related to data centers in both chambers ahead of the rally. The bills address issues including the facilities' energy and water use, environmental impacts and how their development is regulated, as lawmakers face increasing pressure to respond to communities concerned about the effects of these facilities.

artigo.texto: ”Agriculture and blue carbon are the next frontier; this means carbon financing will extend to farmers, fishers, and coastal communities—not just large corporations," Coordinating Minister for Food Affairs Zulkifli Hasan remarked at the Indonesia Sustainability Forum (ISF) 2026 in Jakarta, Tuesday. Hasan, who chairs the Carbon Economic Value (NEK) Steering Committee, explained that carbon economic mechanisms serve as an instrument to assign direct monetary value to environmental preservation while channeling financial benefits to grassroots community managers. Indonesia's annual carbon market potential is estimated to reach US$7.7 billion. The national carbon ecosystem is governed under Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 on Carbon Economic Value, supported by six implementing regulations and the Carbon Unit Registry System (SRUK). The market framework incorporates carbon trading, carbon taxation, and result-based payments. To date, the government has issued registered carbon units for four forestry projects, representing an emission reduction capacity of approximately 30 million tons of CO2 equivalent. These four projects carry an estimated total transaction value of Rp5 trillion (approximately US$279.3 million) and have the potential to generate Rp500 billion (US$27.9 million) in non-tax state revenue. Hasan stressed that carbon market development must prioritize inclusivity, ensuring that localized agricultural and coastal conservation activities generate tangible economic improvements for rural populations. artigo.texto: Power Maryland Backs Two BESS Projects Amid PJM Capacity Push Industrial Info Resources is tracking nearly $3 billion worth of active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland, more than half of which is attributed to grassroot developments Released Thursday, October 08, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary As part of a broader effort to address rising capacity prices, Maryland recently awarded two battery-storage projects with generous capacity credits. Backing Up the PJM The Maryland Public Service Commission recently awarded two battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects under its Energy Storage Capacity Credit (ESCC) program, during the first round of the state's Next Generation Energy Act procurement. Both projects are designed to be connected to the broader power grid. Industrial Info Resources is tracking nearly $3 billion worth of active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland, more than half of which is attributed to grassroot developments. Under the ESCC, Maryland will provide long-term capacity payments--based on stable, flat pricing for a 15-year term--to energy-storage projects that would help to curb market price volatility in the PJM Interconnection. Electricity providers within the state are required to purchase these storage capacity credits at a monthly fixed price, which is proportionate to each provider's capacity obligations. The ESCC program is intended, in part, to address rising capacity prices on the PJM. The PJM Interconnection is the grid manager for an estimated 67 million people living in parts of 13 Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states, including Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois and New Jersey, among others. The two projects selected are Hull Street Energy's Chalk Point Storage Project in Aquasco, which is about 25 miles southeast of Washington, D.C., and LS Power Group's Jade Meadow III Storage Project in Westernport, which sits in the northwestern corner of the state. According to Industrial Info Resources data, both projects currently are expected to begin construction in 2028. The Chalk Point BESS unit would be built next to the operational Chalk Point Power Station, which produces 1,744 megawatts (MW) of gas-fired electricity. The BESS unit would carry 400 MW via lithium-ion batteries and associated facilities. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on this project in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where readers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a project report a profile of the Chalk Point Power Station. The Jade Meadow III BESS unit, which would carry 100 MW, is being developed as part of the Jade Meadow Solar III Plant, which is designed to generate 300 MW from photovoltaic (PV) panels provided by ZnShine PV-TECH Company Limited. Like the Chalk Point project, the BESS unit would use lithium-ion technology. Readers can learn more from a project report and plant profile. The Maryland Public Service Commission said these two ESCC awards will incur a total cost of 6.98 cents per month for the average Maryland residential customer. By the Numbers - Nearly $3 billion: Total investment value (TIV) of active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland - 15 years: How long Maryland will provide capacity payments based on stable, flat pricing for projects awarded under ESCC - 67 million: Estimated number of people living in the PJM area, which covers parts of 13 Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states More Awards on the Horizon By law, the Maryland Public Service Commission must open bidding for the second round of awards under the ESCC program by January 1, 2027, and it must announce the results by October 1. Among the project developers it has invited to participate is Tenaska Incorporated, whose Oystercatcher Battery Storage Project in Maryland Line was not awarded in the first round. Maryland Line sits on the Pennsylvania border, about 35 miles north of Baltimore. The Oystercatcher project would be a stand-alone unit connected to the 500-kilovolt (kV) Conastone Substation, which is managed by Baltimore Gas & Electric Company. It would carry up to 500 MW for the power grid. Readers can learn more from a project report a profile of the Conastone Substation. Other Maryland BESS projects in the works include RWE Renewables Americas LLC's Fourth Quarter Battery Storage Project in Dickerson, which is about 30 miles northwest of Washington, D.C. The stand-alone project, which is proposed to be built at the now-closed coal-fired units at the Dickerson Power Plant, would carry 300 MW. Readers can learn more from a project report a profile of the Dickerson plant. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland. Key Takeaways - Maryland awarded two BESS projects under the first round of its Energy Storage Capacity Credit program. - Both projects currently are expected to begin construction in 2028. - The Maryland Public Service Commission must open a second round of bidding for the ESCC program by January 1, 2027. artigo.texto: Brookwood City Council backs $3.2 billion Applied Digital data center project BROOKWOOD, Ala. (WBRC) - The Brookwood City Council voted Tuesday to support a resolution backing the Tuscaloosa County Economic Development Authority’s (TCEDA) agreement with Applied Digital for the company’s “Delta Forge 2” AI data center project. The TCEDA signed off on Applied Digital’s “Project Highlands” last month. The council’s decision comes after weeks of concerns from the community about environmental impacts and a lack of transparency surrounding the project. Applied Digital says the project would bring thousands of construction jobs, just over 100 full-time jobs, and hundreds of millions of dollars over time for schools and community projects. Brookwood Mayor Joe Barger believes the project is going to be a game changer for the city. “This has been a long time coming. It’s a project that our city has long been fighting for as a community leader. We are excited about what this economic impact comes to for our police, fire, education, infrastructure and a town as a whole,” Barger said. The Alabama Public Service Commission will vote on a power agreement between Applied Digital and Alabama Power. Barger said that vote could happen within weeks. artigo.texto: BYD Da Han EV to launch October 13 with 0.197 Cd drag and 1,008 km range BYD will launch the Da Han EV on October 13, 2026. Ahead of the launch, Autohome reported a 0.197 Cd aerodynamic drag coefficient and official energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km for the 1,008-km RWD version. The Da Han opened pre-sales in August at 249,900 to 299,900 yuan (35,300 to 42,400 USD). Customer deliveries are scheduled to begin within two weeks of launch. Aerodynamics and powertrain efficiency The Da Han measures 5,256 mm long, 1,999 mm wide and 1,510 mm tall, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase. Its 0.197 Cd drag coefficient is among the model’s key efficiency figures. All versions use a 102.3 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) second-generation Blade Battery. The EV is offered in three configurations: - 1008km RWD Premium: 370 kW (496 hp), 500 Nm, 0–100 km/h in 4.9 seconds, 11.5 kWh/100 km, and 1,008 km CLTC range (approx. 820 km WLTP). - 1008km RWD Flagship: It uses the same 370 kW RWD powertrain with additional rear-seat equipment, delivering 1,008 km CLTC range (approx. 820 km WLTP). - 880km AWD Flagship: Dual motors producing 570 kW (764 hp) and 910 Nm, 0–100 km/h in 3.3 seconds, 13.1 kWh/100 km, and 880 km CLTC range (approx. 715 km WLTP). The battery can charge from 10% to 97% in nine minutes at compatible high-output charging stations. Standard DiSus-A and ADAS coverage BYD confirmed that chassis and driver-assistance hardware will be standard across the range. Every Da Han has rear-wheel steering and a 4.95-meter turning radius, along with dual-chamber DiSus-A air suspension. Driver assistance uses BYD’s DiPilot system, marketed in China as the God’s Eye 5.0 driver-assistance system. The roof-mounted LiDAR-equipped system supports high-speed and Urban Navigation on Autopilot (Urban NOA), as well as automated valet parking. BYD also provides a one-year full damage coverage guarantee. Under the policy, BYD covers specified economic losses from qualifying legally liable accidents while Urban NOA is being used in compliance with applicable regulations. The coverage also applies to intelligent parking, subject to the stated conditions. The system remains classified as Level 2+ driver assistance. Cabin technology The cabin features a 17.3-inch floating 3K central display running the DiLink 300 interface with BYD’s in-car AI voice agent, named DiDiXia in the domestic market. Audio uses a 7.1.4-channel Devialet sound system with 31 speakers. Other equipment includes Nappa leather upholstery, front seats with zero-gravity positioning and an active fragrance system. Market positioning BYD positions the Da Han above the existing Han EV in the Dynasty sedan lineup. Domestic sales of BYD’s existing Han sedan lineup have weakened substantially through 2026. The standard Han averaged roughly 7,000 to 8,900 monthly deliveries in late 2025, but monthly volume fell to around 3,000 units during 2026. It delivered 2,997 units in August, down 61.4% year over year, reducing its share of BYD’s domestic sales to 1.6%, according to China EV DataTracker. The higher-spec Han L has declined more sharply. After reaching 2,934 units in December 2025, monthly deliveries fell throughout 2026 to 205 units in August, down 90.7% year over year and accounting for 0.1% of BYD’s domestic sales. BYD will announce final retail pricing and delivery details at the October 13 launch.

artigo.texto: Big Island Wants To Ban Big Data Centers, Once They Agree On What They Are Giant data centers have become the latest bogeyman for residents across the nation wary of industrial development. So far, none are based in Hawaiʻi. Hawaiʻi County is discussing a bill that would restrict large-scale data centers on the island. But the public, officials and state representatives can’t agree on how to define one — or whether they are even a threat. Under Big Island zoning rules, residents and businesses can only use their land in the ways outlined by the county’s code. If it’s not listed as a permitted use, then it’s not allowed. Currently, the code allows for data processing centers in an area with a mouthful of modifiers: industrial-commercial-mixed-use-zoned. Translated, that means if a data center developer wants to build in an industrial area, they would just need to apply. There aren’t any so-called “hyperscale” data centers in Hawaiʻi yet. Zoning codes for Maui, Kauaʻi and Honolulu counties also have a not-listed-not-allowed rule for land use. Some of their codes currently permit data storage and processing facilities. But no other county has put forward regulations and the state is only just beginning to study the issue. Bill 170, introduced by Councilwoman Heather Kimball, seeks to make sure data centers like the ones ruffling feathers across the continent are not permitted anywhere on the Big Island. If it passes, construction of large data centers would be banned with one caveat: they can apply for a special use permit. The bill was heard for a second time by the Windward Planning Commission on Thursday. The Leeward Planning Commission will take up the issue on Oct. 15. So far, however, the biggest hurdle is figuring out how to define what would qualify as a data center under the proposed new rules. “If we get a really good definition, I think that could solve a lot of things,” said Louis Daniele, chair of the Windward Commission. “We keep calling things data centers, data processing facilities – That’s kind of confusing for the layperson.” ‘We Don’t Want It’ Powerful technology corporations are rapidly putting up data centers across the country to power the artificial intelligence boom. The rush has sparked significant backlash from communities over concerns about the impact on the environment, the power grid and their neighborhoods. Hundreds of counties from California to Maine have already introduced regulations or instituted moratoriums on data center construction. The centers, which can cover thousands of acres and consume entire city blocks, are the latest target for those wary about new industrial development, such as Amazon megawarehouses and microwave cellphone towers. “I wanted to make sure we got ahead of the issue,” Kimball said. “I think it’s better to do it now,” she added, before developers start knocking on the door. Her primary concern is the effect a data center could have on the island’s already strained grid and aquifers. The massive centers being built across the country require equally massive amounts of energy and water. A typical hyperscale data center can use up to 100 megawatts of electricity annually, for instance. That could power 100,000 households, according to The International Energy Agency. The increased demand on the grid and the added infrastructure required to support it are raising utilities’ costs to produce electricity elsewhere, and those costs are being passed on to residents. In Maryland, customers pay $168 to $216 more per year on their electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom, according to estimates. Across Hawaiʻi and the country, residents are not only concerned about higher bills. They’re also worried that the energy demand increases the use of fossil fuels and thus pollution, which drives climate change and threatens health. Christina Holt, a Hilo resident who recently ran unsuccessfully for state representative, is leading the local charge against the centers. She’s hosted community Zoom meetings and posts regularly on social media to inform residents and urge them to speak out. Dozens of Big Island residents have shown up at planning commissions meetings. In hours and pages of testimony, residents have made clear that they support an outright ban. “We don’t want it,” Holt said, “and we, as a community, have every right to say no.” Defining ‘Data Center’ No Easy Feat For Bill 170 to be effective, advocates say, it needs to clearly define data centers and distinguish them from a data processing center. Data processing center use was added to the county code in 1996 when the council undertook numerous amendments to the zoning rules. The addition reflected emerging technologies and business activities at the time. It generally referred to office-oriented businesses that used computers to process information, maintain electronic records, or provide administrative and technical services. These types of centers don’t require much electricity and are vital to business and research operations. Today, the state has more than 20 data processing centers, two of them on the Big Island. A Hawaiian Telecom facility in Kawaihae is one of them. Jeannine Souki, manager of government and regulatory affairs for Hawaiian Telecom, testified in front of the Windward Commission, one of two planning commissions on the island, in September. Advocates have two related worries. A definition that’s too broad could exclude necessary infrastructure. Being too specific could create loopholes developers can exploit. Souki urged commissioners to consider whether the way Bill 170 defines data centers could unintentionally ban these essential telecommunication facilities Lawsuits by developers against towns elsewhere in the country that have attempted to prevent construction are adding further pressure to get the definition right. “They’re going to lie, cheat and steal to get what they want,” Chuck Flaherty, secretary of the Hawaiʻi island Sierra Club, said

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Energia nuclear vai abastecer novo data center nos EUA Publicado 06/10/2026 • 10:00 | Atualizado há 21 horas KEY POINTS Foto: AFP A Oracle planeja usar energia nuclear para atender parte da demanda de seu novo campus de data centers nos Estados Unidos. A empresa propôs comprar entre 125 MW e 250 MW da produção da usina nuclear de Point Beach, em Wisconsin. O projeto, chamado Project Lighthouse, deve ficar em Port Washington. A Oracle apresentou a proposta em 2 de outubro de 2026, mas ainda precisa da aprovação do órgão regulador de energia de Wisconsin. Leia também: Oracle fecha contrato de US$ 7 bilhões para fornecer serviços de nuvem à Tencent A quantidade negociada representa a potência que a Oracle pretende adquirir para o novo campus. A usina Point Beach possui dois reatores nucleares e fica às margens do Lago Michigan, de acordo com informações internacionais. A We Energies vendeu a usina para a NextEra Energy em 2007, mas manteve um contrato para comprar a maior parte da geração de Point Beach até 2033. A negociação envolve um fornecimento de energia mais eficaz. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A movimentação da Oracle segue um padrão visto no mercado recentemente. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial e da construção de novos data centers, as empresas buscam um fornecimento de energia mais poderoso e eficaz. Vale destacar que uma energia contínua e sem falhas é essencial para manter o funcionamento das estruturas tecnológicas. Em especial, as usinas nucleares voltaram a receber maior atenção do mercado de tecnologia. Leia também: Entrelinhas de Mercado: IA vai eliminar negócios antes de revelar o que criará, diz VP executivo da Oracle A Public Service Commission of Wisconsin (PSC) precisa analisar e aprovar a negociação. Ainda de acordo com as informações, a vice-presidente de Capacidade e Planejamento de Infraestrutura da Oracle afirmou que a empresa esperava apresentar a proposta à comissão até o fim de 2026. O acordo também se relaciona a uma proposta de aumento de US$ 176 milhões (R$ 878,9 milhões) nas tarifas de eletricidade da concessionária para 2027. artigo.texto: Sen. Britt rallies Mobile County GOP, talks data centers and AI accountability MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Alabama Sen. Katie Britt headlined the Mobile County Republican Party meeting at Regency Church of Christ, rallying voters with less than a month until the midterms. Senator warns against complacency Britt faced a packed house. Her message: don’t get complacent. While Republicans are used to winning big in Mobile County, some polls show Democrat Doug Jones within striking distance of Republican Tommy Tuberville in the governor’s race. In May, more Mobile County voters voted in the Democratic primary than the Republican one. That hasn’t happened since 1994. Data centers divide governor’s race candidates Data centers have emerged as a top issue dividing Republican gubernatorial candidate Tommy Tuberville from his Democratic opponent, Doug Jones. Tuberville considers them essential, while Jones has called for a one-year moratorium. At the Mobile County Republican Party event, Britt sought to strike a middle ground. She said she doesn’t want to stop the construction of data centers, and she doesn’t support a national one-size-fits-all policy. But she said she favors “guardrails” to make sure data centers don’t receive special tax breaks and pay their own way when it comes to electricity and water usage. Britt warned that the U.S. can’t fall behind China. “What we have to understand is what’s good for one community may not be good for another, and that’s why I reject that we have to have a moratorium across the country because for some communities, this is the right pathway forward. And I also don’t believe that we should put one in every corner,” Britt said. “Guys, you don’t want our greatest adversary having capabilities that we do not. So we have to do that, but I think we also have to do that in a very smart and measured way,” Britt said. Britt discusses AI accountability efforts Britt also talked about her efforts to hold artificial intelligence companies accountable. She pointed to conversations she’s had with parents whose children have committed suicide after receiving encouragement to do so from chatbots. Copyright 2026 WALA. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors will consider a proposal Tuesday to develop a zoning amendment prohibiting large-scale data centers in unincorporated parts of the county, citing concerns about the energy and water demands and potential public health effects associated with facilities used to power artificial intelligence. The motion by Supervisor Hilda Solis would direct the Department of Regional Planning to begin drafting an amendment to the county’s zoning code establishing definitions for different types of data centers based on factors including acreage, square footage, energy use and water consumption. The proposed zoning amendment would distinguish hyperscale and artificial intelligence data centers from what the motion calls “beneficial use” facilities, including enterprise, accessory or sole-source data centers used for daily computational needs. The zoning amendment would prohibit all data centers meeting the zoning amendment’s definition of “large-scale” in every zone of unincorporated Los Angeles County. “Given the pressing concerns to immediately prevent the environmental and health effects of data centers powering AI from impacting unincorporated County residents, it is imperative that the Board of Supervisors act on the recommendations to prohibit these facilities expediently,” according to the motion. The proposal comes amid growing interest in the environmental effects of the computing infrastructure required for increasingly powerful AI systems. “Data centers servicing artificial intelligence (AI) consume high rates of energy, over-utilize water resources, contribute to environmental pollution, and impact public health in ways that are still being understood,” according to Solis’ motion. The motion states that the growth of artificial intelligence has fueled development of hyperscale or large-scale data centers that can be larger and consume more resources than facilities traditionally used to service computer networks and store data. It also points to opposition to proposed data centers in the San Gabriel Valley. According to the motion, the Board of Supervisors received 101 pages of public comments, primarily calling for a moratorium on data centers. The motion cites actions by Monterey Park, Montebello, Baldwin Park and El Monte to restrict or halt data center development and notes that Alhambra voters are scheduled to consider a similar ballot measure in November. The county began examining the issue in April, when the board approved a motion directing county departments to study the potential health, environmental and safety effects of data centers, along with their impact on electrical and water resources. A subsequent county report recommended amending Title 22 of the county zoning code to define data centers and prohibit hyperscale facilities in all zones. According to Solis’ motion, the county’s director of Regional Planning on Sept. 17 invoked existing authority under Title 22 to rely on the absence of a similarly defined land use to prohibit large-scale data centers while a comprehensive zoning amendment is developed. Tuesday’s motion would direct Regional Planning to inform residents in unincorporated communities about that action. It would also direct the Department of Public Health, working with County Counsel, to determine whether the county’s noise regulations should be amended to address “low frequency and continuous noise associated with large-scale data centers.” The county’s chief executive officer would be directed to identify funding needed to prepare and implement the zoning amendment, its required California Environmental Quality Act analysis and any changes to the county’s noise regulations. The motion additionally calls for Regional Planning and County Counsel to be prepared to introduce a moratorium if a proposed data center in an unincorporated area presents what the motion describes as a “current and immediate threat to public health, safety, and welfare.” Such a moratorium would target facilities posing a serious risk or nuisance involving health, safety or environmental resources, particularly water and energy resources. The item is scheduled to be considered when the Board of Supervisors meets Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Novo regime tributário busca impulsionar data centers, infraestrutura energética e inteligência artificial no Brasil O REDATA cria incentivos tributários para infraestrutura digital, vinculados a energia limpa, sustentabilidade e investimentos em pesquisa e inovação. quarta-feira, 7 de outubro de 2026 Atualizado em 6 de outubro de 2026 15:01 A lei 15.504/26 instituiu o REDATA - Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, criando um conjunto de incentivos voltados à instalação e à expansão da infraestrutura de processamento de dados no Brasil. A medida insere-se em um cenário de crescimento da demanda por computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e, especialmente, pela infraestrutura necessária ao treinamento e à inferência de modelos de inteligência artificial. O novo regime permite a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins, PIS/Cofins-Importação, IPI e Imposto de Importação incidentes sobre determinados componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação destinados ao ativo imobilizado das empresas habilitadas. No caso do Imposto de Importação, o benefício fica restrito aos bens sem produção nacional equivalente e relacionados em ato do Poder Executivo. Cumpridas as condições previstas na legislação, as suspensões poderão ser convertidas em alíquota zero. A criação do REDATA procura enfrentar um dos principais componentes econômicos dos projetos de data centers: o elevado volume de investimentos necessário à implantação e expansão da capacidade computacional. A redução do custo tributário associado à aquisição e importação de equipamentos pode contribuir para aumentar a competitividade do País na atração de novos projetos e para ampliar a infraestrutura digital disponível no mercado brasileiro. O regime, entretanto, estabelece contrapartidas relevantes. Entre elas estão a disponibilização de, no mínimo, 10% da capacidade instalada com os benefícios para o mercado interno; o atendimento a critérios de sustentabilidade; a observância de Índice de Eficiência Hídrica (WUE) igual ou inferior a 0,05 L/kWh; e a realização de investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação correspondentes a 2% do valor dos produtos adquiridos ou importados com o incentivo. Energia passa a integrar a estratégia tributária dos projetos Um dos aspectos mais relevantes do REDATA está na relação direta entre o benefício tributário e a matriz energética utilizada pelos empreendimentos. Para usufruir do regime, a empresa deverá atender à totalidade de sua demanda de energia elétrica por meio de contratos de suprimento ou de autoprodução provenientes de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, nos termos que ainda serão definidos em regulamento. A exigência aproxima definitivamente três agendas que, até recentemente, eram analisadas de forma relativamente independente: tributação, infraestrutura energética e economia digital. Data centers possuem elevada demanda de energia elétrica e exigem segurança e continuidade no fornecimento. Consequentemente, decisões relacionadas à localização de novos empreendimentos deverão considerar não apenas incentivos tributários e disponibilidade de conectividade, mas também acesso à energia, capacidade da infraestrutura de transmissão, estruturação dos contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução e atendimento aos critérios ambientais estabelecidos para manutenção dos benefícios. Nesse contexto, a análise de viabilidade de novos projetos tende a exigir uma abordagem integrada entre planejamento tributário, estruturação energética, infraestrutura e regulação. Inteligência artificial amplia a relevância dos data centers A própria lei 15.504/26 inclui expressamente no conceito de serviços de data center as atividades de computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e treinamento e inferência de modelos de inteligência artificial, demonstrando assim que o REDATA ultrapassa uma política tributária destinada exclusivamente ao setor tradicional de armazenamento de dados. O regime está diretamente relacionado à expansão da infraestrutura computacional necessária ao desenvolvimento da economia digital e da inteligência artificial no País. O crescimento da IA vem ampliando significativamente a necessidade de capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e energia. Nesse ambiente, a disponibilidade de infraestrutura passa a representar elemento estratégico para empresas de tecnologia, provedores de serviços em nuvem, operadores de data centers e demais agentes envolvidos na cadeia digital. A legislação também procura estimular o desenvolvimento da cadeia tecnológica nacional ao exigir investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação, além de prever tratamento diferenciado para empreendimentos localizados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, onde determinados compromissos previstos no regime são reduzidos em 20%. Implementação ainda exige regulamentação Embora o REDATA já tenha sido instituído, parte relevante de sua operacionalização ainda depende de regulamentação do Poder Executivo, principalmente quanto a definição dos critérios para caracterização das fontes de energia de baixa emissão, a relação dos equipamentos elegíveis aos benefícios, os procedimentos relativos à inexistência de produção nacional equivalente e as regras para comprovação das contrapartidas assumidas pelas empresas. A habilitação e a coabilitação ao regime serão realizadas pela Receita Federal, observadas as condições estabelecidas na legislação e na regulamentação subsequente. Tudo isso só é possível porque a LC 237/26, publicada na mesma data, que incluiu o REDATA entre as exceções às limitações aplicáveis à concessão de benefícios tributários no exercício de 2026, desde que observadas a compatibilidade com a meta de resultado primário e a previsão na lei orçamentária anual. artigo.texto: DeLAND, Fla. — The Volusia County Council is moving forward with a ban on data centers after the first reading of the proposed ordinance. Residents in favor and against them spoke out at the podium, but it wasn't easy to change commissioners' minds. As they reviewed an ordinance written by staff, county commissioners listed concerns discussed two months ago during a meeting in August — like possible sinkholes, public safety and environmental impacts, like water usage. The ordinance said the county will not review or approve any applications, permits, amendments or construction about them. “I, for one, am pleased with what we have in front of us, and unless someone can change my mind, I’ll be voting in favor of it,” District 4 Volusia County Council Member Troy Kent said. The 26-page ordinance references Florida Senate Bill 484, which went into effect in July. The bill allows local governments to regulate large-scale data centers through land development regulations. The proposed ordinance also references studies that say data centers consume large amounts of water, affect the environment and pose health risks for residents. “And if we vote for this ban, it’s not a statement that any of us up here are against data centers," Volusia County Chair Jeff Brower said. "We use them every day. It just means not here.” Council members voted unanimously to move the proposal forward. It is expected to be discussed by the Planning and Land Development Regulation Commission on Oct. 15. Then it’s up for the second and final hearing on Oct. 20. If approved, the ordinance would take effect once filed with the Florida Department of State.

artigo.texto: Linea Energy Closes Financing for 250 MW Mesa View Battery Storage Project in Texas Linea Energy has closed project debt and a preferred equity commitment for Mesa View, a 250 MW / 500 MWh battery storage project in Upton County, with commercial operation expected in 2027. Linea Energy, a renewables developer and independent power producer sponsored by EnCap Investments L.P., has announced the closing of project debt financing and a preferred equity commitment for Mesa View BESS. The standalone 250 MW / 500 MWh battery energy storage project is located in Upton County, Texas. The announcement was made on October 1, 2026. A three-part financing structure According to the company, the debt consists of a construction-to-term loan, a tax equity bridge loan and a letter of credit facility. Norddeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale (NORD/LB) acted as coordinating lead arranger, while Texas Capital participated as a syndicate lender. D.E. Shaw Renewable Investments (DESRI) provided the preferred equity commitment. Linea Energy did not disclose the amount of the debt or of the preferred equity commitment. This type of financing comes in a market where storage projects attract varied structures, as illustrated by CIP's investment in the Kilmarnock South battery storage project in Scotland. Company Linea Energy: company profile Partners already engaged with Linea Cassidy DeLine, Chief Executive Officer of Linea Energy, says the closing illustrates the maturation of the company's platform and its ability to repeatedly deliver investable opportunities to the market. Sondra Martinez, Managing Director at NORD/LB, states that the bank led another financing for Linea, following three previous transactions. Peter Koczanski, Head of Corporate Development at DESRI, notes that the new commitment follows the preferred equity commitment made on Duffy BESS. According to him, the partnership reflects DESRI's confidence in Linea's development platform and execution capabilities. Commercial operation expected in 2027 Mesa View BESS is expected to reach commercial operation in 2027. Once online, the project is to deliver 250 MW of dispatchable capacity into the ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas) market. Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP served as Sponsor counsel to Linea Energy. Winston & Strawn LLP acted as legal counsel to the lenders, and Foley & Lardner LLP advised DESRI. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 %

artigo.texto: Beaufort Co. planning commission recommends a temporary moratorium on data centers BEAUFORT COUNTY, S.C. (WTOC) - Beaufort County leaders are moving forward with a temporary moratorium on data centers. The county’s planning commission voted to send the proposed ordinance to the county council. They also asked council to consider extending the pause from nine months to 12 months. If passed, it would pause acceptance, processing, approval, or issuance of certain applications, permits, and approvals for data centers in the county. County leaders say the moratorium will give them time to define what a data center is and look at the potential impacts one could bring to the county. Several residents spoke during the public comment period, and they were all against the idea of data centers in Beaufort County. They also questioned where one would go. For the moratorium to pass, it will need to go through three different votes and a public hearing. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.
