artigo.texto: Sungrow has been selected to equip Project Blue, Albania’s largest privately developed solar park, with a battery energy storage system of 130 MWh. The project doesn’t benefit from any government subsidies. Matrix Konstruksion and Blessed Investment Group have been expanding their Project Blue photovoltaic complex in Fier in western Albania in phases. Sungrow, a global provider of inverters and energy storage systems, announced that it signed an agreement for the installation of a BESS of 130 MWh at the solar park of 185 MW in peak capacity. The deal concerns 26 PowerTitan 2.0 battery units and 13 MVS3460-LS units. Sungrow’s liquid-cooled BESS solution enhances grid flexibility and facilitates the integration of renewable power, the update reads. Project Blue in Albania is set to expand by 164 MW of PV peak capacity and an 80 MW battery storage system The next phase of Project Blue will add 164 MW of solar capacity in peak terms and an 80 MW / 180 MWh battery system, the company added. “Project Blue demonstrates how strong partnerships, innovative technology, and a clear vision can accelerate renewable energy deployment at scale. It will support Albania’s clean energy transition, strengthen independence, and help meet the growing demand for clean electricity across the region,” said Country Manager of Sungrow Italy Massimo Bracchi. Project Blue is jointly owned and developed by Albania-based Matrix Konstruksion and Blessed Investment Group. As of June 2026, Sungrow has installed over 1.1 TW of power electronic converters worldwide. Founded in Tirana in 1995, Matrix Konstruksion delivers turnkey construction and energy projects. Blessed Investment Group has transitioned from advisory toward principal investing. Over the past two decades, it developed a portfolio that includes renewable energy, real estate and tourism.

artigo.texto: Arnaldo Jardim vê “descritério” no custeio de baterias e quer manter leilão À CNN, deputado defende manter contratação de dezembro apesar do risco de judicialização; divisão da conta entre geradores e consumidores opõe agentes do setor O deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim classificou como um “descritério” a regra que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores de energia os custos das baterias e defendeu manter o leilão previsto para dezembro, apesar do risco de judicialização. Em entrevista ao Mapa da Mina, da CNN, o parlamentar sustentou que o leilão para sistemas de armazenamento deve receber o mesmo tratamento das demais tecnologias contratadas para garantir o abastecimento de eletricidade. Segundo Jardim, os certames anteriores tiveram seus custos rateados entre os consumidores, enquanto a contratação das baterias ficou vinculada ao segmento de geração. “Temos outros leilões que têm o mesmo objeto”, disse. “No caso das baterias, isso ficou vinculado aos geradores. Acho que é um descritério. O projeto que proponho é uma isonomia e uma regra geral para ter uma comparação mais adequada de custos”, disse. A posição do deputado reforça apenas um dos lados da disputa sobre quem deve bancar o custo das baterias. Para Jardim, as baterias oferecem um serviço de segurança ao sistema elétrico, ao permitir que energia produzida em determinados períodos seja guardada e utilizada quando necessária. Nessa avaliação, o benefício ultrapassa as empresas de geração e justifica incluir os consumidores no custeio. “Então precisamos ter baterias para evitar que as oscilações levem a interrupção e blecautes”, afirmou, ao comentar a variabilidade da geração renovável. Baterias também beneficiam empresas O argumento enfrenta um contraponto: o leilão de baterias foi um pleito das empresas que enfrentam os cortes de geração impostos pelo ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico), conhecido pelo termo “curtailment”, por restrições em linhas de transmissão ou por falta de demanda. Quando carregam em momentos de excesso de oferta, os sistemas de armazenamento ajudam a aproveitar energia que poderia ser cortada. Esse efeito alivia parte do "curtailment". O próprio diretor-geral do ONS, Márcio Rea, disse que as baterias devem reduzir os cortes de renováveis em até 50%. Esse benefício sustenta a defesa, por parte de agentes do setor, de que a conta seja compartilhada entre geradores e consumidores, reconhecendo os ganhos de cada grupo. O diretor-geral da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, é contrário a acrescentar esse custo aos consumidores. Ele também questiona a mudança de uma legislação aprovada recentemente, por considerar que isso cria instabilidade para os investimentos. Caso a lei seja alterada, a agência terá de adequar a regulamentação aos novos comandos legais. A legislação vigente determina que os custos da contratação de baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores. O PL 3.716/2026, de Jardim, busca revogar essa obrigação específica e aplicar a regra geral da reserva de capacidade, que contempla os usuários finais de energia e a participação dos geradores nas hipóteses previstas em lei. A controvérsia alcança também o rateio dentro do segmento de geração. Empresas que consideram já oferecer flexibilidade ao sistema contestam sua inclusão na cobrança. Agentes do setor avaliam que divergências sobre essa metodologia podem resultar em ações judiciais e comprometer o calendário ou a contratação dos projetos. Algumas empresas já defendem publicamente adiar o leilão até a definição da fonte pagadora dos custos. Jardim defendeu que esse risco não leve ao adiamento. A contratação está programada para dois certames, em 2 e 4 de dezembro, com início do suprimento em agosto de 2028.

artigo.texto: Fort Smith Board approves data center ordinance, but seeks more restrictions An ordinance making it more difficult to build a data center in Fort Smith was approved Monday (Oct. 5) by the cityâs board of directors, but many on the board want more stringent guidelines and at least one director wants legal clarity on using water sales to limit regional data center development. The ordinance approved Monday by the board requires a development plan review by the Planning Commission and then full board approval of a data center project in the cityâs industrial zoning districts. The ordinance requires an eight-foot opaque wall surrounding the property, 500-foot setbacks from each property line, and âletters from applicable public utilities regarding capacity and proposed load.â Director Christina Catsavis expressed concern about the Fort Chaffee Redevelopment Authority (FCRA), which manages land within city limits, being able to sell land for a data center project without city oversight. The FCRA was formed in 1997 to oversee redevelopment of 6,000 acres of land released by the U.S. Army from Fort Chaffee as part of a Base Realignment and Closure downsizing. Deputy City Administrator Maggie Rice said any property within city limits fall under city development ordinances. “This board still has zoning control over the FCRA property that is in Fort Smith, so you would still have development plan approval that would be required should the FCRA sell property for a data center,â Rice said. As to concerns expressed by some board members about the proposed ordinance not being as tough as that passed by the city of Fayetteville, Rice said the Fort Smith board will have more control over data center development than the Fayetteville City Council. âIn my opinion you donât get much more control over a data center than whatâs being proposed,â Rice said. âThis has to go through two public hearings and this board can ask for anything that it wants. You can make the setback larger, you can make the wall taller, you can require certain facade requirements, you can tell them no.â Rice said the cityâs rules now allow a data center to be built in certain city industrial zones without planning commission or board review. However, Directors AndrÃ© Good and Catsavis wanted to table the proposed ordinance and consider one with more restrictions at a December board meeting. âIâd like to put more teeth in it,â Good said. âIâd like to make it a little bit more difficult.â But Directors Neal Martin and Kevin Settle said they should pass the ordinance because existing city rules now allow a data center project to be built. Martin said the proposed ordinance is a âgood initial step.â âIâd rather pass it tonight, and then have an amendment come back in December,â Settle said. âThat way weâve got protections over these next two months.â Settle, a frequent advocate for using the cityâs water system, which provides water to numerous cities and associations in the region, again pushed city administration to come back with clear and legal options about adding language in water contracts that could restrict or prevent data centers from being built outside city limits. âI want to know if we can have full control over, if they tie in a data center, we should have the right to vote on that as a board,â Settle said in a conversation with City Administrator Jeff Dingman. âYou said yes, but now Iâm hearing that it depends if itâs a contract user, wholesale user. I want this board in the future to have full autonomy that if a data center comes to any city that is connected to our water system, this board votes on that connection, yes or no.â The board voted 6-0 in favor of the ordinance. BACKGROUND Arkansas officials, with support from Gov. Sarah Sanders, have restricted local government actions on data centers. Arkansas Act 851 of 2023 prevents local governments from banning data center development. The law does not prevent local governments from adopting rules that create delays or significant restrictions with data center projects. The cities of Fayetteville and Little Rock have approved more stringent data center development rules. The development of data centers nationwide and in Arkansas has become controversial, with pushback often resulting from local grassroots efforts. Concerns include the potential for massive water use, rising utility rates, excessive noise, and groundwater pollution. The state of New York recently implemented a one-year moratorium on data center construction. According to reporting from CNBC and other outlets, more than 500 local governments nationwide have enacted bans, moratoriums, and other restrictions on data centers. âData centers sit at the intersection of economic development, energy policy and state fiscal health,â according to a report from the National Conference of State Legislatures. âWhile 38 states currently offer dedicated tax incentives to attract data centers, lawmakers across the country are working to balance economic development priorities with sustainable development goals. These capital-intensive projects can generate significant tax revenue for localities, yet data centers also contribute to surging energy demand across the country.â

artigo.texto: The Board of Supervisors Tuesday approved an Interim Urgency Ordinance establishing a 45-day moratorium on land use approvals for new data center development in unincorporated San Joaquin County. The temporary moratorium will allow the County to study the potential impacts of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and determine whether additional land use regulations and infrastructure standards are needed to address their unique demands. “Our communities deserve answers about how large-scale AI data centers could affect water supplies, electricity use, agriculture, noise, and public infrastructure,” said Supervisor Robert Rickman. “That is why the Board directed staff to conduct a six-month study and bring back a proposed temporary moratorium while that work is underway. We need to hear from the public and understand these impacts before deciding whether, and under what conditions, these facilities should be allowed in unincorporated San Joaquin County.” Last month, the Board voted to direct County staff to study the potential impacts on the environment including demands on water, electricity, local infrastructure, and emergency services. The Community Development Department (CDD) recommended the moratorium to preserve public health, safety, and welfare while the County studies, evaluates, and considers adoption of comprehensive land use regulations. Unlike conventional industrial warehouses and other development, large-scale data centers require substantial and continuous electricity and water resources, as well as specialized cooling systems to operate around the clock. The County also must determine whether existing electrical infrastructure can accommodate multiple large-scale data centers. “The County does not currently have specific standards to address the unique impacts of data centers, from noise and energy demands to emergency response and infrastructure capacity,” said Board Chair and Third District Supervisor Sonny Dhaliwal. “Before we consider allowing this type of development, we need to understand the full impact on our community and make sure we have the safeguards in place to protect our residents.” During the moratorium, County staff will evaluate whether the County’s General Plan, Development Title, zoning regulations, and infrastructure standards adequately address large-scale data centers. Staff will also conduct community outreach, consult with stakeholders, research regulations and best practices in other jurisdictions, and return to the Board with recommendations. There are currently no proposals for large-scale AI data centers in unincorporated San Joaquin County.

artigo.texto: Grid-forming capabilities support multiple grid-restoration functions The project plays an important role in supporting voltage and frequency stability at a key point in Cambodia's central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. Its grid-forming capabilities were put through a series of demanding system-restoration scenarios, demonstrating how energy storage can take on a more active role in supporting the power system. Key highlights include: - Large-scale black start from zero voltage: 516 grid-forming PCS units successfully energized the entire plant from zero voltage, establishing stable voltage and frequency across the system. - Restoration of a 240 km transmission network: The system supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations, while maintaining stable operation as the network was progressively restored. - Support for multiple generation sources: The system supported the start-up and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant, before the restored network was operated together with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, energy storage and loads. - Stable operation under challenging grid conditions: During restoration, the system remained stable through five transformer energization events, including a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stability when synchronizing different power sources under a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees, demonstrating its ability to handle challenging conditions during system recovery. - Extended islanded operation: The system operated independently for 3.5 hours, demonstrating that the energy storage system could continue supporting the local network even when separated from the main grid. - Seamless transitions: The project completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, with voltage deviation kept below 2% and transient frequency fluctuation within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. "This project demonstrates that the value of grid-forming energy storage goes far beyond storing electricity.When a power system faces disturbances or loses normal grid support, grid-forming technology can help establish and maintain stable voltage and frequency, support system restoration and keep the grid operating reliably," said Michael Ruan, Regional Director of Sungrow Southeast Asia and South Asia. "Through projects like this, Sungrow is helping turn energy storage into a more active grid-support asset and bringing proven grid-forming capabilities to the evolving power systems of Southeast Asia." Reducing Technical Risk and Ensuring Timely Delivery Faced with strict test protocols, complex power system scenarios, a compressed construction schedule and rainy‑season working conditions with ambient temperature up to 40°C, Sungrow's cross‑functional team covering pre-sales, on‑site delivery and R&D collaborated closely to deliver high‑quality project outcomes: - 20-day commissioning and testing: The on‑site team worked relentlessly under hot and humid conditions for two consecutive months. The team wrapped up hot commissioning plus three rounds of performance tests within 20 days to guarantee timely grid‑connection. - End‑to‑End Service Solution: Sungrow provides full‑lifecycle and one‑stop services spanning integrated design of storage and monitoring systems, EPC‑related support, equipment design, commissioning and O&M services, enabling the customer to fulfill customized grid‑level requirements with reduced management overhead. As Southeast Asia advances its energy transition, Sungrow will continue to bring proven energy storage technologies and solutions to the region, helping customers build more reliable and sustainable power infrastructure. artigo.texto: Webinar "Data Centers no Brasil: Oportunidades, Incentivos e Desafios para Novos Investimentos" Incentivos, aspectos regulatórios e requisitos para projetos de instalação, modernização e expansão de data centers no país estão entre os temas debatidos no webinar. terça-feira, 6 de outubro de 2026 Atualizado às 13:44 Os grupos Tributário, Meio Ambiente e Energia do Trench Rossi Watanabe promovem, no dia 9/10, das 10h às 11h, o webinar "Data Centers no Brasil: Oportunidades, Incentivos e Desafios para Novos Investimentos". O encontro ocorre em meio ao cenário de crescimento da computação em nuvem, da IA e da demanda por processamento e armazenamento de dados, que vem ampliando o interesse por investimentos em data centers no Brasil. O evento será dedicado à análise das principais oportunidades e dos desafios jurídicos, tributários, regulatórios, ambientais e operacionais relacionados a projetos de instalação, modernização e expansão de data centers no país. Entre os temas que serão abordados está a recente instituição do REDATA, que ampliou os incentivos tributários para o setor e estabeleceu requisitos de energia renovável, eficiência hídrica, sustentabilidade, pesquisa e desenvolvimento e oferta de capacidade ao mercado doméstico. A proposta é discutir o novo cenário sob diferentes perspectivas e contribuir para que investidores, operadores e fornecedores possam avaliar os impactos das recentes mudanças, os requisitos aplicáveis aos projetos e os principais pontos de atenção para novos investimentos no setor. Participam como speakers do Trench Rossi Watanabe os sócios Clarissa Machado, Giovani Tomasoni, J. Roberto Martins, Reinaldo Ravelli e Thales Stucky, e a consultora Alessandra Machado. O evento é gratuito e aberto ao público, mediante inscrição prévia. Clique aqui e faça sua inscrição!

artigo.texto: Suzuki utilises BYD’s battery to launch Japan’s most affordable Kei-car EV Suzuki unveiled its first passenger Kei-car EV, the “e-Sky.” With a starting price of 2.12 million yen (13,400 USD), the model aims to become the most affordable Kei-car EV in Japan. While Suzuki has long dominated the Japanese Kei-car market, the e-Sky marks the company’s formal entry into the electric segment. Strategic pricing To achieve its competitive price point, Suzuki collaborated with BYD, utilising the Chinese giant’s battery technology. According to Suzuki, the e-Sky is built on a newly developed dedicated EV platform and features a proprietary “e-Axle” drive system. The vehicle is powered by a 26 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, delivering a WLTP range of 310 km. By comparison, the entry-level BYD Racco, with a 22.4 kWh LFP battery, offers a WLTC range of 210 km, while higher-spec models feature a 35.84 kWh LFP battery and a WLTC range of 320 km. The difference in the two cars’ range is due to their different weights. The Suzuki e-Sky weighs 1,030 kg, while the Racco weighs 1,160 kg with a 22.4 kWh battery and 1,220 kg or 1,230 kg with the 35.84 kWh version. The e-Sky measures 3,395 mm in length, 1,475 mm in width, and 1,625 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 2,460 mm. The Racco measures 3,395 mm long, 1,475 mm wide and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 2,520 mm. Market positioning Suzuki is offering three versions of the e-Sky. The entry-level model, designed primarily for corporate clients, is built-to-order and omits features like fast charging to keep costs low. Suzuki aims for a combined monthly sales volume of 1,000 units across all three trims. With Japanese government subsidies of 568,000 yen (3,600 USD), the effective purchase price for consumers can drop to as low as 1.55 million yen (9,800 USD). This undercuts key rivals, including the BYD Racco (starting at 1.99 million yen after subsidies) and the Nissan Sakura (starting at 1.86 million yen after subsidies). Even without subsidies, the Suzuki e-Sky is still 20,000 yen (126 USD) cheaper than the BYD Racco, making it Japan’s cheapest kei car EV. In 2025, Suzuki sold 556,632 petrol-powered kei cars. Since its July launch, the BYD Racco has sold 1,800 units, and the company plans to enter the Sri Lankan and Macao markets.

artigo.texto: O que a guerra na Ucrânia e a guerra no Irã têm em comum? Ataque de Kiev a um navio iraniano no mar Cáspio expõe uma rede densa de inteligência militar circulando entre os dois conflitos. Gerando resumo Ao menos uma pessoa morreu e outras seis ficaram feridas após um ataque da Ucrânia com cerca de 650 drones contra a capital da Rússia na madrugada desta terça-feira, 6. Trata-se do segundo maior ataque com esses artefatos nos últimos dois anos contra a região de Moscou, localizada a centenas de quilômetros da fronteira ucraniana. Além da vítima fatal, um jovem de 20 anos, e dos feridos, várias casas foram atingidas pelo bombardeio, detalhou o governador regional Andrei Vorobyov. O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia afirmou que suas tropas atingiram quatro centros de processamento de dados em cidades da Ucrânia. Segundo a pasta, os alvos — Parkovyi, Ukrtelecom, Giga e Podolsky — seriam instalações estratégicas das Forças Armadas ucranianas. O ataque foi realizado com drones da brigada Varyag, de acordo com informações da agência estatal russa RIA. Tanto a Ucrânia quanto a Rússia intensificaram, nos últimos meses, os ataques com mísseis contra alvos civis e industriais incluindo infraestruturas de energia, transporte e portuárias, bem como embarcações no Mar Negro. A Rússia já declarou que pretende aumentar ainda mais ataques contra infraestruturas energéticas, inclusive em Kiev, à medida que o inverno se aproxima. /AFP

artigo.texto: Nevada AG Aaron Ford holds Boulder City town hall on data centers, utility bills LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford discussed data centers and their impact on utility costs in Boulder City. Ford, who is running for governor, held a town hall on Sunday in Boulder City focused on data centers’ impact on affordability and his plan as governor to protect Nevada families from higher utility bills. He also outlined his plan to protect taxpayer dollars and state resources. Ford has said he plans to pause new tax abatements and stop attempts to build data centers on federal land. He has also said he will audit data centers to verify whether they have delivered on their commitments. In a release sent to News 3, Ford's campaign claims, "Data Center Joe 'wholeheartedly' supports data centers and has handed them more than $240 million in taxpayer dollars while Nevadans struggle to afford to live in his failed economy. Meanwhile, Joe Lombardo’s campaign has taken $2 million from MAGA data center and Flock billionaires." News 3 reached out to Governor Lombardo's campaign for comment and is awaiting a response.

artigo.texto: Trending MARQUETTE -- From 6-7:30 p.m. on Thursday, the Lake Superior Community Partnership will be hosting a community informational session on data centers in the basement room at Peter White Public Library. "Join us for an informational session about what communities should know about data centers and how to prepare if a project comes your way," said the event description. "Hear from experts, learn about potential benefits and challenges, and have the opportunity to ask questions." Featured speakers at the event will be Ron Akers of the Charter Township of Van Buren and Dakota Baker of the Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance. Van Buren, a township in Macomb County, recently became home to a Google data center project. In a May 11 article by MLive titled "Google pitches Michigan on a different kind of data center. Some don't buy it," Akers is quoted as saying that the Google data center project was "the most extensively researched and evaluated site that I've ever worked on." MLive reports that while Akers and other township representatives have stressed that the project has been heavily vetted and regulated, many Van Buren residents continue to have concerns about certain aspects of the project, such as the non-disclosure agreement Akers and other township officials signed while the project was in its infancy. The full MLive article can be read here: https://www.mlive.com/news/2026/05/google-pitches-michigan-on-a-different-kind-of-data-center-some-dont-buy-it.html. The Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance describes itself on their website as "elevating and advancing local business." Their focus is on advocating for rural business-forward policy at the legislative level. Baker is their director. The Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance has participated in past public information sessions on data centers in other parts of Northern Michigan. "(Thursday's) session is intended to provide information and context around data centers, including potential opportunities, considerations and impacts associated with this type of development," said LSCP in a press release about the event. "The goal of the event is not to advocate for or against data centers, but to create a space where community members can become better informed and engage in the conversation." "As Marquette County's local economic development organization, we have a responsibility to help our community understand the issues and opportunities that could impact our economy," said Natalie Chmiko, CEO of the Lake Superior Community Partnership. "Our role with this event isn't to advocate for or against data centers. It’s to provide an opportunity for community members and municipal leaders to learn more and ask questions.” Those interested in attending Thursday's LSCP event can register for free on LSCP's website at https://members.marquette.org/ap/Events/Register/v5FJw2BUKCyCm. Doors for the event open at 5:30. Annie Lippert can be reached at 906-228-2500, ext. 550. Her email address is alippert@miningjournal.net.

artigo.texto: BYD Song Pro Flex é realmente econômico? Veja preços e versões O BYD Song Pro Flex é o segundo híbrido flex da BYD no Brasil. A montadora chinesa BYD passou de coadjuvante para uma protagonista da indústria automotiva em duas décadas. A trajetória da empresa é meteórica no campo de carros elétricos e híbridos plug-in. Por mais que hoje ela seja tão conhecida e popular nas ruas, a origem dela ainda é pouco conhecida: a marca começa fabricando outro tipo de produto e passa anos voltada apenas ao mercado local. A seguir, conheça a origem dessa companhia, a evolução dela como montadora e como a BYD conseguiu aliar tecnologia e estratégia para virar uma referência do mercado. Como surgiu a BYD? A trajetória da companhia começa em 1995, ano de fundação da Yadi Electronics pelo químico Wang Chuanfu. A empresa nasce em Shenzhen, com apenas 20 funcionários e um dos primos de Wang como sócio. O local fundação era propício para um empreendimento: Shenzen ficou conhecida como “o Vale do Silício da China” pela concentração de investimentos e empresas de eletrônicos. Nascido em uma região pobre em uma família de agricultores, Wang fez mestrado no Instituto de Pesquisa de Metais não Ferrosos de Pequim. Ao longo dos anos, ele chegou ao cargo de vice-presidente na estatal e por um tempo foi a pessoa mais rica da China. A BYD começou fabricando baterias? A meta inicial da empresa não envolvia automóveis, mas produzir baterias de níquel para eletrônicos. Em 1996, ela começa a fabricar baterias de íons de lítio, até hoje o tipo mais usado em produtos como smartphones. As principais clientes da empresa eram as gigantes Motorola, Nokia, Ericsson e Samsung. A situação era tão favorável que, em 1998, ela abre a unidade europeia nos Países Baixos e dois anos depois inaugura o primeiro parque industrial. Quando a BYD começou a fabricar carros? Os planos mudam em 2003, quando a BYD compra uma montadora de veículos chamada Qinchuan Automobile. Ela era de pequeno porte e estava mal financeiramente, mas já tinha uma estrutura pronta que foi vista como oportunidade. Os investidores ficaram desconfiados da movimentação ousada, feita no mesmo ano da fundação da Tesla nos Estados Unidos — que se tornaria uma das suas grandes concorrentes globais no futuro. Os primeiros carros produzidos pela BYD Nos dois primeiros anos, a BYD apenas fabricou modelos que a Qinchuan já tinha, como o Flyer, até começar a sonhar mais alto. Já com a nova divisão estabelecida, ela passou a produzir veículos inéditos. BYD F3 Em 2005, a montadora lançou seu primeiro veículo próprio, o F3. Era um modelo à combustão no formato de sedã e já com um preço bem acessível, mas com um visual inspirado até demais no Corolla da Toyota. Foram 10 mil unidades vendidas no ano, ou 10% da receita de todo o grupo. Nesse ponto, ela percebeu que a fabricação própria era uma ideia a ser seguida. BYD F3DM No fim de 2008, a BYD apresentou o F3DM, o primeiro veículo híbrido plug-in produzido em massa no mundo. Essa é a categoria que até traz tanque de combustível, mas pode ser carregada na bateria. Nesse ponto, ela percebe que poderia unir o conhecimento da fabricação de fontes de energia com o setor automotivo em uma classe de veículos que tinha potencial. BYD e6 O e6 foi o primeiro carro 100% elétrico lançado pela BYD no mercado global, em 2010, além de ser um primeiros a chegar também ao mercado brasileiro. Esse veículo teve o uso mais restrito para frotas de táxis e serviços corporativos. O que ajudou no crescimento da BYD? Uma série de decisões acertadas, visão de negócios e tecnologias ajudaram a BYD a gradualmente se tornar uma referência no mercado automotivo. Inicialmente, ela vendeu carros para o setor corporativo ou governamental, mas percebeu que deveria mirar o consumidor. A estratégia foi lançar carros mais baratos que os modelos estrangeiros na China, com maior preocupação com a qualidade do que as poucas rivais locais do período. Quem acreditou nessa ideia foi a Berkshire Hathaway, de Warren Buffett. Em 2008, ela investe o equivalente a 230 milhões de dólares na BYD. Nessa mesma época, o governo chinês iniciou incentivos para compradores de carros elétricos, o que fortaleceu a presença dele entre o público. Com dinheiro em caixa, ela produz o seu primeiro ônibus elétrico, além de vagões de metrô e empilhadeiras. A companhia também se especializou no desenvolvimento de tecnologias próprias. Elas incluem a e-Platform 3.0, base de montagem de carros com foco em segurança, eficiência e estética, e baterias de alto desempenho. Fabricar a própria bateria é visto como um diferencial, já que as rivais dependem de fornecedoras parceiras mais caras e menos otimizadas ao carro. A BYD tem também sistemas de recarga de veículos que estão entre os mais rápidos do mundo. Como a BYD se expandiu para outros países? Com mais investimentos e estrutura, a BYD amplia o catálogo de veículos com modelos batizados em referência aos nomes de dinastias da China. Eles incluem o sedã Qin (2012), o SUV Tang (2015), que virou só Tan no Brasil e recebeu várias atualizações ao longo dos anos, e os SUVs compactos Song (2015) e Yuan (2016). Além disso, ela também começa o processo de internacionalização, inclusive com parcerias com montadoras. Foi o caso da linha de carros Denza, que estreia em 2014 em parceria com a gigante alemã Daimler. Já 2016 fica marcado por uma mudança na imagem da montadora, que contrata o designer automotivo Wolfgang Egger, com experiência na Audi e na Lamborghini, pra ser o chefe dessa divisão e profissionalizar ainda mais o visual dos modelos. Ela também expande para o setor de transporte ferroviário, muito graças a um investimento feito pela Samsung para iniciar a produção de monotrilhos. Esse é um dos mercados mais fortes dela hoje. Quando a BYD chegou ao Brasil? É em 2015 que a BYD chega no país com uma fábrica de montagem de chassi de ônibus elétricos em Campinas. artigo.texto: China has presented a goal of bringing all-solid-state batteries to an early stage of scaled application by 2030. However, CATL, the world's largest battery maker, is taking a cautious view, saying cost and mass-production technology issues remain and wider adoption will take more time. According to InsideEVs and other outlets, seven government bodies including China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology announced the "15th Five-Year Plan for the New Battery Industry". The plan includes a goal of realising early scaled application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030 and making breakthroughs in core technologies such as advanced electrode materials and new electrolytes. While the government is accelerating efforts to foster the industry, CATL is cautious about the commercialisation timeline. CATL Chairman Robin Zeng (쩡위췬) in June rated the technology maturity of all-solid-state batteries at level 4 out of 9. With level 9 representing mass-producible capability, he said a large technology gap remains. CATL is aiming for small-scale production and vehicle validation in 2027. However, Zeng forecast that "the possibility of scaling all-solid-state batteries to the point of being applied to millions of vehicles is very low before 2030". That is because manufacturing stability and cost, as well as performance, must be solved at the same time. LG Energy Solution offered a similar view. Robert Lee (로버트 리), head of LG Energy Solution in North America, said, "There are still difficulties in mass-producing large all-solid-state cells," adding that they are more likely to be commercialised first in smartphones or specialised uses before expanding to electric vehicles. Market forecasts are also cautious. BloombergNEF projected that "all-solid-state batteries will account for about 10 percent of global demand for electric-vehicle and energy-storage batteries even in 2035." In China, vehicles equipped with semi-solid-state batteries have already appeared, but it is difficult to view this as full-fledged commercialisation of fully all-solid-state batteries. Meanwhile, the Chinese government plans to foster next-generation technologies simultaneously, including sodium-ion and flow batteries, as well as long-life lithium batteries, in addition to all-solid-state batteries. It also set a goal of increasing the charge-discharge cycle life of long-life lithium batteries to 15,000 cycles by 2030.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Two transmission-connected energy storage projects are slated to receive awards in the first round of the Maryland Next Generation Energy Act energy storage procurement, the state public service commission said on Thursday. - The finalists are Flatiron Energy’s 400 MW/1,600 MWh Chalk Point Storage Project in south-central Maryland and REV Renewables’s 40 MW/160 MWh Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in the far western part of the state. Both will receive flat pricing for 15-year terms at a combined cost of 6.98 cents/month for the average Maryland residential customer, the public service commission said. - The award will help address the PJM Interconnection’s capacity woes, which Federal Energy Regulatory Commission chair Laura Swett last week called a “mess.” The grid operator faces a capacity shortfall of 6.8 GW for the 2028-2029 delivery year, up 300 MW from the previous period, as capacity prices remain at the $325/MW-day cap. Dive Insight: Passed in 2025, the Next Generation Energy Act requires Maryland to conduct at least two solicitations for a combined 1.6 GW of energy storage capacity. Eligible projects must be designed to discharge at full power for at least four hours. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced the awards for the first solicitation round on Thursday, the statutory deadline. By law, it must open bidding for the second round by Jan. 1, 2027, and announce project awards by Oct. 1, 2027. Evan Vaughan, executive director of the regional clean energy group MAREC Action, said Thursday’s selections will help mitigate the effects of PJM’s high capacity prices. “These projects can help meet growing electricity demand while reducing exposure to volatile capacity prices that ultimately affect customers’ bills,” Vaughan said in a statement. Also known as the Mid-Atlantic Renewable Energy Coalition, MAREC Action consists of more than 50 developers and manufacturers serving the region’s utility-scale solar, wind and battery storage industry. Flatiron Energy and REV Renewables are both members. Flatiron’s project will be located at NRG’s oil- and gas-fired Chalk Point power plant in the southeastern corner of Prince George’s County, according to the Maryland Public Service Commission. REV will site its project on a portion of a reclaimed coal mine in mountainous Garrett County, near Maryland’s border with West Virginia and Pennsylvania. The commission said it chose not to award the 500-MW/3,000-MWh Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project nor a 135-MW/540-MWh expansion Flatiron requested for the Chalk Point project in a revised filing after the first-round application window closed. The commission said Flatiron could reapply for the Chalk Point expansion and “invited [Oystercatcher] to consider participating” in round two, citing the “desirable electric grid location and characteristics” of the project’s northeastern Maryland site while noting “the need for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County if the project is pursued further.” In addition to near-term cost pressures due to PJM’s capacity crunch, Maryland has ambitious clean energy goals, including a statutory 2045 target for statewide net-zero emissions and a 2035 goal for 100% carbon-free electricity set by gubernatorial order. In a statement, Maryland Public Service Commission Chair Kumar Barve called the first-round award a milestone in the state’s effort to meet its energy policy goals, while acknowledging its relatively modest contribution. “While we are disappointed that these awards are below our 800-MW target for Round 1, our Round 2 solicitation is expected to attract many more offers due to a pool of over 40 additional energy storage projects from PJM’s Cycle 1 interconnection process,” Barve said.

artigo.texto: Data centers ganham disputa por acesso a transmissão de energia em SP Empreendimentos arrematam 228 MW oferecidos pelo governo federal no Estado em temporada de acesso à rede de transmissão Três empresas com empreendimentos de data centers venceram uma disputa pelo acesso a 228 MW (megawatts) no sistema de transmissão em São Paulo, disponibilizados pelo governo federal por meio de um processo competitivo encerrado na 3ª feira (6.out.2026). A capacidade será alocada para os projetos Pahlavan One, Pahlavan Three e Digital DC Brasil. Os 2 primeiros pertencem à Pahlavan Ventures One, que desenvolve e gerencia um projeto de data center integrado ao Complexo Pahlavan, localizado no município de Paulínia (SP). A empresa é controlada pela CloudHQ, uma desenvolvedora global de infraestrutura de data centers de hiperescala. Já a Digital DC Brasil Ltda, que opera comercialmente no Brasil sob a marca NextStream, atende grandes empresas, provedores de serviços de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações e grandes geradores de conteúdo. A companhia atua no setor de infraestrutura digital e serviços de colocation, com 11 data centers distribuídos em 5 países da América Latina. Os empreendimentos arremataram 100% da capacidade disponibilizada em São Paulo no 1º processo competitivo realizado pela Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão). O certame disponibilizou 228 MW de margem de escoamento em 4 pontos de conexão localizados no Estado e teve participação de 7 empreendimentos, que somaram 451 MW de demanda habilitada. A vitória das empresas de data centers vem em um momento em que o setor elétrico demonstra preocupação com a capacidade do sistema de transmissão brasileiro diante da alta demanda energética desse tipo de empreendimento. Representantes do setor afirmam que o ritmo de expansão do sistema brasileiro de transmissão pode ser um gargalo para o estabelecimento de mais data centers no país. Executivos defendem acelerar investimentos em transmissão e mais leilões para esse tipo de infraestrutura, sobretudo depois da implementação do Redata, o regime especial de tributação para data centers recém-aprovado pelo Congresso e sancionado pelo Executivo, que deve atrair cada vez mais empreendimentos para o Brasil. PNAST O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) e o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) realizaram nesta 4ª feira (7.out.2026) a cerimônia de encerramento da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026 da Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão. O evento marca a conclusão do 1º ciclo da política, que criou um novo modelo de entrada de geradores e grandes consumidores na rede básica de transmissão de energia. A medida cria regras padronizadas para pedidos de conexão e estabelece as chamadas Temporadas de Acesso, janelas periódicas nas quais o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) avaliará, de forma conjunta, todos os requerimentos. O sistema foi implementado em decreto baixado pelo governo em dezembro de 2025. O novo modelo substitui o regime de “fila aberta”, em que projetos podiam solicitar conexão a qualquer momento. Esse formato resultava em filas longas, ocupadas por empreendimentos ainda imaturos ou com caráter especulativo, o que dificultava o planejamento da expansão da transmissão. Com a Pnast, os pedidos passam a ser analisados todos de uma vez a cada temporada, considerando a capacidade disponível da rede e critérios técnicos de viabilidade. Ao todo, foram registrados 367 cadastramentos de empreendimentos de geração e consumo, que somaram mais de 20 GW em solicitações de acesso distribuídas por 64 barramentos do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional). Considerando o período de transição e a 1ª Temporada, o ONS analisou mais de 43 GW em solicitações de acesso à Rede Básica, dos quais aproximadamente 30,7 GW foram viabilizados ou habilitados. A partir de 2027, a política contará com duas Temporadas de Acesso por ano.

artigo.texto: CIP invests over â¬270 million in Kilmarnock South battery storage project in Scotland Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners has taken the final investment decision for Kilmarnock South, a 350 MW, 1,400 MWh system. Under construction in southern Scotland, the site is due to enter service in early 2028. Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), through its fourth flagship fund Copenhagen Infrastructure IV, has taken the final investment decision for Kilmarnock South. The 350 MW, 1,400 MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) is located in South Ayrshire, southern Scotland. Construction has begun, and commercial operations are expected in the first quarter of 2028, the company said. A commitment of over â¬270 million CIP says the project represents an investment commitment of more than â¬270 million. UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks, for his part, refers to a battery worth GBP 232 million. With a four-hour duration, Kilmarnock South would become the longest-duration asset in CIP's UK storage portfolio. The system would store surplus Scottish wind power that would otherwise go unused and release it to the grid when the network has capacity. Such projects are part of a market where storage operators are multiplying across Europe, as illustrated by the energy storage contracts secured by ML System in Poland worth â¬4.1 million. Company Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners: company profile Four Scottish projects in total Kilmarnock South is CIP's fourth investment in transmission-connected BESS projects in Scotland. It joins Coalburn 1, which reached commercial operations in August 2026, as well as Coalburn 2 and Devilla. Once all four projects are fully commissioned, their combined storage capacity would reach 4.4 GWh, which CIP describes as the equivalent of almost a third of Great Britain's operational battery storage today. CIP's Scottish portfolio would have a total power capacity of 1.85 GW. According to the company, this capacity would match the electricity demand of over 5.5 million households over a two-hour period. Statements from officials Nischal Agarwal, Partner at CIP, says well-sited storage projects bring flexibility to the power system. In his view, they allow the full benefits of low-cost renewables to be captured, strengthen security of supply and help cut and stabilise consumer bills. Michael Shanks notes that a former coal mine at Coalburn is now home to one of Europe's largest batteries. He says these projects reduce the waste of locally generated power and strengthen energy security. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 % Other storage technologies are also advancing, such as the 12 MWh thermal storage system on which BrenX has started construction at the Wolfson hospital.

artigo.texto: A área portuária de Miramar, no bairro do Barreiro, em Belém, vai receber o primeiro data center para Inteligência Artificial da Amazônia, o BEL1, da Elea Data Centers. O projeto é alvo de um inquérito civil do Ministério Público do Pará (MPPA), que alerta para o risco de formação de “ilhas de calor” em uma região já castigada por temperaturas extremas. O empreendimento também chama atenção para a ausência, no Brasil, de regras ambientais específicas para a instalação de data centers. - 🔎 Data centers (centro de dados, em inglês) são espaços que armazenam e processam informações com equipamentos como servidores de armazenamento e chips de processamento. Para processar grandes volumes de dados, essas máquinas consomem muita energia e geram calor continuamente. Por isso, dependem de sistemas de resfriamento para espalhar esse calor para o ambiente. O projeto vai iniciar com a capacidade de 7,5 megawatts, depois tem previsão de expansão para até 100 megawatts, segundo a empresa. Leia mais: Esses números chamam a atenção de especialistas ouvidos pelo g1, pois só na etapa inicial a potência de 7,5 megawatts seria suficiente para abastecer mais de 22,5 mil residências na região Norte, de acordo com dados da Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), do Ministério de Minas e Energia. Com previsão de começar a funcionar no segundo trimestre de 2027, a empresa Elea promete que o BEL1 vai servir como a infraestrutura necessária para ampliar o acesso da região Norte à IA, à computação em nuvem e a serviços digitais, “aproximando o processamento de dados dos usuários e reduzindo a dependência de servidores em outras regiões do país e até no exterior”. A chegada da infraestrutura levanta questões sobre possíveis impactos ambientais. O empreendimento virou alvo de um inquérito civil do MPPA, sobre os potenciais riscos de criar ‘ilhas de calor’, que superaqueceriam o ambiente urbano, além da ausência de licenciamento ambiental e consultas públicas. O promotor Márcio Maués, 1ª Promotoria de Justiça de Barcarena, quer apurar a legalidade da instalação e os riscos de “dano climático”. A preocupação dele baseia-se em estudo de pesquisadores da Universidade de Cambridge, indicando que data centers podem elevar a temperatura da superfície terrestre em uma média de 2°C, com picos extremos que chegam a 9,1°C, estendendo efeitos térmicos por raio de até 10 km. “Não basta afirmar que não trará consequências, não basta afirmar que será bom. Tem que ser demonstrado tecnicamente”, alerta o promotor Maués. A pesquisa de Cambridge utilizou dados de satélite da NASA para monitorar a temperatura da superfície terrestre no entorno de mais de 8 mil data centers de IA ao redor do mundo entre 2004 e 2024. Os resultados apontaram um aumento médio de 2,07°C na temperatura da superfície terrestre logo após o início das operações dessas estruturas. Os cientistas identificaram que o efeito térmico se propaga por até 10 km, mas sua intensidade decai rapidamente com a distância. O aquecimento médio do solo fica em torno de 1°C em um raio de até 4,5 km das instalações, segundo os resultados. Maués destaca ainda a vulnerabilidade de comunidades ribeirinhas nos arredores da cidade, como a Ilha das Onças, situada a apenas 4,5 km do local. Segundo ele, essas populações não foram ouvidas conforme exige a Convenção 169 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho (OIT). Não foram realizadas consultas públicas com moradores dos bairros Miramar, Barreiro, Sacramenta e Pratinha, que ficam próximos ao local da instalação. “O efeito depende da tecnologia utilizada, mas é algo que precisamos estar atentos. Não acho que seria o caso daqui de Belém, aumentar 9°C, mas é preciso demonstrar se haverá efeito de aumento da temperatura ou não, e em qual proporção”, defende o promotor. O empreendedor e ambientalista Murilo Monteiro é morador do bairro da Sacramenta e disse que acompanha com atenção as discussões sobre o projeto. “Ainda não houve comunicação dirigida à comunidade local nem às instituições que atuam no território. Essa ausência de diálogo gera dúvidas e demonstra a necessidade de ampliar a transparência e a participação social desde as fases iniciais do empreendimento”, afirmou. O pesquisador Juliano Ximenes, da UFPA, concorda com a preocupação, detalhando que estruturas de data center dissipam energia na forma de calor, elevando a temperatura externa em uma área que frequentemente já atinge sensações térmicas de 34°C ou mais, gerando “manchas de calor”. A empresa afirma que usará sistemas de ar-condicionado para resfriar os equipamentos, em vez de água. É a chamada “expansão direta”, um tipo de refrigeração industrial bastante utilizado em data centers. O fundador e CEO da Elea, o italiano Alessandro Lombardi, diz que estudos de impacto térmico mais profundos só seriam realizados para a fase de 100 MW, que ainda não tem data para sair do papel. “Quando se constrói um data center maior, eu penso que essa sugestão de ouvir a sociedade tem que ser vista, mas não nesta fase atual do projeto, que eu posso garantir que não tem nenhum impacto. Será como um shopping center de médio porte, que ainda consome muito mais calor do que um data center deste tamanho na fase inicial”, ele afirma. Para além da temperatura, especialistas alertam para outros possíveis desequilíbrios. O professor Ximenes aponta que manter o resfriamento contínuo dessas máquinas pode gerar uma poluição sonora “severa”: enquanto a Lei Complementar de Controle Urbanístico de Belém limita ruídos a 65 dB, o entorno de data centers pelo mundo pode atingir 96 dB. Lombardi garante que o projeto prevê mecanismos de redução de ruídos. “O ruído eventualmente é dos geradores a diesel, e não do data center em si. Esses geradores emitem um som medido em decibel e ele tem uma legislação sobre o barulho. A contingência a estes ruídos está prevista.” Sem regras no Brasil No Brasil, não há regulamentação específica para instalações de data centers, ou seja, não existem leis ou diretrizes

artigo.texto: Mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de comutadores de fibra óptica até 2035: demanda de data centers impulsiona o crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica entra em uma fase de expansão estrutural, sustentado pelo crescimento incessante da interconexão de data centers (DCI), pelas atualizações de redes de telecomunicações e pela mudança arquitetural em direção a sistemas ópticos abertos e desagregados. Os comutadores de fibra óptica — dispositivos eletro-ópticos ou optomecânicos que encaminham sinais ópticos sem conversão elétrica — são essenciais para gerenciar largura de banda, reduzir a latência e viabilizar redes definidas por software. A demanda se divide entre comutadores de alta confiabilidade e muitos recursos para redes de nível de telecomunicações e comutadores otimizados em custo e com alto número de portas para data centers de hiperescala. O controle sobre plataformas proprietárias de integração fotônica, como MEMS, PLC e fotônica de silício, determina desempenho e custo, enquanto a montagem e o encapsulamento continuam sendo gargalos. As compras são dominadas por relações diretas de design-in com fabricantes de sistemas ópticos, o que torna o sucesso dependente de roteiros tecnológicos plurianuais e de longos ciclos de qualificação. À medida que provedores de nuvem e operadoras buscam maior automação e programabilidade, o mercado migra de componentes isolados para soluções de subsistemas habilitadas por software. Este relatório analisa essas dinâmicas e apresenta uma previsão até 2035, com foco na demanda final, na lógica da cadeia de suprimentos e no posicionamento competitivo. O cenário-base para o mercado de comutadores de fibra óptica até 2035 pressupõe crescimento contínuo do tráfego global de dados, da computação em nuvem e da implantação de 5G/6G, impulsionando a demanda por comutação óptica tanto em telecomunicações quanto em data centers. Espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta anual (CAGR) de 8,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 220 (2025=100) em 2035. Essa perspectiva é sustentada pela transição em curso para redes ópticas abertas e desagregadas, que amplia o número de pontos de comutação e exige maior programabilidade. Nas telecomunicações, a implantação de CDC-ROADMs e OXCs sustentará a demanda por comutadores MEMS com alto número de portas, enquanto os operadores de data centers adotarão cada vez mais comutadores de circuito óptico para reduzir consumo de energia e latência. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico continuará sendo o maior mercado, impulsionada pela infraestrutura de telecomunicações da China e pelos data centers de hiperescala, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão atualizações constantes. Restrições na cadeia de suprimentos, especialmente de ferramentas especializadas de fabricação e wafers eletro-ópticos, podem moderar o crescimento, mas as expansões de capacidade em andamento devem aliviar os gargalos. A pressão sobre os preços persistirá nos segmentos de menor número de portas, mas o valor migrará para subsistemas integrados com controle por software. O cenário-base não pressupõe mudanças tecnológicas disruptivas, e sim melhorias evolutivas na fotônica de silício e na confiabilidade dos MEMS. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Aumento da demanda por interconexão de data centers (DCI), impulsionado por cargas de trabalho de nuvem e IA - Atualização de redes de telecomunicações para 400G/800G e além, exigindo comutação óptica avançada - Migração para redes ópticas abertas e desagregadas, ampliando os pontos de comutação - Necessidade de menor latência e menor consumo de energia em data centers - Iniciativas governamentais de expansão de banda larga e implantação de 5G - Crescimento da computação de borda e da IoT, impulsionando arquiteturas de rede distribuídas Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Altos custos de qualificação e longos ciclos de design-in para comutadores de nível de telecomunicações - Gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos de componentes fotônicos especializados e ferramentas de fabricação - Erosão de preços nos segmentos de comutadores de baixo número de portas e de uso geral - Desafios técnicos para escalar a fotônica de silício para grandes números de portas - Tensões geopolíticas que afetam o comércio e o acesso à tecnologia, sobretudo entre EUA e China Estrutura da Demanda por Setor de Uso Final Telecomunicações (participação estimada: 40%) As operadoras de telecomunicações estão modernizando suas redes de transporte para lidar com o aumento do tráfego gerado por 5G, fibra até a residência e serviços corporativos. Os comutadores de fibra óptica são essenciais em nós ROADM e OXC para o roteamento dinâmico de comprimentos de onda, viabilizando grades flexíveis e arquiteturas incolores, sem direção e sem contenção (CDC). Até 2035, a demanda será impulsionada pela necessidade de maior número de portas, menor perda de inserção e velocidades de comutação mais rápidas. A transição para 400G/800G e, eventualmente, 1,6T exigirá comutadores com desempenho superior. Além disso, a busca por redes abertas e desagregadas aumentará o número de pontos de comutação, à medida que as operadoras procuram evitar a dependência de fornecedores. artigo.texto: - Jocelyn Benson and John James squared off in the first of two Michigan gubernatorial debates - Benson, for the first time, called for a suspension of Michigan’s gas tax to provide relief to motorists - James said he would not push for a statewide moratorium on data centers, countering his campaign’s past statements GRAND RAPIDS — Michigan gubernatorial nominees John James and Jocelyn Benson traded barbs while making some notable policy shifts on data centers and gas taxes Tuesday night during their first televised debate. The meeting between James, a Republican member of the US House, and Benson, the state’s Democratic secretary of state, was mostly cordial. But sparks flew during exchanges over affordability, the Iran war and more. Related: - Gubernatorial candidates’ plans for Michigan’s most pressing issues - Benson’s record: Election fights, faster DMV visits, transparency flop - James says he delivers results. What does his record show? The debate at WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids is the first of two between James and Benson ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. The next will be held at WDIV-TV in metro Detroit Oct. 15, although absentee voting is already underway and more than 201,000 Michiganders have already cast ballots. Read on for takeaways and fact checks from the first debate. James backtracks on moratorium A statewide moratorium on data centers is no longer on the table if James is elected governor, he told reporters after the Tuesday debate. “This will be led by the locals and not by Lansing,” James said. “As a conservative, I don’t like bans or mandates.” James’ stance had been somewhat opaque since August, when his campaign had told The Detroit News he was in favor of a moratorium until standards for local control, electricity use and environmental protections are put in place. After the debate James made it clear he believes local governments should decide the fate of the facilities and he does not favor a statewide block. “If free people decide (a data center is) what they want to do, then the government should get the heck out of their way,” James said. “The moratorium should be imposed on Lansing, not the people.” Fact check: Did James vote against local control? During an exchange over data centers, Benson claimed James “voted four times to block the ability of local communities to have a voice or a say in whether data centers can come to those communities.” As a member of Congress, James didn’t vote for any standalone bills to limit local control on data centers. But he did vote for an early version of the “Big, Beautiful Bill” that included a section called the “Artificial Intelligence and Information Technology Modernization Initiative,” which would have barred state and local jurisdictions from creating laws to regulate artificial intelligence. A bipartisan group representing state legislatures warned the provision would also “circumvent their authority to regulate the permitting, construction and operation of data centers within their borders.” It was not included in the final law. Benson shifts on gas tax Benson said Tuesday night she is “open” to suspending Michigan’s 52-cent gas tax to help motorists facing high prices. That was a shift for Benson, who had previously called for the federal government to suspend its own 18-cent tax but had argued against a state gas tax holiday, suggesting it could “potentially blow in the state budget.” Republican House Speaker Matt Hall has said calls to suspend the state tax are unrealistic given its importance to a bipartisan road funding deal negotiated last year with Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. James made a factual error on the issue during the debate, claiming Michigan could afford a gas tax holiday if Democrats hadn’t “blown” through the state’s “rainy day” savings account the past eight years. In reality, the Budget Stabilization Fund has nearly doubled under Whitmer’s tenure. This year, Senate Democrats proposed withdrawing $350 million to plug budget holes, but House Republicans opposed it, and that plan did not pass the full Legislature. Fact check: Did James vote for Iran war? During the gas tax debate, Benson responded to James: “You voted six times in support of a war in Iran that has directly led to the increase in these gas prices.” James didn’t vote to start the war, but he has voted against six resolutions to try to end it, most recently on Sept. 15, when he opposed a measure to end the conflict unless Congress explicitly authorized a declaration of war. artigo.texto: I visit the hospital rooms of my family and church elders relatively regularly. I have never been to the hospital to visit any of my young cousins, but that changed a week ago. As a heat dome covered Memphis and the Mid-South, my 21-year-old cousin, Ra’Kelle Miller, was struggling to breathe after five minutes outdoors and was rushed to the emergency room. Neither her nebulizer nor asthma pump worked to open her airways. She lives a few miles away from Colossus I and only a couple of miles away from the Valero Oil Refinery. The pollution from these facilities, and the power plant with the illegal gas turbines in neighboring Southaven, are having a real impact on our community’s health now. Politicians and talking heads are leaving the people impacted by hyperscale data centers behind when discussing the “economic development” they think data centers can bring. Memphis is becoming a testing ground for the future of artificial intelligence. But before we rush into that future, we need to pause and ask: What will it cost the people who live here? SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center arrived in Memphis under the cover of NDAs and secret meetings that never included people from the community. That rush to secrecy and to market has led to tons of harmful pollutants being emitted into our air and lungs. SpaceXAI is raking in billions of dollars a month, and all we have to show for it is $30M in city and county tax revenue and temporary construction jobs filled by people from out of town. The tax money is a pittance compared to SpaceXAI’s value and profits. We should be ashamed, not celebrating how we are being treated. SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center has put extraordinary demands on Memphis for electricity, water and other infrastructure. To power those demands, SpaceXAI’s founder, Elon Musk, has relied on dozens of methane gas turbines that emit nitrogen oxides and other pollutants with well-documented health risks. The full health and environmental consequences for Memphis residents continue to worsen. The Memphis City Council has an opportunity to help us learn from this colossal mistake by pausing to think, learn and act in the best interest of the people of Memphis. The council is scheduled for a third reading and vote on Ordinance 5982 on Tuesday. The ordinance proposes pausing new large-scale data center development for 12 months to give Memphis time to study the impact of facilities like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, allow for community input on where they are built, and develop regulations that protect our air, water, land and jobs. There’s more than enough reason to pause and research this before expanding the existing facilities or allowing more. The environmental concerns are substantial. A recent Reuters report found that Musk’s company has installed many more gas turbines than it claimed, and without proper permitting. The majority of those turbines are in neighboring Southaven, near predominantly Black communities of Whitehaven and Westwood that already face elevated rates of respiratory illness. The five-mile affected area extends across the state line into Memphis, including John P. Freeman Middle School. The Reuters report calculated that 30 methane gas turbines with available emissions data could produce nearly 2,500 tons of nitrogen oxides, 4,000 tons of carbon monoxide, and 22 tons of formaldehyde annually, assuming they operate continuously at 80% capacity. The report says that the EPA states that these turbines typically operate around the clock at 80% capacity or more. The American Lung Association states that nitrogen dioxide, one of the nitrogen oxides produced by these turbines, increases toxic smog, which is proven to reduce lung capacity and increase airway inflammation, coughing and wheezing. Toxic smog also worsens asthma and can cause asthma in children, leading to hospital and emergency room visits. Carbon monoxide deprives the body of oxygen, and formaldehyde is a human carcinogen. Cancer rates in South Memphis are already more than 4 times the federal cancer limit. Memphis has become the sacrifice zone for a billionaire’s wealth and profit. An investigative report by ProPublica exposes that this highly elevated cancer rate is due to cancer-causing pollution from industrial sites. Beyond the proposed economic effects of this industrialization are the effects on the lives of the people living in Memphis. People like my cousin, Ra’Kelle. Further, Memphis residents are being asked to not only put themselves in harm’s way for these and future data centers, but also to accommodate this massive land use without the necessary regulation. The current Unified Development Code doesn’t specify regulations for these massive data centers that so heavily consume our water, burden our electrical infrastructure, and threaten our health. The real question isn’t whether Memphis should participate in the AI economy. It’s whether we should allow this unprecedented data center growth to continue under rules written before this technology existed and its adverse health effects were known. We need courage from our City Council to put people at the forefront of these policy decisions. Our lives matter more than hyper-scale data centers. I urge the council to pass Ordinance 5982, which identifies the regulatory gaps and would impose a temporary 12-month moratorium on specified permits for new and expanded data-center development while the city studies and develops permanent regulations. Tennessee is not alone in its quest to understand the impacts of these large-scale facilities before granting permits. Last month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared a halt on new data center construction until the state can conduct an audit of energy and water use and the burden on Texas’ electricity grid. Across the country and across party lines, 65% of Americans are opposed to the construction of new large-scale data centers in their communities. artigo.texto: Ford CEO Jim Farley has pushed back against concerns surrounding the automaker’s relationship with China-based CATL, whose lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery technology Ford has agreed to license. The arrangement has drawn scrutiny over potential national security implications, but Farley has dismissed the growing controversy, urging critics to “stop the drama” and indicating that Ford has no intention of backing away from the partnership. Ford has expanded its ties with Chinese companies beyond its EV battery operations. The automaker works with CATL on electric vehicle batteries, while its new Ford Energy business will focus on battery energy storage systems. The American automaker also announced a partnership with Hangzhou-based Geely Automobile Holdings in July to establish a joint venture focused on the European market. The venture will operate from Ford’s Valencia plant in Spain, which currently produces the Kuga compact SUV for European and other global markets. According to the Detroit Free Press, Ford’s agreement with CATL gives the automaker access to battery technology it will use to produce EV batteries at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall. However, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy raised concerns about Ford’s growing dependence on overseas suppliers for key manufacturing components. In a letter to Farley that Duffy’s team shared, he specifically pointed to China and other countries that the administration considers foreign adversaries as sources of critical parts for the Dearborn-based automaker. The letter stated that Duffy was writing to express “the profound concern of the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) regarding the strategic trajectory of Ford Motor Company (Ford or Company), specifically as it pertains to American national automotive manufacturing integrity, supply chain exposure, and reliance on technologies of foreign adversaries.” Farley responded to the letter, saying Ford will partner with and compete against Chinese suppliers. He said: “We’re going to partner with the Chinese and we’re going to compete with them. Both can be totally fine, they are not mutually exclusive. “So, stop the drama. Just get on with designing good vehicles, great software, great experiences, a great relationship with your owners and suppliers — and we can compete.” Addressing the BlueOval Battery Park in Michigan, where the LFP batteries will be made, Farley said, “That’s our factory,” but noted that CATL is a leader in battery production, so the partnership was a good solution. He added: “It’s American jobs. We’re learning. We’re working with them. We’re solving problems together. It’s better than importing batteries.”

She added that carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits. A carbon market without rigour is merely an exercise in greenwashing a scenario that Nigeria will not accommodate. artigo.texto: Americans have a lot of concerns about AI data centers, but two keep rising to the top. First, the process for approving data centers is very secretive, and the developers are concealing even basic details about their projects from the public. Second, the environmental impacts could be significant, from energy use and bills to water use to noise. In his recent MinnPost Voices commentary, Lindsay Mark Lewis tries to portray the proposed Pine Island, Minnesota, data center as an example of a project that “went through the process” and should therefore be built. But I wonder if Lewis has read any of the documents in the Pine Island “process.” I have, and there simply isn’t enough information in them to evaluate the potential environmental impacts. Key facts were not included in the documents, including how much energy the facility would use and what that might mean for the energy grid or electricity bills; why the facility needs 55 million gallons of water per year and what impact that might have on water resources; how many diesel generators the facility might need on site and what air quality impacts those generators could have; and how much noise or light pollution the facility might cause. The study also neglected to do a required cumulative impact analysis, looking at whether there are other proposed similar facilities nearby and what the cumulative impact of multiple AI data centers might be. Related: The Pine Island blueprint: How Minnesota is setting the standard for data centers The developers have claimed that they didn’t know these details at the time, not that they were deliberately withheld under the non-disclosure agreements they signed with local officials. I don’t know which one is true. But from the perspective of the law, and the residents who wish to know what is being proposed in their town, the result is the same — the environmental study doesn’t include information that the public needs to evaluate and comment on the project. Ironically, Google’s news release about their involvement and anticipated clean energy investments, which was released after the city had voted to approve the project, contained more details about the project than the environmental study. So let’s dig in a bit further to those energy issues, because this is the primary claim at Pine Island — that they are a model of clean energy investment. But the environmental study is silent on the topic of energy demand and clean energy investments. Google doubled down on this secrecy strategy in its recent filings at the Public Utility Commission, where it claimed this information was trade secret and must be withheld from the public. With regard to how much energy the facility would use, here is a direct quote from their filing: “The facilities are anticipated to bring an electrical load of [TRADE SECRET DATA BEGINS TRADE SECRET DATA ENDS] to the Company’s Minnesota system.” Community Voices: Pine Island data center project is far from a gold standard Did that answer your questions? Or are you curious about Google’s plan to build new energy resources? Here is what Google has to say: “At full load ramp and with all resources online, these assets are expected to produce at least [TRADE SECRET DATA BEGINS TRADE SECRET DATA ENDS] of the capacity and [TRADE SECRET DATA BEGINS TRADE SECRET DATA ENDS] of the energy required by the facility.” As long as this veil of secrecy is held around these facilities, this will never be a transparent and democratic public process. Nor can we fully assess this project and its potential impacts. Lewis points to the 2025 law passed in Minnesota on data centers as evidence that we have strong safeguards in place already. That law did have good provisions, such as a requirement that utilities create separate terms of electric service, or “tariffs” for data centers to avoid putting costs onto ratepayers. But we still have significant outstanding issues to address, including nondisclosure agreements, environmental review, and the cumulative impacts of multiple AI data centers on our air, water, and land, among other things. And contrary to Lewis’s claims about clean energy, the law does not prevent our utilities from building fossil fuel plants to service AI data centers, as is happening all around the country right now. There is, in short, a lot more to do. Lewis’s original question about whether it is possible to build and regulate at the same time, the answer is an unequivocal yes. Minnesota is doing it all the time. In its most recent report on permitting efficiency, the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency currently manages air, water, and land permits at over 26,000 facilities across the state. Last year, 99% of the permits submitted met the timeliness requirements set forth by the Minnesota Legislature. Related: In pausing data centers, Minnesota courts did what local officials wouldn’t And yes, there are large, controversial projects that are outliers, including AI data centers. Some folks like to point to these examples to make it seem like all facilities are litigated and challenged. In reality, the vast majority of projects in Minnesota go through environmental review and permitting in a timely manner and are never challenged in court. AI data centers are moving quickly and quietly into the state. They are moving so quickly and under so much secrecy that, without judicial review, communities would have few, if any, tools to protect themselves. The courts do have a role to play in enforcing our bedrock environmental laws, and the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy’s litigation is intended to ensure that these facilities undergo the same process as every other facility in Minnesota. The real question is, who will decide whether these facilities are right for this state — Minnesotans, or the massive technology companies behind these developments? A transparent process is the first step toward putting this decision back where it belongs — in the hands of Minnesotans. Kat
