artigo.texto: Data centers have become the main financiers of new power capacity in Finland, as rising demand for continuous electricity supply reshapes the country’s power contracting landscape. According to a new analysis by Rystad Energy, procurement is shifting from agreements focused mainly on renewable energy volumes toward structures capable of providing a supply profile closer to baseload generation. This change is reflected in the 507 MW agreement signed by Google with Fortum for the Loviisa nuclear power plant, Finland’s first nuclear PPA. Rystad sees the deal as an indication of a broader trend in which large digital consumers will increasingly combine different technologies to secure more stable electricity supply. Finland could reach 5 GW of data center capacity by 2035 Rystad expects Finland to become the fifth-largest data center market in Europe by 2035, with installed capacity rising from 0.8 GW in 2026 to 5 GW. By 2030, data centers could account for around 15% of Finland’s electricity consumption, becoming the country’s main source of new power demand. Rystad points to several factors supporting this growth, including low-cost onshore wind, a strong power grid, low carbon intensity in the electricity system and Finland’s cold climate, which reduces cooling requirements. Data centers overtake industry as long-term power buyers Data centers have already surpassed manufacturing and industrial companies as the largest buyers of electricity through long-term contracts in Finland, with the gap widening rapidly. Google’s 507 MW PPA with Loviisa is the largest individual agreement signed in the country so far, exceeding the 367 MW contract between Amazon and OX2 for the Rajamäenkylä wind project. The nuclear agreement also runs for 22 years, more than twice as long as several major wind and solar PPAs signed in Finland during 2025 and 2026. According to Rystad, the longer duration reflects the growing priority among data center operators to secure stable and predictable electricity volumes over extended periods. Wind will keep expanding, but batteries will be increasingly important Rystad expects onshore wind to continue leading Finland’s renewable capacity growth through 2035. However, rising wind and solar generation has also contributed to a higher number of negative electricity price hours, while battery storage capacity continues to expand. This could support the emergence of hybrid PPAs combining renewable generation with battery energy storage systems, providing a firmer supply profile better suited to the continuous operating needs of data centers. Rystad expects the next generation of power supply contracts in Finland to follow this approach, combining wind, solar and batteries to deliver a profile closer to baseload supply. Grid access could become a key bottleneck The expected growth will also create new challenges for electricity infrastructure. Finland has proposed replacing its current first-come, first-served grid connection system with a prioritization-based approach. According to Rystad, the new framework could affect both data center developers and battery projects by favoring new local and firm generation and rewarding developers able to pair large loads with dispatchable capacity outside congested areas in southern Finland. The analysis points to a broader transformation of Finland’s power market, in which data centers are not only increasing electricity demand but also influencing which technologies receive financing, how PPAs are structured and what type of capacity the system requires. With digital demand growing rapidly, the combination of renewables, storage, firm generation and grid access could become one of the main factors shaping Finland’s power sector expansion over the next decade.

artigo.texto: CINGAPURA, 8 Out (Reuters) - O principal desafio à expansão da BYD é a geopolítica, afirmou Stella Li, vice-presidente executiva da BYD, nesta quinta-feira, meses depois que o presidente da empresa chinesa declarou que a meta é se tornar a maior montadora do mundo em cinco anos. “Quando fazemos negócios, queremos agir com certeza e visibilidade para que possamos controlar a situação e, assim, investir. Mas, com a geopolítica, nunca se sabe qual é a intenção nem o que eles estão fazendo”, disse Li na Cúpula da Ásia do Milken Institute, em Cingapura. Li disse que a empresa decidiu não vender carros de passeio nos EUA por enquanto, apesar de já estar presente no país há “muito tempo”, pois a situação é “complicada”. “Não temos clareza, visibilidade e estabilidade lá, então decidimos esperar e não entrar no mercado norte-americano de carros de passeio neste momento.” Li disse que a BYD não tem planos de fazer parcerias com outras empresas chinesas, dada sua liderança em diversas áreas, como armazenamento de energia e painéis solares. “Somos líderes em vários setores, não apenas em automóveis”, afirmou ela. Li também disse que tem sido difícil contratar pessoal suficiente na China e que a empresa espera utilizar robôs industriais no futuro. Ela destacou que as ações da BYD na bolsa de Hong Kong estavam “extremamente subvalorizadas” em comparação com as empresas americanas, já que a BYD é uma empresa de engenharia e não apenas uma montadora. Ela também disse que a Nvidia continua sendo um parceiro “muito forte” na área de chips para a BYD. (Reportagem de Xinghui Kok)

artigo.texto: ROX Capital Group Launches ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform Targeting UAE and Oman ROX Capital Group, a UAE-headquartered investor and developer of real assets, has introduced the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform, which will focus on utility-scale and commercial storage schemes across the UAE and Oman while also assessing prospects for regional assembly and manufacturing. The platform intends to assess multiple storage technologies, among them vanadium redox flow, lithium iron phosphate and sodium-ion batteries, plus long-duration options such as CO2 batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage. ROX aims to build alliances with chosen technology suppliers, judging them on their record of delivering large-scale storage projects, long-duration storage know-how where applicable, financial and operational strength, and ownership or control of core technology intellectual property. According to the company, preference will go to suppliers offering bankable systems, proven manufacturing capabilities and the capacity to provide long-term technical support, performance guarantees and warranties. Together with its partners, the platform will chase forthcoming energy storage tenders and evaluate local assembly or manufacturing prospects where commercially feasible. Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group, said the Gulf is developing some of the world's biggest solar projects, and the next hurdle is making sure clean power stays available after sunset and through peak demand periods. He observed that no single technology can satisfy every requirement, and that the platform is designed to pair the appropriate technology with each project's needs while, where feasible, backing the growth of local manufacturing capability. Antony further stated that lithium-ion batteries have reshaped energy storage and will continue to be a key part of the answer. Nevertheless, he noted that the Gulf's climate, load profile and energy-security priorities call for a wider mix of technologies. High summer temperatures can drive up cooling needs, while solar-heavy systems demand storage over longer stretches after dark. In his view, technologies such as vanadium flow batteries, CO2 batteries, gravity-based storage and thermal storage have a significant role to play alongside lithium-ion solutions. - 1. artigo.texto: Alabama regulators to decide how data center power deals protect customers MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WBMA) — As Alabama works to attract massive data centers, state regulators are preparing to answer a question that could eventually matter to every Alabama Power customer: Who pays for the electricity and infrastructure those facilities require? The Alabama Public Service Commission is scheduled Tuesday to consider new procedures for reviewing electric-service contracts between Alabama Power and large data centers. The proceeding does not decide whether a particular data center can be built. Instead, the PSC is establishing how it will review the power contracts for some of the state's largest electricity users — including whether the data center is paying the additional costs created by its demand and whether the agreement benefits other Alabama Power customers. The commission received 19 sets of initial comments and 10 sets of reply comments before developing the procedures scheduled for consideration Tuesday. What qualifies as a large data center? Under a new Alabama law, the process applies to a "large load data center customer" with an expected peak electricity demand of at least 150 megawatts at one or more contiguous parcels and meeting other requirements in state law. That threshold is important because the PSC says its existing process for reviewing special electricity contracts was developed long before today's large-scale data centers. Alabama Power's current Flexible Contract Rate, known as Rate FCR, dates to 1996 and applies to qualifying commercial and industrial customers. Under that process, contracts are deemed approved 10 days after filing unless the PSC disapproves them. The commission acknowledged in July that large data center contracts may require more time to review because they can require significantly more electricity capacity and energy than the types of customers contemplated when the existing system was established. Why should an Alabama Power customer care? At the center of the new law is a consumer protection. Before approving one of these contracts, the PSC must determine that its pricing and terms are expected to recover from the data center the incremental costs of providing its electric service and promote positive benefits for other retail customers. Incremental costs include additional expenses involving electricity generation, transmission and distribution that would not have been incurred without the data center, along with fuel costs and taxes. Put more simply: The regulatory framework is intended to determine whether a large data center pays the additional electric costs associated with serving it instead of shifting those costs to existing customers. State law also directs regulators to consider whether a data center agreement could lower costs for other customers, improve the efficiency of the power system and contribute to economic growth in the community where it is located. The PSC's action Tuesday does not itself change residential electric rates. More time to review contracts The PSC proposed in July replacing the existing process for qualifying data center contracts with a dedicated review system. Under the initial proposal, Alabama Power would have to provide regulators with the complete proposed contract and supporting information showing how the agreement complies with the new law. That would include evidence addressing the data center's incremental costs, effects on other customers' costs, power-system efficiency and economic-development benefits. The Alabama Attorney General would also receive an unredacted copy of the filing and supporting documents. PSC staff and the attorney general could then ask Alabama Power questions and request additional information. The proposed formal review period would increase from 10 days to 60 days. However, the original proposal contains an important provision: If the PSC does not issue an order rejecting the contract within those 60 days, the contract would be automatically deemed approved. No affirmative commission vote or approval order would be required. Whether that provision remains in the final procedures is one issue to watch Tuesday. Alabama Power says reviews already happen before contracts are filed Alabama Power told the commission in July that the existing 10-day approval period does not represent the entire review process. The company said it historically works with PSC staff before formally filing a contract and triggering the approval clock. According to Alabama Power, its most recent pre-filing review lasted nearly 60 days, while each of the two proposed contracts before it underwent review for several months. The company said that during the 30 years Rate FCR has existed, it has consistently waited to formally file a contract until it understood PSC staff had enough information to demonstrate that the proposal satisfied the existing criteria. Alabama Power temporarily agreed this summer to extend the formal review period for qualifying data center contracts from 10 to 45 days while the PSC developed permanent procedures. Those temporary changes lasted until the new state law took effect Oct. 1. How much will customers be allowed to see? Transparency also became an issue during the PSC proceeding. The commission's original proposal called for Alabama Power to file a public version of each proposed contract, with information redacted when necessary, while providing unredacted information to regulators and the attorney general. The PSC specifically asked commenters to address what information should be publicly available and what should remain confidential. Regulators also sought input on whether they should monitor contracts after approval to determine their actual effects on other customers and Alabama Power's system. One Alabama resident and ratepayer, Arie Lucille Kimble-Foster, urged the PSC to protect genuinely sensitive infrastructure information while keeping other information available

artigo.texto: O Serpro prepara uma expansão de sua infraestrutura de data centers que poderá transformar Brasília no principal núcleo de uma rede nacional de processamento da estatal. O primeiro e maior empreendimento está sendo negociado com o Parque Tecnológico de Brasília, o Biotic, onde a empresa pretende instalar um centro de dados de aproximadamente 12 MW, preparado para inteligência artificial, GPUs e refrigeração líquida. A estratégia vai além da capital: prevê novas regiões de processamento em São Paulo e Fortaleza, recuperação de infraestrutura no Rio de Janeiro e, posteriormente, presença no Sul do país. O projeto de Brasília já deixou de ser apenas uma intenção anunciada pela direção da empresa. O Plano de Contratações Anual de 2026 do Serpro inclui formalmente a demanda DOD 2024-00234, denominada “Projetar e implementar o novo Data Center de BSA (IN 07) – projeto e obra”. O valor previsto foi tarjado na versão pública do documento. O mesmo plano contém outra iniciativa relacionada à ampliação da capacidade na capital: DOD 2024-00224, destinada a “viabilizar um segundo site em BSA (Brasília) por meio de um colocation privado”. São, portanto, duas frentes diferentes previstas no planejamento da estatal: a construção de um novo centro de dados e a contratação de capacidade em uma infraestrutura privada. Os valores das duas iniciativas foram ocultados pelo Serpro. O novo data center deverá ser instalado dentro do Biotic, na região da Granja do Torto, em Brasília. Até agora, porém, nem Serpro nem Biotic divulgaram publicamente qual lote ou parcela do parque será destinado ao empreendimento. O Lote 4, que aparece nas agendas oficiais das reuniões entre as duas empresas, é o endereço do Edifício de Governança do Biotic, onde ocorreram os encontros, e não há documento público que permita afirmar que será o terreno do data center. A definição é relevante porque o parque já concentra infraestrutura de processamento e energia e abriga instalações ligadas a instituições financeiras públicas. A escolha da área precisará considerar principalmente a disponibilidade de energia, um dos fatores que passaram a determinar a localização dos grandes projetos de data centers. O local já conta com a presença do Data center do Banco do Brasil e da Caixa Econômica Federal, há uma projeção para um data center do BRB (Banco do Brasília). Portanto, falta uma manifestação mkais clara de onde será instalado o novo centro de dados do Serpro. 12 megawatts Em entrevista ao Capital Digital, o presidente do Serpro, Wilton Mota, afirmou que a proposta do Biotic está sendo validada e que a intenção é concluir a negociação ainda em 2026. Segundo ele, o novo centro terá capacidade projetada de aproximadamente 12 MW, muito superior à capacidade atualmente disponível para a estatal em Brasília. Cerca de 3 MW deverão utilizar refrigeração líquida, tecnologia necessária para equipamentos de alta densidade energética, especialmente servidores equipados com GPUs utilizados em inteligência artificial. A infraestrutura deverá ser modular. Isso permitirá que novos módulos sejam acrescentados à medida que a demanda aumentar, evitando que toda a capacidade prevista tenha de ser construída e equipada de uma só vez. O próprio mercado internacional de data centers já começou a registrar o empreendimento como uma instalação planejada de 12 MW dentro do Biotic. Essas bases privadas, entretanto, não identificam o endereço exato dentro do parque, o que reforça que essa informação ainda não está publicamente definida. O dado oficial disponível até agora é a decisão empresarial de implantar o novo centro em Brasília e a negociação com o Biotic. Negociação antiga As conversas são anteriores à atual fase do projeto. Em agosto de 2025, o então presidente do Serpro, Alexandre Amorim, recebeu o presidente do Biotic, Gustavo Dias Henrique, na sede da estatal, em Brasília. A pauta oficial foi registrada apenas como “assuntos institucionais”. A relação entre as duas empresas, na realidade, é ainda mais antiga. O processo SEI 04005-00001054/2018-77 registra a cooperação institucional iniciada entre Biotic e Serpro. O processo original não trata especificamente da construção do novo data center, mas a documentação posterior do próprio Biotic mostra que a relação evoluiu. No Relatório da Administração de 2025, o Biotic registra entre suas ações a parceria com o Serpro para instalação física e evolução de infraestrutura e informa que, “no mesmo eixo”, estavam sendo realizadas tratativas técnicas para implantação de um data center no parque. O documento é particularmente importante porque revela que já haviam sido reunidas informações preliminares e diretrizes de negócio destinadas às avaliações técnica e institucional. O Biotic, entretanto, decidiu preservar as informações consideradas comerciais e estratégicas. Ou seja, os estudos existem, mas ainda não estão disponíveis integralmente ao público. Em 2026, as negociações avançaram. Em 5 de agosto, Wilton Mota e o diretor de Infraestrutura do Serpro, Wallyson Lemos dos Reis Oliveira, reuniram-se com Gustavo Dias no Parque Tecnológico. A audiência ocorreu no Lote 4, Bloco B, onde funciona o Edifício de Governança do Biotic. Em 17 de setembro, Wilton voltou ao parque para nova reunião com Gustavo Dias. Novamente, a pauta divulgada foi apenas “assuntos institucionais”. A sequência de encontros coincide com o período em que, segundo Wilton, a proposta para implantação do novo centro entrou em fase de validação. Conta bilionária O tamanho financeiro do empreendimento ainda não está definitivamente estabelecido. Durante a entrevista ao Capital Digital, Wilton inicialmente mencionou aproximadamente R$ 3 bilhões envolvendo investimento e operação. Depois, ao conferir os números, estimou a construção em aproximadamente R$ 1 bilhão e diferenciou esse investimento inicial dos custos de funcionamento, financiamento e atualização tecnológica ao longo dos anos. artigo.texto: Godawari Power Gets Green Light For 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System In Maharashtra Godawari Power's subsidiary, Godawari New Energy, has received key environmental clearance from Maharashtra's SEAC-3 for a 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System building in AURIC. This critical milestone follows a cumulative capex of ₹501 crore already deployed into the BESS segment as of June 2026 and the recent incorporation of a dedicated clean energy EPC subsidiary. Market snapshot: Godawari Power & Ispat Limited's wholly owned subsidiary, Godawari New Energy Private Limited, has received fresh environmental clearance to construct an industrial building for its upcoming 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System. The greenfield facility is being developed at the AURIC Bidkin Industrial Area in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra, signaling major progress in the company's strategic pivot toward clean energy technology. Data Snapshot - Incurred ₹501 crore in capital expenditure for the BESS project as of June 30, 2026. - Subscribed to ₹150 crore in equity shares on a rights basis on July 3, 2026, taking total investment in subsidiary Godawari New Energy to ₹600 crore. - Reported Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue of ₹1,750.47 crore and a consolidated net profit of ₹222.37 crore. - Offered a 31.45-acre industrial plot at AURIC Bidkin Industrial Area for setting up its downstream Cold Rolling Mill project on September 24, 2026. What's Changed - GPIL's transition from cyclical steel manufacturing to a structural green energy platform is accelerating. The environmental clearance for Godawari New Energy's industrial building in AURIC clears the regulatory path for physical construction of the 20 GWh BESS facility. Parallelly, GPIL incorporated Godawari Energy Solutions on October 1, 2026, establishing a dedicated, in-house EPC and O&M vehicle to manage turnkey execution and capture integrated project margins. Key Takeaways - Environmental Clearance Secured: Godawari New Energy received environmental clearance from Maharashtra's SEAC-3, enabling structural construction of the 20 GWh battery storage facility in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar. - Robust Financial Backing: GPIL has already deployed ₹501 crore in BESS capex as of June 30, 2026, and scaled its equity investment in the subsidiary to ₹600 crore to fund project development. - Synergistic Land Infrastructure: Alongside the BESS facility, GPIL's downstream CRM project has secured a 31.45-acre land allotment at the same AURIC master-planned smart city, consolidating downstream manufacturing operations in Maharashtra. - EPC Ecosystem Integration: The newly incorporated Godawari Energy Solutions arm expands GPIL's capabilities to manage utility-scale clean energy installation and operations internally. SAHI Perspective GPIL's transition strategy is structured to build a highly captive energy storage value chain. By utilizing Godawari New Energy for battery integration and Godawari Energy Solutions for in-house EPC, the group is mitigating execution leakages. Securing environmental clearance for the 20 GWh BESS building is a crucial de-risking milestone that ensures civil works can proceed on schedule for a planned Q1 FY28 commercial launch. Furthermore, opting for AURIC—a master-planned smart city with ready plug-and-play utilities—bypasses the historical infrastructure and water allotment delays that have slowed the company's steel expansions in Chhattisgarh. Market Implications The clearance provides immediate medium-term visibility on GPIL's growth pipeline, which is key as traditional steel divisions remain subject to commodity price cycles. Investors are likely to react favorably to this tangible execution milestone, which validates the feasibility of GPIL's long-term clean energy initiatives. However, core profitability will remain driven by iron ore pellet realizations in the immediate quarters, with the BESS segment requiring further working capital deployment before generating meaningful margins in FY28. Trading Signals Market Bias: Bullish The regulatory clearance for the 20 GWh BESS building substantially de-risks GPIL's clean energy capex pipeline. With ₹501 crore already spent as of Q1 FY27 and the project on track for Q1 FY28 commissioning, GPIL is positioned as a rare first-mover in utility-scale industrial storage. Overweight: Clean Energy, Power Infrastructure, Industrial Engineering Trigger Factors: - Commencement of physical civil construction at the AURIC BESS site. - Operational setup and bagging of first EPC projects by Godawari Energy Solutions. - Formal registration and execution of land deeds for the 31.45-acre CRM plot at AURIC. Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months) Industry Context India's clean energy landscape is experiencing massive grid-scale storage mandates to balance renewable power supply. State and central agencies are aggressively bidding out gigawatt-hour battery storage contracts. GPIL's 20 GWh manufacturing facility—utilizing large-format Grade-1 LFP cells secured via supply deals with EVE Power—positions it strategically to capture early-stage tenders. The integration of its own CRM steel output into structural battery container manufacturing represents a compelling vertical integration play. Key Risks to Watch - Supply Chain Volatility: Dependance on imported lithium-ion cells from global partners exposes the project to geopolitical trade barriers and component pricing shifts. - Execution Timelines: Achieving the target Q1 FY28 commercial launch depends on smooth civil works execution and tech transfers without further regulatory bottlenecks. - Capex Pressure: While backed by solid cash generation (net profit of ₹222.37 crore in Q1 FY27), the overall transition is highly capital-intensive and could strain balance sheet liquidity if steel margins deteriorate. artigo.texto: Drones hit a major data center in Russia’s Ryazan region owned by the country’s leading Artificial Intelligence and technology company Yandex, the company said on Thursday. It added that the attack caused a fire and forced the company to fully suspend the center’s operations. The company said it was dealing with the consequences and restoring affected services. The company said that its core consumer services were not affected. Yandex runs YandexGPT, one of Russia’s leading generative AI models. The attack on the Yandex data center followed a wave of Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in recent weeks. Previously there were no confirmed major Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian data centers. On the website of its Yandex Cloud service, the company said there were problems with the electricity supply at one data center “zone”, and recommended customers use other zones.

artigo.texto: Resumo - LG firmou contrato plurianual de 'chillers' para data centers de IA nos EUA - Empresa fecha acordo com a AIR Control Concepts, da Virgínia - Projetos somam mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade; valor não foi revelado - Ação da LG Electronics subiu até 8,8% no pregão em Seul - Nova fábrica na Virgínia deve começar a produzir no 1º semestre de 2027 - Encomendas anuais podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até fim de 2026 Fornecer soluções de refrigeração para data centers voltados à inteligência artificial é o objetivo de um contrato de longo prazo que a unidade norte-americana da LG Electronics selou, conforme a empresa divulgou nesta terça-feira (6). Do outro lado do negócio está a AIR Control Concepts, operadora de data centers com sede na Virgínia, cujos projetos somam capacidade superior a 5 gigawatts. Diante do anúncio, as ações da fabricante avançaram até 8,8% na bolsa de Seul. As partes não revelaram o valor do contrato. A fabricante sul-coreana afirma, no entanto, que esse entendimento de vários anos impulsiona sua expansão no mercado mundial de refrigeração destinado à infraestrutura de IA. O salto das ações em Seul quase representou o maior movimento registrado em um único dia nos últimos dois meses. Apelidados de ‘chillers’, tais sistemas de refrigeração industrial se tornaram alvo de expansão acelerada na LG. Por trás disso está a multiplicação de data centers pelo planeta, cuja disseminação fez disparar a demanda por formas eficazes de controle térmico, necessárias para manter funcionando as cargas de inteligência artificial. Expansão para além dos Estados Unidos Além dos acordos fechados recentemente em território norte-americano, a companhia afirma que tem avançado também em iniciativas relevantes na Indonésia e no Oriente Médio. Ainda neste mês, a companhia havia anunciado a intenção de expandir a fabricação de ‘chillers’ nos Estados Unidos e também na Coreia do Sul. O plano prevê erguer uma unidade na Virgínia, voltada a atender a demanda dos data centers americanos, cuja produção deve começar no primeiro semestre de 2027. Na Coreia, por sua vez, a LG quer ampliar a capacidade das fábricas de Changwon e Pyeongtaek, que já estão em operação. Meta de receita antecipada As projeções da companhia são ambiciosas. Tendo garantido US$ 426 milhões já no primeiro semestre, a LG estima que, até o encerramento de 2026, os pedidos anuais de resfriamento voltados a data centers cheguem à casa dos vários bilhões de dólares. Segundo a empresa, a meta de 2027, US$ 680 milhões em receita com ‘chillers’, deve ser alcançada antes do previsto.

artigo.texto: Polônia lança programa de subsídios de 1 bilhão de zlotys para armazenamento residencial de energia e calor O Ministério do Clima e Meio Ambiente da Polônia apresentou uma nova iniciativa de subsídios que abrange sistemas residenciais de armazenamento de energia elétrica e térmica. A iniciativa é voltada para pessoas que já possuem uma microinstalação de energia renovável conectada à rede. O financiamento se aplicará a unidades de armazenamento de energia elétrica com capacidade nominal de pelo menos 10 kWh e a unidades de armazenamento térmico com capacidade de pelo menos 100 litros. As despesas de compra e instalação de unidades residenciais de armazenamento estão dentro do escopo do programa. Prosumidores no regime de net billing que comprarem sistemas de armazenamento de energia elétrica poderão obter até 16 mil zlotys, ou US$ 4.127,57, enquanto os que estão no regime de net metering têm direito a no máximo 8 mil zlotys. Para sistemas de armazenamento térmico, os candidatos podem receber até 1.000 zlotys, além de um bônus extra que chega a 2.000 zlotys para dispositivos produzidos na UE. O teto total de apoio é de 19 mil zlotys por ponto de energia. Um total de 1 bilhão de zlotys está sendo fornecido pelo governo polonês por meio do Fundo de Modernização. As inscrições serão aceitas a partir de 20 de outubro, e o programa deve continuar até o início de outubro de 2027, ou até que o dinheiro acabe. Paulina Hennig-Kloska, ministra do Clima e Meio Ambiente da Polônia, descreveu a instalação de armazenamento de energia em instalações solares residenciais como uma prioridade de seu ministério. Segundo ela, o programa tem dois objetivos principais: aumentar a eficiência do uso de energias renováveis e reforçar a segurança energética. Análises do ministério observam que a ajuda anterior para a compra de instalações de armazenamento contribuiu para um aumento no número de armazenamentos residenciais de energia na Polônia, de 10.000 em 2024 para cerca de 150.000 até junho deste ano. O ministério agora busca a meta de ultrapassar 200.000 instalações residenciais de armazenamento na Polônia até o fim do próximo ano. O vice-ministro do Clima e Meio Ambiente, Slawomir Cwik, observou que as instalações elegíveis devem incluir um sistema de gestão de energia e ter capacidade de ilhamento. Segundo ele, isso permite que as residências mantenham o fornecimento de energia mesmo quando a rede cai. Dados do ministério indicam que uma rodada inicial de apoio financiada pelo Programa Nacional de Energia da Polônia destinou cerca de 112 milhões de zlotys à instalação de mais de 5.000 sistemas residenciais de armazenamento. Separadamente, a Agência de Reestruturação e Modernização da Agricultura da Polônia lançou um programa de subsídios para energias renováveis voltado a agricultores, com inscrições abertas em 5 de outubro. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado de sistemas de armazenamento de energia residencial na Polônia, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. Cobertura do Produto Este relatório abrange o mercado global de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia Residencial (HESS), incluindo unidades integradas baseadas em baterias projetadas para uso residencial, a fim de armazenar eletricidade da rede ou de fontes renováveis, como a solar fotovoltaica em telhados. O escopo engloba sistemas completos, subsistemas-chave e componentes de equilíbrio de planta utilizados em aplicações residenciais de armazenamento de energia. Incluídos - Sistemas completos de armazenamento residencial por bateria (ex.: íon-lítio, chumbo-ácido, baterias de fluxo) - Componentes do sistema: conjuntos de baterias, sistemas de gerenciamento de bateria (BMS), inversores/carregadores - artigo.texto: Florida is making a big bet on artificial intelligence. Tech companies want to build enormous data centers here, and our electric utilities are getting ready to build the power plants and power lines to run them. The question for every family in Central Florida is simple: if the bet goes wrong, who pays? Start with what happens if it goes right. A data center brings construction jobs, some permanent ones, and a large new taxpayer. When a big customer pays its full share, the cost of running the grid is spread across more users, and that can help hold down everyone’s rates. That is a real benefit, and it is why so many communities want these projects. Now set aside the environmental questions, which are serious in their own right, and ask the money question. What happens if the data center leaves? Data centers run on contracts, and contracts end. Companies merge, move, or find cheaper power somewhere else. But the power plant built for that customer doesn’t leave with it. Utilities pay for new plants over decades and recover the cost through our monthly bills. If the customer that new power generation was built for walks away, the remaining cost doesn’t disappear. Unless the contract says otherwise, the cost of the new plant lands on the rest of us. That is not a guess about the far future. One Florida utility’s own filing for these rules shows about $1 billion of new power plants still being paid off in 2047. For context, a child starting kindergarten this fall will be 26 that year. If the customer those plants were built for has left by then, that child could be helping pay for them on their own utility bill. The Legislature saw this coming. A new state law says these giant customers have to pay their own way, and that the risk of one failing to pay can’t be pushed onto everyone else. On Oct. 1, the state’s investor-owned utilities had to file their rules for meeting that promise. I read them. The fairest test of those rules is whether a departing customer has to pay for what was built for it. That’s an exit fee. The new law lets state regulators approve one. It doesn’t require one. Tampa Electric included a strong exit fee for any customer that leaves during its 20-year contract. After 20 years, though, a customer can give notice and walk away owing nothing more, while plants built for it are still being paid off. Florida Power and Light has an exit fee too, but it covers only part of the cost, and FPL’s rules don’t reach every customer the law covers. Duke Energy Florida, which serves much of Central Florida, is still waiting on regulators to rule on its proposal. None of these companies is ignoring the law. Each filed something, and some of what they filed is good. But the question isn’t whether the rules exist. It’s whether they protect you if things go wrong. And if your power comes from the Orlando Utilities Commission, there’s something else you should know. The new law doesn’t cover city-owned utilities at all. Any protection for OUC customers comes from OUC’s own contracts and board, not from this law. Here’s what you can do. The Florida Public Service Commission takes public comments on its website, and it is reviewing Duke’s proposal now. Tell the commissioners you want every data center contract to include an exit fee that covers everything built for it. If you’re an OUC customer, ask OUC’s board the same question. The promise has already been made: other customers won’t carry the risk. Whether it’s kept depends on what goes into these contracts now, while the people paying attention still have a say. Mark McNees is director of the masters degree program in Social and Sustainable Enterprises at Florida State University’s Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship.

artigo.texto: How Data Center Power Went from Utility to Strategy Not so long ago, a data center's power strategy was relatively straightforward. Secure a high-capacity utility grid connection, install uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, and deploy backup generators to handle rare grid outages. Today, the global demand for computational infrastructure, driven by AI workloads, hyperscale cloud facilities, and digital connectivity, has pushed traditional power paradigms to their limits. Grid constraints and long interconnection timelines that can stretch far beyond the schedules on which AI infrastructure is being developed are forcing data center operators to look for more control over long-term energy needs. What we're seeing at Rehlko is that backup generation is increasingly considered part of a broader onsite power strategy. As grid bottlenecks persist and AI-driven load dynamics challenge conventional electrical designs, emergency generators can no longer be treated as isolated safety nets. By embedding backup assets into a broader onsite power framework, operators are taking control of their development timelines, ensuring continuous resilience, and future-proofing their digital infrastructure. Conversations once focused on what happens if the grid goes down are now turning into much deeper discussions about ensuring the facility has enough reliable power in the first place, and that there's a capability to control that power as requirements change. Because the availability of grid power affects site selection, construction schedules, phasing and capital investment, data center developers need to understand their potential power architecture much earlier: what the grid can provide; when it can provide it; what onsite generation might contribute; how much storage is appropriate; and how the system could evolve as the facility expands. Ability to Evolve With Modular Development Generators remain critical for backup, but they also become a piece in an onsite power jigsaw that is all about resilience. Operators are starting to look more closely at how generation, battery storage, and grid power can work together. The emerging model is one in which onsite generation can help bridge the gap between when a data center needs power and when the grid can provide it. Instead of waiting years for a connection or network upgrade, capacity can be brought online through onsite generation with a system that evolves as the grid becomes available. This is particularly important for large AI facilities, where power requirements can increase in phases rather than arriving all at once. A modular onsite system can therefore provide an additional route to capacity, allowing a facility to grow while the grid connection catches up. Clarke Energy, a Rehlko company and part of our end-to-end energy ecosystem, recognizes this paradigm shift. It describes how a future-ready data center runs a combination of gas engines, diesel generators, battery energy storage system (BESS), and onsite renewables with microgrid controls, designed to scale as demand grows and energy priorities evolve. Single-System Control of Multiple Resources The emerging architecture is not necessarily about replacing the grid – which will remain fundamental to most data centers – it's about creating layers of resilience and flexibility around it. Fast-responding diesel or continuous gas-fueled engines deliver bulk energy during utility outages or bridge grid constraints. Advanced batteries and grid-forming inverters smooth out sudden spikes in power demand, keep voltage steady, and respond instantly to frequency changes. Renewable generation provides the option of lower-carbon electricity when available. Intelligent controls sit on top, coordinating the different resources to make them operate as a single system. For an AI data center, this kind of flexibility is particularly important. GPU-driven workloads can create demanding and rapidly changing electrical loads. Batteries can respond almost instantaneously to short-duration changes, while engines can provide longer-duration support. Meanwhile, the grid remains part of the equation rather than being treated as an all-or-nothing proposition. Such a strategy also addresses one of the biggest challenges around the environmental impact of modern data centers, how to square-off the demand for more energy with sustainability goals. Pathway Towards Lower-Carbon Operation A carefully executed energy strategy should also aim to put the data center on a path towards lower-carbon operation. Hybrid energy systems combining generation and battery storage with fuel flexibility – including hydrogen-ready engines and renewable fuels – can help facilitate a longer-term transition. This is a shift towards designing energy infrastructure that meets the here-and-now demand for power-hungry capacity and resilience, while retaining the flexibility to support a lower-carbon energy system in the future. The sometimes-ad hoc investment in individual assets, whether they are generators or batteries, is giving way to integrated systems where the different assets are coordinated through a layer of advanced controls. Rather than view backup power in isolation as a passive safeguard, for example, make it part of a broader power strategy designed around resilience, speed to power, scalability and future energy requirements. The future of resilient data-center power is unlikely to be defined by a single technology. It will be defined by how effectively grid power, generation, storage, controls and future energy technologies are brought together into a system that can respond to what the facility needs today and adapt to what it will need tomorrow. artigo.texto: Rox wagers on the Gulf’s storage gap Rox Capital Group, a Dubai-based asset manager focused on sustainability, is in talks with potential partners for a new energy-storage platform targeting utility-scale and commercial projects in the UAE and Oman, founder Robin Antony tells EnterpriseAM UAE. Rox’s plans will focus on storage technologies ranging from lithium-ion, flow, and sodium-ion batteries to longer-duration options such as thermal, gravity, and compressed-air storage, according to a press release. The plan includes jointly submitting bids for upcoming storage tenders. Depending on the project, Rox could invest directly, co-develop with partners, or broker contracts between technology providers, investors, and project owners, Antony said. The pitch is that Gulf projects need a mix of technologies: Summer heat raises cooling needs for batteries, and solar-heavy grids need storage that lasts longer after dark, Antony argues. Demand is building: Masdar and EWEC are developing a USD 6.1 bn Abu Dhabi plant that pairs 5.2 GW of solar with 19 GWh of storage, and Masdar’s Ibri III project is Oman’s first solar-plus-storage plant. Still no specifics: Rox hasn’t named partners, projects, or target tenders, and Antony declined to give a capital target or timeline. Following up on A:5 (xNF>AF) A UAE delegation was in Washington last week pushing for deeper tech ties, including follow-through on the US decision to ease export controls on the UAE. The trip was led by Omran Sharaf, assistant minister for advanced science and technology at the Foreign Affairs Ministry, according to a ministry statement. The delegation met White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios and Under Secretary of State for Economic Growth Jacob Helberg. Talks covered AI, cybersecurity, space, quantum computing, and post-quantum encryption. With the Commerce Department, the agenda covered trade facilitation and export management. BACKGROUND- Washington moved the UAE into Country Group A:5, its allies-only export tier, in July. That lets G42 and other approved firms buy advanced chips without a license, as we’ve reported. But G42’s access lapses in April 2027 unless it’s extended, and G42 is reportedly in exploratory talks about selling a majority stake to US firms to secure access beyond that date. The two countries are working together on a 5 GW UAE-US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, anchored by the 1 GW Stargate UAE cluster.

artigo.texto: Grid-forming capabilities support multiple grid-restoration functions The project plays an important role in supporting voltage and frequency stability at a key point in Cambodia's central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. Its grid-forming capabilities were put through a series of demanding system-restoration scenarios, demonstrating how energy storage can take on a more active role in supporting the power system. Key highlights include: - Large-scale black start from zero voltage: 516 grid-forming PCS units successfully energized the entire plant from zero voltage, establishing stable voltage and frequency across the system. - Restoration of a 240 km transmission network: The system supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations, while maintaining stable operation as the network was progressively restored. - Support for multiple generation sources: The system supported the start-up and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant, before the restored network was operated together with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, energy storage and loads. - Stable operation under challenging grid conditions: During restoration, the system remained stable through five transformer energization events, including a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stability when synchronizing different power sources under a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees, demonstrating its ability to handle challenging conditions during system recovery. - Extended islanded operation: The system operated independently for 3.5 hours, demonstrating that the energy storage system could continue supporting the local network even when separated from the main grid. - Seamless transitions: The project completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, with voltage deviation kept below 2% and transient frequency fluctuation within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. "This project demonstrates that the value of grid-forming energy storage goes far beyond storing electricity.When a power system faces disturbances or loses normal grid support, grid-forming technology can help establish and maintain stable voltage and frequency, support system restoration and keep the grid operating reliably," said Michael Ruan, Regional Director of Sungrow Southeast Asia and South Asia. "Through projects like this, Sungrow is helping turn energy storage into a more active grid-support asset and bringing proven grid-forming capabilities to the evolving power systems of Southeast Asia." Reducing Technical Risk and Ensuring Timely Delivery Faced with strict test protocols, complex power system scenarios, a compressed construction schedule and rainy‑season working conditions with ambient temperature up to 40°C, Sungrow's cross‑functional team covering pre-sales, on‑site delivery and R&D collaborated closely to deliver high‑quality project outcomes: - 20-day commissioning and testing: The on‑site team worked relentlessly under hot and humid conditions for two consecutive months. The team wrapped up hot commissioning plus three rounds of performance tests within 20 days to guarantee timely grid‑connection. - End‑to‑End Service Solution: Sungrow provides full‑lifecycle and one‑stop services spanning integrated design of storage and monitoring systems, EPC‑related support, equipment design, commissioning and O&M services, enabling the customer to fulfill customized grid‑level requirements with reduced management overhead. As Southeast Asia advances its energy transition, Sungrow will continue to bring proven energy storage technologies and solutions to the region, helping customers build more reliable and sustainable power infrastructure. Contact: Luly Wang, luly.wang@sungrow-hq.com Source: Sungrow Power

artigo.texto: LG Electronics fecha contrato nos EUA para resfriamento de data centers de IA As ações da LG Electronics avançaram depois que a companhia fechou um novo contrato plurianual para fornecer sistemas de resfriamento a data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos. A gigante sul-coreana de eletrônicos de consumo vem expandindo rapidamente o negócio de equipamentos de refrigeração industrial, conhecidos como “chillers”, impulsionada pelo boom global de data centers, que aumenta a demanda por soluções eficientes de gestão térmica para infraestrutura de IA. A LG informou nesta terça-feira (6) que sua subsidiária nos EUA firmou um acordo de longo prazo com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia, para fornecer “chillers” a data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. A empresa não revelou o valor do contrato, mas afirmou que o acordo acelera a expansão da LG no mercado global de resfriamento para data centers de IA. Em Seul, as ações da LG Electronics chegaram a subir 8,8% no início do pregão, caminhando para a maior alta diária em cerca de dois meses. A LG disse que, apoiada por vitórias recentes na América do Norte, também está ampliando presença em projetos relevantes de data centers no Oriente Médio e na Indonésia. No início deste mês, a empresa anunciou que vai aumentar a produção de “chillers” tanto nos EUA quanto na Coreia do Sul. A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia para atender à demanda crescente de data centers americanos, com início de produção previsto para o primeiro semestre de 2027. Paralelamente, pretende elevar a produção em unidades já existentes em Changwon e Pyeongtaek, na Coreia. Segundo a LG, as novas encomendas anuais de soluções de resfriamento para data centers podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após a companhia garantir US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A empresa também afirmou esperar atingir antes do prazo a meta de 2027 de US$ 680 milhões em receita no negócio de “chillers”.

artigo.texto: Amprius Technologies Pioneer in silicon nanowire anode technology According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Lithium Silicon Battery market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global lithium silicon battery market is positioned for significant expansion through 2035, driven by escalating demand for higher energy density in electric vehicles and premium stationary storage applications. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries with graphite anodes, lithium silicon batteries incorporate silicon into the anode, enabling substantially greater energy capacity per unit of weight and volume. This technological advantage is critical for automotive OEMs seeking to extend driving range without increasing battery pack size, and for commercial and industrial storage operators where physical space is at a premium. However, market growth is tempered by challenges including silicon's volumetric expansion during cycling, which necessitates specialized binders, electrolytes, and mechanical designs, creating a high barrier to system integration. The supply chain for high-purity engineered silicon anode materials remains nascent, and qualification cycles for automotive and aerospace applications are lengthy. Despite these hurdles, ongoing material innovations and manufacturing scale-up are expected to reduce costs and improve cycle life, unlocking broader adoption. The market is forecast to grow at a robust CAGR from 2026 to 2035, with Asia-Pacific leading in production and demand, followed by North America and Europe. As automotive manufacturers strive to meet stricter emissions regulations and consumer expectations for longer range, silicon anode technology offers a viable path to higher energy density without compromising safety. The market will likely experience a gradual decline in costs as production scales and material innovations improve cycle life and safety. The electric vehicle sector represents the largest and most dynamic end-use market for lithium silicon batteries. artigo.texto: GlobalFoundries brings massive solar array, battery storage online in Essex Junction ESSEX JUNCTION, Vt. (WCAX) - A massive new solar array and battery storage system are now online at GlobalFoundries’ Essex Junction campus to offset demand on the power grid and lower electric bills. With the flip of the ceremonial breakers, GlobalFoundries’ new on-site solar array and 16-megawatt battery energy storage system are now online, marking a milestone for the Green Mountain State. “It’s the largest battery ever installed in Vermont, right here behind our own meter,” said GlobalFoundries’ Dan Colello. The battery goes hand in hand with the solar array, which sits on more than 30 acres of already developed but underutilized land that includes an old parking lot and brownfield. The energy from the panels is then stored in the four-hour, or 16-megawatt-hour, battery energy storage system. Related Story: “The battery is positioned to be able to reduce peak. Over that four hours of duration, it will discharge to reduce the consumption by the facility in its footprint on the regional grid,” said Rory Jones, co-founder of Lightshift Energy. Gov. Phil Scott joined in on the celebration Monday, commending the project on saving Vermonters money. “In fact, it should reduce costs by more than $40 million over the next 25 years. That’s real money. The savings is important to GlobalFoundries, and the Vermonters that work here. It’s also important for all of us as ratepayers,” Scott said. The project, part of GlobalFoundries’ net-zero goals, won’t disrupt the company’s energy needs for manufacturing. “The project demonstrates how battery storage can be integrated into advanced manufacturing, while maintaining the quality our operations require. And it provides a valuable lesson about future projects across the whole of GlobalFoundries,” said GlobalFoundries’ CEO Tim Breen. Copyright 2026 WCAX. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Data centers, Flock cameras discussed in city council meeting adopting 2027 budget EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - City council members approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center development Monday night, pausing all related construction while officials study its potential impact on the city. City leaders say the pause gives them time to research effects on infrastructure, utilities and neighborhoods, and to finalize zoning rules before any new projects move forward. The moratorium can be extended if officials need more time. Council President, Ben Trockman said the decision followed sustained public pressure. “We had multiple conversations — I’ve heard in council quite frequently, and I think something that we see in our inboxes quite often as well, is that there is concern,” Trockman said. $152 Million Budget Approved for 2027 Council also adopted the city’s 2027 budget, totaling more than $152 million. Major allocations include: - ~$6 million for restoring 27 miles of city roads - ~$20 million for parks and recreation - ~$30 million for water and sewer projects - $182,000 for Flock Safety cameras — a line item that drew criticism from residents Flock Camera Funding Sparks Privacy Concerns Some residents like Philip Elpers say the automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras amount to an invasion of privacy and argue they were installed without public input. “There has to be a commitment in the budget that actually stops all of this in the future until we say it’s okay,” Elpers said. Police Chief Defends Flock Camera Use Evansville Police Chief Philip Smith addressed the concerns directly at Monday’s meeting, saying the department has strict procedures in place to prevent misuse. He pointed to the cameras’ role in solving crimes, including a 2022 child kidnapping case. Smith said the technology has not been found unconstitutional and defended the department’s track record. “Not one time, in not one courtroom in the United States has ALPR been ruled as a violation of the 4th Amendment,” Smith said. “We’ve had Flock here since 2021, and we’ve not had one officer violate the policy or procedure of Flock usage in Evansville, Indiana.” Officials say even though the budget was adopted, they can still bring up flock cameras in future meetings if needed. artigo.texto: Economia Digital Exponential Summit: Rodrigo Abreu detalha retorno do Pátria aos data centers Por Fernando Benevides - Em 07/10/2026 às 7:20 AM CEO da Omnia associou a retomada do grupo à expansão da inteligência artificial. No painel sobre a nova economia digital, projeto no Pecém para a ByteDance deu dimensão à aposta. A venda da Odata, anunciada pelo Pátria em dezembro de 2022, marcou a saída do grupo daquele ciclo de investimentos em data centers. No Exponential Summit, em 6 de outubro, Rodrigo Abreu explicou que a expansão da inteligência artificial generativa mudou a equação do setor e levou o Pátria a voltar ao segmento com a Omnia Data Centers. Abreu participou do painel “Data Centers: o Brasil no centro da nova economia digital”, ao lado de Lucas Vanzin, da Eveo; Sergio Abela, da Ascenty; e Renan Lima Alves, da ABDC e da Boost. À frente da Omnia e como operating partner do Pátria, ele apresentou a infraestrutura digital como uma nova frente de investimento impulsionada pela demanda por capacidade computacional para inteligência artificial e serviços em nuvem. Ao distinguir data centers de inferência, que atendem às solicitações dos usuários, daqueles voltados ao treinamento de modelos de IA, Abreu resumiu a disputa por projetos de grande porte: “Os de treinamento, a gente está brigando para trazer para cá”. Ele apontou a disponibilidade de energia como uma vantagem competitiva do Brasil. A trajetória do executivo passa por empresas de tecnologia e telecomunicações. Antes de assumir a Omnia, Abreu foi CEO da Oi entre 2020 e janeiro de 2024 e ocupou posições de liderança na TIM e na Cisco. A experiência em telecomunicações conecta sua atuação atual à expansão de redes e infraestrutura que sustenta serviços digitais. O projeto que materializa a estratégia no Ceará é o Data Center Pecém, desenvolvido pela Omnia em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos para atender à ByteDance, controladora do TikTok. A primeira etapa começou a ser construída em janeiro de 2026. O plano divulgado pelo governo estadual prevê investimento superior a R$ 200 bilhões ao longo de quatro fases até 2033; a fase inicial foi estimada em R$ 55 bilhões. A unidade foi anunciada com 200 megawatts de capacidade de tecnologia da informação, enquanto a demanda elétrica projetada pode chegar a 300 megawatts. A previsão divulgada para o início da operação é 2027. Em janeiro de 2026, a Omnia assumiu o controle integral da CDV DC I, empresa responsável por parte da infraestrutura do empreendimento na ZPE do Pecém. A Casa dos Ventos permaneceu ligada ao projeto como parceira energética. Em maio, as empresas anunciaram um contrato de autoprodução de cerca de US$ 2 bilhões, com fornecimento de até 300 megawatts médios de energia renovável a partir de projetos eólicos no Ceará e no Piauí. A Casa dos Ventos desenvolverá e operará esses ativos, e a Omnia também terá participação neles. O cronograma também está sob questionamento judicial. Em setembro, o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União ajuizaram ação para que o empreendimento não entre em operação antes da consulta ao povo Anacé e da elaboração de estudo de impacto ambiental e relatório de impacto ambiental (EIA/Rima). A ação também pede medidas de monitoramento ambiental e energético. O pedido se refere ao início da operação; não determina a paralisação das obras em curso. À reportagem, Rafael Sá, presidente da ZPE Ceará, afirmou que foi feito um acordo com os Anacé. Ele não detalhou os termos do entendimento nem explicou como ele se relaciona com as medidas solicitadas na ação. A Omnia, por sua vez, declarou em manifestação pública que o licenciamento ambiental segue o rito conduzido pela Superintendência Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Semace). A atuação do Pátria no Ceará também alcança o mercado de crédito. Em janeiro de 2026, a gestora concluiu a aquisição de 51% da Solis Investimentos .

artigo.texto: Beaufort County commissioners holding public hearing & vote on data center moratorium The above video is our WITN+ livestream and may not reflect the content in this story. BEAUFORT COUNTY, N.C. (WITN) - Tonight, Beaufort County commissioners will hear public input and vote on a moratorium for data center developments. The public hearing on the one-year moratorium was originally scheduled for last month but was postponed so the community could have an additional opportunity to share input. Commissioners will then vote on the proposal following the hearing. The moratorium would pause building or expanding large computer facilities used to power artificial intelligence. The commissioners offered an informal hearing during last month’s meeting, where several residents spoke in favor of the moratorium. Residents voiced concerns about noise pollution, emissions and electricity costs from potential data centers. Several residents said they support a moratorium lasting longer than one year. The commissioners’ meeting will start at 5:30 p.m. at 136 W. Second Street in Washington. County commissioners say a public hearing sign-up sheet will be placed on the podium before tonight’s meeting. Copyright 2026 WITN. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Mercado Voluntário de Carbono alarga metodologias para projetos florestais O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passou a contar com duas novas metodologias para projetos de Reflorestação e de Gestão Florestal Melhorada, juntando-se à já existente para Novas Florestações. A informação consta de um comunicado do Ministério do Ambiente e Energia (MAEN), que considera este alargamento uma forma de aumentar as possibilidades de investimento privado em projetos de sequestro de carbono em Portugal. Com estas alterações, ficam disponíveis três metodologias de carbono destinadas a diferentes tipos de intervenção florestal. Segundo o comunicado do MAEN, a medida pretende também incentivar práticas de gestão sustentável que produzam benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais, reforçando a capacidade de geração de créditos de carbono no país. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, citada no comunicado do MAEN. A governante acrescenta que o alargamento das metodologias pretende reforçar a credibilidade e o crescimento do MVC e mobilizar financiamento privado para projetos relacionados com a neutralidade carbónica e a resiliência das florestas. A plataforma tem atualmente dois projetos registados, ambos na categoria de Novas Florestações, enquanto um terceiro se encontra em validação inicial. Estão disponíveis para venda 977 créditos de carbono e estão registados 29 utilizadores. O comunicado do MAEN indica ainda a existência de 10 verificadores qualificados, responsáveis pela validação inicial e pela verificação periódica dos projetos. Para Maria da Graça Carvalho, o mercado está a ganhar “escala e maturidade”. De acordo com o MAEN, estão já a ser desenvolvidas novas metodologias relacionadas com o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, com o objetivo de abranger também os ecossistemas costeiros no âmbito da ação climática e da valorização do capital natural.

artigo.texto: Noah Berger/Getty Images via Amazon Web Services Over the next five years, Amazon will invest more than $1 billion in education, energy and water conservation, as well as in infrastructure in communities that host their data centers, the company said last week. As part of its “Built Together” framework, residents of Amazon’s data center communities will receive free community college and hands-on workforce training to prepare them for in-demand career fields, such as HVAC, IT, health care, education, public safety and advanced manufacturing. When the initiative launches in a few months, Amazon will cover all out-of-pocket expenses that remain after a student receives financial aid. The company anticipates that the program will help some 300,000 students access degree programs over the next five years. In addition, Amazon is expanding the network of physical training facilities at and near its data centers. These facilities provide free skilled trade certification programs and direct pathways to jobs with Amazon and its construction partners. The company projects that by the end of 2028, they will train 100,000 workers a year “for real jobs in their hometowns—fully funded by Amazon,” Matt Garman, CEO of Amazon Web Services, wrote in the announcement. The announcement comes amid growing backlash against the AI-fueled proliferation of data centers over the past few years. According to a recent Gallup poll, 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their area, citing strained natural resources, cost-of-living increases, noise pollution and job losses, as well as general negative views about AI. But Amazon, which has at least 900 data centers across 50 countries, claimed in the announcement that many of those concerns stem from “misinformation” and “outright lies,” and that the United States can’t afford to fall behind on building more data centers. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run,” Garman said. “The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so.”

artigo.texto: Quando se fala em projetos REDD+, a discussão costuma começar, e muitas vezes terminar, nas toneladas de carbono. Quantas emissões foram evitadas? Quantos créditos foram gerados? Qual foi a redução do desmatamento? Essas são perguntas essenciais. Afinal, o objetivo central do REDD+ é reduzir as emissões provenientes do desmatamento e da degradação florestal. Mas olhar apenas para o carbono deixa de fora uma parte importante daquilo que pode determinar o sucesso de um projeto no longo prazo. Uma floresta não permanece em pé simplesmente porque existe uma meta de carbono associada a ela. Conservá-la exige presença territorial, monitoramento, prevenção de incêndios, instituições capazes de tomar decisões, recursos para enfrentar pressões externas e, em muitos casos, alternativas econômicas compatíveis com a manutenção da área. Por isso, quando bem estruturados, projetos REDD+ podem produzir benefícios que vão além das toneladas de CO₂ evitadas. A própria estrutura internacional de salvaguardas do REDD+ reconhece a importância da governança florestal, dos direitos e da participação de povos indígenas e comunidades locais, da biodiversidade e dos benefícios sociais e ambientais associados à conservação. Proteger a floresta exige infraestrutura Grandes áreas florestais precisam ser acompanhadas continuamente para identificar abertura de estradas, invasões, focos de incêndio, extração ilegal de madeira, garimpo, novas áreas de ocupação e outros sinais de pressão. É nesse contexto que recursos provenientes de projetos REDD+ podem financiar sistemas de monitoramento por satélite, equipamentos, capacitação de equipes locais e ações de vigilância em campo. A tecnologia permite acompanhar mudanças na cobertura vegetal em grandes extensões territoriais. O trabalho em campo, por sua vez, acrescenta uma dimensão que o satélite sozinho não oferece: compreender o que está acontecendo, quem está entrando no território, quais áreas são mais vulneráveis e como responder às ameaças. A combinação entre instrumentos tecnológicos, conhecimento territorial e capacidade de atuação local transforma monitoramento em proteção. Governança também é conservação Projetos florestais são implementados em territórios onde já existem pessoas, organizações, conhecimentos, direitos, relações sociais e estruturas próprias de decisão. Por isso, uma das questões mais importantes em REDD+ é quem decide o que será feito com os recursos gerados pela conservação. As prioridades podem ser construídas por meio das estruturas de governança da própria comunidade: assembleias, associações, lideranças, conselhos ou outras formas legítimas de representação. Esse processo pode fortalecer organizações locais, ampliar sua capacidade administrativa e financeira e criar mecanismos mais estruturados para planejamento, execução de recursos, prestação de contas e tomada coletiva de decisões. Gerar renda sem derrubar florestas Talvez uma das maiores possibilidades dos projetos REDD+ esteja na capacidade de conectar conservação com desenvolvimento econômico local. Em muitas regiões amazônicas, isso significa fortalecer atividades que dependem da floresta em pé. Açaí, castanha-do-brasil, óleos, sementes, frutas, artesanato e outros produtos da sociobiodiversidade podem compor cadeias econômicas baseadas na manutenção dos recursos florestais. No entanto, fortalecer uma cadeia produtiva exige mais do que financiar a coleta. É possível investir em beneficiamento, armazenamento, equipamentos, boas práticas de produção, logística, organização de cooperativas, acesso a mercados e agregação de valor. Nesse contexto, a lógica econômica começa a mudar. A floresta deixa de ser percebida apenas como uma área que não pode ser convertida e passa a fazer parte de uma atividade econômica cuja continuidade depende da conservação florestal. É preciso evitar a explicação simplista de que comunidades desmatam apenas porque possuem baixa renda. Os vetores do desmatamento são muito mais complexos e incluem mercados de commodities, ocupação irregular de terras, infraestrutura, exploração ilegal de recursos naturais, fragilidade institucional e diferentes incentivos econômicos. A lição é relevante: conservar floresta exige olhar para décadas, não só para o próximo ciclo de emissão de créditos. Proteção além da fronteira do projeto Há outro desafio fundamental: uma área pode estar protegida enquanto seu entorno continua submetido às mesmas forças que provocam o desmatamento. Nesse cenário, existe o risco de que determinada atividade simplesmente se desloque. É o chamado leakage ou vazamento de emissões. Se um projeto impede o desmatamento em determinada área, mas a atividade responsável por aquela pressão migra e derruba floresta em outro local, parte do benefício climático pode ser anulada. Metodologias atuais de REDD+ tratam esse risco de maneira explícita. É nesse ponto que benefícios sociais, produtivos e climáticos começam a convergir. Quando um projeto investe exclusivamente dentro dos seus limites, existe a possibilidade de parte das pressões simplesmente migrar para regiões próximas. Quando combina conservação com alternativas de renda, recuperação produtiva, assistência técnica, engajamento de comunidades vizinhas e fortalecimento da governança territorial, cria condições para atacar alguns dos fatores que poderiam provocar o leakage. Estrutura maior A tonelada de CO₂ é a unidade utilizada para medir o resultado climático de um projeto REDD+. Mas ela não descreve tudo o que precisa acontecer para que essa quantidade de dióxido de carbono deixe efetivamente de ser emitida. Esses elementos não devem ser considerados automaticamente como prova de integridade climática. Um projeto continua precisando demonstrar adicionalidade, utilizar uma linha de base robusta, contabilizar incertezas e leakage e verificar de forma independente suas reduções de emissões. artigo.texto: Elestor has won the Waterstof Innovatie Award 2026 for its hydrogen–iron flow battery technology, recognising its approach to using hydrogen as an active component of the battery system. The company was one of three nominees selected from 14 submissions, with the jury highlighting the innovative use of hydrogen in a technology designed to make renewable electricity available when it is needed. The award recognises Elestor’s work on large-scale, long-duration electricity storage, with its hydrogen–iron flow battery designed to store renewable energy for periods ranging from several hours to multiple days. Using hydrogen for long-duration energy storage Flow batteries can use different chemistries and active materials, known as redox couples. While a range of approaches can work from a scientific perspective, Elestor says only some have the potential to succeed commercially. Its hydrogen–iron flow battery is designed around the need for longer-duration energy storage. The technology can also be integrated with hydrogen infrastructure, while supporting more continuous electrolyser operation. This creates a connection between long-duration electricity storage and the production of green hydrogen and clean fuels. Recognition for Elestor’s team The Waterstof Innovatie Award was presented by Lijs Groenendaal of NLHydrogen to Dries Kleuskens of Elestor. For the company, the recognition reflects more than the award ceremony itself. Elestor said it represents the work of its wider team as it continues developing and commercialising its hydrogen–iron flow battery technology. The award highlights the growing role of hydrogen-based technologies in approaches to renewable energy storage, while recognising Elestor’s specific contribution to the development of long-duration battery systems.

artigo.texto: - 01AVL-Tyfast MOU to assess oxide for LVO batteries. - 02No supply or price commitments; qualification required. - 03AICIS approval supports electrolyte scale-up. Australian Vanadium (ASX: AVL) has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with US-based Tyfast Energy Corp to evaluate its planned Australian vanadium oxide products for Tyfast’s proprietary lithium vanadium oxide (LVO) anode technology and explore potential future supply and offtake arrangements. The MOU has an 18-month term and is non-exclusive, with no agreed minimum supply volume, price, purchase commitment, or financial consideration, and any future pilot, development, supply, or offtake arrangement requiring successful technical and commercial evaluation and definitive agreements. Tyfast is developing LVO lithium-ion batteries for heavy-duty applications including mining, trucking, construction, and defence, giving Australian Vanadium a potential additional market alongside its established focus on vanadium flow batteries (VFBs). The staged collaboration will assess product forms and specifications, sample material, bench-scale and pilot-scale qualification, and possible demonstration projects before any commercial supply or offtake arrangement is considered. The move follows Australian Vanadium receiving an Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme (AICIS) assessment certificate earlier this week for a key component of vanadium electrolyte, supporting its proposed expansion to industrial-scale electrolyte production in Australia. Heavy-Duty Battery Pathway Under the MoU, Australian Vanadium and Tyfast intend to assess Australian vanadium oxide against Tyfast’s battery-material requirements, including potential vanadium pentoxide or other mutually agreed oxide or intermediate products. The program is expected to examine sample delivery and acceptance criteria, material optimisation, indicative quantities, and delivery schedules, with successful qualification potentially leading to mine-site pilots, fleet trials, pre-commercial supply and commercial negotiations. “Emerging opportunities such as this reinforce the rationale for considering the potential production of higher-purity vanadium products as part of the Optimised Feasibility Study,” chief executive officer Graham Arvidson said. “As new markets for vanadium emerge, we want the Australian Vanadium project to have the flexibility to respond to a broader range of customer requirements.” Tyfast reports its LVO technology is being developed to combine fast charging, long cycle life, broad-temperature performance and high energy density, with target markets spanning heavy-duty industrial and defence applications. Electrolyte Scale-Up Advances The AICIS certificate covers a key industrial chemical component of vanadium electrolyte, authorising Australian Vanadium to introduce the assessed chemical by import or manufacture within a specified annual limit and subject to certificate conditions. Based on the company’s current electrolyte formulation and conversion assumptions, that annual limit is estimated to support sufficient electrolyte production for approximately 2.5 gigawatt-hours of deployed VFB capacity. Australian Vanadium has separately received an AICIS assessment certificate for vanadium trioxide, which may be used as a raw material in its electrolyte production process. The company’s VSUN Energy subsidiary continues to develop the domestic VFB market. The two developments broaden Australian Vanadium’s battery-market strategy across both VFBs and emerging lithium-ion applications as it advances the Australian Vanadium project and evaluates higher-purity vanadium products for a wider range of customer requirements.
