artigo.texto: Hermantown council unanimously passes AUAR review for proposed data center HERMANTOWN, Minn. (Northern News Now) - The Hermantown city council voted unanimously on Monday to approve an Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for the proposed Google data center. Read: Heated data center debate results in pause to Hermantown city council meeting An AUAR is a state-authorized environmental review process used to study how different development scenarios could affect the environment before construction begins. The 2,700-page AUAR for the proposed Google Data Center includes comments from five government agencies and more than 200 residents. Public concerns listed in the AUAR include environmental impacts, wetlands and transparency to the public. Many data center opponents over the past year have pushed back on the AUAR, arguing it is not as comprehensive as an Environmental Impact Statement. Project leaders who presented at the meeting, including Kimley Horn and Mortenson Construction, said they addressed the public’s concerns in the AUAR. “Many of those items are the direct result of the public process the city facilitated through the AUAR, and demonstrate Google’s commitment to incorporating public input in the development of the project,” said Chris Bates with Mortenson. Public Comment Supporters at the meeting agreed, arguing that Google is acting in good-faith by making these changes, and that the AUAR is a comprehensive framework for the city. They also emphasized the economic benefits of the data center. “One thing I appreciate about the AUAR process is that it allows us to be excited about economic development while also doing the necessary work to understand its impacts,” said Hermantown Chamber of Commerce President Kim Parmeter. On the other hand, opponents of the data center pushed back on the AUAR, asking the city to instead do an Environmental Impact Statement, which they view as a more comprehensive review that would bring in an outside entity to complete it. “They can’t make promises for what’s happening in 5 years,” said Duluth resident Jim Klukkert. “How long has Google been in existence, and they want to tell you that they understand they are making a commitment of 20-25 years?“ MN DNR Letter Another big topic of conversation from both the public and presenters Monday night was the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. The DNR sent a letter to the city in August asking for clarification and revision on the AUAR. That included mitigation plans and additional monitoring for impacts to wetlands from this project. Presenters on Monday said they made changes based on these letters, and that the DNR never formally objected to the environmental review Vote on Thursday The environmental review for Minnesota Power’s transmission line, which would power the data center, was also up for vote on Monday night. However, city leaders announced that due to the long public comment period on the AUAR vote, they moved for council to reconvene this Thursday. artigo.texto: O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) encerrou a primeira temporada de acesso da Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast) com a alocação de 228 MW de capacidade remanescente da Rede Básica para três data centers em São Paulo. A capacidade, distribuída em quatro pontos de conexão, foi totalmente destinada aos empreendimentos das empresas Pahlavan One e Pahlavan Three, empresas cotroladas pela Cloud HQ, e da Digital DC Brasil, que opera sob a marca NextStream, controlada pelo fundo de private equity Actis. Em agosto deste ano, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) negou pedido de medida cautelar das empresas Pahlavan Ventures One, Pahlavan Ventures Two e Pahlavan Ventures Three para manter três projetos de data centers na fila de acesso à rede básica até que surgisse capacidade para ampliar o consumo dos empreendimentos, que integram o Complexo Pahlavan, em Paulínia, São Paulo, com conexão compartilhada no barramento de 440 kV da subestação Replan. Realização da 1° temporada de acesso O primeiro ciclo da Pnast, instituída pelo Decreto nº 12.772/2025, estabeleceu um novo modelo de acesso à Rede Básica, com foco em transparência, previsibilidade e eficiência na conexão de empreendimentos ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A etapa final da 1ª Temporada de Acesso foi concluída na terça-feira, 6 de outubro, com a realização do primeiro processo competitivo previsto pela política. Ao longo da 1ª Temporada de Acesso, foram registrados 367 cadastramentos de empreendimentos de geração e consumo, que somaram mais de 20 GW em solicitações de acesso distribuídas por 64 barramentos do SIN. Considerando também a fase transitória, o ONS analisou mais de 43 GW em pedidos de acesso à Rede Básica. Desse total, aproximadamente 30,7 GW foram viabilizados ou habilitados. Para este primeiro processo competitivo, sete projetos participaram da disputa, somando 451 MW de demanda habilitada. Ao final, os 228 MW de capacidade disponível, equivalente a 100% da margem ofertada, foram alocados para três data centers das empresas Pahlavan One, Pahlavan Three e Digital DC Brasil. “Quando desenhamos essa política, tivemos como objetivo superar uma lógica de espera e construir uma política de estado, baseada em planejamento, critérios técnicos e processos competitivos. Com a Pnast, damos mais previsibilidade aos agentes, aumentamos a eficiência dos investimentos e garantimos que a expansão da transmissão esteja alinhada às necessidades do desenvolvimento do país. É uma mudança que fortalece o planejamento do setor elétrico, amplia a segurança do sistema e cria as condições para que o Brasil avance com infraestrutura adequada e visão de longo prazo”, afirmou o ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira. O diretor-geral do ONS, Marcio Rea, destacou os resultados do primeiro ciclo da política. “Encerramos este primeiro ciclo com resultados que demonstram a efetividade do novo modelo de acesso à transmissão. Além dos volumes expressivos de capacidade analisada e viabilizada, realizamos com sucesso o primeiro Processo Competitivo da Pnast, consolidando um ambiente mais previsível, transparente e eficiente para investidores, consumidores e para o planejamento da expansão do sistema elétrico brasileiro”, declarou. Para o diretor de TI, Relacionamento com Agentes e Assuntos Regulatórios do ONS, Maurício de Souza, os resultados do primeiro ciclo devem contribuir para o aprimoramento da política. “A elevada participação dos agentes e a realização bem-sucedida do primeiro processo competitivo demonstram a maturidade do setor para esse novo modelo. Os aprendizados deste ciclo fornecerão subsídios importantes para os aperfeiçoamentos previstos nas próximas edições da Política”, destacou.

artigo.texto: City of Ozark, Mo., passes an ordinance that imposes restrictions on data center development OZARK, Mo. (KY3) - It’s about to be a lot tougher for data center developers to build in Ozark. On Monday night, the city’s board of aldermen voted unanimously to add more hurdles to data center development. Additions to the city ordinance tackle issues like water use and noise regulations, and others point to public input and transparency. “They would have to hold a mandatory neighborhood meeting for surrounding residents to allow residents to voice their opinions with regard to the development. They would have to submit ongoing noise monitoring and, in fact, maintain a public website,” said Ozark’s Mayor Pro Tem, Chris Aiken. “They will have to document and make public all complaints that they receive as well as their responses to those complaints.” Ozark resident Justin Wisdom says water consumption is towards the top of his list of concerns when it comes to data centers. “They do take a lot of water, and I’ve heard that water rights kind of get a little restricted when data centers are in your vicinity,” said Wisdom. “So, I mean, that’s kind of a pretty big worry.” Aiken says that the board of aldermen believes these changes to the city ordinance also address citizen concerns over potential data centers’ water and electricity consumption. “We’ve included design requirements within our ordinance to make sure that if there is a data center here, it’s using the most efficient cooling systems available,” said Aiken. “They actually have to submit a report from the utility company analyzing the impact that the facility would have on our electrical infrastructure.” Aiken says the city chose to add restrictions to the existing ordinance rather than impose a moratorium or outright ban on data centers. “I think our city determined that, legally, that was maybe a little more risky and that we’d be better off getting out ahead of these developments, placing reasonable restrictions on them so that they’re not going to constitute a nuisance for the people of Ozark,” said Aiken. “I think that’s a good strategy,” said Wisdom. “Make the companies just not even want to come around due to the restrictions and stuff. I think that’s honestly a good way to go.” To read the full ordinance, click here. The ordinance begins on page 105; new additions are in red. artigo.texto: Maryland Conditionally Selects Two Energy Storage Projects Totaling 440 MW in First Round Maryland's Public Service Commission conditionally selects Chalk Point (400 MW) and Jade Meadow III (40 MW), below the 800 MW target set for the first round. A second call for applications is due by January 1, 2027. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced on October 1, 2026 that it has conditionally selected two transmission-connected energy storage projects. They will receive Energy Storage Capacity Credits under the first round of procurement required by the state's Next Generation Energy Act. The sector is also seeing other deals, such as Usva Energia's sale of a 100 MW battery storage project in Finland to Enlight and the â¬37.9 million secured by Qair for two solar-plus-storage plants in Chad. According to the commission, the credits help large projects obtain financing by hedging against price uncertainty in the PJM Interconnection capacity market, through a more stable revenue stream. Two projects selected for 440 MW The commission selected the 400 MW Chalk Point Storage Project in Aquasco, Prince George's County, and the 40 MW Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in Barton, Garrett County. Together they would provide 440 MW of potential storage capacity, with four-hour durations and flat 15-year award terms. The awards remain subject to the commission's approval conditions and obligations. The combined estimated cost of the two projects is 6.98 cents per month for a typical Maryland residential customer, according to the commission. The Chalk Point project would be located at the site of the existing power plant of the same name. Jade Meadow III would be a combined solar-and-storage facility on a reclaimed coal mine in Western Maryland. A framework set by the 2025 law Enacted during the Maryland General Assembly's 2025 legislative session, the law directs the commission to conduct at least two solicitations for a cumulative 1,600 MW of front-of-the-meter, transmission-connected storage with a minimum four-hour duration. The first solicitation, which sought 800 MW, was issued through a Request for Applications on December 24, 2025. Five applicants submitted proposals in Round 1. The commission, assisted by its consultant Power Advisory LLC, found all five applications administratively complete and eligible. It then evaluated and ranked them using qualitative and quantitative criteria, including cost-effectiveness and potential ratepayer impacts. Two applicants subsequently withdrew: the 300 MW Fourth Quarter Battery Energy Storage System project in Montgomery County and the 135 MW Pulaski Energy Storage Project in Baltimore County. Decision after the summer hearings After a public hearing on July 30, 2026, and evidentiary hearings involving multiple parties from August 4 to 6, 2026, the commission determined that Chalk Point and Jade Meadow III were the most cost-effective and highest-ranked remaining proposals. It did not select the 500 MW Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project in Harford County, citing its lower ranking and considerations of cost-effectiveness and ratepayer impacts. The commission nonetheless recognized the project's desirable grid location and characteristics, and invited the applicant to consider Round 2. It also noted the need for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County. The commission also denied Chalk Point's proposed increase from 400 MW to 535 MW for Round 1. It said the revised capacity was offered after the application window closed and was not evaluated through the competitive solicitation process. The project may submit its expanded proposal in Round 2. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 % Next steps ahead of Round 2 "These awards are an important milestone for Maryland in our efforts to meet state energy policy goals set by the legislature in recent years," said Commission Chair Kumar Barve. He added that the commission is disappointed the awards fall below the 800 MW target for Round 1. He expects the Round 2 solicitation to attract many more offers, owing to a pool of over 40 additional storage projects from PJM's Cycle 1 interconnection process. The developers of Chalk Point and Jade Meadow III will have to apply to the commission for construction approval. That step will involve additional public and evidentiary hearings on non-financial aspects, including safety, siting and environmental impacts. The commission will continue the capacity credit awards process through a second Request for Applications, which is due to be issued by January 1, 2027.

artigo.texto: Spain is Raising its Stake in Utility-Scale Battery Storage Renewable energy developers Zelestra and EDP have signed two long-term power purchase agreements (PPA) that will expand their combination of utility-scale solar energy and battery storage brought together for the first time in Spain’s grid history. The companies announced Tuesday that the two new PPAs would add about 462 MWh of battery storage to 181 MW of direct-current solar capacity across the portfolio. The new PPAs are built on an original 2025 agreement which detailed the hybrid solar and storage project in the Trujillo, Extremadura region. Altogether it brings the EDP-Zelestra partnership to four Spanish projects totaling more than 500 MWh of renewable capacity with four-hour duration storage. Portuguese utility and global renewables project developer EDP will be the off-taker for both power generation resources. “Zelestra and EDP have built something together that is unique in the Spanish market: a commercial partnership that is unlocking large-scale storage capacity that will benefit the wider energy system,” Jaime Burguete, CEO of Zelestra in Spain, said in a statement. “These four hybrid projects show that energy storage is bankable in Spain, and we expect this segment of the market to be the main growth area in the years ahead. It also means that every megawatt-hour moved into the evening or early morning is clean power the system would otherwise have had to find elsewhere.” Earlier this year, Zelestra and EDP moved to hybridize an existing solar energy plant in Cáceres. The plans for the developing 160 MWh of battery energy storage is intended to balance and complement the 50-MW Pizarroso solar facility which began operations in 2023. “We are continuously developing new solutions that combine technology, market expertise and flexibility assets to unlock greater value from clean energy,” said Pedro Neves Ferreira, CEO of global energy management at EDP. “By integrating storage with renewable generation, we can enhance system resilience, improve efficiency and accelerate the electrification and decarbonization of the economy.” Spain’s electricity planners are increasingly adopting renewable energy resources. Low-carbon energy accounts for about 75% of the nation’s electricity resource mix, led by solar, wind, nuclear and hydropower. Spanish grid operator Red Eléctrica has tallied the installed battery energy storage capacity at nearly 200 MW across the country. While far below the battery capacity in the U.S., Spain’s installed energy storage has grown nearly 600% in the past year. artigo.texto: THE PHILIPPINES and South Korea are negotiating two cooperation agreements involving joint work on carbon market mechanisms, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources said. Environment Secretary Juan Miguel T. Cuna said the two governments are expediting talks on a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on environmental cooperation and another on climate change cooperation, both of which meet the requirements of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. They hope to conclude talks before a bilateral summit in November, to be held during the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila. According to Mr. Cuna, the MoUs will also cover greenhouse gas emissions reduction, water resource management, and ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement sets out how countries can cooperate through carbon markets, including the cross-border transfer of emissions reductions. Mr. Cuna met with South Korean Deputy Minister for Climate Change Jongho Kyun on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly High-Level Week and Climate Week NYC 2026 in New York. “As we move toward COP31, we see the priority increasingly shifting from commitments to implementation and delivery, translating climate goals into policies, investments, technologies, and measurable outcomes,” Mr. Cuna said. Mr. Cuna also thanked South Korea for its official development assistance through the Korea International Cooperation Agency, for its support for marine plastics reduction, emergency aid during the Mindoro oil spill, and the recent transfer of the marine clean-up vessel MV Nilad for use in Manila Bay. The two officials also discussed the need for a clear pathway for vulnerable countries to access the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, following the floods in Nepal. Mr. Cuna said access arrangements are particularly important for the Philippines, which continues to face significant climate-related hazards. Mr. Cuna said partnership with South Korea will remain important for regional sustainability. — Moureen Ylessandra B. Dizon

artigo.texto: ‘It’s a nuisance’: Harlem neighbor raises concerns over data center noise HARLEM, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - Construction at Google’s Pumpkin Center data center in Harlem is running around the clock, according to a neighbor, raising questions about whether the project is following county rules on construction hours. Gregory Guido, who lives near the more than 3,000-acre site, said he moved to the area for peace and quiet, only for the noise to begin almost as soon as work started. “I moved out here to the country, where it was going to be nice and quiet, a nice place to settle down and raise families,” Guido said. A county ordinance allows construction sites to operate only between 6 a.m. and 11 p.m. Developers can apply to the Inspection and Permit Department for a permit to work beyond those hours. Guido said the noise continues well outside those hours and questioned why it isn’t regulated more closely, given the impact on families with children and people who work. Augusta leaders set hearing on major rewrite of zoning ordinance Augusta residents will get a chance to weigh in on a rewrite of the city’s zoning rules later this month. “If there’s kids that have to go to sleep and they have to wake up early to go to school or if somebody’s working and they got to get up and they got to go to work, they should not have to hear this,” Guido said. “Twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, where’s the protection?” A county spokesperson said they were not able to confirm by the end of the day Wednesday whether the Pumpkin Center site has applied for or received a permit to work beyond normal construction hours. Guido said he expects the noise to continue for some time as the project moves forward. “It’s a nuisance,” Guido said. “This is just the start, this is just the beginning, right, we haven’t even had any data centers go up yet.” He hopes for a change, as the construction scene near the Harlem exit seems to grow with each passing night. “This is all night and it does not stop,” Guido said. “Now that the weather’s cooled off, right, October, everybody’s outside, we got trick or treating coming up. When all the kids are outside trick or treating, this is what they are going to hear.” There is no further information available on the project’s permit status at this time. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. artigo.texto: Data centers are a hot-button issue right now, but many executives in Northern Virginia are looking beyond the controversy. Related stories - Despite skyrocketing rates, real estate agent says DC-area homebuyers still have ‘upper hand’ - How Alexandria hopes to transform Duke Street into a more unified corridor - From napkin drawing to final product, this Fairfax business helps inventors through the process A majority of D.C.-area business leaders now believe the centers will have a positive impact on the regional economy, according to a survey. A survey from the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce and Pinkston found 53% of top executives view data centers positively while 34% have doubts. One in eight leaders, 13%, had no opinion. “A majority of them see data centers as a positive economic force, but there is some concern,” Julie Coons, president and CEO of the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce, told WTOP News. “I believe that what business leaders see is that our economy today, and as it evolves into the future, the toehold we have here in Northern Virginia and the greater DMV is so important,” she said. “And data centers do enable those industries that we want to continue to keep here and attract here — cybersecurity, commercial space, quantum of the future. So they’re critical to our economic standing today and certainly in the future.” While many business leaders in the Northern Virginia region are embracing data centers, Tim Tkacz is a bit more guarded. The CEO of Blue Sky Innovators, a Reston-based defense and national security company, said he is “whole hog optimistic” about the technology behind data centers. “We need these,” Tkacz said. “But at the same time, we have to be responsible about the impact that they have on the local communities that they go into.” This was the first time the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce and Pinkston asked about the economic impact of data centers in their quarterly survey. They surveyed 169 CEOs, executives and business owners from companies based in Fairfax, Loudoun, Arlington and Prince William counties as well as the cities of Fairfax, Falls Church and Alexandria. Growing doubts about the economy The survey also found growing pessimism among business leaders about the economy, both nationally and locally. Thirty-six percent of executives expect the regional economy to grow in the next six months, down from 40% in the second quarter. Some 23% believe the local economy will decline slowly or significantly in the coming months. Coons said business leaders expressed a level of caution. “While they maintain high, high confidence in their own business capacity,” Coons said. “They do see regional headwinds.” Pessimism has swelled about the national economy in recent months too, with 47% of leaders now downbeat about the national landscape. That’s up from 38% in the second quarter. Only 34% are optimistic about the national economy. Almost half business leaders, 49%, said their companies are being hurt by President Donald Trump’s foreign policy decisions, led by international trade, tariffs and the war in the Middle East. Hiring and spending plans Two-thirds of business leaders are optimistic about their own company’s outlook. While strong, that’s still down from 77% in the last survey. This rise in pessimism about the local economy has business leaders moving cautiously as they plan for 2027. Some 40% do not plan to change their spending plans in the next six months while 37% plan to increase spending slightly. Only 6% plan to increase spending significantly. As for hiring, a third of business leaders in Northern Virginia, 32%, plan to increase their payrolls and add positions heading into the new year. Almost three in five, 58%, plan to keep staffing about the same. “Let’s watch how things go over the next year or so,” Coons said. artigo.texto: Amazon ends secret data center pacts and pledges $1 billion to host towns — AWS promises 30,000 home efficiency retrofits amid 100 proposed bans It will also invest more than $1 billion over five years in communities hosting its facilities. Amazon will no longer require nondisclosure agreements (NDA) with government agencies involved in its data center projects and will adhere to its new Data Center Commitment program designed to address mounting opposition to AI infrastructure, it disclosed on Friday in a blog post. The company also unveiled plans to invest more than $1 billion over five years in communities hosting its facilities. The announcements come as more than 100 data center moratoriums are being considered across the U.S., so AWS wants to make data centers more attractive to locals. No NDAs Amazon's decision to no longer require NDAs from government officials working with it is part of the company's newly announced Data Center Commitment program aimed at making data center building more transparent and somewhat less unpleasant to people living nearby. Among other things, the company vows to hold community open houses, disclose information about projects as early as possible, and listen to local concerns as development proceeds. Amazon also vows annual disclosure of its energy consumption and efficiency, water consumption and efficiency, and the proportion of electricity supplied by carbon-free sources. Speaking of power usage efficiency (PUE), Amazon reports a global PUE of 1.14 for 2025, compared with an industry average of 1.25 and 1.63 for on-premises enterprise data centers. It also says its facilities were 7x more water-efficient than the industry average and that it had reached 75% of its goal to become water-positive by 2030. Many concerns Also, new sites will use backup generators compliant with EPA Tier 4 emissions standards. While Amazon emphasizes that new sites will use backup generators meeting EPA Tier 4 emissions standards, the commitment is somewhat ambiguous in general, as the specification limits vary by engine power and generator classes, whereas Amazon does not specify the generator classes it intends to deploy. The company says an average U.S. data center consumes around 170,000 gallons of water per day, whereas an average Amazon facility uses less than 13,000 gallons, equivalent to 42 U.S. households. However, Amazon does not distinguish between the water consumption of a typical AWS data center designed for general-purpose cloud workloads and newly built AI data centers packed with power-hungry AI accelerators, which certainly have substantially different cooling requirements. In general, Amazon is trying to counter concerns about the resource requirements of data centers, although some of its comparisons remain rather ambiguous. When it comes to energy efficiency, the new Built Together initiative will add more than $1 billion to Amazon’s existing community spending. The company expects to provide more than 300,000 students with access to free community-college education over five years. It currently operates three Modular Training Centers, has six more under development, and plans another 16. Each facility can train roughly 2,000–4,000 people annually, with Amazon targeting as many as 100,000 trained workers per year by the end of 2028. Separately, more than 65 contracted water projects are expected to return over 8 billion gallons annually, more than twice the water Amazon says its data centers consumed in 2025. The bus and its small crew of conservative activists from a group called Humans First had just completed an over 8,000-mile whistle-stop marathon of a road trip on perhaps the most uniting theme today: anti-data-center sentiment. “This technology is being shoved down people’s throats,” said Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, admiring the bus’ artwork from a nearby sidewalk. She said the group aimed to push back against AI giants and their assumption that they can build billions of dollars of AI infrastructure without residents’ input. “That’s not the American way,” she said. Founded this year as a coalition of left- and right-wing activists who worry that the rush to embrace AI is being spearheaded by tech oligarchs steamrolling Americans’ ability to steer the technology, Humans First has since morphed into a conservative-only effort led by Kremer to advocate for better guardrails on data center construction and AI in general. Kremer, a veteran conservative organizer who played noted roles in the tea party and the organization that helped create the rally preceding the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol attack, has spearheaded cross-country bus trips to extol MAGA talking points and deny the outcome of the 2020 election. Composed of Kremer, her husband, her daughter and her dog, Lovie — “He’s been with me the entire trip,” Kremer said — along with staffers and security guards, the Humans First squad has made more than 35 stops in communities across the country over the past five weeks. The trip culminated in Monday’s visits to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta and Nvidia — widely regarded as the world’s largest and most influential AI companies. Kremer and her daughter, Kylie Jane Kremer, fielded questions from reporters about the tour’s goals and its accomplishments. On Sunday, Kremer participated in a panel at a gathering of AI luminaries in nearby Berkeley, where she laid out the future of conservative AI approaches to mitigate such potential outcomes. artigo.texto: Uma decisão do Tribunal Regional Federal da 1ª Região (TRF1) determinou que a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) analise em até 48 horas um pedido cautelar de três data centers da Pahlavan e impeça, até essa deliberação, que eventual capacidade remanescente na subestação Replan, em São Paulo, seja definitivamente comprometida com terceiros no processo competitivo da Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast). A liminar foi concedida na terça-feira, 6 de outubro, mesmo dia em que os data centers Pahlavan One e Pahlavan Three foram vencedores no processo competitivo que alocou 228 MW de capacidade de conexão. O resultado foi apresentado pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) nesta quarta-feira, 7, durante a cerimônia de encerramento da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026. Além das duas empresas da Pahlavan, a Digital DC Brasil também foi selecionada. Os três empreendimentos ficaram com 100% dos 228 MW ofertados, em uma disputa que teve sete projetos habilitados, com demanda total de 451 MW. A Pahlavan Two foi a única das três empresas que integram a ação judicial que não apareceu entre as vencedoras. Como a Aneel ainda não foi intimada da decisão, o prazo de 48 horas ainda não começou a correr. A determinação judicial se restringe a eventual capacidade que o ONS identifique no barramento de 440 kV da subestação Replan como existente e tecnicamente apta, total ou parcialmente, ao atendimento dos incrementos de Montante de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão (Must) pretendidos pelas empresas para 2029. Até a análise do pedido cautelar, essa capacidade não poderá ser definitivamente adjudicada, contratada ou comprometida com terceiros. A restrição deixa de produzir efeitos automaticamente após a manifestação da Aneel, independentemente do resultado. A decisão não reconhece prioridade para os projetos, não reserva capacidade e não suspende a Temporada de Acesso. Projetos da Pahlavan foram estruturados antes da Pnast O processo envolve os data centers Pahlavan Ventures One, Pahlavan Ventures Two e Pahlavan Ventures Three, em Paulínia, com conexão ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) pelo barramento de 440 kV da subestação Replan. Segundo as empresas, os empreendimentos foram estruturados sob as regras anteriores à Pnast e já contavam com portaria do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), atos autorizativos da Aneel, pareceres de acesso favoráveis do ONS e Contratos de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão (Custs). A controvérsia envolve a ampliação do Must de cada projeto, de 71 MW para 157 MW a partir de 2029. As empresas alegam que os pedidos de revisão dos pareceres para incluir o aumento somente poderiam ser formalizados a partir de janeiro de 2026, devido à regra então vigente que limitava os Custs aos quatro anos civis seguintes. >>> Pnast terá regras para evitar concentração de capacidade na transmissão Em dezembro de 2025, entrou em vigor o Decreto 12.772/2025, que criou a Pnast e instituiu as Temporadas de Acesso. As empresas protocolaram os pedidos de revisão em 1º de janeiro deste ano, mas os novos pareceres do ONS concluíram pela inviabilidade dos incrementos. De acordo com informações da Aneel reproduzidas na decisão judicial, os estudos apontaram sobrecarga na linha de transmissão Fernão Dias-Bom Jardim, em 440 kV, na hipótese de contingência simples da linha Fernão Dias-REC Bandeirantes, também em 440 kV. A agência também informou, com base em nota técnica do ONS, que a capacidade remanescente no barramento de 440 kV da Replan era zero para os produtos de 2028 e 2029. Recurso aguardava decisão Após a Aneel indeferir o pleito, as empresas apresentaram recurso à diretoria da agência em 10 de setembro, acompanhado de novo pedido cautelar. O pedido ainda não havia sido analisado quando o processo competitivo da primeira Temporada de Acesso foi marcado para 6 de outubro. Ao conceder parcialmente a liminar, o relator, desembargador Rafael Paulo Soares Pinto, considerou que havia risco de a apreciação administrativa ocorrer depois da alocação da capacidade, quando já não haveria objeto a preservar. O tribunal rejeitou, porém, o pedido para suspender os pareceres de acesso negativos do ONS e preservar capacidade atual ou futura até a decisão final dos processos administrativos. A decisão também estabelece que a restrição só alcança eventual capacidade que o próprio ONS identifique como existente e apta ao atendimento dos incrementos de 2029. Caso não haja capacidade nessas condições, a vedação temporária não produz efeito sobre o processo competitivo.

artigo.texto: City council meeting erupts into chaos after planned data center vote postponed See more of our coverage in your search results. Chaos erupted at the end of a Tennessee city council hearing when officials postponed a vote on Elon Musk’s data centers, sparking a fistfight and protesters taking over the meeting hall. A mob of enraged protesters harassed members of the Memphis City Council Tuesday night after they had just voted to delay the vote on a moratorium of data centers in the city. Councilors voted 7 to 5 Tuesday night to table the remaining items on the agenda for a later date before the meeting devolved into a loud disarray of shouting between council members and the residents. One protester broke out a bullhorn and began to lead a chant of “ain’t no power like the power of the people.” Council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen Washington had called for a recess to the meeting and ordered police officers to clear out the hall, according to a livestream. The frenzied mob worked its way to the dais and began shouting at the city councilors who were huddled around. The protesters accused the elected officials of being “sellouts,” according to video from KWAM News Radio. Officers had successfully removed the protesters from the meeting hall as the mob continued to shout “this is our city” and “show me what democracy looks like.” At least two women engaged in a fight near the exits during the chaotic meeting, but no arrests were made, WREG reported. Roughly 100 protesters had attended the meeting for the scheduled final vote on the data centers that sit south of the city on the Memphis, Tenn.-Southaven, Miss. border. Two large data center facilities, named Colossus and Colossus 2, are run by Musk’s artificial intelligence company SpaceXAI. The original Colossus facility was built to serve X’s Grok AI bot but was later part of an agreement in May that will see Anthropic use the full computing power of the facility The delayed motion was rescheduled to October 20, Action News 5 reported. If passed, a 12-month moratorium would be enacted on data centers to allow for a study on the impact the facilities have on the city’s health, engineering, power and water infrastructure. City council infighting occurred amid the chaos as one councilor accused another of confusing people. “That’s all he does; he brings up mess, he… that’s all you do, JB Smiley, confuse the people over, over, over and over! Anytime there is an election,” Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, according to Action News 5. Councilman Smiley, who voted against delaying the vote, called for a civilized discussion on the subject instead of the shouting and fighting. “When the community shows up, we just have to listen to them. I’m disappointed that we didn’t listen with ears, okay, I hear you, I understand. Let’s figure out how we can do what you want, but also what we believe would be in the best interest of the community,” said Smiley, who was the lead sponsor on the moratorium proposal. Councilman Jeff Warren, an opponent of any moratorium, warned that the year-long pause would give incentive to companies to not do business with the city and find another area to build the complexes. “If we pass a moratorium, there’s not reason for them to think they need to come here. They get the same benefit from going to Desoto County, Crittenden County, Fayette County, Tipton County,” said Councilman Jeff Warren Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - Business and economic experts told members of the Ohio Valley’s business community that data centers would be beneficial to the economic future of the community. Data centers, a hot topic in the region, was discussed at length Tuesday morning at the annual Economic Outlook Conference sponsored by the Wheeling Area Chamber of Commerce. The conference was held at the Wheeling Island Hotel-Casino-Racetrack. David H. McKinley, president and chief investment officer at McKinley-Carter Wealth Services, supported construction of data centers locally, pointing out the financial success in Loudoun County, Virginia. There are 234 data centers located in the county, and the collective property tax on them comes in at $1.8 billion, according to McKinley. This accounts for 38-40% for the county's tax base. "Technology investments are huge. We take them all for granted," he said. "The ramp up is significant and not to be overlooked. "I'm disappointed there is so much negativity about data centers." Former Delegate Erikka Storch, R-Ohio, now external affairs manager for American Electric Power, and James Bailey, a member attorney at Spilman, Thomas and Battle, participated in a panel discussion pertaining to the energy industry in the state that was led by John Deskins, assistant dean at the WVU John Chambers College of Business and Economics. both Storch and Bailey indicated support for data centers. "From our perspective, data centers operating in our area would help our customers," Storch said. "It would give us a larger population in which to spread our costs, and we would welcome them. "It would send the message that it would diversify the economy when there are opportunities, and it would increase tax revenue." The money has been "very transformational” for counties that already have data centers or are building them, such as in Putnam County, she added. Google is developing a multi-billion-dollar hyperscale data center campus in Buffalo, West Virginia. "There are incredible opportunities, but unfortunately there are tons of misinformation out there," said Bailey, whose law firm represents those wanting to build a data center in Ohio County. "The water use isn't nearly what you hear. These things are self-contained now." Newer technology allows the water at the plant to be recycled and it uses about the same amount of water as any industrial facility, he explained. "You never hear from people who are for something. You only hear from people who are against it," Bailey said. Deskins provided a statewide economic outlook, and said that West Virginia needs more working-age adults in the workforce and a more diversified business climate if it is to grow economically. Deskins predicts there will be economic growth in West Virginia in the coming years, though it will happen at a slower rate than is typical. "We still have uncertainty ... over tariff policy, the war in Iran," he said. "Certainly, we have uncertainty around interest rates, but that uncertainty has diminished and that's a good thing. "Here in West Virginia, we think the state is going to remain stable over the next five years. There will be growth in some regions, but stability overall statewide." West Virginia has many successes, but they are "too concentrated geographically," Deskins noted. These are occurring in Jefferson and Berkeley counties in the Eastern Panhandle, and in Putnam County near Charleston and Kanawha County. "We have a lot of regions that are stagnant, and we need to find ways to have growth in those regions that are healthy to broaden out geographically," he continued. Despite the fact that West Virginia has low unemployment rates and people are working, the state continues to rank last in the number of adults actively participating in the workforce. The national workforce participation rate is 64%, while West Virginia continues to lag at 54.5%. "It is the biggest economic challenge we face," Deskins said. "There is no way West Virginia can achieve the prosperity we hope for until we get more people in the workforce. It is virtually a mathematical impossibility to imagine that West Virginia would have some form of economic prosperity on par with the nation... and have mathematically the smallest share of adults in the workforce. "It should be our biggest economic development challenge, and it should be our biggest priority. But fixing this is very hard." Among West Virginia counties, Wetzel County has the lowest workforce participation rate at 47.9%, according to U.S. Census statistics. This reflects a measurement of people between the ages of 16 and 64 who are not in school. Sharon Campbell, executive director of the Wetzel-Tyler Chamber of Commerce, suggested workforce participation in the region is lower because of a lack of any childcare facilities there and a lack of public transportation. These factors particularly affect women in the workforce, she added. The area also has been hit hard with drug addiction issues, Campbell noted. Deskins noted the years West Virginia has outperformed the nation in gross domestic product growth were when oil and gas industries performed strongly. The healthcare industry, led by WVU Medicine, also has been growing in the state, he added, as has the information industry. More diversification among businesses located in the state would lead to more economic growth, Deskins said. He also suggested the state should make more effort to retain and attract people to increase population. West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack spoke about "how inefficient state government is," and how when a bad decision is made, "government keeps going on." "West Virginia is at a crossroads, and this demand is being brought to us by the demand for electricity nationwide," he explained. "Most of it is needed by AI (artificial intelligence and data centers). "America cannot produce that electricity for West Virginia. They have to have us." artigo.texto: Ukraine will receive $16.2 million to develop renewable energy and energy storage systems The Board of the Climate Investment Funds (CIF) has approved Ukraine’s $16.2 million investment plan. The funds will be directed toward the development of renewable energy, cross-border power interconnections, and energy storage systems. According to the minister, this funding is part of the “Renewable Energy Integration” (REI) program. “This will help accelerate the integration of the Ukrainian power grid into the European energy network and will also strengthen the transformation of the Ukrainian energy sector,” Shmyhal said. The implementation of the approved program involves both public and private sectors. As Denys Shmyhal noted, as part of the public sector component, an investment package with an estimated value of $200 million has been put together in collaboration with the World Bank and NPC “Ukrenergo.” It includes a number of important projects to strengthen the Ukrainian power grid. Specifically, the following are planned: - construction of the 400 kV Chernivtsi–Suceava cross-border interconnector; - the creation of additional transmission capacity of 880 MW toward Ukraine and 445 MW toward European power grids; - the modernization and reinforcement of five high-voltage substations; - providing engineering support for the implementation of investment projects; - modernizing the IT, telecommunications, and operational infrastructure of NPC “Ukrenergo.” The implementation of these measures is expected to contribute to the further strengthening of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and its integration with the European power system. The second component of the program focuses on attracting private investment into modern energy infrastructure. According to Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal, this component is being developed by the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Specifically, the plan includes: - support for private investment in energy storage systems; - the development of autonomous BESS systems, which are expected to provide 610 MW of battery storage capacity; - implementation of renewable energy generation projects in combination with energy storage systems; - the implementation of other distributed energy solutions. Thus, the investment plan approved by the CIF is intended to simultaneously support the development of renewable generation, electricity storage, and the expansion of Ukraine’s capacity to exchange electricity with European countries. This was announced on October 6 by Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal. As a reminder, Ukraine and Germany plan to expand cooperation in the energy and transportation sectors. Among the agreements are potential purchases of German equipment to restore the power grid and locomotives for Ukrzaliznytsia, which are intended to help offset losses caused by Russian attacks. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi announced this following a conversation with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Ukraine and Germany have signed a series of agreements in the energy sector totaling more than 155 million euros. The agreements concern the restoration of damaged infrastructure, the supply of critical equipment, and the development of distributed generation. Separately, Germany announced a contribution of 250 million euros to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund.

artigo.texto: Corning Incorporated Broad portfolio including adapters According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Lc Fiber Optic Adapters market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global market for LC fiber optic adapters is a specification-driven, high-volume component business whose demand trajectory is tightly coupled to optical port density growth in data centers, telecom networks, and enterprise infrastructure. LC adapters, which provide precise alignment between LC connectors, are foundational passive components in fiber-to-the-x, hyperscale cloud, and 5G transport architectures. Between 2026 and 2035, the market is expected to expand at a moderate single-digit CAGR, supported by sustained investment in bandwidth infrastructure and the ongoing shift toward higher fiber counts per rack. The competitive landscape is shaped by qualification cycles with major network equipment manufacturers and hyperscalers, creating high barriers to entry and sticky supply relationships. Supply chain control over high-precision ceramic alignment sleeves remains a critical bottleneck and value driver. Geographically, manufacturing and assembly are concentrated in Asia, while design authority and high-reliability sourcing remain in North America, Europe, and Japan. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of demand architecture, supply chain dynamics, pricing, and competitive positioning through 2035. The baseline scenario for the LC fiber optic adapters market through 2035 anticipates steady expansion, with global demand rising at a CAGR of approximately 5.8% from 2026 to 2035. This outlook assumes continued growth in optical port deployments across hyperscale data centers, 5G transport networks, and enterprise LAN environments, alongside incremental replacement and upgrade cycles in existing fiber infrastructure. The market index, set at 100 in 2025, is projected to reach 176 by 2035. Growth is not uniform: high-performance, low-loss LC adapters for OEM design-in will outpace standard-grade adapters sold through distribution, as hyperscalers and NEMs tighten specifications for insertion loss, durability, and reliability data. The supply side remains concentrated in Asia for component manufacturing and assembly, but qualification and design authority stay in North America, Europe, and Japan, creating complex cross-regional supply chains. Pricing pressure is expected to persist in commodity segments, partially offset by value capture in premium, application-specific adapter variants. Key risks include demand cyclicality in telecom capex, trade policy disruptions, and the rising cost of ceramic ferrules and alignment sleeves. Overall, the market offers attractive opportunities for suppliers with vertical integration or secured ceramic supply, as well as for specialists that can meet stringent qualification requirements and provide design-in support. Data centers and cloud infrastructure represent the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for LC fiber optic adapters. Hyperscale operators and colocation providers are deploying higher fiber counts per rack to support cloud, AI, and machine learning workloads, directly increasing the number of LC adapters per server rack and switch port. LC adapters are preferred for their small form factor and high port density, enabling efficient cable management in high-density patch panels. Demand-side indicators include data center capex, server shipment volumes, and optical transceiver port counts. Through 2035, the shift to 400G/800G and future 1.6T Ethernet will require more adapters per port and higher-performance low-loss variants. Hyperscalers increasingly set their own specifications, demanding extensive reliability data and audit rights, which favors qualified suppliers with proven track records. This segment is expected to grow at a CAGR above the market average, driven by sustained cloud infrastructure investment and the buildout of AI-ready data centers. artigo.texto: Jinko ESS, a leading global energy storage company and a subsidiary of JinkoSolar Co., Ltd., is advancing a 135MWh green battery energy storage project in Germany. Connected with a photovoltaic plant and structured to support a hybrid power purchase agreement (PPA), the project is designed to strengthen the delivery and commercial value of renewable electricity. As Germany expands its renewable energy capacity, co-located and connected storage is becoming increasingly important. Battery energy storage can capture surplus solar generation, shift renewable electricity to periods of higher demand, and help create a more stable delivery profile for customers and the grid. By integrating 135MWh of green BESS capacity with the PV plant, the project is intended to support more effective use of solar generation and provide the flexibility required for a hybrid PPA. The approach brings together renewable production, energy storage, and contracted energy delivery within one coordinated project concept. The project is built on the Jinko Tera liquid-cooled energy storage system (5.01MWh). With a tested 94.1% conversion efficiency, the system captures surplus solar output with minimal charging and discharging losses, while its mirrored AB-cabinet layout reduces footprint by 17.7% and DC cabling by 50%, significantly shortening on-site delivery and grid-connection cycles — enabling storage capacity to enter service alongside the PV plant faster and supporting the reliable execution of the hybrid PPA. Roberto Murgioni, General Manager of Jinko ESS Europe, said: “We are delighted to continue strengthening our cooperation in Germany through this 135MWh project. By bringing together PV, storage and a hybrid PPA structure, this project reflects the kind of integrated approach that will make renewable energy more flexible and dependable.” Looking ahead, Jinko ESS will continue to collaborate with partners across Europe to deliver high-quality battery energy storage solutions that enhance renewable energy utilisation, strengthen grid flexibility, and support new routes to market for clean power.

artigo.texto: Data center emissions dispute prompts Virginia trip by Spartanburg officials Environmental group says public was misled on data center’s cancer-causing emissions SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - The Southern Environmental Law Center is asking the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services to reconsider its decision involving the Valara data center project in Spartanburg County, arguing the public did not have an opportunity to review updated information about the facility’s formaldehyde emissions. SELC sent a letter to DES on Oct. 1 asking the agency to reopen the public comment period for Valara’s air permit. Emissions estimates changed The dispute centers on formaldehyde emissions from natural gas-fired turbines planned for the data center. In its permitting documents, DES previously calculated controlled formaldehyde emissions at less than 10 tons per year. DES’ September permit sets a federally enforceable limit of less than 10 tons per year for any individual hazardous air pollutant, including formaldehyde. The permit also limits total hazardous air pollutants to less than 25 tons per year. SELC argues updated calculations put Valara’s controlled formaldehyde emissions at 10.58 tons per year. Frank Holleman, a senior attorney with SELC, said Valara’s original application relied on an emission reduction associated with technology the company was not using. “They reduced the estimates of that by using a reduction based on a technology they were not using and is no longer marketed,” Holleman said. DES later acknowledged that an incorrect emission factor had been used, according to SELC. The agency reviewed additional information provided by Valara and recalculated the emissions before issuing the permit. Holleman said the public has not been given enough information to independently review the updated calculation. “They also say they had some industry information that Valara provided, but they didn’t give the numbers. They didn’t show how they calculated it. And we’ve got this black box of additional information, all done behind closed doors,” Holleman said. DES says its permitting staff reviewed the application, supplemental information and public comments before issuing the Sept. 18 permit. The agency says it is required by law to issue the permit if an application demonstrates compliance with applicable state and federal regulations and the conditions of the permit. Why the 10-ton limit matters The permit places a limit of less than 10 tons per year on any individual hazardous air pollutant. Exceeding a permit limit could put the facility out of compliance and subject it to enforcement. Formaldehyde is classified as a known human carcinogen. Holleman said DES should give the public more information about how the updated emissions figure was calculated. “And what we’re saying is, no, no, no. The law doesn’t allow that. Simple fairness doesn’t allow it,” Holleman said. SELC is asking DES to reopen the public comment period. FOX Carolina reached out to DES for a response. The agency said it would answer questions the following day. Valara is also facing at least two active lawsuits, both led by the Southern Environmental Law Center. Valara had not responded as of the report. Spartanburg County officials travel to Virginia’s Data Center Alley The dispute comes as several Spartanburg County Council members and county officials travel to Loudoun County, Virginia, an area known for its concentration of data centers. According to a county travel notice, council members Monier Abusaft and Paul Abbott are traveling to Loudoun County from Sunday, Oct. 4, through Tuesday, Oct. 6. They are joined by county staff and others to learn from community leaders, utility executives and industry experts about Loudoun County’s experience with data center development. Monday’s schedule included a data center industry tour, discussions with Loudoun County supervisors and board members, a meeting with Amazon data center representatives and a session with other data center industry representatives. Tuesday’s schedule includes meetings with Loudoun Water, Loudoun County Economic Development and a state delegate. Loudoun County is about an hour and a half drive northwest of Washington, D.C. FOX Carolina reached out to county officials for comment but no one was available for an interview. Holleman, whose organization was told about the trip when it was announced Friday night, said he believes county leaders should hear from people who have raised concerns about data center development. “It really is yet another disgrace. And here they have county councilmen traveling up to Virginia. And if you look at their agenda, they’re meeting with one industry representative after another. Why are they not meeting with environmental advocates, community advocates, people who are concerned? Who do they represent? Do they represent the people of Spartanburg? Or do they represent the data center operators, owners, and investors and hedge funds in major corporations?” Holleman said. What Loudoun County says about data centers Loudoun County officials point to the tax revenue generated by the data center industry as a major economic benefit. According to Loudoun County, data centers generated $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue during fiscal year 2026, representing 39% of the county’s overall budget. The county’s adopted fiscal year 2027 budget projects $1.3 billion in data center revenue, or about 40% of the total budget. Loudoun County also says more than 17,000 direct and indirect data center-related jobs have been created. Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. artigo.texto: During their first face-to-face debate, candidates for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, Democrat William Lawrence and incumbent Republican Tom Barrett, faced off on immigration policy, the Iran war and data center development. Throughout the debate on Tuesday, Barrett continually referenced old statements posted by Lawrence on social media, while Lawrence repeatedly took a stance of connecting Barrett to President Donald Trump. A 'humane' immigration policy Upon being asked about budgeting for the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Lawrence said border security and ICE personnel should be regarded as separate. Lawrence said he supported a “secure border” paired with a “humane, efficient and orderly” immigration system. The congressional hopeful referenced the deaths of two Minneapolis, Minnesota, residents, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during Operation Metro Surge in January, saying the current immigration system is “un-American.” “We need to remember the words on the Statue of Liberty, which call us to our high values and remind us that we should welcome immigrants because we are immigrants,” Lawrence said. Barrett also established a desire for a “humane” system of immigration that is also “firm” and “fair.” He further advocated a need for a “secure border,” saying current border security legislation has reduced fentanyl overdose rates. The Department of Homeland Security's renewed focus on immigration enforcement under the second Trump administration led to a 31% decrease in the number of hours spent on fentanyl-related criminal investigations, according to a recent DHS Office of the Inspector General report. “We have to start with the border security first policy,” Barrett said. “Then we can have a conversation about the remaining immigration questions that are out there that we need to continue to work on.” Barrett also referred to Lawrence’s old social media posts advocating for “free and open migration” and “amnesty to all 12 million illegal immigrants in the country,” saying Lawrence’s plan would make “communities less safe.” Lawrence said they were “hypothetical statements" and later said he has since changed his mind. Future data center development Data centers have been a bipartisan source of strain in the Greater Lansing Area, with residents concerned about the hyper-scale projects' toll on the environment and the job market. Barrett said local governments should be in charge of data center development projects. The incumbent Republican candidate disparaged the pursuit of the Green New Deal due to it “taking away local control" from future development. “I've been on the side of local control,” Barrett said. “I've been on the side of local residents for this.” Lawrence, who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, championed his “nationally recognized” fight against data centers and advocacy for “safe AI.” He referenced past appearances at local council meetings where Lawrence condemned data center development, calling out Barrett’s lack of presence in such areas. “Residents across the political spectrum — Democrats, Independents, Republicans — have been fighting back and saying, ‘No, we don't want this in our communities,’” Lawrence said. The Iran War Barrett said he was “one of the very first Republicans” to vote against continuing the war in Iran. He said this “continued vote” was not of "convenience" but "conviction,” advocating for "separating" himself from Trump with regard to the nation’s part in the war. “Our national leaders, whether it's the president or anybody else, (have) to be contemplating the downstream effects of every decision that we make,” Barrett said. While Lawrence also supported an end to the conflict, he emphasized the economic impacts, saying, “We can’t afford for this war to continue.” Lawrence also criticized Barrett’s initial support of Trump, condemning his decision to “arm the Israeli government.” Support student media! Please consider donating to The State News and help fund the future of journalism. “We have got to put a stop to this,” Lawrence said. “I am a strong supporter that we should bring our money home, stop arming Israel and stop these endless wars that are not making us any safer.” Lawrence called for Barrett to “condemn the president for his words” in reference to recent comments suggesting that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if cleared to develop nuclear weaponry. While Barrett agreed that this language “wasn’t acceptable,” he fired back, challenging Lawrence to denounce leftist streamer Hasan Piker’s remarks that “Americans deserved 9/11.” Lawrence denounced Piker's comments, saying, “It was a despicable statement.” The event was livestreamed through WKAR’s YouTube channel on Tuesday and will air on Oct. 7 at 7 p.m. through local news outlets.

artigo.texto: KUALA LUMPUR – The deferment of Malaysia’s carbon tax implementation will give the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry (NRES) more time to finalise the regulatory and policy framework needed before emission caps are enforced. Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup said the decision to postpone the tax, which was initially scheduled to be introduced this year, was also influenced by global geopolitical developments that had contributed to energy price volatility. Speaking during a Concorde Club dialogue session at Wisma Bernama here today, he said the delay would provide industries with additional time to adjust while the government strengthens the legal framework governing carbon emissions. He said this included the National Carbon Market Policy and the proposed Climate Change Act, which he hoped could be tabled soon. “(The postponement) is also right because we need to have the proper framework and all that in place first. That’s why we’ve been successful in launching the National Carbon Market Policy and I hope that we can table the Climate Change Act soon. “Once that is up, then we have the framework and the policies all clearly in place, including the regulation, enforcement, the regulatory powers to give us to set the emission ceiling, and then we can know anything above the ceiling, then the carbon tax will come into place as a penalty to the polluters. “So, we’re not looking at this year for the carbon tax,” he said. On exemptions under the Clean Air Regulations, Arthur said industrial plants would only be considered for extensions if their operators could demonstrate concrete efforts to adopt the necessary technologies. He said the ministry would not issue further blanket exemptions, adding that operators whose existing exemptions expire by January next year would need to demonstrate progress towards compliance. He said 2030 remained the final deadline for all industries to achieve full compliance. “We had the Clean Air Regulations, which came into force in 2014, where plants, factories are not allowed to pollute above the 600 milligram per cubic meter…that was the regulation set…however, they’ve been enjoying exemptions up to this year. “So when I came in as the Minister, I decided that I will not be issuing any more exemptions because the technology is available, the technology is accessible and if we are to meet our target of net zero emissions by 2050, we need to have all this in place and we definitely need the cooperation from the industries as well,” he said. Arthur said operators would still be given sufficient time to conduct feasibility studies and carry out necessary modifications, but they would have to demonstrate meaningful progress to qualify for any temporary extension. The session, titled “Building A Resilient Malaysia: Environment, Climate And Our Future”, was moderated by Malaysian National News Agency (Bernama) chairman Datuk Seri Wong Chun Wai. Also present were Bernama chief executive officer Datin Paduka Nur-ul Afida Kamaludin and members of the local and foreign media based in Malaysia. - October 5, 2026 The post Carbon tax deferment gives NRES time to finalise regulatory, policy framework: Arthur appeared first on Scoop.

artigo.texto: Tecnologia criada na FEEC utiliza células cilíndricas, eletrólito aquoso e circulação interna por turbina, elimina mangueiras e bombas externas e pode evoluir para sistemas estacionários de armazenamento conectados à rede Pesquisadores da Faculdade de Engenharia Elétrica e de Computação da Unicamp (FEEC) desenvolveram uma nova arquitetura de bateria de fluxo voltada ao armazenamento estacionário de energia em larga escala, com aplicação potencial em sistemas associados à geração solar e eólica. A solução chama atenção por abandonar parte da configuração tradicional dessas baterias. Em vez de placas empilhadas, mangueiras e bombas externas para movimentação do eletrólito, a tecnologia desenvolvida na Unicamp utiliza eletrodos cilíndricos, células seladas individualmente e uma pequena turbina instalada dentro da própria bateria. - Brasil já tem 35 GW em energia eólica, concentra 90% das turbinas no Nordeste e agora enfrenta o gargalo que pode limitar a expansão até 2035 - China coloca em operação nova unidade de 660 MW em Zhongwei para dar estabilidade a base de 13 GW de energia renovável no deserto de Tengger e levar eletricidade até Hunan - Europa inaugura complexo híbrido com 242 MW de energia solar e bateria de 773 MWh na Bulgária e prepara expansão com mais 250 MW em turbinas eólicas - Nordeste já produz energia solar e eólica para exportar ao restante do Brasil, mas expansão esbarra em falta de armazenamento, gargalos na transmissão e impactos sobre fauna, flora e comunidades Nos ensaios realizados em laboratório, o equipamento alcançou aproximadamente 400 ciclos de carga e descarga, além de cerca de 98% de eficiência de carga e 82% de eficiência energética. O projeto nasceu no grupo Brazilian Renewable Energies (BREnergies) durante o doutorado do engenheiro eletricista João Pedro Aguiar dos Santos, sob orientação de César Pagan e coorientação de Hudson Zanin, ambos da FEEC. A arquitetura já resultou em um pedido de patente depositado no Instituto Nacional da Propriedade Industrial (INPI), com estratégia conduzida pela Agência de Inovação Inova Unicamp. Eletrodos cilíndricos substituem pilhas de placas Nas baterias de fluxo convencionais, os eletrodos normalmente são organizados em placas empilhadas. O eletrólito circula por tubos e mangueiras ligados a bombas externas. Essa arquitetura funciona, mas aumenta o número de conexões hidráulicas e, consequentemente, os pontos em que podem surgir falhas ou vazamentos. A proposta desenvolvida pela Unicamp parte de outra geometria. Cada célula é selada individualmente e utiliza dois eletrodos posicionados de forma concêntrica: um deles forma um anel maior, enquanto o outro ocupa a região interna. Essas células podem ser ligadas em série sem necessidade de formar uma pilha convencional. A mudança não é apenas geométrica. Ela altera também a maneira como o eletrólito se movimenta dentro do sistema. Pequena turbina dentro da bateria elimina bombas e mangueiras externas Um dos diferenciais centrais da tecnologia está no sistema de circulação interna. Uma pequena turbina instalada dentro da própria bateria movimenta o eletrólito. Com isso, o projeto dispensa parte das bombas e tubulações externas utilizadas em sistemas convencionais. A ideia é reduzir componentes hidráulicos e simplificar a arquitetura. Esse foi também um dos maiores desafios do trabalho. Segundo João Pedro Aguiar dos Santos, a equipe não encontrou equipamentos comerciais capazes de atender à configuração pretendida. Foi necessário construir praticamente toda a estrutura experimental. “Durante os estudos, percebi que não existia nenhum tipo de design ou setup experimental que pudéssemos comprar para montar a bateria. Isso foi um grande desafio, porque tivemos que montar desde as células até os reatores maiores para fazer os experimentos no laboratório.” O pesquisador também destaca que o desenvolvimento exigiu conhecimentos de diferentes áreas. “Foi um sistema multidisciplinar, unindo engenharia mecânica, eletrônica e eletroquímica, e tivemos que construir tudo do zero.” Bateria chegou a aproximadamente 400 ciclos sem aditivos Nos testes de carga e descarga, a bateria de fluxo giratório chegou a aproximadamente 400 ciclos sem a utilização de aditivos no eletrólito. Segundo os pesquisadores, esse desempenho superou referências de sistemas semelhantes avaliados sob condições comparáveis, que alcançaram cerca de 100 ciclos. Um dos problemas encontrados nesses sistemas é o crescimento de dendritos. Essas estruturas podem se formar durante os processos eletroquímicos e, em determinados casos, provocar curto-circuitos e comprometer a bateria. No protótipo da Unicamp, o ensaio não terminou por falha eletroquímica. A interrupção ocorreu devido a uma limitação mecânica no anel coletor responsável pelo contato elétrico do eletrodo interno. Esse detalhe importa porque indica que a limitação observada não estava diretamente relacionada à química da bateria. A próxima etapa será justamente aprimorar esse componente. Pesquisadores querem superar 3 mil ciclos A equipe trabalha agora com a perspectiva de melhorar a durabilidade do sistema. Além da mudança no mecanismo de contato elétrico, o projeto prevê a utilização de aditivos no eletrólito. A expectativa dos pesquisadores é superar 3 mil ciclos de operação. Nos testes já realizados, a bateria apresentou aproximadamente 98% de eficiência de carga e 82% de eficiência energética. Em uma demonstração prática, o sistema conseguiu operar durante duas horas alimentando LEDs e um ventilador. O objetivo dessa etapa ainda não era demonstrar uma aplicação comercial em grande escala, mas verificar o comportamento integrado da bateria durante a operação. Sistema eletrônico acompanha até pH e formação de dendritos Os pesquisadores também precisaram criar um sistema próprio de gerenciamento. artigo.texto: Três data centers ficaram com os 228 MW de capacidade da rede básica de transmissão ofertados em São Paulo no primeiro processo competitivo da Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast), realizado na terça (6/10). Dois deles são da norte-americana CloudHQ. O resultado foi divulgado nesta quarta (7/10) pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). A CloudHQ venceu com a Pahlavan One e a Pahlavan Three, empresas pelas quais desenvolve um campus de data centers em Paulínia (SP). O terceiro projeto é da Digital DC Brasil, que opera no país sob a marca NextStream. A disputa envolveu a margem de escoamento em quatro pontos de conexão no estado. Sete empreendimentos participaram, com 451 MW de demanda habilitada, quase o dobro da capacidade disponível. Os lances médios ficaram na ordem de R$ 800 por kW, segundo a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Transmissão de Energia Elétrica (Abrate). Foi a primeira vez que a capacidade remanescente da rede básica foi alocada por meio de um mecanismo competitivo, segundo o ONS. O processo era a etapa final da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026, encerrada nesta quarta em cerimônia na sede do operador. O diretor-geral do ONS, Marcio Rea, avalia que o primeiro ciclo comprovou a efetividade do novo modelo de acesso. “Além dos volumes expressivos de capacidade analisada e viabilizada, realizamos com sucesso o primeiro Processo Competitivo da Pnast, consolidando um ambiente mais previsível, transparente e eficiente para investidores, consumidores e para o planejamento da expansão do sistema elétrico brasileiro”, disse. Para a Abrate, que representa as transmissoras de energia, a política é necessária para disciplinar a fila de pedidos de conexão à rede básica diante, de um lado, da expansão das fontes eólica e solar e da geração distribuída (GD) e, de outro, da chegada de grandes cargas, como data centers, projetos de hidrogênio verde e a eletrificação da demanda. A associação avalia que o modelo coloca o Brasil à frente de outros países no atendimento à demanda dos data centers. “Enquanto diversos países enfrentam dificuldades para atender à crescente demanda computacional, recorrendo com frequência à geração própria local para evitar a dependência da rede elétrica tradicional, o Brasil tomou a dianteira”, afirma a presidente executiva da Abrate, Talita Porto, em nota. Segundo a entidade, Rea foi convidado a apresentar os resultados da política em Washington (EUA), no início de novembro, em evento que reunirá operadores elétricos de todo o mundo. Quem levou a capacidade A Pahlavan Ventures One e a Pahlavan Ventures Three aparecem, em lista de solicitações de acesso publicada pelo ONS (.pdf), como controladas pela CloudHQ e associadas a um data center em Paulínia. A CloudHQ lançou o campus de Paulínia em março de 2023, com investimento anunciado de até US$ 3 bilhões. O projeto prevê três prédios com 48 MW de capacidade de TI cada, com possibilidade de expansão para seis. A Digital DC Brasil tem um data center no campus de Tamboré, em Santana de Parnaíba (SP), e pediu ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), em maio de 2025, a conexão de nova carga para ampliar a estrutura. A NextStream opera 11 data centers, quase todos na América Latina. A empresa surgiu depois que a gestora britânica Actis comprou, em 2023, ativos da Nabiax, construídos originalmente pela Telefónica. ONS analisou 43 GW em pedidos Na temporada, o ONS registrou 367 cadastramentos de empreendimentos de geração e consumo, que somam mais de 20 GW em solicitações de acesso, distribuídas por 64 barramentos do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Somada a fase transitória da política, o operador analisou mais de 43 GW em pedidos de acesso à rede básica. Desse total, cerca de 30,7 GW foram viabilizados ou habilitados. A experiência da primeira temporada servirá de base para ajustes nas próximas edições, segundo o diretor de TI, Relacionamento com Agentes e Assuntos Regulatórios do ONS, Maurício de Souza. A partir de 2027, serão duas temporadas de acesso por ano. O cronograma da primeira delas já foi publicado pelo ONS (.pdf). A Pnast foi instituída pelo decreto 12.772/2025 e reorganiza a fila de pedidos de conexão de grandes projetos ao SIN. O ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira, afirmou que a política substitui a lógica de espera por “planejamento, critérios técnicos e processos competitivos”. Editado por Gustavo Gaudarde
