artigo.texto: A capital paulista recebe, entre os dias 6 e 8 de outubro de 2026, a edição de estreia do Data Center World Brasil, conferência internacional voltada à infraestrutura crítica de tecnologia da informação. Conforme anunciado pela organizadora Informa Markets, o congresso ocorre nas instalações do São Paulo Expo, funcionando em paralelo às atividades do evento Futurecom. O encontro reúne mais de 2.500 executivos e cerca de 300 congressistas com o objetivo de discutir os rumos da capacidade de processamento em larga escala no território nacional. Segundo informações divulgadas pela promotora, a agenda prioriza os impactos decorrentes da rápida expansão dos ecossistemas de inteligência artificial sobre a malha operacional brasileira. A programação foi estruturada para contrapor a crescente demanda por poder computacional aos desafios técnicos de suprimento elétrico, conectividade em hiperescala e segurança jurídica. A entidade promotora sustenta que os debates ocorrem em uma conjuntura na qual decisões regulatórias e logísticas moldarão a atratividade do país perante o fluxo global de capital intensivo voltado à computação em nuvem. Competitividade tributária e regime especial para infraestrutura De acordo com a programação detalhada pela Informa Markets, a rodada de abertura do congresso concentra-se nos instrumentos de atração de capital produtivo, com ênfase no debate sobre o Redata — regime especial de tributação formulado especificamente para o setor de processamento de dados. A organizadora aponta que o painel inaugural visa mapear os efeitos dessa política sobre a competitividade fiscal brasileira em um horizonte estimado entre cinco e dez anos. Especialistas escalados para a plenária avaliam como o alinhamento de diretrizes entre o Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) e as alíquotas estaduais de ICMS incide sobre a viabilidade financeira das construções civis e da importação de insumos tecnológicos de ponta. A promotora assinala que a discussão tributária transcende o escopo contábil e assume caráter geopolítico. Países vizinhos na América Latina disputam aportes de provedores globais conhecidos como hyperscalers, tornando a clareza nas regras de incentivo e desoneração de bens de capital um diferencial competitivo relevante. O cronograma do evento prevê a participação de lideranças do Ministério das Comunicações, do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (Brasscom) e da gestora Patria Investments para abordar entraves de funding, modelos de garantias e arquitetura de crédito de longo prazo. Restrições energéticas e viabilidade de suprimento elétrico A disponibilidade de potência elétrica desponta como o principal gargalo estrutural identificado pelos organizadores do congresso. De acordo com a Informa Markets, a transição para clusters computacionais dedicados a modelos generativos de inteligência artificial multiplicou o consumo por metro quadrado útil nos centros de processamento. A programação técnica inclui mesas dedicadas à análise da intermitência da matriz limpa, modelos de autoprodução de energia e sistemas avançados de armazenamento para garantir que as instalações sustentem contratos de nível de serviço com operação contínua e ininterrupta. O debate abrange as variáveis determinantes na seleção de sítios imobiliários industriais para a instalação dessas estruturas físicas. Conforme destacam os documentos informativos da organização, contratantes corporativos examinam indicadores de performance que exigem equilíbrio milimétrico entre proximidade dos anéis de transmissão, redundância de subestações e proximidade dos grandes polos consumidores para evitar perdas de transmissão e oscilações de voltagem. A busca por áreas com capacidade de expansão modular de megawattagem tornou-se premissa mandatória nos planos de negócios do segmento. - Segurança de suprimento: análise de interconexões com a Rede Básica do Sistema Interligado Nacional. - Contratos de longo prazo: estruturação de acordos bilaterais de compra de energia renovável certificada. - Sistemas de contenção de falhas: implementação de usinas de geração de backup e módulos de baterias químicas. - Arquitetura de missão crítica: redundância elétrica baseada em tolerância a falhas sem paradas programadas. Transformação da arquitetura térmica e expansão do resfriamento líquido A Informa Markets relata que a evolução de processadores gráficos e aceleradores de tensores provocou uma ruptura nos padrões tradicionais de engenharia predial. O diretor do Data Center World Brasil, Leonardo Benedicto, declarou na apresentação do fórum que a inteligência artificial exige repensar integralmente o ecossistema dos edifícios dedicados, articulando fornecimento energético, controle microclimático e flexibilidade modular para acomodar atualizações tecnológicas contínuas ao longo do ciclo de vida dos empreendimentos. Conforme sustentam os relatórios técnicos que embasam os painéis, a densidade energética por rack ultrapassou patamares históricos, forçando o abandono gradual dos sistemas convencionais de resfriamento exclusivamente por ar comprimido. O congresso programou demonstrações sobre o avanço de soluções de resfriamento líquido direto no chip (liquid cooling ou direct-to-chip) e tecnologias de imersão total. Essa migração técnica reduz substancialmente o indicador de eficácia no uso de energia (PUE), permitindo elevar a capacidade de cálculo instalada no mesmo espaço físico sem sobrecarregar os limites térmicos dos componentes semicondutores. Conectividade avançada e impactos macroeconômicos regionais Outro vetor abordado na agenda técnica trata da infraestrutura de telecomunicações associada às rotas de cabos submarinos e redes de fibra óptica de alta capacidade. A entidade promotora salienta que a proximidade física com pontos de troca de tráfego e nós de distribuição na borda (edge computing) dita o nível de latência suportado

artigo.texto: Yesterday morning we launched our National Data Center Tracker, and within hours we had a major new project to add to it, as well as legislation aimed at preventing projects like it from being built on federal public lands. The ground is moving fast. NPR reported Wednesday that nuclear startup Valar Atomics is proposing a massive data center complex on more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land near Price, Utah. The project, called Project Beehive, would include data centers powered by roughly 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and facilities for storing nuclear waste. According to company documents reviewed by NPR, the reactors would collectively produce around 9.6 gigawatts of electricity for the data centers, plus additional thermal energy for other industrial uses. Utah currently produces around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average, though its peak generating capacity can reach roughly 10 gigawatts during the summer. At almost the same time, Oregon Senator Ron Wyden introduced legislation that would prohibit the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands for new data centers and associated infrastructure nationwide. Project Beehive Valar’s federal proposal is still at the beginning of the process. BLM’s Utah office confirmed to NPR that it has received the company’s application and is reviewing it for completeness. The agency said that if the application moves forward through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, the public will have opportunities to weigh in. Valar is already laying out a timeline. Company documents call for non-nuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. The 9,000-plus acres of BLM land are only part of the project. Utah state records show that Valar also sought a special-use lease covering roughly 640 acres of state trust land in Carbon County. The Trust Lands Administration Board unanimously approved the lease on September 17, according to KSL. The federal application is much larger. Project Beehive would spread across more than 9,000 acres near Price and combine the data centers, hundreds of reactors, nuclear fuel production and nuclear waste storage in a single proposed complex. And we’d already come across Valar before any of this surfaced. We’ve Seen Valar Before Our tracker already contained another Valar project near Green River, Utah. The company had applied for roughly 10,200 acres of BLM land for a data center co-located with small nuclear reactors before deciding not to pursue the site. We kept it in the tracker as withdrawn. That history looks a little more important today. A roughly 10,200-acre Valar proposal near Green River appeared in the federal record and was later dropped. Now another Valar proposal has surfaced near Price involving more than 9,000 acres of BLM land and hundreds of nuclear reactors. The Public Lands Fight Is Already Bigger Than Valar Our Public Lands tracker now has 16 data center sites sitting on land the public owns, each tied to a public document placing it there. South of Boise, Rhea Data’s Blacks Creek Campus would put a four-million-square-foot data center campus on 3,226 acres of BLM land beside Blacks Creek Reservoir. In Nevada, Copia Digital’s Bergen Data Center is proposed on 744 acres of BLM land north of Las Vegas. In Arizona, the Frontier Data Center would occupy 620 acres of BLM land in Pinal County, while the Harquahala Data Center would occupy another 275 acres in Maricopa County. All three remain proposed. The tracker also includes public-land projects that are much further along or have already run into trouble. Townsite Solar 2 outside Boulder City, Nevada was proposed on 89 acres of BLM land about 1.6 miles from Lake Mead National Recreation Area. Its approval was challenged, and BLM later asked the Interior Board of Land Appeals to set aside the agency’s own approval so the application could undergo additional review. Federal land controlled by other agencies is part of the buildout too. The tracker includes proposed or active data center projects at Energy Department sites in Kentucky, Ohio and South Carolina, along with projects on state-owned land and other BLM applications scattered across the West. And the 16 mapped sites still don’t capture everything sitting in the federal pipeline. BLM records also contain applications that don’t yet have enough public location information to map, including a Prometheus Hyperscale proposal in Wyoming involving rights-of-way for a road, telecommunications line and water pipeline, and another Valar nuclear-powered data center proposal in Utah whose public record still doesn’t disclose its size or exact location. The federal push behind these projects is coming from the top. President Trump’s July 2025 executive order directed federal agencies to make appropriate federal sites available for qualifying data center projects, and our tracker shows Interior later telling BLM state directors to identify public lands that could take data centers. Now there’s movement in the other direction. Wyden’s new legislation would prohibit the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands for new data centers and associated infrastructure. His office said the bill followed reporting that more than 17,000 acres of public land across Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, Idaho, Wyoming and Utah were being considered for data center development. None of that changes the law today. Valar’s application is still before BLM, the other proposed projects remain in various stages of the process, and Wyden’s legislation has only been introduced. But one day after launching the tracker, there’s already another 9,000-plus-acre project to follow and another major federal response to add to the record. artigo.texto: A Researcher in Denmark Aims to Reduce AI Reliance on Data Centers New Technology Can Move AI Calculations to the Electricity Grid The EU [European Union] wants to make data centres a more sustainable part of the energy system. A researcher from the leading energy research university in Europe, Aalborg University, has developed a technology that can allow existing energy plants to take over part of the AI calculations and thus relieve both data centers and electricity grids. Data centres are crucial for Europe’s digital development, but their increasing electricity consumption is also putting pressure on the energy system. This summer, the European Commission published a strategic roadmap for digitalisation and artificial intelligence in the energy sector. Among other things, it will promote digital solutions for optimising the electricity grid and ensure that data centres are integrated more sustainably into Europe’s energy system. According to the European Commission, data centers already account for 2.5 percent of the EU’s electricity consumption. Therefore, a model for tripartite agreements between data center operators, energy players and public authorities is being worked on to support a more sustainable integration of data centers. The European agenda hits directly at the challenge that Associate Professor Subham Sahoo from Aalborg University in Denmark is trying to solve with the technology Power to Compute, P2C. Instead of letting all AI calculations take place in data centers, he will use parts of the existing energy infrastructure to carry out part of the calculation work. “We are facing a challenge where both the green transition, electrification of companies and digital development pull in the same direction. Everyone needs more power and more capacity. Therefore, we also need to think about how we can use the existing infrastructure more wisely,” says Subham Sahoo, associate professor at the Department of Energy at Aalborg University. Energy Plants Can Help Data Centers The basic idea of P2C is that some of the electronic devices that are already connected to the electricity grid can also contribute to calculations. For example, it can be control electronics in a solar cell system. Instead of just handling power, the device can receive a small computational task from a data center, solve it, and send back the response. In this way, P2C will not replace data centers, but distribute part of their computational work on equipment that is already in the energy system. The technology thus links two tracks in the EU’s new strategy: the use of AI and digital solutions in the energy sector, and a more sustainable integration of data centers. “We do not see P2C as a competitor to the data centers. We see it as a supplement. The data centers will continue to be necessary, but if we can move some of the computational work to existing energy infrastructure, we can reduce the need for new physical infrastructure,” says Subham Sahoo. Can Reduce Power Consumption and Cooling Preliminary calculations indicate that P2C can lower data centers’ energy consumption by about 10 percent and reduce the cost of cooling the servers by 10 to 20 percent. The results are early, and it is still too early to draw definitive conclusions about the large-scale effect. The perspective is that the data centers can solve more tasks without a corresponding expansion of their physical capacity, while at the same time making better use of existing equipment in the energy system. The Next Step Is Testing Outside the Laboratory P2C has so far been tested in the laboratory. Several Danish companies have already shown interest in participating in a large-scale trial, and according to the researcher, the technology can be brought closer to practical application if the right partners and data are in place. “This is not something we see as a distant vision far into the future. Our preliminary results are promising, and the ambition is to get out of the laboratory and into real test environments as soon as possible,” says Subham Sahoo. Contact information: Subham Sahoo Associate Professor, AAU Energy Aalborg University (+45) 9141 0380 sssa@energy.aau.dk power2compute.ai Caspar Birk Press Advisor Aalborg University (+45) 2249 1303 cabi@adm.aau.dk Aalborg University (AAU) is a Danish public research university conducting interdisciplinary research across science, engineering, social sciences, humanities and health. en.aau.dk

artigo.texto: AI Energy Parks: From Speed to Power to Power That Lasts Why This Matters Up to 10 years. That's how long a large new grid connection can take in North America. So developers are chasing time-to-power, and they should be. But a site that gets power first and gets the architecture wrong has only traded one bottleneck for another. Every shortcut taken to energize on schedule becomes technology debt, and the bill comes due when the load changes, the technology moves, and the site has to be rebuilt while the data center is running. The alternative is the AI Energy Park. Think of it as a microgrid built for AI: a large, optimized, behind-the-meter power system designed for the scale, density, and dynamic load of AI data centers. It integrates grid supply, on-site generation, storage, power distribution, and controllable demand into one coordinated, software-enabled campus. But speed to power can’t be the only objective. Sites designed only to hit an energization date lock in today's assumptions: boundaries drawn around the first equipment, bespoke software, interfaces that fit one configuration. Over a multi-decade lifecycle, generation technologies, market rules, utility capacity, and AI load profiles will all change. An AI Energy Park should be treated as long-term infrastructure, not a temporary bridge to utility service. The goal is not to predict the next 20 years perfectly, but to build an architecture that can evolve without costly rip-and-replace cycles. So how do you get both: power on a credible schedule and an architecture built to last? Stop designing every site from scratch. A Repeatable Model for Speed and Certainty Custom designs add engineering effort, integration complexity, cost, and execution risk. They also force each project to repeat key decisions about system boundaries, operations, protection, procurement, and commissioning. Repeatability speeds delivery. Standard power blocks, controls, cybersecurity zones, data structures, and commissioning methods can be validated once and adapted to each site. This allows for earlier procurement and lets engineers focus on site-specific needs. Four principles make that model scalable and future-ready: - Connectivity links assets and systems, reducing integration effort and speeding commissioning. - Interoperability allows systems from different vendors to work together, preserving choice and simplifying expansion. - Visibility gives operators a real-time view of system health, capacity, risk, and performance. - Optimization uses that visibility to balance cost, reliability, emissions, and grid services. Design for Lifecycle Value Over a 20-year horizon, generation technologies, utility capacity, power density, market rules, software platforms, and renewable economics will all evolve. A future-ready design preserves options so the site can respond without rebuilding its core power architecture. That means designing for change through configuration and modular expansion. Standards-based interfaces, clear system boundaries, repeatable building blocks, and shared digital capabilities allow technologies and vendors to change without redesigning the entire system, reduce dependence on any single supplier, and allow capacity to be added as demand becomes firm. The objective is not a static design that is frozen on day one, but a durable framework that can absorb innovation over time. Reliability for AI Workloads A flexible Energy Park can operate in grid-connected, islanded, or hybrid modes; add generation, storage, and renewables without rebuilding supervisory controls; and actively manage demand. For AI workloads, coordinated controls across UPS, batteries, generation, and the grid provide load smoothing and fault ride-through. This protects compute uptime while preventing rapid load changes and grid disturbances from cascading across the campus. Reliability depends on coordinated system behavior, not just redundant equipment. The controls must detect changing conditions, protect critical loads, manage transitions between operating modes, and support predictable recovery. Validated sequences and clear visibility into available capacity help operators act before asset limits become campus-wide disruptions. Value Beyond the Fence Line A well-designed Energy Park can operate as a grid asset rather than an isolated private power plant: a flexible participant that can support both the anchor load and the broader energy system. For utilities, measurable curtailment, load shifting, and self-supply create more flexible interconnection options and can defer infrastructure during constrained periods. For communities, purpose-built infrastructure can strengthen local reliability, support future electrification, and provide measurable grid services. Community acceptance will depend on making those benefits tangible and transparent, while addressing concerns about local cost, reliability, land use, noise, emissions, water, and construction. Where market rules and utility agreements allow, these capabilities can also support demand response, reserve services, renewable balancing, and restoration. These remain secondary; the primary mission is reliable power for the data center. Power That Lasts Speed to power delivers the first megawatt. Power that lasts protects the investment over the decades that follow. A purpose-built Energy Park must absorb volatile AI loads, ride through grid disturbances, adapt as supply options and technologies change, and contribute measurable value beyond the fence line. A repeatable reference design and delivery model is how an Energy Park delivers both: power on a credible schedule, and an architecture built to last. artigo.texto: Council moves to extend Lexington's pause on data center development, restart zoning process In a lengthy public hearing, Council heard from dozens of residents who pressed for more time to get Lexington data center regulations right. Following a lengthy public hearing Tuesday, Lexington’s Urban County Council moved to extend Fayette County’s pause on data center development until October 31, 2027, as the body continues working to regulate them. Spurred on by the sale of a former Lexmark property to a data center developer, Council has spent the last few months studying the facilities, along with their environmental and electrical grid impacts. In June, the body unanimously passed a moratorium – or temporary pause – on their development in Fayette County, effective through October 31, 2026. Council had also directed the Planning Commission to develop a zoning ordinance text amendment (updates to Lexington’s zoning laws) so it could modernize its regulation of data centers. Councilmembers discussed the Planning Commission’s recommendations Tuesday after a public hearing that lasted for several hours and saw nearly 60 residents and individuals sign up to address the Council. From representatives of Lexington’s business community to members of the Bluegrass Democratic Socialists of America, their message was clear: Lexington needs more time to properly regulate data centers, including determining where they should go and what types of restrictions they should have. Most speakers opposed data centers or wanted much stricter limits on the facilities. Many in the room called for a ban on hyperscale data centers (those with an energy capacity exceeding 25 megawatts) and some supported a complete ban on new data centers in Fayette County. Speakers raised several concerns about data centers’ potential land use impacts, from electricity and water consumption to higher utility bills, strains on the electrical grid, noise, pollution, waste heat and potential negative health effects for nearby residents. Representatives of Commerce Lexington, banks, telecommunications companies, and the University of Kentucky stressed that smaller data centers and server rooms already exist in Lexington and support local businesses and institutions here, particularly those that rely on data storage and processing, from hospitals to schools. They cautioned against overly broad restrictions that could hurt Lexington’s economic development. The deciding motions came from District 1 Councilmember Tyler Morton and District 4 Councilmember Emma Curtis. Morton successfully moved to remove most of the Planning Commission’s recommendations for data centers and server rooms from the draft zoning ordinance text amendment (ZOTA), allowing the Council to move forward with its own approach to regulating data centers in Fayette County. Morton had previously questioned the fairness of the recommendations, which proposed allowing smaller-scale data centers in Lexington’s industrial and commercial zones – which are concentrated in District 1 and on the city’s northside. Morton also successfully moved to advance a resolution launching a new zoning ordinance text amendment process that will look at creating a separate zoning category for data centers. The new process will not be under the tight timeline Lexington’s Planning Commission faced to deliver its recommendations to Council, and it will include more opportunities for residents to engage, Morton told CivicLex in an interview after the hearing. Curtis moved to advance a resolution extending the current data center moratorium through to October 31, 2027. Morton and Curtis’ resolutions will move through Council’s regular legislative process, with final votes expected at an upcoming Council meeting.

artigo.texto: Raleigh leaders voted to put a pause on developing new, larger data centers for six months, as community advocates push for a 32-month pause to study the impacts and give residents more say. The measure passed in a 7-1 vote, with councilmember Christina Jones voting against the moratorium. A group advocating for a longer moratorium expressed frustration after the moratorium passed, saying it wasn't long enough. Other WRAL Top Stories The moratorium is shorter than the 12-month pause Apex approved in April and the 18-month pause Cary adopted in August. Raleigh’s draft sets aside 60 days for research and drafting rules, followed by 120 days to move proposed changes through the legislative process. Mary Black, who served on Raleigh City Council from 2022 to 2024 and is now a community organizer for the Raleigh Anti-Data Center Coalition, says that leaves too little time to involve people who could live near the facilities. “What we want is transparency and input in the process, and that’s going to take more than six months,” Black said. WRAL contacted Mayor Janet Cowell and every council member on Monday and Tuesday morning to ask why six months was chosen, whether that would be enough time, and whether they would support an extension if new guidelines were not ready. They had not responded as of publication. Why six months? The draft ordinance says Raleigh needs time to address the development, infrastructure, and environmental impacts of larger data centers. It identifies potential concerns, including electricity and water demand, noise, light pollution and heat islands. While Raleigh has general industrial development rules, the draft says it lacks standards specific to larger data centers. It also warns that infrastructure needed to serve those facilities could create significant burdens for the city’s water utility and its ratepayers. During the first 60 days, staff would study impacts, draft proposed changes and examine how other communities regulate data centers. A team of staff experts would coordinate that work. The final 120 days would be used to propose code amendments and follow the legislative adoption process. The draft calls that six-month period necessary to complete the work. It does not explain why Raleigh’s schedule is shorter than those in Cary and Apex. Black said adopting regulations within six months may be possible, but meaningful community engagement would take longer. She said the coalition’s request for 32 months would allow more time for research, rulemaking and public involvement. In September, Cowell told WRAL the pause would allow a conversation about an issue that had become highly emotional. She also said Raleigh wanted to protect residents while preserving its role as a technology and research hub. “This is a tech center,” Cowell said. Neighboring towns have longer timelines Cary unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium Aug. 27 to study power demand and grid capacity, water consumption, noise and vibration, site design and buffering. Staff will provide progress updates, with a decision on an ordinance expected in February 2028. Cary’s schedule includes technical studies, community engagement and regional coordination through spring 2027, followed by draft ordinance review that summer and public hearings and board consideration before a council decision. Apex unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on April 14 after a developer withdrew a proposed data center near the Shearon Harris Nuclear Plant. Mayor Jacques Gilbert previously told WRAL the pause would allow more research into water and electricity use and potential costs to residents. Pushback over neighborhood impacts and transparency Raleigh’s debate follows substantial opposition to a proposed data center near Jones Sausage and Rock Quarry roads in Southeast Raleigh. In August, 30 of the 32 people expected to speak at a public hearing had signed up in opposition, according to a sign-up sheet WRAL obtained. The developer subsequently withdrew its annexation request. Mayor Pro Tem, Jane Harrison, said in August that she wanted residents to better understand the approval process and wanted more notice when larger projects came before the Board of Adjustment. “I just want to make sure that we all understand how this process currently works,” Harrison said. Black said public hearings alone do not provide enough opportunity to reach residents and understand their concerns. She wants council members to engage people where they live, work and play. Supporters point to jobs, tax revenue and innovation Data center supporters say the facilities can generate investment and tax revenue while supporting the technology behind modern services and artificial intelligence. During a recent visit to Duke Energy’s Roxboro coal plant in Person County, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright described data centers as “intelligence factories” and linked their growth to the Trump administration’s economic agenda. “So we can spur economic growth, generate revenues for local communities, drive up wages for workers,” Wright said. “To do that, you need more energy, not less energy.” In a statement to WRAL, the Data Center Coalition, an industry group representing companies including Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta, urged local leaders to pursue regulations instead of moratoriums. “Rather than enacting moratoriums, which will discourage investment and send signals that the community is closed for business, local leaders should work with the industry and all stakeholders to establish reasonable regulatory frameworks that meet the needs of the community without deterring the industry and the benefits it can bring,” said Christy Tarallo, the group’s Southeast director of government affairs. artigo.texto: Companhia reforça investimentos em infraestrutura elétrica, transformadores e geração de energia, mirando o avanço dos centros de dados até 2030 A WEG (BOV:WEGE3) reforçou sua estratégia de crescimento em centros de dados e infraestrutura elétrica durante o WEG Day 2026, realizado na sexta-feira (02/10). A companhia apresentou planos de expansão da capacidade produtiva até 2030, com destaque para transformadores, geradores, sistemas elétricos e soluções de refrigeração. A avaliação apresentada pelo banco responsável pela análise é de que a WEG ampliou sua posição competitiva para capturar a demanda relacionada à expansão dos centros de dados. A companhia reúne em seu portfólio soluções de transmissão e distribuição de energia, máquinas rotativas, automação e revestimentos industriais, além de equipamentos voltados à infraestrutura necessária para essas operações. Os centros de dados aparecem como um dos principais vetores de crescimento da WEG. A companhia estima que seu portfólio atual, combinado às expansões planejadas até 2030, poderá representar uma fatia equivalente a aproximadamente 15% do custo de construção de um centro de dados, sem considerar os servidores. O mercado brasileiro ainda apresenta espaço para expansão. O país conta com aproximadamente 215 centros de dados, enquanto os Estados Unidos possuem 4.766 unidades. Além disso, apenas cerca de 30% dos dados gerados no Brasil são processados em estruturas instaladas no próprio país. A WEG participa de diferentes etapas da implantação desses projetos. Na primeira, negociada diretamente com o cliente final, fornece equipamentos de alta tensão, como subestações, transformadores de potência, painéis elétricos e sistemas de proteção. Na etapa seguinte, a companhia oferece soluções de média e baixa tensão, incluindo estruturas elétricas pré-montadas, transformadores a seco, sistemas de distribuição de energia, equipamentos para energia crítica, motores, inversores e geradores. A atuação também se estende à refrigeração e à geração auxiliar de energia, principalmente por meio do fornecimento de equipamentos para fabricantes desses sistemas. A procura por transformadores permanece elevada nos principais mercados atendidos pela WEG. Nos Estados Unidos, os centros de dados responderam por 18,5% das entradas de pedidos de transformadores da companhia nos últimos 12 meses. A empresa já está envolvida em projetos de grande escala. Um deles prevê 23 transformadores de 70 megavolt-amperes cada, enquanto outro contempla oito equipamentos de 250 megavolt-amperes. No México, a WEG fornece 14 transformadores a seco de 3,3 megavolt-amperes para um projeto. No Brasil, a companhia também atende iniciativas ligadas à expansão da infraestrutura de centros de dados. Segundo a administração, a participação em diferentes etapas da cadeia aumenta a vantagem competitiva da WEG, já que concorrentes tendem a concentrar sua atuação em partes específicas desse mercado. A estratégia de expansão inclui investimentos relevantes na produção de geradores. A primeira etapa prevê R$ 122 milhões e tem conclusão estimada para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Com o projeto, a capacidade diária deverá passar de 10 para 20 geradores. A segunda fase envolve R$ 718 milhões em investimentos e prevê maior integração da produção. A meta é alcançar uma capacidade de 50 geradores por dia até 2030. Mesmo nesse nível, a produção corresponderia a aproximadamente 30% da demanda do maior cliente da companhia, indicando espaço para a WEG buscar novos contratos à medida que a capacidade produtiva avance. A WEG investiu R$ 1,4 bilhão no primeiro semestre de 2026, equivalente a 4,3% da receita. O percentual ficou acima da média histórica e teve como prioridades os transformadores e equipamentos associados à expansão da infraestrutura elétrica. Para o médio prazo, a companhia espera manter os investimentos entre 3% e 5% da receita. Entre os projetos previstos estão ampliações na produção de transformadores no México, na Colômbia, em Washington, nos Estados Unidos, e em unidades brasileiras localizadas em Betim, Itajubá e Gravataí. Às 14h39 de segunda-feira (05/10), as ações WEG eram negociadas a R$ 50,48, com queda de 1,89%. O papel abriu o pregão a R$ 52,50, mesmo nível da máxima registrada até o momento, e chegou à mínima de R$ 49,95. Nas últimas 52 semanas, WEGE3 oscilou entre R$ 35,41 e R$ 54,53, mostrando que o mercado segue acompanhando de perto as perspectivas de crescimento e execução dos investimentos da companhia. Com isso, a ação operava abaixo da abertura e próxima da mínima do dia. O movimento ocorre enquanto investidores avaliam as perspectivas de crescimento da WEG e os investimentos necessários para ampliar a capacidade produtiva, especialmente diante da demanda relacionada aos centros de dados e à infraestrutura de energia. A WEG atua no setor de equipamentos elétricos e industriais, com operações que abrangem motores, geradores, transformadores, automação, sistemas de energia e outras soluções utilizadas na infraestrutura industrial. A diversificação do portfólio permite à companhia atender diferentes etapas de projetos de eletrificação e expansão da capacidade energética. QUER SABER COMO GANHAR MAIS? artigo.texto: Romania’s renewable energy associations have called on the country’s energy regulator, ANRE, to slash the required financial guarantee for standalone battery projects sixfold, from EUR 30,000 per MW of installed capacity to EUR 5,000 per MW. They claim the “excessive” guarantee amount hinders investment in energy storage amid increasing flexibility needs. The current regulation, issued by the Romanian Energy Regulatory Authority (ANRE) this summer, treats energy storage projects and new power generation plants equally, despite considerable differences in investment profile, revenue structure, and economic risks, according to the Romanian Wind Energy Association (RWEA) and the Romanian Photovoltaic Industry Association (RPIA), Economica reported. “Independent (standalone) electricity storage facilities have a distinct technical and functional specificity compared to electricity generation capacities. Consequently, the investment profile, revenue structure, and related economic risks differ considerably and require a proportionate approach in terms of the financial guarantee related to the issuance of the establishment authorization,” according to RWEA and RPIA. Battery projects would face a disproportionate financial burden if treated equally as power generation plants The uniform treatment creates an unequal financial burden for standalone storage projects, which may affect their economic viability and create an additional barrier to their development, amid the increased need for flexibility and at a time when more and more investors plan to install large-scale batteries, they claim. The two associations have sent an amendment to ANRE calling for the required financial guarantee for standalone battery energy storage projects to be set at EUR 5/kW of installed capacity, down from EUR 30/kW. Romania has tightened the rules for energy projects in an attempt to filter out “serious” investors from “speculators.” Other measures include raising the financial guarantee for grid connection from 5% of the connection fee to 20% and introducing auctions to allocate grid capacity. Romania’s total battery storage capacity currently stands at about 2.31 GWh and is expected to reach 4 GWh by the end of 2027, according to Economica’s report.

artigo.texto: Finlândia interrompe construção de data centers do Google pelo impacto ambiental De acordo com a Agência de Supervisão Finlandesa, mais de 300 hectares de floresta foram cortados sem avaliação de impacto A Agência de Supervisão Finlandesa (LVV) ordenou nesta terça-feira, 6, que o Google suspenda a construção de novos ‘data centers’ em dois municípios da Finlândia até no máximo 23 de outubro de 2026, à espera de uma avaliação de seu impacto ambiental. Estes projetos fazem parte de um investimento de 13 bilhões de euros (R$ 72,7 bilhões) anunciado na Finlândia, o maior investimento da gigante tecnológica americana na Europa no âmbito da inteligência artificial. Durante uma visita na semana passada à cidade de Muhos, uma jornalista da AFP observou o ir e vir de retroescavadeiras. Em frente à fazenda de um dos moradores com quem conversou, a floresta tinha desaparecido de um terreno adquirido pelo Google. A agência finlandesa de supervisão exigiu, em um comunicado, que sejam suspensas “todas as medidas preparatórias suscetíveis de modificar de forma significativa o meio ambiente no âmbito dos projetos de ‘data centers’ previstos em Muhos e Kajaani”, no noroeste do país. A agência abriu uma investigação pela suspeita de que a empresa Tuike Finland, que representa o Google, cortou mais de 300 hectares de floresta em Muhos sem realizar previamente a avaliação de impacto ambiental. As obras devem ser interrompidas até que seja feita esta avaliação, detalhou a agência. “Entendemos as preocupações expressas e reconhecemos que, neste caso concreto, não estivemos à altura de nossos próprios padrões, que são elevados”, admitiu Sondre Ronander, porta-voz do Google, em uma mensagem enviada à AFP. “Estudaremos as conclusões da agência e seguiremos suas recomendações”, acrescentou. Graças a um clima ameno, uma eletricidade relativamente estável e barata, produzida majoritariamente mediante energia nuclear, além de uma ampla capacidade eólica e hidrelétrica, a Finlândia experimentou recentemente um auge dos investimentos em ‘data centers’. (com AFP)

artigo.texto: Woke up, fell out of bed Dragged a comb across my head Found my way downstairs and drank a cup And looking up, I noticed I was late —“A Day in the Life” by The Beatles Ah, those were simpler days. When John Lennon and Paul McCartney wrote that in 1967, there were no such things as data centers. Today, though, the protagonist of that song might have already used a data center twice — once if he or she relied on an alarm connected to the internet to wake up by and a second time if he or she had checked the time on a Wi-Fi clock. Maybe even more. Did the singer happen to order the coffee or tea in that cup from a grocery store delivery service? If so, that order went through a data center. Is that coffeemaker, by chance, plugged into the “internet of things”? Is the thermostat for the residence connected to the internet? If so, more data centers. Over the past year, data centers have become politically despised by both left and right, according to recent polling (including the Commonwealth Poll from Virginia Commonwealth University). At the same time, we’ve increased the number of things we do that require data centers. This is a form of cognitive dissonance — where we say we want all the conveniences of modern life but don’t want the facilities that make those conveniences possible. On the one hand, this is no different than how people feel about energy generation. Everybody wants the lights to come on, but nobody wants a power plant (or, these days, a solar farm) nearby. On the other hand, we all understand that we do turn on the lights, but we may not recognize all the times we tap into data centers. Our current frenzy over data centers led me to wonder: What is our data center footprint? We’re all familiar with the concept of a carbon footprint — how much carbon we’re all responsible for pumping into the atmosphere. What’s the data center equivalent? To what extent are each of us driving the demand for data centers? Here’s what I found. American life has changed to require data centers — We’ve stopped writing checks, and we’ve stopped spending cash When this century began, 67% of us were paying bills by check, or occasionally by cash, according to The Financial Brand. Now that figure appears to be just 10% or so, according to the Federal Reserve. Some of us never carry cash anymore. We swipe a plastic card. That means almost all of our bill-paying nowadays is digital — and each transaction may involve at least six different data centers, according to Bluefin. It starts on your computer or phone, goes to the store, then to a payment processor, a bank, then back to the store, with some additional “payment processors” along the way. — Almost one-fifth of our shopping is now online Once, shopping required going to a store. Now 17.1% of all sales take place online, according to the Federal Reserve. Many of us have ordered online and tracked the shipment. (Why is it going through Terre Haute a second time?) What if we could track that order as it pings among data centers? A single order may bounce among a half dozen or more different data centers, from your local internet provider to the company you’re buying from to the payment processor to a fraud alert service to your bank to the delivery companies along the way. Each of those might involve multiple data centers, as the data is shuffled around. — Almost half of our entertainment is now online. Probably more. Once upon a time, we had three channels and not even all of those came in clearly. I grew up learning how to “jiggle the antenna” if the reception wasn’t clear. Now, Nielsen tells us that 48.6% of our television time is devoted to streaming services. Cable services have fallen to 20.5%, over-the-air broadcasts to 19.2%. That other 11.8% or so may also involve data centers because some of that is devoted to gaming. Every time we stream “House of the Dragon,” we’re really streaming “House of the Data Center.” And those multiplayer online games? Data centers. How many data centers are involved in all these activities? That’s hard to tell. Many entertainment companies don’t disclose this data. Netflix says only that it has 18,000 servers spread across 6,000 locations around the world, but there could be multiple servers in a single data center. Hulu doesn’t have its own data centers but contracts through Amazon Web Services, which has at least 914 data centers around the world. Of those, 96 are in Virginia, almost entirely in Northern Virginia, although there’s one in Louisa County. For some, social media is entertainment. Meta, the parent company of Facebook, now has 165 data centers, with seven of those in Virginia, according to the Data Center Map. It’s unclear how many TikTok has; the company rents storage space, and some of those facilities are in Virginia, according to Forbes. One way or another, the amount of data being generated each year has doubled since 2020 and is projected to keep growing. Exploding Topics says 90% of the data in the world has been generated in the past two years. All of that has to be stored somewhere. Data centers are being built to keep up with this geometrically increasing amount of data. JLL, a global commercial real estate company that tracks data centers, says that the vacancy rate in data centers is just 1% (and 0.6% in Northern Virginia) and that “data center vacancy is likely to remain zero through 2028.” Why that date? “Most tenants securing space today are contracting for 2028 deliveries,” JLL says. Will the amount of data level off after that? Doubtful, based on all these trends. We have set in motion a chain of events that appears to have no end in sight — and we haven’t even talked about artificial intelligence yet (although we will soon). — Americans are online more than 10 hours a day For the very first Earth Day in 1970, the cartoonist Walt Kelly had his character Pogo say: “We have met the enemy and he is us.” The same admonition applies today. artigo.texto: Energy storage researchers have long chased a deceptively simple goal: electrode materials that can soak up and release charge quickly, repeatedly, and cheaply. A team led by Gu Gong and Zongcheng Miao of Xijing University, working with collaborators at Xi’an Polytechnic University, Hubei University of Automotive Technology, Åbo Akademi University and Northwestern Polytechnical University, now reports a striking step toward that goal in the journal Ionics. The group has crafted a two-dimensional, sponge-like form of nickel disulfide, NiS2, whose hierarchical porous architecture allows it to perform double duty as the working electrode in both aqueous supercapacitors and rechargeable nickel-zinc batteries. The design, published on 5 October 2026, pairs a remarkably high specific capacitance of 1227.5 farads per gram at a modest current density of 0.5 amperes per gram with good cycling stability in alkaline electrolyte, numbers that place the material among the more capable transition metal sulfide electrodes described to date. The trick behind the material lies in how it is made. Rather than precipitating nickel sulfide particles directly from solution, the researchers used a metal-organic framework, or MOF, as a sacrificial template. MOFs are crystalline lattices built from metal ions connected by organic linker molecules, and they are famous for being riddled with regularly spaced pores at the molecular scale. By converting this framework through a sulfurization strategy, the team preserved a memory of the original porous structure while transforming the chemistry from a hybrid organic-inorganic framework into a pure inorganic sulfide. The result is a sponge-like NiS2 architecture in which mesopores, pores in the range of roughly two to fifty nanometers, are abundant and interconnected, producing a high specific surface area that would be difficult to achieve by conventional synthesis routes. That architecture matters because the performance of a battery or supercapacitor electrode is governed largely by how easily ions can reach the electroactive sites where charge storage happens. In a dense, poorly connected material, ions from the electrolyte must diffuse long distances through tortuous pathways, and much of the interior of the material is effectively wasted. In the sponge-like NiS2, the abundant mesopores act as highways for hydroxide ions and other electrolyte species, shortening diffusion lengths dramatically, while the large surface area exposes a vast number of electroactive sites for the surface redox reactions that store charge. The hierarchical porosity also helps accommodate the volume changes that accompany repeated charging and discharging, a key factor in the material’s observed cycling stability. The electrochemical results are the heart of the study. When tested as a supercapacitor electrode in alkaline electrolyte, the NiS2 electrode delivered a specific capacitance of 1227.5 F g−1 at 0.5 A g−1, a value that reflects an exceptional density of accessible charge-storage sites. Specific capacitance measures how much electric charge a gram of electrode material can hold per volt of potential, and values above one thousand farads per gram are characteristic of high-performance pseudocapacitive materials, which store charge through fast, reversible surface reactions rather than purely electrostatic adsorption. Nickel sulfides are well suited to this role because nickel can shuttle between multiple oxidation states during charging and discharging, enabling rich redox chemistry at the electrode surface. Perhaps the most commercially interesting finding is that the material is bifunctional. The same NiS2 electrode that excels in a supercapacitor configuration can also serve as the cathode in an aqueous nickel-zinc battery, where it delivers high specific capacity and stable long-term performance. Ni-Zn batteries are an attractive technology because they use water-based electrolytes, which are inherently safer and cheaper than the flammable organic solvents found in lithium-ion cells, and because zinc is abundant and easy to handle. The catch has historically been finding cathode materials that can withstand the demanding alkaline environment while storing enough charge to make the cells competitive. The demonstration that a single MOF-derived sulfide can serve both device types suggests a versatile platform rather than a one-off material. The study situates itself within a broader surge of interest in aqueous energy storage. Water-based devices occupy a compelling middle ground between supercapacitors, which charge in seconds but store limited energy, and conventional batteries, which store more energy but charge more slowly and carry greater safety burdens. Recent literature highlighted in the paper’s reference list spans electrochemical activation tactics for aqueous devices, rechargeable zinc-based storage, molecularly crowding electrolytes for micro-supercapacitors, and flexible yarn-like Ni-Zn batteries for wearable electronics. Transition metal sulfides, including nickel sulfides such as Ni3S4 and NiS2, have emerged as leading candidates in this space because they combine high theoretical capacity, good electrical conductivity relative to oxides, and low cost. The MOF-derived approach itself is part of a wider design philosophy in materials chemistry. By using a preassembled framework as a template, chemists can impose order on a material at the nanoscale that would be hard to achieve through direct synthesis. In this case, the sulfurization step converts the nickel-containing framework into NiS2 while retaining the sponge-like morphology, a process analogous to casting a sculpture in a mold. artigo.texto: LAS VEGAS (KTNV) — When it comes to bringing businesses to Southern Nevada, data centers aren't the top focus. But neither are they off the table. That's what Danielle Casey, president and CEO of the Las Vegas Global Economic Alliance, told Channel 13 in an interview marking her one-year anniversary in the job. She said the alliance has decided to focus on five key areas, including advanced manufacturing concentrated on national defense, a job she said requires human employees. Data centers, which don't generate the kinds of jobs that other industries targeted by the alliance do, are not on the priority list. "So, in terms of the larger question, the community conversations, I would say no, because the proactive work that we are doing to advance our strategic plan is not focused on attracting data centers," she said. "I'll be clear, though, it's also not focused on completely disallowing them." WATCH | Economic development chief talks data centers Although some data centers — such as Switch — have operated for years in Las Vegas and elsewhere without complaints, data centers have become controversial of late, as artificial intelligence requires more and larger centers. In Reno, the city council voted for a temporary moratorium on data centers, and in Pahrump, the Nye County Commission voted to ban data centers in a particular hydrographic basin because of concerns over water. The Henderson City Council voted to reject a data-center ban, but a planned center in that city has been scrapped. And in Boulder City, a controversial data center drew vocal opposition before developers moved it to federal land, where it's been stalled by an administrative judge. The controversy surrounding data centers led Gov. Joe Lombardo to issue an executive order to prevent data centers from raising electricity rates or using water for cooling, and to force the centers to pay the portion of the state sales tax that goes to pay for schools. Meanwhile, state Sen. Dina Neal, D-Clark County, has requested a bill that would repeal data center tax breaks first passed in 2015 and impose a moratorium on new data centers in the state. According to a memo from the Legislative Counsel Bureau, there are 70 data centers either operating or planned for Nevada. For her part, Casey said an outright ban would not be helpful, especially for rural communities. "A ban would prevent the good projects from coming forward," she said. "The ones that are truly beneficial, and you're also seeing a lot of different data centers and other investments. Some of them are really well suited for certain rural communities because they're a large capital investment." Casey said data centers — which have their own association here in Nevada — are trying to become more a part of local communities. "So many have been or are becoming much more outwardly clear about their social consciousness, meaning how do they invest back in the community, and that's a good thing," she said. "So yes, completely banning anything prevents other good things. But guardrails are always important." Among those guardrails: the demand for new energy. NV Energy, in a fact sheet posted on its website, said "...the scale and pace of this potential growth is unlike anything previously planned for in Nevada." While the utility is planning to serve large data centers, it said it will protect existing customers from increased costs, maintain reliable service and meet the state's long-term energy and economic goals. One of those goals? A voter-approved constitutional mandate to generate 50% of the state's energy from renewable sources by 2030. A company official said it will likely miss that goal because of high demand from data centers, according to The Nevada Independent.

artigo.texto: O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passou a disponibilizar duas novas metodologias para projetos de reflorestação e de gestão florestal melhorada, juntando-as à metodologia já existente para novas florestações, anunciou o Ministério do Ambiente e Energia. Com o alargamento, o mercado passa a contar com três metodologias de carbono, destinadas a aumentar as oportunidades de desenvolvimento de projetos de sequestro de carbono em território nacional e a captar investimento privado para soluções baseadas na natureza. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática”, afirmou a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, citada no comunicado. Segundo a governante, o alargamento das metodologias permite reforçar a credibilidade e a capacidade de crescimento do MVC, mobilizando financiamento privado para projetos que contribuam para a neutralidade carbónica, a valorização do território e a resiliência das florestas portuguesas. As novas metodologias abrangem um conjunto mais diversificado de intervenções florestais, reforçando o potencial de geração de créditos de carbono em Portugal e incentivando práticas de gestão sustentável com benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais. Atualmente, o MVC tem dois projetos registados na tipologia de novas florestações, enquanto um terceiro se encontra em fase de validação inicial. A plataforma disponibiliza 977 créditos de carbono para venda, conta com 29 utilizadores registados e dispõe de 10 verificadores qualificados. Os verificadores asseguram a validação inicial e a verificação periódica dos projetos, de acordo com o Ministério do Ambiente e Energia. A criação das novas metodologias constitui, segundo a tutela, mais uma etapa na consolidação do MVC enquanto instrumento de apoio à ação climática, permitindo direcionar investimento para projetos de sequestro de carbono, conservação e valorização dos recursos florestais nacionais. Maria da Graça Carvalho adiantou ainda que estão a ser desenvolvidas novas abordagens para valorizar o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, com o objetivo de incluir os ecossistemas costeiros nas políticas de ação climática e de valorização do capital natural. O MVC foi criado para apoiar projetos de redução ou remoção de emissões de gases com efeito de estufa através de um mecanismo voluntário de geração e comercialização de créditos de carbono. artigo.texto: Publicidade O avanço dos investimentos em data centers no Brasil pode abrir uma nova frente para o mercado de fundos imobiliários (FIIs). De um lado, a AZ Quest Panorama estruturou um fundo temático para financiar ativos da Scala, uma das principais empresas do setor no país. De outro, a Alianza mantém no radar a possibilidade de transformar seus ativos de data center em um veículo próprio, em um movimento que poderia ampliar o acesso de investidores de varejo a esse mercado. A estratégia ganhou força em um momento em que o Brasil busca se posicionar como um polo regional para infraestrutura digital. A regulamentação do setor, especialmente com o Redata, é vista pelas gestoras como um passo importante para aumentar a competitividade brasileira e destravar novos projetos. Para Marcos Freitas, gestor de fundos imobiliários da AZ Quest Panorama, o modelo de fundo de data centers funciona como uma nova fonte de capital para empresas que precisam financiar uma expansão intensiva em investimentos. A estrutura criada pela gestora envolve a aquisição de ativos da Scala, que permanece como locatária por meio de contratos de longo prazo. Atualmente, a Scala opera 13 unidades no Brasil, com cerca de 200 MW instalados, e é controlada pela DigitalBridge. Segundo ele, as empresas de data centers já utilizam equity, dívida corporativa e project finance, mas o modelo imobiliário acrescenta uma nova alternativa. “A gente traz uma nova fonte de capital, que é usar os ativos imobiliários que elas possuem como forma de financiamento do capital de giro e dos investimentos dessas companhias” explica o gestor ao InfoMoney. No caso, a AZ Quest estruturou um fundo imobiliário cetipado com prazo determinado de dez anos e remuneração previamente definida. Continua depois da publicidade A Scala aluga os ativos adquiridos pelo fundo durante o período e, ao final, tem a obrigação de recomprá-los. A remuneração, segundo Freitas, parte de IPCA + 9,5% ao ano no cenário de permanência até o décimo ano e pode chegar a IPCA + 10,5% em determinadas hipóteses de recompra antecipada. Leia Mais: FIIs sobem forte após 1º turno da eleição presidencial; veja maiores altas FIIs de data centers buscam combinar renda previsível e exposição à expansão da infraestrutura digital Segundo Freitas, o AZ Quest Panorama Data Centers (AZDC) foi desenhado para oferecer ao investidor uma exposição ao setor sem que ele precise assumir diretamente os riscos de desenvolvimento de um novo data center. Continua depois da publicidade O fundo captou R$ 482 milhões na primeira emissão de cotas e reuniu mais de 7 mil investidores. “A gente achou que seria interessante levar para o mercado um produto temático desse setor, que pudesse dar um pouco para o investidor a sensação de que ele está participando do segmento, mas com ativo real, não tendo que entrar em projetos com uma incerteza mais alta”, afirma. O gestor destaca ainda que o prazo determinado pode ser uma característica atrativa para investidores que buscam previsibilidade. “É um fundo que tem começo, meio e fim”, diz. Para a pessoa física, diz ele, a proposta é oferecer uma renda de longo prazo com isenção fiscal, sem a volatilidade diária típica dos fundos imobiliários listados. Continua depois da publicidade A tese da AZ Quest não depende, necessariamente, da expansão do fundo para outros ativos imediatamente. A gestora avalia conversas com outras empresas de data centers para estruturas semelhantes, mas mantém a característica temática do produto como parte central da estratégia. “Eu acho que nesse momento de mercado, o nosso plano é seguir com fundos cetipados, que é um fundo temático, com uma empresa específica para comprar data centers”, pontua Freitas. Leia Mais: Galpão perto do consumidor vale mais: FII BRCO11 explica força do “last mile” Continua depois da publicidade Alianza mantém plano de spin-off de data centers do ALZR11 A estratégia da Alianza segue uma direção diferente. A gestora já possui exposição a data centers dentro de sua estrutura e mantém a possibilidade de realizar, no futuro, um spin-off dos ativos, transformando a carteira em um veículo listado dedicado ao segmento. Segundo Fabio Carvalho, sócio da Alianza, a ideia continua de pé, mas depende principalmente de uma melhora das condições de mercado. O tamanho dos projetos e o nível dos juros são hoje os principais obstáculos para uma operação desse tipo. “O interesse do spin-off ainda existe, mas em um momento de juros mais baixo, pra conseguir evoluir com outro ativos”, comenta Carvalho. O executivo explica que o próprio crescimento dos data centers tornou a estrutura mais desafiadora. Projetos que antes exigiam algumas centenas de milhões de reais passaram a ter dimensões muito maiores, dificultando a aquisição integral de determinados ativos por um único fundo. “Os data centers estão ficando grandes, isso é um problema também. Os projetos estão ficando cada vez maiores. (…) Antigamente tinham data centers médios, que eram de R$ 200 milhões, agora você tem um médio de R$ 700 milhões, isso é um negócio enorme”, diz. Nesse cenário, a Alianza avalia alternativas para participar de projetos maiores sem necessariamente comprar 100% dos ativos. Contratos longos podem transformar data centers em ativos de renda Para Carvalho, a principal característica que pode tornar os data centers interessantes para um eventual fundo dedicado é a duração dos contratos. Segundo ele, os ativos já existentes possuem contratos longos e novos projetos podem ser estruturados com prazos ainda maiores. Segundo o executivo, há contratos com mais de uma década restante e novos ativos poderiam ser adquiridos com contratos de 15 ou até 20 anos. A Alianza já possui exposição ao segmento por meio de fundos com estratégia mais ampla. O ALZR11, por exemplo, é citado por Carvalho como um dos fundos de perfil multiestratégia que poderia ter maior flexibilidade para adquirir ativos de data center. artigo.texto: Electricity and Energy Minister Dr Kgosientsho Ramokgopa has confirmed that South Africaâs first section 34 determination under the Integrated Resource Plan 2025 (IRP 2025) will prioritise 4,600MW of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 5,000MW of gas-to-power. Electricity 1Min South Africa Ramokgopa prioritises battery storage and gas-to-power in new electricity plan Electricity and Energy Minister Kgosientsho Ramokgopa says the first section 34 determination under the Integrated Resource Plan 2025 will prioritise 4,600MW of battery energy storage and 5,000MW of gas-to-power to reduce curtailment and strengthen reliable electricity supply. Electricity and Energy Minister Dr Kgosientsho Ramokgopa has confirmed that South Africaâs first section 34 determination under the Integrated Resource Plan 2025 (IRP 2025) will prioritise 4,600MW of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 5,000MW of gas-to-power. The combined 9,600MW allocation is aimed at addressing the electricity systemâs immediate need for energy storage, flexibility and dependable, dispatchable power. The first determination will not include new wind or solar capacity. According to the Department of Electricity and Energy, a subsequent determination will address additional wind and solar projects, including hybrid developments paired with energy storage, as well as longer-term pumped storage options. Ramokgopa said the IRP 2025 should be viewed not only as an electricity planning framework but also as an infrastructure investment blueprint. He said new investment must deliver electricity that the system can accommodate and supply when households and businesses need it, while keeping costs as low as possible. The department said rising electricity curtailment was placing additional pressure on system costs. Curtailment occurs when available electricity generation cannot be accommodated because of network constraints or operating conditions, including periods when supply exceeds demand. This means electricity that could otherwise be supplied to consumers is left unused, while infrastructure and contractual costs remain. The procurement approach will therefore first focus on making better use of electricity that is already available before additional variable generation is added through the next determination. Batteries to reduce curtailment Battery energy storage will be central to the government's approach. The batteries will be able to charge using electricity that would otherwise be curtailed and discharge that electricity during evening peak periods or when demand increases. The department said this would help convert surplus electricity into usable power while providing rapid balancing and grid-support services. Storage projects will be located and operated in areas where they can access surplus electricity and discharge it without creating the same network constraints. Procurement will be aligned with the requirements of the System Operator, with enforceable availability and performance obligations. The department said the effectiveness of battery storage would be measured by the amount of electricity shifted into periods when it is needed and the reliability services provided to the grid. South Africa already has a foundation for expanding battery storage. By June 2025, all five projects in the first battery storage bid window, totalling 513MW, had reached commercial close and entered construction, attracting R15.4 billion in investment. The proposed 4,600MW allocation would significantly expand the country's procurement of storage services. 5,000MW gas-to-power allocation The proposed 5,000MW gas-to-power allocation will complement battery storage by providing dispatchable electricity when renewable generation declines or demand rises. Unlike batteries, gas generation does not absorb surplus electricity. Instead, its role will be to operate flexibly, allowing renewable energy to meet demand when output is high and supplying the remaining electricity requirement when renewable generation falls. The procurement design will consider factors including plant start-up times, ramping capability and minimum operating levels. The department said fuel availability, delivered gas prices, port and pipeline infrastructure, grid connections and commissioning schedules would also need to be assessed together. The affordability of gas-to-power projects will be evaluated against their expected operating profiles. The battery storage and gas procurement programmes will form part of a broader strategy involving transmission expansion, new industrial electricity demand and regional electricity trade. While battery storage can help reduce curtailment, the department said sustained progress would also depend on delivering the grid infrastructure needed to transport electricity to consumers. The procurement programme is also expected to support local manufacturing, engineering, construction, skills development and broader ownership of energy infrastructure through measurable commitments. âThis approach advances the seventh administrationâs priorities by improving the use of available electricity, supporting dependable supply for industrial production and employment, and addressing avoidable costs that place pressure on electricity affordability,â Ramokgopa said.

artigo.texto: CHARLESTON, Ill. (WCIA) — The Charleston City Council approved an ordinance establishing a temporary moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage systems Tuesday night. City Manager Steve Bennett confirmed with WCIA over email that the council approved the moratorium in a 5-0 vote. According to city documents online, Charleston has determined data centers, battery energy storage systems and related battery uses have “unique characteristics” that warrant “consideration of appropriate regulations.” Currently, the City’s Unified Development Code does not have specific regulations addressing the location, development, and operation of data centers or battery energy storage systems. With this moratorium, the city plans to conduct research and update the code, before considering related applications. The Board of Zoning Appeals and Planning had a public hearing Sept. 24. During that hearing, the board recommended the council approve the moratorium. You can read more details about the ordinance online.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de baterias de lítio-silício: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de baterias de lítio-silício até 2035: demanda por densidade energética impulsiona o crescimento Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de baterias de lítio-silício, o setor entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de baterias de lítio-silício está posicionado para uma expansão significativa até 2035, impulsionado pela crescente demanda por maior densidade energética em veículos elétricos e em aplicações premium de armazenamento estacionário. Diferentemente das baterias de íons de lítio convencionais, que usam ânodos de grafita, as baterias de lítio-silício incorporam silício ao ânodo, o que permite capacidade energética substancialmente maior por unidade de peso e de volume. Essa vantagem tecnológica é decisiva para as montadoras que buscam ampliar a autonomia sem aumentar o tamanho do pack de baterias, e para operadores de armazenamento comercial e industrial em que o espaço físico é escasso. O crescimento do mercado, porém, é limitado por desafios como a expansão volumétrica do silício durante os ciclos de carga e descarga, que exige aglutinantes, eletrólitos e projetos mecânicos especializados, criando uma barreira elevada à integração de sistemas. A cadeia de suprimentos de materiais de ânodo de silício engenheirados de alta pureza ainda é incipiente, e os ciclos de qualificação para aplicações automotivas e aeroespaciais são longos. Apesar desses obstáculos, espera-se que inovações contínuas em materiais e a ampliação da escala de fabricação reduzam custos e melhorem a vida útil dos ciclos, abrindo caminho para uma adoção mais ampla. A projeção é de crescimento a uma taxa composta robusta entre 2026 e 2035, com a Ásia-Pacífico na liderança tanto da produção quanto da demanda, seguida pela América do Norte e pela Europa. Este relatório traz uma análise abrangente do tamanho de mercado, da segmentação, da dinâmica competitiva e das tendências regionais, oferecendo insights estratégicos para os agentes de toda a cadeia de valor. O cenário-base para o mercado de baterias de lítio-silício entre 2026 e 2035 prevê crescimento robusto, sustentado pela aceleração da adoção em veículos elétricos e em armazenamento estacionário premium. À medida que as montadoras buscam atender a regulamentações de emissões mais rigorosas e às expectativas dos consumidores por maior autonomia, a tecnologia de ânodo de silício oferece um caminho viável para maior densidade energética sem comprometer a segurança. No setor de armazenamento estacionário, a demanda deve ser de nicho, mas de alto valor, concentrada em aplicações comerciais e industriais em que as restrições de espaço justificam o prêmio de preço. O mercado provavelmente verá uma queda gradual de custos à medida que a produção ganha escala e as inovações em materiais melhoram a vida útil dos ciclos e a segurança. O crescimento, no entanto, será limitado pela complexidade de gerenciar a expansão do silício, que exige redesenho em nível de sistema e componentes especializados. A cadeia de suprimentos de materiais de silício engenheirados se ampliará, mas gargalos em silício de alta pureza e em aditivos para eletrólitos podem persistir, influenciando preços e prazos de entrega. A dinâmica competitiva favorecerá desenvolvedores integrados de célula a sistema e parcerias entre fornecedores de materiais e gigafábricas. Geograficamente, a Ásia-Pacífico manterá a liderança em fabricação e consumo, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão forte crescimento, impulsionadas por incentivos locais e metas de independência energética. Até 2035, o mercado deve alcançar uma valorização substancial, com taxa composta de crescimento de 18,5% entre 2026 e 2035, refletindo tanto o amadurecimento tecnológico quanto a demanda crescente por soluções de armazenamento de energia de alto desempenho. Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Aumento da demanda por veículos elétricos com maior autonomia e densidade energética mais alta - Restrições de espaço em aplicações urbanas e comerciais de armazenamento estacionário, que valorizam soluções compactas - Regulamentações e incentivos governamentais que promovem transporte de emissão zero e integração de energias renováveis - Avanços em materiais de ânodo de silício e em formulações de eletrólitos, melhorando vida útil dos ciclos e segurança - Aumento dos investimentos em capacidade de fabricação de baterias e na localização da cadeia de suprimentos - Adoção crescente em eletrônicos de consumo, que exigem baterias mais finas, leves e de maior capacidade Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Desafios técnicos ligados à expansão volumétrica do silício, que provocam perda de capacidade e preocupações de segurança - Custos de fabricação elevados e complexidade de integrar ânodos de silício às linhas de produção existentes - Ciclos longos de qualificação e testes para aplicações automotivas e aeroespaciais - Disponibilidade limitada de materiais de silício engenheirados de alta pureza e de aditivos especializados para eletrólitos - Concorrência das baterias de íons de lítio com grafita, já maduras, e de químicas alternativas, como as de estado sólido Estrutura da demanda por setor de uso final Veículos elétricos (participação estimada: 65%) O setor de veículos elétricos representa o maior e mais dinâmico mercado de uso final para as baterias de lítio-silício.
