artigo.texto: Eastern Nebraska village becomes first to permanently ban data centers By Noelle Annonen , Multimedia Reporter Oct. 5, 2026, 6 a.m. · Nehawka, a village in Cass County, recently became the first known village in Nebraska to set in place a permanent ban against data centers. A local leader said the idea might be spreading to other villages. Chad Krueger, co-chair of the Nehawka Village Board of Trustees, said data center developers were seeking to buy up land, and the optioned land was getting closer and closer to Nehawka. “One of our residents said, ‘Maybe we should do something about it,’” Krueger said. Cass County approved a data center moratorium, which is a temporary ban on data centers that will buy the county time until regulations around the projects can be drafted, but Krueger said it doesn’t help Nehawka. Cass County’s jurisdiction only covers up to the edge of Nehawka’s extraterritorial jurisdiction, he said, which includes the village itself and a one-mile buffer zone. This is standard for small Nebraska villages, Krueger said, and the village has zoning authority over what happens within that boundary. “Obviously we could always rewrite our (zoning) code again later in the future,” Krueger said. “But at this point, it’s an all-out-ban of data centers in our territory.” Only one Nehawka resident cautioned the board about broadly banning development, according to Krueger, but the majority of residents who weighed in were all in favor of the plan. “The last thing they wanted was a big data center or a natural resources vacuum near our village,” Krueger said. At least 19 counties now have moratoriums, typically ranging from six months to a year, against data centers. The counties are Box Butte, Butler, Cass, Custer, Dundy, Furnas, Gage, Garfield, Hayes, Harlan, Howard, Johnson, Kearney, Logan, Otoe, Rock, Saline, Seward and Sioux Counties. Other counties have drafted regulations controlling how data centers will interact with their natural resources. For instance, Buffalo County approved data center regulations in August and required any development that uses water for cooling to use a closed-loop system. This addresses a common concern that data centers continually pull from the regional water supply, with some fearing that a center could take up to 5 million gallons a day. Closed-loop systems will still use water for cooling but only take in water one time and recycle it. Lincoln County also approved regulations in August, following a controversial denial of a moratorium. These regulations require closed-loop or recycled-water cooling systems as well as protections for public power customers by prohibiting any costs associated with electric service to the data center from being passed on to residents. Noise pollution, electricity use, protection of wildlife and especially water resources were all key factors for Nehawka residents, Krueger said. “Nehawka has been in a slight drought for a good while now,” Krueger said. “We have ponds that used to exist around our village that no longer exist because the water table has dropped down so far the springs don’t feed (them) anymore. Our villagers are always concerned with water and with our natural resources.” Krueger said the village has been getting calls from village clerks across the state looking for information on Nehawka’s ban. L. Lynn Rex, executive director of the Nebraska League of Municipalities, said her organization is unaware of any villages outside of Nehawka banning data centers.

artigo.texto: KANSAS CITY, Mo. — A motions hearing is set for October 22 on a lawsuit related to the Nebius data center project in Independence. The Independence GUARD (Guardians United Against Reckless Development) Alliance filed the lawsuit to halt construction of the Nebius hyperscale AI data factory in the Little Blue Valley. Named in the lawsuit are the city of Independence, Missouri ADC Holdings LLC (data center developer) and Independence Power Partners LP. Residents along Bly Road in the Little Blue Valley of Independence are hoping to stop construction near their homes. The lawsuit alleges the city violated zoning and sunshine laws, as well as the city charter, and has failed to enforce city laws. Residents are asking a judge to pause the project. A hearing has been set for October 22 at 9 a.m. on their motion for a temporary restraining order and the defendants' motion to dismiss. The Independence City Council approved billions of dollars in incentives for Dutch tech company, Nebius, to build and operate the 2.1-million-square-foot hyperscale AI data factory on 400 acres at the south end of Bly Road in March. Nebius broke ground on the first phase of the project in April. Nebius — which is party to the lawsuit through a subsidiary, Missouri ADC Holdings — provided us a statement about the lawsuit when it was filed earlier this year in Jackson County Circuit Court. “We are reviewing the claims and cannot comment on the case specifics,” Nebius Vice President of Public Affairs John Sutter said in a statement. “Nebius remains committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations, and being a responsible partner for the community as our historic investment in Independence takes shape.”

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Aneel propõe consulta de 30 dias sobre custos de sistemas de baterias Publicado 06/10/2026 • 18:56 | Atualizado há 12 horas KEY POINTS Divulgação/Aneel A diretoria da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) decidiu nesta terça-feira (6), abrir uma consulta pública de 30 dias para aperfeiçoar a proposta de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias na modalidade de reserva de capacidade. As contribuições poderão ser apresentadas entre 8 de outubro e 9 de novembro. A principal questão em discussão é a forma de distribuir os custos da contratação. Em parecer elaborado em agosto, a área técnica da agência apontou como alternativa preferencial o rateio do encargo entre todos os geradores de energia elétrica, com valores diferentes conforme o Índice de Flexibilidade (IF) de cada usina. Pelo modelo proposto, os geradores com maior flexibilidade arcariam com 25% do encargo, enquanto aqueles com menor flexibilidade pagariam 100%. Para a área técnica, essa opção oferece o “melhor equilíbrio” entre a finalidade do encargo, a estabilidade do custeio, a objetividade técnica e a viabilidade regulatória. A definição desse mecanismo ocorre em meio a uma controvérsia sobre o rateio. Há projetos de lei no Congresso que pretendem derrubar a previsão de distribuição dos custos. A Lei nº 15.269/2025, que trata da modernização do setor elétrico, estabeleceu que as despesas relacionadas à contratação de baterias sejam rateadas exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia elétrica, sem participação dos consumidores no financiamento. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O modelo em análise poderá ser aplicado aos sistemas de armazenamento que forem contratados nos dois leilões de baterias previstos para dezembro de 2026, descritos como inéditos. Relator do processo, o diretor Gentil Nogueira afirmou que a proposta corresponde à chamada “norma perene”. Caso seja aprovada, ela poderá servir de referência para definir o custeio dos sistemas de armazenamento contratados no leilão previsto para dezembro. Nogueira destacou, porém, que o edital do próprio leilão ainda precisa ser aprovado e poderá estabelecer regras específicas para o custeio. artigo.texto: LG lands multibillion dollar deal to cool North American AI data centers LG Electronics will supply chillers for 5 gigawatts of AI data center capacity under a long-term agreement with U.S.-based AIR Control Concept. From top left, Don Kwack, chief executive of LG Electronics' North America; James Lee, president and head of LG Electronics' Eco Solutions business; and, from bottom left, Chris Ahn, president of LG Electronics USA’s Air Conditioning Technology division, and Hayden Bland, president of AIR Control Concept (AIR), and other AIR executives pose for a photo at the signing ceremony for a long-term chiller supply contract between LG and AIR. The location and date of the photo are unspecified. LG ELECTRONICS LG Electronics has won a long-term contract to supply chillers for AI data centers (AIDC) in North America, with a total capacity of 5 gigawatts. The company's U.S. subsidiary said Monday that it recently signed a long-term supply agreement with AIR Control Concept (AIR), a North American infrastructure platform company. The contract value was not disclosed, but an LG Electronics spokesperson said it was worth several trillion won, or several billion dollars. LG will supply chillers and other cooling equipment in phases for AIDCs totaling 5 gigawatts. AIR designs and builds data centers in the United States and Canada and also handles public procurement and aftermarket services. It executes large projects through its data center subsidiary, AIR Mission Critical, and counts major data center operators worldwide as clients. LG said the long-term contract, which guarantees large volumes, shows that its products meet the technical and reliability standards of hyperscale data centers. Cooling has become one of the main constraints in building AI data centers. AI servers rely on high-performance GPUs, which consume far more power and give off far more heat than conventional servers. Overheated chips slow down or fail, which is why chillers are a central piece of equipment in most data center cooling systems. Traditional data centers mostly use air cooling, which blows cold air across the servers. As power density per rack rises, air alone is often not enough, and operators are increasingly adding liquid cooling, which brings cold water or other coolant close to the chips to absorb heat directly. In such systems, a coolant distribution unit (CDU) manages the flow and temperature of the coolant that reaches the chips. LG and AIR are discussing expanding the supply to include CDUs. LG is also broadening its portfolio to cover thermal management for both air and liquid cooling. The cooling business is expected to grow as AI drives demand for more data center capacity. Worldwide data center power capacity is expected to grow by 108 gigawatts in a single year, from 226 gigawatts in 2026 to 334 gigawatts in 2027, according to market researcher Omdia. LG's AIDC cooling orders topped 600 billion won ($446.4 million) in the first half of this year, and the company expects cumulative orders to reach several trillion won by year-end. It also expects to reach its target of 1 trillion won in chiller sales ahead of the original schedule of the end of 2027. LG began supplying and installing cooling equipment this year for a large North American AIDC project it won last year. It has also won deals for major data centers elsewhere in the world, including the Middle East and Indonesia. "Based on our differentiated technologies, including high-efficiency chillers and high-performance liquid cooling solutions, and our experience supplying rapidly expanding large-scale data centers, we will lead the global AIDC cooling market," said James Lee, president and head of LG Electronics' global heating, ventilation and air conditioning and AI data center thermal management operations. BY LEE JAE-LIM [lee.jaelim@joongang.co.kr]

artigo.texto: Governor and Representatives Ocasio-Cortez and Ryan Hold Roundtable in Dutchess County With Farmers and Community Stakeholders To Discuss Impacts of Potential Data Center Development Governor Highlighted Key Policies from Data Center Moratorium and AI Safety Regulations Governor Kathy Hochul and U.S. Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan today toured Fishkill Farms, a family-owned, multigenerational farm in East Fishkill, Dutchess County and held a roundtable discussion with several local farmers, advocates and businesses to discuss the impacts of hyperscale data centers. Today’s discussion highlighted New York’s nation-leading moratorium on hyperscale data center construction, which is helping to protect local communities amid concerns over water and land use, energy costs, and proposed data center development, including in East Fishkill. New York State is experiencing an unprecedented surge in proposals for data center development driven by artificial intelligence and other computing operations that could require massive amounts of energy and water to run and cool thousands of computer servers. This summer, Governor Hochul signed an Executive Order hitting pause on new hyperscale data center development. This action has temporarily paused discretionary State environmental permits for up to one year in order to build a regulatory framework that will protect ratepayers, the environment, the energy grid and communities across the state. By pausing discretionary state environmental permits for new hyperscale data center construction for up to one year and imposing strict new rules that hold data center developers accountable and ensure benefits for local residents, Governor Hochul’s moratorium is addressing the ongoing concerns being raised by communities statewide. “As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and transforms our world as we know it, I’m standing up for New York’s farmers, small businesses and families — ensuring they aren’t left behind,” Governor Hochul said. “I enacted a nation-leading data center moratorium to protect our communities and hold developers accountable because I believe New Yorkers deserve a say in the decisions that affect their future. I’m proud to stand with Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan as we deliver a government that’s committed to fighting for working families across New York.” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, “Across the country, Silicon Valley billionaires are trying to impose data centers on communities that don’t want them. Today, Governor Hochul, Representative Ryan, and I heard directly from Hudson Valley farmers on the impacts these data centers have on the farming communities in New York State. In July, Governor Hochul took action to protect farmers and working New Yorkers by instituting a one-year moratorium on data center construction. New York is once again showing Americans what is possible when we put working people at the center of our agenda.” Representative Pat Ryan said, “I’m so proud that here in the Hudson Valley we’re standing together and fighting back against these data center projects. We’re not going to let anyone — especially not a bunch of billionaire tech oligarchs — come in here and poison our water, drive up our utility bills, and build this powerful technology that even they acknowledge could have devastating impacts for humankind. This is a fight that transcends so many of the divides in our country right now because we’re all united in putting our community ahead of corporate profits. From our town boards, to the Governor’s nation-leading moratorium, to urgently needed action at the federal level, we’re going to continue our fight to ensure that we the people are the ones to decide what happens in our lives and in our communities.” State Senator Michelle Hinchey said, “Tech companies are racing to profit off the AI boom, building data centers wherever they can and leaving communities to bear the costs through increased pressure on water supplies, energy infrastructure, and utility bills. New York is responding the right way — with Governor Hochul’s nation-leading moratorium, which is critical to giving the state time to understand the risks involved and, above all, protect ratepayers from higher bills and our natural resources from depletion. New York has an opportunity to lead in responsible innovation, and I thank Governor Hochul for her leadership and Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez for bringing this fight to the federal level.” State Senator Kristen Gonzalez said, “Across New York State, communities are struggling with the impacts of unchecked data center development from demands on our natural resources to strains on our energy grid. On my New York Fights AI Data Centers Statewide Tour, I visited 13 proposed or existing data centers and met with communities, just like East Fishkill, fighting to protect their air, water, and land. I want to thank the Governor for her first-in-the-nation moratorium on the largest data centers and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for her work introducing federal data center legislation.” “As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and transforms our world as we know it, I’m standing up for New York’s farmers, small businesses and families — ensuring they aren’t left behind.” Assemblymember Didi Barrett said, “It’s clear there is still more work to do in regulating data centers, and I look forward to working with Governor Hochul and her team to address many of the priorities in the Responsible Data Center Development Act, which includes ratepayer protections, robust host community benefits, renewable energy requirements and strong labor standards. artigo.texto: A inteligência artificial vai gerar bilhões em ganhos de eficiência. Para o bolso de quem? O dinheiro poupado pela IA pode ir para consumidores, empresas ou sumir numa briga de algoritmos. A inteligência artificial está redefinindo o valor no mercado acionário, com o setor de software caindo para a 31ª posição no ranking da BCG. A demanda por infraestrutura física, como chips e energia, impulsiona fabricantes de hardware. Paulo Mattosinho, da BCG, e Moisés Cona, do GRI Institute, destacam a necessidade de infraestrutura para IA. O estudo Value Creators Rankings 2026 mostra que empresas de infraestrutura têm bons retornos, enquanto software enfrenta desafios para monetizar a IA. A inteligência artificial está mudando o mapa de criação de valor no mercado acionário. O setor de software e serviços de tecnologia, que antes estava entre os quatro que mais geravam retorno aos acionistas, agora está na lanterna do ranking da Boston Consulting Group (BCG). Os novos dados mostram que a área caiu para a 31ª posição entre 35 segmentos. Enquanto isso, chips, componentes elétricos, energia e outras empresas ligadas à infraestrutura física da IA ganharam espaço. “Por mais de uma década, o segmento de tecnologia dominou o topo das nossas classificações. Agora, porém, o setor de software e serviços de TI despencou 27 posições. Isso acontece porque a IA, na sua fase atual de implantação, é altamente intensiva em infraestrutura (física e computacional)”, explica Paulo Mattosinho, diretor executivo e sócio do Boston Consulting Group (BCG). Segundo o estudo Value Creators Rankings 2026, a atual fase de implementação da inteligência artificial demanda investimentos em chips, data centers, energia e conectividade. Neste contexto, fabricantes de hardware, produtores de componentes elétricos e empresas de energia ganham espaço. “A capacidade computacional para treinar e rodar modelos de IA em escala relevante não existe sem chip, data center, energia e conectividade”, diz Moisés Cona, sócio e managing director do GRI Institute Infrastructure. Por isso, o dinheiro começa chegando às empresas que fornecem a estrutura necessária para a tecnologia funcionar. O executivo afirma que esse padrão não é inédito e já foi observado em ciclos tecnológicos anteriores. “O boom de investimentos em fibra óptica e infraestrutura de telecomunicações antecedeu o aumento de valor das empresas de internet que passariam a rodar sobre essa infraestrutura. Décadas atrás, investimentos em rede elétrica precederam os ganhos de produtividade das fábricas”, exemplifica Cona. Software e TI em baixa O estudo mostra que, enquanto as empresas de infraestrutura garantem bons retornos aos acionistas, as companhias de software ainda não conseguiram transformar o avanço da IA em crescimento de receita. “Elas enfrentam incertezas e custos elevados para monetizar a IA em escala sem perder suas margens”, complementa Mattosinho. “A própria IA começou a mudar a cadeia de valor do mercado de software: modelos de IA generativa e ferramentas de automação avançada começam a substituir licenças, processos e serviços de TI tradicionais”, acrescenta. Veja mais - Como a IA vai dar dinheiro? Empresas buscam modelo lucrativo apesar dos altos custos - Meta AI, Grok, Gemini e ChatGPT espalham desinformação e imprecisões sobre eleições, mostra estudo - Empresas brasileiras podem movimentar R$ 500 milhões com vendas de data centers Os números da Morningstar ajudam a ilustrar esse movimento. Em 2025, o índice que acompanha as empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos subiu 21,4 pontos porcentuais, dos quais 11,9 pontos vieram da indústria de semicondutores. Fabricantes de chips que impulsionam a computação de IA, como a Nvidia e a Broadcom, registraram forte crescimento em 2025. Em contrapartida, as empresas de software tiveram dificuldades. A empresa de gerenciamento de relacionamento com o cliente (CRM) baseada em nuvem, Salesforce, por exemplo, registrou uma queda de 20,2%. A provedora de serviços de TI corporativos ServiceNow teve queda de 27,8%. “O grande desafio para os executivos de software é equilibrar duas exigências: precisam continuar investindo no desenvolvimento de soluções de IA para não perderem relevância no longo prazo, mas precisam entregar metas de curto prazo e margens saudáveis”, afirma o sócio da BCG. O economista Felipe Araújo, doutorando em economia pela FGV, afirma que existe um hiato entre a adoção da inteligência artificial e conseguir, de fato, aumentar a produtividade. “Muitas organizações estão incentivando a implementação de IA, mas ainda estão descobrindo exatamente onde a tecnologia consegue gerar ganhos efetivos. Algumas dessas experiências vão funcionar e aumentar a produtividade, mas existe um processo de aprendizado sobre quais aplicações realmente geram valor”, diz. Criação de valor ou euforia do mercado A ruptura tecnológica promovida pela inteligência artificial impulsiona uma movimentação significativa entre empresas de todos os segmentos. Uma projeção da consultoria Gartner diz que o gasto global em IA deve superar US$ 2,59 trilhões em 2026. Segundo Araújo, essa não é a primeira vez que se observa uma euforia em torno de uma ruptura tecnológica. “Eu teria cautela em afirmar que estamos diante de uma migração estrutural da criação de valor do software para a infraestrutura física”, contrapõe. “Falaria mais em um possível overshooting (excesso de investimento): existe uma corrida para antecipar uma transformação potencialmente muito grande, e o risco é que o investimento em capacidade se antecipe à velocidade efetiva de monetização da tecnologia”, afirma. No Brasil, um relatório da GRI mostrou que 76% dos investidores do segmento planejam ampliar os investimentos. “O próprio mercado reconhece que essa é uma janela de cerca de dois anos, e que, uma vez fechada, dificilmente se reabre na mesma dimensão”, afirma Cona. “Se falharmos em enfrentar os desafios necessários para garantir atratividade, que passam, entre outras, pelas e

artigo.texto: Reforma Tributária é um Redata permanente para os setores de Telecom e data center "Todos os investimentos em 5G a partir de agora serão desonerados de tributo. Isso é um feito para o setor", observou o advogado Daniel Loria. Ele admitiu que é possível pensar em um adiamento. "Pode ser bom para o governo e para alguns setores". A Reforma Tributária é um Redata permanente para o setor de telecom e data center, afirma o advogado Daniel Loria, que participou de painel sobre o tema na Futurecom 2026 nesta quarta-feira, 07 de outubro, em São Paulo. “O Redata nasceu para antecipar os efeitos da Reforma Tributária e desonera o setor produtivo. Na reforma, os investimentos em 5G serão recuperados em até 60 dias ou já vão ter equipamentos em alíquota zero”, observou o especialista. Daniel Loria admitiu que há incertezas e desafios atuais a menos de 100 dias da vigência da Reforma Tributária como a nota fiscal de venda, a nota fiscal de compra e como o crédito será apropriado. “Mas ainda assim a Reforma Tributária é muito boa para o setor de Telecom”, atestou. À CDTV, do portal Convergência Digital, Daniel Loria, ao ser indagado se a vigência da Reforma deveria ou não ser adiada, disse que governo e setores poderiam negociar. “Para o governo adiar pode ser bom para cumprir tudo que foi prometido. Para alguns setores será a oportunidade de entrarem de vez no novo regime””. Assista a íntegra da entrevista com Daniel Loria.

artigo.texto: PIERCE TOWNSHIP, Ohio — A new data center proposal in Pierce Township turned what was scheduled to be a regular Zoning Commission meeting into an hour-long referendum on how the controversial facilities should be regulated Tuesday. People packed the Locust Corner Elementary School gymnasium to get their turn telling Zoning Commission members what they'd like to see done to limit the potential impact on utility rates, water consumption, noise levels, lighting and more. To get inside, just about everyone had to pass through a net of Pierce Township residents passing out fliers against them being welcomed to town. Kathy Cummins told us she was against the facilities being built in Pierce Township for many reasons, but the location of Crane Data Center's 300-acre proposal directly across US 52 from the now-closed Walter C. Beckjord Generating Station, still contaminated with toxic coal ash, was the most concerning. "That's what makes this site particularly challenging," Cummins told us before the meeting began. WATCH: Pierce Township residents pack a meeting on data center rules with a proposal looming A Crane representative told us after their presentation to Pierce Township Trustees that they had considered building on the Beckjord site, but ruled against it due to the ongoing contamination. We asked another member of the group passing out fliers, Bruce Cummins, what he thought about a deal allowing Crane to move in if they agreed to clean up Beckjord. "If the site was remediated, the coal ash was removed, I think that's a different conversation," he said. Bob Hucker told us he attended the meeting because he was against any new large-scale data center construction. "People need to know about this," Hucker said. Zoning Commission Chairman Jeff Stitt told the crowd before public comment began that they have been tasked with establishing data center rules for the entire township, and no official application had been submitted. Therefore, he said there was no specific project they could address directly. When asked about Crane's proposal, Stitt said that was not a formal submission they could review. "There is no one who has submitted an application, so there is no area planned," he said. "That was just an area someone expressed concern in." That sentiment was echoed weeks earlier when Pierce Township Trustee Allen Freeman talked with our I-Team. "It's basically a sales pitch, but it was not a proposal. It wasn't a zoning request. It doesn't even rise to that level, so we're not entertaining it," he said. At Tuesday's meeting, Freeman pledged transparency as the Zoning Commission built data center regulations and the trustees considered them. "This stays open. This stays transparent. Anything that we discuss, you're not going to see an NDA (non-disclosure agreement) that's going to block it," he said. Stitt urged patience as the process could take months to complete. "We don't want to make a snap decision because we live here," he said. Pierce Township has a moratorium on data center construction through May 31, 2027. Stitt said if the rules aren't prepared by the time the moratorium expires, it could be extended. Click here to see Crane's full presentation.

artigo.texto: Contemporary Amperex Technology unveils TECTRANS II battery platform Published on 10/06/2026 at 09:00 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) unveiled its TECTRANS II next-generation commercial vehicle battery solution at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hannover on September 14, 2026, according to the company’s announcement. Modular commercial vehicle platform CATL said TECTRANS II is designed for multiple commercial vehicle applications and can be configured with different numbers of standardized battery packs. The platform supports a maximum driving range of up to 1,000 kilometers and is compatible with both e-axle and central-drive architectures, as well as charging and battery swapping. Range, charging and fleet economics According to CATL, the battery offers a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg. Its maximum configuration supports 80% charging in 25 minutes with megawatt-level fast charging. CATL also said the platform is designed to support a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometer service life for heavy-duty truck applications. Cooperation with DHL Group CATL said it also signed a memorandum of understanding with DHL Group at the show. The companies plan to develop green freight corridors across Europe and work with vehicle manufacturers and other partners on electric-vehicle pilot deployments.

artigo.texto: UKIAH, CA., 10/6/26 — Mendocino County’s ban on new data centers will run until August 2028, with an exception about the size of a shipping container. The ban was put in place while a committee works with staff on a permanent ordinance that would govern how and whether the county permits data centers in the future. Supervisors voted 4-1 Tuesday to extend the moratorium they adopted Sept. 1 by 22 months and 15 days, to Aug. 21, 2028, the longest stretch state law allows. They also narrowed the terms. As Supervisor Ted Williams described the change to the board, facilities that draw less than 3 megawatts of electricity are no longer subject to the moratorium. The ad hoc committee of Williams and District 3 supervisor John Haschak met with county staff over lunch, worked out the change, and the board adopted it the same afternoon. Supervisor Maureen Mulheren voted no, calling the threshold “not fully developed.” “This idea that we’re having three megawatts coming up during a meeting as a path forward,” she said, was something she would’ve wanted staff and the community to work out first. The first version of the moratorium, a 45-day urgency ordinance, was set to expire Oct. 16. Deputy County Counsel Matthew Kiedrowski told the board the next meeting would’ve fallen outside the 45-day limit. Why 3 megawatts Williams, reporting for the board’s two-supervisor ad hoc committee of Haschak and himself, said 3 megawatts is roughly what PG&E will deliver through standard service before a project needs its own transformers or a substation. “3 megawatts would allow a data center the size of a shipping container,” he said. The point, he said, was to let local businesses use small data projects without tripping over the ordinance while the county spends the next 20 months writing a permanent rule, and still keep out “gigawatt-size facilities.” Richard Angley, the interim director of Planning and Building Services, said he believed the ordinance his staff has been drafting uses 20 megawatts as a threshold, a figure drawn from other jurisdictions. “The three megawatts came up today,” he said. Supervisor Madeline Cline said she was “not particularly in love with this arbitrary setting” of a number, but preferred allowances to a blanket ban. Williams, who proposed the figure, said it was “still somewhat arbitrary.” The board took the item up at 9:33 a.m. and couldn’t finish it before lunch break. Williams and Cline wanted a power threshold so telecommunications facilities wouldn’t be caught by the ban. Mulheren said she wouldn’t vote for any megawatt figure that day. “I do not know what that should be,” she said. “From a politics standpoint, a ban on data centers is great politics,” Cline said. As actual policy, she said, a flat-out ban is problematic. A two-year clock The board also asked whether two years was too long. Interim CEO Sara Pierce said Planning and Building is short-staffed and anything sooner than two years “would be stretched.” Later in the same discussion, senior planner Mark Cliser said the permanent ordinance “is just about done,” and a first draft could reach the Planning Commission in six or seven months. However, in the afternoon, Angley said 10 months was possible “in an absolute perfect world,” but “the likelihood of that is very slim.” Supervisor John Haschak said these things can take a while, explaining that the county has worked on an ordinance for low-intensity camping, the Hipcamp model, for about five years and still doesn’t have one. Adam Gaska, executive director of the Mendocino County Farm Bureau, told the board the bureau opposed the blanket ban. “We believe a ban is a knee-jerk reaction stemming from fear and not out of a real and actual present threat,” he said. Eileen Russell of Mendocino Forest Products, who asked the board in September to leave room for a data center at the Ukiah sawmill, said in the morning that “people have stopped the conversation” about investing here since word of the moratorium got out. In the afternoon, after the 3-megawatt change, she said a data center the size of a storage container is “not really allowing the type of development or innovation that could take Mendocino Forest Products into the next generation.” She described a power plant burning forest residuals next to the sawmill, selling its power to a data center. Doug Stewart, president of the Anderson Valley Winegrowers Association, said he wanted a limit, not a two-year moratorium. After the change, he said it “did address what I came here to discuss.” Dolly Riley, chair of the Redwood Valley Municipal Advisory Council, supported the full extension. “Mendocino County does not have the water to spare,” she said. What else changed over lunch The lunch rewrite made two other changes. The ordinance had exempted ordinary office, retail, school, hospital and industrial computer equipment. Williams said that under that wording a large retailer could have built a data center for its own operations. That exemption is gone. Hospitals and healthcare facilities are now exempted as public safety and emergency facilities, and the requirement that those be owned and operated by a public agency was dropped, because the county’s hospitals aren’t. The ordinance doesn’t name a project. It says the county “anticipates receiving” inquiries and applications. The moratorium can end sooner than 2028. Kiedrowski said the board can terminate it once it adopts a permanent data center ordinance. Haschak moved the amended ordinance with two conditions: a report back to the board every four months, and a new ad hoc committee to work with staff on the permanent ordinance. Chair Bernie Norvell named Cline and Williams to it. Mulheren said she assumed that committee would take up the question she voted no over. “If three megawatts is too small, what isn’t too small?” she asked.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 7 de outubro de 2026, às 12:20 Por Ana Paula Machado São Paulo, 07/10/2026 – A BYD depende de uma mudança na regra sobre conteúdo local de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) para definir investimentos de R$ 500 milhões no País. O vice-presidente sênior da empresa no Brasil, Alexandre Baldy, disse à Broadcast que a companhia tem conversado com o governo para aumentar o porcentual de localização dos equipamentos. Pelas regras atuais, é considerada nacional uma bateria que tenha até 15% de componentes produzidos no mercado brasileiro. Segundo Baldy, na estrutura de uma bateria para armazenamento de energia elétrica, os packs contêm entre 80% e 83% dos componentes. Já os inversores, onde se concentram os transformadores, respondem por 15% a 17% das peças. “Do jeito como está, isso não estimula a fabricação de BESS, porque posso trazer da China, onde é mais competitivo”, disse o executivo. “Queremos fazer aqui no Brasil os packs de bateria não somente os inversores. O plano é importar a célula da bateria, porque isso envolve transferência de tecnologia e é uma decisão de governos, não de uma empresa.” Baldy ressaltou ainda que, caso a regra seja mudada, a BYD vai instalar a fábrica de BESS na Zona Franca de Manaus (ZFM) e poderá gerar entre 400 e 500 empregos. A unidade, de acordo com ele, teria capacidade para produzir até 10 gigawatts (GW). “Não posso passar o que passei com a fábrica de painel solar em Campinas (SP), que hoje trabalha com 82% de ociosidade. Lá já tivemos 700 funcionários, hoje, trabalhamos com 300 empregados em um turno de produção e mais de 50% de capacidade ociosa”, disse Baldy. Isso aconteceu, segundo ele, porque o governo anterior zerou as tarifas de importação de painel solar e a medida, completa Baldy, prejudicou os investimentos realizados pela companhia. “Quando se mudou a regra do jogo, quebrou o nosso planejamento. Por isso, vamos aguardar um retorno do governo para decidirmos se vamos ou não investir em uma fábrica de BESS no Brasil.” O executivo ressaltou que os recursos, de R$ 500 milhões, são próprios e garantidos pela matriz, mas disse que a China só vai liberar o investimento após essa definição e com todos os documentos assinados para a instalação da unidade. “Nós precisamos que o BNDES financie os nossos clientes, aqueles que devem participar do leilão (armazenamento de capacidade de potência) de dezembro. Dinheiro nós temos.” Quanto ao pedido de aumento de carga na fábrica de Camaçari, na Bahia, Baldy disse que a companhia teve de pedir à Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) um reforço para sustentar os investimentos de expansão da unidade. Segundo ele, a empresa havia pedido uma elevação de fornecimento somente para a distribuidora local, a Coelba, mas teria de fazer o pedido também à Aneel por comprar energia no Mercado Livre. “Hoje, a fábrica usa 1,5 megawatts (MW) e precisamos de 13 MW com a estimativa de chegarmos a 22 MW”, disse Baldy. “Sem energia não tem indústria.” Contato: ana.machado@estadao.com Veja também

artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series on the United States and the Evolution of Energy Storage Stanislav Kondrashov on American Style energy storage The relationship between the United States and energy storage stretches across several generations of technological development. Long before contemporary battery installations became part of the electrical landscape, American engineers and industries were already exploring ways to preserve usable energy through mechanical, gravitational, thermal, and electrochemical methods. Electrification gradually gave storage a different role: it could become an active component of increasingly complex electrical networks. Key takeaway: the American history of energy storage is fundamentally a history of timing. Generation and consumption do not always occur at the same moment, and storage creates a technological bridge between them. As American electrical infrastructure expanded, that bridge became increasingly sophisticated, combining physical equipment with manufacturing, electronics, software, monitoring, and specialized engineering. The Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series examines this progression as more than the history of the battery. Energy storage includes several technological families. What connects them is a simple objective: retain useful energy in one form and make it available later. That principle has remained remarkably consistent even as the technologies surrounding it have changed. How Did Energy Storage Develop in the United States? Energy storage in the United States developed alongside industrialization and electrification, progressing through mechanical systems, elevated-water methods, electrochemical batteries, thermal techniques, and increasingly sophisticated electrical storage installations. More recently, electronics and software have added a digital layer to storage infrastructure. The historical sequence was not a straight replacement of one technology by another. Different storage methods solved different problems. Some were suited to large infrastructure. Others became useful in relatively compact applications. Modern electrical networks can contain several approaches simultaneously. This diversity is central to understanding the American storage landscape. Storage Began With a Problem Older Than Electricity The fundamental challenge of storage predates electrical networks. Energy may become available at one moment but become useful at another. Mechanical systems provided early answers. A moving component could preserve kinetic energy. Compressed systems could retain energy for later release. Elevated water could preserve potential energy through gravity. Thermal methods could retain useful differences in temperature. These approaches differ technically, but each introduces flexibility between availability and use. That flexibility became increasingly important as industrial systems grew more sophisticated. Electrification Changed the Storage Question Electricity introduced a distinctive challenge. Electrical generation and consumption need close coordination. As American electrification expanded, engineers needed increasingly sophisticated ways to manage changing patterns of demand and generation. Storage offered one possible response. It could absorb electricity at one moment and make electricity available at another. The significance of this capability increased as electrical networks became larger. “The history of storage becomes especially revealing when electricity enters the picture, because engineers are no longer thinking only about preserving energy; they are also thinking about how timing can become an active part of an interconnected electrical system,” Stanislav Kondrashov says. Storage was becoming part of network architecture. Elevated Water Introduced Storage at Large Scale One historically important approach uses gravity and water. Electricity can be used to move water upward. The elevated water represents stored potential energy. When electricity is needed later, the water can move downward through generating equipment. The concept is straightforward. Its implementation requires substantial engineering. Reservoirs, turbines, pumps, electrical equipment, transmission connections, and monitoring systems must operate together. This illustrates an important feature of energy storage history. Storage is rarely just the medium retaining energy. It is the complete system that makes storing and recovering that energy practical. Batteries Created a Different Kind of Flexibility Electrochemical storage changed the possibilities considerably. Batteries could be manufactured as discrete units. They could be installed in different places. They could operate across different scales. They could serve applications far removed from large gravitational infrastructure. This introduced modularity. Modularity is historically significant because it allows capacity to be assembled from multiple units rather than requiring every storage installation to follow a single physical model. As manufacturing developed, batteries became relevant across an expanding range of applications. Portable Storage Changed Everyday Technology One important chapter in American storage history occurred far from large electrical infrastructure. Portable batteries allowed electrical energy to travel with devices. This changed the relationship between electricity and location. An electrical product no longer always needed an immediate connection to fixed infrastructure while operating. Stored electricity could accompany the device. That principle became increasingly important as electronics expanded into professional and everyday activities. Portable storage therefore represents another historical dimension of the American relationship with energy storage: mobility. artigo.texto: Cisco's Jeetu Patel: AI Agents Are Coming, and Data Centers Are a National Security Issue Jeetu Patel is bullish on AI, especially AI agents. He also thinks the technology brings real national security stakes. Patel is Cisco's president and chief product officer. He was in Austin for WebexOne, Cisco's major user conference, where the company showed off its next wave of AI tools. Cisco has a significant presence in Austin, including an innovation hub. "One of the most seismic shifts in history" Patel says AI is moving fast. He believes it can help solve some of the world's biggest problems, including disease, poverty, and education. "This technology is one of the most seismic innovations and shifts that we have experienced in the history of humanity," Patel said. "But it also has a meaningful amount of risk that we have to make sure that we mitigate." His outlook is optimistic, with a clear view of the downsides. "I am, on balance, a net optimist," he said. "I feel like this is going to be one of the most amazing technologies that allows us to do things we could never dream of doing before. But I don't wear rose-colored glasses." ALSO| This vest simulates getting shot in the line of duty so officers can train for it before What are AI agents? Patel says the next big wave is AI agents. These are tools that take on tasks, make decisions, and do more work on our behalf. Cisco sits on the front lines of cybersecurity, and Patel says the company is working to reduce the risks that come with that shift. As agents get more powerful, he says, they create new challenges. One is network strain. "Agents consume about five times more network bandwidth for conducting the same exact task as a human does," Patel said. The data center debate Data centers have become a hot topic across Texas. Patel says the stakes go beyond the economy and changing the landscape. His warning is that if the country does not keep up with demand for computing power, it could face a national security problem as AI agents and bad actors multiply their capabilities. "You're going to have trillions of agents around the world, and they can start attacking critical infrastructure if we're not careful," Patel said. "That could cost lives. The only way you can defend against it is by making sure that your defenses are also at machine scale." Machine-scale defense takes computing power, and computing power takes data centers. "So I feel like for the safety and security of humanity, data centers are actually a very essential ingredient," he said. "It's not something that's an elective that we can either choose to do or not do, because it actually won't keep us safe." Texas and the AI buildout Patel says Texas is well positioned for the AI buildout. He adds that the country as a whole will need more power, computing capacity, network bandwidth, and security to keep pace.

artigo.texto: Cabinet Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Deborah Barasa speaking during the launch of the Kenya Guide for Strategic Engagement in Carbon Markets 2026./KNA Kenya has moved to strengthen its participation in global carbon markets with the launch of a new guide aimed at attracting high-integrity climate investments while protecting communities, ecosystems and the country’s national climate targets. Cabinet Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Deborah Barasa said the Kenya Guide for Strategic Engagement in Carbon Markets 2026 would provide a framework for ensuring that carbon-market investments generate genuine environmental benefits and lasting value for Kenyans. The guide was officially launched in Nairobi on Monday in the presence of Environment and Climate Change Principal Secretary Dr Eng Festus Ng’eno and senior representatives from Switzerland, South Korea, the European Union, the United Kingdom and Norway. Barasa said the guide marked a critical milestone in making Kenya’s engagement in carbon markets more strategic, transparent and aligned with national interests. “Kenya is open to responsible and high-integrity carbon investment. We are seeking quality, integrity and lasting development value,” she said. She noted that carbon markets presented a major opportunity to mobilise private capital into renewable energy, forestry, agriculture, waste management and clean cooking, while creating jobs, supporting innovation and facilitating technology transfer. However, she cautioned that such investments must not come at the expense of communities or the environment. The guide is expected to provide greater clarity and predictability for investors, project developers and communities, while complementing ongoing reforms, including the establishment of the National Carbon Registry and strengthening of Kenya’s legal framework for implementing Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Barasa called for partnerships that deliver measurable climate benefits, strong environmental and social safeguards and equitable sharing of benefits generated by carbon projects. She said the government’s priority was now to translate the new policy framework into concrete action and position carbon markets as a credible pathway towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient and inclusive economy. Environment and Climate Change Principal Secretary Dr Eng. Festus Ng’eno said Kenya was moving beyond viewing carbon markets as a future opportunity and was positioning itself as a key player in shaping the emerging global carbon trading system. “For years, carbon markets were discussed as a future opportunity. That future is now here,” Ng’eno said, noting that international trading frameworks under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were becoming operational. He said the new guide would strengthen Kenya’s strategic, transparent and high-integrity participation in international carbon markets. A key provision of the guide is a 10 million-tonne cumulative ceiling for international transfers of carbon dioxide equivalent between 2025 and 2030. Ng’eno said the ceiling would help safeguard Kenya’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets and minimise the risk of the country overselling its carbon credits. He said Kenya’s carbon-market strategy was anchored on four principles: predictability, uncompromising integrity, putting people before carbon, and creating value beyond carbon. Under the framework, carbon projects will be expected to provide tangible benefits to local communities through equitable benefit-sharing, technology transfer, skills development, employment and local value creation. The government said the approach would ensure that carbon markets contribute to national development without undermining Kenya’s climate commitments or the rights and livelihoods of communities hosting carbon projects. The launch brought together Switzerland’s Ambassador to Kenya Mirko Giulietti, South Korean Ambassador Kang Hyung-shik, EU Deputy Ambassador Ondrej Simek, British Deputy High Commissioner and Development Director Diana Dalton, and Norwegian Minister Counsellor and Deputy Head of Mission Christian Gahre. Kenya is now expected to focus on implementing the new framework as it seeks to attract climate finance while maintaining strong safeguards against environmental degradation, inequitable benefit-sharing and risks to the country’s carbon budget.

artigo.texto: Amazon to invest $1B into data center communities amid backlash against data center rollouts Published 3:03 pm Monday, October 5, 2026 NEW YORK — Amazon is investing more than $1 billion over the next five years into communities where it operates data centers for education, job training, water and energy preservation projects and other local priorities as it reacts to a growing backlash from politicians and consumers to the tech industry’s rollout of the massive buildings. According to a blog post on Friday by Matt Garman, Amazon’s CEO of its cloud computing arm, Amazon has already spent more than $1 billion in communities with a large data center presence over the past three years. Garman also said that Amazon is no longer using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies it works with on its projects, and it said it hosts open houses in communities where it operates to share information about what it’s doing. He also warned against the spread of what he believes is misinformation about data centers’ impact on the environment and energy rates — and he cited the dangers of over 100 moratoriums against these centers being considered across the country. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” he wrote. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position. There is urgency to this data center build out because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security.” Garman’s pledge comes as data centers, which power artificial intelligence and cloud computing, have become a hot political issue heading into the midterms as tech giants race to invest more money in expanding these infrastructures. Small, under-the-radar data centers have been around for decades. But the explosion of artificial intelligence chatbots has resulted in data centers that are bigger than anything just about any town has ever seen. Some of them dwarf football stadiums and factories and consume more energy than small cities. By 2030, data centers will account for nearly 3% of the world’s projected electricity use, with 935 trillion watt-hours, according to a United Nations University report released in June on these buildings’ environmental footprint. Amazon said in July that it now expects to spend $220 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, including on data centers and other technology investments. That’s up from its prior estimate of $200 billion. President Donald Trump has embraced the building of more data centers, but there is growing wariness from voters. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans. And a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 7 de outubro de 2026, às 15:50 Por Aramis Merki II São Paulo, 07/10/2026 – O avanço da inteligência artificial está levando empresas a rever como armazenam e processam dados, em um movimento que combina a busca por soberania da informação com a necessidade de controlar custos de infraestrutura. No caso da B3, ter data center próprio é uma escolha para proteger informações do mercado financeiro, de acordo com o líder da área responsável por alocar equipamentos de processamento de dados em data centers externos (colocation, no termo em inglês), Eduardo Yukio Kashiwakura. Segundo ele, a B3 armazena informações de brasileiros e de clientes institucionais, incluindo dados sobre carteiras de investimentos, posições e operações no mercado financeiro. “Para nós, ter um data center próprio, é questão de soberania dos dados”, disse durante painel no evento Data Center World Brasil, em São Paulo. Já empresas que não têm escala para operar estruturas próprias buscam alternativas híbridas para garantir segurança e governança sobre os dados. É o caso do Grupo Santa Cruz Distribuidora de Medicamentos, segundo o diretor de informação da companhia, Jorge Stakowiak. Ele afirma que a empresa não tem capacidade para manter um data center próprio e, por isso, busca combinar diferentes ambientes de infraestrutura, com regras de governança para determinar quais dados podem ser utilizados em aplicações de inteligência artificial. Para o diretor, a arquitetura de infraestrutura precisa ser flexível e pode combinar ambientes próprios, terceirizados e híbridos, de acordo com o tipo de informação e as necessidades do negócio. A definição de onde cada dado será armazenado e processado passa, nesse contexto, por critérios de segurança, governança e custo, e não apenas pela propriedade do data center. artigo.texto: A diretoria da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) decidiu, nesta terça-feira (6/10), abrir consulta pública de 30 dias para o aprimoramento da proposta de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), na modalidade de reserva de capacidade. A consulta ficará aberta de 8 de outubro a 9 de novembro de 2026. A área técnica da agência apontou, em parecer de agosto, que a melhor alternativa para os custos da contratação de baterias é o rateio entre todos os geradores de energia. Contudo, a proposta é que o pagamento seja modulado em função do chamado Índice de Flexibilidade (IF). Com esse critério, aquelas usinas com maior flexibilidade pagariam menos (25% do encargo), enquanto aquelas com menor flexibilidade pagariam 100%. A alternativa, ainda de acordo com a área técnica, apresenta o “melhor equilíbrio entre aderência à finalidade do encargo, estabilidade do custeio, objetividade técnica e viabilidade regulatória”. O tema é controverso, especialmente porque há projetos de lei no Congresso buscando derrubar essa previsão de rateio dos custos. A Lei nº 15.269/2025, de modernização do setor elétrico, previu expressamente que os custos decorrentes da contratação de baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia elétrica, excluindo a possibilidade de custeio pelos consumidores. Os dois leilões de baterias, inéditos, estão previstos para dezembro deste ano. O diretor Gentil Nogueira, relator, comentou que a proposta em discussão trata da “norma perene”, que, se aprovada, poderá ser utilizada para o custeio dos sistemas de armazenamento que devem ser contratados no leilão de baterias marcado para dezembro. No entanto, ele salientou que o próprio edital do leilão, ainda a ser aprovado, pode trazer disciplina para esse custeio específico. O edital precisa ser aprovado até o fim de outubro, de maneira a cumprir a regra de publicação com 30 dias de antecedência. Por Renan Monteiro e Luciana Collet

artigo.texto: Turbo Energy's technology integrates battery storage with solar power for efficient energy management across three Spanish industrial sites. Quiver AI Summary Turbo Energy, S.A. announced the successful integration of its battery storage technology with rooftop solar systems at three industrial sites in Spain, part of the Pamesa Net Zero initiative. The company has activated 62.5 MWh of battery storage capacity as part of a larger $53 million contract to implement a total of 366 MWh across ten factories. This integration allows for the efficient management of renewable energy, coordinating battery usage with solar generation and each site's energy demands. Since the systems began operation, they have reportedly avoided 421 metric tons of CO₂ emissions. Turbo Energy’s intelligent energy management system continuously optimizes energy usage based on real-time data from various sources, enhancing the efficiency of renewable energy consumption at the facilities. The successful deployment at these sites marks a significant step in the broader project development, showcasing Turbo Energy's capabilities in managing complex energy systems in industrial environments. Potential Positives - Turbo Energy has successfully integrated 62.5 MWh of intelligent energy storage capacity across three industrial sites, marking a significant milestone in the company's $53 million contract to supply a total of 366 MWh of battery storage. - The operating systems at these sites are now fully functional, demonstrating Turbo Energy's capability to execute complex energy management projects under real industrial conditions. - The project has contributed to the avoidance of 421 metric tons of CO₂ emissions, highlighting the environmental benefits of Turbo Energy's technology in industrial applications. - This deployment advances Turbo Energy's position in the market, providing a strong operational reference for future multi-site energy management projects. Potential Negatives - Despite achieving operational status of 62.5 MWh of battery storage, the press release emphasizes that a significant portion of the remaining delivered capacity is still undergoing installation and commissioning, which may indicate delays in the overall project timeline. - The press release includes a cautionary statement regarding forward-looking information, suggesting that there are inherent uncertainties and risks that could negatively impact future performance and operational goals. - While the 421 metric tons of CO₂ avoided is a positive outcome, the press release does not quantify the overall environmental impact or energy savings relative to the broader scale of the project, which may raise questions about its effectiveness and efficiency. FAQ What is the main achievement of Turbo Energy in Spain? Turbo Energy has successfully integrated 62.5 MWh of intelligent energy storage across three industrial sites in Spain, enhancing renewable energy management. How does Turbo Energy's technology optimize energy usage? The technology coordinates battery charging, solar generation, and industrial demand to improve energy efficiency and reduce costs for manufacturing facilities. artigo.texto: Data Centers: Dalton Utilities details water usage, power costs, citizens repeat pause request Published 3:01 am Wednesday, October 7, 2026 City officials said Monday night that work is continuing behind the scenes to examine issues surrounding data centers and other large power users, while Dalton Utilities offered new details about the financial safeguards and revenue associated with serving the rapidly growing industry. The discussion came amid repeated calls from some residents for the city to impose a six-month moratorium on new data center development while it considers regulations specifically governing the facilities. Before the public comment portion of Monday’s meeting, Mayor Sams said city staff are continuing work the council has requested involving large power users. “I want to make [clear] that our staff are continuing to work on doing their due diligence as we have asked of them as it relates to large power users, which would include but not be limited to data centers,” Sams said. Sams did not announce a decision on a moratorium or a data center-specific ordinance. City Administrator Andrew Parker said he had invited Dalton Utilities CEO John Thomas to speak because of the amount of public comment council members have heard about data centers during recent meetings. Parker cautioned that the utility’s role represents only one part of the broader discussion and that some issues surrounding large power users and data centers fall outside Dalton Utilities’ purview. “We’ll continue to provide more information as we move forward,” Parker said. Water use Thomas addressed water use, electricity supply and rates, financial protections for other utility customers and revenue generated by data center customers. On water, Thomas said the large data center being developed in Whitfield County is being built with a closed-loop cooling system in which water is initially added and then recirculated rather than continuously replaced. Thomas said some water can be lost through evaporation or other means but said the amount is expected to be small. “It’s not expected to use really much more water than a restaurant, two restaurants or so that you might think of around town,” Thomas said. Thomas also said Dalton Utilities has water capacity available because its industrial customers now use about one-third as much water as they once did. Power and protecting other customers Thomas said Dalton Utilities has always purchased some of its electricity from the regional wholesale market and has never supplied its entire electric load solely from resources it owns. As population, manufacturing and other economic activity grow across the Southeast, increased demand can constrain that regional market and put upward pressure on wholesale electricity costs, he said. Thomas emphasized that electric providers do not all have the same mix of owned and purchased power and therefore may experience those pressures differently. When Dalton Utilities serves a data center directly, Thomas said, the utility uses several measures intended to protect its other customers from financial exposure created by the enormous electric loads involved. Data center customers are subject to what Thomas described as exceptional deposit requirements. They also pay a fixed monthly demand charge tied to the amount of electric capacity available to them, regardless of whether they use that full capacity during a particular month. Dalton Utilities’ largest data center customer is treated differently still. Thomas said the customer is billed weekly for electricity rather than monthly and maintains a prepaid account. Each week, the customer pays for the amount of electricity Dalton Utilities expects it to consume during the following week. Data center customers also pay upfront for local infrastructure Dalton Utilities must construct to connect their facilities to the electric grid, Thomas said, rather than leaving the utility to recover those costs through rates over time. Millions in revenue Thomas also put numbers Monday night to the financial benefits Dalton Utilities says data centers provide. According to Thomas, the utility’s two largest data center customers generated just under $5 million in state and local sales tax revenue in 2025. Data center revenue has also substantially increased the amount Dalton Utilities transfers annually to the city’s general fund, according to Thomas. Dalton Utilities transfers 5% of its revenue to the city. Thomas said that in each of the past four years, the annual transfer would have been approximately $3.5 million to $4 million lower without revenue from data center customers. The city’s adopted 2026 General Fund budget includes $15.55 million from the Dalton Utilities transfer, compared with $9.1 million in budgeted property-tax revenue. Councilmember Steve Farrow noted that the utility transfer reduces the amount of revenue the city must raise through property taxes. Parker said the city’s 2026 budget includes approximately $15.5 million from Dalton Utilities transfer payments, compared with approximately $9.1 million in budgeted property tax revenue. Resident renews call for moratorium The presentation did not resolve the broader questions that have brought residents to recent city and county government meetings. During public comment, Carmen Shuler again asked the city to adopt a six-month moratorium on data center development while officials develop a data center-specific ordinance. Shuler said a group of concerned residents has submitted a proposal seeking the moratorium and argued that a temporary pause would give the city time to research standards and best practices. “A moratorium is a pause, not a ban,” Shuler said. She asked whether city officials have made decisions on either the requested moratorium or development of a data center ordinance and questioned whether the city has sought consultants or impact studies to help evaluate future development. Oct 7, 2026 Foss & Company Closes $58 Million Tax Equity Deal for GridStor Battery Storage in Hidalgo County, Texas Foss & Company has finalized a $58 million partnership flip deal to fund a utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) in Hidalgo County, Texas, constructed by GridStor, as announced in a press release. This transaction, which yields Section 48 Investment Tax Credits, is the second collaboration between the tax equity syndicator and the battery storage developer. The battery storage asset remains on track to be operational in October 2026, according to the release. Bryen Alperin, Partner and Managing Director at Foss & Company, stated that the deal highlights the strength of the firm's partnership with GridStor and its ongoing confidence in utility-scale battery storage as an asset class. He added that with grid operators increasingly depending on storage to balance supply and demand, the firm is pleased to assist in bringing projects like this one in Hidalgo County online, and anticipates expanding its pipeline with GridStor in the coming years. Spencer Mash, SVP of Finance and Head of Capital Markets at GridStor, expressed satisfaction with completing the financing with Foss and gratitude for their backing of the BESS asset class. He noted that the transaction mirrors the sector's continued maturation and the rising confidence of financing partners in the role battery energy storage can play in supporting grid reliability and flexibility where it is most needed. The deal adds another utility-scale battery storage asset to Foss & Company's expanding renewable energy tax equity portfolio. Established in 1983, Foss & Company is a national tax equity investor and fund sponsor that has allocated over $11 billion in tax equity for insurance, banking, and other large corporate clients into historic rehabilitation projects, renewable energy, and advanced energy production facilities. The firm positions itself as a full-service advisor with demonstrated expertise in guiding partners through tax equity investments. GridStor builds and operates battery projects aimed at enhancing the reliability of America's power system by storing electricity for delivery when and where it is most needed. The company develops, acquires, builds, and operates utility-scale, standalone battery storage projects primarily across North America. artigo.texto: Actis adds 244MW / 1,141MWh battery storage portfolio to Polish platform within three months of launch - Transaction advances Actis’ 1.5GW wind, solar, and BESS target for new Central & Eastern Europe platform - Actis has committed more than US$1.1 billion across three platforms in CEE LONDON, 6 October 2026: Actis, a leading growth market investor in sustainable infrastructure, today announced it is acquiring two battery energy storage system (BESS) projects as it rapidly scales its recently launched Polish renewable energy platform. The projects are being acquired from DRI, with one 112MW / 518MWh project in Kozienice already acquired and ready for construction by Actis, and the other – a 132MW / 623MWh project in Trzebinia – signed and set to complete once operational. These projects will represent some of the first utility-scale BESS projects to reach commercial operation in Poland, with a total 244MW of power capacity and 1,141MWh of four-hour plus duration energy storage. Both assets benefit from a secured revenue base through a 17-year inflation-indexed capacity market contract. Building on Actis’ acquisition of Klara Renewables – a 171MW onshore wind portfolio with approximately 275MW of hybridisation potential, signed in July 2026 – these two assets support Actis’ integrated approach, combining renewable power generation with BESS to create a system-level portfolio that aims to mitigate volatility and maximise value capture across the power system while increasing Poland’s grid flexibility and renewable energy integration capability. With Poland expected to retire approximately 18GW of coal while adding 50GW of renewables and 14GW of gas capacity by 2040, the country’s structural transition away from coal offers significant growth opportunities for assets like BESS, particularly given electricity demand is forecast to more than double by 2050 due to industrial and transport electrification and economic growth. This transformation is underpinned by attractive financial mechanisms, including a strong capacity market providing long-term and stable cashflows, alongside robust corporate PPA demand. Jaroslava Korpanec, Head of Central & Eastern Europe at Actis, commented: "The CEE region has historically been underinvested in, and the need to drive decarbonisation and invest in independent energy supply is, in our view, absolutely crucial. Poland is a major European power market but a carbon-intensive one that needs to transition from coal to renewables while keeping the grid steady. These two projects will help build the grid flexibility required and in doing so support Poland in managing its energy transition, energy competitiveness and resilience.” Murat Cinar, Chief Executive Officer of DRI, said: “Battery storage is expected to play an increasingly important role in Poland’s energy system as the share of renewables continues to grow. We believe Kozienice and Trzebinia are strong projects that can provide significant flexibility to the grid and we are pleased to see them moving into their next stage with Actis. This transaction also reflects the strength, in our view, of DRI’s capability to develop and advance meaningful energy projects in Europe’s most important growth markets.” ENDS RELATED ARTICLES The statements contained herein, including those made by Jaroslava Korpanec are as of 6 October 2026 and represent the views of Actis which is not research and should not be treated as research. artigo.texto: A gigante sul-coreana LG Electronics assinou um contrato de longo prazo para fornecer sistemas de refrigeração industrial a data centers de inteligência artificial nos Estados Unidos. O acordo, que impulsionou as ações da empresa em Seul, visa atender à demanda crescente por infraestrutura térmica eficiente para o boom de IA no mundo. As ações da LG Electronics avançaram no mercado financeiro depois que a companhia fechou um novo contrato plurianual para fornecer sistemas de resfriamento a data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos. A gigante sul-coreana de eletrônicos de consumo vem expandindo rapidamente o negócio de equipamentos de refrigeração industrial, conhecidos como "chillers", impulsionada pelo boom global de data centers, que aumenta a demanda por soluções eficientes de gestão térmica para infraestrutura de IA. Pontos-chave sobre o contrato - Contrato plurianual firmado com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia. - O acordo prevê o fornecimento de "chillers" para data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. - As ações da LG subiram 8,8% no início do pregão em Seul, marcando a maior alta diária em dois meses. - A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia, com início da produção no primeiro semestre de 2027. - Encomendas anuais podem chegar a bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A LG informou nesta terça-feira (6) que sua subsidiária nos EUA firmou um acordo de longo prazo com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia, para fornecer "chillers" a data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. A empresa não revelou o valor exato do contrato, mas afirmou que o acordo acelera a expansão da LG no mercado global de resfriamento para data centers de IA. Em Seul, as ações da LG Electronics chegaram a subir 8,8% no início do pregão, caminhando para a maior alta diária em cerca de dois meses. A LG disse que, apoiada por vitórias recentes na América do Norte, também está ampliando sua presença em projetos relevantes de data centers no Oriente Médio e na Indonésia. Expansão industrial e metas de receita No início deste mês, a empresa anunciou que vai aumentar a produção de "chillers" tanto nos EUA quanto na Coreia do Sul. A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia para atender à demanda crescente de data centers americanos, com início da produção previsto para o primeiro semestre de 2027. Paralelamente, pretende elevar a produção em unidades já existentes em Changwon e Pyeongtaek, na Coreia do Sul. Segundo a LG, as novas encomendas anuais de soluções de resfriamento para data centers podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após a companhia garantir US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A empresa também afirmou esperar atingir, antes do prazo, a meta de 2027 de US$ 680 milhões em receita no negócio de "chillers".
