artigo.texto: U.S. data center capacity growth projections appear to be on track for 2026 and 2027 despite mounting opposition to projects that support the build-out of artificial intelligence technologies. Goldman Sachs now projects that total U.S. data center capacity will reach 64 gigawatts by year’s end, an increase in its prior forecast by 5 gigawatts. But the financial services firm also decreased its 2027 forecast by 5 gigawatts, expecting it to reach 90 gigawatts in that year. U.S. capacity stands at about 62.7 gigawatts, according to energy data firm Cleanview. The latest big development announcements include plans in Virginia by LG Electronics to build its first U.S. plant focused on production of chillers for data center cooling. On the investment side, facility operator Sabey Data Center Properties reported a significant new commitment from global equity firm Ares Management Corp. to support expansion. Nearly 400 U.S. cities and towns, along with at least 14 states, are considering moratoriums or other restrictions on data center development. This comes as more than 1,500 data center projects are in various stages of planning nationwide, according to the Pew Research Center. “While U.S. data center development faces increasing political and community opposition, project data and our updated capacity estimates suggest that the U.S. data center growth outlook through 2027 remains largely unchanged,” Goldman analysts said in a research note issued Sunday. Goldman’s 2026-2027 projections are based on its forecast of a 38% increase in U.S. power demand in 2026 and another 38% rise in 2027, much of it driven by data centers. A single gigawatt is roughly enough to power up to around 1 million homes, based on energy industry standards. Power consumption plays a big part in nationwide opposition to data centers, with communities concerned about energy, water and land usage amid worries that projects could also drive up utility bills for residents and businesses near the facilities. Several technology and energy firms have pledged to pay costs for needed utility upgrades as states and cities seek to put those policies into law. Data center projects increasingly include on-site power generation facilities designed to prevent taking power from regional grids, but those components add considerably to development costs. Goldman previously projected that U.S. capital investment in data centers and related AI support systems would hit $765 billion for 2026 alone. The firm expects cumulative global capital spending to reach $7.6 trillion by 2031. More companies boost investment Much of the current and future spending is coming from the largest tech company “hyperscalers,” such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Facebook parent Meta. Multiple other data center operators, investors and suppliers are responding to the AI build-out. LG Electronics, a division of the South Korean industrial giant, said it is expanding its global chiller manufacturing capacity with its first facility in the U.S., planned for a 43-acre site near Windsor in southeastern Virginia. Production is scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027 at a 350,000-square-foot industrial building completed in 2025 by developers of the Shirley T. Holland Intermodal Park, according to an LG statement and regional reports. The new plant is expected to employ more than 150 people and is part of LG Electronics’ strategy to "expand production capacity for advanced cooling technologies and better serve the rapidly expanding customer base in North America,” Don Kwack, CEO of LG Electronics North America, said in the statement. LG plans to invest more than $100 million in the new U.S. facility and expansions of two existing South Korean factories to meet North American demand, the company said. Its first U.S. chiller factory “is addressing the growing need for advanced cooling solutions for data centers across the country,” said Chris Ahn, president of LG Electronics USA’s air conditioning technology division. In another transaction, leaders of Sabey Data Center Properties, the operator of more than 4 million square feet of U.S. data centers, announced on Monday an expanded investment by minority owner Ares Management Corp. That takes the equity firm’s stake to more than $500 million since the first investment was announced in July. Sabey Data Center Properties is majority-owned by Seattle-based Sabey Corp. and National Real Estate Advisors LLC of Washington, D.C. A statement from the two companies and Los Angeles-based Ares said new funding will go toward planned U.S. capacity expansion by Sabey Data Center Properties. Sabey’s development pipeline would take its data center computing capacity from its current 275 megawatts to a planned 737 megawatts by 2033, company officials said. A single megawatt powers up to about 1,000 homes, according to industry standards.

artigo.texto: There’s a growing need for long-duration storage to meet energy demand and balance out renewables on the grid. Energy Dome uses compressed carbon dioxide gas in its massive grid batteries, which can deliver power for up to 24 hours. As the world races to meet growing electricity demand, solar and onshore wind power have become the cheapest and quickest-to-deploy sources to install on the grid. But, despite their upsides, both are subject to variations in weather patterns, which means supplies can be intermittent. Energy Dome is using stored carbon dioxide to help smooth out gaps between supply and demand. Advertisement The key component of an Energy Dome plant is a huge white dome that covers an area about the size of seven soccer fields and holds about 2,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide. When energy is available—say, from a connected solar farm—compressors squeeze the gas, turning it into a liquid that’s then stored in carbon-steel tanks. That process generates heat, which the system holds in a proprietary thermal storage material. Then, when the grid needs power, the carbon dioxide is released from the tanks and warmed with the stored heat, turning it back into a gas. That gaseous carbon dioxide then passes through a turbine to generate electricity and flows back into the dome, ready to begin the cycle again. This story is only available to subscribers. Don’t settle for half the story. Get paywall-free access to technology news for the here and now. Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new—utilities have been using compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades. But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world. Energy Dome turned on its first commercial plant in Sardinia, Italy, in 2025. The facility has a capacity of 200 megawatt-hours. That’s enough to power about 18,000 Italian homes for 10 hours. Key indicators Industry: Energy storage Founded: 2020 Headquarters: Milan, Italy Notable fact: Energy Dome has plans for 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of projects across five continents. Potential for impact Cheaper energy storage could help wind and solar meet more of the world’s electricity demand. Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate new installations for short-duration applications of up to four hours. But the economics aren’t competitive for longer durations: A lithium-ion system that provides eight hours of storage at the same power output requires doubling the number of cells. Energy Dome estimates that its technology is roughly 10% to 15% cheaper than lithium-ion batteries for an eight-hour system, and that the economics are even better for longer-duration systems of up to 24 hours. The company says its ability to scale bigger and faster than lithium-ion boils down to the fact that its design uses existing commercially available equipment like compressors and storage tanks. Its plants that are either operational or under contract have eight or 10 hours of capacity. Caveats Energy Dome only has one commercial project that’s operational. It’ll need to build many more to provide the 30 gigawatt-hours of storage it has planned. The technology also isn’t quite as efficient as lithium-ion. Overall, Energy Dome’s process can return about 70% of the electricity it stores to the grid (a measure known as roundtrip efficiency). Lithium-ion batteries average roughly 90%. But some other long-duration storage techniques clock in lower; some iron-air batteries, for example, are around 50%. Advertisement Energy Dome’s plants may not all be benign from a planet-warming perspective. The company offers a version of its system that pairs its carbon dioxide battery with natural gas turbines. That version replaces internal heat storage with waste heat from the gas turbines to help evaporate carbon dioxide. That helps the plant run more efficiently but ultimately results in greenhouse-gas emissions from the natural gas turbines. Next steps Energy Dome has a pipeline of about 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of plants in the works around the world, and many of these projects could come online by the end of the decade. Because the company uses off-the-shelf components, the time from a signed contract to delivered capacity is only two years. In June 2026, for example, it signed a deal with Google to build a 200 MWh plant in Ireland, which is expected to come online in 2028.

artigo.texto: New data center development in Anne Arundel County is on hold while county leaders decide how to regulate the rapidly growing industry. The Anne Arundel County Council voted 7-0 Monday night to approve an amended version of Bill 63-26, establishing a temporary moratorium on new data center development. The moratorium will run until Jan. 31, 2028, or until the county adopts comprehensive data center legislation, whichever comes first. The measure differs significantly from the bill as originally introduced. Council members initially considered banning new privately operated data centers in the county, then unanimously amended the proposal in September to replace the ban with a temporary moratorium. Projects already in the development process will generally be allowed to continue. The amended measure also includes future phases of existing data centers on adjacent or adjoining properties. During the moratorium, the county will establish a work group to study data center development and recommend permanent regulations to the county executive and County Council. The group is expected to consider energy and water use, utility infrastructure, noise, air quality, environmental impacts, and economic development. The debate comes as data centers continue to expand in Anne Arundel County. Microsoft, which is developing a data center campus at Annapolis Junction Business Park, previously testified against the original ban. The company said it supported developing regulations and creating a work group, but wanted existing campuses to continue development. The legislation also calls for repealing a personal property tax assessment reduction for qualified data storage centers. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates. artigo.texto: Zelestra and EDP have signed two new power purchase agreements (PPAs) to hybridise operational solar plants in Spain with battery energy storage systems (BESS), taking their partnership to four hybrid projects and more than 1 GWh of contracted storage capacity in the country. The long-term agreements cover Zelestra’s operational Pedroso solar plant in Seville and Valkyria solar plant in Castilla-La Mancha. Under the agreement, Zelestra will develop a 25 MW BESS with approximately 100 MWh of storage capacity at the 31 MWdc Pedroso solar plant. At the Valkyria project, a 90.45 MW BESS with approximately 362 MWh of storage capacity will be integrated with the 150 MWdc solar plant. Both battery systems will have a four-hour duration. EDP, which is already the offtaker for both solar plants, is expanding its role in the Spanish battery storage market through the new agreements. The latest PPAs bring the companies’ Spanish hybridisation partnership to four projects. In 2025, EDP and Zelestra signed what they described as Spain’s first combined solar and BESS PPA, covering 170 MWdc of solar capacity and 400 MWh of storage at a project in Trujillo, Extremadura. Earlier in 2026, the companies signed an agreement to hybridise an operational solar plant, adding a 160 MWh BESS to the 50 MW Pizarroso solar plant in Cáceres. Across the four projects, the partnership now represents more than 1 GWh of contracted battery storage capacity. The companies said hybridising existing operational solar plants can provide a faster route to increasing grid flexibility, as the projects already have land, grid connections and renewable generation infrastructure in place. Pedro Neves Ferreira, CEO of Global Energy Management at EDP, said the company is developing solutions that combine renewable generation with flexibility assets to improve the value and efficiency of clean energy. He added that integrating energy storage with renewable generation can strengthen system resilience and support electrification and decarbonisation. Jaime Burguete, CEO of Zelestra in Spain, said the partnership is enabling large-scale storage capacity in the Spanish market and described energy storage as a growing segment of the country’s renewable energy sector. artigo.texto: JUWI GmbH, based in Wörrstadt, has recently signed contracts with three leading companies in the energy sector for the technical operation, servicing and maintenance of six further battery energy storage systems (BESS). The facilities are currently under construction and are due to be commissioned within the next six months. For more than five years, the JUWI Group’s O&M experts have been managing battery storage systems in Germany and Belgium. With these newly secured contracts, JUWI is expanding its portfolio of managed battery storage systems to around 700 megawatt-hours of storage capacity. The new projects are being carried out for three different companies and involve storage capacities ranging from 4 to 100 megawatt-hours. JUWI’s services include technical operations management as well as servicing and maintenance for the first few years of the plants’ operational phase. The new contracts underscore the growing importance of battery storage systems for a secure and flexible energy supply, as well as market participants’ confidence in JUWI’s long-standing expertise in operations management and service provision. Oliver Otte, Head of O&M at JUWI GmbH, explains: “We are delighted that three renowned companies in the energy sector have chosen us as their O&M partner for the servicing, maintenance and technical operation of their battery storage systems. With our many years of experience in operating battery storage systems, we create real added value for investors and operators. Our aim is to operate the systems reliably, safely and cost-effectively throughout their entire life cycle.” By further expanding the BESS portfolio, JUWI is strengthening its position as an experienced operations management and service partner for battery storage and renewable energy systems in Europe.

artigo.texto: Indiana has heard plenty about the data center boom: billions in proposed investment and construction jobs. The more consequential question is whether the benefits will extend beyond the project site and be shared by all Hoosier families and businesses. One early answer is coming from Indiana Michigan Power, which has proposed a rate reduction plan to the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. The proposal would reduce Indiana customer bills by about $59 million in 2027, freeze all rates on the monthly bill for three years and, by I&M’s estimate, save its average residential customer about $100 annually. I&M explains why: “This rate decrease is made possible by the load growth and increased revenue it is experiencing from large customers including data centers.” I&M’s proposal offers a concrete early indication of how the economics can work. Large customers bring more than new demand. Their steady, substantial revenue can create room for utilities to invest in transmission, substations and the technology that makes the grid stronger. That means more capacity, fewer and shorter outages, and a system prepared for the factories, homes and businesses that will need dependable electricity in the years ahead. South Bend Mayor James Mueller called the proposal “the power of growth and getting more for less.” It is a concise description of how growth can work for the people of Indiana. Indiana is only beginning to see these investments reach the system. As projects move to construction and operations, the benefits of growth should become easier to recognize: stronger infrastructure, greater capacity and, if I&M is a guide, lower bills for Hoosier households. Data center investment can generate significant local tax revenue to help communities pay for schools, police and fire protection, infrastructure and amenities. A larger tax base can also mean less pressure to raise property tax rates on homeowners and businesses. Water use is changing, too. A new data center planned for Lebanon will use a water-efficient closed-loop system designed to use zero water for most of the year. The developer says a typical AI-optimized data center using this kind of system uses less water annually than two full-service restaurants. Just as important is the people side of this growth. Last month, Indianapolis celebrated the first graduating class of Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy. Indiana is one of four states in the initial pilot for Meta’s $115 million nationwide initiative, which trains people for the skilled trades needed to build and maintain digital infrastructure, power generation and grid modernization. Participants need no prior experience. They are paid while completing the program and graduate with industry credentials and a guaranteed job with a Meta partner. Ethan Blake, a graduate from Fishers, put its value more directly: “They gave me an on ramp to success in a way, and they gave me the tools that I needed to be able to navigate this new workforce. They gave me the knowledge that I needed to be able to navigate the new workforce, and they gave me a job.” That is why this moment matters. Indiana has abundant energy resources, a skilled manufacturing tradition, strategic location and workers ready to build. The data center boom can create jobs for electricians, fiber technicians, equipment operators, construction workers and the many local businesses that support them. It can also catalyze the grid improvements that help every employer and family. I&M’s proposed rate reduction is not the end of the conversation. It is a promising early sign of what Indiana can achieve through new investment, a growth-oriented mindset, and confidence in ourselves and the future. Jim Merritt of Carmel is a former Indiana state senator.

artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons Limited (JWL), through its energy business arm JEM Energy, has strengthened its presence in India’s battery energy storage system (BESS) market by securing a 41 MW/102.5 MWh standalone BESS project in Uttarakhand in partnership with Madhav Infra Projects Limited. The joint venture emerged as the L1 bidder for Cluster C of the Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL) tender issued under the Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) mechanism. The project includes the supply and commissioning of BESS systems with an estimated value of approximately ₹100 crore. The award marks JEM Energy’s entry into the Uttarakhand energy storage market. JWL has also received a formal Letter of Award (LoA) from the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (WBSEDCL) for a 50 MW/200 MWh standalone BESS project. The project will be located at the Jeerat 132 kV substation in North 24 Parganas, West Bengal. JWL had originally secured the project in August 2026, while the latest LoA formalizes the award. Together, the two projects represent a combined BESS capacity of 91 MW/302.5 MWh and strengthen JEM Energy’s pipeline in the rapidly expanding energy storage segment. The company’s expansion comes as India accelerates investments in battery storage to support renewable energy integration and improve grid flexibility. The Union Cabinet’s approval of the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III includes plans to add 50 GWh of battery energy storage capacity along with the development of stronger intra-state transmission infrastructure. Substation-level storage projects such as those being developed in Uttarakhand and West Bengal are expected to support this broader grid modernization strategy. Vivek Lohia, Managing Director of Jupiter Wagons Limited, said that winning the Uttarakhand project and receiving the formal award for the Jeerat project represent important milestones in scaling JEM Energy into a significant energy storage business. The company has set a target of building a BESS order book of approximately ₹1,000 crore by FY27. JWL also expects its electric mobility business to turn EBITDA positive in the third quarter of FY27 and achieve profitability by FY28. JEM Energy plans to continue a disciplined bidding strategy for utility-scale as well as Commercial and Industrial (C&I) energy storage opportunities across India. The company’s growing presence in BESS reflects JWL’s broader strategy of diversifying beyond its traditional railway and mobility operations and participating in high-growth segments linked to India’s energy transition. artigo.texto: Ecopro BM said on Monday it signed a memorandum of understanding with Samsung SDI to cooperate on developing materials for all-solid-state batteries. The two companies will begin joint research and development with the goal of commercialising sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in 2027. They plan to establish a cooperation system from early development through quality evaluation and building a mass-production system. Samsung SDI will take charge of developing all-solid-state battery cells and advancing mass-production technology, while Ecopro BM will be responsible for developing key materials. The cooperation will cover a range of key materials, starting with cathode materials and including electrolytes for cathodes and electrolytes for separators. All-solid-state batteries are seen as next-generation technology that can improve safety and performance. They are cited as a core technology for electric vehicles and humanoid robots because they can be used longer on a single charge and have a lower fire risk. Ecopro BM has secured proprietary process technology in the field of sulfide-based solid electrolytes. It is also operating a pilot plant with annual capacity of 40 tons, the company said. Based on competitiveness in powder-control and quality-management technologies, it is also developing cathode materials suitable for solid electrolytes on the back of its high-nickel cathode material technology. On the back of these results, Ecopro BM was selected in August for the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's "Super Eul" project. The project is an R&D support programme aimed at fostering materials, parts and equipment companies that will lead global supply chains by securing world-leading and first-of-its-kind technologies. Companies propose growth strategies and technology development plans, and selections are made through plan evaluation, technology verification and comprehensive assessment. Ecopro BM passed evaluation with a sulfide-based solid-electrolyte task, and the government plans to support selected companies for at least 7 years with 20 billion won per task. Kong Bo-hyun (공보현), an executive director in charge of research and development at Ecopro BM, said at the time on solid-electrolyte development, "We are currently reviewing pilot mass production with leading customers, and we expect the earliest mass-production timing to be 2027. We have completed mass-production line design and are preparing so that we can immediately begin construction in line with customer demand."

artigo.texto: Environmental Air Systems is scaling in-house capabilities to meet surging data center demand From high-end home installations in North Carolina to gigawatts of modular cooling for some of the world’s biggest data center clients, Environmental Air Systems (EAS) has spent decades bringing every part of the job under one roof. As a complete mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) solutions provider, the business delivers building services, controls, and engineered modular solutions, occupying an unusual position as both a manufacturer and a contractor. While most of the company’s clients today are Fortune 500 companies, EAS has modest roots dating to 1953. To learn more about how EAS has evolved, we sit down with Bill Bullock, Senior VP, Strategic Business Solutions. “We got our start doing residential-type installations for high-end homes, installing some of the first air conditioning and heating in the Greensboro area of North Carolina,” Bill opens. “As we grew, the textile industry came to the Southeast, and we engineered many of the systems that supported it, including custom air handling units and air washers. That work gave rise to our manufacturing division, and we became a sheet metal powerhouse able to do really anything made from sheet metal. “When that market began to decline and jobs moved first to Mexico and then to China, EAS looked elsewhere,” he continues. “We moved to the pharmaceutical industry and built one of the first buildings in North Carolina’s Research Triangle Park for Glaxo Wellcome, now GlaxoSmithKline. In the 1980s, we formed Envirotrol, our controls and building automation business unit.” The next major shift was between 2010 and 2015 when EAS was purchased by Comfort Systems USA. Comfort Systems, which trades under the ticker FIX, is now a $9 billion annual revenue company, and EAS is one of more than 40 operating companies across its fleet. “We’re unique in that we’re both a manufacturer and a contractor, whereas most of the companies Comfort Systems owns are primarily mechanical or electrical contractors,” Bill explains. “Comfort Systems purchased Starr Electric Company in Greensboro and tucked it under EAS to give us the full total solution: mechanical contracting, manufacturing, controls and service, and electrical contracting. “We provide highly customized mechanical and electrical infrastructure such as central utility plants, mechanical rooms, custom air handling equipment, and modular electrical systems. Essentially, we modularize that infrastructure for highly sophisticated and complex industrial-scale projects primarily in the data center, pharmaceutical, and life sciences sectors. Think big infrastructure and utilities, and lots of chilled water, steam, and hot water.” Today, around 80 percent of the company’s work supports data center infrastructure, with the rest split across semiconductor, pharmaceutical, and advanced manufacturing clients. “The concentration of data center work has developed over the last five years or so,” Bill reflects. “We had a more balanced market split before then, but the scale-up of cloud and now AI has fueled growth and offset that sector for us. While growth isn’t a new mindset for us as the company has historically grown every three to five years, the data center industry has seen us experience unprecedented demand.” With demand in the data center markets increasing, EAS has evolved its capabilities for building data center cooling systems off-site. “A modular cooling plant, or a cooling plant of any kind for a data center client is a very complex thing,” Bill explains. “It requires some of the largest chillers and pumps made, and we need highly skilled individuals to handle and assemble such heavy and complex equipment. Everything is expensive and one misstep can cause damage; putting all those parts and pieces together in an efficient system is the most difficult part. However, EAS has manufactured thousands of modular cooling plants, providing gigawatts of cooling to date. We take for granted how easy it has become for us, but it is no joke!” Throughout its extensive history, EAS has continuously strived to bring more aspects of a project in-house, with its total solution model combining engineering, fabrication, controls, electrical work, logistics, and execution under one roof. “Management at EAS has consistently added services and solutions that now enable us to provide a total solution for our clients, hence the addition of Envirotrol,” Bill confirms. “We now also operate freight and logistics, and we’ve expanded our engineering and design capabilities to meet client demand, which has allowed us to support some of the most sophisticated clients on the globe. “What we can provide differs from a company that finds subcontractors and cobbles together a solution,” he adds. “We are one company with one goal, one team, and one focus in mind. The alternative is that each company has its own agenda, with its own cost structure and profit margins. EAS has our client in mind throughout the whole process, and it’s our own solution without other outside forces potentially working in silos.” For mission-critical projects, the clearest advantage EAS offers is time, as it can typically reduce a build schedule by 25 percent or more. “Time savings begin at the design stage,” Bill says. “We ensure the design considers manufacturability, constructability, cost, and schedule, rather than the design changing hands between multiple firms or entities, which can cause delays or cost issues. We own the model and we design it with the trades in mind, meaning we avoid a situation where someone finishes a portion of the design and it clashes with another. “It also helps that we’re building in a manufacturing environment, applying advanced manufacturing principles. artigo.texto: Demanda por Interconexão de Data Centers de IA Dispara: Quais Ações de Comunicação Óptica Mais se Beneficiam? 5 Ações dos EUA para Acompanhar A expansão dos data centers de IA impulsiona a demanda por infraestrutura de transmissão de dados de alta velocidade, priorizando conexões ópticas sobre cabos de cobre para evitar gargalos nas GPUs. Cinco empresas destacam-se nesse mercado: Lumentum, Coherent, Applied Optoelectronics, Credo Technology e Ciena. Lumentum lidera em crescimento de componentes ópticos; Coherent oferece um portfólio diversificado e escala; Applied Optoelectronics apresenta alta elasticidade em módulos de 800G e 1,6T; Credo destaca-se por margens elevadas em chips de conectividade; e Ciena foca em redes ópticas de grande escala para data centers. TradingKey - A competição nos data centers de IA está se expandindo para além do simples aumento no número de GPUs, voltando-se para o aprimoramento da eficiência da transmissão de dados em todo o cluster de computação. À medida que milhares ou mesmo dezenas de milhares de aceleradores de IA são conectados em um único cluster, os cabos de cobre tradicionais enfrentam limitações crescentes em distância de transmissão, largura de banda e consumo de energia, impulsionando o desenvolvimento acelerado de tecnologias como módulos ópticos de 800G e 1,6T, comutação óptica e óptica co-empacotada. A comunicação óptica para IA refere-se à transmissão de informações por meio de sinais ópticos entre chips, servidores, racks e data centers. Em comparação com as conexões tradicionais de cobre, as conexões ópticas oferecem vantagens na transmissão a longas distâncias, alta largura de banda e controle de eficiência energética, tornando-se particularmente adequadas para os clusters de computação de IA em constante expansão. O treinamento de grandes modelos de IA não é realizado de forma independente por uma única GPU; em vez disso, exige um vasto conjunto de processadores trocando parâmetros e dados continuamente. Quando as velocidades de transmissão de rede não acompanham o ritmo das velocidades de computação, as GPUs podem ficar ociosas à espera de dados. Como resultado, os data centers de IA exigem não apenas mais chips, mas também atualizações sincronizadas em switches, chips de conectividade, módulos ópticos, lasers e sistemas de redes ópticas. Em comparação com a computação em nuvem tradicional, o treinamento de IA exige a transmissão frequente de volumes massivos de dados entre servidores. Se a velocidade da rede não acompanhar o poder de processamento das GPUs, até mesmo os chips mais caros podem não operar em capacidade máxima por ficarem aguardando a chegada dos dados. Consequentemente, a comunicação óptica está deixando de ser um simples equipamento de suporte para se tornar um componente vital da infraestrutura de IA. No mercado de ações dos EUA, a Coherent (COHR), a Lumentum (LITE), a Credo Technology (CRDO), a Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) e a Ciena (CIEN) são atualmente ações representativas no segmento de interconexão de alta velocidade para IA. No entanto, as cinco empresas diferem em seu posicionamento de negócios, abrangendo componentes ópticos, módulos ópticos, chips de conectividade, sistemas de redes ópticas e equipamentos de interconexão para data centers. Lumentum: Fornecedora Principal de Componentes Ópticos de Alta Velocidade e Lasers A Lumentum vem se tornando uma das empresas de crescimento mais rápido no atual ciclo de comunicação óptica para IA. Seus produtos abrangem componentes de comunicação óptica, módulos ópticos para nuvem, sistemas de comutação de circuitos ópticos e lasers de alta potência necessários para a tecnologia de óptica empacotada (co-packaged optics). A receita recém-divulgada pela Lumentum para o quarto trimestre do ano fiscal de 2026 atingiu US$ 1,006 bilhão, uma alta de 109,3% na comparação anual, com lucro por ação não-GAAP de US$ 3,23. A empresa projeta que a receita do primeiro trimestre do ano fiscal de 2027 alcance de US$ 1,225 bilhão a US$ 1,275 bilhão, indicando que a demanda por comunicações ópticas de alta velocidade continua crescendo rapidamente. Mais importante ainda, a diretoria da Lumentum declarou explicitamente que, à medida que as cargas de trabalho de computação de IA exigem maior velocidade e largura de banda, a arquitetura dos data centers está se voltando para a conectividade óptica. A empresa está avançando em produtos relacionados à tecnologia 1,6T e expandindo sua presença em soluções de conectividade óptica. A força da Lumentum reside em seus componentes essenciais de comunicação óptica e tecnologia laser, garantindo-lhe maior sensibilidade às mudanças na demanda por interconexão óptica de alta velocidade em comparação com fabricantes dedicados exclusivamente a equipamentos para data centers. No entanto, a LITE tornou-se uma ação de infraestrutura de IA amplamente monitorada, apresentando alta volatilidade no preço de suas ações e em seu valuation. Consequentemente, qualquer desaceleração nas expectativas de alto crescimento pode exercer uma pressão significativa sobre o seu valuation. Coherent: Abrangendo Múltiplos Segmentos de Dispositivos Ópticos, Módulos Ópticos e Data Centers de IA A Coherent é uma das empresas de fotônica com o escopo de atuação mais amplo entre essas cinco companhias, com produtos que abrangem comunicações ópticas, lasers, módulos ópticos e outras tecnologias fotônicas. A receita da empresa atingiu US$ 2,05 bilhões no quarto trimestre do ano fiscal de 2026, uma alta de 34% na comparação anual, com margem bruta GAAP de 38,5% e margem bruta não GAAP de 40,2%. A empresa afirmou que os data centers de IA estão migrando de conexões de cobre para interconexões ópticas, e que o portfólio fotônico abrangente e a escala de fabricação da Coherent a posicionam bem para capturar essa demanda de longo prazo. artigo.texto: After months of negotiations and tense public meetings, Colleton County has reached an agreement with two landowners over data center development in the county. The settlement establishes a “data center exclusion area,” which prohibits data centers in sensitive areas, including the ACE Basin, one of the largest undeveloped estuaries on the East Coast and the South Carolina’s crowning conservation achievement. The Southern Environmental Law Center filed the lawsuit on behalf of Jennifer Singleton and Miles Crosby, both of whom own property near the previously proposed 1,000-megawatt data center southwest of Walterboro. The project proposal surfaced after county council changed the zoning code so the Zoning Board of Appeals could approve data centers in a single vote. About 400 people attended a December 2025 Zoning Board of Appeals meeting to oppose the plans. Singleton and Crosby filed the lawsuit soon after, arguing the approval process violated state law, the county’s comprehensive plan and the county’s own zoning code. What’s in the settlement? The settlement bans data centers in portions of the county that include the ACE Basin, as well as along sensitive rivers. K.C. Campbell, a spokesperson for the county, said that county staff are going to continue to refine the map before sending it to the planning commission and, later, county council for approval. It will then become part of the county’s comprehensive plan, a master document that guides long-term development. The data center exclusion zone covers about 62 percent of the county, said Robby Maynor, a policy advocate with the Southern Environmental Law Center. Both parties in the lawsuit were happy with the outcome. For Singleton, who set out to prevent a 859-acre data center near her home, the added protections across broader swaths of the county are a big win. The settlement assigns the Southern Environmental Law Center an advisory role. The environmental advocacy group will help guide decisions related to data centers and development more broadly, Maynor and Campbell said. “I think that this is a model that could probably be replicated elsewhere,” Singleton said. She’s relieved but said work still needs to be done since other areas of the state remain vulnerable to data centers. “It’s a win, but not the win,” said Belvin Olasov, director of the Charleston Climate Coalition, which was not involved in the negotiations. In his view, there has been some positive news on data centers across the state, including a number of data center moratoriums that municipalities passed in recent months. A number of large projects have been approved across the state as well. Maynor, a Colleton County resident, said that while he is optimistic about the outcome in Colleton County, the settlement is a “building block,” and it doesn’t replace much-needed statewide regulation. A new site A few months after SELC filed the lawsuit, Colleton County Council approved a six-month moratorium on data center development. Soon after the moratorium went into affect, the county approved an overhaul of its data center zoning regime with little explanation. Council can now apply a “digital infrastructure overlay district” to various areas in the county. It also amended the comprehensive plan to include the “unique nature” of data centers and applied the overlay to a property near the unincorporated community of Smoaks. County officials and developer Ken Loeber of Eagle Rock Partners gathered for a public information session on Sept. 22. Eagle Rock Partners had abandoned the plan for a data center outside Walterboro, which would now fall firmly within the settlement’s data center exclusion zone. The developer has settled on a site within the northern reaches of Colleton County, which now sits within the new “digital infrastructure overlay district.” Posters around the room touted a number of benefits, including a 200-foot forested buffer, noise limits and opportunities for local businesses in catering, landscaping and other areas. Brantley Strickland, executive director of the Colleton County Economic Alliance, said he was unable to go into specifics, but data center developers were still interested in the county. When speaking about the settlement, Maynor said that Colleton County has not grown in the same way as its neighbors to the north and south, which include Beaufort and Charleston counties. That has been a good thing when it comes to preserving rural life and character, but it has also meant the area continues to cope with a lack of opportunities that come with economic growth. Hopefully, the county can strike a balance, fostering economic development while protecting sensitive areas such as the ACE Basin, Maynor said.

Contemporary Amperex Technology stock sits 38.83 percent below its high Published on 10/08/2026 at 11:56 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Contemporary Amperex Technology (ISIN CNE100003662) proposed a EUR 50 million shareholder loan for its Spanish battery joint venture. EnergyTrend reported on October 8, 2026, that the proposal dated to September 30 and was intended to fund construction investment and daily operations. Spain plant gets working capital Contemporary Star Energy S.L. is the controlled subsidiary responsible for the joint battery factory with Stellantis in Spain. Contemporary Amperex Technology indirectly owns 50 percent of the venture, while Stellantis subsidiaries hold the remaining 50 percent, according to EnergyTrend. The loan carries a fixed annual interest rate of 3.55 percent and can be drawn in several tranches. The principal and accrued interest may be converted into equity, while the maximum term is 12 months; the proposal still requires approval by the general meeting of shareholders, the same report said. Strong first-half operating figures The financing decision comes against a strong operating backdrop. In the first half of 2026, revenue reached CNY 276.92 billion, up 54.80 percent from the prior-year period, while net profit attributable to shareholders rose 41.98 percent to CNY 43.28 billion, Gate News reported on September 16, 2026. Power battery revenue was CNY 192.13 billion in that period, up 46.02 percent year over year, while energy storage battery revenue rose 87.54 percent to CNY 53.26 billion. Capacity utilization reached 94.86 percent, giving investors a more detailed measure of the company's operating scale than revenue alone. Targets remain above the A-share Goldman Sachs named CATL a top China battery pick and set a 12-month target of RMB 565 for its A-shares on October 2, 2026, according to EconoTimes. The bank cited scale, technology and cost advantages, while identifying weaker demand, raw material prices and competition as risks. Stock stays near its yearly low The Shenzhen-listed A-share was last at CNY 286.75 on October 8, 2026 at 3:04 p.m. CST, down 1.50 percent from CNY 291.11. Its CNY 285.17 to CNY 468.75 52-week range places the price 0.55 percent above the low and 38.83 percent below the high, while market capitalization stood at CNY 1.3 trillion. artigo.texto: Crédito de carbono de alta qualidade sobe 75%, diz MSCI Levantamento apresentado na Climate Week NYC mostra expansão de sistemas regulados e US$ 5,5 bilhões em contratos futuros. Laura Albuquerque, co-CEO da Future Climate, analisa o que os números indicam para o financiamento de projetos no Brasil Os créditos de carbono classificados como de alta qualidade pela MSCI tiveram valorização de 75% em 12 meses e chegaram a US$ 14 por tonelada, enquanto os de menor qualidade são negociados abaixo de US$ 2. Os dados foram apresentados por Guy Turner, diretor-geral da área de mercados de carbono da companhia, durante a Climate Week NYC, realizada em Nova York em setembro de 2026, e indicam avanços em três frentes: ampliação dos sistemas regulados, diferenciação de preços por qualidade e mobilização de capital. Segundo a apresentação, foram registrados US$ 5,5 bilhões em investimentos em contratos futuros e projetos, distribuídos em mais de 200 transações, com um quarto dos recursos destinado a iniciativas de remoção de carbono. Os contratos de compra antecipada de créditos de restauração da natureza monitorados pela MSCI, com entrega prevista para 2035, alcançaram US$ 45 por tonelada, alta de 10% em relação ao primeiro semestre de 2025. Sistemas regulados ganham escala No período analisado, a União Europeia passou a incluir integralmente as emissões do transporte marítimo no comércio de emissões do bloco, o EU ETS. A Indonésia avançou em normas para dar clareza e amplitude às negociações de carbono, e o México se comprometeu a lançar um sistema nacional em 2027, com cobertura de 40% de suas emissões. Na Ásia, a Índia colocou em operação um portal para administrar registros e transações do período de conformidade de 2025 a 2027, que abrange 740 entidades e mais de 700 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e). O Vietnã contabilizou as primeiras operações de seu sistema, referentes ao ciclo 2025 a 2026, e o Japão tornou obrigatório o GX-ETS, que cobre 40% das emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa e reúne entre 300 e 400 empresas. Para Laura Albuquerque, co-CEO da Future Climate e membra do Comitê da Ambição Net Zero da Rede Brasileira do Pacto Global da ONU, durante cerca de duas décadas a defesa desses mercados se apoiou em estudos sobre seu potencial para reduzir o custo de cumprimento das metas climáticas. "A lógica econômica permanece: direcionar recursos para oportunidades de redução e remoção de emissões que permitam alcançar essas metas com maior eficiência. A diferença é que, hoje, a experiência acumulada oferece dados concretos para orientar decisões de política pública e investimento", afirma. Demanda corporativa e integridade No segmento de créditos, os números da MSCI mostram atividade consistente. Cerca de 4 mil empresas definiram metas pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), o equivalente a 4 bilhões de toneladas de emissões, e um quarto delas assumiu compromissos de emissões líquidas zero (net zero). Em 12 meses, mil novos projetos foram registrados, outros 1.150 entraram na carteira em preparação e empresas aposentaram créditos provenientes de 2.850 projetos. A projeção da MSCI indica que as aposentadorias globais de 2026 devem ficar próximas do volume de 2025, em torno de 200 milhões de toneladas. Na leitura da co-CEO, o sinal mais relevante está na distância de valor entre projetos, que torna a avaliação de qualidade parte central da decisão de alocação de recursos para compradores e investidores. A executiva observa ainda que a convergência em torno dos Core Carbon Principles, definidos pelo Conselho de Integridade para o Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (ICVCM, na sigla em inglês), cria uma linguagem comum sobre integridade, mas exige que preços e financiamento reconheçam os custos de desenvolvimento. Capital antes da receita Para as desenvolvedoras, o cenário evidencia a necessidade de recursos antes da geração de receita. "Projetos exigem recursos para estruturação, implantação, monitoramento, ratings para a verificação ao longo de anos. A valorização dos créditos de qualidade precisa se traduzir em condições de financiamento que permitam produzir essa oferta", diz Laura. Segundo ela, os contratos futuros podem contribuir nesse processo ao conectar a demanda dos compradores ao ciclo de investimento dos projetos. O Brasil tem diferentes vias de demanda em construção: o mercado voluntário; o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042, de 11 de dezembro de 2024, com os Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs); os mecanismos do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris; o programa de combustível sustentável de aviação (SAF, na sigla em inglês) previsto na Lei nº 14.993; e o Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional (Corsia). Na avaliação da executiva, são caminhos com regras e escalas distintas, que precisam ser considerados na estruturação dos investimentos. Laura pondera que preços, investimentos e aposentadorias não substituem a mensuração dos resultados climáticos, embora demonstrem uma base observável de atividade econômica, demanda e alocação de capital. "Para o país, a oportunidade está em usar essa experiência para desenvolver um mercado capaz de financiar projetos de qualidade, e o próximo avanço dependerá de transformar os sinais de demanda em capital disponível para quem entrega reduções e remoções verificáveis", conclui a executiva. Para mais informações, basta acessar: https://futureclimate.com

artigo.texto: Por que Data Centers são importantes? E quais os problemas? Guia do Adulto Premium te explica as polêmicas em torno das estruturas que sustentam a inteligência artificial. Crédito: Larissa Burchard/Estadão Gerando resumo O presidente da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel), Carlos Baigorri, afirmou que o governo federal não deve se meter na definição dos data centers que serão implementados no Brasil. Essa escolha deve ficar por conta das empresas, defendeu. “Não dá para esperar que tenha um agente do Estado definindo onde vão estar os data centers”, afirmou Baigorri. “Não tem esse planejamento aqui. Tudo é business, é mercado. Na Anatel, não somos bons em fazer negócio. Não somos empreendedores, não é esse o nosso know how. Se fizermos um planejamento disso, não vai ficar bom.” O presidente da Anatel deu uma palestra nesta terça-feira, 6, durante a Futurecom, feira de telecomunicações que reúne empresários e autoridades públicas. Baigorri argumentou que o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura digital – como redes de fibra óptica, cabos submarinos e data centers – deve ter uma regulamentação mínima, dando liberdade para que as empresas façam os investimentos que julgarem necessários. “O mercado tecnológico, com dinâmica acelerada, funciona se tiver boas regras”, afirmou, citando a necessidade de segurança institucional e jurídica. O presidente da Anatel avaliou ainda que as telecomunicações são um exemplo a ser seguido por outros setores. Ele afirmou que há milhares de provedores de banda larga fixa, três grandes operadoras nacionais de redes móveis e novos entrantes no setor de internet por satélite. Essa diversidade, disse, garante a qualidade do sinal e uma cobertura ampla no País. “Telecom não é mais um problema no Brasil”, disse. “O setor funciona com o mínimo de intervenção do Estado. A intervenção existe, é necessária, mas muito menor que em outros setores.” O que aconteceu na implantação da TV a cabo Baigorri lembrou que, muitos anos atrás, a Anatel e o Ministério das Comunicações tinham um controle rigoroso do mercado. Isso envolvia até um planejamento para liberação de outorga para implantação de TV a cabo nas cidades. Na sua visão, esse foi um fatores que encareceram a TV a cabo e impediram a sua popularização no País. “Tinha empresário querendo investir, mas não conseguia outorga”, relembrou. Como exemplo, citou que a banda larga no Brasil trafega por redes de fibra óptica, com mais velocidade de navegação, enquanto na Europa, há lentidão para substituição dos cabos de cobre, pois há regras e obrigações que oneram as empresas locais. “No Brasil, o cobre vale mais arrancado do solo e derretido, porque as redes de fibra óptica são diversificadas, e ninguém quer explorar o cobre”, disse. “No Brasil, o cobre foi recolhido não por desejo do Estado, mas das empresas, que enxergaram aí uma oportunidade de negócio, com melhor serviço.”

artigo.texto: A previsão do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) de reunir baterias, hidrelétricas e termelétricas nos próximos leilões de reserva de capacidade reforça a necessidade de dividir os custos dessas contratações entre todo o setor, defende a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). Para a entidade, a possibilidade de contratar as tecnologias nos mesmos certames exige tratamento igual no custeio, com a revisão da regra introduzida pela Lei 15.269/2025 que atribui apenas aos geradores o pagamento pela contratação das baterias. Até aqui, os certames para baterias foram organizados separadamente dos destinados às demais fontes de potência, que contratou, em um leilão caro, realizado em março, 19 gigawatts (GW) de potência por meio de 100 projetos, a maioria de térmicas a gás. O calendário anunciado pelo MME para 2027 a 2029 abre a possibilidade de contratação conjunta — mudança que, para o diretor-executivo da Absae, Fabio Lima, reforça a necessidade de eliminar a diferença de tratamento. “Essa lei [Lei 15.269/2025], quando diz ‘pague a bateria de uma forma diferente’, ela é uma ferramenta para impedir a competição neutra entre soluções”, afirmou o executivo à agência eixos. A Absae avalia positivamente a Portaria Normativa MME 143/2026, publicada em edição extra do Diário Oficial da União em 29 de setembro. A norma prevê leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência no segundo semestre de 2027, 2028 e 2029, condicionados às necessidades identificadas nos estudos do planejamento setorial. O cronograma permite considerar baterias, armazenamento hidráulico por usinas reversíveis, hidrelétricas e termelétricas, inclusive a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos. Antes disso, os primeiros leilões dedicados exclusivamente às baterias estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro deste ano, com a regra de custeio gerando atrito no setor. Para Lima, o calendário sinaliza que a contratação de potência deve continuar nos próximos anos e que diferentes tecnologias podem atender às necessidades do sistema, conforme os atributos exigidos. A comparação, segundo ele, deve considerar a duração da entrega de potência e o nível de flexibilidade das soluções. “Eu preciso de potência com qual duração, com qual nível de flexibilidade? A partir desses atributos, eu vejo em que ponto dessa régua eu sou atendido por uma solução, por duas soluções, por três soluções. E fazê-las competir para alcançar o menor custo global, alcançar maior eficiência para o setor”, disse. Congresso e Aneel A regra específica para o armazenamento está no parágrafo 6º do artigo 3º-A da Lei 10.848/2004, alterada pela Lei 15.269/2025. O deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP) apresentou o PL 3716/2026 para revogar esse dispositivo e submeter as baterias à regra geral de custeio da reserva de capacidade, que prevê a participação de usuários finais e geradores. A discussão ocorre paralelamente à preparação dos leilões de dezembro pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). A diretora Agnes da Costa disse, em conversa com o estúdio eixos na ROG.e 2026, esperar que a decisão do Congresso sobre o rateio aconteça após os certames. A agência seguirá a legislação vigente enquanto não houver alteração. Lima avalia que cabe ao Congresso corrigir a distinção entre tecnologias, enquanto a Aneel deve regulamentar a regra existente e conduzir os leilões. “A Aneel não pode trabalhar com a hipótese de se a lei vai ser ou não corrigida. Ela tem que cumprir o seu papel de regular o dispositivo e de fazer o leilão.” Benefícios para os consumidores A defesa de um rateio mais amplo também se apoia nos benefícios econômicos do armazenamento para os consumidores, segundo a Absae. Estudo desenvolvido pela Volt Robotics para a entidade estima que, no cenário de referência utilizado pela Análise de Impacto Regulatório da Aneel, a instalação de 4,5 gigawatts (GW) de sistemas de armazenamento por baterias (BESS) pode gerar benefícios de R$ 8,9 bilhões por ano para os consumidores, enquanto os ganhos atribuídos aos geradores chegam a R$ 550 milhões anuais. Os benefícios estimados para os consumidores são cerca de 16 vezes os atribuídos aos geradores. O rateio está entre os principais pontos de divergência na consulta pública da Aneel sobre a minuta do edital. O processo ficou aberto de 30 de julho a 14 de setembro e recebeu 88 contribuições, divulgadas em 21 de setembro. Também foram discutidos a participação de baterias instaladas junto a usinas existentes e os efeitos das exigências de conteúdo local sobre prazos e custos. Associações de geradores e desenvolvedores defendem compartilhar o custeio com os consumidores por entenderem que os benefícios são sistêmicos. Já Abrace, Concen e Abradee sustentam que a expansão das renováveis intermitentes gerou a necessidade de capacidade firme e que o custo deve permanecer com a geração, conforme a legislação atual. Risco de inadimplência Além da mudança no rateio, a Absae pede que a Aneel reveja o tratamento do risco de inadimplência na minuta do edital. Para Lima, o empreendedor contratado tem direito a receber pelo serviço prestado, e a regulação deve assegurar essa receita. “O risco do empreendedor é aquilo que ele pode manejar, é comprar um bom sistema, implantar e operá-lo adequadamente.” O argumento está ligado ao modelo escolhido para os leilões. Segundo o executivo, as baterias atenderão ao Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), que decidirá os horários de carga e descarga, e dependerão da receita pela disponibilidade de potência. Ao contrário de modelos adotados em outros mercados, os empreendimentos não poderão complementar essa remuneração com receitas obtidas pela compra e venda de energia em horários com preços diferentes. “No Brasil é uma receita integral, o projeto todo tem que caber dentro daquela receita. Justamente por isso o risco da inadimplência não pode ser do empreendedor, porque eu não estou indo para o mercado privado fazer contratos bilaterais

artigo.texto: Air Liquide Major player in hydrogen infrastructure According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Hydrogen Storage Materials market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global hydrogen storage materials market is positioned for transformative growth through 2035, driven by the urgent need for bankable long-duration energy storage and the scaling of hydrogen mobility. This market, encompassing solid-state materials and engineered systems that store hydrogen via adsorption or chemical bonding, is evolving from niche technology demonstration to commercial deployment. Demand is bifurcating: high-performance, high-cost materials serve mobility applications such as fuel cell vehicles, aviation, and maritime, while cost-optimized, scalable materials target stationary energy storage. Material selection is increasingly a systems engineering decision, influenced by balance-of-plant complexity, power conversion compatibility, and thermal management. Supply chain resilience remains a critical bottleneck due to dependencies on rare earth elements and specialized alloys, exposing the market to geopolitical risks. The qualification and certification burden is immense, particularly for mobility and large-scale stationary storage, creating time-to-market barriers that favor established players. Project economics for hydrogen-based long-duration storage are currently dominated by electrolyzer and power conversion costs, placing intense pressure on storage material costs to achieve total system bankability. The competitive landscape is fragmenting into advanced material specialists, integrated system providers, and energy majors, with channel control shifting toward those offering certified, bankable sub-systems. Regional strategies diverge, with some geographies acting as demand hubs and others as manufacturing hubs, creating complex trade flows and local content requirements. The baseline scenario for the hydrogen storage materials market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust expansion, underpinned by the global energy transition and the imperative to decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors. The market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 18.5%, reaching a market index of 450 by 2035 (2025=100). This growth is not uniform; it is characterized by a bifurcation between mobility and stationary storage applications. In mobility, demand is driven by fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs), buses, trucks, and maritime vessels, where high gravimetric and volumetric density are paramount, favoring metal hydrides and complex hydrides despite higher costs. In stationary storage, the focus is on long-duration energy storage (LDES) to support renewable integration, where cost per kilowatt-hour and cycle life are critical, driving adoption of lower-cost materials and engineered systems. The supply chain will face significant challenges, including limited high-volume production of specialized alloy powders and dependence on critical minerals like rare earth elements. However, these challenges also spur innovation in alternative chemistries and recycling. The qualification and certification burden will remain a key barrier, but as standards evolve and more materials achieve certification, the market will broaden. Project economics will improve as scale and manufacturing efficiencies reduce costs, but the pace of growth will be sensitive to policy support, hydrogen infrastructure build-out, and the cost of competing technologies like lithium-ion batteries. Overall, the market is poised for a decade of dynamic growth, with significant opportunities for companies that can navigate the technical and commercial complexities. The mobility sector represents the most dynamic and demanding application for hydrogen storage materials. Currently, fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs), buses, and trucks rely predominantly on compressed hydrogen tanks (Type IV), but solid-state materials offer the potential for higher volumetric density, lower pressure, and improved safety. Through 2035, as FCEV adoption accelerates in heavy-duty transport, maritime, and aviation, demand for advanced metal hydrides and complex hydrides will surge. Key demand-side indicators include vehicle production volumes, refueling infrastructure build-out, and total cost of ownership parity with diesel. The mechanism is straightforward: as fleet operators seek zero-emission solutions with long range and fast refueling, hydrogen storage materials that enable compact, lightweight, and safe onboard storage become critical. However, cost and durability remain challenges, with ongoing R&D focused on reducing material costs and improving cycle life. The sector's growth will be punctuated by regional differences, with Asia-Pacific leading in FCEV deployment, followed by Europe and North America. Current trend: Rapid growth driven by decarbonization targets and expanding model availability.. Major trends: Shift toward heavy-duty FCEVs and buses, requiring higher capacity storage, Development of low-pressure, high-density storage systems for maritime and aviation, Increasing partnerships between material suppliers and OEMs for integrated storage solutions, and Government mandates and subsidies for zero-emission commercial vehicles. Representative participants: Toyota Motor Corporation, Hyundai Motor Company, Nikola Corporation, Ballard Power Systems Inc, Cummins Inc, and Hexagon Purus ASA. The stationary power sector, including utilities and grid operators, is increasingly turning to hydrogen storage materials for long-duration energy storage (LDES) to balance renewable intermittency and provide backup power. Currently, deployment is limited to pilot projects and demonstration plants, but through 2035, as renewable penetration exceeds 50% in many regions, the need for cost-effective, scalable LDES will drive significant demand. artigo.texto: Tesla Powerwall, Megapack According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Storage Racks market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global battery storage racks market is entering a phase of sustained expansion, underpinned by the accelerating deployment of energy storage systems across utility, commercial, and residential applications. Battery storage racks are engineered structural frameworks that securely house, organize, and support battery modules, integrating thermal management, wiring, and safety components. As renewable energy penetration rises and grid operators seek flexibility, the demand for robust, modular, and containerized rack solutions is intensifying. The market is characterized by a diverse competitive landscape, ranging from specialized engineering firms to diversified industrial manufacturers and system integrators. Between 2026 and 2035, growth will be propelled by utility-scale storage projects, data center UPS requirements, and the proliferation of residential solar-plus-storage systems. However, supply chain volatility, evolving safety standards, and intense price competition present notable challenges. This report provides a data-driven analysis of market size, segmentation, regional dynamics, and key trends, offering stakeholders a transparent view of the opportunities and risks shaping the industry's trajectory through 2035. The baseline scenario for the world battery storage racks market anticipates robust growth from 2026 to 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.2%, reaching a market index of 220 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook assumes continued policy support for renewable energy, declining battery costs, and rapid expansion of utility-scale storage capacity. The market's expansion is closely tied to global energy storage installations, which are projected to multiply several times over the forecast period. Stationary and containerized racks will dominate demand, particularly for grid-scale projects, while modular and rack-mounted systems gain traction in commercial and residential segments. Asia-Pacific will remain the largest market, driven by China's aggressive storage targets, followed by North America and Europe. Supply chain constraints for steel and aluminum, along with logistical bottlenecks, may temper growth in the short term, but innovation in materials and modular designs will enhance cost efficiency. The competitive landscape is expected to consolidate, with larger players leveraging scale and integrated solutions. Overall, the market is poised for a period of dynamic expansion, with significant opportunities for manufacturers that can offer standardized, safety-compliant, and thermally optimized rack solutions. Utility-scale energy storage is the largest and fastest-growing end-use segment for battery storage racks, driven by the global shift toward renewable energy and the need for grid stability. These projects require large-scale, containerized or stationary racks that can house thousands of battery modules, often in harsh outdoor environments. Demand is propelled by national renewable portfolio standards, capacity auctions, and declining battery costs. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from the integration of solar and wind farms, where storage racks are essential for smoothing output and providing peak capacity. Key demand-side indicators include the volume of utility-scale storage projects announced, grid interconnection queues, and government tenders. The trend is toward higher energy density, modular designs for faster installation, and integrated thermal management to ensure safety and longevity. Major companies supplying racks for this segment include Vertiv, Eaton, and Sungrow, often in partnership with battery manufacturers and EPC contractors. Current trend: Rapid expansion. Major trends: Shift toward containerized and modular rack systems for faster deployment, Integration of advanced thermal management and fire suppression within racks, Increasing use of steel and aluminum alloys for lightweight, corrosion-resistant structures, Standardization of rack designs to reduce costs and lead times, and Growing adoption of digital monitoring and predictive maintenance features. Representative participants: Vertiv Holdings, Eaton Corporation, Sungrow Power Supply, Fluence Energy, Tesla Inc, and BYD Company. Commercial and industrial (C&I) backup power applications are a significant driver of battery storage rack demand, as businesses seek to ensure operational continuity amid grid instability and rising energy costs. These systems typically require modular or rack-mounted battery configurations that can be scaled to match facility load profiles. Demand is particularly strong in regions with unreliable grid infrastructure, as well as in sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare, and retail, where power interruptions can cause substantial financial losses. Through 2035, the segment will expand as more companies adopt on-site storage to manage demand charges, participate in demand response programs, and integrate renewable generation. Key indicators include commercial construction activity, electricity price volatility, and the adoption of energy-as-a-service models. Rack solutions for C&I must balance compactness, safety, and ease of installation, often incorporating integrated power management hardware. Companies like Schneider Electric, ABB, and Rittal are prominent in this space. Current trend: Steady growth. Major trends: Growing adoption of behind-the-meter storage for demand charge management, Integration of racks with building management systems for smart energy control, Increased focus on safety and code compliance in urban installations, Rise of energy-as-a-service models reducing upfront costs for businesses, and Modular rack designs enabling incremental capacity expansion. artigo.texto: De 1946 ao Data Center do TikTok no Ceará: a evolução da infraestrutura tech no mundo e no Brasil! Dos porões do ENIAC em 1946 aos megaprojetos com usinas nucleares e instalações no Brasil: conheça a história completa dos Data Centers!. Entidades que representam o segmento de data centers querem uma redução de 90% no Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços (ICMS) dos equipamentos necessários para a infraestrutura, conforme reportou o site Telesíntese. O tema foi abordado durante a abertura do evento Data Center World, na última terça-feira (6). A negociação envolve o Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) e objetiva complementar os benefícios oferecidos pelo Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), sancionado pelo governo federal no mês passado. Porém, os estados resistem à proposta, conforme Walter Wolff, presidente da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais (Brasscom). Outros pontos em discussão Os equipamentos que seriam beneficiados com a redução do ICMS não contemplam toda a infraestrutura física dos centros de dados, segundo Wolff. A lista ainda está em discussão com fabricantes brasileiros e deve ser concentrada em eletrônicos, incluindo cerca de 25 dispositivos. - Para o representante da Brasscom, a participação dos estados na iniciativa, junto com os benefícios federais, é importante para aumentar a competitividade do Brasil no cenário internacional; - Vale lembrar que o ICMS é um tributo de responsabilidade estadual que incide sobre a venda de produtos e a prestação de serviços, com a alíquota variando conforme a unidade federativa; - Junto com a redução do imposto, as entidades também pedem a regulamentação do Redata, que pode ser concluída nas próximas semanas; - Apesar da expectativa de um desfecho rápido, alguns pontos ainda são discutidos, o que pode resultar em atrasos. Um deles é sobre a disponibilidade de energia para os data centers, conhecidos por enormes demandas de eletricidade e água. As indefinições também afetam os equipamentos beneficiados, as classificações fiscais dos produtos e os procedimentos para solicitar inclusões. Outra pendência é quanto à previsibilidade dos benefícios do programa. O setor defende um prazo de cinco anos, o que ofereceria maior segurança na tomada de decisões de investimentos de longo prazo, pois a construção da infraestrutura geralmente é demorada. Ampliando a infraestrutura nacional Os benefícios tributários, a regulamentação do Redata e a adaptação à reforma tributária representam uma grande oportunidade de crescimento para os data centers no Brasil, segundo Victor Arnaud, presidente da Equinix. Para ele, a redução de custos incentiva as empresas a transferirem cargas de processamento para o país. Essas capacidades computacionais que atendem aos usuários brasileiros estão hospedadas no exterior. Mas com os novos incentivos, Arnaud acredita que as empresas vão ampliar os investimentos no território nacional. A necessidade de ampliação da infraestrutura, diante do crescimento da IA, também pode levar os centros de dados para o espaço. Saiba mais sobre os planos do setor para a órbita terrestre. artigo.texto: A Kingston Technology, empresa mundial em produtos de memória e soluções de armazenamento, participa da primeira edição da Data Center World (DCW) em São Paulo, evento que acontece entre os dias 6 e 8 de outubro na capital paulista. O movimento reforça o DNA corporativo global de uma marca que há mais de três décadas é fornecedora chave para as maiores infraestruturas de Nuvem e gigantes globais de tecnologia. A presença da Kingston na feira simboliza um movimento estratégico de aceleração e fortalecimento das suas operações no mercado B2B e de infraestrutura da América Latina, impulsionado pela alta demanda de Inteligência Artificial alinhado ao fato do Brasil liderar consecutivamente, há cinco anos, o mercado regional de servidores. No estande da marca, os visitantes e profissionais de TI conhecerão produtos e serviços focados no mercado B2B e corporativo, destacando soluções voltadas para empresas, infraestrutura, armazenamento e aplicações de negócios. Em termos de portfólio, a fabricante apresenta no Brasil suas soluções OEM (Embedded) para projetos embarcados — atendendo desde iniciativas de cidades inteligentes até a indústria robótica —, além do SSD DC3000ME, desenvolvido sob medida para as demandas críticas e intensivas de data centers. Para completar o ecossistema expositivo, um painel interativo exibirá desde componentes de entrada para upgrades, como o SSD NV3, até memórias profissionais e dispositivos com criptografia como a linha IronKey e cartões industriais. Além da demonstração e usabilidade dos produtos, a Kingston também fará durante o evento o lançamento oficial do Clube Kingston, canal inédito de relacionamento direto com clientes e parceiros B2B que oferecerá eventos exclusivos, conteúdos técnicos – incluindo webnairs e treinamentos – e um programa de engajamento baseado em pontuação. Embora seja amplamente reconhecida pelo consumidor brasileiro por suas soluções de memória e armazenamento, especialmente entre entusiastas de tecnologia e gamers, a Kingston tem uma atuação global que vai muito além do mercado B2C. Com décadas de experiência no desenvolvimento de soluções para ambientes corporativos, a companhia atende desde pequenas e médias empresas até grandes corporações, fabricantes de tecnologia, Data Centers e provedores de serviços de Nuvem, com soluções desenvolvidas para infraestruturas críticas e cargas de trabalho de alta demanda. O grande diferencial competitivo no País reside na oferta de um departamento de engenharia próprio focado no desenho de projetos customizados, aliado a uma agilidade no atendimento local e consultoria especializada de pré e pós-venda para empresas de todos os portes. “O mercado latino-americano de infraestrutura e Data Centers vive um momento de forte expansão, e o Brasil lidera essa transformação com uma demanda crescente por soluções de alta performance e disponibilidade. Embora sejamos conhecidos pelo consumidor final no Brasil, a Kingston sempre teve sua essência fincada no segmento corporativo, sendo parceira estratégica das maiores infraestruturas de nuvem do mundo. Participar da Data Center World é o palco ideal para reforçar nossa expertise no segmento B2B, nosso extenso portfólio de soluções para o universo corporativo e também todo o nosso suporte local”, afirma Paulo Vizaco, gerente de Negócios do País na Kingston Brasil & diretor-Regional Etail América Latina. Parcerias estratégicas aceleram atuação no ecossistema corporativo Para maximizar sua presença no evento e aproximar a tecnologia dos compradores corporativos, a Kingston destaca sua colaboração com o KaBuM!, referência no varejo de tecnologia que vem expandindo sua atuação na frente B2B. A parceria ganha materialidade com o ecossistema Kingston para Empresas, plataforma exclusiva no site da KaBuM! projetada para simplificar a aquisição de memórias e SSDs para servidores e workstations. No estande, os visitantes poderão interagir com o REX, assistente de Inteligência Artificial da Kingston integrado à plataforma que auxilia gestores a encontrarem produtos compatíveis por meio de comandos de texto e voz. De forma pontual, a Kingston também realiza demonstrações em conjunto com a ASUSTOR, ilustrando a integração de seus SSDs e memórias de alta performance em dispositivos corporativos e sistemas de armazenamento em rede (NAS) da fabricante.
